date: c. 815 BC (Encyclopaedia Iranica; the year of Shamshi-Adad V's Median campaign is uncertain)
name: Sagbita
place: Sagbita, royal city of Hanasiruka (unidentified, central Zagros), Iran
how the result was decided: Shamshi-Adad V's annals record 2,300 Medes killed, 140 of their horsemen captured and Hanasiruka's royal city taken; there is no other source.
Iranian force: The warriors of the Median chief Hanasiruka, including horsemen (140 were captured); the annals give no other detail.
why it counts: Media: an Iranian-led state
borderline: an episode of an Assyrian campaign record, not a named battle in modern lists
doubts and flags: Borderline: an episode of an Assyrian campaign record, not a named battle in modern lists.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Inscriptions of Shamshi-Adad V (Grayson, RIMA 3); Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: The annals also claim 1,200 nearby settlements destroyed and tribute imposed on the Median tribes. Sagbita lay in the district later called Sagbat, in the Assyrian province of Kishesim (Iranica).

name: Harhar
place: Harhar, renamed Kar-Sharrukin (unidentified, central Zagros, perhaps the Kermanshah area), Iran
how the result was decided: Sargon besieged and took Harhar, which became the seat of the Assyrian province of Kar-Sharrukin.
commanders B: unknown (the townsmen, who had driven out their lord Kibaba)
Iranian force: The people of Harhar in revolt against their pro-Assyrian lord; no numbers or units are recorded.
why it counts: Media: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a town of the Median borderland: whether its defenders counted as Medes is uncertain, and the siege is known only from Sargon's own texts
doubts and flags: Borderline: a town of the Median borderland: whether its defenders counted as Medes is uncertain, and the siege is known only from Sargon's own texts.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Annals of Sargon II; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: Iranica adds that Harhar revolted in 715 and the Assyrians had to conquer it again; no detail of that second capture survives, so it is not a separate entry.

name: Kishesim (716 BC)
place: Kishesim, renamed Kar-Nergal (unidentified, central Zagros), Iran
how the result was decided: Kishesim fell to Sargon II, who captured its lord Bel-sharru-usur and made the town an Assyrian provincial seat under the name Kar-Nergal.
Iranian force: The townsmen and retainers of Bel-sharru-usur, lord of Kishesim; Sargon's texts give no numbers or units.
why it counts: Media: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a town of the Median borderland: whether its lord and defenders counted as Medes is uncertain, and the capture is known only from Sargon's own texts
doubts and flags: Borderline: a town of the Median borderland: whether its lord and defenders counted as Medes is uncertain, and the capture is known only from Sargon's own texts.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Annals and Display Inscription of Sargon II; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'; en.wikipedia Sargon II
note: Iranica treats Kishesim and Harhar, both made provinces in 716, as the start of the Assyrian conquest of Media; Sargon received tribute from 28 Median city lords in the same campaign. Wikipedia spells the town Kisheshim.

date: c. 714-713 BCE (Assyrian intelligence letters to Sargon II; date approximate)
name: Cimmerian defeat of Rusa I
place: Urartu, eastern Anatolia (Uasi/Guriania region; exact site unknown)
how the result was decided: Assyrian reports say the Urartian army and its king were beaten by the Gimirrai, which left Rusa too weak to meet Sargon's 8th campaign (714).
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Assyrian state letters to Sargon II (State Archives of Assyria vols 1 and 5); Sargon's letter to the god Assur on the 8th campaign; Ivantchik, Les Cimmeriens au Proche-Orient (1993); Diakonoff, CHI 2 (1985)
note: The Cimmerians' language is unknown; many scholars call them Iranian-speaking, others Thracian or unclassified. The fight is known only from Assyrian secondhand reports and details are vague.

name: Halule
place: Halule on the Tigris (unidentified, perhaps near Samarra), Iraq
how the result was decided: Sennacherib claims a crushing victory but the Babylonian Chronicle says the Elamite king forced an Assyrian retreat, and modern historians treat the battle as indecisive.
commanders A: Humban-nimena III of Elam, Mushezib-Marduk of Babylon, Humban-undasha (Elamite commander, killed), Nabu-shuma-ishkun (captured)
Iranian force: The contingents of Parsuash (the Persians) and Anzan (Anshan) among the allies of Elam listed by Sennacherib, beside Ellipi, Pashiru and the Chaldean and Aramaean tribes; no numbers are given.
why it counts: Persians (Anshan): an Iranian-led state
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Sennacherib's annals (Chicago and Taylor prisms); Babylonian Chronicle (ABC 1); en.wikipedia Battle of Halule; Encyclopaedia Iranica
note: Contingent: the Persians were a small part of Elam's coalition. Whether Parsuash here means the Persians of Fars or the Zagros Parsua, and whether Anzan was then Persian-ruled, is debated; Wikipedia's infobox names Achaemenes as a commander, an unproven modern identification, and gives an 'Assyrian victory' while its text calls the battle indecisive.

date: c. 679 BCE (early in Esarhaddon's reign; exact year uncertain)
name: Hubushna (Esarhaddon v Teushpa)
place: Hubushna (Hupisna), on the Cilician/Cappadocian border near Eregli, Turkey
how the result was decided: Esarhaddon's prism inscriptions claim that he defeated Teushpa the Cimmerian in the land of Hubushna.
commanders A: Esarhaddon (or a field commander in his name)
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Esarhaddon Nineveh Prism A (Borger, Die Inschriften Asarhaddons); Ivantchik 1993; Diakonoff, CHI 2 (1985)
note: Teushpa is the first Cimmerian leader named in cuneiform; the report is a royal claim, so the scale of the fighting is unknown. Cimmerian speech is unclassified (probably Iranian, perhaps not).

date: c. 676-675 BCE (Assyrian dating; Schmitt gives c. 675)
name: Esarhaddon v Ishpakaia (Scythians and Mannaeans)
war: Esarhaddon's wars on the north-eastern frontier
place: Mannaean country and the Hubuskia border, in the Median borderlands of north-western Iran (site unknown)
how the result was decided: Esarhaddon's inscriptions say that he defeated the Ashkuzai (Scythian) force and killed Ishpakaia, who had joined the Mannaeans against Assyria.
commanders B: Ishpakaia the Scythian (killed); Ahsheri, king of the Mannaeans
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Esarhaddon Nineveh Prism A and the Babylon Prism; Assyrian oracle queries (SAA 4); Ivantchik 1993; Diakonoff 1985; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishpakaia; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scythians
note: This is the first Scythian leader named in Assyrian sources. The Scythians were allies of the Mannaeans, with Cimmerians possibly on the same side; the fight itself is told only in royal inscriptions, and the place is given variously as Mannaean or Median territory.

date: c. 672 BC (the oracle queries are dated c. 672-669)
name: Kishassu (c. 672 BC)
how the result was decided: Esarhaddon's oracle queries only ask whether Kashtaritu's coalition would take Kishassu and its neighbours and record no result, though the revolt as a whole freed the Medes from Assyrian rule (Iranica).
commanders A: Kashtaritu (city lord of Kar-kashshi), Mamitiarshu (city lord of the Medes), Dusanni of Saparda
Iranian force: Kashtaritu's Medes of Kar-kashshi and the Medes of Mamitiarshu, with Mannaean, Cimmerian and Saparda allies; no numbers survive.
why it counts: Media: an Iranian-led state
borderline: known only from oracle queries that name the threatened towns but record no fighting or result; not a named battle in modern lists
doubts and flags: The sources consulted do not give the result, so the battle is listed but not scored. Borderline: known only from oracle queries that name the threatened towns but record no fighting or result; not a named battle in modern lists.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Esarhaddon's oracle queries to Shamash (Starr, SAA 4); Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'; en.wikipedia Kashtariti
note: Kishassu is usually taken as the later spelling of Kishesim, whose Sagbat district held Kashtaritu's seat Kar-kashshi; Iranica says the rebels attacked the fortresses of Harhar and Kishesim. Kashtaritu has been identified with Herodotus' Phraortes, but many reject this. Wikipedia also counts Scythians in his alliance and mentions a planned raid on Kilman.

date: c. 653 BC (shortly after Phraortes' death; some put it c. 625)
name: Nineveh (Cyaxares, c. 653 BC)
how the result was decided: Herodotus says Cyaxares met and defeated the Assyrians and then sat down before Nineveh; the siege was broken off only when the Scythians arrived.
Iranian force: Cyaxares' army, which Herodotus says he gathered from all his subjects and was the first to divide into separate units of spearmen, archers and horsemen.
why it counts: Media: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no conventional name; the field battle is recorded in a single clause of Herodotus
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from Herodotus 1. Borderline: no conventional name; the field battle is recorded in a single clause of Herodotus.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Herodotus 1.103; en.wikipedia Cyaxares
note: Herodotus makes the attack revenge for Phraortes. The siege that followed is not scored separately: it was abandoned because of the Scythian invasion, not an Assyrian defence (see the next entry).

date: c. 653 BC (traditional dating of Phraortes' death; c. 625 if Herodotus' reign lengths are counted back from 550 without a separate Scythian interval)
name: Nineveh (Phraortes, c. 653 BC)
how the result was decided: Herodotus says Phraortes perished with most of his army in his campaign against the Assyrians of Nineveh.
commanders A: unknown (the Assyrian king, Ashurbanipal by the usual dating)
Iranian force: The Median army of Phraortes, who according to Herodotus had first subdued the Persians and other peoples of Asia; no units or numbers are given.
why it counts: Media: an Iranian-led state
losses B: Phraortes and most of his army (Herodotus)
borderline: no conventional name: Herodotus names the enemy (the Assyrians of Nineveh) but not the site
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from Herodotus 1. Borderline: no conventional name: Herodotus names the enemy (the Assyrians of Nineveh) but not the site.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Herodotus 1.102; en.wikipedia Phraortes
note: Wikipedia (Phraortes) gives his reign as c. 675-653 and says he was killed by the Assyrian king, generally taken to be Ashurbanipal.

date: c. 653 BC (Wikipedia dates Scythian rule over Media c. 653-625; Iranica c. 653/635-625/615)
name: Scythian invasion of Media
how the result was decided: Herodotus says the Medes met the Scythians, were beaten in the battle and lost their rule.
Iranian force: Cyaxares' Median army, called back from the siege of Nineveh; Herodotus gives no detail.
why it counts: Media: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the name is Wikipedia's title for the war; the battle itself has no name or site
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from Herodotus 1. Borderline: the name is Wikipedia's title for the war; the battle itself has no name or site.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Herodotus 1.103-106; en.wikipedia Scythian invasion of Media; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: Herodotus says the Scythians, pursuing the Cimmerians, came upon Cyaxares while he was besieging Nineveh. Cyaxares later ended Scythian rule by murdering their leaders at a banquet (a massacre, not a battle; not an entry). Wikipedia's infobox result ('Medes victory') contradicts its own text.

date: c. 652 BCE (other dates for Gyges' death and the sack: c. 644 or c. 637 BCE)
name: Sardis (Cimmerian capture, c. 652 BC)
how the result was decided: Strabo says Lygdamis' Cimmerians took Sardis except the citadel; Ashurbanipal's inscriptions say that they killed Gyges.
commanders B: Gyges (killed in the war); his son Ardys
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Strabo 1.3.21, 13.4.8; Herodotus 1.6, 1.15; Callinus fr. 5a; Ashurbanipal's prisms (Rassam cylinder, on Gyges); Ivantchik 1993
note: The Lydian king Gyges died fighting the Cimmerians; the Lydians kept the acropolis and the Cimmerians later withdrew or were driven out (Ardys, Alyattes). The Cimmerians' Iranian speech is uncertain, so this is a doubtful qualifier.

name: Arrapha
war: Medo-Babylonian conquest of the Assyrian Empire
how the result was decided: The Medes took Arrapha and its region and used it as their base against Assyria in 614; the chronicle line itself is broken.
Iranian force: The Median army of Cyaxares; the chronicle gives no detail of units or numbers.
why it counts: Media: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the chronicle breaks off after 'the Medes went down to Arrapha'; the capture is inferred and no fighting is described
doubts and flags: Borderline: the chronicle breaks off after 'the Medes went down to Arrapha'; the capture is inferred and no fighting is described.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3 (Fall of Nineveh Chronicle), year 11; en.wikipedia Sinsharishkun; Cyaxares; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: Not the Babylonian victory over the Assyrians at Madanu near Arrapha in 616, in which no Medes are recorded. Wikipedia (Sinsharishkun) dates the Median move to late 615 or 614.

name: Assur (siege)
war: Medo-Babylonian conquest of the Assyrian Empire
how the result was decided: Assur fell to the Medes, who stormed and sacked it; Nabopolassar's Babylonians arrived only after the city had fallen.
Iranian force: Cyaxares' Median army; the chronicle gives no numbers or units.
why it counts: Media: an Iranian-led state
losses B: heavy: the chronicle says the Medes 'inflicted a terrible defeat on a great people'
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3, year 12; en.wikipedia Fall of Assur; Sinsharishkun; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: Wikipedia titles it 'Fall of Assur'. Cyaxares and Nabopolassar met by the city and made their alliance, later sealed by the marriage of Nebuchadnezzar and Amytis.

name: Tarbisu
war: Medo-Babylonian conquest of the Assyrian Empire
place: Tarbisu (Sherif Khan, just north of Nineveh), Iraq
how the result was decided: The chronicle records that the Medes captured Tarbisu, a city in the district of Nineveh.
Iranian force: Cyaxares' Median army; no units or numbers are recorded.
why it counts: Media: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a capture recorded in one line of the chronicle; the fighting is not described
doubts and flags: Borderline: a capture recorded in one line of the chronicle; the fighting is not described.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3, year 12; en.wikipedia Sinsharishkun; Cyaxares; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: The broken line before it is usually restored as a Median march on Nineveh in the same month (Wikipedia's Sinsharishkun adds Nimrud; Cyaxares calls it a feint); Nineveh did not fall and that attack is not a separate entry. Wikipedia's article on the war misdates Tarbisu to 615.

date: Simanu to Abu (June-August) 612 BC; the city fell in August
name: Nineveh (siege, 612 BC)
war: Medo-Babylonian conquest of the Assyrian Empire
how the result was decided: Nineveh fell to the Medes and Babylonians in August 612 after a three-month siege.
Iranian force: Cyaxares' Median army (the Umman-manda of the chronicle), which Iranica and Wikipedia say played the major part; whether Scythian or other steppe contingents served with it is debated.
why it counts: Media: an Iranian-led state
losses B: unknown; the city was sacked and burned
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3, year 14; Herodotus 1.106; en.wikipedia Battle of Nineveh (612 BC); Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: Wikipedia titles it 'Fall of Nineveh' and lists Scythians as allies of the Babylonians, without detail. Sinsharishkun is commonly held to have died in the defence; Ashur-uballit II then took the throne at Harran.

date: Arahsamnu (November) 610 BC; the city was taken in 610 or early 609
name: Harran (siege)
war: Medo-Babylonian conquest of the Assyrian Empire
how the result was decided: Ashur-uballit and his Egyptian allies abandoned Harran, which the Babylonians and Medes then captured and plundered.
commanders A: Nabopolassar; the Umman-manda (Medes; Wikipedia names Cyaxares)
Iranian force: The Umman-manda (Medes), who came to help the king of Akkad and joined their army to his as a separate force; no numbers.
why it counts: Media: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the defenders fled before the main attack; one translation of the chronicle has the Babylonian king fight a battle before taking the city
doubts and flags: Borderline: the defenders fled before the main attack; one translation of the chronicle has the Babylonian king fight a battle before taking the city.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3, year 16; en.wikipedia Fall of Harran; Medo-Babylonian conquest of the Assyrian Empire; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: The Medes plundered the temple Ehulhul and went home (Iranica). In 609 Ashur-uballit and an Egyptian army besieged the Babylonian garrison of Harran until Ululu and failed; no Median force is recorded then, so that siege is not an entry. Wikipedia's 'Fall of Harran' treats 610-609 as one event.

date: c. 625-585 BCE (after the Scythians' return from Asia; no firm date)
name: Scythian slaves' revolt (Herodotus)
place: the Scythian ditch between the Tauric mountains and Lake Maeotis, Crimea/steppe (site unknown)
how the result was decided: Herodotus says the Scythians failed with spears and bows but routed the slaves' sons by charging with whips.
doubts and flags: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Herodotus 4.1-4
note: Told by Herodotus as a story of the Scythians' return from their 28 years in Asia. It is more legend than record, but it is a named engagement of Scythians against Scythians.

date: 28 May 585 BC (the date of the solar eclipse; alternatives 582 or 581 BC, or a lunar eclipse in 609 or 587)
name: Halys
place: near the Halys (Kizilirmak) river (site unknown), Turkey
how the result was decided: Herodotus says the fighting stopped when day turned to night and both sides at once made peace, with no victor.
Iranian force: Cyaxares' army after the conquest of Assyria; Herodotus gives no composition, so presumably the Median spearmen, archers and horsemen with contingents of subject peoples.
why it counts: Media: an Iranian-led state
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from Herodotus 1.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Herodotus 1.73-74; en.wikipedia Eclipse of Thales; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Media'
note: Also called the Battle of the Eclipse. The war lasted five years with victories on both sides (Herodotus). Syennesis of Cilicia and Labynetus of Babylon mediated a peace fixing the Halys as the border, sealed by the marriage of Astyages and Aryenis, daughter of Alyattes. Herodotus does not name the site; the Halys is an assumption. Iranica gives 29 May.

date: 552 BC (uncertain; Wikipedia gives winter-spring 552; some accounts put all the battles of the revolt in 550)
name: Hyrba
place: Hyrba (unidentified, on the road from Media into Persis), Iran
how the result was decided: In Nicolaus' account Cyrus' men killed 250 of the 300 Median horsemen sent after him and the rest fled.
commanders B: unnamed commander of Astyages' horsemen (Nicolaus); Harpagus in Herodotus' first battle
Iranian force: Cyrus' side: the inhabitants of Hyrba, whom he armed, and Persian troops (1,000 horse and 5,000 foot were asked of his father); Astyages' side: 300 Median horsemen.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
strength A: 1,000 cavalry and 5,000 infantry requested from Persia (Nicolaus; whether they fought is uncertain)
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from Nicolaus of Damascus (after Ctesias), whose story of Cyrus' revolt is full of legendary elements; Herodotus has instead a first battle in which Harpagus and most of the Medes went over to Cyrus.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Nicolaus of Damascus, FGrH 90 F66; Herodotus 1.127; en.wikipedia Battle of Hyrba; Medo-Persian conflict
note: Civil: Persians (Anshan) against Media. Ctesias (as summarised by Wikipedia) has Cyrus defeat the Medes near Hyrba before Astyages won the next fight. Iranica (Astyages) counts only three battles in Nicolaus and Justin, so Hyrba is the preliminary clash.

name: Persian Border
place: on the border of Media and Persis, on the road from Ecbatana to Pasargadae (site unknown), Iran
how the result was decided: After two days' fighting the Persians fell back to Pasargadae and Astyages took the town they had defended, so the Medes held the field (Nicolaus).
commanders B: Cyrus, Oebares, Cyrus' father (Atradates in Nicolaus; Cambyses I in Wikipedia), who died of his wounds or in captivity
Iranian force: Astyages' Median army, said to be enormous, against Cyrus' Persian tribal levy; no credible figures survive.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from Nicolaus of Damascus (after Ctesias); Polyaenus and Justin also speak of early Persian defeats, but the details are legendary and the battle is absent from the Babylonian sources.
period: The Medes, the Scythians and the first Persians
sources: Nicolaus of Damascus, FGrH 90 F66; Polyaenus 7.6; Justin 1.6; en.wikipedia Battle of the Persian Border; Medo-Persian conflict; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Astyages'
note: Civil: Media against the Persians (Anshan). Wikipedia's article on this battle gives a 'Persian victory' (a first-day success) and an infobox of 60,000 horse and 3,000 chariots for the Medes and 50,000 horse and 100 chariots for the Persians, figures of unclear origin; the Medo-Persian conflict article and Iranica (Cyrus lost the first two battles) support the Median victory followed here.

name: Ecbatana (550 BC)
how the result was decided: Cyrus marched to Ecbatana and carried off its treasure to Anshan (Nabonidus Chronicle); no defence or fighting is recorded.
commanders B: Astyages (already captured; in Ctesias hiding in the palace)
Iranian force: Cyrus' Persian army with the Median troops who had gone over to him; nothing is known of any defenders.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a capture after the Median army's collapse; no fighting is recorded (Wikipedia's Persian Revolt suggests the walls may have allowed some resistance)
doubts and flags: Borderline: a capture after the Median army's collapse; no fighting is recorded (Wikipedia's Persian Revolt suggests the walls may have allowed some resistance).
sources: Nabonidus Chronicle (ABC 7) ii 1-4; Ctesias (Photius); en.wikipedia Medo-Persian conflict; Persian Revolt; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Astyages'
note: Civil: Persians (Anshan) against Media. In Ctesias Astyages hid in the palace with his daughter Amytis and her husband Spitamas; Oebares carried the treasure to Persia. Ecbatana became an Achaemenid royal capital.

date: 550 BC (the Nabonidus Chronicle dates Astyages' fall to Nabonidus' sixth year, 550/549)
name: Pasargadae
place: near Pasargadae (perhaps the Morghab plain), Iran
how the result was decided: On the second day the Persians, shamed by their women on the mountain, routed the Medes and took their camp (Nicolaus), and Strabo too places Cyrus' last victory over Astyages at Pasargadae.
Iranian force: Cyrus' Persian tribal levy (Herodotus 1.125: the Pasargadae, Maraphii and Maspii, the farming tribes and the nomad Dai, Mardi, Dropici and Sagartii) with Median deserters, against Astyages' Median royal army.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
doubts and flags: Traditional: The battle story (two days, the women baring themselves to shame the fleeing men) comes from Nicolaus of Damascus after Ctesias, with echoes in Polyaenus, Justin and Plutarch, and is legendary; the decisive defeat and capture of Astyages c.
sources: Nicolaus of Damascus, FGrH 90 F66; Herodotus 1.127-128; Strabo 15.3.8; Polyaenus 7.6, 7.45; Justin 1.6; Nabonidus Chronicle (ABC 7) ii 1-4; Sippar cylinder of Nabonidus; en.wikipedia Medo-Persian conflict; Persian Revolt; Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Astyages'
note: Civil: Persians (Anshan) against Media. Herodotus (1.128) says Astyages armed the remaining Medes, was defeated and captured; the Nabonidus Chronicle says his army mutinied and handed him over to Cyrus; the Sippar cylinder that Cyrus 'scattered the large army of the Umman-manda with his small army'. Wikipedia's campaign box lists a 'Siege of Pasargadae Hill' (no article), apparently the mountain phase of this battle, which is not a separate entry here. Accounts differ on whether Astyages was taken in this battle, in a later fight or hiding at Ecbatana.

date: autumn 547 BC (traditional date; possibly later in the 540s)
name: Pteria
place: Pteria (probably Kerkenes Dag, near Sorgun), Turkey
how the result was decided: Night parted the armies with neither side victorious (Herodotus 1.76); Croesus marched back to Sardis the next day, which is a strategic matter.
Iranian force: Cyrus's Persians and Medes, joined by levies of 'all who dwelt in the lands between' gathered on the march (Herodotus 1.76); no numbers in the sources.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses A: heavy (Herodotus: many fell on both sides)
sources: Herodotus 1.76-77; Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander; en.wikipedia Battle of Pteria
note: Pteria is usually identified with Kerkenes Dag (some prefer Bogazkoy). Wikipedia's 95,000 Lydians and 20,000 Persians are not in Herodotus. The 547 date rests on a now doubted reading of the Nabonidus Chronicle; many date the Lydian war c. 547-541.

date: late 547 BC or 546 BC (14 days; possibly later in the 540s)
name: Sardis (siege, 547 BC)
how the result was decided: Sardis fell to the besiegers on the fourteenth day, when Persians climbed an unguarded stretch of the acropolis cliff (Herodotus 1.84).
commanders A: Cyrus II; Hyroeades the Mardian led the escalade
Iranian force: Cyrus's Persian and Median army after the victory before Sardis; the assault was led by Hyroeades of the Mardi, a Persian mountain tribe (Herodotus 1.84).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Herodotus 1.80-87; Xenophon, Cyropaedia 7.2; Nabonidus Chronicle ii.15-18 (disputed); en.wikipedia Siege of Sardis (547 BC)
note: The Nabonidus Chronicle entry for 547 (Cyrus marched to 'Lu-...' and killed its king) was long read as Lydia; the reading is now doubted, so the fall of Sardis may date anywhere from 547 to c. 541. Herodotus has Croesus spared on the pyre.

date: late 547 BC (traditional date; possibly later in the 540s)
name: Thymbra
place: the plain before Sardis (Thymbra in Xenophon), near Sart, Turkey
how the result was decided: The Lydian cavalry was broken (by the smell of the camels, in Herodotus) and the Lydians fled into Sardis, leaving the field to the Persians.
Iranian force: Persian infantry and cavalry with the baggage camels, mounted by men armed as horsemen, placed in front on Harpagus' advice (Herodotus 1.80); Xenophon adds Medes, Armenians, Hyrcanians, Arabs, scythed chariots and siege towers.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
doubts and flags: Traditional: A battle on the plain before Sardis is told by Herodotus (1.
sources: Herodotus 1.79-80; Xenophon, Cyropaedia 6.2-7.1; en.wikipedia Battle of Thymbra
note: Modern estimates (Wikipedia) put the Persians at 20,000-50,000. Wikipedia lists Arab, Babylonian and Egyptian mercenaries with Croesus (Xenophon); Herodotus says Croesus had dismissed his mercenaries and fought with the Lydians alone. Xenophon's Egyptians later took service with Cyrus.

name: Phocaea (siege)
how the result was decided: The city fell: under siege by a mound, the Phocaeans sailed away during a truce and Harpagus occupied the empty town (Herodotus 1.164).
Iranian force: Harpagus' army, the Persian and Median force left in Asia Minor after the Lydian war; it took the Ionian cities by mounds (Herodotus 1.162-164). Not described further.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a siege with siege works but no recorded assault; the city was abandoned
doubts and flags: Borderline: a siege with siege works but no recorded assault; the city was abandoned.
sources: Herodotus 1.162-167; en.wikipedia Phocaea
note: Phocaea is the city in the Greek list; most Phocaeans went to Chios and then to Alalia in Corsica, later founding Elea (the battle of Alalia against Carthaginians and Etruscans involved no Persians).

date: 546 BC or 545 BC (the year after the fall of Sardis)
name: Sardis (siege, 546 BC)
how the result was decided: The siege was abandoned: Pactyes fled to Cyme at the approach of Mazares' relief army, and Tabalus kept the acropolis (Herodotus 1.154-157).
commanders A: Tabalus (commander of the acropolis); Mazares (relief army)
Iranian force: Tabalus' Persian garrison shut in the acropolis, relieved by an army under the Mede Mazares sent by Cyrus (Herodotus 1.153-157).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a siege with little recorded fighting
doubts and flags: Borderline: a siege with little recorded fighting.
sources: Herodotus 1.153-161
note: Pactyes, a Lydian in charge of Croesus's treasure, hired mercenaries on the coast and raised the coastal Greeks. Mazares then enslaved Priene and plundered the Maeander plain and Magnesia (Herodotus 1.161); no battle is recorded there.

date: c. 545-540 BCE (Ctesias' story, no firm date)
name: Cyrus v Amorges (Saka)
war: Cyrus the Great's wars in Central Asia
place: Saka country east of the Caspian (site not given by Ctesias)
how the result was decided: Ctesias says that Cyrus took Amorges but that Sparethra then defeated the Persians and recovered him, and the two peoples made peace as allies.
commanders B: Amorges (Amorges, king of the Saka); his wife Sparethra
doubts and flags: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
sources: Ctesias, Persica (Photius' epitome; the Saka and Amorges episode); Polyaenus, Strategemata, book 7 (Cyrus); Lenfant, Ctesias de Cnide (2004); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saka
note: Ctesias is an unreliable source and Herodotus has no such war; the Saka here are the Haumavarga of Amorges, not the Massagetae of Tomyris. Included because the Saka are named opponents and Cyrus (Persian) leads the other side.

name: Teos (siege)
how the result was decided: Harpagus took the walls by a mound, and the Teians took ship and sailed off to found Abdera in Thrace (Herodotus 1.168).
Iranian force: Harpagus' Persian and Median army (not described).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: fighting is implied (the wall taken by a mound) but not described
doubts and flags: Borderline: fighting is implied (the wall taken by a mound) but not described.
sources: Herodotus 1.168-169
note: Herodotus adds that the other Ionians except Miletus fought Harpagus city by city and were defeated (1.169); those fights are unnamed and not listed.

name: Lide (siege)
place: Mount Lide, near Pedasa (Gokceler, near Bodrum), Turkey
how the result was decided: The Pedasians held out for a long time on fortified Mount Lide but were finally subdued (Herodotus 1.175).
Iranian force: Harpagus' Persian and Median army with the Ionian and Aeolian levies he compelled to serve against the Carians, Caunians and Lycians (Herodotus 1.171).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Herodotus 1.171, 1.175
note: The Pedasians were the only Carians to resist; the site of Mount Lide is uncertain (near Pedasa on the Bodrum peninsula). Herodotus dates nothing in Harpagus' campaign; it is placed c. 546-540 BC.

name: Caunus (siege, 540 BC)
how the result was decided: The Caunians, like the Lycians of Xanthos, fought to the end and their city fell (Herodotus 1.176).
Iranian force: Harpagus' Persian and Median army with Ionian and Aeolian levies (Herodotus 1.171).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: most of the defenders (Herodotus: 'for the most part' they did as the Lycians)
borderline: known from one sentence of Herodotus
doubts and flags: Borderline: known from one sentence of Herodotus.
sources: Herodotus 1.172, 1.176
note: Herodotus treats the Caunians as distinct from the Carians (they claimed Cretan origin) though they spoke Carian; listed under Carians. The year in the name distinguishes it from any later Caunus entry (e.g. 396 BC).

name: Xanthos (siege)
how the result was decided: The Lycians were beaten on the Xanthian plain, burned their families in the acropolis and died in a last sally, and Xanthos fell (Herodotus 1.176).
Iranian force: Harpagus' Persian and Median army with Ionian and Aeolian levies (Herodotus 1.171, 1.176).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: all the fighting men killed; only 80 families who were away survived (Herodotus 1.176)
sources: Herodotus 1.171, 1.176; en.wikipedia Xanthos
note: A field battle on the plain north of the city followed by a siege and last stand; one entry. Date c. 540 (Harpagus' campaign is undated, c. 546-540).

date: month Tashritu (late September or early October) 539 BC, before 10 October
name: Opis
place: Opis, on the Tigris (perhaps Tell al-Mujailat, southeast of Baghdad), Iraq
how the result was decided: The Babylonian army was defeated at Opis and the town plundered (Nabonidus Chronicle iii.12-14); Sippar surrendered without battle a few days later.
commanders A: Cyrus II; Ugbaru (Gobryas), governor of Gutium
Iranian force: Cyrus's army of Persians and Medes, with the troops of Gutium under Ugbaru (Gobryas), a Babylonian governor who had gone over to Cyrus (Nabonidus Chronicle).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Nabonidus Chronicle iii.12-16; Cyrus Cylinder; en.wikipedia Battle of Opis; Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander
note: Translators disagree whether the Chronicle's massacre of 'the people of Akkad' was Cyrus's work or Nabonidus's. Wikipedia's 70,000 Persians attributed to Herodotus is not reliable (Herodotus does not mention Opis). The site of Opis is uncertain.

date: 12 October 539 BC (16 Tashritu); Cyrus entered on 29 October
name: Babylon (siege, 539 BC)
how the result was decided: Babylon fell: the army of Gutium under Ugbaru entered the city on 16 Tashritu (12 October 539) and Nabonidus was taken.
Iranian force: Cyrus's Persian and Median army with Ugbaru's troops of Gutium, who made the entry (Nabonidus Chronicle iii.15-16).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the Nabonidus Chronicle and Cyrus Cylinder say the city was taken 'without battle'; Herodotus and Xenophon tell of a siege and a night entry along the lowered Euphrates
doubts and flags: Borderline: the Nabonidus Chronicle and Cyrus Cylinder say the city was taken 'without battle'; Herodotus and Xenophon tell of a siege and a night entry along the lowered Euphrates.
sources: Nabonidus Chronicle iii.15-18; Cyrus Cylinder; Herodotus 1.188-191; Xenophon, Cyropaedia 7.5; Daniel 5; en.wikipedia Fall of Babylon
note: Wikipedia title: Fall of Babylon. Briant doubts the 'without battle' claim as Persian court propaganda. Xenophon and Daniel have Belshazzar killed that night; unconfirmed.

date: 530 BC (between August and December, from the Babylonian dating of Cyrus's death)
name: Massagetae (530 BC)
place: beyond the Araxes (probably the Syr Darya), Kazakhstan
how the result was decided: In Herodotus's account the Massagetae won the field, destroying most of the Persian army and killing Cyrus (1.214).
Iranian force: Cyrus's royal army of Persians and Medes (not described beyond 'the Persians'; Herodotus 1.214).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: most of the Persian army and Cyrus (Herodotus)
doubts and flags: Traditional: Herodotus says his version was the most credible of several; Ctesias has Cyrus mortally wounded fighting the Derbices and their Indians, Berossus has him fall against the Dahae, Xenophon has him die in bed.
sources: Herodotus 1.205-216; Ctesias, Persica (Photius' epitome); Berossus; Xenophon, Cyropaedia 8.7; en.wikipedia Tomyris, Cyrus the Great
note: In Ctesias the Derbices, with elephants and Indian allies, wound Cyrus, but the Saka of Amorges come to his aid and the Persians win; Cyrus dies three days later. Under Herodotus's version, which this entry follows, the Massagetae won. Site unknown (Araxes = Syr Darya, Amu Darya or Uzboy).

name: Massagetae (camp ambush, 530 BC)
place: beyond the Araxes (probably the Syr Darya), Kazakhstan
how the result was decided: The Persians returned on the drunken Massagetae in the captured camp, killed many and took Spargapises and many others prisoner (Herodotus 1.211).
Iranian force: Cyrus's royal army of Persians and Medes; the weakest part was left in the camp with the feast and was killed before the main body returned (Herodotus 1.207-211).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: a third of the Massagetae army (Herodotus)
losses A: the troops left in the camp
borderline: an episode without a conventional name
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from Herodotus, who tells a folktale-like ruse (a camp left with wine) in a campaign of which he admits several versions; Ctesias and Berossus tell Cyrus's last war differently. Borderline: an episode without a conventional name.
sources: Herodotus 1.205-211
note: Herodotus's Araxes has been taken as the Syr Darya, the Amu Darya or the Uzboy; the site is unknown. Spargapises was Tomyris' son.

date: probably 526-525 BC (Cambyses' march on Egypt); undated
name: Gaza (siege, 525 BC)
how the result was decided: Polybius says only that Gaza alone withstood a siege when the Persians invaded; it was under Persian rule afterwards, but whether it fell or came to terms is not recorded.
Iranian force: Presumably Cambyses' invasion army (Persians and Medes with subject levies); not described.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: known only from a passing remark of Polybius; date, commander and outcome are not stated
doubts and flags: The sources consulted do not give the result, so the battle is listed but not scored. Borderline: known only from a passing remark of Polybius; date, commander and outcome are not stated.
sources: Polybius 16.22a; Herodotus 3.5; en.wikipedia Battle of Pelusium
note: Gaza (Herodotus' Cadytis) was a Philistine city, so 'Philistines' is used as the opponent (a new name). Wikipedia's History of Gaza has a confused entry on a failed Persian attack in 529 BC; not used.

name: Memphis (siege, 525 BC)
how the result was decided: Memphis surrendered after a siege and Psamtik III was captured (Herodotus 3.13).
Iranian force: Cambyses' Persian and Median army with Greek subjects and a river fleet (a Mytilenean ship carried the herald; Herodotus 3.13).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses A: a Persian herald and the 200 men of a Mytilenean ship, killed before the siege
losses B: 2,000 young Egyptian nobles executed after the fall, ten for each Mytilenean (Herodotus 3.14)
sources: Herodotus 3.13-15; en.wikipedia Battle of Pelusium, First Achaemenid conquest of Egypt
note: Wikipedia's conquest article calls it 'a long siege'. The later expeditions to the Ammonians (Siwa) and to Kush ended without battles (the army lost in the sand, the march abandoned for hunger) and are not listed.

name: Pelusium (525 BC)
how the result was decided: After a hard fight with many dead on both sides the Egyptians broke and fled to Memphis, leaving the field to the Persians (Herodotus 3.11).
Iranian force: Cambyses' Persian and Median army with his Ionian and Aeolian Greek subjects (Herodotus 3.1), backed by a Phoenician, Cypriot and Ionian fleet; the Arab king of the desert road supplied water (Herodotus 3.4-9, 3.19).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Herodotus 3.1-13; Ctesias, Persica; Polyaenus 7.9; en.wikipedia Battle of Pelusium, First Achaemenid conquest of Egypt
note: Psamtik's Greek and Carian mercenaries killed the sons of the turncoat Phanes before the battle (Herodotus 3.11). Polyaenus' story of cats held before the Persian ranks is late and doubtful. The Arabs (Qedar) gave passage and water across Sinai; Herodotus does not say they fought.

name: Sikayauvati
place: the fortress of Sikayauvati, district of Nisaya, Media (unlocated), Iran
how the result was decided: Darius and his fellow conspirators killed Gaumata and his foremost followers in the fortress (Behistun §13).
commanders A: Darius I with Intaphernes, Otanes, Gobryas, Hydarnes, Megabyzus and Ardumanish
Iranian force: Darius and six Persian nobles 'with a few men' (Behistun §13).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
strength A: seven nobles and a few men
losses B: Gaumata and his foremost followers killed
borderline: a palace coup and assassination rather than a battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: a palace coup and assassination rather than a battle.
sources: Behistun (DB) §§10-13; Herodotus 3.61-79; Ctesias; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bisotun iii
note: Herodotus (3.76-79) describes a fight in the royal apartments; Ctesias names the Magus Sphendadates. Whether Gaumata was an impostor or the real Bardiya, son of Cyrus, is disputed. Nisaya is often placed near Bisotun; the coordinates are regional.

name: Izala
place: Izala district (Mount Izla, Tur Abdin), 'in Assyria', Turkey
how the result was decided: The inscription says Vaumisa's army defeated the rebels who came against him (Behistun §29).
Iranian force: An army under the Persian Vaumisa sent by Darius; not described (the royal army was Persian and Median).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Behistun (DB) §29; Livius.org Behistun translation
note: Vaumisa afterwards waited in Armenia for Darius, which suggests the victory was not decisive. The rebels belong to the inscription's Armenian section, though the battle was fought in Assyria; Izala is the Tur Abdin (Mount Izla) near Mardin.

name: Kapishakanish
place: the fortress of Kapishakanish, Arachosia (unlocated), Afghanistan
how the result was decided: Vivana's army defeated the rebel army at the fortress (Behistun §45).
factions B: Vahyazdata (the army he sent to Arachosia)
Iranian force: Vivana's satrapal army of Arachosia, loyal to Darius; not described (presumably Arachosian levies and Persian garrison troops).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Behistun (DB) §45; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bisotun iii
note: Vahyazdata, who claimed to be Bardiya, son of Cyrus, had risen in Persis and sent this army east. Kapishakanish has been compared with Kapisa (Bagram), which lies outside Arachosia; unlocated.

name: Tigris (522 BC)
place: a crossing of the Tigris (unlocated, probably near Opis), Iraq
how the result was decided: Darius crossed the river on inflated skins, camels and horses and routed the Babylonian army holding the bank (Behistun §18).
Iranian force: Darius's own army, which he calls 'the Persian and Median army which was with me' (Behistun §25); some crossed on skins, some on camels and horses (§18).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Behistun (DB) §§16-18; Livius.org Behistun translation; en.wikipedia Nebuchadnezzar III
note: Nidintu-Bel claimed to be Nebuchadnezzar, son of Nabonidus; his troops held the reed thickets and boats on the river. The site of the crossing is not named.

name: Zazana
place: Zazana, on the Euphrates (unlocated, probably near Sippar), Iraq
how the result was decided: The Babylonians were routed and partly driven into the river; Nidintu-Bel fled to Babylon with a few horsemen (Behistun §19).
Iranian force: Darius's Persian and Median field army (Behistun §§19, 25).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Behistun (DB) §§19-20; Livius.org Behistun translation; en.wikipedia Nebuchadnezzar III
note: Darius then took Babylon and Nidintu-Bel (§20); the first Babylonian tablet dated by Darius is of 22 December 522, so the city fell within days and no separate siege entry is made. Herodotus' 19-month siege and the Zopyrus story (3.150-160) fit neither Babylonian revolt.

date: 521 BC (undated in the inscription; Chiçantakhma was a prisoner by mid-July 521)
name: Sagartia
how the result was decided: Takhmaspada's army defeated the rebels and captured Chiçantakhma, who was impaled at Arbela (Behistun §33).
Iranian force: A Persian and Median army under the Mede Takhmaspada (Behistun §33).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: the inscription names no site or date
doubts and flags: Borderline: the inscription names no site or date.
sources: Behistun (DB) §33; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bisotun iii; en.wikipedia Behistun inscription
note: Chiçantakhma claimed descent from Cyaxares. Iranica (after Borger's reading of the Babylonian version) puts his capture by 15 July 521. Sagartia is variously placed in the Zagros or eastern Media; coordinates regional.

name: Marush
how the result was decided: The only source, the inscription, says Hydarnes' army defeated the Median rebels (Behistun §25); he then halted at Kampanda to wait for Darius.
Iranian force: A detachment of Darius's small 'Persian and Median army' under the Persian Hydarnes (Behistun §25).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Behistun (DB) §§24-25; Livius.org Behistun translation
note: Many historians judge Marush indecisive, since Hydarnes waited at Kampanda until Darius came; the field test follows the inscription. Fravartish claimed to be Khshathrita of the line of Cyaxares.

name: Gandutava
how the result was decided: Vivana again routed the rebel army (Behistun §46); its commander fled to the fortress of Arshada, where Vivana caught and killed him.
factions B: Vahyazdata (the army he sent to Arachosia)
Iranian force: Vivana's satrapal army of Arachosia (not described).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Behistun (DB) §§46-47; Livius.org Behistun translation
note: The capture of the rebel commander at Arshada (§47) is a pursuit and capture, not listed separately.

name: Vishpauzatish
how the result was decided: The inscription says Vishtaspa defeated the rebels (Behistun §35), though he needed reinforcements before he could finish the revolt.
factions B: Parthian and Hyrcanian rebels (partisans of Fravartish)
Iranian force: Vishtaspa's loyal forces of Parthia, before the Persian reinforcement arrived (Behistun §35).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Behistun (DB) §35; Livius.org Behistun translation; en.wikipedia Patigrabana
note: Parthia and Hyrcania rose for Fravartish of Media. Historians often treat this battle as indecisive because Vishtaspa waited for reinforcements.

name: Kunduru
how the result was decided: Darius routed Fravartish's army; Fravartish fled towards Raga with a few horsemen and was caught and impaled at Ecbatana (Behistun §§31-32).
Iranian force: Darius's own field army, 'the Persian and Median army which was with me' (Behistun §§25, 31).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Behistun (DB) §§31-32; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bisotun iii
note: The decisive battle of the Median revolt. The identification of Kundurush with Kangavar is a guess.

name: Rakha
how the result was decided: Artavardiya defeated Vahyazdata, who fled with a few horsemen to Paishiyauvada (Behistun §41).
Iranian force: Part of 'the Persian and Median army which was with me', detached under the Persian Artavardiya while the rest went with Darius to Media (Behistun §41).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Behistun (DB) §§40-41; Livius.org Behistun translation
note: Vahyazdata claimed to be Bardiya, son of Cyrus, and rose at Tarava in Yautiya with Persian support.

name: Tigra
place: the stronghold of Tigra, Armenia (unlocated), Turkey
how the result was decided: The inscription says Dadarshi's army defeated the rebels at the stronghold (Behistun §27).
Iranian force: Dadarshi's army (not described; see Zuzahya).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Behistun (DB) §27; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Dadarsis
note: A battle at a stronghold, not described as a siege.

name: Zuzahya
how the result was decided: The inscription says Dadarshi's army defeated the rebels (Behistun §26).
commanders A: Dadarshi, an Armenian in Darius's service
Iranian force: An army sent with Dadarshi; the inscription does not describe it (presumably royal Persian and Median troops, perhaps with loyal Armenians).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Behistun (DB) §26; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Dadarsis
note: Achaemenid Armina lay around Lake Van and the upper Euphrates; Zuzahya is unlocated (coordinates regional). The rebels' names are Urartian rather than Armenian (Iranica).

name: Autiyara
how the result was decided: The inscription says Vaumisa's army defeated the rebels (Behistun §30); the Babylonian version counts the rebel dead and prisoners.
Iranian force: Vaumisa's army (not described; the royal army was Persian and Median).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Behistun (DB) §30; Babylonian version lines 55-57 ('On the rocks: the unfinished story of the Babylonian version of the Bisotun inscription', Iraq, 2025); Livius.org Behistun translation
note: Vaumisa then waited in Armenia until Darius came to Media, suggesting the revolt was not yet over.

name: Uyama
place: the fortress of Uyama, Armenia (unlocated), Turkey
how the result was decided: The inscription says Dadarshi's army defeated the rebels at the fortress (Behistun §28).
Iranian force: Dadarshi's army (not described; see Zuzahya).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Behistun (DB) §28; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Dadarsis
note: Dadarshi then waited in Armenia until Darius came to Media; Iranica calls Uyama the decisive defeat of the Armenian rebels.

name: Parga
place: Mount Parga, Persis (unlocated; perhaps Forg near Darab), Iran
how the result was decided: Artavardiya routed Vahyazdata's second army and captured him; he was impaled at Uvadaicaya (Behistun §§42-43).
Iranian force: Artavardiya's Persian and Median detachment (Behistun §§41-42).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Behistun (DB) §§42-43; Livius.org Behistun translation; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bisotun iii
note: Vahyazdata had raised a new army at Paishiyauvada after Rakha. The Forg identification is old and uncertain; coordinates regional.

name: Patigrabana
place: Patigrabana, Parthia (unlocated; Mashhad has been suggested), Iran
how the result was decided: Vishtaspa, reinforced from Raga, routed the rebels and Parthia submitted (Behistun §36).
factions B: Parthian and Hyrcanian rebels (partisans of Fravartish)
Iranian force: Vishtaspa's Parthian loyalists reinforced by a Persian army that Darius sent from Raga (Behistun §36).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Behistun (DB) §36; Livius.org Behistun translation; en.wikipedia Patigrabana
note: Wikipedia dates it 'around 520 BC'; the inscription's date converts to 11 July 521. The Mashhad identification is speculative.

name: Babylon (siege, 521 BC)
how the result was decided: Babylon fell to Intaphernes on 22 Markazanash (27 November 521) and Arakha and his chief followers were taken (Behistun §50).
Iranian force: An army sent by Darius under the Persian Intaphernes, his bow-bearer; not described (Behistun §50).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: Arakha and 2,497 of his followers executed (Babylonian version)
sources: Behistun (DB) §§49-50; Livius.org Behistun translation; en.wikipedia Nebuchadnezzar IV, Fall of Babylon
note: Arakha, son of Haldita, an 'Armenian' (Urartian), revolted on 25 August 521 claiming to be Nebuchadnezzar, son of Nabonidus. Herodotus' 19-month siege and Zopyrus' stratagem (3.150-160) are sometimes referred to this revolt but fit neither; his 3,000 impaled may echo it. Parts of the walls were pulled down after the capture.

date: 28 December 521 BC (23 Aciyadiya; 10 December 522 is the alternative)
name: Margiana
how the result was decided: Dadarshi's army crushed the Margians (Behistun §38).
Iranian force: The army of the Bactrian satrapy under its satrap Dadarshi (Behistun §38).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: 55,243 killed and 6,972 captured (Aramaic version); 55,2[..] killed and 6,572 captured (Babylonian version)
sources: Behistun (DB) §§38-39 with the Babylonian and Aramaic versions; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Frada and Dadarsis; Livius.org Behistun translation
note: No site is named beyond Margiana. Iranica prefers 28 December 521 because Frada is the last rebel on the relief. The casualty figures are generally thought inflated.

date: 520 or 519 BC (Darius's second or third year)
name: Elam (520 BC)
how the result was decided: Gobryas defeated the Elamites and captured their leader Atamaita, who was brought to Darius and killed (Behistun col. V).
Iranian force: An army under the Persian Gobryas; not described (the royal army was Persian and Median).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the inscription names no site
doubts and flags: Borderline: the inscription names no site.
sources: Behistun (DB) col. V (§71); Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bisotun iii
note: The third Elamite revolt. The first two (Açina, Martiya, 522-521) ended without battles: Açina was handed over bound and the Elamites killed Martiya themselves.

name: Saka campaign of Darius I
place: beyond the 'sea' (draya): the Caspian, Aral, Amu Darya or Syr Darya, Central Asia
how the result was decided: After crossing the 'sea' with all his army Darius routed the Saka and their chief Skunkha was captured and brought to him (Behistun col. V).
Iranian force: Darius's royal army, not described in the inscription (normally a Persian and Median core).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a campaign entry: the inscription records a victory but names no site
doubts and flags: Borderline: a campaign entry: the inscription records a victory but names no site.
sources: Behistun (DB) col. V (§74) and relief; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bisotun iii; en.wikipedia Skunkha
note: Against the Saka tigraxauda ('pointed caps'). A few scholars refer the 'sea' to the Bosporus and the campaign to the European Scythians. Polyaenus' tale of the herdsman Sirakes leading Darius's army into the desert (7.12) is legendary and not listed.

name: Samos (517 BC)
how the result was decided: The Persians drove Charilaus' mercenaries back into the acropolis after their surprise sortie, then massacred the Samians and handed the island to Syloson (Herodotus 3.146-149).
Iranian force: Otanes' Persian army, carried by sea to install Syloson (Herodotus 3.141-147); the ships were presumably from the subject Ionians and Phoenicians.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses A: many Persians of high rank killed in the sortie (Herodotus 3.146)
sources: Herodotus 3.139-149; en.wikipedia Syloson
note: Herodotus calls Samos the first of all Greek and barbarian cities that Darius took. Maeandrius escaped by a secret passage and sailed to Sparta.

name: Barca (siege)
how the result was decided: Barca fell after a nine-month siege, taken by a broken oath sworn over a plank-covered trench (Herodotus 4.200-202).
commanders A: Amasis, a Maraphian (army); Badres, a Pasargadan (fleet); sent by Aryandes, satrap of Egypt
Iranian force: 'All the army of Egypt, by land and sea' under two Persian commanders (Herodotus 4.167): the Persian garrison troops of Egypt with subject levies and a fleet; miners dug under the walls.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the leaders impaled by Pheretime and the rest enslaved; some deported to Bactria (Herodotus 4.202-204)
sources: Herodotus 4.145, 4.165-167, 4.200-205; en.wikipedia Barca (ancient city)
note: Sent at the request of Pheretime of Cyrene; Herodotus thinks the real aim was the conquest of Libya. The army went on to Euesperides, and Libyans harried it on the march home (4.203), unnamed skirmishes not listed. Herodotus puts it at the time of the Scythian campaign; Wikipedia's Barca article says 515.

name: Scythian campaign of Darius I
place: the steppe north of the Danube towards the Oarus (southern Ukraine), Ukraine
how the result was decided: No pitched battle was fought; after weeks of Scythian raids Darius withdrew by night, leaving his sick and his camp, and the Scythians held the field (Herodotus 4.128-136).
Iranian force: The royal army of all the subject nations, 700,000 men with 600 ships in Herodotus (4.87); the Ionian, Aeolian and Hellespontine Greeks guarded the Danube bridge while the land army marched into Scythia.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: 700,000 men and 600 ships (Herodotus 4.87); 80,000 left with Megabazus afterwards (4.143)
losses B: heavy; the sick and weak abandoned in the camp (Herodotus 4.135)
borderline: a campaign of raids and skirmishes without a pitched battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: a campaign of raids and skirmishes without a pitched battle.
sources: Herodotus 4.1, 4.83-144; Ctesias; en.wikipedia Scythian campaign of Darius I
note: Wikipedia's infobox calls it a Persian victory, its text a costly stalemate; the field test gives it to the Scythians, whom the Sauromatae (listed as Sarmatians), Budini and Geloni joined. On the way the Getae resisted and were at once subdued (Herodotus 4.93), and the empty wooden town of Gelonus was burned (4.123); neither is listed. Herodotus' figures are impossible.

name: Perinthus
how the result was decided: The Perinthians fought bravely for their freedom but were overcome by the numbers of Megabazus' army and the city was subdued (Herodotus 5.2).
Iranian force: Megabazus' army of 80,000 left in Europe by Darius after the Scythian campaign (Herodotus 4.143, 5.1-2).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
note: Same as Ancient Greek Battles: Perinthus, c. 512 BC, Persian victory; the opponent there is named 'Perinthus'. If Perinthus (siege, 340 BC) is also in this set, this entry should become 'Perinthus (512 BC)'. Megabazus then subdued Thrace and deported the Paeonians without a recorded battle.

name: Lemnos
how the result was decided: The Lemnians fought hard but were in time overcome, and the Persians set Lycaretus over the survivors (Herodotus 5.27).
Iranian force: Otanes' Persian army carried on ships supplied by the Lesbians (Herodotus 5.26).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: known from two sentences of Herodotus
doubts and flags: Borderline: known from two sentences of Herodotus.
sources: Herodotus 5.25-27
note: The Lemnians were then 'Pelasgians' (Tyrsenians), not Greeks; listed under Greek cities. In the same campaign Otanes took Constantinople, Chalcedon, Antandrus, Lamponium and Imbros (Herodotus 5.26) with no fighting described; not listed.

date: 499 BC (a siege of about four months)
name: Naxos (siege, 499 BC)
how the result was decided: An initial attack was repelled and after four months the besiegers ran out of money and sailed away without taking the town.
commanders A: unknown (the Naxian people, who had expelled their oligarchs)
commanders B: Megabates (cousin of Darius), Aristagoras of Miletus; sent by the satrap Artaphernes
Iranian force: A royal fleet of about 200 triremes raised by Artaphernes, carrying 'many Persians and other allies' (Herodotus 5.32), with Aristagoras' Milesians and the Naxian exiles; the ships were crewed by Aegean subjects (a ship of Myndus in Caria is named).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Herodotus 5.28-34; en.wikipedia Siege of Naxos (499 BC); en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt
note: Allies_b 'Greek cities' = Miletus under Aristagoras and the exiled Naxian oligarchs. Herodotus' story that Megabates warned the Naxians after a quarrel with Aristagoras may be Aristagoras' later excuse. The failure set off the Ionian Revolt.

name: Ephesus (498 BC)
how the result was decided: The Persians caught the Greeks retreating from Sardis outside Ephesus and routed them; the survivors scattered to their cities.
commanders A: the Persian commanders west of the Halys (unnamed by Herodotus; Wikipedia gives Artaphernes)
Iranian force: The Persians holding lands west of the Halys, who gathered to relieve Sardis and followed the Greeks to Ephesus (Herodotus 5.102); probably mostly cavalry (Holland).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: many killed, among them Eualcides of Eretria (Herodotus 5.102)
sources: Herodotus 5.102-103; en.wikipedia Battle of Ephesus (498 BC)
note: Name kept as in Ancient Greek Battles; Wikipedia: Battle of Ephesus (498 BC). Side_b 'Greek cities' = Eretria. Afterwards the Athenians left the revolt.

name: Sardis (siege, 498 BC)
how the result was decided: The attackers took and burned the lower city but failed to take the citadel held by Artaphernes and withdrew when the Persians and Lydians massed against them in the agora, so the place did not fall.
commanders B: Charopinus (brother of Aristagoras) and Hermophantus (Milesians), Melanthius (Athenians)
Iranian force: Artaphernes' garrison of the citadel and the Persians and Lydians of the city, who gathered in the agora by the Pactolus and fought the Greeks there (Herodotus 5.100-101).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: unknown (the Ionian army with the crews of 20 Athenian and 5 Eretrian ships)
sources: Herodotus 5.97-105; en.wikipedia Siege of Sardis (498 BC)
note: Side_b 'Greek cities' = Eretria. Wikipedia's infobox reads 'Greek retreat, city burned'; the fire destroyed most of the lower city and the temple of Cybebe and moved Darius to vow vengeance on Athens (Herodotus 5.105).

name: Labraunda
place: sanctuary of Zeus Stratios, Labraunda (near Milas), Turkey
how the result was decided: The Persians attacked the Carians and the Milesian relief army at the sanctuary and routed them, the Milesians losing most heavily.
Iranian force: Daurises' army of Persians, as at the Marsyas.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no standalone Wikipedia article (treated as a battle in the Ionian Revolt article)
doubts and flags: Borderline: no standalone Wikipedia article (treated as a battle in the Ionian Revolt article).
sources: Herodotus 5.119-120; en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt
note: Ionian rebels = the Milesians and their allies.

name: Marsyas River
place: the White Pillars on the Marsyas (Cine river), near its confluence with the Maeander, Turkey
how the result was decided: After a long fight the Carians were beaten and fled to Labraunda, leaving the field to the Persians.
commanders B: unnamed Carian leaders (Pixodarus son of Mausolus of Cindye proposed fighting with the river behind them)
Iranian force: Daurises' army, fresh from retaking the Hellespontine towns; Herodotus calls its men Persians.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no standalone Wikipedia article (treated as a battle in the Ionian Revolt article)
doubts and flags: Borderline: no standalone Wikipedia article (treated as a battle in the Ionian Revolt article).
sources: Herodotus 5.117-119; en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt
note: The site of the White Pillars is unknown; coordinates are for the lower Marsyas valley. Most date the Carian battles to 497, some to 496.

name: Pedasus
place: the road to Pedasa (Gokceler, near Bodrum), Turkey
how the result was decided: The Carians ambushed the Persian army at night on the road to Pedasus and destroyed it with its generals.
commanders A: Heraclides son of Ibanollis of Mylasa
commanders B: Daurises, Amorges, Sisimaces, Myrsus son of Gyges (all killed)
Iranian force: Daurises' army of Persians marching on the Carian cities (Herodotus 5.121).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the army destroyed with its generals (Herodotus 5.121)
borderline: no standalone Wikipedia article (a named ambush, treated as a battle in the Ionian Revolt article)
doubts and flags: Borderline: no standalone Wikipedia article (a named ambush, treated as a battle in the Ionian Revolt article).
sources: Herodotus 5.121; en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt
note: Which Pedasus is meant is uncertain (the Lelegian Pedasa near Halicarnassus is usual); coordinates approximate. Wikipedia notes a 496 date would give the Carians time to regroup.

name: Salamis in Cyprus (497 BC)
how the result was decided: The Cypriot line broke after Stesenor of Curium and the Salaminian chariots went over to the Persians, Onesilus fell, and the Persians held the field.
commanders B: Onesilus of Salamis (killed), Aristocyprus of Soli (killed), Stesenor of Curium (changed sides)
Iranian force: Artybius' 'great army of Persians' shipped over from Cilicia (Herodotus 5.108-112), probably with Cilician levies; the loyal Amathusians were on the Persian side.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Herodotus 5.104, 5.108-115; en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt
note: Side_b = Salamis, Soli, Curium and the other rebel Cypriot kingdoms. Fought the same day as the sea battle off Salamis, which the Ionians won.

name: Salamis in Cyprus (sea) (497 BC)
how the result was decided: The Ionian fleet defeated the Phoenician fleet off Salamis (Herodotus 5.112).
Iranian force: The Phoenician fleet that brought Artybius' army to Cyprus (Herodotus 5.108, 5.112).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Herodotus 5.108-112; en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt
note: The victory was wasted by the defeat on land the same day; the Ionians sailed home.

name: Soli in Cyprus (siege, 497 BC)
how the result was decided: Soli fell in the fifth month after the Persians undermined its wall (Herodotus 5.115).
commanders B: unknown (King Aristocyprus had fallen at Salamis)
Iranian force: The Persian army victorious at Salamis, with Phoenician naval support; its make-up at the siege is not recorded.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no Wikipedia battle article; Herodotus describes the siege (mining) in one sentence
doubts and flags: Borderline: no Wikipedia battle article; Herodotus describes the siege (mining) in one sentence.
sources: Herodotus 5.115-116
note: Herodotus says the other rebel cities were besieged and retaken within the year and Soli held out longest. The excavated Persian siege mound and Cypriot counter-mines at Old Paphos (Kouklia) belong to the same campaign, but no written account of that siege survives.

name: Lade
place: sea off the island of Lade (now silted up, near Balat), Turkey
how the result was decided: The Ionian line collapsed when most of the Samians and the Lesbians fled, the Chians withdrew after heavy losses, and the Persian fleet held the sea off Miletus.
commanders A: unnamed Persian generals (Wikipedia suggests Datis may have commanded the fleet)
Iranian force: A fleet of 600 ships from the Phoenicians (the keenest), the Cypriots, the Cilicians and the Egyptians (Herodotus 6.6, 6.9).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: heavy, above all the Chians; 49 of 60 Samian ships and the Lesbians deserted (Wikipedia's infobox: 246 ships)
sources: Herodotus 6.6-17; en.wikipedia Battle of Lade
note: Some modern historians doubt Herodotus' Samian story of desertion, which he probably had from Samian sources.

name: Miletus (siege, 494 BC)
how the result was decided: Miletus fell to the besiegers after they mined its walls and brought up engines, in the sixth year of the revolt (Herodotus 6.18).
Iranian force: The Persian land armies of Asia Minor, combined into one army for the siege (Herodotus 6.6), with the victorious fleet blockading by sea.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: most of the men killed, the women and children enslaved, the survivors deported to Ampe on the Persian Gulf (Herodotus 6.19-20)
sources: Herodotus 6.6, 6.18-21; en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt; en.wikipedia Battle of Lade
note: No standalone Wikipedia article for this siege. Phrynichus' play 'The Capture of Miletus' was staged at Athens soon after.

name: Malene
place: Malene, territory of Atarneus (near Dikili), Turkey
how the result was decided: After a long fight a Persian cavalry charge routed Histiaeus' men and he was captured in the flight.
Iranian force: A large Persian army under Harpagus; the Persian cavalry decided the battle (Herodotus 6.28-29).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: unknown (Histiaeus' foragers, Ionians and Aeolians from Lesbos)
losses B: many killed; Histiaeus captured and impaled at Sardis by Artaphernes
sources: Herodotus 6.26-30; en.wikipedia Ionian Revolt
note: Histiaeus, the former tyrant of Miletus, was by then fighting as a freebooter with a Lesbian fleet; Wikipedia places the battle in 494-493 without a firm date.

name: Brygian night raid
war: First Persian invasion of Greece (Mardonius' campaign)
place: Mardonius' camp in Macedonia (site unknown), Greece
how the result was decided: The Brygi killed many Persians and wounded Mardonius in their night attack but did not take the camp, which the Persians held (Herodotus 6.45); their later subjection is a separate matter.
Iranian force: Mardonius' land army that crossed the Hellespont in 492 (the fleet had been wrecked off Athos); its make-up is not recorded. Achaemenid field armies of the time were built round Persian and Median infantry and Iranian cavalry with subject levies.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a night raid told in one sentence by Herodotus; no Wikipedia battle article (named 'Brygian night raid' in the campaign article)
doubts and flags: Borderline: a night raid told in one sentence by Herodotus; no Wikipedia battle article (named 'Brygian night raid' in the campaign article).
sources: Herodotus 6.43-45; en.wikipedia First Persian invasion of Greece
note: Side_b 'Thracians' = the Brygi (Bryges), whom Herodotus calls Thracians. Their homeland is placed near Mt Bermion or further north-west (Lake Ohrid, Pelagonia, now North Macedonia), so the site is uncertain. Judged by the raid alone, the Brygi inflicted the heavier recorded loss.

date: 490 BC (August or September, a week before Marathon)
name: Eretria (siege, 490 BC)
war: First Persian invasion of Greece (Datis and Artaphernes)
how the result was decided: After six days of assaults with heavy losses on both sides, Eretria fell on the seventh when Euphorbus and Philagrus opened the gates.
commanders B: unknown (Euphorbus son of Alcimachus and Philagrus son of Cyneas betrayed the city)
Iranian force: Datis' expeditionary army, landed at Tamynae, Choereae and Aegilia (Herodotus 6.101), with cavalry; modern estimates about 25,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: heavy; the city sacked, its temples burned and its people deported to Arderikka in Kissia (Herodotus 6.101, 6.119)
sources: Herodotus 6.99-101, 6.119; en.wikipedia Siege of Eretria
note: Side_b 'Greek cities' = Eretria. The 4,000 Athenian cleruchs of Chalcis sent to help left before the siege (Herodotus 6.100-101).

name: Karystos (siege, 490 BC)
war: First Persian invasion of Greece (Datis and Artaphernes)
how the result was decided: The Carystians, besieged and their land ravaged, submitted to the Persians (Herodotus 6.99).
Iranian force: Datis' expeditionary army (modern estimates about 25,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry), carried by a fleet with Ionian and Aeolian contingents (Herodotus 6.98).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: about 25,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry (modern estimate for the expedition)
borderline: Herodotus records a siege and the ravaging of the land but no assault; it ended in surrender
doubts and flags: Borderline: Herodotus records a siege and the ravaging of the land but no assault; it ended in surrender.
sources: Herodotus 6.99; en.wikipedia First Persian invasion of Greece
note: Side_b 'Greek cities' = Karystos (Carystus).

name: Lindos (siege, 490 BC)
war: First Persian invasion of Greece (Datis and Artaphernes)
how the result was decided: By the Lindian Chronicle, Datis ended the blockade with a pact of friendship while the town was still invested, after rain relieved its water shortage.
Iranian force: Datis' expeditionary fleet and army on its way into the Aegean (600 triremes for the whole expedition, Herodotus 6.95); the force at Lindos is not described.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a blockade with no recorded fighting, known only from a temple chronicle
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from a miracle story of Athena in the Lindian Chronicle (inscribed 99 BC), not from Herodotus; Datis' fleet may well have touched Rhodes, but the siege and its ending are temple legend. Borderline: a blockade with no recorded fighting, known only from a temple chronicle.
sources: Lindian Chronicle (Epiphany D); en.wikipedia First Persian invasion of Greece
note: Side_b 'Greek cities' = Lindos (and the country people of Rhodes who fled there). Wikipedia says the attempt 'failed'; under the siege test a siege ended by treaty is a draw.

name: Marathon
war: First Persian invasion of Greece (Datis and Artaphernes)
how the result was decided: The Athenian and Plataean wings routed the Persian wings and then the victorious Persian centre, driving the Persians to their ships and holding the field.
commanders A: Miltiades, Callimachus (killed), Aristides, Themistocles, Stesilaus (killed); Arimnestus (Plataeans)
commanders B: Datis, Artaphernes (son of Artaphernes); the exiled tyrant Hippias as guide
Iranian force: Datis' expeditionary army: the Persians and the Saka held the centre and broke through (Herodotus 6.113); the cavalry may not have been engaged.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: about 25,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry (modern estimates); 600 ships (Herodotus)
losses B: 6,400 killed and 7 ships captured (Herodotus 6.115-117); modern estimates 1,000-2,000 killed
sources: Herodotus 6.102-117; Nepos, Miltiades 4-6; Pausanias 1.32; en.wikipedia Battle of Marathon
note: Allies_a 'Greek cities' = Plataea. The traditional date (Boeckh) is 12 September; some prefer August. The Persians then sailed round Sunium but found the Athenian army back at Athens and returned to Asia.

date: winter 480/479 BC (during the siege of Potidaea)
name: Olynthus (siege, 480 BC)
how the result was decided: Artabazus took Olynthus and massacred its Bottiaean defenders by a nearby lake (Herodotus 8.127).
Iranian force: Artabazus' corps of 60,000 picked from Mardonius' army (Herodotus 8.126).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: Herodotus records the siege and capture but not the fighting
doubts and flags: Borderline: Herodotus records the siege and capture but not the fighting.
sources: Herodotus 8.127; en.wikipedia Second Persian invasion of Greece
note: Side_b 'Greek cities' = Olynthus, then held by the Bottiaeans (a people driven out of Macedonia, not Greeks in the strict sense). Artabazus gave the town to Critobulus of Torone and the Chalcidians.

name: Potidaea (siege, 480 BC)
how the result was decided: After three months Artabazus' attack across the shallows at low tide was caught by a great flood, many drowned or were killed by the Potidaeans in boats, and he raised the siege (Herodotus 8.129).
Iranian force: Artabazus' 60,000 men picked from Mardonius' army to escort Xerxes to the Hellespont (Herodotus 8.126); in 480 Artabazus had led the Parthians and Chorasmians (Herodotus 7.66).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: many drowned or killed in the flood (Herodotus 8.129)
sources: Herodotus 8.126-129; en.wikipedia Second Persian invasion of Greece
note: Side_a 'Greek cities' = Potidaea, which had revolted with the other towns of Pallene (Herodotus 8.126). The flood is often read as a tsunami; Herodotus blamed Poseidon. Some date the end of the siege to early 479.

date: August or September 480 BC (three days, the same days as Thermopylae)
name: Artemisium
place: strait off Cape Artemisium, northern Euboea, Greece
how the result was decided: On the third day the fleets broke off with heavy losses, the Persians having lost more ships (Herodotus 8.16) but the Greeks leaving the strait that night, so the ships lost and the sea area point opposite ways.
commanders B: Achaemenes, Ariabignes, Prexaspes, Megabazus (the four admirals), Artemisia I, Damasithymus
Iranian force: The royal fleet (1,207 ships at Doriscus by Herodotus' count, reduced by storms): Phoenician, Egyptian, Cypriot, Cilician, Ionian, Hellespontine, Carian, Lycian, Pamphylian and other ships, each with 30 Persian, Median or Saka marines (Herodotus 7.89-96, 7.184).
languages: Greek; Phoenician; Anatolian; Egyptian; Persian; Median; East Iranian
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: 1,207 ships at the start of the campaign less storm losses (Herodotus); modern estimates far lower
losses A: heavy; half the Athenian ships damaged (Herodotus 8.18); Wikipedia's infobox: 100 ships
losses B: about 30 ships on day 1, a Cilician squadron on day 2 and more than the Greeks on day 3 (Herodotus); about 200 more wrecked in a storm off Euboea; Wikipedia's infobox: 400 ships
sources: Herodotus 8.1-23; Diodorus 11.12-13; en.wikipedia Battle of Artemisium
note: Outcome kept as a draw, as in Ancient Greek Battles; Wikipedia's infobox calls it a Persian victory (the Persians then took Euboea). The preliminary skirmish off Sciathus, where Persian scouts took two Greek guard ships, is counted within this battle.
