Allies_a 'Greek cities' = Corinth, Aegina, Megara, Chalcis, Sicyon, Epidaurus, Eretria, Troezen and others.

date: August or September 480 BC (Wikipedia gives 21-23 July, 20 August or 8-10 September; three days)
name: Thermopylae
how the result was decided: On the third day the Persians, having turned the pass by the Anopaea path, destroyed the Greek rearguard and held the pass.
commanders B: Leonidas I (killed), Demophilus of Thespiae (killed), Leontiades of Thebes
Iranian force: Xerxes' land army: the Medes and Kissians attacked first, then the Immortals (the 10,000 Persian guard) under Hydarnes, then picked troops of every nation; the Immortals turned the pass (Herodotus 7.210-225).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: 40,000-300,000 (modern estimates); Herodotus gives 2,641,610 fighting men for the whole army
sources: Herodotus 7.175-233; Diodorus 11.4-10; en.wikipedia Battle of Thermopylae
note: Allies_b 'Greek cities' = Thespiae, Phocis, Opuntian Locris, Tegea, Mantinea, Corinth, Phlius, Mycenae and other Peloponnesians. Fought on the same days as Artemisium; the date is disputed.

name: Athens (siege, 480 BC)
how the result was decided: The Persians took the Acropolis by climbing the cliff near the shrine of Aglauros and killed its defenders (Herodotus 8.53).
Iranian force: Xerxes' land army: Persians posted on the Areopagus shot fire-arrows into the wooden barricade, and a party climbed the north face (Herodotus 8.52-53).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: a few: the temple treasurers and poor Athenians behind a wooden barricade (Herodotus 8.51)
sources: Herodotus 8.50-55; en.wikipedia Achaemenid destruction of Athens; en.wikipedia Second Persian invasion of Greece
note: Wikipedia's article 'Achaemenid destruction of Athens' covers this siege and the burning of 480 and Mardonius' razing of 479, which saw no fighting and is not a separate entry. Exiled Pisistratids accompanied Xerxes and parleyed with the defenders.

name: Delphi (480 BC)
place: below the sanctuary of Athena Pronaia, Delphi, Greece
how the result was decided: Herodotus says the Persian detachment fled when thunderbolts and falling rocks struck it near the shrine of Athena Pronaia, and the Delphians pursued and killed many.
Iranian force: A detachment of Xerxes' army sent through Phocis to plunder Delphi; its units are not recorded.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: unknown (60 Delphians stayed, the rest fled to Parnassus)
borderline: a miracle story; no Wikipedia battle article
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from Herodotus' miracle story (8. Borderline: a miracle story; no Wikipedia battle article.
sources: Herodotus 8.35-39; Diodorus 11.14
note: Side_a 'Greek cities' = Delphi.

date: late September 480 BC (26 or 27 September per Wikipedia)
name: Salamis
place: straits between Salamis and Attica, Greece
how the result was decided: The Greeks broke the Persian fleet in the straits, sinking or taking some 200 ships, and held the sea; the Persian fleet fell back to Phaleron and then to Asia.
commanders A: Themistocles, Eurybiades, Adeimantus of Corinth, Aristides (at Psyttaleia)
commanders B: Xerxes I (watching from the shore), Ariabignes (killed), Achaemenes, Artemisia I of Halicarnassus, Damasithymus (killed)
Iranian force: The royal fleet: Phoenicians on the west wing facing the Athenians, Ionians on the east facing the Spartans, with Egyptian, Cypriot, Cilician, Carian, Pamphylian and Lycian ships; Persian, Median and Saka marines aboard; and about 400 troops on Psyttaleia (Herodotus 8.85, 8.95).
languages: Greek; Phoenician; Anatolian; Egyptian; Persian; Median; East Iranian
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Herodotus 8.40-96; Aeschylus, Persians; Diodorus 11.15-19; Plutarch, Themistocles 11-15; en.wikipedia Battle of Salamis
note: Allies_a 'Greek cities' = Aegina, Corinth, Megara, Chalcis, Sicyon, Epidaurus, Eretria, Troezen, Naxos, Leucas, Ambracia and others. The destruction of the Persian troops on Psyttaleia by Aristides' hoplites is counted within this battle.

name: Sestos (siege, 479 BC)
war: Second Persian invasion of Greece (Greek counter-offensive)
how the result was decided: Sestos fell after the starving Persian garrison slipped out by night and the townspeople opened the gates to the Athenians (Herodotus 9.118).
Iranian force: Artayctes' garrison: the Persians of Sestos and the neighbouring towns and Oeobazus' party from Cardia, with the Aeolian townspeople (Herodotus 9.115-118).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: Artayctes and his son captured and executed; Oeobazus caught and sacrificed by the Apsinthian Thracians
sources: Herodotus 9.114-121; Thucydides 1.89; en.wikipedia Greco-Persian Wars
note: Allies_a = the Ionian and Hellespontine allies who stayed with the Athenians after Leotychides' Peloponnesians went home. Herodotus ends his history with this siege; the town fell in winter 479/478 or spring 478. Wikipedia has no standalone article (Siege of Sestos redirects to Greco-Persian Wars).

date: August 479 BC (the eighth day of the stand-off on the Asopus)
name: Dryoskephalai
war: Second Persian invasion of Greece (Plataea campaign)
place: Dryoskephalai pass over Mt Cithaeron (near Eleutherae), Greece
how the result was decided: The Persian cavalry caught a convoy of 500 pack animals coming down the pass, killed men and beasts and drove the rest back to the Persian camp (Herodotus 9.39).
commanders A: Mardonius (on the advice of Timagenidas of Thebes)
Iranian force: Mardonius' cavalry, sent by night to the pass (Herodotus 9.39).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: a supply convoy of 500 pack animals with drivers
borderline: a cavalry raid on a supply convoy within the Plataea campaign, named only by its pass
doubts and flags: Borderline: a cavalry raid on a supply convoy within the Plataea campaign, named only by its pass.
sources: Herodotus 9.38-39; en.wikipedia Battle of Plataea
note: Side_b 'Greek cities' = the supply train of the Greek allied army. Wikipedia's Plataea article mentions the raid without naming the pass.

date: August 479 BC (about ten days before Plataea)
name: Erythrae (479 BC)
war: Second Persian invasion of Greece (Plataea campaign)
place: foothills of Cithaeron near Erythrae (near Erythres), Greece
how the result was decided: The Persian cavalry fell back after Masistius was killed and failed to recover his body, leaving the field to the Greeks (Herodotus 9.22-25).
commanders A: Pausanias; Olympiodorus son of Lampon (300 Athenians and archers)
Iranian force: The whole of Mardonius' cavalry attacking by squadrons under Masistius (Herodotus 9.20); his horse were Persians, Medes, Bactrians, Indians and Saka.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: 3,000 Megarians, relieved by 300 Athenian picked men and archers
borderline: a preliminary engagement of the Plataea campaign, described in the Plataea article but not separately named
doubts and flags: Borderline: a preliminary engagement of the Plataea campaign, described in the Plataea article but not separately named.
sources: Herodotus 9.19-25; Plutarch, Aristides 14; en.wikipedia Battle of Plataea
note: Side_a 'Greek cities' = Megara. The Greeks then moved down from Erythrae to the Asopus ridge near Plataea.

date: August 479 BC (traditionally the same day as Plataea)
name: Mycale
place: shore beneath Mt Mycale (near Priene), Turkey
how the result was decided: The Greeks broke the Persian shield-wall, stormed the stockaded camp and burned the beached fleet, holding the field.
Iranian force: Tigranes' army left to guard Ionia (60,000 by Herodotus 9.96) with the marines and crews of the beached fleet; the Persians fought hardest, while the disarmed Samians, the Milesians and other Ionians turned on them (Herodotus 9.99-104).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: the crews and marines of 110 ships (Herodotus 8.131)
losses B: most of the army killed; the camp and ships burned (about 4,000 killed by a modern estimate)
sources: Herodotus 9.90-106; Diodorus 11.34-36; en.wikipedia Battle of Mycale
note: Allies_a: 'Greek cities' = Corinth, Sicyon, Troezen; 'Ionian rebels' = the Samians, Milesians and other Ionians who changed sides during the battle. The Phoenician ships had been sent away before the battle.

date: August 479 BC (27 or 28 August per Wikipedia)
name: Plataea
war: Second Persian invasion of Greece (Plataea campaign)
how the result was decided: The Spartans and Tegeans killed Mardonius and routed the Persians, and the Greeks stormed the Persian stockade and held the field; Artabazus marched off with 40,000 men.
commanders B: Mardonius (killed), Artabazus; Theban leaders Attaginus and Timagenidas
Iranian force: Mardonius' picked army: Persians (with the Immortals), Medes, Bactrians, Indians and Saka, foot and horse, with Phrygian, Thracian, Mysian, Paeonian, Ethiopian and Egyptian units and about 50,000 Medising Greeks (Herodotus 8.113, 9.31-32).
languages: Persian; Median; East Iranian; Greek; Indian
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: all but 3,000 of those not with Artabazus (Herodotus 9.70); 100,000 (Diodorus)
sources: Herodotus 9.12-89; Diodorus 11.29-33; Plutarch, Aristides 11-21; en.wikipedia Battle of Plataea
note: Allies_a 'Greek cities' = Tegea, Corinth, Megara, Sicyon, Plataea, Aegina, Phlius, Epidaurus, Troezen, Eretria, Chalcis and others. Allies_b 'Greek cities' = the other Boeotians, Thessalians, Locrians, Malians and Phocians; the Thebans fought the Athenians hard. Traditionally fought on the same day as Mycale.

name: Byzantium (siege, 478 BC)
how the result was decided: Constantinople fell to the besiegers and its Persian garrison was captured.
commanders A: Pausanias (with Aristides and Cimon leading the Athenians, per Plutarch)
Iranian force: The Persian garrison of Byzantium ('held by the Medes'), which included Persian nobles who were kinsmen of the King (Thucydides 1.94, 1.128).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: 20 Peloponnesian ships, 30 Athenian and many other allied ships (Thucydides 1.94)
losses B: the garrison captured, including kinsmen of the King (later released secretly by Pausanias)
sources: Thucydides 1.94, 1.128; Plutarch, Aristides 23, Cimon 6; en.wikipedia Greco-Persian Wars, Wars of the Delian League
note: Thucydides puts it after Pausanias' campaign in Cyprus in the same year, where he 'subdued most of the island' (no named battle).

name: Eion
place: Eion at the mouth of the Strymon (near Amphipolis), Greece
how the result was decided: Cimon beat the Persians outside the walls and starved Eion into falling; the governor Boges burned himself rather than surrender.
Iranian force: The Persian garrison of the governor Boges, supplied by Thracian allies until Cimon drove them off (Herodotus 7.107; Plutarch, Cimon 7).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the garrison destroyed; Boges killed himself; the inhabitants enslaved
sources: Herodotus 7.107; Thucydides 1.98; Plutarch, Cimon 7; en.wikipedia Wars of the Delian League
note: The battle outside the walls and the siege are one entry, as in Ancient Greek Battles.

name: Doriskos (siege)
place: Doriskos, near the mouth of the Hebrus (Evros), Greece
how the result was decided: Mascames held Doriskos against every Greek attempt and the fort was never taken (Herodotus 7.106).
Iranian force: The garrison of the governor Mascames, appointed by Xerxes in 480; its make-up is not recorded (an Achaemenid garrison was normally Persians with local troops).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: several unsuccessful attempts mentioned in one sentence by Herodotus; no single described engagement
doubts and flags: Borderline: several unsuccessful attempts mentioned in one sentence by Herodotus; no single described engagement.
sources: Herodotus 7.105-106; en.wikipedia Wars of the Delian League
note: Herodotus says 'the Greeks' tried; Wikipedia takes them to be Athenian attempts. The Persians probably withdrew the garrison around 465 BC, and the King sent gifts every year to Mascames' descendants for his defence.

name: Eurymedon
place: banks of the Eurymedon (Koprucay) near Aspendos, Antalya, Turkey
how the result was decided: Cimon's landed hoplites routed the Persian army after a hard fight and took its camp.
commanders B: Pherendates (army, per Ephorus); Ariomandes son of Gobryas (overall, per Callisthenes)
Iranian force: The royal army gathered at Aspendos under Pherendates, joined by the crews of the beached Phoenician ships; no ancient source gives its size.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: the hoplite marines of about 200 triremes (perhaps 5,000)
sources: Thucydides 1.100; Plutarch, Cimon 12-13; Diodorus 11.60-62; en.wikipedia Battle of the Eurymedon
note: Wikipedia's infobox marks Pherendates as killed. Diodorus puts the sea battle off Cyprus and the land battle at the Eurymedon the same day.

name: Eurymedon (sea)
place: off the mouth of the Eurymedon (Koprucay), Antalya, Turkey
how the result was decided: The Persian fleet was broken at the river mouth and 200 Phoenician triremes were taken or destroyed (Thucydides 1.100).
Iranian force: The royal fleet of 200 Phoenician triremes (Thucydides; 350 per Ephorus, 600 per Phanodemus), waiting for 80 more Phoenician ships from Cyprus; marines probably Iranian, as in 480.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Thucydides 1.100; Plutarch, Cimon 12-13; Diodorus 11.60-61; en.wikipedia Battle of the Eurymedon
note: Plutarch adds that Cimon then destroyed the 80 Phoenician ships coming from Cyprus; Thucydides is silent and some historians doubt it, so it is not entered separately.

name: Chersonese (465 BC)
how the result was decided: Cimon with four triremes took 13 Persian ships and drove the Persians out of the Chersonese (Plutarch, Cimon 14).
Iranian force: Persians who had stayed in the Chersonese with at least 13 ships, and Thracians from the interior whom they called in (Plutarch, Cimon 14).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: at least 13 ships, with Thracian allies
borderline: minor action known only from Plutarch, with no conventional name
doubts and flags: Borderline: minor action known only from Plutarch, with no conventional name.
sources: Plutarch, Cimon 14.1; en.wikipedia Wars of the Delian League

name: Nile
war: Wars of the Delian League (Egyptian revolt of Inaros)
how the result was decided: Charitimides' 40 Athenian ships captured 20 of the 50 Persian ships with their crews and sank the other 30 (Ctesias).
Iranian force: A royal fleet of 50 ships supporting Achaemenes' army, probably Phoenician (Ctesias calls them Persian ships; Wikipedia, Phoenician).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Ctesias, Persica (Photius' summary) 36; en.wikipedia Inaros II, Wars of the Delian League
note: Known only from Ctesias' summary; the site and exact date are unknown, but it belongs to the campaign of Achaemenes.

name: Papremis
war: Wars of the Delian League (Egyptian revolt of Inaros)
place: Papremis, western Nile Delta (site unidentified), Egypt
how the result was decided: Inaros' Egyptians and the Athenians broke Achaemenes' army, which fled to Memphis; Achaemenes was killed.
Iranian force: The army of the satrap Achaemenes, brother of Xerxes, raised from the empire: over 300,000 horse and foot (Diodorus 11.74) or 400,000 with 80 ships (Ctesias), figures much exaggerated.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: the Egyptian rebels and the Athenian expedition (200 ships came from Cyprus)
losses B: Achaemenes and, by Ctesias' figure, 100,000 men killed
sources: Herodotus 3.12, 7.7; Thucydides 1.104; Diodorus 11.74; Ctesias (Photius) 36; en.wikipedia Inaros II, Wars of the Delian League
note: Thucydides does not name the battle; Herodotus and Ctesias do. Some date it to 459.

date: c. 456 BC (relief of the White Castle, besieged since c. 459)
name: Memphis
war: Wars of the Delian League (Egyptian revolt of Inaros)
how the result was decided: Megabyzus beat the Egyptians and Athenians in battle and drove them from Memphis, raising their siege of the White Castle.
Iranian force: The White Castle garrison (Persians and Medes, with the Egyptians who had not joined the revolt, Thucydides 1.104) and Megabyzus' relief army, drilled for a year in Cilicia (300,000 per Diodorus, 200,000 per Ctesias; modern estimate about 25,000), with Phoenician, Cilician and Cypriot ships.
languages: Persian; Median; Aramaic; Egyptian; Phoenician; Anatolian
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: 300,000 men and 300 triremes (Diodorus 11.75); 200,000 men and 300 ships under Oriscus (Ctesias); modern estimate about 25,000
sources: Thucydides 1.104, 1.109; Diodorus 11.74-77; Ctesias (Photius) 37; en.wikipedia Inaros II, Megabyzus, Wars of the Delian League
note: One entry for the siege of the White Castle (c. 459-456, at least three years) and the relief battle, as in Ancient Greek Battles.

name: Prosopitis (siege)
war: Wars of the Delian League (Egyptian revolt of Inaros)
place: island of Prosopitis, western Nile Delta (near Nikiou), Egypt
how the result was decided: After 18 months Megabyzus drained the channel round the island, took it and destroyed the Athenian fleet; only a few Athenians escaped through Libya to Cyrene (Thucydides 1.109-110).
Iranian force: Megabyzus' army and the Phoenician fleet (Thucydides 1.109-110).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: the Athenian expedition's remaining fleet and the Egyptian rebels
losses B: the fleet burned or taken; the whole Egyptian expedition cost Athens about 250 ships (modern estimate)
sources: Thucydides 1.109-110; Diodorus 11.77; Ctesias (Photius) 37-38; en.wikipedia Inaros II, Wars of the Delian League
note: Diodorus says the Egyptians went over and the Athenians left under a truce; Ctesias says Megabyzus took Inaros and the Greeks at Byblos on terms. Either way the place fell. Not in Ancient Greek Battles.

name: Mendesian mouth
war: Wars of the Delian League (Egyptian revolt of Inaros)
place: Mendesian mouth of the Nile (Lake Manzala area), Egypt
how the result was decided: The Phoenician fleet and the Persian land army destroyed most of the 50 relief triremes; only a few escaped (Thucydides 1.110).
Iranian force: The Phoenician fleet attacking from the sea and Persian infantry from the shore (Thucydides 1.110).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Thucydides 1.110; en.wikipedia Inaros II, Wars of the Delian League
note: The squadron arrived unaware that Prosopitis had fallen.

name: Kition (siege, 450 BC)
war: Wars of the Delian League (Cimon's Cyprus campaign)
how the result was decided: The Athenians gave up the siege for lack of food after Cimon's death and sailed away (Thucydides 1.112).
Iranian force: The Phoenician kingdom of Kition defending its city as a subject of the King; Persian royal forces (Artabazus' fleet, Megabyzus' army) were in the region (Diodorus 12.3) but none is said to have been inside.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: 200 ships at the start, less 60 sent to Amyrtaeus in Egypt (Thucydides 1.112)
losses B: Cimon died (of sickness or a wound)
borderline: the defenders were the Phoenician kingdom of Kition, a Persian vassal; no Persian troops are named in the siege
doubts and flags: Borderline: the defenders were the Phoenician kingdom of Kition, a Persian vassal; no Persian troops are named in the siege.
sources: Thucydides 1.112; Plutarch, Cimon 18-19; Diodorus 12.3; en.wikipedia Wars of the Delian League
note: Diodorus (12.3) says Cimon took Kition and Marion by storm; Thucydides, followed here, says the siege was abandoned. Not in Ancient Greek Battles.

date: c. 450 BC (about 30 days after the Athenians left Kition)
name: Salamis in Cyprus (450 BC)
war: Wars of the Delian League (Cimon's Cyprus campaign)
how the result was decided: The Athenians beat the Phoenicians, Cyprians and Cilicians on land as well as at sea and then sailed home unhindered (Thucydides 1.112).
Iranian force: Phoenicians, Cyprians and Cilicians (Thucydides 1.112); Diodorus places the royal army of Megabyzus (300,000) in Cilicia.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: the fleet of about 140 ships and its troops (200 less 60 sent to Egypt)
sources: Thucydides 1.112; Diodorus 12.3-4; Plutarch, Cimon 18-19; en.wikipedia Wars of the Delian League
note: Diodorus tells the campaign differently: Cimon took 100 of Artabazus' 300 ships off Cyprus, then landed in Cilicia and beat Megabyzus' army, before besieging Salamis.

name: Salamis in Cyprus (sea) (450 BC)
war: Wars of the Delian League (Cimon's Cyprus campaign)
how the result was decided: The Athenians defeated the Phoenician, Cyprian and Cilician fleet off Salamis (Thucydides 1.112); Diodorus says they took 100 ships.
Iranian force: The royal fleet of Phoenicians, Cyprians and Cilicians (Thucydides 1.112); 300 ships under Artabazus (Diodorus 12.3).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: 100 ships taken with their crews, many sunk (Diodorus)
sources: Thucydides 1.112; Diodorus 12.3-4; en.wikipedia Wars of the Delian League
note: The Peace of Callias, if historical, followed; Thucydides does not mention it.

date: c. 448-445 BC (after the defeat of Usiris; date uncertain)
name: Megabyzus' revolt (Menostanes)
how the result was decided: Ctesias says Megabyzus wounded Menostanes and the royal army fled.
Iranian force: Megabyzus' Syrian army against a second royal army under the King's nephew Menostanes; no numbers given.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no conventional name; known only from Ctesias
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from Ctesias (Photius' summary 41), whose account of the revolt is a court romance; modern historians doubt the details and some the battles themselves. Borderline: no conventional name; known only from Ctesias.
sources: Ctesias, Persica (Photius' summary) 41; en.wikipedia Megabyzus
note: Megabyzus then submitted on terms negotiated by Artarius, Amytis and Artoxares and was pardoned.

date: c. 448-445 BC (some years after the execution of Inaros; date uncertain)
name: Megabyzus' revolt (Usiris)
how the result was decided: Ctesias says Megabyzus routed Usiris' royal army after the two generals wounded each other, and took Usiris prisoner.
Iranian force: Megabyzus' army of 150,000 foot raised in his satrapy of Syria against Usiris' royal army of 200,000 (Ctesias), both figures incredible.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no conventional name; known only from Ctesias
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from Ctesias' romantic court history (Photius' summary 40), with incredible numbers and a duel of generals; Wikipedia's Megabyzus article treats the encounters as duels rather than pitched battles. Borderline: no conventional name; known only from Ctesias.
sources: Ctesias, Persica (Photius' summary) 40; en.wikipedia Megabyzus
note: Usiris is called an Egyptian by Ctesias.

date: c. 420 BC (early in the reign of Darius II; date uncertain)
name: Arsites' revolt (first battle)
how the result was decided: Ctesias says the royal general Artasyras was defeated by Artyphius.
Iranian force: Artyphius' army with Greek mercenaries against the royal army of Artasyras; no numbers given (Ctesias).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no name or place; one of three battles known only from one sentence of Ctesias' summary
doubts and flags: Borderline: no name or place; one of three battles known only from one sentence of Ctesias' summary.
sources: Ctesias, Persica (Photius' summary) 52
note: Arsites was a full brother of Darius II. The site is unknown; Syria is a guess because Artyphius' father Megabyzus had been satrap there.

name: Arsites' revolt (second battle)
how the result was decided: Ctesias says Artasyras was defeated a second time.
Iranian force: Artyphius' army with Greek mercenaries against the royal army of Artasyras; no numbers given (Ctesias).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no name or place; known only from one sentence of Ctesias' summary
doubts and flags: Borderline: no name or place; known only from one sentence of Ctesias' summary.
sources: Ctesias, Persica (Photius' summary) 52

name: Arsites' revolt (third battle)
how the result was decided: Ctesias says Artasyras won the third battle after bribing Artyphius' Greek mercenaries, all but three Milesians, and Artyphius surrendered.
Iranian force: The royal army of Artasyras against Artyphius, whose Greek mercenaries had been bought off (Ctesias).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no name or place; known only from one sentence of Ctesias' summary
doubts and flags: Borderline: no name or place; known only from one sentence of Ctesias' summary.
sources: Ctesias, Persica (Photius' summary) 52
note: Artyphius and later Arsites surrendered on promises of safety and were put to death in the ashes at Parysatis' urging.

name: Iasos
war: Peloponnesian War (Ionian War); revolt of Amorges
how the result was decided: The Peloponnesian and Syracusan fleet took Iasos by a surprise assault, captured Amorges and handed him and the town to Tissaphernes (Thucydides 8.28).
Iranian force: The rebel Amorges, bastard son of the satrap Pissouthnes, with his mercenaries, mostly Peloponnesian, and the people of Iasos (Thucydides 8.28).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: the Peloponnesian and Syracusan fleet of 55 ships
losses B: Amorges captured; his mercenaries taken into Peloponnesian service; the town sacked
borderline: the Persian side was a rebel against the King; the attackers acted at the urging and in the pay of the loyal satrap Tissaphernes, who received the town (could be treated as civil or left out)
doubts and flags: Borderline: the Persian side was a rebel against the King; the attackers acted at the urging and in the pay of the loyal satrap Tissaphernes, who received the town (could be treated as civil or left out).
sources: Thucydides 8.5, 8.26-28 (no Wikipedia article)
note: Amorges had held Caria in revolt since about 414 with Athenian support; Syracusans were with the Peloponnesians (Greek cities).

name: Miletus (412 BC)
how the result was decided: The Athenians routed the Peloponnesians and Tissaphernes' troops, set up a trophy and began to wall off Miletus, though the Milesians beat the Argives on the other wing (Thucydides 8.25).
commanders B: Tissaphernes; Milesian and Peloponnesian commanders unnamed
Iranian force: Tissaphernes in person with his cavalry and a body of foreign mercenaries (Thucydides 8.25); no numbers given.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: 800 Milesian hoplites, the Peloponnesians of Chalcideus' fleet, Tissaphernes' mercenaries and cavalry
sources: Thucydides 8.25-27
note: Miletus (Greek cities) and the Peloponnesians led the defending side. The Athenians withdrew to Samos when a Peloponnesian and Syracusan fleet of 55 ships arrived (a strategic matter). No Wikipedia article; Persian role could be judged a contingent.

name: Abydos (411 BC)
place: off Abydos (Nara Burnu), Dardanelles, Canakkale, Turkey
how the result was decided: Alcibiades' arrival turned the day; the Peloponnesians fled to Abydos and lost 30 ships, while Pharnabazus' troops on the shore saved the rest (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.1.4-7).
Iranian force: Pharnabazus' army of cavalry and foot, which he led down to the beach, riding into the sea himself, to protect the Peloponnesian ships (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.1.6).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: 97 ships (as given in Wikipedia's infobox), with Pharnabazus' army
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 1.1.4-7; Diodorus 13.45-46; en.wikipedia Battle of Abydos
note: Wikipedia's infobox lists only Athens and Sparta; the Persian role rests on Xenophon and Diodorus. The land battle of 409/408 at the same place keeps its set-12 name 'Abydos' below; the merged list may need years on both.

date: spring 410 BC (usually May or June; one view March)
name: Cyzicus
place: off Cyzicus and on the shore near Cleri, Sea of Marmara (near Erdek), Turkey
how the result was decided: The Athenians destroyed or took the whole Peloponnesian fleet and beat the Spartans and Pharnabazus' troops on the beach, killing Mindarus; Cyzicus surrendered the next day.
Iranian force: Pharnabazus' satrapal army, foot and an important cavalry force, drawn up on the beach where Mindarus ran his ships ashore (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.1.14-18; Diodorus 13.49-51).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the entire fleet (the Syracusans burned their own); Mindarus killed
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 1.1.11-18; Diodorus 13.49-51; Plutarch, Alcibiades 28; en.wikipedia Battle of Cyzicus
note: Syracusan ships fought with the Peloponnesians (Greek cities).

name: Abydos
place: near Abydos (Nara Burnu), Dardanelles, Canakkale, Turkey
how the result was decided: Pharnabazus came to the relief of Abydos with many horsemen and was routed; Alcibiades pursued with his cavalry and 120 hoplites until dark (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.2.15-17).
Iranian force: Pharnabazus with a large force of cavalry and foot from his satrapy of Hellespontine Phrygia.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: the combined army of Thrasyllus and Alcibiades (30 ships with Thrasyllus)
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 1.2.15-17; Plutarch, Alcibiades 29; en.wikipedia Thrasyllus
note: Name and date as in Ancient Greek Battles; the sea battle of 411 at the same place is entered as 'Abydos (411 BC)'. The Athenians did not take Abydos; the Abydenes (Greek cities) fought with Pharnabazus.

name: Ephesus (409 BC)
place: before Ephesus, near Koressos and the marsh (near Selcuk), Turkey
how the result was decided: The Ephesians, Tissaphernes' troops and the Syracusan and Selinuntine crews routed both Athenian landing forces, at Koressos and at the marsh, and set up two trophies (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.2.6-10).
commanders A: Tissaphernes; the Syracusan and Selinuntine captains (unnamed)
Iranian force: The troops Tissaphernes mustered to save the shrine of Artemis, with his Persian cavalry and the levy of the countryside (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.2.6).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: 1,000 hoplites, 100 cavalry and 50 triremes, with 5,000 sailors armed as peltasts (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.2.1)
losses B: several hundred killed (Xenophon and Diodorus give different figures)
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 1.2.6-10; Diodorus 13.64; en.wikipedia Thrasyllus
note: Ancient Greek Battles lists Ephesus, Persia and Syracuse as the winners; Ephesus had been under Tissaphernes since 412. The Ionian revolt's battle of 498 BC at Ephesus may require a year in the merged list.

name: Chalcedon
place: before the Athenian siege wall at Chalcedon (Kadikoy, across the Bosporus from Constantinople), Turkey
how the result was decided: Thrasyllus beat Hippocrates' sortie and killed him while Alcibiades held off Pharnabazus, who could not break through the siege wall and fell back to his camp at the Heracleion (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.3.4-7).
Iranian force: Pharnabazus' army of foot and a large cavalry force, which came up to the Heracleion of Chalcedon to relieve the town (Xenophon, Hellenica 1.3.5).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: Hippocrates and many of his men killed
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 1.3.4-7; Diodorus 13.66; Plutarch, Alcibiades 30
note: The siege then ended in an agreement with Pharnabazus: Chalcedon to pay tribute to Athens again, and Pharnabazus to escort Athenian envoys to the King.

name: Centrites
war: Revolt of Cyrus the Younger (retreat of the Ten Thousand)
place: the Centrites (Botan) near its confluence with the Tigris, Siirt, Turkey
how the result was decided: The Greeks forced the ford after a feint; the Persian cavalry on the bank and the infantry on the bluffs fled, and the rearguard beat off the Carduchians (Xenophon, Anabasis 4.3).
Iranian force: Cavalry on the far bank and infantry on the bluffs: the troops of Orontas and Artuchas, Armenians, Mardians and Chaldaean mercenaries (Xenophon, Anabasis 4.3.3-4).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: an episode of the Anabasis with no battle article
doubts and flags: Borderline: an episode of the Anabasis with no battle article.
sources: Xenophon, Anabasis 4.3; en.wikipedia Ten Thousand (Greek mercenaries)
note: Kentrites in Greek; usually identified with the Botan (Bohtan) Su. The Carduchians who attacked the rear were not Persian allies.

name: Tiribazus' camp
war: Revolt of Cyrus the Younger (retreat of the Ten Thousand)
place: western Armenia, between the Teleboas and the Euphrates (north-west of Lake Van), Turkey
how the result was decided: The Greeks fell on Tiribazus' camp before he could spring his ambush in the pass, routed his men and took his tent with its silver-footed couches and his household (Xenophon, Anabasis 4.4.18-22).
Iranian force: Tiribazus, hyparch of western Armenia, with his own troops and Chalybian and Taochian mercenaries (Xenophon, Anabasis 4.4.18).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: a few killed; camp, tent and household taken
borderline: camp raid of the retreat with no conventional name
doubts and flags: Borderline: camp raid of the retreat with no conventional name.
sources: Xenophon, Anabasis 4.4.4-22; en.wikipedia Ten Thousand (Greek mercenaries)

name: Tissaphernes' attacks (Tigris valley)
war: Revolt of Cyrus the Younger (retreat of the Ten Thousand)
place: Tigris valley north of Mespila (Nineveh, at Mosul) and the hills beyond, Iraq
how the result was decided: The Greek slingers and archers outranged Tissaphernes' missile troops near Mespila and the Greeks won the race for the summit in the hills, so Tissaphernes drew off each time without stopping the march (Xenophon, Anabasis 3.4.13-49).
Iranian force: Tissaphernes' own cavalry, the army of Orontas (satrap of Armenia, the King's son-in-law), Cyrus' former Asian troops and troops given by the King, with many archers and slingers (Xenophon, Anabasis 3.4.13).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: several days of skirmishing grouped as one entry; no conventional name
doubts and flags: Borderline: several days of skirmishing grouped as one entry; no conventional name.
sources: Xenophon, Anabasis 3.4.13-3.5.1; en.wikipedia Ten Thousand (Greek mercenaries), Anabasis (Xenophon)
note: Tissaphernes then burned the villages and the Greeks entered the Carduchian mountains, where no Persian forces fought them.

date: autumn 401 BC (a few days after the arrest of the Greek generals)
name: Zapatas
war: Revolt of Cyrus the Younger (retreat of the Ten Thousand)
place: beyond the Great Zab (Zapatas) near its confluence with the Tigris, Iraq
how the result was decided: On the second day the Greek slingers and new cavalry charged Mithradates' horse and missile troops at a ravine and routed them, taking 18 horsemen alive (Xenophon, Anabasis 3.4.1-5).
Iranian force: Mithradates' force: on the first day about 200 horse and 400 archers and slingers, on the second 1,000 horse and 4,000 archers and slingers lent by Tissaphernes (Xenophon, Anabasis 3.3.6, 3.4.2).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: the Ten Thousand, with 200 Rhodian slingers and 50 horsemen newly formed
losses B: some foot killed in the ravine; 18 horsemen captured
borderline: a skirmish of the retreat with no conventional name; named after the river
doubts and flags: Borderline: a skirmish of the retreat with no conventional name; named after the river.
sources: Xenophon, Anabasis 3.3.6-3.4.5; en.wikipedia Ten Thousand (Greek mercenaries)
note: On the first day (Anabasis 3.3.6-11) Mithradates harassed the Greeks without loss and drew off; this entry scores the second day.

name: Cunaxa
place: Cunaxa, on the Euphrates north of Babylon (near Baghdad), Iraq
how the result was decided: Cyrus was killed and his Asian troops fled the field with Ariaeus; only the Greek mercenaries held their ground, and they withdrew to their plundered camp at nightfall.
Iranian force: Royal army: Tissaphernes' cavalry, 6,000 horse under Artagerses, wicker-shield infantry, Egyptian heavy infantry, archers and 200 scythed chariots. Cyrus' army: 10,400 Greek hoplites and 2,500 peltasts, about 1,000 Paphlagonian horse, his 600 Persian horsemen, Ariaeus' Asian levies and 20 scythed chariots (Xenophon, Anabasis 1.7-8).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
strength A: 900,000 present of a nominal 1,200,000, with 200 scythed chariots (Xenophon); 400,000 (Ctesias); about 40,000 (modern estimate in Wikipedia)
strength B: 10,400 Greek hoplites, 2,500 peltasts, 100,000 Asian troops and 20 scythed chariots (Xenophon); modern estimates of the Asian troops 10,000-20,000
sources: Xenophon, Anabasis 1.7-10; Plutarch, Artaxerxes 7-13; Diodorus 14.22-24; Ctesias (Photius) 63-64; en.wikipedia Battle of Cunaxa
note: Xenophon and Ctesias stress that the Greeks were victorious on their wing; under the test the royal side won, as the rebel army left the field and its claimant was dead. Abrocomas' 300,000 arrived five days late.

name: Calpe
how the result was decided: The Greeks routed the Bithynian infantry and Pharnabazus' horsemen and held the field (Xenophon, Anabasis 6.5).
commanders A: Xenophon and the generals of the Ten Thousand
commanders B: Bithynian chiefs; commanders of Pharnabazus' cavalry (not named)
Iranian force: The cavalry of Pharnabazus, satrap of Hellespontine Phrygia, sent to help the Bithynian Thracians keep the Greeks out of Phrygia; the day before it had cut up a Greek foraging party under Neon (Anabasis 6.4.23-24).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: the Ten Thousand, reunited (several thousand hoplites and peltasts)
losses A: about 500 of Neon's foragers killed the day before (Xenophon)
borderline: no conventional battle name; a minor battle known from Xenophon
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional battle name; a minor battle known from Xenophon.
sources: Xenophon, Anabasis 6.4.23-6.5.32
note: Persia is listed as the Bithynians' ally: Pharnabazus sent his cavalry to their aid. Calpe Harbour was the Ten Thousand's base on the Black Sea coast.

date: late 400 BC (raised at the onset of winter 400/399)
name: Cyme (siege)
war: Persian-Spartan War (prelude: Tissaphernes against the Ionian and Aeolian cities)
how the result was decided: Tissaphernes ravaged Cyme's territory but could not take the city and raised the siege as winter came on, releasing his captives for ransom (Diodorus 14.35.7).
Iranian force: Tissaphernes' satrapal army; the source gives no composition. Western satrapal armies then combined Persian and other Iranian cavalry with Anatolian (Carian, Lydian) levies and Greek mercenaries (said here, not in the source).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses A: many captives taken in the countryside, later ransomed
borderline: a minor siege known only from Diodorus
doubts and flags: Borderline: a minor siege known only from Diodorus.
sources: Diodorus 14.35.6-7
note: Tissaphernes' attacks on the Greek cities led them to appeal to Sparta, which sent Thibron (399).

name: Asidates' tower (raid)
war: Persian-Spartan War (the Ten Thousand join Thibron)
place: Plain of the Caicus near Pergamum (Bergama), Turkey
how the result was decided: The night assault failed to take Asidates' fortified tower, and the Greeks withdrew with their booty under attack from the Persian relief forces, leaving the field to them (Xenophon, Anabasis 7.8.12-19).
Iranian force: Asidates' household defending his tower, then the relief forces: Itabelius with his own troops, Assyrian hoplites and about 80 Hyrcanian horsemen in the King's pay from Comania, about 800 peltasts, and men from Parthenium and Apollonia, including horsemen (Anabasis 7.8.15).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: the tower garrison and relief forces (above)
strength B: a picked force of a few hundred of Xenophon's men, with more horse and peltasts sent after them
borderline: a raid on a Persian noble's estate; no conventional name
doubts and flags: Borderline: a raid on a Persian noble's estate; no conventional name.
sources: Xenophon, Anabasis 7.8.8-23
note: Xenophon's account ends with Asidates captured with his family and goods in a second sortie soon afterwards, so the raid as a whole ended in the Greeks' favour; the fight at the tower is scored as above.

name: Larisa (siege)
place: Larisa 'the Egyptian' (probably Larisa Phrikonis, near Buruncuk), Turkey
how the result was decided: The defenders filled Thibron's water-shaft and burned his siege shed in sorties, and he abandoned the siege when ordered to Caria (Xenophon, Hellenica 3.1.7).
Iranian force: The townsmen of Larisa, held for the King; Xenophon (Cyropaedia 7.1.45) says their ancestors were Egyptian soldiers settled there by Cyrus.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a Persian-held town defended by its own colonists; no Persian army present
doubts and flags: Borderline: a Persian-held town defended by its own colonists; no Persian army present.
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 3.1.7; Cyropaedia 7.1.45
note: Dercylidas took Larisa without a fight later in 399.

name: Magnesia (399 BC)
place: Magnesia on the Maeander (near Tekin), Turkey
how the result was decided: Thibron took Magnesia, a town subject to Tissaphernes, at the first assault (Diodorus 14.36.2).
Iranian force: The town's defenders under Tissaphernes' rule; no Persian troops are named.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: Thibron's army: about 5,000 Peloponnesians and neodamodeis, 2,000 Asiatic Greeks and the Cyreans (Xenophon, Hellenica 3.1.4-6)
borderline: a Persian-held Greek town taken at the first assault; no Persian army is named
doubts and flags: Borderline: a Persian-held Greek town taken at the first assault; no Persian army is named.
sources: Diodorus 14.36.2-3
note: Thibron then moved the unwalled town to the hill Thorax. Xenophon's account of 399 does not mention Magnesia or Tralles.

name: Tralles (siege)
how the result was decided: Thibron could achieve nothing against the strong town and abandoned the siege (Diodorus 14.36.3).
Iranian force: The garrison of a town held for Tissaphernes; composition not given. Tissaphernes' cavalry soon forced Thibron back to Ephesus.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a siege known only from Diodorus; no fighting described
doubts and flags: Borderline: a siege known only from Diodorus; no fighting described.
sources: Diodorus 14.36.3

name: Caunus (siege)
how the result was decided: Pharax raised his blockade of Conon at Caunus when Artaphernes and Pharnabazus came up with strong forces, and sailed back to Rhodes (Diodorus 14.79.5).
Iranian force: Conon's 40 triremes of the King's fleet (raised in Cyprus, Cilicia and Phoenicia) and the land forces of Pharnabazus and Artaphernes.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: 40 triremes, then land forces of two satraps
borderline: a blockade raised without recorded fighting
doubts and flags: Borderline: a blockade raised without recorded fighting.
sources: Diodorus 14.79.4-5; Hellenica Oxyrhynchia 9 (Conon at Caunus)
note: Rhodes revolted from Sparta soon afterwards and received Conon.

name: Gordium (siege)
how the result was decided: Agesilaus attacked the well-provisioned hill fortress for several days without success and marched away (Hellenica Oxyrhynchia).
Iranian force: The garrison of Gordium under the Persian Rathines; its composition is not given (Phrygian strongholds were normally held by Persian officers with local troops).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: known only from the Hellenica Oxyrhynchia
doubts and flags: Borderline: known only from the Hellenica Oxyrhynchia.
sources: Hellenica Oxyrhynchia (Agesilaus' march through Phrygia, autumn 395)
note: On the same march Agesilaus also failed against the fortresses of Leonton Kephalai and Miletou Teichos before going on to Paphlagonia.

name: Kaue
place: Kaue, a village in Hellespontine Phrygia (site unknown, in the region of Dascylium), Turkey
how the result was decided: Herippidas' dawn attack overran Pharnabazus' camp; the satrap fled and the Greeks took the camp and its booty (Xenophon, Hellenica 4.1.20-26).
Iranian force: Pharnabazus' field camp with his household troops and outposts; Xenophon gives no numbers. Earlier that winter the satrap had attacked Greek foragers with two scythed chariots and about 400 horsemen (Hellenica 4.1.17-19).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: a picked force of hoplites and peltasts with Spithridates' cavalry
borderline: a raid on a camp; no conventional name
doubts and flags: Borderline: a raid on a camp; no conventional name.
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 4.1.20-27; Plutarch, Agesilaus 11
note: The quarrel over the booty made Spithridates and the Paphlagonians desert Agesilaus. The village is Kaue in Xenophon (translated 'Cave').

name: Sardis (395 BC)
place: plain near the Pactolus, outside Sardis (Sart), Turkey
how the result was decided: Agesilaus routed the Persian cavalry by the Pactolus and took its camp; the Spartans held the field.
commanders A: Agesilaus II (Xenocles led the ambush in the Hellenica Oxyrhynchia and Diodorus)
commanders B: Tissaphernes (in Sardis during the battle, according to Xenophon)
Iranian force: Tissaphernes' Persian cavalry, fighting without its infantry, which had not come up (Xenophon); Diodorus gives the satrap 10,000 horse and 50,000 foot shadowing Agesilaus.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: Agesilaus' army: 30 Spartiates, 2,000 neodamodeis, 6,000 allies, with the Cyreans and Asiatic Greeks (Xenophon)
strength B: 10,000 cavalry and 50,000 infantry with Tissaphernes (Diodorus 14.80.1); only the cavalry engaged
losses B: over 6,000 killed (Diodorus 14.80.4); much lower in the Hellenica Oxyrhynchia
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 3.4.20-25; Hellenica Oxyrhynchia 11-12; Diodorus 14.80; Pausanias 3.9.6; en.wikipedia Battle of Sardis (395 BC)
note: Ancient Greek Battles calls it 'Sardis'; the year is added because the Persian set has other Sardis entries (547, 498 BC). Xenophon describes a set battle by the Pactolus, the Hellenica Oxyrhynchia and Diodorus an ambush by Xenocles on the march. Tissaphernes was executed soon afterwards.

date: August 394 BC (shortly before the eclipse of 14 August)
name: Cnidus
how the result was decided: The royal fleet routed Peisander's fleet, captured 50 triremes (Diodorus) and held the sea off Cnidus.
Iranian force: The King's fleet of more than 90 triremes (Diodorus): Phoenician squadrons under Pharnabazus and the Greek squadron under Conon, largely Cypriot (Evagoras of Salamis), with Cilician ships.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: 50 triremes and about 500 men captured (Diodorus 14.83.7); Peisander killed
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 4.3.10-12; Diodorus 14.83.4-7; Isocrates, Evagoras 56; Pausanias 1.1.3; en.wikipedia Battle of Cnidus
note: Ancient Greek Battles lists Salamis (Cyprus) as Persia's ally; here 'Cypriot kingdoms' (Evagoras of Salamis supplied most of Conon's ships).

name: Cythera
how the result was decided: Conon took the town of Cythera at the first assault and sent the Cytherians to Laconia under truce (Diodorus 14.84.5).
Iranian force: The royal fleet after Cnidus, Phoenician and Cypriot Greek ships with the troops they carried, under Pharnabazus and Conon.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a capture with little recorded fighting
doubts and flags: Borderline: a capture with little recorded fighting.
sources: Diodorus 14.84.4-5; Xenophon, Hellenica 4.8.7-8
note: On the same cruise the fleet raided the Laconian coast (Pherae, Phoenicus). A garrison under the Athenian Nicophemus was left on Cythera.

name: Maeander (Thibron)
how the result was decided: Struthas' cavalry caught Thibron's disorderly raiding force, killed Thibron and most of his men and drove the rest off the field (Xenophon, Hellenica 4.8.18-19).
Iranian force: Struthas' cavalry, which Xenophon makes the only arm engaged.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: Thibron, Diphilas and most of the force killed (Xenophon)
sources: Xenophon, Hellenica 4.8.17-19; Diodorus 14.99.1-3
note: Diodorus dates it 390/389. The survivors were taken over by Diphridas.

name: Egypt (invasion, 385-383 BC)
how the result was decided: Isocrates says the King's generals suffered more harm than they did in three years of fighting in Egypt and then withdrew, leaving Hakor in possession (Panegyricus 140); no single battle is described.
Iranian force: The royal army of Abrocomas, Tithraustes and Pharnabazus; no composition survives. Royal armies of the time joined Persian and other Iranian troops with levies of the western satrapies and Greek mercenaries (said here, not in the source).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a campaign known only in outline; no named battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: a campaign known only in outline; no named battle.
sources: Isocrates, Panegyricus 140-141; en.wikipedia Battle of Pelusium (373 BC) (background)
note: The Athenian Chabrias served Hakor in these years, but his part in this war is uncertain.

name: Citium
how the result was decided: Glos' fleet defeated Evagoras' fleet off Citium, destroying or taking many ships, and Evagoras fled to Salamis (Diodorus 15.3.4-6).
Iranian force: The royal fleet of about 300 triremes under Glos, raised in Ionia, Cilicia and Phoenicia (the army assembled at Phocaea and Cyme), with marines of the royal army.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Diodorus 15.2-4; Isocrates, Evagoras 60-64; en.wikipedia Evagoras I
note: Evagoras' Salamis is 'Cypriot kingdoms' (Ancient Greek Battles: Salamis (Cyprus)). Glos was the son of Tamos, an Egyptian of Memphis in Persian service. Cimon's siege of Kition (450/449 BC) is a separate entry.

name: Salamis in Cyprus (siege, 381 BC)
how the result was decided: Salamis was still invested by land and sea when Orontes ended the war by treaty: Evagoras kept his city as a tribute-paying vassal king (Diodorus 15.8-9).
Iranian force: The royal army of Tiribazus and Orontes, put by Diodorus at 300,000 men, with Glos' fleet: Persian and other Iranian troops with levies of the western satrapies and Greek mercenaries.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Diodorus 15.4, 15.8-9; Isocrates, Evagoras 64; en.wikipedia Evagoras I
note: Egypt (Hakor) gave Evagoras some help during the siege. Wikipedia's Evagoras article keeps an older chronology (invasion 385, peace 376).

name: Pelusium (373 BC)
place: Pelusium (Tell el-Farama) and the Mendesian mouth of the Nile, Egypt
how the result was decided: In the one battle described, the Persians and Iphicrates' mercenaries routed the Egyptian force that came out against their landing at the Mendesian mouth and stormed the fort (Diodorus 15.42.4-5); the halt short of Memphis and the withdrawal when the Nile rose are strategic matters.
Iranian force: Pharnabazus' royal army, given as 200,000 'barbarians' with 20,000 Greek mercenaries under Iphicrates, 300 triremes and 200 thirty-oared ships (Diodorus 15.41.3).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses A: many killed and taken at the Mendesian fort
sources: Diodorus 15.41-43; Nepos, Iphicrates 2; en.wikipedia Battle of Pelusium (373 BC)
note: Wikipedia also calls it the Battle of Mendes. Pelusium was too strongly fortified to attack, so the fleet entered the Mendesian mouth, where the fort was stormed (a Persian success); Pharnabazus refused Iphicrates' plan to march on Memphis. Coordinates are for the Mendesian mouth (approximate). Wikipedia's 'Port Said' for Pelusium is wrong.

name: Assos (siege)
how the result was decided: Autophradates raised the siege on Agesilaus' approach and Mausolus sailed away, so the defender won (Xenophon, Agesilaus 2.26).
Iranian force: Both sides Persian: Ariobarzanes' satrapal troops and mercenaries, helped by Agesilaus' mercenaries; the besiegers were the satrapal army of Lydia under Autophradates and Mausolus' Carian forces, with 100 ships (Xenophon).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a siege raised without recorded fighting
doubts and flags: Borderline: a siege raised without recorded fighting.
sources: Xenophon, Agesilaus 2.26-27; en.wikipedia Ariobarzanes of Phrygia (as Adramyttium); en.wikipedia Revolt of the Satraps
note: Xenophon names Assos; Wikipedia and the Cambridge History of Iran place the siege of Ariobarzanes at Adramyttium. Cotys of Thrace besieged Sestos at the same time.

name: Datames against Autophradates
place: a defile in Cappadocia near the Cilician Gates, Turkey
how the result was decided: Datames caught the royal army in a narrow defile, killed many thousands for the loss of about 1,000, set up a trophy on the field, and Autophradates made a truce and withdrew to Phrygia (Nepos, Datames 8).
Iranian force: Both sides Persian. Autophradates' royal army (Nepos, Datames 8): 20,000 horse and 100,000 Cardaces infantry, 3,000 slingers, with Cappadocian, Armenian, Paphlagonian, Phrygian, Lydian, Aspendian and Pisidian, Cilician and Captianian contingents, 3,000 Greek mercenaries and many light troops; Datames' army, mainly Cappadocians, was 'not a twentieth part' as large.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
strength A: under a twentieth of the royal army (Nepos)
borderline: an unnamed campaign known only from Nepos; date uncertain
doubts and flags: Borderline: an unnamed campaign known only from Nepos; date uncertain.
sources: Nepos, Datames 7-8; en.wikipedia Revolt of the Satraps; en.wikipedia Datames
note: Nepos alone tells it; the chronology of Datames' revolt is obscure.

name: Samos (siege, 366 BC)
war: Satraps' Revolt (Athens against the King's garrison in Samos)
how the result was decided: Samos fell to Timotheus after a ten-month siege.
Iranian force: The garrison put into Samos by Cyprothemis with the backing of Tigranes, the King's hyparch (Demosthenes 15.9); probably mercenaries.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: 8,000 peltasts and 30 ships (Isocrates 15.111, for the expedition)
sources: Isocrates, Antidosis 108-111; Demosthenes 15.9; Nepos, Timotheus 1; en.wikipedia Timotheus (general)
note: Timotheus was sent to aid Ariobarzanes but, finding him in open revolt, attacked Samos instead. Athens then settled cleruchs on Samos.

name: Bosporus (Leucon v Heracleots)
why it counts: Scythians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Polyaenus 6.9.3–4
note: The Heracleots landed from a large fleet and raided. Leucon posted Scythian archers behind his hoplites to cut down anyone who fled, then defeated the invaders. Date and site are uncertain.

name: Datames against Artabazus
how the result was decided: Datames pursued his father-in-law's cavalry as it deserted to Artabazus and cut it down beside the royal army, which was defeated and withdrew (Diodorus 15.91.2-7).
Iranian force: Both sides Persian: Datames' Cappadocian cavalry and mercenary infantry against the royal army of Artabazus; no breakdown is given.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: an unnamed battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: an unnamed battle.
sources: Diodorus 15.91.2-7; Nepos, Datames 6; en.wikipedia Datames; en.wikipedia Artabazus II
note: Nepos (Datames 6) tells the same stratagem against Mithrobarzanes' desertion, but in a war against the Pisidians; the two may be versions of one event.

name: Chares' victory over the satraps
how the result was decided: Chares' mercenary army and Artabazus defeated the royal satraps' army (Diodorus 16.22.1).
Iranian force: Both sides Persian: Artabazus' own small force, with Chares' Athenian mercenary army doing most of the fighting, against the royal satraps' army of 70,000 (Diodorus).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
strength A: Artabazus' few troops and Chares' army
borderline: an unnamed battle; Athens fought as Artabazus' paid ally
doubts and flags: Borderline: an unnamed battle; Athens fought as Artabazus' paid ally.
sources: Diodorus 16.22.1-2; Demosthenes 4.24 and scholia; en.wikipedia Chares of Athens; en.wikipedia Artabazus II
note: Artaxerxes III's protest and threat to aid Athens' rebel allies made Athens recall Chares and end the Social War.

name: Pammenes' victories over the satraps
how the result was decided: Pammenes' Thebans and Artabazus defeated the satraps in two great battles (Diodorus 16.34.1-2).
Iranian force: Both sides Persian: Artabazus' forces with 5,000 Theban troops under Pammenes, against the royal satraps' armies.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: two unnamed battles combined in one entry
doubts and flags: Borderline: two unnamed battles combined in one entry.
sources: Diodorus 16.34.1-2; en.wikipedia Artabazus II
note: Artabazus later fell out with Pammenes; the revolt collapsed and Artabazus fled to Philip II with Memnon.

name: Halicarnassus (c. 352 BC)
war: Wars of the Hecatomnids (Caria against Rhodes)
how the result was decided: In Vitruvius' story Artemisia's men seized the Rhodian ships in the harbour, killed the Rhodians who had landed, and then took Rhodes with the captured fleet.
Iranian force: The fleet and troops of the Hecatomnid satrapy of Caria under Artemisia, using Mausolus' secret harbour.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the Rhodian landing party killed, the fleet captured (Vitruvius)
borderline: a Carian satrap's own war; counted as Persian because the Hecatomnids were the King's satraps
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from Vitruvius (2. Borderline: a Carian satrap's own war; counted as Persian because the Hecatomnids were the King's satraps.
sources: Vitruvius 2.8.14-15; Demosthenes 15; en.wikipedia Artemisia II of Caria
note: The Rhodian oligarchs were backed by Caria; Demosthenes' speech On the Liberty of the Rhodians (351) shows Rhodes under Carian control.

name: Egypt (invasion, 351 BC)
how the result was decided: The Egyptians, led by their Greek generals Diophantus and Lamius, repulsed the royal invasion and the King withdrew without reconquering Egypt (Diodorus 16.40.3, 16.48.2; Isocrates, Philippus 101).
commanders A: Nectanebo II; Diophantus of Athens and Lamius of Sparta
Iranian force: Artaxerxes III's royal army; no composition survives. It will have been like the army of 343: Persian and other Iranian troops, imperial levies and Greek mercenaries (said here, not in the sources).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a campaign; no named battle known
doubts and flags: Borderline: a campaign; no named battle known.
sources: Diodorus 16.40.3-6, 16.44.1, 16.48.1-2; Isocrates, Philippus 101; en.wikipedia Second Achaemenid conquest of Egypt
note: The failure set off the revolts of Phoenicia (Sidon) and Cyprus.

date: c. 346 BC (date uncertain; Diodorus narrates the revolt under 351/350)
name: Mentor's victory over the satraps
how the result was decided: Tennes and Mentor's 4,000 Greek mercenaries defeated the two satraps and drove them out of Phoenicia (Diodorus 16.42.1-2).
commanders A: Tennes of Sidon; Mentor of Rhodes
commanders B: Belesys (satrap of Syria), Mazaeus (satrap of Cilicia)
Iranian force: The satrapal armies of Syria (Belesys) and Cilicia (Mazaeus); no figures. Such armies combined Persian cavalry and garrison troops with Syrian, Cilician and mercenary infantry (said here, not in the source).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: the Sidonians with 4,000 Greek mercenaries sent by Nectanebo II (Diodorus)
borderline: an unnamed battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: an unnamed battle.
sources: Diodorus 16.41-42; en.wikipedia Tennes; en.wikipedia Mentor of Rhodes
note: The mercenaries were lent by Nectanebo II of Egypt, hence Egypt as ally.

name: Sidon (siege)
how the result was decided: Sidon fell to Artaxerxes III when Tennes and Mentor betrayed it; the Sidonians burned the city with themselves inside (Diodorus 16.45).
commanders A: Artaxerxes III; Mentor of Rhodes (after changing sides)
Iranian force: Artaxerxes III's royal army (Diodorus: 300,000 foot, 30,000 horse, 300 triremes, 500 transports) with about 10,000 Greek mercenaries (1,000 Thebans under Lacrates, 3,000 Argives under Nicostratus, 6,000 Asiatic Greeks), joined by Mentor's 4,000.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: over 40,000 dead in the fire (Diodorus 16.45); 100 leading citizens and 500 suppliants killed
borderline: taken by betrayal, with little fighting at the walls
doubts and flags: Borderline: taken by betrayal, with little fighting at the walls.
sources: Diodorus 16.41-45; en.wikipedia Tennes
note: The Sidonians had burned their own ships to prevent flight. Tennes was executed afterwards.

name: Salamis in Cyprus (siege, 344 BC)
how the result was decided: Besieged by land and sea, Pnytagoras surrendered Salamis by submitting to the King and was left as his vassal (Diodorus 16.46.1-3).
commanders A: Evagoras II and Phocion of Athens (for Idrieus, satrap of Caria)
Iranian force: The force sent by Idrieus, satrap of Caria, on the King's orders: 40 triremes and 8,000 mercenaries under Evagoras II and Phocion (Diodorus 16.42.7).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Diodorus 16.42.3-9, 16.46.1-3; Plutarch, Phocion
note: The other Cypriot kingdoms were reduced in the same campaign; Evagoras II, who hoped to recover Salamis, was set aside. Pnytagoras' submission is treated as a surrender (the place fell); if read as a negotiated peace the result would be a draw.

name: Pelusium (343 BC)
how the result was decided: Pelusium surrendered to Lacrates on terms after Nicostratus' division crossed the Nile and destroyed Cleinius' counterattack and Nectanebo fell back on Memphis (Diodorus 16.48-49).
commanders A: Artaxerxes III; Lacrates of Thebes and Rhosaces; Nicostratus of Argos and Aristazanes; Mentor of Rhodes and Bagoas
commanders B: Nectanebo II; Philophron (garrison of Pelusium); Cleinius of Cos (killed)
Iranian force: Artaxerxes III's royal army (Diodorus: 300,000 foot, 30,000 horse) with about 14,000 Greeks in three divisions, each under a Greek and a Persian commander: Lacrates' Thebans with Rhosaces' cavalry and Asiatic infantry, Nicostratus' Argives with Aristazanes and 80 triremes, Mentor's mercenaries with Bagoas.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: about 100,000: 20,000 Greek mercenaries, 20,000 Libyans, 60,000 Egyptians (Diodorus 16.47); 5,000 Greeks in Pelusium
losses A: part of the army lost earlier in the Barathra marshes
losses B: Cleinius and over 5,000 of his men killed (Diodorus)
sources: Diodorus 16.46.4-16.51; en.wikipedia Battle of Pelusium (343 BC) (archived); en.wikipedia Second Achaemenid conquest of Egypt
note: Wikipedia has merged the battle article into 'Second Achaemenid conquest of Egypt', which dates the conquest 340/339. Bubastis and the other Delta towns then surrendered, and Nectanebo fled south.

name: Perinthus (siege)
how the result was decided: Philip failed to take Perinthus and broke off the siege to attack Byzantium (Diodorus 16.74-77).
commanders A: Apollodorus (commander of the force sent by Arsites); the Perinthians
Iranian force: Mercenaries, money, grain and missiles sent by the coastal satraps on Artaxerxes III's orders (Diodorus 16.75.1-2); Pausanias (1.29.10) names Apollodorus as commander of the mercenaries sent by Arsites, satrap of Hellespontine Phrygia.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: unknown (larger than the defenders, with siege engines)
borderline: the size of the Persian force is unknown; it may have been only a contingent
doubts and flags: Borderline: the size of the Persian force is unknown; it may have been only a contingent.
sources: Diodorus 16.74-77; Pausanias 1.29.10; Arrian 2.14.5; en.wikipedia Siege of Perinthus
note: Constantinople also sent troops and artillery. 'Greek cities' = Perinthus and Constantinople.

name: Ateas (Scythians)
place: Dobruja, south of the Danube delta
why it counts: Scythians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Justin 9.2; Frontin. Str. 2.8.14; Strabo 7.3.18; Lucian Macr. 10
note: About 20,000 women and children reportedly captured. Site unknown.

name: Magnesia (336 BC)
war: Macedonian advance force in Asia Minor (Parmenion and Attalus)
place: near Magnesia (probably on the Maeander), Turkey
how the result was decided: Memnon surprised the Macedonians at their evening meal, killed or captured many and drove the survivors into Magnesia (Polyaenus 5.44.4).
Iranian force: Memnon's mercenary army of about 4,000 men (Polyaenus 5.44.4), Greek mercenaries in Persian pay.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Polyaenus 5.44.4; Diodorus 17.7.8-10 (the campaign); en.wikipedia Memnon of Rhodes; Livius, Memnon of Rhodes
note: Ancient Greek Battles calls it 'Magnesia'; the year is added because of the separate entry for Thibron's capture of Magnesia (399 BC). Polyaenus places it near Magnesia held by Parmenion and Attalus; Memnon's later actions (Cyzicus, Pitane, the Troad) belong to 335.

date: 335 BC (Diodorus' year; some date it to 336)
name: Cyzicus (335)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Macedonian advance force in Asia Minor)
how the result was decided: Memnon's surprise attack narrowly failed to take the city, and he withdrew after ravaging its territory (Diodorus 17.7.3).
Iranian force: Memnon's 5,000 Greek mercenaries (Diodorus 17.7.3).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a failed surprise attack on a city; the fighting is barely described
doubts and flags: Borderline: a failed surprise attack on a city; the fighting is barely described.
sources: Diodorus 17.7.3; livius.org Memnon of Rhodes
note: Cyzicus was on the Macedonian side. Diodorus narrates the operations of Memnon and Parmenion under 335; Livius dates them to 336.

date: 335 BC (Diodorus' year; some date it to 336)
name: Pitane (siege)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Macedonian advance force in Asia Minor)
how the result was decided: Parmenion raised the siege when Memnon's relief army appeared (Diodorus 17.7.10).
Iranian force: Memnon's relief army, not described; earlier that year he led 5,000 Greek mercenaries (Diodorus 17.7.3), and the Persian forces of the north-west were then mercenaries with the satrapal cavalry of Hellespontine Phrygia.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a siege raised when a relief army approached; no fighting is recorded
doubts and flags: Borderline: a siege raised when a relief army approached; no fighting is recorded.
sources: Diodorus 17.7.9-10; livius.org Memnon of Rhodes
note: Just before, Parmenion stormed Grynium and enslaved its people (Diodorus 17.7.9); no Persian force is recorded there, so it is not listed.

date: 335 BC (Diodorus' year; some date it to 336)
name: Troad
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Macedonian advance force in Asia Minor)
how the result was decided: Calas, far outnumbered, was beaten and withdrew to Rhoeteum (Diodorus 17.7.10).
Iranian force: A Persian army many times larger than Calas' force (Diodorus), not described; the western satraps then fielded Persian cavalry with Greek mercenaries and local levies.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Diodorus 17.7.10; livius.org Memnon of Rhodes
note: Name, year and site as in Ancient Greek Battles. Diodorus does not name the Persian commander; Memnon is often assumed.

name: Halicarnassus (siege)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
how the result was decided: After their sorties were beaten back, Memnon and Orontobates set fire to the town and withdrew to the citadels and Cos, and the town fell.
commanders B: Memnon of Rhodes, Orontobates, Ephialtes (killed), Thrasybulus
Iranian force: Orontobates' Persian and Carian troops and Greek mercenaries (among them Athenian exiles under Ephialtes and Thrasybulus), supported by the Persian fleet (Arrian 1.20-23; Diodorus 17.24-27).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses A: about 40 killed in the last sortie (Arrian 1.22.7); 16 killed and 300 wounded in an earlier fight
losses B: about 1,000 killed in the last sortie (Arrian 1.22.7); 170 in an earlier fight
sources: Arrian 1.20-23; Diodorus 17.23-27; en.wikipedia Siege of Halicarnassus
note: Ancient Greek Battles lists this as 'Halicarnassus (sortie)', autumn 334, because it counts a siege only through a battle fought in it (here Ephialtes' sortie from the Tripylon gate); this entry covers the whole siege, the sorties included, and the result is the same. The citadels Salmakis and Zephyrion held out into 333 (see 'Caria').

name: Miletus (siege, 334)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
how the result was decided: Miletus was stormed after Nicanor's fleet at Lade cut it off from the Persian fleet.
Iranian force: Hegesistratus' garrison of Greek mercenaries with the Milesians; the Persian fleet of 400 ships, mainly Phoenician and Cypriot, lay off Mycale but could not intervene (Arrian 1.18-19).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: garrison unknown (Wikipedia: 300 Milesians); 400 ships offshore, not engaged
losses B: heavy; 300 mercenaries who fled to an islet were taken into Alexander's service (Arrian 1.19.6)
sources: Arrian 1.18-19; Diodorus 17.22; en.wikipedia Siege of Miletus
note: A raid by five Persian ships on the Macedonian anchorage was beaten off (Arrian 1.19.9-11); it is counted here as part of the siege. Not in Ancient Greek Battles, which counts sieges only through a battle fought in them.

name: Granicus
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
how the result was decided: The Persian cavalry broke and fled and the Greek mercenaries were surrounded and cut down; the Macedonians held the field.
commanders B: Arsites, Spithridates (killed), Arsames, Rheomithres, Memnon of Rhodes, Omares (killed), Mithrobuzanes (killed), Mithridates (killed)
Iranian force: The cavalry of the western satraps along the river (Persian horse, 1,000 Medes, 2,000 Bactrians, Hyrcanians under Spithridates, Paphlagonians under Arsites) with Greek mercenary infantry under Omares behind; Arrian gives 20,000 horse and nearly 20,000 mercenary foot.
languages: Persian; Greek; Median; East Iranian; other Iranian; Anatolian
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: about 18,000 engaged (modern estimate); the whole expedition about 32,000 foot and 5,100 horse (Diodorus 17.17)
strength B: 20,000 horse and nearly 20,000 mercenary foot (Arrian); 10,000 horse and 100,000 foot (Diodorus); modern estimate about 14,000-15,000 (Devine)
losses B: about 1,000 cavalry killed, most of the mercenaries killed and 2,000 captured (Arrian 1.16.2); Diodorus: over 10,000 foot and 2,000 horse killed, over 20,000 captured
sources: Arrian 1.13-16; Diodorus 17.18-21; Plutarch, Alexander 16; en.wikipedia Battle of the Granicus
note: Macedon's allies were the Thessalian cavalry and the Hellenic League contingents (Ancient Greek Battles lists 'Thessaly'). Arsites killed himself after the battle.

name: Caria
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
how the result was decided: Ptolemy and Asander defeated Orontobates in battle, killing about 700 foot and 50 horse (Arrian 2.5.7).
Iranian force: Orontobates' satrapal army of Caria, not described; it held the citadels of Halicarnassus and would have been Persian, Carian and Greek mercenary troops.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: about 700 foot and 50 horse killed, at least 1,000 captured (Arrian 2.5.7)
sources: Arrian 2.5.7
note: Afterwards the Macedonians took Myndus, Caunus, Thera, Callipolis, Cos and Triopium (Arrian 2.5.7). Name, year and site as in Ancient Greek Battles.

name: Memphis (333)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (after Issus)
how the result was decided: Amyntas first beat the garrison before Memphis, but Mazaces' sally caught his men scattered for plunder and killed him and most of them (Curtius 4.1.30-33; Diodorus 17.48.3-5).
Iranian force: The Persian garrison of Memphis under the satrap Mazaces; not described, but the Achaemenid garrisons of Egypt were Persian troops with Aramaean, Jewish and other soldiers.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: about 4,000 mercenaries (Diodorus 17.48.2; Arrian 2.13.2 has 8,000 escape from Issus with Amyntas and others) and Egyptian supporters
losses B: Amyntas and most of his men killed
borderline: no conventional name; it is the fight of Amyntas' mercenaries with the Persian garrison before Memphis
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name; it is the fight of Amyntas' mercenaries with the Persian garrison before Memphis.
sources: Curtius 4.1.27-33; Diodorus 17.48.2-5; Arrian 2.13.2-3; en.wikipedia Amyntas (son of Antiochus)
note: Amyntas, a Macedonian exile in Persian service, fled from Issus with Greek mercenaries via Tripolis and Cyprus to Pelusium, claimed to act for Darius, and tried to take Egypt for himself; Arrian says only that he was killed by the Egyptians. New entity: 'Greek mercenaries'.

date: spring-summer 333 BC (Memnon died during the siege)
name: Mytilene (siege, 333)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Memnon's Aegean campaign)
how the result was decided: Mytilene, walled off by land and blockaded by sea, capitulated to Pharnabazus and Autophradates and took a Persian garrison (Arrian 2.1).
commanders A: Memnon of Rhodes (died during the siege), Pharnabazus, Autophradates
commanders B: unknown (the Mytileneans and Alexander's mercenary garrison)
Iranian force: The Persian fleet (about 300 ships, mainly Phoenician and Cypriot: Diodorus 17.29.2) and Memnon's Greek mercenaries, who shut the city in with a double stockade and five camps (Arrian 2.1.1-2).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Arrian 2.1; Diodorus 17.29; livius.org Memnon of Rhodes
note: Mytilene was allied to Alexander. The terms expelled his mercenaries and restored the exiles; Lycomedes of Rhodes commanded the Persian garrison and Diogenes became tyrant (Arrian 2.1.4-5). Before this Memnon took Chios by betrayal and most of Lesbos without a battle.

name: Siphnos
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Memnon's Aegean campaign)
how the result was decided: Proteas surprised Datames' squadron at dawn and captured eight of its ten ships.
Iranian force: Datames' squadron of 10 ships detached from the Persian fleet of Pharnabazus and Autophradates (Arrian 2.2.4-5); its crews are not described.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Arrian 2.2.4-5
note: Name, year and site as in Ancient Greek Battles.

name: Issus
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
place: river Pinarus (Payas or Deli Çay) near Issus, Turkey
how the result was decided: Darius fled and his army broke and was pursued off the field; the Macedonians took his camp and family.
commanders B: Darius III, Nabarzanes, Arsames (killed), Rheomithres (killed), Atizyes (killed), Sabaces (killed), Thymondas
Iranian force: Darius' royal army: Greek mercenary hoplites (Arrian 30,000; modern estimates about 10,000-12,000), the Cardaces (Persian infantry), the Persian guard (Immortals, the kinsmen cavalry), the Persian, Median and Hyrcanian heavy cavalry under Nabarzanes on the seaward wing, and light-armed levies (Arrian 2.8; Curtius 3.9).
languages: Persian; Greek; Median; other Iranian; Anatolian
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: 600,000 (Arrian, Plutarch), 400,000 (Diodorus, Justin), 250,000 (Curtius); modern estimates mostly under 100,000
losses A: 182 killed, 504 wounded, 302 missing (Curtius 3.11.27); 300 foot and 150 horse killed (Diodorus 17.36.6)
losses B: 100,000 foot and 10,000 horse killed (Arrian 2.11.8; Diodorus); modern estimates far lower (Wikipedia: 20,000-40,000)
sources: Arrian 2.6-11; Curtius 3.8-11; Diodorus 17.32-36; Plutarch, Alexander 20; en.wikipedia Battle of Issus
note: The day (5 November) is a modern calculation and is not in the ancient sources. Macedon's allies were the Thessalian cavalry and Hellenic League troops.

date: autumn 332 BC (about two months; Wikipedia: October)
name: Gaza (siege, 332)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
how the result was decided: Gaza was stormed at the fourth assault and its defenders were killed.
Iranian force: Batis' garrison of Persian troops and the Arab mercenaries he had hired (Arrian 2.25.4; Curtius 4.6.7-30).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: about 10,000 Persians and Arabs killed (Curtius 4.6.30); the men killed and the women and children enslaved (Arrian 2.27.7)
sources: Arrian 2.25-27; Curtius 4.6.7-30; Diodorus 17.48.7; en.wikipedia Siege of Gaza (332 BC)
note: Ancient Greek Battles lists this as 'Gaza (sortie)', autumn 332 (the defenders' sally against the siege works, in which Alexander was wounded: Arrian 2.26.4-27.2); this entry covers the whole siege, the sortie included, with the same result. Curtius (4.6.29) says Batis was dragged behind a chariot.

name: Hellespont
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (after Issus)
how the result was decided: The Macedonian fleet defeated Aristomenes, sent by Darius to recover the Hellespont coast, and took or sank his ships (Curtius 4.1.36).
commanders A: the Macedonian fleet summoned from Greece (commanders not named)
Iranian force: Aristomenes' squadron, not described; the Persian fleet was then crewed mainly by Phoenicians, Cypriots and Greeks.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Curtius 4.1.36
note: Known only from Curtius' short notice. The Macedonian Hellespont fleet raised in 333 was under Amphoterus and Hegelochus. Name, year and site as in Ancient Greek Battles.

name: Lydia
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (after Issus)
place: Lydia and neighbouring regions (three battles, sites unknown), Turkey
how the result was decided: Antigonus defeated the Persian generals in three battles in different places (Curtius 4.1.35).
commanders B: Persian generals who escaped from Issus (not named)
Iranian force: The commanders and troops who escaped from Issus, reinforced with Cappadocian and Paphlagonian recruits (Curtius 4.1.34).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
