note: One entry for three battles, as in Ancient Greek Battles. Heckel identifies the three as Antigonus in Lycaonia, Calas in Paphlagonia and Balacrus at Miletus (Curtius 4.5.13), so this entry may overlap 'Miletus (332)'.

name: Miletus (332)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (after Issus)
how the result was decided: Balacrus defeated Hydarnes, Darius' general, and recovered Miletus (Curtius 4.5.13).
Iranian force: Hydarnes' force, not described; the Persian counter-offensive of 332 used Issus survivors, Anatolian levies and mercenaries.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Curtius 4.5.13
note: Ancient Greek Battles calls this 'Miletus'; the year is added here because of 'Miletus (siege, 334)'. See also 'Lydia'.

name: Mytilene (siege, 332)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (after Issus)
how the result was decided: Hegelochus besieged Mytilene and Chares surrendered it on terms and left with his men (Arrian 3.2.6).
Iranian force: About 2,000 troops 'of the Persians' (Arrian 3.2.6) under the Athenian Chares, probably mostly mercenaries in Persian pay.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a blockade ended by capitulation; no assault is recorded
doubts and flags: Borderline: a blockade ended by capitulation; no assault is recorded.
sources: Arrian 3.2.3-7; Curtius 4.5.14-22
note: In the same campaign Hegelochus recovered Tenedos, Chios (where the citizens let him in and Pharnabazus was captured) and Cos without battles; those captures are not listed.

name: Scythia
place: Scythia, north-west of the Black Sea (site unknown)
why it counts: Scythians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
note: Zopyrion, Alexander's governor in Thrace ('Pontus' in Justin), invaded Scythia with 30,000 men and besieged Olbia (Macrobius). He then perished with his whole army. Justin dates it c. 331; Curtius puts the news in 325. No details of the battle survive.

date: 1 October 331 BC (fixed by the Babylonian astronomical diaries)
name: Gaugamela
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
place: Gaugamela (probably Tel Gomel, near Erbil), Iraq
how the result was decided: Darius fled, the Persian centre and left broke and Mazaeus' wing withdrew; the Macedonians held the field and pursued to Arbela.
Iranian force: The levy of the whole empire: Persian guards (Immortals, kinsmen) and about 2,000 Greek mercenaries in the centre; Bactrian, Sogdian, Dahae, Saka, Arachosian, Persian, Susian and Cadusian horse under Bessus on the left; Median, Parthian, Hyrcanian, Tapurian, Syrian, Mesopotamian, Armenian, Cappadocian and Albanian horse under Mazaeus on the right; Indians, Mardian archers, scythed chariots and 15 elephants (Arrian 3.8, 3.11).
languages: Persian; East Iranian; Median; Parthian; other Iranian; Aramaic; Armenian; Indian; Greek; other Caucasian; Anatolian
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: 1,000,000 foot and 40,000 horse (Arrian 3.8.6); 800,000 foot and 200,000 horse (Diodorus 17.53.3); 200,000 foot and 45,000 horse (Curtius); modern estimates about 50,000-120,000
sources: Arrian 3.8-15; Curtius 4.12-16; Diodorus 17.53-61; Plutarch, Alexander 31-33; en.wikipedia Battle of Gaugamela
note: Arrian (3.8.3) says the Saka came not as Bessus' subjects but as allies of Darius. Macedon's allies were the Thessalian cavalry and Hellenic League troops.

name: Uxian Defile
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
place: the Uxian pass on the road from Susa to Persis (site disputed), Iran
how the result was decided: Alexander turned the pass, and the Uxians, caught between his column and Craterus on the heights, were routed and sued for terms (Arrian 3.17).
Iranian force: The Uxian hillmen (Arrian) or Madates' garrison holding the pass and his town for Darius (Curtius 5.3); numbers not given.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: Persian role depends on the source: Arrian's Uxians were independent hillmen who took tolls even from the Persian kings, while Curtius makes it a stand by Darius' kinsman Madates, governor of the Uxians
doubts and flags: Borderline: Persian role depends on the source: Arrian's Uxians were independent hillmen who took tolls even from the Persian kings, while Curtius makes it a stand by Darius' kinsman Madates, governor of the Uxians.
sources: Arrian 3.17; Curtius 5.3.1-16; Diodorus 17.67; en.wikipedia Battle of the Uxian Defile
note: Curtius has Madates besieged in his town and pardoned at Sisygambis' plea. The tribute imposed was 100 horses, 500 cattle and 30,000 sheep a year (Arrian 3.17.6). Wikipedia's coordinates are those of Susa; the pass was in the Zagros east of Susa. New entity: 'Uxians'.

name: Artacoana (siege)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Bessus' war)
how the result was decided: Alexander took the rebels' wooded rock by setting fire to it, and those who had joined the revolt were killed or enslaved (Curtius 6.6.23-34; Diodorus 17.78.1-2).
Iranian force: Arian rebels who had risen for Satibarzanes when he went over to Bessus (Curtius: 13,000 armed men on the rock).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a minor siege known from Curtius and Diodorus; Arrian mentions only the pursuit and punishment of the rebels
doubts and flags: Borderline: a minor siege known from Curtius and Diodorus; Arrian mentions only the pursuit and punishment of the rebels.
sources: Curtius 6.6.20-34; Diodorus 17.78.1-2; Arrian 3.25.5-7
note: Satibarzanes, satrap of Aria, submitted to Alexander and then revolted for Bessus, who had taken the title Artaxerxes V; hence 'Achaemenid Empire'.

date: January 330 BC (some date it to December 331)
name: Persian Gate
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (conquest of the Achaemenid Empire)
place: the Persian Gates pass (north of Yasuj), Iran
how the result was decided: Alexander's flanking column came down behind the Persian wall while Craterus attacked from the front, and the defenders were destroyed or scattered.
commanders A: Alexander the Great, Craterus, Philotas, Ptolemy
Iranian force: Ariobarzanes' army of Persis behind a wall across the pass: 40,000 foot and 700 horse (Arrian 3.18.2), 25,000 foot (Curtius; Diodorus, with 300 horse); modern estimates are far lower.
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: Alexander's division (Wikipedia: about 17,000); Parmenion took the rest by the wagon road
strength B: 40,000 foot and 700 horse (Arrian); 25,000 foot and 300 horse (Diodorus 17.68.1); modern estimates as low as 700-2,000 (Wikipedia)
losses A: unknown; heavy in the first frontal attack
sources: Arrian 3.18; Curtius 5.3.17-5.4.34; Diodorus 17.68; en.wikipedia Battle of the Persian Gate
note: Arrian says Ariobarzanes escaped with a few horsemen; Curtius (5.4.33-34) that he broke out, was refused entry at Persepolis and died fighting. The modern Iranian story of his sister Youtab is not in the ancient sources.

name: Aria
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Bessus' war)
how the result was decided: Satibarzanes was killed in single combat by Erigyius and his army fled (Arrian 3.28.3; Curtius 7.4.33-40).
Iranian force: Satibarzanes' Arian rebels with 2,000 horsemen sent by Bessus (Arrian 3.28.2).
why it counts: Achaemenid Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: 6,000 Greek foot and 600 horse, with Phrataphernes' troops (Arrian 3.28.2)
strength B: 2,000 horse from Bessus and the Arian rebels
note: Bessus (Artaxerxes V) was still free, so this counts as 'Achaemenid Empire'. The Persian nobles Artabazus and Phrataphernes fought on Alexander's side. Name, year and site as in Ancient Greek Battles.

name: Cyropolis (siege)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
how the result was decided: The Macedonians got in by a dry watercourse and opened the gates, and the citadel surrendered for lack of water (Arrian 4.3.1-4).
Iranian force: About 15,000 Sogdian fighters, the best of the region (Arrian 4.3.4).
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
sources: Arrian 4.2-3; Curtius 7.6.16-23; en.wikipedia Siege of Cyropolis
note: Ptolemy said the town surrendered, Aristobulus that it was stormed (Arrian 4.3.5). Curtius' siege of the city of the Memaceni is probably the same. Wikipedia's coordinates (40.28, 69.63) are those of Khujand (Alexandria Eschate).

name: Gaza (Sogdiana)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
place: Gaza (perhaps Nau, south-west of Khujand), Tajikistan
how the result was decided: Alexander stormed the town with ladders on the first day; the men were killed and the women and children enslaved (Arrian 4.2.3-4).
Iranian force: Sogdian townsmen and the rebels of the region gathered in the seven Jaxartes towns (Arrian 4.2.1-2).
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the first of seven towns taken in a few days; a minor assault
doubts and flags: Borderline: the first of seven towns taken in a few days; a minor assault.
sources: Arrian 4.2.2-4
note: Arrian says five of the seven towns fell within two days; Cyropolis is entered separately. Site identification uncertain.

name: Jaxartes (329 BC)
place: north bank of the Jaxartes (Syr Darya) opposite Alexandria Eschate (Khujand), Tajikistan/Uzbekistan
how the result was decided: Alexander crossed the river under a catapult barrage, routed the Scythian horse (Saka) and pursued them into the steppe (Arrian 4.4).
commanders B: no commander named (a Saka king and his brother Carmanes are mentioned in Curtius)
sources: Arrian, Anabasis 4.2.1-4.4.9; Curtius 7.6.1-7.9.17; Plutarch, Alexander 45; Bosworth, Conquest and Empire (1988); Ancient Greek Battles ('Jaxartes')
note: The Saka (the 'Asiatic Scythians' of Arrian) had helped the Sogdian rebels. Alexander fell ill from the river water; the fight was a quick cavalry victory that kept the frontier on the Jaxartes.

name: Maracanda (siege)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
how the result was decided: Spitamenes twice gave up the blockade of the citadel, first when Pharnuches' relief column approached and again when Alexander came (Arrian 4.5.2-3, 4.6.3-4).
commanders A: the garrison of the citadel (commander not named)
Iranian force: Spitamenes' Sogdian rebels, joined in the second blockade by Scythian (Saka) horsemen (Arrian 4.5-6).
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
note: In the first blockade the garrison made a sortie and then withdrew into the citadel (Arrian 4.5.2).

name: Polytimetus
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
how the result was decided: Spitamenes' horse archers surrounded the Macedonian column at a river crossing and destroyed it; only about 300 foot and 40 horse escaped (Arrian 4.5.4-4.6.2).
Iranian force: Spitamenes' Sogdians with about 600 Scythian horse archers (Arrian 4.5.4), probably Massagetae or Dahae.
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
strength B: about 2,360: 60 Companions, 800 mercenary horse, 1,500 mercenary foot (Arrian 4.3.7); Curtius: 3,000 foot and 800 horse
sources: Arrian 4.3.7, 4.5-6; Curtius 7.6.24, 7.7.30-39; en.wikipedia Battle of the Polytimetus
note: Arrian (4.6.1-2) also gives Aristobulus' version, an ambush in a wooded park. Ancient Greek Battles lists the winners as 'Sogdians' and 'Saka'.

name: Gabai
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
place: near Gabai (Bagae), on the border of Sogdiana and the Massagetae (site unknown), Uzbekistan
how the result was decided: Coenus routed Spitamenes' horsemen, killing over 800, and the Sogdian and Bactrian rebels deserted him (Arrian 4.17.4-7).
Iranian force: About 3,000 Massagetae horsemen with Spitamenes' Sogdian and Bactrian rebels (Arrian 4.17.4-5).
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
strength B: about 3,000 Massagetae horse with Sogdians and Bactrians
sources: Arrian 4.17.4-7; en.wikipedia Wars of Alexander the Great
note: Afterwards the Massagetae killed Spitamenes and sent his head to Alexander (Arrian 4.17.7); Curtius (8.3) says his wife killed him. Name, year and site as in Ancient Greek Battles.

name: Xenippa
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
place: Xenippa (site unknown, perhaps the Baysun area), Uzbekistan
how the result was decided: After a long and even fight the Bactrian exiles broke, losing 700 killed and 300 captured (Curtius 8.2.16-17).
Iranian force: About 2,500 Bactrian exiles, all horsemen, driven out of Xenippa (Curtius 8.2.15).
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
borderline: known only from Curtius
doubts and flags: Borderline: known only from Curtius.
sources: Curtius 8.2.14-18
note: Curtius says the exiles were pardoned. The site is unknown; it lay on the Bactrian-Sogdian border, possibly near Baysun.

name: Zariaspa
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
place: edge of the desert near Zariaspa (Bactra, Balkh), Afghanistan
how the result was decided: Craterus caught the raiders at the edge of the desert and beat them; about 150 were killed and the rest escaped into the desert (Arrian 4.17.1).
Iranian force: Spitamenes' raiders: the Massagetae with over 1,000 other horsemen (Arrian 4.17.1); Curtius calls them Dahae.
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
strength B: the Massagetae and over 1,000 other horse
sources: Arrian 4.17.1; Curtius 8.1.6
note: Ancient Greek Battles has this as 'Zariaspa' (Macedon against the Saka, with Sogdian allies). It counts here as Spitamenes' force because the raiders were his band; Spitamenes himself is not named in the fight, which would make the Massagetae the principals.

name: Zariaspa (ambush)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
how the result was decided: Spitamenes' horsemen ambushed the sortie from Zariaspa as it returned with the recovered booty, killing most of it and taking Peithon (Arrian 4.16.6-7).
commanders B: Peithon son of Sosicles (captured), Aristonicus the harpist (killed)
Iranian force: Spitamenes and the Sogdian exiles with about 600 Massagetae horsemen (Arrian 4.16.4).
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
strength A: about 600 Massagetae horse with the Sogdian exiles
strength B: about 80 mercenary horse with some royal pages and Companions (Arrian 4.16.6)
borderline: no conventional name; Arrian's account of the sortie from Zariaspa
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name; Arrian's account of the sortie from Zariaspa.
sources: Arrian 4.16.4-7; Curtius 8.1.3-5
note: Just before, Spitamenes stormed a Bactrian fort and captured its commander (Arrian 4.16.4). Curtius (8.1.3-5) tells of Attinas, killed with his 300 horsemen in a Massagetae ambush, probably the same event.

name: Paraetacene (327)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
place: Paraetacene (the Hissar region, site unknown), Tajikistan
how the result was decided: Craterus won a hard-fought battle in which Catanes fell and Austanes was captured (Arrian 4.22.2).
Iranian force: The rebels of Paraetacene, horse and foot, under the local lords Catanes and Austanes (Arrian 4.22.1-2).
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
sources: Arrian 4.22.1-2; Curtius 8.5.2
note: The last fight of the Sogdian and Bactrian revolt; the year is added to the name to keep it apart from the Diadochi battle of Paraitacene (317).

name: Rock of Chorienes (siege)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
place: Rock of Chorienes (probably Kuh-e Nur on the Vakhsh), Tajikistan
how the result was decided: Chorienes surrendered after the Macedonians filled the ravine and brought the rock within bowshot (Arrian 4.21; Curtius 8.2.19-33).
Iranian force: Chorienes' Sogdian followers in Paraetacene (numbers not given).
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
losses B: unknown (Curtius: many killed by slings and arrows)
sources: Arrian 4.21; Curtius 8.2.19-33; iranicaonline.org Chorienes
note: Encyclopaedia Iranica takes Arrian's Chorienes and Curtius' Sisimithres to be the same man (Bosworth thought them different) and places the rock at Kuh-e Nur by the Vakhsh. Chorienes was restored as governor.

name: Sogdian Rock (siege)
war: Wars of Alexander the Great (Sogdian and Bactrian revolt)
place: Sogdian Rock, or Rock of Ariamazes (site disputed, perhaps near Derbent in the Baysun range), Uzbekistan
how the result was decided: The defenders surrendered when 300 climbers reached the heights above them (Arrian 4.18.4-4.19.4).
Iranian force: Ariamazes' Sogdians (Curtius 7.11.1: 30,000 armed men), sheltering the family of the Bactrian lord Oxyartes, Roxane among them.
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
losses B: none in fighting; Curtius says Ariamazes and his kin were crucified
sources: Arrian 4.18.4-4.19.6; Curtius 7.11; en.wikipedia Siege of the Sogdian Rock
note: Wikipedia places the rock at 40.4 N, 69.4 E (near Khujand); most modern proposals are in the south, in the Baysun-Hissar ranges. The coordinates are a regional guess.

name: Hydaspes
place: left bank of the Hydaspes (Jhelum), Punjab, Pakistan
how the result was decided: Alexander's cavalry, opened by the Dahae mounted archers, drove Porus' horse back on his infantry and the Macedonian phalanx finished it (Arrian 5.14-18).
sources: Arrian, Anabasis 5.12.2, 5.14-18 (the Bactrian, Sogdian and Scythian horse and 1,000 Dahae horse archers); Curtius 8.13-14; Diodorus 17.87-89; Plutarch, Alexander 60; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Hydaspes
note: Alexander's cavalry included Bactrian, Sogdian and Scythian (Saka) squadrons and about 1,000 Dahae horse archers, who began the fight by harassing the Indian right wing. The Iranian horse formed a large part of the cavalry but a small part of the whole army, so this counts as a named unit rather than a fifth.

name: Cappadocia (322)
war: Wars of the Diadochi (Perdiccas' conquest of Cappadocia)
how the result was decided: Perdiccas defeated Ariarathes in battle, killing about 4,000 and capturing 5,000 with the king (Diodorus 18.16.2).
Iranian force: Ariarathes' army, mainly Cappadocian: 30,000 foot and 15,000 horse (Diodorus 18.16.2).
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
borderline: Ariarathes was the Achaemenid satrap of Cappadocia and never submitted to Alexander, but Cappadocia is not one of this set's Persian states and this set counts the Iranian resistance only to 327: probably out
doubts and flags: Borderline: Ariarathes was the Achaemenid satrap of Cappadocia and never submitted to Alexander, but Cappadocia is not one of this set's Persian states and this set counts the Iranian resistance only to 327: probably out.
sources: Diodorus 18.16.1-3; Appian, Mithridatic Wars 8; Plutarch, Eumenes 3
note: His nephew Ariarathes II recovered Cappadocia about 301 with Armenian help (Diodorus 31.19.5); that fight is not listed.

name: Paraitacene
how the result was decided: As in Ancient Greek Battles: Eumenes' phalanx routed Antigonus' and Antigonus lost far more men, but Antigonus' cavalry broke Eumenes' left and Antigonus camped on the field and claimed victory. Wikipedia infobox: Eumenes victory
why it counts: Peucestas brought 10,000 Persian archers and slingers and 3,000 Persians armed in the Macedonian manner, besides the levies of the upper satraps (Diod. 19.14, 19.27-28)
sources: Diod. 19.26–32; Plut. Eum. 15; Nep. Eum. 8
note: Peucestas brought 10,000 Persian archers and slingers and 3,000 Persians armed in the Macedonian manner, besides the levies of the upper satraps (Diod. 19.14, 19.27-28)

name: Parthia (Peithon v the upper satraps)
how the result was decided: As in Ancient Greek Battles: Peucestas and the satraps of the upper provinces defeated Peithon, satrap of Media, after he had killed Philip of Parthia. Both sides Macedonian.
why it counts: The upper satraps (Peucestas of Persis and others) drove Peithon out of Parthia with their native levies (Diod. 19.14)
note: The upper satraps (Peucestas of Persis and others) drove Peithon out of Parthia with their native levies (Diod. 19.14)

name: Gabiene
how the result was decided: As in Ancient Greek Battles: Tactically mixed: Eumenes' Silver Shields routed Antigonus' phalanx, but Antigonus' cavalry won and captured the baggage; the Silver Shields then handed Eumenes over. Wikipedia: inconclusive, Antigoni
why it counts: Peucestas' Persians and the upper satraps' levies in Eumenes' army (Diod. 19.40-43)
sources: Diod. 19.39–43; Plut. Eum. 16–17; Nep. Eum. 10; Polyaen. 4.6.13
note: Peucestas' Persians and the upper satraps' levies in Eumenes' army (Diod. 19.40-43)

name: Callatis
war: Third War of the Diadochi (Lysimachus v Pontic cities)
why it counts: Scythians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
note: Pitched battle against the Scythians who came to help rebel Callatis; the Thracians changed sides before the fighting. Followed by a siege of Callatis.

name: Tigris
place: marshes by the Tigris, east of Babylonia (site unknown)
how the result was decided: As in Ancient Greek Battles: Night attack from concealment in the marshes; Evagoras killed, most of Nicanor's army went over to Seleucus.
commanders B: Nicanor (satrap of Media), Evagoras (satrap of Aria, killed)
why it counts: Nicanor, satrap of Media, led a force raised in Media and the upper satrapies (Diod. 19.92)
note: Nicanor, satrap of Media, led a force raised in Media and the upper satrapies (Diod. 19.92)

date: 310/309 BCE (after the battle on the Thates)
name: Aripharnes' fortress (siege, 310 BC)
war: Bosporan civil war (Satyrus II v Eumelus)
place: the stronghold of Aripharnes, king of the Siraces, across the Thates (Kuban), Taman/Kuban region (site unknown)
how the result was decided: Satyrus II was wounded in the assaults and died; his son Prytanis raised the siege and withdrew, so the fortress held (Diodorus 20.23).
sources: Diodorus Siculus 20.22.3-23; Ancient Greek Battles (note to 'Thates River'); Minns, Scythians and Greeks (1913); Rostovtzeff, Iranians and Greeks (1922)
note: Satyrus' army was mostly Scythian; Aripharnes' Siraces were Sarmatian-type nomads. The siege followed Satyrus' victory at the Thates and ended the war in Eumelus' favour.

name: Thates River
place: across the Thates river, Asian Bosporus (Kuban; site unknown)
commanders B: Eumelus; Aripharnes, king of the Siraces
why it counts: Scythians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
note: Satyrus' army was mostly Scythian (c. 20,000 foot, 10,000 horse); Eumelus' mostly the Siraces (Sarmatians) of Aripharnes. Satyrus was killed soon afterwards besieging Aripharnes' fortress (siege, not listed). Diodorus spells the river Thates (often 'Thatis').

name: Cappadocia (Ariarathes v Amyntas)
how the result was decided: As in Ancient Greek Battles: Diodorus says only that Ariarathes 'slew Amyntas the Macedonian general' and drove out the Macedonians while the Successors fought each other. Amyntas' master (probably Antigonus, possibly a post-Ipsu
commanders A: Ariarathes II, with troops of Ardoates of Armenia
why it counts: Ariarathid dynasty of Cappadocia, of Persian descent (Ariarathes I a Persian satrap; Diod. 31.19)
note: Ariarathid dynasty of Cappadocia, of Persian descent (Ariarathes I a Persian satrap; Diod. 31.19)

name: Ancyra
how the result was decided: As in Ancient Greek Battles: Trogus credits the Gauls with the victory; Eusebius says it was against Mithridates and that about 20,000 of Seleucus' men fell. Seleucus barely escaped, and Asia Minor west of the Taurus was left to
commanders A: Antiochus Hierax; Mithridates II of Pontus
why it counts: Mithridatid dynasty of Pontus, Persian in the male line (founder Mithridates I Ktistes of a Persian noble house; App. Mith. 9, 112) and Greek through its Seleucid queens: Mithridates VI's mother Laodice VI was a Seleucid, and Justin 38.7 has him claim Cyrus and Darius on his father's side and Alexander and Seleucus on his mother's; his kingdom was Greek, and its battles are Greek battles in Ancient Greek Battles and Battles of the Romans; Mithridates II of Pontus led his own army as Hierax's ally
sources: Trogus Prol. 27; Justin 27.2.10–11; Porphyry FGrH 260 F32.8
note: Mithridatid dynasty of Pontus, Persian in the male line (founder Mithridates I Ktistes of a Persian noble house; App. Mith. 9, 112) and Greek through its Seleucid queens: Mithridates VI's mother Laodice VI was a Seleucid, and Justin 38.7 has him claim Cyrus and Darius on his father's side and Alexander and Seleucus on his mother's; his kingdom was Greek, and its battles are Greek battles in Ancient Greek Battles and Battles of the Romans; Mithridates II of Pontus led his own army as Hierax's ally

date: c. 238 BC (dates between c. 247 and 238 BC are proposed)
name: Parni conquest of Parthia
place: Parthia (Astabene and Parthyene; site unknown), Iran
how the result was decided: Arsaces overpowered and killed the satrap Andragoras and took Parthia (Justin 41.4.7); no battle is described, so the result rests on the conquest itself.
commanders A: Arsaces I, Tiridates (his brother, in Arrian's version)
Iranian force: The Parni, a tribe of the Dahae steppe horsemen from the Ochus (Tejen) region, led by Arsaces (Strabo 11.9.2-3; Justin 41.4); no numbers.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a conquest campaign rather than a named battle: Andragoras was killed, but no battle is described
doubts and flags: Borderline: a conquest campaign rather than a named battle: Andragoras was killed, but no battle is described.
sources: Justin 41.4.6-7; Strabo 11.9.2-3; Arrian, Parthica (in Photius and Syncellus); en.wikipedia Parni conquest of Parthia; Seleucid-Parthian Wars
note: Andragoras had probably made himself independent of Seleucus II before the invasion (his coins), so the opponent is a breakaway Seleucid satrapy. Arrian's version (via Syncellus) has Arsaces and Tiridates kill a satrap called Pherecles or Agathocles instead. Hyrcania was taken soon after.

name: Parthia (Arsaces I v Seleucus II)
how the result was decided: Justin reports that Arsaces defeated Seleucus in battle, a day the Parthians kept ever after as the beginning of their liberty; Seleucus withdrew.
Iranian force: Arsaces' Parni and Parthian horsemen, perhaps reinforced from the Apasiacae, the steppe nomads to whom he had first withdrawn (Strabo 11.8.8); no figures.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
borderline: known only from Justin; no site or conventional name
doubts and flags: Borderline: known only from Justin; no site or conventional name.
sources: Justin 41.4.8-10; Strabo 11.8.8; Athenaeus 4.153a (Posidonius); en.wikipedia Seleucid-Parthian Wars
note: Strabo says only that Arsaces fled from Seleucus to the Apasiacae, and some historians doubt a pitched battle; a report that Seleucus was captured (Posidonius in Athenaeus 4.153a) is disputed and may refer to a later Seleucus. Seleucus was recalled west by a rising (Justin). Date disputed (c. 235-227 BC).

date: c. 220 BCE (Polybius 4.56, in his narrative of 220)
name: Sinope (siege, c. 220 BC)
war: Pontic-Sinopean war (Mithridates of Pontus against Sinope)
how the result was decided: Sinope, supplied by Rhodes, was not taken and stayed independent until Pharnaces I took it in 183 BCE (Polybius 4.56; Strabo 12.3.11).
commanders B: not recorded (the Sinopeans, with a general sent from Rhodes)
sources: Polybius 4.56; Strabo 12.3.11; Wikipedia 'Mithridates III of Pontus'
note: The Pontic king belonged to the Mithridatid house of Persian descent; Polybius gives only the blockade and the Rhodian relief, not an assault, and the king's numbering (II or III) varies between scholars. Weak entry: a blockade with no recorded fighting.

name: Raphia
place: Raphia (Rafah), on the Egyptian-Palestinian border, Gaza Strip
how the result was decided: Ptolemy's phalanx broke the Seleucid left and centre after Antiochus' wing had routed the Ptolemaic left, and Antiochus withdrew.
commanders A: Ptolemy IV, Arsinoe III, Echecrates, Andromachus
commanders B: Antiochus III; Aspasianus the Mede, Byttacus, Menedemus
sources: Polybius 5.79-86; Walbank, Commentary on Polybius vol. 1; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Raphia
note: The Seleucid order of battle lists 5,000 Medes, Cissians, Cadusians and Carmanians under Aspasianus the Mede, 5,000 light-armed Dahae, Carmanians and Cilicians under Byttacus, and 2,000 Persian and Agrianian archers and slingers: perhaps a seventh of the army, and several named units. The Dahae are the steppe element.

date: c. 212 or 211 BCE (Polybius 8.23-25; the year is inferred from his narrative order)
name: Arsamosata (siege, c. 212 BC)
war: Antiochus III's Armenian expedition (submission of Xerxes of Armenia and Sophene)
place: Arsamosata (Haraba, near Elazig), Turkey; site approximate
how the result was decided: Shut up in Arsamosata, Xerxes came to terms: he paid tribute, kept his kingdom and married Antiochus' sister Antiochis (Polybius 8.25).
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Polybius 8.23-25; Wikipedia 'Xerxes of Sophene' and 'Arsamosata'; Strabo 11.14.15
note: Xerxes belonged to the Orontid (Eruandid) house, of Iranian origin that claimed Achaemenid descent (uncertain; some regard the Orontids as only Iranianised). Polybius calls him king of Armenia; modern historians place him as ruler of Sophene (and Commagene). The siege ended by agreement rather than assault, so the 'result' is the Seleucid gain of submission and tribute.

name: Mount Labus
place: pass over Mount Labus (Elburz range), between Hecatompylos and Hyrcania, Iran
how the result was decided: After a day-long fight the Parthian defenders of the pass were outflanked by Seleucid light troops at night and abandoned the summit to Antiochus (Polybius 10.29-31).
commanders A: Antiochus III; Diogenes, Nicomedes of Cos, Nicolaus the Aetolian, Polyxenidas
commanders B: Arsaces II (overall command; Polybius names no commander at the pass)
Iranian force: The 'barbarians' sent by Arsaces II to hold the pass with ambushes and rolled stones: Parthian and Hyrcanian light troops and mountaineers (Polybius 10.29-31); no numbers.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
sources: Polybius 10.28-31; en.wikipedia Battle of Mount Labus; Seleucid-Parthian Wars
note: en.wikipedia (Seleucid-Parthian Wars) describes the fight as a stalemate turned into a Seleucid success by the night flank attack. Arsaces II later accepted Seleucid suzerainty (208 BC).

name: Syrinx (siege)
place: Syrinx (Sirynx), Hyrcania (site unknown, in the Gorgan plain), Iran
how the result was decided: Antiochus filled the ditches, mined the walls and took Syrinx by assault after the defenders had killed its Greek inhabitants (Polybius 10.31).
Iranian force: The Parthian garrison and the Hyrcanian 'barbarians' who had gathered in Syrinx after the loss of the Labus pass (Polybius 10.31); no numbers.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
sources: Polybius 10.31; en.wikipedia Seleucid-Parthian Wars; List of wars involving Iran (before 1979)
note: Polybius calls the defenders only barbarians; en.wikipedia says the city held a Parthian garrison while Arsaces II was at Nisa. Tambrax, a nearby unwalled city with a palace, fell without a fight.

name: Arius
war: Eastern anabasis of Antiochus III (Bactrian campaign)
place: ford of the river Arius (Hari Rud), on the road from Aria into Bactria
how the result was decided: As in Ancient Greek Battles: A cavalry battle: Antiochus forced the ford at night, then routed the 10,000 Bactrian horse at dawn; he was wounded in the mouth and his horse was killed. Euthydemus fell back to Zariaspa/Bactra, and
commanders B: cavalry of Euthydemus I (Euthydemus himself was at 'Tapuria'/Guriana)
why it counts: Euthydemus' 10,000 horse at the Arius were Bactrian cavalry (Polyb. 10.49)
note: Euthydemus' 10,000 horse at the Arius were Bactrian cavalry (Polyb. 10.49)

name: Magnesia
place: plain near Magnesia ad Sipylum (Manisa), Lydia, Turkey
how the result was decided: Eumenes' cavalry routed the Seleucid left, panicked the scythed chariots and the phalanx was shot down and broken.
commanders A: Lucius Cornelius Scipio, Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, Eumenes II
sources: Livy 37.37-44 (37.40, army list); Appian, Syriaca 30-36; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Magnesia
note: Antiochus III's right wing, where he commanded, included 1,200 Dahae horse archers (Livy), with Cyrtian slingers and Elymaean archers; the Dahae are a named unit, far below a fifth of the army. Also in Ancient Greek Battles and Battles of the Romans.

name: Elymais (death of Antiochus III)
war: Seleucid wars in the east (Antiochus III's raid on the temple of Bel)
place: temple of Bel in Elymais (site unknown, in the Zagros foothills of Khuzestan), Iran
how the result was decided: The Seleucid force that attacked the temple by night was overwhelmed by the local Elymaeans and Antiochus III was killed with his men (Diodorus 28.3, 29.15; Strabo 16.1.18; Justin 32.2.1-2).
commanders A: unknown (the Elymaeans of the temple district)
Iranian force: The Elymaean highlanders around the temple, who rose against the plunderers (Strabo's 'neighbouring barbarians'); no numbers or leaders recorded.
why it counts: Elymais: an Iranian-led state
losses B: Antiochus III and his force killed
borderline: a fight over a temple raid, not a named battle; Elymais was still a Seleucid province, so whether it 'fought on its own account' is a judgment
doubts and flags: Borderline: a fight over a temple raid, not a named battle; Elymais was still a Seleucid province, so whether it 'fought on its own account' is a judgment.
sources: Diodorus 28.3, 29.15; Strabo 16.1.18; Justin 32.2.1-2; en.wikipedia Elymais
note: Elymais counts here only because the Elymaeans fought on their own account against the king; Elymais became an independent kingdom only under Kamnaskires I (c. 147 BC). A similar attempt by Antiochus IV in 164 BC was foiled without a recorded battle (Polybius 31.9; 1 Maccabees 6.1-4).

name: Sinope (siege, 183 BC)
war: Pharnaces I's expansion on the Black Sea (Pontic capture of Sinope)
how the result was decided: Pharnaces took Sinope and made it his capital; Rhodes' protest to Rome came to nothing (Polybius 23.9; Strabo 12.3.11).
sources: Polybius 23.9.2 and 24.1; Strabo 12.3.11; Wikipedia 'Pharnaces I of Pontus' (fetched 1 Nov 2026)
note: Pharnaces I belonged to the Mithridatid house of Pontus, of Persian descent (claimed Achaemenid ancestry; Wikipedia: 'of Persian and Greek ancestry'). Sinope fell to a sudden attack and the details of the fighting are not recorded, so this is a thin 'siege'; the war with Eumenes II and Ariarathes IV that followed (181-179 BCE) has no named battle.

name: Media (capture of Demetrius II)
place: mountains of Media (exact site unknown), Iran
how the result was decided: Demetrius' army was destroyed and he himself was captured (Justin 36.1, 38.9; Josephus Ant. 13.186; Babylonian astronomical diaries).
commanders A: Mithridates I (his general Bagasis had held the Seleucids for a year)
Iranian force: Mithridates I's Parthian army, chiefly cavalry, with the forces of his governor in Media, Bagasis; no figures.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
sources: Justin 36.1.2-6, 38.9.2; Josephus Ant. 13.184-186; 1 Maccabees 14.1-3; Appian, Syriaca 67; en.wikipedia Seleucid-Parthian Wars
note: Justin says Demetrius was taken by a ruse during peace talks after winning several fights; the Babylonian diaries date the capture to summer 138 BC. Justin says the Persians (of Persis), Elymaeans and Bactrians aided Demetrius in the war, not necessarily in this battle; Persis and Elymais are thus on the Seleucid side here, as allies only.

name: Lycus (Great Zab)
place: river Lycus (Great Zab), northern Mesopotamia, Iraq
how the result was decided: Antiochus defeated the Parthian general Indates and set up a trophy by the Lycus (Nicolaus of Damascus in Josephus, Ant. 13.251-252).
commanders A: Antiochus VII Sidetes; John Hyrcanus (Jewish contingent)
Iranian force: Indates' Parthian field army in Mesopotamia; the sources give no details, and it was presumably Parthian cavalry with local levies.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
strength A: about 80,000 armed men for the whole campaign (Justin 38.10)
sources: Josephus Ant. 13.249-253 (Nicolaus of Damascus); Justin 38.10; Diodorus 34/35.15-17; en.wikipedia Battle of Ecbatana
note: One of three Seleucid victories in 130 BC (Justin 38.10); the other two are unnamed. The army halted two days at the river at Hyrcanus' request for a Jewish festival.

name: Ecbatana (129 BC)
how the result was decided: Antiochus' column was destroyed and he was killed (or killed himself); the Seleucid troops in their Median winter quarters were killed or captured.
Iranian force: Phraates II's Parthian army, chiefly cavalry, supported by the Median towns that rose against the Seleucid troops billeted on them (Justin 38.10; Diodorus 34/35.17).
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
strength B: Antiochus' own column small (probably the royal guard); the whole army about 80,000 armed men with 300,000 camp followers (Justin 38.10)
losses B: Antiochus killed; his guard destroyed; most of the army in winter quarters killed or captured
sources: Justin 38.10, 39.1; Diodorus 34/35.15-17; Appian, Syriaca 68; Josephus Ant. 13.253; en.wikipedia Battle of Ecbatana
note: The sources place the battle only in Media; 'Ecbatana' is the conventional label. Antiochus' son Seleucus was captured. The Seleucid prisoners were drafted into Phraates' army and deserted him against the Saka.

name: Phraates II v Saka
war: Parthian wars with the Saka and Yuezhi
how the result was decided: When the Parthian line wavered the Greek prisoners in Phraates' army went over to the Saka; the Parthian army was cut to pieces and the king killed (Justin 42.1.4-5).
Iranian force: Phraates II's Parthian army, with the Greek soldiers captured from Antiochus VII's army, who deserted in the battle (Justin 42.1).
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the army destroyed; Phraates II killed
borderline: no conventional name or site; known only from Justin
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name or site; known only from Justin.
sources: Justin 42.1.1-5; en.wikipedia Phraates II
note: The Saka had been hired for the war against Antiochus VII, arrived too late, were refused pay and ravaged Parthia; Phraates left Himerus in charge of Babylonia when he marched east. Date 128 or 127 BC.

name: Artabanus I v Tocharians
war: Parthian wars with the Saka and Yuezhi
place: eastern frontier of Parthia (site unknown), Turkmenistan

why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state

name: Yucheng (siege, 104 BC)

Yucheng fell to Shangguan Jie in 102 and its king fled to the Kangju.

Whether the Dayuan were Iranian-speaking is doubtful (see the note on Yucheng); the earlier note about a Saka king of Ferghana named Mauakes is a modern guess at the name Wugua.

commanders A: the Saka overlord (Shahanushahi) and his chiefs, led by Kalakacharya
doubts and flags: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
sources: Kalakacharya-katha (Jain; Prabhavakacarita, Kahavali); Brown, The Story of Kalaka (1933); Sircar, Studies in Indian Coins
note: The tradition says Vikramaditya, Gardabhilla's son, later drove the Saka out (the Vikrama era of 57 BCE). The historical Indo-Scythian conquest of Ujjain and Malwa seems later (1st century CE), so the date and the fight itself are doubtful.

name: Seleucia (siege, 55 BC)
war: Parthian civil war (Mithridates IV against Orodes II)
place: Seleucia on the Tigris (Tell Umar), Iraq
how the result was decided: Surena took Seleucia by storm, being himself the first man on the wall (Plutarch, Crassus 21.6).
Iranian force: Orodes' army led by Surena with his household horse from Sakastan, against Mithridates' Parthian partisans and the Greek citizens of Seleucia who held the city for him.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Plutarch, Crassus 21.6; Justin 42.4.1-4; en.wikipedia Mithridates IV of Parthia
note: en.wikipedia (after Bivar) puts the siege in 54 BC and has Mithridates offer battle and lose; Justin has him surrender at Babylon after a long siege. Older numbering calls him Mithridates III. Gabinius had brought him to the Euphrates in 55 BC before turning to Egypt.

name: Babylon (siege, 54 BC)
war: Parthian civil war (Mithridates IV against Orodes II)
how the result was decided: Mithridates, besieged in Babylon for a long time, surrendered because of famine and was put to death (Justin 42.4.2-4).
Iranian force: Orodes' Parthian army against Mithridates' remaining partisans in Babylon; no details.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a siege ended by famine; no fighting is described
doubts and flags: Borderline: a siege ended by famine; no fighting is described.
sources: Justin 42.4.2-4; en.wikipedia Mithridates IV of Parthia
note: Some modern accounts merge this with the fall of Seleucia (above) and have Mithridates defeated in battle near Seleucia.

name: Ichnae
place: near Ichnae, on the Balikh south of Carrhae, Syria
how the result was decided: The satrap's small force was beaten and Silaces fled wounded to Orodes; the Romans held the field (Dio 40.12).
commanders B: Silaces (Dio's Talymenus Ilaces), satrap of Mesopotamia
Iranian force: The satrap Silaces with a few horsemen (Dio 40.12); no figures.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
sources: Cassius Dio 40.12-13; Plutarch, Crassus 17; en.wikipedia Battle of Carrhae
note: After the fight Crassus stormed Zenodotium, a Greek town whose people had killed his soldiers; no Parthian force fought there.

date: 9 June 53 BC (Republican calendar; day by tradition, Ovid Fasti 6.465)
name: Carrhae
place: the plain south of Carrhae (Harran), near the Balikh, Turkey
how the result was decided: The Parthians held the field; the Roman army abandoned it at night, leaving 4,000 wounded, and was destroyed in the retreat.
commanders B: Marcus Licinius Crassus, Publius Crassus (killed), Gaius Cassius Longinus
Iranian force: Surena's household army of no fewer than 10,000 horsemen, his vassals and slaves: about 1,000 mail-clad cataphracts and the rest horse archers, supplied with arrows by a train of 1,000 camels (Plutarch, Crassus 21, 24-25).
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
strength B: about 42,000: seven legions (about 34,000), 4,000 cavalry and 4,000 light troops (Plutarch)
sources: Plutarch, Crassus 17-33; Cassius Dio 40.16-27; en.wikipedia Battle of Carrhae; Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Carrhae' (Shahbazi)
note: The Arab chief of Osroene (Plutarch's Ariamnes, probably Abgar II), a Parthian client, guided Crassus while in Parthian pay and is not counted as a Roman ally; Crassus had Gallic cavalry under Publius, and Artavasdes II of Armenia, who had promised troops, stayed away. Crassus was killed a few days later in a scuffle at a parley near Sinnaca, and Varguntius' detachment was destroyed in the retreat. Orodes II was meanwhile in Armenia with the main army.

date: autumn 51 BC (the Parthians besieged Antioch again in 50 BC)
name: Antioch (siege, 51 BC)
war: Roman-Parthian Wars (Parthian invasion of Syria, 51-50 BC)
place: Antioch on the Orontes (Antakya), and the ambush near Antigonea, Turkey
how the result was decided: The Parthians failed to take Antioch and withdrew, and their force was ambushed near Antigonea, where Osaces was mortally wounded (Dio 40.29; Cicero).
Iranian force: A large Parthian cavalry raiding army under the general Osaces with the young prince Pacorus (Dio 40.28-29; Cicero, Ad Familiares 15.1-4); no figures.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
strength A: unknown (the remnants of Crassus' army and local levies)
losses B: many killed in the ambush; Osaces mortally wounded
sources: Cassius Dio 40.28-30; Cicero, Ad Atticum 5.20-21 and Ad Familiares 2.10, 15.1-4; en.wikipedia Siege of Antioch (51 BC)
note: Named 'Antioch (siege)' in Battles of the Romans; the year is added because the Sasanians besieged Antioch later. The Parthians wintered in Cyrrhestica and besieged Bibulus in Antioch in 50 BC without success before leaving Syria. A small Parthian raid of 52 BC had also been repelled by Cassius (Dio 40.28).

name: Nicopolis
how the result was decided: As in Ancient Greek Battles: Pharnaces II, king of the Cimmerian Bosporus, fighting to recover his father's Pontic kingdom (counted as Pontus). Two of Calvinus' four legions were Deiotarus' Galatians; Ariobarzanes III of Cappadoc
why it counts: Mithridatid dynasty of Pontus, Persian in the male line (founder Mithridates I Ktistes of a Persian noble house; App. Mith. 9, 112) and Greek through its Seleucid queens: Mithridates VI's mother Laodice VI was a Seleucid, and Justin 38.7 has him claim Cyrus and Darius on his father's side and Alexander and Seleucus on his mother's; his kingdom was Greek, and its battles are Greek battles in Ancient Greek Battles and Battles of the Romans
sources: [Caes.] B. Alex. 34–40; App. Mith. 120; Dio 42.46
note: Mithridatid dynasty of Pontus, Persian in the male line (founder Mithridates I Ktistes of a Persian noble house; App. Mith. 9, 112) and Greek through its Seleucid queens: Mithridates VI's mother Laodice VI was a Seleucid, and Justin 38.7 has him claim Cyrus and Darius on his father's side and Alexander and Seleucus on his mother's; his kingdom was Greek, and its battles are Greek battles in Ancient Greek Battles and Battles of the Romans

name: Pelusium (siege, 47 BC)
war: Alexandrian War (Caesar's relief army from Syria)
allies A: Judaea; Nabataean, Syrian and Cilician levies
how the result was decided: Mithridates stormed Pelusium on the day he arrived (Bellum Alexandrinum 26; Josephus, BJ 1.187-190).
commanders B: Egyptian garrison of Ptolemy XIII (commander not recorded)
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Caesar (Bellum Alexandrinum) 26; Josephus BJ 1.187-192, AJ 14.127-136; Appian BC 2.89; Wikipedia 'Mithridates of Pergamon' (fetched)
note: Mithridates of Pergamon was reputed a son of Mithridates VI by the Galatian Adobogiona (Wikipedia accepts it; Strabo 13.4.3 records the claim as a report), so a Mithridatid of Persian-Greek descent (uncertain). His army was Levantine, so the Iranian part is only the leader.

name: Pharnaces II v Asander (47 BC)
place: European Bosporus, near Panticapaeum (Kerch), Crimea (site unknown)
how the result was decided: Pharnaces, who had retaken Theodosia and Panticapaeum with Scythian and Sarmatian troops, was beaten and killed by his governor Asander.
sources: Appian, Mithridatica 120; Dio 42.47.5; Strabo 13.4.3
note: Appian says Pharnaces raised Scythian and Sarmatian troops for the reconquest, and also lists him as a Mithridatid of claimed Persian descent. Ancient Greek Battles has the fight as 'Bosporus (Pharnaces v Asander)'; Scythian and Sarmatian numbers are not given.

name: Zela
how the result was decided: As in Ancient Greek Battles: 'Veni, vidi, vici.' Pharnaces II (king of the Bosporus) counted as Pontus.
why it counts: Mithridatid dynasty of Pontus, Persian in the male line (founder Mithridates I Ktistes of a Persian noble house; App. Mith. 9, 112) and Greek through its Seleucid queens: Mithridates VI's mother Laodice VI was a Seleucid, and Justin 38.7 has him claim Cyrus and Darius on his father's side and Alexander and Seleucus on his mother's; his kingdom was Greek, and its battles are Greek battles in Ancient Greek Battles and Battles of the Romans
sources: [Caes.] B. Alex. 72–77; Plut. Caes. 50; Suet. Caes. 35, 37; App. BC 2.91, Mith. 120; Dio 42.47
note: Mithridatid dynasty of Pontus, Persian in the male line (founder Mithridates I Ktistes of a Persian noble house; App. Mith. 9, 112) and Greek through its Seleucid queens: Mithridates VI's mother Laodice VI was a Seleucid, and Justin 38.7 has him claim Cyrus and Darius on his father's side and Alexander and Seleucus on his mother's; his kingdom was Greek, and its battles are Greek battles in Ancient Greek Battles and Battles of the Romans

name: Nile (47 BC)
place: Nile Delta, between the Jewish Camp (Tell el-Yahudiya) and Alexandria, Egypt; exact site unknown
side A (victor if decisive): Rome and the relief army of Mithridates of Pergamon
how the result was decided: The Egyptian army was routed, Ptolemy XIII drowned and Alexandria passed to Caesar (Bellum Alexandrinum 28-31).
Iranian side: Rome and the relief army of Mithridates of Pergamon
commanders A: Julius Caesar; Mithridates of Pergamon (commanding the relief army)
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Caesar (Bellum Alexandrinum) 26-31; Appian BC 2.90; Dio 42.43; Josephus BJ 1.187-192; Wikipedia 'Mithridates of Pergamon' (fetched)
note: Mithridates of Pergamon commanded the relief army that joined Caesar; his descent from Mithridates VI (uncertain) is what qualifies the battle. The army was Levantine, so the Iranian part is only the leader.

date: 45-44 BC (to 43 BC in Battles of the Romans)
name: Apamea (siege, 45 BC)
war: Roman civil wars (Caecilius Bassus' revolt in Syria)
place: Apamea on the Orontes (Qalaat al-Mudiq), Syria
how the result was decided: Apamea never fell: the first Caesarian siege was given up and the second ended in 43 BC when both armies went over to Cassius.
commanders A: Quintus Caecilius Bassus (Pompeians); Pacorus (Parthian force); Alchaudonius the Arab
commanders B: Gaius Antistius Vetus; then Lucius Staius Murcus and Quintus Marcius Crispus (Caesarians); Antipater
Iranian force: A Parthian force (under the prince Pacorus, per en.wikipedia) that came at Bassus' invitation but left because of winter without achieving anything important (Dio 47.27); size unknown.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
strength A: Bassus' two legions with slaves and levies, Arab archers
strength B: three legions (Murcus) and three (Crispus), with a Jewish force from Antipater
borderline: Dio says the Parthians came but left for the winter without doing anything important; en.wikipedia says Pacorus and Alchaudonius drove off Antistius' army. Parthian fighting is uncertain, hence 'contingent'
doubts and flags: Borderline: Dio says the Parthians came but left for the winter without doing anything important; en.wikipedia says Pacorus and Alchaudonius drove off Antistius' army. Parthian fighting is uncertain, hence 'contingent'.
sources: Cassius Dio 47.26-28; Appian, Civil Wars 3.77-78, 4.58-59; Strabo 16.2.10; Josephus Ant. 14.268-272; en.wikipedia Siege of Apamea
note: A Roman civil siege in Battles of the Romans ('Apamea (siege)', civil); not civil here, since only one Persian side took part. The year is added because the Sasanians took Apamea in 540 and 573. Dio credits the archery of Alchaudonius' Arabs with Bassus' success in the first fighting.

name: Philippi
how the result was decided: In the second battle (23 October) Brutus' army was routed and then surrendered; the first battle (3 October) was indecisive, each side taking one enemy camp.
commanders B: Marcus Junius Brutus, Gaius Cassius Longinus (Liberators)
Iranian force: Parthian and Median horse archers in the Liberators' cavalry: Cassius had 4,000 mounted bowmen, Arabs, Medes and Parthians, and Brutus 2,000 'Parthian and Thessalian' horse (Appian, Civil Wars 4.88).
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
losses B: about 8,000 in the first battle; the army surrendered after the second
borderline: the Parthian horse archers joined Cassius drawn by his reputation (Appian 4.59) and may not have been a force of the Parthian state
doubts and flags: Borderline: the Parthian horse archers joined Cassius drawn by his reputation (Appian 4.59) and may not have been a force of the Parthian state.
sources: Appian, Civil Wars 4.59, 4.88, 4.105-131; Plutarch, Brutus 38-52; Cassius Dio 47.35-49; en.wikipedia Battle of Philippi; Roman-Parthian Wars
note: en.wikipedia lists a 'Parthian Empire (cavalry force)' among the Liberators. Labienus had been sent to Orodes II to ask for help, but no royal army arrived before the battle. One entry for both engagements; Cassius killed himself after the first.

name: Decidius Saxa's defeat
how the result was decided: Saxa was beaten in the field and fled to Antioch and then Cilicia, where he was caught and killed (Dio 48.25).
Iranian force: Orodes II's Parthian cavalry army under Pacorus and the Roman renegade Quintus Labienus, joined by Roman garrison troops in Syria who had served Brutus and Cassius (Dio 48.24-25).
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
strength A: Parthian cavalry, about 14,000-20,000 for the whole invasion (modern estimates on en.wikipedia)
strength B: unknown (Saxa's remaining troops, most having gone over)
losses B: army destroyed or gone over; standards taken
sources: Cassius Dio 48.24-26; Plutarch, Antony 30; Livy, Periochae 127; Florus 2.19; en.wikipedia Parthian invasion of 40 BC; Quintus Labienus
note: Persian role principal: Labienus commanded a Parthian army in Orodes' service. Apamea first repulsed Labienus, then surrendered on a false report of Saxa's death; Antioch surrendered too.

name: Stratonicea (siege)
how the result was decided: Labienus besieged Stratonicea for a long time but could not take it (Dio 48.26); the siege ended with Ventidius' advance in 39 BC.
Iranian force: Labienus' army in Asia: Parthian troops given him by Orodes with Roman deserters and local levies (Dio 48.24-26, 48.39).
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a minor siege with no conventional name; the Persian role is through Labienus' Parthian-backed army
doubts and flags: Borderline: a minor siege with no conventional name; the Persian role is through Labienus' Parthian-backed army.
sources: Cassius Dio 48.26; Tacitus, Annals 3.62; en.wikipedia Quintus Labienus
note: Stratonicea's resistance was later rewarded by Rome (Tacitus, Annals 3.62). Labienus took Alabanda and razed the deserted Mylasa after both had killed his garrisons; no battle is recorded there.

name: Amanus Pass
war: Roman-Parthian Wars (Parthian invasion of 40 BC; Ventidius' counter-offensive)
place: Amanus pass (Belen pass, the Syrian Gates), between Cilicia and Syria, Turkey
how the result was decided: Pharnapates' Parthians, who were getting the better of Silo's advance guard, were routed when Ventidius came up, and Pharnapates was killed (Dio 48.41).
Iranian force: A Parthian force under Pacorus' lieutenant Pharnapates holding the pass: horse archers and cataphracts; no figures.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
sources: Cassius Dio 48.41; Plutarch, Antony 33; en.wikipedia Battle of Amanus Pass
note: After the defeat Pacorus withdrew beyond the Euphrates and Syria was recovered.

name: Cilician Gates (39 BC)
war: Roman-Parthian Wars (Parthian invasion of 40 BC; Ventidius' counter-offensive)
place: Cilician Gates (Gulek pass), Taurus mountains, Turkey
how the result was decided: The Parthian cavalry charged Ventidius' camp on high ground without waiting for Labienus and was thrown back with heavy loss; Labienus' army then broke up in Ventidius' night ambushes (Dio 48.39-40).
commanders B: Quintus Labienus; Parthian cavalry commanders (Pharnapates, per en.wikipedia)
Iranian force: Parthian cavalry (horse archers and cataphracts) sent to Labienus, with Labienus' Roman and locally levied infantry camped apart (Dio 48.39-40).
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
strength A: unknown (light troops ahead of the main legions)
losses B: heavy; Labienus' army dispersed or went over
sources: Cassius Dio 48.39-40; Plutarch, Antony 33; en.wikipedia Battle of the Cilician Gates; Quintus Labienus
note: Dio places the fight near the Taurus; en.wikipedia names it the Cilician Gates. Labienus fled, was found in Cilicia and killed (other sources have him die in battle).

name: Samosata (siege)
how the result was decided: As in Battles of the Romans: The assaults failed and Antony withdrew on terms, taking 300 talents (Plutarch). Commagene was a Hellenistic kingdom with a Greek-speaking court under an Iranian (Orontid) dynasty.
why it counts: Antiochus I of Commagene, who claimed descent from Darius I on his father's side and from Alexander and the Seleucids on his mother's (his mother Laodice Thea was a Seleucid; the two ancestor galleries at Nemrut Dag); Orontid line (Commagene; Artaxiad Armenia as its branch) widely described as of Iranian origin, but disputed
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Plutarch Antony 34; Cassius Dio 49.20-22; Josephus BJ 1.321-322, AJ 14.439-447
note: Antiochus I of Commagene, who claimed descent from Darius I on his father's side and from Alexander and the Seleucids on his mother's (his mother Laodice Thea was a Seleucid; the two ancestor galleries at Nemrut Dag); Orontid line (Commagene; Artaxiad Armenia as its branch) widely described as of Iranian origin, but disputed

date: 9 June 38 BC (by tradition, the anniversary of Carrhae)
name: Mount Gindarus
war: Roman-Parthian Wars (Pacorus' second invasion of Syria)
how the result was decided: The Parthians charged the Roman camp on high ground, were routed by the legionaries and slingers, and Pacorus fell (Dio 49.20; Plutarch, Antony 34).
Iranian force: Pacorus' Parthian army of horse archers and cataphracts (Dio 49.20); no figures.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
losses B: very heavy; Pacorus killed with his guard
sources: Cassius Dio 49.19-21; Plutarch, Antony 34; Strabo 16.2.8; Frontinus, Strategemata 1.1.6, 2.2.5; Justin 42.4.7-10; en.wikipedia Battle of Mount Gindarus
note: Ventidius lured Pacorus across the Euphrates at an unexpected point by a deliberate leak (Frontinus; Dio 49.19). The date on the anniversary of Carrhae is a tradition (Dio 49.21; Eutropius).

name: Phraaspa (siege)
place: Phraaspa (Praaspa), royal city of Media Atropatene (perhaps Maragheh), Iran
how the result was decided: Antony failed to take Phraaspa and abandoned the siege in October, his siege train lost and his foragers harassed by the Parthian cavalry.
commanders A: Phraates IV; Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene
Iranian force: The garrison of the Median royal city, which made sorties (Plutarch, Antony 39), and Phraates IV's Parthian cavalry with the horse of Atropatene, about 24,000 (2,000 cataphracts and 22,000 horse archers) by the estimate given on en.wikipedia.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
strength B: about 100,000: 60,000 Roman infantry, 10,000 Spanish and Celtic horse and 30,000 allies (Plutarch, Antony 37)
sources: Plutarch, Antony 38-40; Cassius Dio 49.25-28; Strabo 11.13.3-4; en.wikipedia Antony's Atropatene campaign
note: In a foraging battle before the walls Antony put the Parthians to flight but killed only 80 and took 30 (Plutarch, Antony 39). The site of Phraaspa is disputed (Maragheh, or less likely Takht-e Soleyman).

name: Statianus' convoy (ambush)
place: on the road to Phraaspa, Media Atropatene, Iran
how the result was decided: The Parthian and Median cavalry destroyed the baggage train and its two legions, killing Statianus and burning the siege engines (Plutarch, Antony 38; Dio 49.25).
commanders A: Phraates IV or his general Monaeses; Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene
commanders B: Oppius Statianus (killed), Polemon I of Pontus (captured)
Iranian force: Phraates IV's Parthian cavalry with the horse of his ally Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene (Dio 49.25); no figures.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
strength B: two legions (about 10,000) escorting 300 wagons of siege engines (Plutarch)
losses B: 10,000 killed (Plutarch); Polemon captured; the siege train destroyed
sources: Plutarch, Antony 38; Cassius Dio 49.25; Velleius 2.82; en.wikipedia Antony's Atropatene campaign; Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene
note: Artavasdes II of Armenia left with his cavalry before the attack, so the Armenian role is nominal. Media Atropatene, itself a Persian state in this set, fought as Phraates' ally. Kelly makes Phraates himself the commander.

name: Zhizhi (36 BC)
place: Zhizhi's fortress on the Talas river near Taraz, Kazakhstan
how the result was decided: Han and allied troops stormed the fortress, killed Zhizhi and about 1,500 of his men after repelling Kangju cavalry attacks.
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Hanshu 70 (Chen Tang biography) and 94b; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zhizhi; Hill, Through the Jade Gate
note: Zhizhi's father-in-law, the Kangju king, sent several thousand horse (10,000 in one count). The Kangju (north of Sogdiana) were perhaps Iranian-speaking (Saka or Sogdian type) but this is uncertain, so the entry qualifies only if they are counted. Zhizhi's own Xiongnu are not Iranian.

name: Antony's retreat from Phraaspa
place: the mountain road from Phraaspa to the Araxes, Media Atropatene, Iran
how the result was decided: In 27 days and 18 engagements the Parthian cavalry harried an army that left the field to them each day until it crossed the Araxes, having lost about 20,000 foot and 4,000 horse (Plutarch, Antony 40-50).
Iranian force: Phraates IV's Parthian horse archers and cataphracts with Median (Atropatenian) cavalry (Plutarch; Dio 49.28-31); no figures.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
losses B: about 20,000 foot and 4,000 horse, more than half by disease (Plutarch, Antony 50)
borderline: a fighting retreat of many engagements, not a single battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: a fighting retreat of many engagements, not a single battle.
sources: Plutarch, Antony 40-51; Cassius Dio 49.28-31; Velleius 2.82; en.wikipedia Antony's Atropatene campaign
note: The best known engagement is the destruction of Flavius Gallus' force (3,000 killed, 5,000 wounded; Plutarch, Antony 42-43), which Antony's legions finally checked. A Mardian guide led the army by a mountain road. Antony lost about 8,000 more in the winter march through Armenia (Plutarch, Antony 51).

date: c. 32 BC (between Antony's treaty with the Mede in 33 BC and Actium)
name: Artavasdes I of Media v Phraates IV
side B: Phraates IV, with Artaxias II of Armenia
how the result was decided: Dio says only that the Median king, with Roman soldiers lent by Antony, defeated the Parthians and Artaxias (Dio 49.44).
factions B: Phraates IV (Parthia), with Artaxias II of Armenia
commanders B: unknown (forces of Phraates IV and Artaxias II)
Iranian force: Artavasdes' Median (Atropatenian) cavalry with Roman troops lent by Antony, against the Parthian army and Artaxias' Armenians.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no named battle; known only from a summary sentence of Dio
doubts and flags: Borderline: no named battle; known only from a summary sentence of Dio.
sources: Cassius Dio 49.33, 49.44; Plutarch, Antony 52-53; en.wikipedia Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene
note: Civil because two states of the list (Atropatene and Parthia) fought each other; en.wikipedia says only that the Roman reinforcements helped Artavasdes repel a Parthian attack.

name: Artaxias II v Artavasdes I of Media
place: Media Atropatene or Armenia (site unknown), Iran
side A (victor if decisive): Phraates IV and Artaxias II of Armenia; Armenia
how the result was decided: After Antony recalled his Roman troops the Median king was defeated and captured (Dio 49.44.4).
factions A: Phraates IV (Parthia) and Artaxias II of Armenia
Iranian force: The Parthian army with Artaxias II's Armenians against Artavasdes' Median forces, left without their Roman auxiliaries; no details.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no named battle; known only from a summary sentence of Dio, and the Parthian share of the victors' army is unclear (en.wikipedia names only Artaxias)
doubts and flags: Borderline: no named battle; known only from a summary sentence of Dio, and the Parthian share of the victors' army is unclear (en.wikipedia names only Artaxias).
sources: Cassius Dio 49.44.4, 51.16.2; Res Gestae 32-33; en.wikipedia Artavasdes I of Media Atropatene
note: If Artaxias fought without Parthian forces this would be a defeat of Atropatene by Armenia rather than a civil battle. Artavasdes later escaped during a Parthian civil war and took refuge with Octavian, who gave him Lesser Armenia.

name: Artabanus' first defeat
war: Parthian succession war (Vonones I against Artabanus II)
place: probably near the borders of Media, Iran (site unknown)
how the result was decided: Artabanus was routed in the first clash and fell back to the borders of Media (Tacitus; Josephus).
factions B: Artabanus II (then king of Media Atropatene)
Iranian force: Parthian noble cavalry on both sides: Vonones had the retinues of the nobles (the Karin and Suren factions) who had brought him from Rome; Artabanus came with forces from Media Atropatene and, Tacitus says, had grown up among the Dahae.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of the succession war, known only in outline
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of the succession war, known only in outline.
sources: Tacitus, Annals 2.3; Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.46-50; en.wikipedia Vonones I; en.wikipedia Artabanus II of Parthia
note: The dates rest on coins: Vonones reigned c. 8-12 and Artabanus struck coins from c. 10/11.

date: c. 10 CE (the date is drawn from coins and the Mathura Lion Capital; uncertain by a decade)
name: Sagala (Rajuvula v Strato II, c. 10 CE)
how the result was decided: Strato II's coinage ends and Rajuvula takes over Sagala, the Indo-Greek capital of the Punjab.
sources: Mathura Lion Capital inscription; coin evidence (Bopearachchi, Monnaies gréco-bactriennes et indo-grecques, 1991); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Scythians
note: No fighting is described; the conquest is inferred from coin overstrikes and the end of Strato's coinage, so the entry is a marker for the end of Greek rule in the Punjab.

name: Vonones' defeat
war: Parthian succession war (Vonones I against Artabanus II)
how the result was decided: Artabanus beat Vonones, who fled from the field with a few horsemen to Seleucia and then to Armenia (Josephus).
Iranian force: Artabanus' rebuilt army of Median and Parthian nobles, perhaps with Dahae horse, against Vonones' following among the Parthian nobility (no details survive).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no conventional name: the decisive but unnamed battle of the succession war
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name: the decisive but unnamed battle of the succession war.
sources: Tacitus, Annals 2.3-4; Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.46-52; en.wikipedia Vonones I
note: Vonones became king of Armenia in 12 and was later held by the Romans in Syria and Cilicia, where he was killed in 19.

name: Orodes' defeat
place: Armenia, probably in the Araxes plain (site unknown), Armenia
how the result was decided: Pharasmanes wounded Orodes in single combat and the Parthians, believing their prince dead, fled the field (Tacitus).
commanders A: Pharasmanes I of Iberia, his brother Mithridates (the Roman candidate for Armenia)
Iranian force: Orodes' Parthian army, mostly horse archers and noble cavalry; Tacitus contrasts it with the Iberian and Albanian foot and the Sarmatian horse of Pharasmanes, and says Orodes failed to hire Sarmatians because the Iberians held the passes.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no conventional name: the one pitched battle of the Iberian invasion of Armenia
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name: the one pitched battle of the Iberian invasion of Armenia.
sources: Tacitus, Annals 6.33-35; en.wikipedia Iberian invasion of Armenia; en.wikipedia List of wars involving Iran (before 1979)
note: Rome backed the invasion but sent no troops; Mithridates of Iberia took the Armenian throne.

name: Seleucia (siege, 40-42)
war: Revolt of Seleucia (c. 35-42) and the war of Vardanes I and Gotarzes II
place: Seleucia on the Tigris (near al-Mada'in), Iraq
how the result was decided: Seleucia submitted to Vardanes in 42, in the seventh year of its revolt, after a siege interrupted by Gotarzes' return.
Iranian force: Vardanes' Parthian royal army; the sources give no details (Parthian armies of the time were noble cavalry, cataphracts and horse archers, with levies).
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a siege known only in outline; the fighting is not described
doubts and flags: Borderline: a siege known only in outline; the fighting is not described.
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.8-9; en.wikipedia Vardanes I; en.wikipedia Gotarzes II
note: Seleucia, the Greek city opposite Ctesiphon, revolted c. 35. Gotarzes used the long siege to raise an army and drive Vardanes east; after the two brothers came to terms, Vardanes took the city's surrender and its right to coin (Wikipedia: June 42).

date: c. 45 (between 43 and 46; Tacitus tells it under AD 47)
name: Erindes
war: Parthian succession war (Vardanes I against Gotarzes II)
place: the river Erindes (Charinda), on the border of Media and Hyrcania (unidentified), Iran
how the result was decided: Vardanes won the fierce fight for the river crossing and Gotarzes withdrew (Tacitus).
Iranian force: Vardanes' Parthian royal cavalry against Gotarzes' army from Hyrcania; in the earlier round of the war Gotarzes had called on the Dahae and Hyrcanians (Tacitus 11.8).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Tacitus, Annals 11.10; en.wikipedia Vardanes I; en.wikipedia Gotarzes II
note: The manuscripts and translations give the river as Erindes or Charinda; Vardanes then subdued the peoples as far as the river Sindes, between the Dahae and the Arians, in unnamed fights.

date: 49 (Tacitus tells it under AD 49; some date it 50 or 51)
name: Corma
war: Parthian succession war (Gotarzes II against Meherdates)
place: near Mount Sanbulos, across the river Corma (perhaps near Bisotun, Kermanshah), Iran
how the result was decided: Meherdates' army broke after Carenes pursued too far, and Meherdates was betrayed by Parraces and handed to Gotarzes, who cut off his ears (Tacitus).
commanders B: Meherdates, Carenes (of the house of Karen)
Iranian force: Gotarzes' Parthian royal army against Meherdates' Parthian partisans led by Carenes; the contingents of Abgar of Edessa and Izates of Adiabene deserted Meherdates before the battle.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Tacitus, Annals 12.10-14; en.wikipedia Meherdates; livius.org (Behistun, Parthian relief of Gotarzes II defeating Meherdates)
note: Meherdates, a son of Vonones I raised in Rome, was escorted to the Euphrates by Cassius Longinus but had no Roman troops in the battle. Neither Mount Sanbulos nor the Corma is securely identified; Gotarzes' victory relief is at Bisotun.

date: 49 CE (summer?); the fight is an episode of the campaign that ends at Uspe
name: Panda River (Aorsi and Romans v Dandarii, 49 CE)
war: Bosporan war of Mithridates VIII v Cotys I
place: River Panda, in the land of the Dandarii (Kuban/Taman region, Russia; exact river unknown)
side A (victor if decisive): Bosporan kingdom of Cotys I; Aorsi
how the result was decided: Tacitus has the Aorsi cavalry and Roman foot beat the Dandarii and cross the Panda, after which Soza falls and the army goes on to Uspe.
Iranian side: Bosporan kingdom of Cotys I v Mithridates VIII
factions A: Bosporan kingdom of Cotys I, Aorsi
commanders A: Eunones (king of the Aorsi); Cotys I; C. Julius Aquila (Roman prefect)
commanders B: Mithridates VIII (deposed Bosporan king); Zorsines (king of the Siraces, until he changed sides at Uspe)
sources: Tacitus, Annals 12.15-21; Rostovtzeff, Iranians and Greeks in South Russia (1922); Minns, Scythians and Greeks (1913)
note: Tacitus does not give the fight a name and may be summarising a running cavalry action; check that it is not already counted inside the Uspe siege. Whether Zorsines' Siraces fought here (as opposed to at Uspe) is not certain.

name: Uspe (siege)
place: Uspe, town of the Siraces beyond the river Panda (site unknown, Kuban region)
commanders A: Gaius Julius Aquila, Cotys I, Eunones
why it counts: Sarmatians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Tacitus Ann. 12.15-17; en.wikipedia Roman–Bosporan War
note: Opponent: the Siraces, allies of the deposed Mithridates of the Bosporus; allies_a Sarmatians = the Aorsi. The town was stormed after its offer of 10,000 slaves was refused, and Zorsines submitted.

date: c. 50 CE (Tacitus places it in the 12th book under 50)
name: Vannius' defeat (50 CE)
war: Revolt against Vannius, king of the Danubian Suebi
place: Danube frontier of the Suebic kingdom of Vannius (Moravia / western Slovakia); exact site unknown
how the result was decided: Tacitus says Vannius' Iazyges horsemen would not be shut in the forts, so he fought in the open, was beaten and fled to the Danube fleet; Claudius settled him in Pannonia.
commanders A: Vibilius (king of the Hermunduri); Vangio and Sido (Vannius' nephews)
commanders B: Vannius (king of the Suebi); the Iazyges chiefs (not named)
sources: Tacitus, Annals 12.29-30; Wolfram, The Roman Empire and Its Germanic Peoples (1997)
note: The Iazyges are the first Sarmatians named in the Middle Danube. Their share of Vannius' army is not given, but Tacitus makes them the decisive part (the cavalry).

name: Artaxata
how the result was decided: As in Battles of the Romans: The en.wikipedia list calls it the Sack of Artaxata. Its 'Capture of Tigranocerta' (59) was a surrender without fighting and is not entered; the resistance of Legerda is entered separately.
why it counts: Tiridates I of Armenia, brother of the Parthian king Vologases I (Tac. Ann. 13.37-41)
sources: Tacitus Ann. 13.39-41; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles (Sack of Artaxata)
note: Tiridates I of Armenia, brother of the Parthian king Vologases I (Tac. Ann. 13.37-41)

name: Volandum (siege)
how the result was decided: As in Battles of the Romans: Stormed within a day, with three smaller forts; Artaxata surrendered soon after.
why it counts: Partisans of the Arsacid Tiridates I (Tac. Ann. 13.39)
sources: Tacitus Ann. 13.39; en.wikipedia Roman–Parthian War of 58–63
note: Partisans of the Arsacid Tiridates I (Tac. Ann. 13.39)

date: 61 CE (Hou Hanshu: the 4th year of Yongping)
name: Suoju (Yarkand), 61 CE
war: Khotan's wars against the oasis states of the Tarim basin
how the result was decided: The Hou Hanshu says Guangde of Khotan attacked and killed Xian and Suoju was ruled by Khotan, with thirteen states submitting.
sources: Hou Hanshu 88 (Western Regions: Yutian); Hill, The Western Regions according to the Hou Hanshu (2009); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Khotan
note: Khotanese is an eastern Iranian (Saka) language; the Hou Hanshu records only the result. Dates in the tradition differ by a year or two.

name: Tigranocerta (siege)
how the result was decided: The Parthian assault was beaten off by a sally and the siege was given up for want of fodder; Tigranocerta held.
commanders A: Tigranes VI of Armenia with the Roman garrison (Corbulo in overall command)
commanders B: Monaeses, Monobazus II of Adiabene (Vologases I at Nisibis)
Iranian force: Monaeses' picked Parthian cavalry, with the infantry of Monobazus of Adiabene, who carried the scaling ladders (Tacitus).
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
strength A: unknown (Tigranes' Armenians and a Roman garrison)
losses B: Adiabenians cut down in the sally (Tacitus)
sources: Tacitus, Annals 15.1-6; Cassius Dio 62.20; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 58-63; en.wikipedia Battle of Rhandeia
note: Tigranes' raid into Adiabene provoked the siege. The site of Tigranocerta is disputed (Arzan near Batman or Silvan/Mayafarqin).

date: c. 62-66 CE (the inscription falls under Silvanus' governorship, c. 60-67)
name: Chersonesus (siege, c. 62 CE)
war: Scythian (Crimean) attack on Chersonesus and its relief by Rome
how the result was decided: Silvanus' inscription says he compelled the king of the Scythians to raise the siege of Chersonesus, beyond the Borysthenes.
commanders B: Ti. Plautius Silvanus Aelianus (governor of Moesia)
sources: CIL XIV 3608 (Silvanus Aelianus' elogium from Tibur); Vinogradov and Zolotarev, Chersonesus and Rome (1990); Minns, Scythians and Greeks (1913)
note: Silvanus's Roman force and the Bosporan fleet are said to have been used. The Scythians are the late (Crimean) Scythians, an Iranian people by the usual account.

name: Rhandeia
place: Paetus' winter camp at Rhandeia, on the Arsanias (Murat) near Arsamosata, Turkey
how the result was decided: Paetus, blockaded in his camp, capitulated and the Romans left Armenia before Corbulo's relief arrived.
commanders A: Vologases I, Tiridates I of Armenia
Iranian force: Vologases' Parthian royal army of cavalry with Tiridates' Armenians; on the way it destroyed the Roman detachments that Paetus had posted in the Taurus passes.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
strength B: two legions (IV Scythica, XII Fulminata) with auxiliaries
losses B: the army capitulated; the forts and stores were surrendered
sources: Tacitus, Annals 15.7-17; Cassius Dio 62.21; en.wikipedia Battle of Rhandeia; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 58-63
note: Wikipedia's infobox coordinates (39.40 N, 43.80 E) do not fit its own text; the Roman-set site on the Arsanias is kept. The Romans had to bridge the Arsanias for Vologases; the treaty of Rhandeia (63/64) made Tiridates king of Armenia, crowned by Nero.

name: Moesia
place: Moesia, south of the lower Danube (site not given)
why it counts: Sarmatians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Tacitus, Histories 1.79
note: Roxolani (Sarmatians).

date: 72 CE (Josephus dates it to the 4th year of Vespasian, after the Commagene war)
name: Alan invasion of Media and Armenia
war: Alan raid through the Caucasus (called in by the king of Hyrcania)
place: Media Atropatene and Armenia (Iranian Azerbaijan, Armenia)
how the result was decided: Josephus says the Alans routed Pacorus (who fled and later ransomed his wife and concubines for 100 talents) and defeated Tiridates in a battle in which he was nearly lassoed, then went home with plunder.
commanders B: Pacorus (king of Media, brother of Vologases I); Tiridates I of Armenia (also a brother of Vologases)
sources: Josephus, Jewish War 7.244-251; Cassius Dio 66.15; Bivar, 'The Political History of Iran under the Arsacids', CHI 3(1) (1983)
note: Both sides were Iranian (the Arsacid brothers of Vologases I were Parthians). Josephus gives no place name for the fight with Tiridates.

name: Commagene
place: Commagene, near Samosata on the Euphrates
how the result was decided: As in Battles of the Romans: The battle lasted a whole day without decision; the princes then fled to Parthia and Commagene, a Hellenistic kingdom with a Greek court, was annexed.
commanders B: Epiphanes and Callinicus, sons of Antiochus IV
why it counts: Sons of Antiochus IV of Commagene; Orontid line (Commagene; Artaxiad Armenia as its branch) widely described as of Iranian origin, but disputed
