doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Josephus, Jewish War 7.219-243
note: Sons of Antiochus IV of Commagene; Orontid line (Commagene; Artaxiad Armenia as its branch) widely described as of Iranian origin, but disputed

name: Gumo (Ban Chao, 78 CE)
war: Ban Chao's reconquest of the Western Regions
how the result was decided: Ban Chao led the troops of Khotan, Shule and other states against Gumo and cut off about 700 heads, according to the Hou Hanshu.
commanders B: the king of Gumo (name not preserved)
sources: Hou Hanshu 47 (Ban Chao biography); Hill (2009); Yu Taishan, Sino-Platonic Papers 131 (2004)
note: The troop numbers and the part played by the Khotanese are from Chinese sources; the summary of the campaign is brief. Khotan is named among the allied states.

date: 87 CE (Zhanghe 1); Wikipedia's Ban Chao article has the Yarkand fight in 88
name: Shache (Ban Chao, 87 CE)
war: Ban Chao's reconquest of the Western Regions
how the result was decided: Ban Chao ambushed the 50,000-strong Kucha relief force on the night it marched past, killed 5,000, and Shache surrendered.
commanders A: Ban Chao; the king of Khotan (Guangde or his successor)
commanders B: the marshals of Kucha (about 50,000 men); the king of Shache
sources: Hou Hanshu 47 (Ban Chao biography); Hill (2009); Yu Taishan (2004)
note: Ban Chao drew his 25,000 men from Khotan and other allied states; the share of the Khotanese is not given, but Khotan is the first named and the chief ally of the Han in this region. The date is not identical in all modern accounts.

date: 90 CE (second year of Yongyuan; month not given)
name: Ban Chao's defeat of the Kushan army (90 CE)
place: Shule (Kashgar) region, western Tarim Basin, Xinjiang
how the result was decided: Xie's army, short of supplies and robbed of its couriers to Kucha, asked leave to withdraw and the Kushans later sent tribute (Hou Hanshu 47).
commanders A: Xie (Kushan deputy king); Kushan king (probably Vima Takto)
why it counts: A Kushan army led by the deputy king Xie (Hou Hanshu 47) fought Ban Chao; the Kushans are uncertain Iranians (see note).
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Hou Hanshu 47 (biography of Ban Chao) and 88 (Western Regions); Hill, J. E., Through the Jade Gate to Rome (2009); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ban_Chao
note: The Han text gives 70,000 Kushans, almost certainly inflated; Ban Chao won by scorched-earth defence and by intercepting envoys sent to the king of Kucha, with little actual fighting. The Kushans ruled Bactria and wrote Bactrian (an Eastern Iranian language), but the dynasty came from the Yuezhi, whose own language is disputed (Tocharian or Iranian), so the identification is uncertain.

date: 92 CE (spring or early summer; the year is certain, the month is not)
name: Destruction of Legio XXI Rapax (92 CE)
place: Pannonia, on the middle Danube (exact site unknown; between Carnuntum and Brigetio is the usual guess)
how the result was decided: Suetonius says the Sarmatians cut a legion and its legate to pieces; the legion is not heard of again.
commanders B: the legate of Legio XXI Rapax (name not preserved), killed with the legion
sources: Suetonius, Domitian 6.1; Cassius Dio 67.5-7; Jones, The Emperor Domitian (1992); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iazyges
note: Suetonius names the Sarmatians as the destroyers; Dio blames the Marcomanni and Quadi, and some modern accounts add Dacians. The identification of the legion as XXI Rapax rests on its disappearance from the record after 92.

name: Yanqi (Ban Chao, 94 CE)
war: Ban Chao's reconquest of the Western Regions
allies A: Khotan; Kucha; Shanshan; Shule; other Tarim states
how the result was decided: Ban Chao's army of Han officers and troops of the Tarim states took Yanqi; King Guang was captured and executed.
commanders B: Guang (king of Yanqi, captured and executed)
sources: Hou Hanshu 47 (Ban Chao biography); Hill (2009); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ban_Chao
note: Khotan is among the allied states named; the Khotanese share of the 70,000 is not given. Ban Chao's earlier defeat of the Kushans (90) is left out, since the Kushans are an uncertain case.

name: Adamclisi
why it counts: Sarmatians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Trajan's Column; Tropaeum Traiani; en.wikipedia Battle of Adamclisi; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: Dacians with Roxolani (Sarmatians) and Bastarnae. The Tropaeum Traiani (109) commemorates the victory; the altar may instead commemorate Fuscus' or Oppius Sabinus' dead.

name: Nicopolis ad Istrum
place: Near the later city of Nicopolis ad Istrum, on the Yantra
why it counts: Sarmatians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Trajan's Column; Jordanes, Getica 101; en.wikipedia Trajan's Dacian Wars; en.wikipedia Battle of Adamclisi
note: en.wikipedia's Adamclisi article calls the night battle near Nicopolis indecisive; its Dacian Wars article calls it a Roman victory.

name: Ctesiphon (116)
place: Ctesiphon, on the Tigris (near Salman Pak), Iraq
how the result was decided: Trajan took Ctesiphon with Osroes' daughter and golden throne; the king had fled and no defence is described.
Iranian force: Whatever garrison Osroes I left in his capital; no Parthian field army is recorded (the empire was split between Osroes and Vologases III).
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
borderline: capture without described fighting; kept to agree with Battles of the Romans
doubts and flags: Borderline: capture without described fighting; kept to agree with Battles of the Romans.
sources: Cassius Dio 68.28; en.wikipedia Trajan's Parthian campaign
note: Trajan took the title Parthicus in February 116, which is why some put the capture in late 115; Wikipedia's campaign article dates it to 115.

name: Maximus' defeat
how the result was decided: Maximus' army was defeated in battle and he was killed (Cassius Dio).
commanders A: probably Sanatruces, nephew of Osroes I
Iranian force: Parthian cavalry under Sanatruces, perhaps with Saka archers, acting with the rebellious cities of Mesopotamia.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no place name; kept to agree with Battles of the Romans
doubts and flags: Borderline: no place name; kept to agree with Battles of the Romans.
sources: Cassius Dio 68.30; John Malalas, Chronicle 11; en.wikipedia Trajan's Parthian campaign
note: Dio says Maximus was sent 'against the rebels'; Battles of the Romans credits the victory to the Parthians, and Wikipedia does not say whether Parthian troops took part.

name: Sanatruces' defeat
how the result was decided: Sanatruces' army was beaten and he was killed after Parthamaspates went over to the Romans (Malalas).
commanders A: Trajan, Lusius Quietus, Erucius Clarus, Julius Alexander (with Parthamaspates, who deserted Sanatruces)
Iranian force: The Parthian cavalry that Sanatruces had kept together, perhaps reinforced with Saka archers (Wikipedia, after Malalas).
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no place name; known mainly from Malalas
doubts and flags: Borderline: no place name; known mainly from Malalas.
sources: John Malalas, Chronicle 11; Cassius Dio 68.30; en.wikipedia Trajan's Parthian campaign
note: Trajan then crowned Parthamaspates at Ctesiphon; Dio credits Erucius Clarus and Julius Alexander with retaking and burning rebel Seleucia.

date: 117 CE (the end of Trajan's reign and the first months of Hadrian's)
name: Quadratus Bassus' defeat (117 CE)
place: Roman Dacia and Lower Moesia, along the Danube/Banat frontier (exact site unknown)
how the result was decided: The Roman governor of Dacia, Quadratus Bassus, was killed in the fighting, and Hadrian had to hurry to the Danube and make terms; the Roxolani were soon won over by a tribute adjustment.
commanders B: C. Julius Quadratus Bassus (governor of Dacia, killed); Q. Marcius Turbo sent to restore the frontier
sources: Historia Augusta, Hadrian 5-6; the honorific inscription for Quadratus Bassus from Pergamon; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iazyges
note: That Bassus died fighting the Sarmatians is attested; the circumstances of the fight are not. Treat as a minor, thinly sourced defeat.

date: c. 120 CE (Nashik Cave 10 inscription, year 42 of the Saka era)
name: Uttamabhadras relief (Ushavadata v Malavas, c. 120 CE)
war: Western Satrap (Kshaharata) wars in Rajasthan and Malwa
place: Pushkar region (Pokkhara), Rajasthan, India; exact site unknown
how the result was decided: The Nashik Cave 10 inscription says the Malayas fled 'at the mere roar' of Ushavadata's approach, and the Uttamabhadras they had besieged were freed.
commanders A: Ushavadata (son-in-law of Nahapana and his viceroy; son of Dinika)
sources: Nashik Cave 10 inscription of Ushavadata (Epigraphia Indica 8); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Satraps
note: Ushavadata (Rishabhadatta) is an Indian-named relative of the Saka Nahapana; the inscription is a boast, and the fight, if any, is not described.

date: c. 124 CE (range c. 105-130; Gautamiputra's inscriptions are dated by regnal years 18-19)
name: Gautamiputra Satakarni v Nahapana (c. 124 CE)
war: Satavahana reconquest of Maharashtra from the Western Satraps (Kshaharatas)
place: Nashik / Govardhana region, western Deccan (exact site unknown)
how the result was decided: Gautamiputra's inscriptions (through his mother Gautami Balasri) say he 'rooted out the Khakharata family' and destroyed Sakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas; the Jogalthembi hoard of Nahapana's coins overstruck by Gautamiputra shows the recovery of Nashik.
commanders B: Nahapana (Kshaharata satrap); Ushavadata (his son-in-law and viceroy)
sources: Nashik (Pandavleni) Cave 3 inscription of Gautami Balasri; Jogalthembi coin hoard; Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India (2008); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Satraps
note: No battle is described; the war is known from inscriptions and the overstruck coin hoard. The Kshaharatas are called Saka or Pahlava (Parthian) in different accounts; either way they are Iranian.

date: c. 127 CE (the date is that of Kanishka's accession in the Khotan tradition; uncertain)
name: Saketa (Khotan and Kanishka, c. 127)
war: Khotanese-Kushan campaign in the Ganges plain (Tibetan Khotan annals)
how the result was decided: The Tibetan Li yul lung bstan pa says the Khotanese king Vijaya Kirti and Kanishka took Saketa together.
doubts and flags: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
sources: Li yul lung bstan pa (Prophecy of the Li Country), as in Emmerick, Tibetan Texts Concerning Khotan (1967); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Khotan
note: Known only from a late Tibetan Buddhist tradition about Khotan; no independent source. Included because the Khotanese king is named as a leader.

date: 130 (traditional; modern guesses range from the 2nd to the 3rd century)
name: Salut
place: Salut, near Bisya and Bahla, Oman
how the result was decided: In the Omani tradition the Azd won the battle and the Persians left the interior of Oman.
commanders A: Malik ibn Fahm al-Azdi, Amr ibn Fahm
commanders B: the Persian marzban of Oman (named in the tradition Bara son of Dara son of Bahman)
Iranian force: In the tradition, the Persian garrison and settlers of Oman under their marzban; no reliable details.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a traditional battle of uncertain date and Persian state
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from Omani and Arab traditions written down many centuries later; modern scholars read it as a memory of the Azd migration rather than a documented event, and the date given by Wikipedia (130) is not explained. Borderline: a traditional battle of uncertain date and Persian state.
sources: Omani tradition (al-Awtabi, Ansab al-Arab; the Kashf al-Ghumma); en.wikipedia Battle of Salut (Ulrich 2008, 2019; Wilkinson)
note: Wikipedia's infobox says Parthian forces, its text 'Persian'; if the battle is historical but later, it belongs to the Sasanian period.

name: Kashgar's victory over Khotan (132 CE)
war: Khotan's wars against Keriya and the Han governors
place: Khotan / Keriya area, southern Tarim basin (Xinjiang, China)
how the result was decided: The Hou Hanshu says Chenpan's army of 20,000 beat the Khotanese, cut off several hundred heads, and the king of Keriya was replaced.
commanders A: Chenpan (king of Kashgar), with about 20,000 men
sources: Hou Hanshu 88 (Yutian); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Khotan
note: Fangqian had killed the king of Keriya (129) and kept it against Han orders; this is the Han reply. Details of the fight are thin.

name: Kanishka's war with Parthia
place: west of the Kushan realm, perhaps Aria or Bactria (site unknown), Afghanistan
how the result was decided: The only source says Kanishka won after a great slaughter of the Parthian army.
commanders B: the Parthian king (unnamed; perhaps Vologases III)
Iranian force: In the Buddhist account the Parthian king led mounted bowmen, armoured troops, foot archers and spearmen.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a war known from one Buddhist text; no battle or site is named
doubts and flags: Traditional: Attested only in the Fu fazang yinyuan zhuan, a Buddhist text translated into Chinese in the 470s, as a moral tale of Kanishka's remorse; the Parthian king is unnamed and the date is a modern inference. Borderline: a war known from one Buddhist text; no battle or site is named.
sources: Fu fazang yinyuan zhuan (Taisho 2058); en.wikipedia Kanishka's war with Parthia
note: Wikipedia's List of wars involving Iran also lists a first Parthian-Kushan war (45-50s), fought mainly by the Indo-Parthians, with no named battle.

date: before 150 CE (the Junagadh inscription is dated Saka year 72 = 150 CE); the fights are undated
name: Rudradaman v Vasishthiputra Satakarni (c. 140-150 CE)
place: Dakshinapatha (northern Deccan and the Konkan); exact sites unknown
how the result was decided: The Junagadh inscription says Rudradaman twice completely defeated the lord of Dakshinapatha, Satakarni, but spared him because of their close relationship.
sources: Junagadh (Girnar) rock inscription of Rudradaman (Epigraphia Indica 8); Kanheri inscription of Vasishthiputra Satakarni's queen; Sircar, Select Inscriptions (2005); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Satraps
note: Two battles are implied; entered as one event. Rudradaman's dynasty (Kardamaka, descended from Chashtana) is Saka by the usual account.

date: c. 150 CE (the Junagadh inscription of Saka year 72)
name: Rudradaman v the Yaudheyas (c. 150 CE)
place: Yaudheya country (Haryana / eastern Rajasthan); exact site unknown
how the result was decided: The Junagadh inscription says Rudradaman 'forcibly uprooted' the Yaudheyas, who were proud of their title 'heroes among all Kshatriyas' and would not submit.
sources: Junagadh (Girnar) rock inscription of Rudradaman, line 11; Sircar (2005); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Satraps
note: Known only from a royal inscription's boast; the place and the fighting are not described.

name: Elegeia
place: Elegeia, beyond the Cappadocian frontier near the headwaters of the Euphrates (probably Ilica, near Erzurum), Turkey
how the result was decided: Severianus' army was trapped and destroyed within three days, and he killed himself.
Iranian force: The Parthian army that Vologases IV sent into Armenia under Osroes; the sources say only 'the Parthians', i.e. the usual horse archers and cataphracts of the noble levy.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
strength B: one legion (perhaps IX Hispana) with auxiliaries
sources: Cassius Dio 71.2; Lucian, How to Write History and Alexander 27; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166

name: Cornelianus' defeat
how the result was decided: The governor's army was beaten and fled in disorder (Historia Augusta).
commanders B: Lucius Attidius Cornelianus, governor of Syria
Iranian force: The Parthian army that invaded Syria in 161-162; no details survive (normally the noble cavalry levy).
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no place name; known only from brief mentions
doubts and flags: Borderline: no place name; known only from brief mentions.
sources: Historia Augusta, Marcus 8.6; Fronto; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166

name: Artaxata
place: Artaxata, the Armenian capital on the Araxes (near Artashat), Armenia
how the result was decided: Statius Priscus captured and destroyed Artaxata.
Iranian force: Parthian troops supporting the Parthian-installed king Pacorus, with Armenian forces; no details survive.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
strength A: including I Minervia and V Macedonica
sources: Historia Augusta, Marcus 9.1; Fronto; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: The Romans founded a new capital, Kaine Polis, in 164 and made Sohaemus king of Armenia.

name: Edessa (siege, 163)
how the result was decided: The Parthians took Edessa and installed Wa'el son of Sahru as their client king.
Iranian force: A Parthian army of Vologases IV, with the Edessan partisans of Wa'el; no details survive.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the siege is known from coins and the Edessan king list; the fighting is not described
doubts and flags: Borderline: the siege is known from coins and the Edessan king list; the fighting is not described.
sources: Wa'el's coins with the Parthian king's portrait; Edessan king list; en.wikipedia Siege of Edessa (163)
note: Ma'nu VIII fled to the Romans; Wa'el ruled Edessa as a Parthian client from 163 to 165.

name: Sura (163)
place: Sura, on the right bank of the Euphrates (near Mansoura), Syria
how the result was decided: Lucian mentions a battle at Sura only in passing and no source says who won; the Parthians still held the right bank there in 163.
Iranian force: Parthian forces holding the south bank of the Euphrates; nothing more is known.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
doubts and flags: The sources consulted do not give the result, so the battle is listed but not scored.
sources: Lucian, How to Write History; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: The year is added to the Roman-set name because Khosrow I's capture of Sura (540) is another entry.

name: Ctesiphon (165)
place: Ctesiphon and Seleucia, on the Tigris (near Salman Pak), Iraq
how the result was decided: Avidius Cassius took Ctesiphon and burned the royal palace; Seleucia opened its gates and was sacked.
Iranian force: The defenders of the Parthian capital under Vologases IV's officers; no details survive.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
sources: Cassius Dio 71.2; Historia Augusta, Verus 8; en.wikipedia Battle of Ctesiphon (165); en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: Wikipedia names it the Battle of Ctesiphon (165) but describes a siege and capture. Avidius Cassius went on into Media in 166 without a recorded battle.

name: Dura-Europos (165)
place: Dura-Europos, on the middle Euphrates (near Salhiyeh), Syria
how the result was decided: Lucian reports a great Roman victory at Europos, and Dura passed into Roman hands.
Iranian force: The Parthian army on the middle Euphrates and the garrison of Dura, a Parthian-held town of Greek and Aramaic speakers; no units are named.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
losses A: 2 killed, 7 wounded (a historian mocked by Lucian)
sources: Lucian, How to Write History; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: The year is added to the Roman-set name because Shapur I's siege of Dura (256) is another entry.

name: Edessa (siege, 165)
how the result was decided: The citizens killed the Parthian garrison and opened the gates, so Edessa fell to the Roman besiegers.
commanders A: Lucius Verus (nominal), probably Martius Verus or Avidius Cassius; Ma'nu VIII
commanders B: Wa'el son of Sahru and the Parthian garrison
Iranian force: The Parthian garrison of Edessa with the Edessan partisans of Wa'el.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Edessa (165); en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
note: Ma'nu VIII was restored with the title Philorhomaios.

name: Nisibis (siege, 165)
how the result was decided: Nisibis was besieged and taken; the Parthian army dispersed and Osroes escaped by swimming the Tigris (Lucian).
Iranian force: The Parthian army that fell back from Edessa to Nisibis under Osroes; no units are named.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
sources: Lucian, How to Write History; en.wikipedia Roman-Parthian War of 161-166

date: 170 CE (the year is certain; Fronto died early in the Marcomannic invasion of Dacia)
name: Death of Fronto (170 CE)
place: Roman Dacia (the Alburnus Maior and Banat approaches; exact site unknown)
how the result was decided: Fronto's tomb inscription says he fell fighting 'against the Germans and the Iazyges' after earlier successes; it does not say who held the field.
commanders B: M. Claudius Fronto (governor of the Dacias, killed)
doubts and flags: The sources consulted do not give the result, so the battle is listed but not scored.
sources: CIL VI 1377 (Fronto's monument inscription); Historia Augusta, Marcus Aurelius 22.1; Birley, Marcus Aurelius (1987); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iazyges
note: The Iazyges hold Dacia's western edge, so they were the natural party in the attack; the inscription names them alongside the Germans.

name: Frozen Danube
place: On the frozen middle Danube (site unknown)
why it counts: Sarmatians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Cassius Dio 71.7
note: Iazyges (Sarmatians).

name: Sauromates II's defeat of the Scythians (c. 180-210)
war: Bosporan wars against the Crimean Scythians
how the result was decided: The Wikipedia summary of the Bosporan kingdom says Sauromates II inflicted a critical defeat on the Scythians and brought the whole Crimean peninsula into his state.
sources: Bosporan inscriptions (CIRB); Mielczarek, The Army of the Bosporan Kingdom (1999); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosporan_Kingdom
note: Known from inscriptions and brief summaries; no named battle. Bosporan kings after Sauromates I (93-124) are of mixed (Thracian, Greek and Sarmatian) descent, so only the Scythians are counted here.

name: Nisibis (siege, 197)
how the result was decided: Laetus held Nisibis and the Parthians raised the siege as Severus approached.
Iranian force: Vologases V's royal army, a seasonal levy of the nobles' cavalry; the sources give no breakdown.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
sources: Cassius Dio 76(75).9; en.wikipedia Septimius Severus' Parthian campaigns
note: The earlier siege of Nisibis (194) was by Abgar VIII of Osrhoene, Adiabene and Hatra without Parthian forces, and is left out.

date: late 197 or January 198 (Severus took the title Parthicus Maximus on 28 January 198)
name: Ctesiphon (198)
place: Ctesiphon, on the Tigris (near Salman Pak), Iraq
how the result was decided: Severus stormed and sacked Ctesiphon after strong resistance, and Vologases fled.
Iranian force: The garrison and people of the Parthian capital under Vologases V; the sources give no breakdown.
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
sources: Cassius Dio 76(75).9; Herodian 3.9; en.wikipedia Battle of Ctesiphon (198); en.wikipedia Septimius Severus' Parthian campaigns
note: Severus failed twice before Hatra (198 and 199), which was defended by the Hatrene army without recorded Parthian troops; those sieges are left out.

name: Nisibis (217)
how the result was decided: Cassius Dio, a contemporary, says Macrinus was beaten in the three days of fighting before Nisibis, and Herodian, who makes the slaughter even, does not have the Parthians leave the field; the 200 million sesterces Macrinus then paid for peace is a strategic matter.
Iranian force: Artabanus IV's great levy: horse archers, cataphracts, and armoured lancers mounted on camels (Herodian 4.14-15).
why it counts: Parthia: an Iranian-led state
sources: Cassius Dio 79(78).26-27; Herodian 4.15; en.wikipedia Battle of Nisibis (217); en.wikipedia Parthian war of Caracalla
note: Kept as a Parthian victory as in Battles of the Romans and Wikipedia; Caracalla had been murdered on 8 April 217. His surprise attack on Artabanus' court in 216 (Herodian) was a massacre, not a battle, and is left out.

name: Ardashir's conquest of Kerman
how the result was decided: Ardashir defeated and captured the king of Kerman and took the province (al-Tabari).
Iranian force: Ardashir's army from Persis, the Persian nobility and their mounted retainers, against the local Iranian levy of Kerman.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of Ardashir's rise, known from al-Tabari; date uncertain
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of Ardashir's rise, known from al-Tabari; date uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, History (tr. Noldeke 1879; tr. Bosworth vol. V); en.wikipedia Ardashir I
note: Al-Tabari's account comes from Sasanian royal tradition; modern historians accept the conquest but not every detail. Ardashir made his son, also named Ardashir, king of Kerman.

name: Ardashir's conquest of Isfahan
how the result was decided: Ardashir defeated and killed Shadh-Shapur, ruler of Isfahan (al-Tabari).
Iranian force: Ardashir's army of Persian nobles and their retainers, against the levy of the Parthian vassal of Isfahan.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of Ardashir's rise, known from al-Tabari; date uncertain
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of Ardashir's rise, known from al-Tabari; date uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, History (tr. Noldeke 1879; tr. Bosworth vol. V); en.wikipedia Ardashir I
note: The sequence Kerman, Isfahan, Khuzestan, Mesene, Hormozdgan follows al-Tabari; the dates are approximations.

name: Ardashir's conquest of Khuzestan
place: Khuzestan (al-Ahwaz or Susa; site unknown), Iran
how the result was decided: Ardashir defeated and killed the ruler of Khuzestan and annexed the province (al-Tabari).
Iranian force: Ardashir's army of Persian nobles and their retainers, against the forces of the Parthian vassal of Khuzestan (Elymais/Susiana).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of Ardashir's rise, known from al-Tabari; date uncertain
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name: an unnamed battle of Ardashir's rise, known from al-Tabari; date uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, History (tr. Noldeke 1879; tr. Bosworth vol. V); en.wikipedia Ardashir I
note: Wikipedia calls the slain ruler the governor of Susa; al-Tabari names Nirufar, king of al-Ahwaz, whom Artabanus had ordered to march against Ardashir.

name: Ardashir's conquest of Mesene
place: Mesene, at the head of the Persian Gulf (near Charax Spasinou), Iraq
how the result was decided: Ardashir killed the king of Mesene with his own hand and annexed Characene (al-Tabari).
factions B: Bandu, king of Mesene (Characene, a Parthian vassal)
Iranian force: Ardashir's army of Persian nobles and their retainers, against the forces of the vassal kingdom of Characene.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no conventional name: known from al-Tabari; Characene was a Parthian vassal kingdom, treated here as Parthian (civil); date uncertain
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name: known from al-Tabari; Characene was a Parthian vassal kingdom, treated here as Parthian (civil); date uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, History (tr. Noldeke 1879; tr. Bosworth vol. V); en.wikipedia Ardashir I
note: Ardashir founded Astarabadh-Ardashir (Karkh Maysan) there. Characene had been ruled by Parthian princes since Vologases IV's conquest of 151.

name: Hormozdgan
war: Sasanian overthrow of the Parthians (rise of Ardashir I)
place: plain of Hormozdgan, probably near Ram-Hormoz (Khuzestan), Iran
how the result was decided: Artabanus IV was killed and his army broke; Ardashir held the field.
commanders B: Artabanus IV (killed), the chief secretary Dad-windad
Iranian force: Ardashir's army of Persis, about 10,000 horse (later tradition), partly in mail, with his sons and the lords of Persis, Kerman and Elymais; Artabanus led the larger Parthian army of noble cavalry in lamellar armour.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: heavy; Artabanus IV killed, Dad-windad taken or killed
sources: Tabari 1.818-819; Nihayat al-arab; Bal'ami; Firuzabad relief; Iranica, Ardasir I; en.wikipedia Battle of Hormozdgan
note: Also spelled Hormozgan or Hormizdagan. The site is disputed: Ram-Hormoz (Bal'ami) is usually preferred; Iranica puts the plain in Media and Widengren at Golpayegan.

name: Hatra (siege, 227)
war: Ardashir I's western campaigns (first Mesopotamian campaign)
how the result was decided: Ardashir failed to take Hatra and marched away to Media (Cassius Dio 80.3.2).
commanders A: the king of Hatra (probably Sanatruq II)
Iranian force: Ardashir's new royal army, the Persian and Parthian noble cavalry that had joined him after Hormozdgan, with levied foot; the sources name no units.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Cassius Dio 80.3.2; Iranica, Ardasir I; en.wikipedia First Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I; en.wikipedia Fall of Hatra
note: Iranica dates the attempt c. 226-227, the Wikipedia campaign article c. 229. Dio says Ardashir breached the wall but lost many men in an ambush. Hatra, an Arab kingdom, was then probably a Roman ally.

name: Nisibis (siege, 230)
how the result was decided: The Persians besieged Nisibis but failed to take it and withdrew.
Iranian force: Ardashir's invading army, which also sent cavalry raids into Syria and Cappadocia; no units named. It was a levy of Persian and Parthian nobles fighting mainly as horse archers and armoured cavalry.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Zonaras 12.15; Herodian 6.2; Cassius Dio 80.4; Iranica, Ardasir I; en.wikipedia Sasanian campaign of Severus Alexander
note: Called Nisibis (siege) in Battles of the Romans.

name: Severus Alexander's southern column
place: lower Mesopotamia, on the march towards Ctesiphon (site unknown), Iraq
how the result was decided: Ardashir's main army caught the southern column on its own and destroyed most of it (Herodian 6.5).
commanders B: unknown (Severus Alexander led the campaign with the central column)
Iranian force: Ardashir's whole field army of mounted archers and armoured cavalry; the Historia Augusta's 120,000 cataphracts, 700 elephants and 1,800 scythed chariots (Alex. 55-56) are not credible.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: very large (Herodian); 120,000 cataphracts, 700 elephants, 1,800 scythed chariots (Historia Augusta)
borderline: no conventional name (Battles of the Romans's descriptive name)
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name (Battles of the Romans's descriptive name).
sources: Herodian 6.5-6; Historia Augusta, Alexander 55-56; en.wikipedia Sasanian campaign of Severus Alexander
note: Herodian says the Persians won by numbers; the Historia Augusta instead claims a great Roman victory, which modern historians reject. The northern column was checked by Ardashir in Media and wrecked by the Armenian winter, without a named battle.

name: Nisibis (siege, 237)
war: Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
how the result was decided: Nisibis fell to the Persians.
Iranian force: Ardashir's and Shapur's royal army, which took Carrhae next and later Hatra; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Syncellus p. 681; Zonaras 12.18; Iranica, Ardasir I; en.wikipedia Siege of Nisibis (237)
note: Called Nisibis (siege) in Battles of the Romans. The Cambridge Ancient History dates the capture of Nisibis and Carrhae to 237 and 238.

name: Carrhae (siege, 238)
war: Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
how the result was decided: Carrhae fell to the Persians.
Iranian force: Ardashir's and Shapur's royal army; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Syncellus p. 681; Zonaras 12.18; Iranica, Ardasir I; en.wikipedia Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
note: Called Carrhae (siege) in Battles of the Romans. Nothing is known of the fighting.

name: Dura-Europos (siege, 239)
war: Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
how the result was decided: The Persian attack on Dura was beaten off and the town stayed Roman until 256.
commanders B: Ardashir I and Shapur I (as rulers; field commander unknown)
Iranian force: A Sasanian raiding army; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: known mainly from a graffito saying the Persians 'came down upon us'; perhaps a raid or short attack rather than a full siege
doubts and flags: Borderline: known mainly from a graffito saying the Persians 'came down upon us'; perhaps a raid or short attack rather than a full siege.
sources: graffito SEG VII 743b; Iranica, Ardasir I; en.wikipedia Sasanian campaign of Gordian III; en.wikipedia Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
note: Iranica calls it a major raid; the Wikipedia campaign articles speak of a siege of Dura repulsed (239-241).

name: Hatra (siege, 240)
war: Second Mesopotamian campaign of Ardashir I
how the result was decided: Hatra fell after a long siege and was plundered and abandoned.
commanders B: Sanatruq II of Hatra (probably killed); a Roman garrison (cohors IX Maurorum Gordiana)
Iranian force: Ardashir's and Shapur's royal army with siege engineers; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the city destroyed; the Roman garrison probably wiped out
sources: Cologne Mani Codex; Tabari 1.827-830 (legend of al-Nadira); Iranica, Ardasir I; en.wikipedia Fall of Hatra
note: Called Hatra (siege) in Battles of the Romans. Iranica dates the fall between April and September 240; the Cologne Mani Codex points to April 241. The siege lasted one year (or two, Tabari). The tale of the princess al-Nadira betraying the city to Shapur is legend. Hatra's own army bore most of the defence.

name: Resaena
how the result was decided: The Romans routed the Persian army, which withdrew from Roman Mesopotamia (Ammianus 23.5.17).
Iranian force: Shapur I's royal army; no units named. Normally Persian and Parthian noble cavalry (armoured lancers and horse archers) with levied foot.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Ammianus 23.5.17; Historia Augusta, Gordian 26-27; Iranica, Shapur I; en.wikipedia Battle of Resaena
note: The Romans then recovered Carrhae, Nisibis and Singara without recorded battles.

name: Misiche
place: Misiche (later Peroz-Shapur, al-Anbar near Fallujah), Iraq
how the result was decided: Shapur's inscription records a great frontal battle in which the Roman army was beaten; Gordian died and Philip bought peace.
commanders B: Gordian III (died), Philip the Arab, Gaius Julius Priscus
Iranian force: Shapur I's royal army; the inscription (ŠKZ) names no units. Normally Persian and Parthian noble cavalry with levied foot.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Shapur I's inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam (ŠKZ) 3-4; Zosimus 3.32; Oracula Sibyllina 13; en.wikipedia Battle of Misiche
note: Roman sources hide the defeat and blame Philip for Gordian's death; some modern scholars think Gordian died later near Zaitha. Shapur renamed the place Peroz-Shapur ('victorious is Shapur').

name: Nisibis (siege, 252)
how the result was decided: Shapur took Nisibis.
Iranian force: Shapur I's royal army; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Tabari; Chronicle of Seert; Liber Caliphorum; en.wikipedia Siege of Nisibis (252)
note: Not mentioned in Shapur's own inscription; dated to his 11th year (252, Potter) by Syriac and Arabic sources. Nothing is known of the siege itself.

name: Antioch (siege, 253)
how the result was decided: Antioch fell to the Persians and was sacked.
commanders A: Shapur I, Hormizd(-Ardashir); the Antiochene renegade Mariades (Cyriades) as guide
Iranian force: Shapur I's royal army after Barbalissos, guided by Mariades and his Antiochene followers; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the city sacked and many deported
borderline: Ammianus says the city was taken by surprise while the people sat in the theatre: little fighting is recorded
doubts and flags: Borderline: Ammianus says the city was taken by surprise while the people sat in the theatre: little fighting is recorded.
sources: Ammianus 23.5.3; Shapur I's inscription (ŠKZ); Malalas 12; en.wikipedia Siege of Antioch (253)
note: The date of the first capture of Antioch (253 or 256) is disputed.

name: Barbalissos
place: Barbalissos (Qal'at Balis), on the Euphrates, Syria
how the result was decided: Shapur's inscription says a Roman force of 60,000 was destroyed at Barbalissos.
Iranian force: Shapur I's royal army; the inscription names no units.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Shapur I's inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam (ŠKZ) 4-5; Iranica, Shapur I; en.wikipedia Battle of Barbalissos
note: Known only from Shapur's inscription; Wikipedia dates it 252.

name: Emesa (253)
how the result was decided: The Persian force fell back from Emesa after its commander was killed, as most modern historians accept.
commanders A: Uranius Antoninus (Sampsigeramus), priest of Emesa; Odaenathus in the pursuit
commanders B: an unnamed Persian general (killed), of Shapur I's army
Iranian force: A detachment of Shapur I's army under a Persian general; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Malalas 12; Domninus of Antioch; Baldus; en.wikipedia Siege of Emesa (253)
note: Disputed: Malalas tells of the Emesene priest and his slingers routing the Persians; Overlaet argues from the Bishapur reliefs that Emesa submitted. Wikipedia calls it a siege (November 253).

name: Dura-Europos (siege, 256)
how the result was decided: Dura fell to the Persians after mining and assaults, and was abandoned.
commanders B: unknown (garrison with cohors XX Palmyrenorum and legionary detachments)
Iranian force: Shapur I's siege army with engineers who drove mines under the walls and used burning sulphur and pitch against Roman countermines; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the garrison lost; about 20 soldiers suffocated in one countermine (excavations)
sources: excavations at Dura (du Mesnil du Buisson; S. James 2011); Iranica, Dura-Europos; en.wikipedia Siege of Dura-Europos (256)
note: Called Dura-Europos (siege) in Battles of the Romans. Dated by a coin of 256 found with the dead in the countermine; some prefer 257.

name: Antioch (siege, 260)
how the result was decided: Shapur broke through the walls and took Antioch for the second time.
Iranian force: Shapur I's royal army after Edessa; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the city sacked and its people deported
sources: Shapur I's inscription (ŠKZ); Zonaras 12.23; Orosius 7.22; Iranica, Antioch; en.wikipedia Siege of Antioch (260)
note: Some scholars think Antioch fell only once, in 253 or 256 or 260.

name: Caesarea (siege, 260)
how the result was decided: The Persians took Caesarea by a night attack along a way into the city revealed by a tortured captive (Zonaras 12.23).
Iranian force: One of the columns of Shapur I's army raiding Asia Minor after Edessa; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: unknown (the city had some 400,000 people, Zonaras)
losses B: the garrison killed; the city sacked
sources: Zonaras 12.23; Shapur I's inscription (ŠKZ); en.wikipedia Siege of Caesarea in Cappadocia (260)
note: Called Caesarea (siege) in Battles of the Romans. Demosthenes broke out through the Persians and escaped (Zonaras).

name: Edessa
how the result was decided: The Roman army was beaten and Valerian was captured with the prefect, the senators and much of the army (Shapur's inscription).
Iranian force: Shapur I's royal army; his inscription lists the many provinces of Valerian's 70,000 but not his own troops.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the emperor and most of the army captured or killed
sources: Shapur I's inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam (ŠKZ) 9-11; Zosimus 1.36; Zonaras 12.23; Lactantius, De mortibus 5; en.wikipedia Battle of Edessa
note: Roman sources say Valerian was seized during a parley; the course of the battle is unclear. The first Roman emperor taken prisoner.

name: Odaenathus' attack on Shapur's retreat
place: on the Euphrates during Shapur's withdrawal (site unknown), Turkey or Syria
how the result was decided: Odaenathus fell on the Persians as they recrossed the Euphrates and took baggage, booty and some of the king's women; the Persians went on retreating.
Iranian force: The rear and baggage train of Shapur I's army returning from Syria and Asia Minor with booty and captives.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: baggage, booty and some of the royal women
borderline: no conventional name; scholars of the Persian side treat it as a minor raid on the baggage train, exaggerated by Roman writers
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name; scholars of the Persian side treat it as a minor raid on the baggage train, exaggerated by Roman writers.
sources: Historia Augusta, Gallieni 10, Tyranni triginta 15; Festus 23; Zosimus 1.39; en.wikipedia Odaenathus' Sasanian campaigns
note: Odaenathus fought as a Roman commander, with his Palmyrene army of archers, cataphracts and Arab horse. Not in Battles of the Romans.

name: Pompeiopolis
place: near Pompeiopolis (Soli, near Mersin), and Sebaste (Elaiussa), Turkey
how the result was decided: Balista broke through the Persian lines, relieved Pompeiopolis and routed the Persians, who left Cilicia.
commanders B: detachments of Shapur I's army (commanders not named)
Iranian force: Persian raiding columns besieging the Cilician coast towns, laden with booty and captives; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Zonaras 12.23; Syncellus p. 716; Historia Augusta, Gallieni 3; en.wikipedia Odaenathus' Sasanian campaigns
note: Battles of the Romans dates this to 260. Balista used ships along the coast, but the fighting was on land.

name: Ctesiphon (siege, 263)
how the result was decided: Odaenathus ravaged the country round Ctesiphon but could not take it and withdrew.
Iranian force: The garrison of the capital and the forces of Asoristan; Shapur avoided a field battle. No units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Historia Augusta, Gallieni 10; Zosimus 1.39; Festus 23; en.wikipedia Siege of Ctesiphon (263)
note: Called Ctesiphon (siege) in Battles of the Romans. Roman sources say Odaenathus beat Shapur's lieutenants in several engagements and sent prisoners to Rome for Gallienus' triumph.

name: Ctesiphon (siege, 266)
how the result was decided: Odaenathus abandoned the siege when the Goths invaded Asia Minor.
Iranian force: The garrison of the capital; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a second siege reported only by late and doubtful sources; some modern historians accept a campaign of 266/267, others doubt it
doubts and flags: Borderline: a second siege reported only by late and doubtful sources; some modern historians accept a campaign of 266/267, others doubt it.
sources: Historia Augusta, Gallieni 12; en.wikipedia Odaenathus' Sasanian campaigns
note: One tradition even claims Odaenathus took Ctesiphon. Odaenathus was murdered on his way back. Not in Battles of the Romans.

name: Carus' victory over the Sarmatians
why it counts: Sarmatians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Historia Augusta, Carus 9.4; Eutropius 9.18
note: Carus then marched against the Persians.

name: Ctesiphon (283)
place: Ctesiphon and Seleucia (Coche), on the Tigris (near Salman Pak), Iraq
how the result was decided: Carus routed the Persians and took Seleucia (Coche) and Ctesiphon (Zonaras 12.30).
commanders B: unknown (Bahram II was in the east)
Iranian force: The garrison of the capital and the troops left in Asoristan while Bahram II fought the revolt of his brother Hormizd; the Persians tried to flood the Roman camp by diverting a canal (Zonaras).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Zonaras 12.30; Historia Augusta, Carus 8; Eutropius 9.18; en.wikipedia Carus' Sasanian campaign
note: Called Ctesiphon in Battles of the Romans. Carus died soon after near Ctesiphon (struck by lightning, the story goes) and the army withdrew.

name: Meinas Sabatha (siege)
place: Meinas Sabatha, on the Royal Canal near Seleucia, Iraq
how the result was decided: Carus besieged and took Meinas Sabatha after stiff resistance.
Iranian force: The garrison and local forces of Asoristan; Bahram II and his main army were away fighting his brother Hormizd's revolt in the east, which was backed by Sakas and Kushans.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Zosimus 3.23; en.wikipedia Carus' Sasanian campaign
note: Called Meinas Sabatha (named here as a siege, as the campaign article describes 'the siege and capture of the city') in Battles of the Romans.

name: Carrhae (296)
how the result was decided: Narseh routed Galerius' army in the last of the engagements between Carrhae and Callinicum; Galerius and Tiridates fled with the remnant.
Iranian force: Narseh's royal army, partly raised on the Euphrates frontier; no units named. Normally Persian and Parthian noble cavalry with levied foot.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Eutropius 9.24; Festus 25; Orosius 7.25; Ammianus 14.11.10; en.wikipedia Battle of Carrhae (296)
note: Called Carrhae in Battles of the Romans. Orosius counts three engagements, the first two indecisive; here one entry, as in Battles of the Romans.

name: Satala (298)
place: Armenia, probably at Osxay in the district of Basean east of Erzurum (Satala was the Roman base), Turkey
how the result was decided: Galerius surprised Narseh's camp at dawn and routed his army, taking his harem and treasury.
Iranian force: Narseh's royal army, mostly cavalry, encamped with the king's household, women and treasury; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: about 25,000 (Roman sources), with the Armenian royal army
losses B: very heavy; the royal household captured
sources: Festus 25; Eutropius 9.25; Lactantius, De mortibus 9; Buzandaran III.21; en.wikipedia Battle of Satala (298); en.wikipedia Galerius' Sasanian campaigns
note: Called Satala in Battles of the Romans. Also called the battle of Erzurum or of Osxay. It led to the Peace of Nisibis (299).

date: 322 CE (323 for the law that follows; the campaign is often given as 322)
name: Rausimodus' crossing of the Danube (322 CE)
place: Middle Danube frontier (Pannonia/Moesia), then across the river in barbarian territory (exact site unknown)
how the result was decided: Constantine drove the raiders back, pursued them over the Danube and killed Rausimodus there.
sources: Zosimus 2.21; Origo Constantini Imperatoris (Anonymus Valesianus); Wolfram, History of the Goths (1990); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rausimod
note: Rausimodus is usually called a king of the Sarmatians, but some readings of the sources make him a Goth. The Wikipedia article calls him 'Sarmatian or Maeotian' and suggests he may be the Bosporan king Rhadamsades. Identification disputed.

name: Arest
war: Shapur II's wars in Armenia (Persian invasion of 337-338)
place: Arest, on the north shore of Lake Van, Turkey
how the result was decided: The Armenian army routed the Persian invaders (Armenian tradition).
commanders B: unknown (the army was let in by the Armenian traitor Databen Bznuni)
Iranian force: A Persian invading army said to number 30,000; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from later Armenian tradition; its date (336-338) and the Persian figure of 30,000 are uncertain and the story may be embellished.
sources: later Armenian tradition (Movses Khorenatsi); Syvänne, Military History of Late Rome 284-361, p. 307; en.wikipedia Vache I Mamikonian; en.wikipedia Khosrov III the Small
note: Databen was stoned as a traitor afterwards. Soon after, perhaps in 338, Vache Mamikonian was killed in an unnamed defeat by the Persians (Buzandaran III.11).

name: Narasara
place: Narasara, in upper Mesopotamia; perhaps Nararra east of Amida, or near Nineveh or Singara, Turkey
how the result was decided: The Persian army was beaten and its commander Narseh killed (Festus 27).
commanders B: Narseh, brother (or son) of Shapur II (killed)
Iranian force: A Persian army under the prince Narseh which had taken Amida; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Festus 27; Libanius; Theophanes AM 5829; en.wikipedia Battle of Narasara
note: Date (335, 337, 341 or 343) and site are disputed; some think it is the same as the battle of Singara. The Romans then retook Amida.

name: Nisibis (siege, 338)
how the result was decided: Shapur raised the siege after about sixty days and Nisibis held.
Iranian force: Shapur II's whole army of cavalry, infantry and elephants, with siege engines, towers, mines and a dam on the river (Theodoret).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: heavy, with plague in the camp
sources: Theodoret, Historia ecclesiastica 2.30 and Historia religiosa 1; Chronicon Paschale; Jerome, Chronicle; en.wikipedia Siege of Nisibis (338)
note: Called Nisibis (siege) in Battles of the Romans. Theodoret's account (flood and wall rebuilt overnight) may mix this siege with that of 350. Wikipedia dates it 15 June to August 338.

name: Singara (344)
how the result was decided: The Romans drove the Persians back and stormed their camp but were thrown out at night with heavy losses; both sides claimed the victory and modern scholars call it indecisive.
Iranian force: Shapur II's royal army of armoured cavalry, archers and infantry with a fortified camp (Julian, Oration 1; Libanius, Oration 59); no peoples named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Julian, Oration 1; Libanius, Oration 59; Festus 27; Eutropius 10.10; Jerome, Chronicle; en.wikipedia Battle of Singara (344)
note: Called Singara in Battles of the Romans. Jerome's Chronicle puts a night battle at Singara in 348; Wikipedia's war article also describes a night raid on a Persian camp at Singara in 348, perhaps the same battle.

name: Nisibis (siege, 346)
how the result was decided: Shapur was repulsed and gave up the siege.
Iranian force: Shapur II's royal army; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Jerome, Chronicle; Theophanes; Dodgeon and Lieu; en.wikipedia Perso-Roman wars of 337-361
note: Called Nisibis (siege) in Battles of the Romans. Little is known of this second siege.

name: Nisibis (siege, 350)
how the result was decided: The assault through the breach made by the flood stuck in the mud and failed, and Shapur raised the siege.
Iranian force: Shapur II's army of armoured cavalry, archers and war elephants with towers, with boats floated on the flooded plain after the Mygdonius was dammed (Julian, Orations 1 and 2).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Julian, Orations 1 and 2; Ephrem, Carmina Nisibena; Zonaras 13.7; en.wikipedia Siege of Nisibis (350)
note: Called Nisibis (siege) in Battles of the Romans. Shapur left for the east, where nomads (Chionites) had invaded.

name: Satala (350)
place: the Persian camp at Osxay (Voskha) in Basean, near Satala, Turkey
how the result was decided: The Persian camp was taken and the shah fled, losing his treasure and women (Buzandaran).
commanders A: Armenian princes with Roman forces (names uncertain)
commanders B: the shah (called Narseh by Faustus; Shapur II at this date)
Iranian force: The shah's army and household in a fortified camp; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the camp, treasure and royal women taken
borderline: possibly a doublet of Satala (298)
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from the Buzandaran (Faustus of Byzantium, III. Borderline: possibly a doublet of Satala (298).
sources: Buzandaran Patmut'iwnk' III.21 (Garsoïan 1989, pp. 98-100); en.wikipedia Shapur II's invasion of Armenia (350)
note: Listed in Wikipedia's campaign box as Battle of Satala (c. 350); also called Voskha.

date: 358 CE (spring-summer; follows the Sarmatian raid on Pannonia Valeria of 357)
name: Constantius II against the Sarmatians (358)
place: Middle Danube and the Tisza (Parthiscus) confluence, Sarmatian lands (Serbia / Hungary)
how the result was decided: Ammianus has the Sarmatian prince Zizais throw himself at the emperor's feet and the Limigantes give hostages after Roman and allied forces attacked them from three sides.
commanders B: Zizais (Sarmatian prince); Limigantes chiefs; Vitrodorus and Agilimundus (Quadi)
sources: Ammianus Marcellinus 17.12-13; Barnes, Ammianus Marcellinus and the Representation of Historical Reality (1998); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iazyges
note: Ammianus describes a campaign with some fighting and a submission, not a named pitched battle; kept low because the Acimincum ambush of 359 (already in the dataset) is the real fight of this war.

name: Acimincum
place: Acimincum (Stari Slankamen), on the Danube, Pannonia Secunda
why it counts: Sarmatians among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Ammianus 19.11.1-16
note: The Limigantes were the former subject people of the Sarmatians.

name: Amida (siege, 359)
how the result was decided: Amida fell to the besiegers after 73 days.
commanders A: Shapur II, Tamsapor, Grumbates king of the Chionites, the king of the Albani (Urnayr)
commanders B: Aelianus (crucified afterwards); Ursicinus outside the city
Iranian force: Shapur II's royal army of cataphracts, archers and infantry with the royal guard, the Segestani (Sakas of Sistan) with elephants, the Gelani and the Vertae, and the allied Chionites under Grumbates and the Albani (Ammianus 18.6, 19.1-2).
languages: Persian; Parthian; East Iranian; Daylami and Caspian; other Caucasian; other
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: seven legions with some cavalry, plus townsmen and refugees; modern estimates 5,300 to 20,000 soldiers
losses B: most of the garrison killed or captured; the city sacked and its people deported
sources: Ammianus Marcellinus 18.6-19.9 (eyewitness); en.wikipedia Siege of Amida (359)
note: Called Amida (siege) in Battles of the Romans. The son of Grumbates was killed before the walls, which provoked the siege. Ammianus was inside the city and escaped.

name: Bezabde (Roman siege)
place: Bezabde (Phoenice, near Cizre), on the Tigris, Turkey
how the result was decided: Constantius gave up the siege when the winter rains came, and the Persian garrison held the town.
Iranian force: The strong garrison left by Shapur II, archers and picked men, who sallied and burned the Roman rams and engines (Ammianus 20.11).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Ammianus 20.11; en.wikipedia Constantius II's siege of Bezabde
note: Constantius withdrew to Antioch.

name: Bezabde (siege)
place: Bezabde (Phoenice, near Cizre), on the Tigris, Turkey
how the result was decided: A ram brought down a tower and the Persians stormed Bezabde.
commanders B: garrison of legiones II Flavia, II Armeniaca and II Parthica with Zabdicene archers (commander unknown)
Iranian force: Shapur II's army with rams, archers and armoured assault troops; no peoples named (Ammianus 20.7).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Ammianus 20.7; en.wikipedia Shapur II's siege of Bezabde
note: Shapur repaired the walls and left a strong garrison.

name: Singara (siege, 360)
how the result was decided: A ram brought down a newly repaired tower and Singara fell after a few days.
commanders B: garrison of legio I Flavia and legio I Parthica (commander unknown)
Iranian force: Shapur II's army with battering rams and archers; no peoples named (Ammianus 20.6).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the garrison and people taken captive to Persia
sources: Ammianus 20.6; en.wikipedia Siege of Singara (360)
note: Called Singara (siege) in Battles of the Romans.

name: Virta (siege)
place: the fortress of Virta (Birtha, probably Tikrit), Iraq
how the result was decided: The garrison beat off the assaults and Shapur withdrew across the Tigris.
Iranian force: Shapur II's army returning from Bezabde; no peoples named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Ammianus 20.7.17-18; en.wikipedia Perso-Roman wars of 337-361
note: The identification of Virta with Tikrit is probable but not certain.

name: Ganzak (363)
place: Ganzak in Atropatene (near Takab or Leylan), Iran
how the result was decided: Vasak surprised the Persian army before it had assembled; it broke and fled, and he pursued it (Buzandaran).
commanders A: Vasak Mamikonian, for King Arshak II
Iranian force: Shapur II's army gathering in Atropatene for the invasion of Armenia; no units named.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from the Buzandaran (Faustus of Byzantium), whose stories of Vasak Mamikonian's victories over Shapur are exaggerated and loosely dated; the year 363 and Shapur's presence are uncertain.
sources: Buzandaran Patmut'iwnk' IV; en.wikipedia Battle of Ganzak (363); en.wikipedia Armeno-Sasanian Wars of 363-371
note: Wikipedia lists the Romans with the Armenians in the war box; the Buzandaran account is Armenian only.

name: Pirisabora (siege)
how the result was decided: After two days of fighting the defenders gave up the walls and then surrendered the citadel.
Iranian force: A strong Persian garrison under Mamersides with the townspeople; about 2,500 people in all (Wikipedia, after Zosimus).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the garrison surrendered; the city burned
sources: Ammianus 24.2.9-22; Zosimus 3.17-18; Libanius, Oration 18; en.wikipedia Siege of Pirisabora
note: Called Pirisabora (siege) in Battles of the Romans. Soon after, Surena surprised three Roman squadrons of scouts nearby, an unnamed skirmish.

name: Ctesiphon (363)
place: the east bank of the Tigris before Ctesiphon (near Salman Pak), Iraq
how the result was decided: The Romans forced the river crossing and drove the Persians into Ctesiphon with about 2,500 dead to 70 Roman.
Iranian force: Ranks of mailed cataphract cavalry, close-order infantry with oblong wicker shields behind them, and elephants in the rear (Ammianus 24.6.8).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Ammianus 24.6; Zosimus 3.24-25; Libanius, Oration 18; en.wikipedia Battle of Ctesiphon (363)
note: Called Ctesiphon in Battles of the Romans. Shapur II and his main army were away; Julian then decided not to besiege the city and burned his fleet.

name: Maiozamalcha (siege)
how the result was decided: The Romans broke into the city through a mine and took it.
Iranian force: A Persian garrison under Nabdates (he and 80 of his men were taken alive) with the armed townspeople; a sally hit the Roman cattle.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the inhabitants massacred; Nabdates and 80 men captured
sources: Ammianus 24.4.1-27; Zosimus 3.20-22; Libanius, Oration 18; en.wikipedia Siege of Maiozamalcha
note: Called Maiozamalcha (siege) in Battles of the Romans.

name: Maranga
place: Maranga, on the Tigris north of Ctesiphon, Iraq
how the result was decided: The Persian attack was beaten off and the Persians withdrew, leaving the Romans the field.
commanders B: Merena, commander of the cavalry, two sons of Shapur II and many satraps (Ammianus 25.1.11)
Iranian force: Mail-clad cataphracts in close order, archers, and elephants (Ammianus 25.1.12-14).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: Julian's main army (about 65,000 at the start, Zosimus)
sources: Ammianus 25.1.11-19; Zosimus 3.28; en.wikipedia Battle of Maranga
note: A three-day truce followed.

name: Samarra (363)
place: on the Tigris south of Samarra, Iraq
how the result was decided: The Romans drove off the Persian attack on their column with heavy loss, Merena and Nohodares among the dead, and held the field at nightfall; Julian's mortal wound is not a battlefield result (Ammianus 25.3).
Iranian force: Cavalry with elephants attacking the Roman rear and left flank (Ammianus 25.3); fifty nobles and satraps fell.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: Julian's main army (about 65,000 at the start, Zosimus)
losses B: heavy; two commanders and fifty nobles and satraps killed (Ammianus)
sources: Ammianus 25.3; Zosimus 3.28-29; Libanius, Oration 18; en.wikipedia Battle of Samarra (363)
note: Called Samarra in Battles of the Romans, which scores it a draw because of Julian's death; here the battlefield result decides: the Romans held the field. Wikipedia's campaign article misdates it to 26 July. Jovian's retreat after it brought further unnamed fighting (Sumere, Charcha, four days at Dura) and the peace of 363, ceding Nisibis and Singara.

date: winter 367/368 - spring 368 (some date the fall to 369 or 370)
name: Artogerassa (siege)
place: Artogerassa (Artagers), in Arsharunik on the Araxes; probably near Kagizman, Turkey
how the result was decided: The fortress fell to Shapur's blockade and assaults and the queen and the royal treasure were taken; the night sortie that routed the first besiegers did not end the siege.
commanders A: Shapur II; at first the Armenian renegades Cylaces (Glak) and Artabannes (Vahan)
commanders B: Queen Pharandzem (Parandzem), wife of Arsaces II
Iranian force: First a siege corps under the Armenian renegades Cylaces and Artabannes (who went over to the queen and let her sortie rout their camp), then Shapur II's main army (Ammianus 27.12.5-12). No composition given.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: most of the garrison died of disease and hunger (Faustus)
sources: Ammianus 27.12.5-12; Faustus of Byzantium (Buzandaran) book 4; Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002); en.wikipedia Siege of Artogerassa
note: Faustus says the siege lasted 13 months. It followed the capture of Arsaces II by treachery.

name: Bagavan
place: near Bagavan (Vagabanta), in Bagrevand, at the foot of Mount Npat near the source of the Arsanias (Murat), Turkey
how the result was decided: After answering a Persian cavalry attack the Romans and Armenians routed the Persians, who withdrew with heavy losses (Ammianus 29.1.3).
commanders A: Traianus and Vadomarius; Mushegh Mamikonian (Armenian sparapet), with King Pap watching from Mount Npat
commanders B: Shapur II's generals; King Urnayr of Albania (wounded), Meruzhan Artsruni
Iranian force: The army sent by Shapur II, with the contingent of his ally King Urnayr of Caucasian Albania and Armenian renegades under Meruzhan Artsruni (Faustus 5.4).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Ammianus 29.1.2-4; Faustus of Constantinople 5.4-5; Movses Khorenatsi; en.wikipedia Battle of Bagavan
note: Also called Dzirav (Movses Khorenatsi), which Manandian and Garsoian regard as an error or a conflation with Faustus' battle of Gandzak (a Faustus-only battle with Shapur present, not listed separately). A truce followed.

date: 374 CE (autumn; Theodosius the Younger was dux of Moesia Prima)
name: Moesia Prima (Theodosius v Sarmatians, 374)
war: Sarmatian and Quadi invasions under Valentinian I
place: Moesia Prima, on the Danube (Viminacium region, Serbia); exact site unknown
how the result was decided: Ammianus says Theodosius, as dux of Moesia, beat off a Sarmatian invasion with heavy losses to the invaders.
commanders A: Theodosius (later Theodosius I), dux of Moesia Prima
sources: Ammianus Marcellinus 29.6.15; Zosimus 4.16; Pacatus, Panegyric of Theodosius; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodosius_I
note: The best-attested fight of Theodosius before his accession, but brief and undated in detail. The invaders may have included Quadi.

date: c. 370-375 CE (Ammianus gives no year; modern dates run c. 370 to 375)
name: Tanais (Huns v Alans, c. 374)
place: Steppe between the Don (Tanais) and the Volga, the land of the Tanaite Alans (Russia)
how the result was decided: Ammianus says the Huns killed and plundered many Alans and joined the rest to themselves by treaty.
sources: Ammianus Marcellinus 31.3.1-3; Jordanes, Getica 123-126; Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973); Thompson, The Huns (1996); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alans
note: This is the opening of the Hun westward move that led to the Gothic crossing of the Danube in 376. Several fights are summarised in one sentence; entered as one event.

date: c. 375-376 CE (after the death of Ermanaric)
name: Vithimiris' last battle (c. 376)
place: Gothic steppe north of the Black Sea, between the Dniester and the Don (exact site unknown)
how the result was decided: Ammianus says Vithimiris held out for a while with Alan hirelings but was beaten and killed in battle.
commanders B: Vithimiris (Greuthungian king, killed); Alatheus and Saphrax (regents for his son Viderichus)
sources: Ammianus Marcellinus 31.3.3; Heather, The Goths (1996); Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)
note: Whether the hired force was Alan or Hun is a textual problem in Ammianus; most editors read Alans. The Alan share is unknown.

name: Dibaltum
place: outside Dibaltum (Deultum, Debelt), near the Black Sea coast of Thrace
why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Ammianus 31.8.9-10; en.wikipedia Battle of Dibaltum

name: Constantinople
commanders A: unknown; the empress Dominica paid volunteers (Socrates)
why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Ammianus 31.16.4-7; Socrates, Ecclesiastical History 5.1; Sozomen 7.1; Zosimus 4.22; en.wikipedia Gothic War (376-382)
note: Ammianus tells of a Saracen who drank the blood of a slain Goth, which unnerved the Goths.

name: Adrianople
place: north of Adrianople (Edirne), at the Gothic wagon laager
why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Ammianus 31.12-13; Zosimus 4.24; Orosius 7.33; Socrates, Ecclesiastical History 4.38; en.wikipedia Battle of Adrianople
note: Valens' body was never found. The Greuthungi and Alans under Alatheus and Saphrax decided the battle.

name: Poetovio
war: Civil war of Theodosius I and Magnus Maximus
why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Panegyrici Latini 2(12).35-36; Orosius 7.35.4; Zosimus 4.46; en.wikipedia Battle of Poetovio
note: Maximus was handed over at Aquileia and executed on 28 August 388.

name: Save
war: Civil war of Theodosius I and Magnus Maximus
place: on the Save near Siscia (Sisak), Pannonia Savia
why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Panegyrici Latini 2(12).32-34; Orosius 7.35.3-4; Zosimus 4.46; en.wikipedia Battle of Poetovio
note: Also called the battle of Siscia.

name: Frigidus (Theodosius v Eugenius, 394)
war: War of Theodosius against Eugenius and Arbogast
place: River Frigidus (Vipava), Julian Alps, Slovenia (exact field disputed)
allies A: Gothic, Iberian, Hunnic and Alan federates
how the result was decided: Theodosius' army, aided by the bora wind on the second day, broke Arbogast's; Eugenius was captured and executed and Arbogast killed himself.
commanders A: Theodosius I; Timasius; Stilicho; Gainas; Saul; Bacurius the Iberian (killed); Alaric (Gothic contingent)
sources: Zosimus 4.57-58; Orosius 7.35; Rufinus (via Socrates 5.25, Sozomen 7.24); Claudian, III Cons. Honorii; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Frigidus
note: Zosimus names Gainas, Saul and Bacurius as the federate commanders; Saul is described as a pagan barbarian of uncertain nation, an Alan in some accounts (the Saul of Pollentia, 402). The Wikipedia article does not mention Alans, so the Alan element rests on Saul and is weak.

name: Hunnic raid of 395
place: the Tigris-Euphrates lands near Ctesiphon, Iraq
how the result was decided: The Huns fled before the Persian army; one column was overtaken and partly destroyed and the Persians recovered the booty and 18,000 captives.
commanders A: the Sasanian army of Bahram IV (no general named)
Iranian force: The Sasanian royal army; no composition recorded (normally the asawaran cavalry of the Iranian nobility with infantry levies).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: part of one column killed; 18,000 captives freed
borderline: a pursuit during a raid; known as an engagement only from a campaign article, not a named battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: a pursuit during a raid; known as an engagement only from a campaign article, not a named battle.
sources: Priscus; Greatrex and Greatrex, Byzantion 69 (1999) 65-75; Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns 54; en.wikipedia Hunnic raid of 395
note: The Huns came through the Caucasus, raided Roman Armenia and Syria and then went down the Euphrates; the second column escaped through the Derbent pass.

name: Pollentia
why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Claudian, De bello Getico; Orosius 7.37; Prudentius, Contra Symmachum 2; Jordanes, Getica 154-155; en.wikipedia Battle of Pollentia
note: Result disputed: Roman sources claim a clear victory (the Gothic camp, with Alaric's wife, was taken), Jordanes a Gothic one; Alaric withdrew in good order.

date: c. 395-410 CE (Rudrasimha III's reign is given as c. 388-415; Chandragupta's Udayagiri inscription of 401 and Sanchi inscription of 412-413 show him holding Malwa)
name: Chandragupta II v Rudrasimha III (c. 395-410 CE)
war: Gupta conquest of the Western Satraps
place: Malwa and Gujarat (Ujjain region); exact site unknown
how the result was decided: The Satrap coinage ends and Gupta silver coins imitating it appear in Gujarat and Malwa; Chandragupta's Sanchi and Udayagiri inscriptions record his conquest of the region.
commanders B: Rudrasimha III (last Western Satrap, killed in the later tradition)
doubts and flags: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
sources: Udayagiri and Sanchi inscriptions of Chandragupta II (401-413); Visakhadatta, Devichandragupta (fragments quoted in the Natyadarpana and Shringaraprakasha); Upinder Singh (2008); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Satraps
note: The conquest is attested by coins and inscriptions; the story of Chandragupta killing the Saka king in disguise is from the lost play and is a doubtful tradition. Dates in the range 395-415 are all argued.

name: Florence (siege)
why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Zosimus 5.26; Orosius 7.37; Paulinus, Vita Ambrosii 50; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles; en.wikipedia Stilicho
note: Stilicho's arrival ended the siege and drove Radagaisus onto the hills of Faesulae (next entry); Florence was nearly lost.

date: summer-autumn 406 CE (before the Rhine crossing of 31 December 406)
name: Rhine frontier (Franks v Vandals and Alans, 406)
war: Vandal, Alan and Suebic invasion of Gaul
place: Rhine frontier, probably near Mainz (Germany; exact site unknown)
how the result was decided: The Franks killed Godigisel and about 20,000 Vandals, until Respendial's Alans came up and routed the Franks, saving the Vandals.
sources: Renatus Profuturus Frigeridus, in Gregory of Tours, Histories 2.9; Orosius 7.38; Prosper (Chronicle, 406); MacDowall, Germanic Warrior AD 236-568 (2016); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respendial
note: Likely several actions summarised as one. Respendial's Alans decided the day; the other Alan group under Goar had already gone over to the Romans.

name: Faesulae
place: The hills of Faesulae (Fiesole), above Florence
why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Zosimus 5.26; Orosius 7.37; Augustine, De civitate Dei 5.23; Olympiodorus fr. 9; en.wikipedia List of Roman battles
note: Radagaisus' host (Goths with others) was surrounded and starved rather than beaten in a pitched battle; 12,000 of his best men were taken into Roman service. Radagaisus was executed on 23 August 406.

date: 416-418 CE (Hydatius puts the final defeat of the Alans in 418; some scholars 426)
name: Wallia's war on the Alans and Silings (Spain, 416-418)
war: Visigothic campaigns in Spain for Honorius
place: Baetica and Lusitania (Andalusia and Portugal); exact sites unknown
how the result was decided: Hydatius says Wallia annihilated the Silingi, and the Alans were so cut up that Addac fell and the survivors, leaderless, joined the Asding king Gunderic.
commanders B: Addac or Attaces (Alan king, killed); Fredbal (Siling king, captured)
sources: Hydatius, Chronicle (years 416-418); Orosius 7.43; Kulikowski, Late Roman Spain and Its Cities (2004); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alans
note: The campaign spans several years and several fights that the sources do not separate. After it the Alans fought as part of the Vandal kingdom.

name: Nervasos Mountains
place: The Nervasian mountains (Nerbasii montes), Gallaecia; site unknown
why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Hydatius 71, 74; en.wikipedia Battle of the Nervasos Mountains
note: The Vandals lifted their siege of the Suebi when Asterius approached, but on their retreat they killed some of Maurocellus's men at Bracara (Braga); the usurper Maximus, backed by barbarians, was put down at the same time.

name: Arzanene
place: Arzanene, east of the Tigris, Turkey
how the result was decided: Ardabur defeated Narses' army, which retreated (Socrates 7.18).
Iranian force: Narses' frontier army; no composition recorded (the Sasanian field army of the period was built around the asawaran heavy cavalry and horse archers of the Iranian nobility, with infantry levies).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Socrates, Historia Ecclesiastica 7.18; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Roman-Sasanian War of 421-422
note: Narses then tried to strike into Roman Mesopotamia but was intercepted by Ardabur.

name: Nisibis (siege, 421)
how the result was decided: Ardabur raised the siege and withdrew when Bahram V's relief army approached; the Persians kept Nisibis.
commanders A: the garrison of Nisibis; Bahram V (relief army); al-Mundhir I (Lakhmid)
Iranian force: The Persian garrison of Nisibis and Bahram V's relief army, with the Lakhmid Arabs of al-Mundhir I (Socrates 7.18).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Socrates, Historia Ecclesiastica 7.18; Malalas; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Roman-Sasanian War of 421-422
note: Socrates also tells how al-Mundhir's Arabs panicked and drowned in the Euphrates and how the Persian 'Immortals' were ambushed; neither is a separately named battle. Battles of the Romans lists the Lakhmids as 'Arabs'.

name: Theodosiopolis (siege, 421)
place: Theodosiopolis, probably in Armenia (Erzurum), Turkey; possibly Resaina in Osrhoene
how the result was decided: The Persians lifted the siege after about 30 days, when a stone-thrower killed one of their vassal kings (Theodoret 5.37).
commanders B: Bahram V's army (a vassal king was killed by a stone-thrower)
Iranian force: 'Many thousands' of soldiers with siege engines including a helepolis (Theodoret); composition not given.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Theodoret, Historia Ecclesiastica 5.37.6-10; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Theodosiopolis
note: The town is usually taken to be Theodosiopolis in Armenia (Erzurum); some identify it with Theodosiopolis-Resaina (Ras al-Ayn) in Osrhoene. Theodoret's account is hagiographic.

name: Tarraco
why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Hydatius 77; Prosper s.a. 422; Salvian 7.11; en.wikipedia Battle of Tarraco
note: The battle was fought in Baetica; the name Tarraco comes from a modern addition to an online translation of Hydatius (Castinus may have retreated to Tarraco). The Vandals kept Baetica.

name: Ravenna (425)
war: War of the Eastern Empire against the usurper Joannes
how the result was decided: Aspar's cavalry crossed the marsh by an unguarded path and took Ravenna; Joannes was captured and killed.
commanders A: Aspar (Alan by descent); Ardabur (Aspar's father, an Alan); Candidianus
commanders B: Joannes; Castinus; Aetius (arrived after the fall)
sources: Socrates, Church History 7.23; Philostorgius 12.13; Prosper (425); Martindale, PLRE 2, 'Fl. Ardabur Aspar'
note: Counted by the leader rule: Aspar is described as of Alanic (or Alanic-Gothic) descent. His troops were Eastern Roman, so the contingent is not Alan.

name: Merv (427)
how the result was decided: In the tradition Bahram surprised and routed the invaders near Merv, killing their king and capturing his wife.
commanders B: the Kidarite king ('khaqan of the Turks' in Tabari), killed
Iranian force: A picked force of the Persian nobility's cavalry, raised partly in Armenia and Azerbaijan while Mihr Narseh stayed as regent (Tabari).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from Tabari, Dinawari, Thaalibi and the Shahnameh, which draw on the Sasanian royal tradition and the romance of Bahram Gur; modern historians accept a Persian success against the Kidarites about 427 but not the details.
sources: Tabari (tr. Bosworth, vol. 5, 95-96); Daryaee (2000); en.wikipedia Bahram V; en.wikipedia Sasanian-Kidarite wars
note: A general then pursued the enemy into Transoxiana and defeated them again (Tabari). The enemy is called Turks or Hephthalites in the Arabic sources; modern historians identify them as Kidarites.

date: 428 CE (Wikipedia; Hydatius' sequence puts it in 428-429, shortly before the Vandal crossing to Africa)
name: Mérida (Vandals and Alans v Suebi, 428)
war: Vandal and Suebic wars in Gallaecia and Lusitania
how the result was decided: Hydatius says Gaiseric turned back, caught the Suebi near Mérida and drove them into the Guadiana, where Heremigarius drowned.
commanders A: Gaiseric (king of the Vandals and Alans)
commanders B: Heremigarius (Suevic leader, drowned in the Guadiana)
sources: Hydatius, Chronicle (years 428-429); Thompson, Romans and Barbarians (1982); Kulikowski (2004)
note: Hydatius and the standard accounts name the Vandals only; no source says Alans fought here. After 418 the Alans were part of the Vandal kingdom (Gaiseric is 'king of the Vandals and Alans'), so an Alan contingent is likely but not recorded.

name: Hippo Regius (siege)
