why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Possidius, Vita Augustini 28-29; Procopius, Wars 3.3.30-36; en.wikipedia Siege of Hippo Regius
note: Augustine died in the besieged city on 28 August 430. The Vandals raised the siege after about 14 months (a technical Roman success), but occupied the abandoned city after the battle of 431/432.

date: 431 (Procopius places it after the long siege of Hippo; some date it 432)
name: Africa (Boniface and Aspar's defeat by the Vandals, 431)
war: Vandal conquest of Africa (Roman relief expedition from the East)
place: near Hippo Regius (Annaba), Algeria; site not recorded
side B: Western Roman army and the Eastern relief army of Aspar
how the result was decided: The combined Roman army was defeated, Boniface sailed for Italy and Hippo was abandoned (Procopius, Vand. 3.3.35-36; Prosper Tiro).
Iranian side: Western Roman army and the Eastern relief army of Aspar
sources: Procopius, Wars 3.3.35-36; Prosper Tiro, Chronicle s.a. 431; Hydatius; Wikipedia 'Aspar'
note: Aspar, magister militum of the Eastern army, was of Alan descent (his father Ardabur and his own name are Alan); the Eastern army that he brought is not described as Alan, so the qualification is the commander. Procopius gives no place or numbers and the Vandals' own Alan element is not counted here. Weak: a defeat known only from short notices.

name: Avarayr
place: the plain of Avarayr, in Artaz (near Chors, Chaypareh County), Iran
how the result was decided: The Persians broke the Armenian army and held the field, killing Vardan and eight other generals; the later religious concessions are a strategic matter.
Iranian force: Mushkan's army of asawaran cavalry with the royal 'Immortals' and war elephants, joined by the Armenian loyalists of Vasak Siwni (Elishe; his 300,000 is rhetorical).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: 1,036 killed (Elishe), including Vardan and eight generals
sources: Elishe, History of Vardan and the Armenian War; Lazar Parpetsi; Hewsen, 'Avarayr', Encyclopaedia Iranica; en.wikipedia Battle of Avarayr
note: A revolt of a Persian-ruled province (Persarmenia), hence opponent group 'Rebels'. Yazdegerd II afterwards dismissed Vasak and eased religious pressure.

name: Catalaunian Plains
place: The Catalaunian Plains (Campus Mauriacus), Champagne; site unknown
commanders A: Flavius Aetius; Theodoric I (killed); Thorismund; Sangiban
why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Jordanes, Getica 190-218; Hydatius 150; Prosper s.a. 451; en.wikipedia Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
note: Wikipedia's infobox calls it inconclusive; Attila was driven back to his laager and then withdrew from Gaul. Date 20 June after Bury (others: early July or 27 September). Proposed sites: Montgueux near Troyes, Méry-sur-Seine, La Cheppe. Attila's allies included Ostrogoths and Gepids.

name: Orléans (siege)
commanders A: Bishop Anianus (in the city); Flavius Aetius and Theodoric I (relief)
why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Jordanes, Getica 194-195; Gregory of Tours 2.7; Vita Aniani; en.wikipedia Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
note: Attila broke off his final assault when the relief army approached; some historians see the defence of Orléans as the real turning point of 451.

date: c. 455-457 CE (Bhitari pillar, undated; Junagadh inscription of 457-458 mentions the mlecchas)
name: Skandagupta's war with the Hunas (c. 455-457)
place: North-western frontier of the Gupta empire (battlefield not named; Punjab and Indus approaches), India/Pakistan
how the result was decided: The Bhitari pillar claims Skandagupta's arms made the earth tremble in the clash and the Gupta heartland stayed intact.
why it counts: The Bhitari pillar says Skandagupta met the Hunas in battle; the Hunas of c. 456 are identified as Kidarites or Alchon Huns, both of uncertain Iranian identity.
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Bhitari pillar inscription of Skandagupta; Junagadh rock inscription of Skandagupta (year 138); Bakker, H., The Alkhan (2020); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skandagupta
note: The only evidence is a vague royal praise-inscription and the identification of the mlecchas and Hunas is inferred; the site, scale and even the date within 455-467 are unknown. The Huna enemy is called Kidarite or Alchon depending on the scholar; both are of disputed Iranian identity.

date: c. 455-459 (the Life of Vakhtang puts it in his sixteenth year; a reconstruction)
name: Ossetians (Vakhtang I's first campaign, c. 455-459)
war: Wars of Vakhtang I Gorgasali (Ossetian raid on Iberia)
place: Dvaleti and the Darial approaches, north Georgia / North Ossetia; approximate
how the result was decided: Vakhtang won the single combat with the enemy champion and freed his sister Mirandukht; the raiders were beaten (Life of Vakhtang Gorgasali).
commanders A: Vakhtang I Gorgasali (then a youth, with his father Mirdat)
doubts and flags: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition. Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Juansher, Life of Vakhtang Gorgasali (Georgian Chronicles); Wikipedia 'Vakhtang I of Iberia' (fetched 1 Nov 2026); Suny, The Making of the Georgian Nation
note: Vakhtang belonged to the Chosroid house, which the Georgian Chronicles trace to the Persian Mihranids (Mirian III), and his mother Sagdukht is called Persian; 'Ossetians' (Ovsi) is the Georgian name for the Alans, though Wikipedia says they may have been Huns. Known only from the Life of Vakhtang; the date is reconstructed.

name: Arelate
why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Sidonius, Carmen 5; Hydatius 197; Gregory of Tours 2.11; en.wikipedia Battle of Arelate; en.wikipedia Majorian
note: Also called the Battle of Arles (458). Theodoric II had been besieging Aegidius in Arles; after the defeat the Visigoths returned to federate status and gave up Septimania.

name: Cartagena
place: Portus Ilicitanus (Santa Pola), bay of Alicante
why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Hydatius 200; Marius of Avenches s.a. 460; en.wikipedia Battle of Cartagena (461)
note: Despite the name it was fought near Elche (Ilici), not at Cartagena; 13 May 460 is sometimes given. Majorian made peace and was deposed and killed in 461.

name: Bergamo
why it counts: Alans among the belligerents in Ancient Greek Battles or Battles of the Romans
sources: Fasti Vindobonenses priores s.a. 464; Marcellinus Comes s.a. 464; Jordanes, Getica 236; en.wikipedia Battle of Bergamo
note: The day is flagged as uncertain on Wikipedia.

date: c. 466 CE (war began c. 464; victory announced at Constantinople in 467)
name: Peroz I's defeat of the Kidarites (c. 466)
how the result was decided: Peroz briefly took Tokharistan, minted gold at Balkh on Kidarite models and sent victory embassies in 467-468.
commanders A: Peroz I; Mehama (Hephthalite or Alchon lord of Kadag)
why it counts: Peroz I, a Persian king, led the Sasanian army with Hunnic allies against the Kidarite king Kunkhas (Priscus fr. 41; Bactrian documents).
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Priscus fr. 41 (Blockley); Sims-Williams, N., Bactrian Documents from Northern Afghanistan; Rezakhani, K., ReOrienting the Sasanians (2017); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peroz_I; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidarites
note: No battle narrative survives: the war is known from Priscus (Peroz's trick marriage offer and the 300 Persian officers maimed at Balaam), the victory embassy and Peroz's Balkh coinage. The Kidarites are Huns of disputed Iranian identity.

name: Bolia (Ostrogoths v Suebi and allies, 468)
war: Ostrogothic wars on the middle Danube
place: River Bolia, south of the Danube in Pannonia (Hungary; proposals include Pilismarot and Csem)
side B: Suebi; Sarmatae; Gepids; Rugi; Sciri; Heruli
how the result was decided: Jordanes says the Goths beat the coalition of Suebi, Sarmatians, Gepids, Rugi and Sciri, though the Wikipedia article notes that Hyun Jin Kim argues the Goths lost and left for the south.
commanders A: Theodemir (Valamir had already fallen); the young Theodoric
commanders B: Hunimund (king of the Suebi); Beuca (named with the coalition, apparently the Sarmatian king); Hunulf (Sciri)
sources: Jordanes, Getica 53 (277-279); Wolfram, History of the Goths (1990); Gracanin and Skrgulja (2014); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bolia
note: Jordanes lists Sarmatae among the coalition. By this date 'Sarmatians' of the Pannonian plain were remnants of the Iazyges and Limigantes mixed with Goths and Huns, so their Iranian character is doubtful; the Sarmatian leader's name is not certain.

date: c. 469-474 CE (Wikipedia gives c. 474; sources are vague)
name: Peroz I's first defeat by Akhshunwar (c. 474)
place: Hephthalite frontier near Gurgan (Gorgan), north-eastern Iran/Turkmenistan
how the result was decided: Peroz was captured and had to be ransomed (Procopius says by the emperor Zeno) and to swear to keep the peace.
why it counts: Peroz I (a Persian king) led the Sasanian army against the Hephthalite king Akhshunwar and was ambushed and captured (Procopius, Wars 1.3-4; Tabari).
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.3-4; al-Tabari; Pseudo-Joshua the Stylite; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peroz_I
note: The Procopius account (the prostration to the rising sun, the concealed ditch) is anecdotal and the ditch trick is also told of the 484 battle, so which war it belongs to is disputed; some scholars count only two Hephthalite wars before 484. Not to be confused with the 484 battle (Herat), already in the dataset.

name: Akori
place: Akori (Arguri), on the northern slope of Mount Ararat, Turkey
how the result was decided: Vahan's rebels routed the marzban's army and killed Adhur Gushnasp (Lazar Parpetsi).
Iranian force: The marzban's army of about 7,000 horsemen (Lazar Parpetsi), Persian cavalry with some Armenian loyalists.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Lazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians; en.wikipedia Vahan Mamikonian
note: A revolt of a Persian-ruled province, hence opponent group 'Rebels'.

name: Akesga
how the result was decided: The Armenians, left without the Iberian help they expected from Vakhtang, were routed and two of their leaders killed.
commanders B: Vahan Mamikonian; Vasak Mamikonian and Sahak II Bagratuni (both killed)
Iranian force: Shapur Mihran's army sent against the Iberian and Armenian rising; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: unknown; Vasak Mamikonian and Sahak Bagratuni killed
sources: Lazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians; en.wikipedia Vahan Mamikonian
note: Wikipedia does not name the Persian commander at Akesga; Shapur Mihran led the Persian army in the area (Lazar Parpetsi).

name: Nersehapat
how the result was decided: Vahan defeated the Persian reinforcements and held the field (Lazar Parpetsi).
commanders B: commander of the Persian reinforcements (not named in Wikipedia)
Iranian force: Persian reinforcements sent by Peroz I; no numbers or units given.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Lazar Parpetsi, History of the Armenians; en.wikipedia Vahan Mamikonian

name: Herat (484)
place: near Balkh or Herat (the site is uncertain), Afghanistan
how the result was decided: The Persian army was ambushed and destroyed (in Procopius' account in a hidden trench) and Peroz was killed.
Iranian force: Peroz's 'enormous' royal army of the asawaran and the great houses (a Mihran among the commanders); no numbers or units given.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the whole army; Peroz and four of his sons and brothers killed, his daughter and treasure captured
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.4; Joshua the Stylite; Tabari; Schindel, 'Kawad I', Encyclopaedia Iranica; en.wikipedia Hephthalite-Sasanian War of 484
note: Wikipedia's article is titled 'Hephthalite-Sasanian War of 484' and places Peroz's last camp near Balkh after an advance from Herat; the battle is often called after Herat. Khonsarinejad and Khorashadi (2021) doubt the trench story. Peroz had earlier been defeated and captured by the Hephthalites (c. 474-481) in battles that have no name.

name: Sukhra's Hephthalite campaign
how the result was decided: In Tabari's account Sukhra heavily defeated the Hephthalites and made Khushnavaz return Peroz's treasure, his daughter and the chief priest.
commanders A: Sukhra (Zarmihr) of the house of Karen
Iranian force: The remnant of the Sasanian army rallied by Sukhra ('the majority of the Sasanian army', Tabari).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a campaign rather than a named battle
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known only from Tabari and the later Perso-Arabic tradition, which glorifies the Karen family; the Roman and Syriac sources know only that Persia then paid tribute to the Hephthalites, and modern historians treat the victory as doubtful or as a negotiated return of the captives. Borderline: a campaign rather than a named battle.
sources: Tabari; Pourshariati, Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire (2008); Schindel, 'Kawad I', Encyclopaedia Iranica; Rezakhani, ReOrienting the Sasanians (2017); en.wikipedia Sukhra's Hephthalite campaign

date: c. 502 (Javakhishvili) or c. 522-527 (Sanadze); undated in the Life
name: Iberia (Vakhtang I's last battle against the Iranians, c. 502 or 522)
war: Persian invasion of Iberia under Kavadh I (death of Vakhtang I)
place: Kartli near Mtskheta, Georgia; the Life names Mtskheta as his burial place
how the result was decided: Vakhtang died fighting the invaders and an Iranian viceroy governed Tiflis by 518 (Wikipedia; Life of Vakhtang).
commanders B: Vakhtang I Gorgasali (died of his wounds)
doubts and flags: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
sources: Juansher, Life of Vakhtang Gorgasali; Wikipedia 'Vakhtang I of Iberia' (fetched 1 Nov 2026); Suny, The Making of the Georgian Nation
note: Vakhtang is said to have refused Kavadh's summons to join the war against Rome; the Iranian army that invaded Iberia fought him (the Life says he died at the hands of a renegade slave). Sasanian side Persian; Vakhtang's Chosroid house is of Persian Mihranid descent by the Georgian tradition (uncertain). Known only from the Life; no place or date is firm.

name: Amida (siege, 502)
how the result was decided: Amida fell to Kavad's assault in January 503 after a three-month siege.
commanders B: Cyrus (governor of Mesopotamia), Leontius, Paul bar Zainab
Iranian force: Kavad I's royal army with Armenian and Arab (Lakhmid) allies (Joshua the Stylite, Zacharias); Hunnic troops are mentioned in some accounts.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: no regular troops; the citizens defended the walls
losses B: 80,000 dead including civilians (Wikipedia infobox, from the Syriac sources)
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.7; Joshua the Stylite; Zacharias of Mytilene book 7; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Amida (502-503)
note: Kavad had earlier taken Theodosiopolis (by betrayal) and Martyropolis (by surrender) in 502; those captures without real fighting are not listed.

name: Amida (siege, 503)
how the result was decided: After a blockade of more than a year the starving Persian garrison gave Amida back to the Romans.
Iranian force: A garrison of 3,000 Persians under Glones (Joshua the Stylite); Patricius also defeated a Persian relief force.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: Glones and many of the garrison killed
sources: Joshua the Stylite; Procopius, Wars 1.9; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: The garrison surrendered the city in early 505 in return for payment under the truce (Procopius gives 1,000 lb of gold); scored as a besieger's success as in Battles of the Romans.

date: 503 (before the attack on Edessa in September)
name: Constantia (siege, 503)
how the result was decided: Kavad failed to take Constantia and moved on to Edessa.
commanders A: the garrison and citizens of Constantia
Iranian force: Kavad's main army; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the fighting was slight; the townspeople even supplied Kavad's army
doubts and flags: Borderline: the fighting was slight; the townspeople even supplied Kavad's army.
sources: Joshua the Stylite; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: Constantia and Constantina are the same city (Viransehir).

name: Nisibis (503)
how the result was decided: After an early Roman success Kavad's counter-attack drove Areobindus' army back westward.
Iranian force: Kavad's main army at Nisibis; no composition recorded (asawaran cavalry with levies).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: about 12,000 (Areobindus' division of the 52,000-man Roman army)
sources: Joshua the Stylite; Procopius, Wars 1.8; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: Asouades was probably a Kindite chief (Battles of the Romans lists 'Arabs').

name: Tell Beshme
place: between Apadna (Opadna) and Tell Beshme, between Amida and Nisibis, Turkey
how the result was decided: Hypatius and Patricius were routed and fled to Samosata, losing much of their cavalry in the retreat.
Iranian force: Kavad's main army (no composition recorded), which had just plundered Areobindus' fort at Apadna.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: about 40,000 (the divisions of Hypatius and Patricius)
sources: Joshua the Stylite; Procopius, Wars 1.8; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: Also called the battle of Apadna (Opadna).

name: Edessa (siege, 503)
how the result was decided: The Persian assaults on Edessa failed and Kavad withdrew to Persia.
Iranian force: Kavad's army with Lakhmid Arab allies, who overran much of Osrhoene (Joshua the Stylite).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Joshua the Stylite; Procopius, Wars 1.8; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Anastasian War
note: A Hunnic raid into Persian Armenia helped persuade Kavad to withdraw.

date: c. 510 CE or slightly earlier (the Eran pillar of Goparaja is dated Gupta year 191 = 510 CE and records the battle as past; the 29 June date in some summaries is the date of the pillar, not of the fight)
name: Second Battle of Eran (c. 510)
place: Eran (ancient Airikina), Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: The Eran inscription records a great battle in which Goparaja died but does not say who won; Toramana's boar inscription shows him ruling Eran soon after.
why it counts: Toramana, king of the Alchon Huns (of disputed Iranian identity), is the probable enemy of the Gupta army in the Eran inscription of Goparaja; the inscription does not name him.
doubts and flags: The sources consulted do not give the result, so the battle is listed but not scored. Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Eran inscription of Goparaja (Gupta year 191); Eran boar inscription of Toramana; Bakker, H., The Alkhan (2020); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Battle_of_Eran
note: Wikipedia's infobox says Gupta victory, but Bakker notes the inscription is silent on the outcome and Goyal argues the battle may precede Toramana's conquest of eastern Malwa. The opponent is not named in the text; the identification with Toramana's Huns is inferred.

name: Rishtal (Aulikara-Huna war, c. 515)
war: Gupta-Huna wars (Aulikara-Hunnic war, end of the First Hunnic War)
place: Rishtal near Sitamau/Mandsaur (Dasapura), Madhya Pradesh, India (site approximate)
how the result was decided: The Rishtal inscription claims Prakashadharma ambushed the Huns, routed them and sacked Toramana's camp.
why it counts: Toramana, Alchon Hun king (disputed Iranian identity), is named as the defeated Huna overlord in the Rishtal inscription of Prakashadharma.
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Rishtal inscription of Prakashadharma (discovered 1983; edited by Salomon); Bakker, H., The Alkhan (2020); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aulikara%E2%88%92Hunnic_War
note: A single victory inscription gives the only account; the fight at Rishtal is as the inscription says, the identification of the Huna with Toramana is by the editors. Toramana's death at Varanasi is a later and weak claim.

name: Persarmenia
how the result was decided: Narses and Aratius defeated the second Roman raid into Persarmenia (Procopius 1.12.20-22).
Iranian force: Persian forces in Persarmenia under the Armenian brothers Narses and Aratius (Kamsarakan), then in Persian service; no numbers given.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.12.20-22; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Iberian War
note: The first Roman raid had plundered Persarmenia unopposed. Narses and Aratius later went over to Rome (530).

name: Thebetha (siege)
place: Nisibis, then the Persian fortress of Thebetha, fifteen parasangs from Dara, Turkey
how the result was decided: Libelarius' attacks on Nisibis and Thebetha achieved nothing and he withdrew in the summer heat; the Persian strongholds held.
commanders A: the garrisons of Nisibis and Thebetha
Iranian force: Persian frontier garrisons; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: little fighting is described
doubts and flags: Borderline: little fighting is described.
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.12.23-24; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Iberian War

name: Mindouos
place: Mindouos (Melebasa, modern Ogunduk), north of Nisibis, Turkey
how the result was decided: The Persians defeated the Roman army building a fort at Mindouos and the survivors fled to Dara (Procopius 1.13.1-8).
commanders A: Persian army (commander not named by Procopius)
Iranian force: A Persian field army; no composition recorded (asawaran cavalry with levies).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.13.1-8; Zacharias of Mytilene book 9; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Thannuris
note: Possibly the same engagement as Thannuris (Hughes); kept separate as in Wikipedia and Battles of the Romans.

name: Sondani (Yashodharman v Mihirakula, c. 528)
place: Sondani (Sondni), near Mandsaur (Dasapura), Madhya Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: The Mandasor pillar says Yashodharman made Mihirakula bow his head and the Huns lost their Indian possessions soon after.
why it counts: Mihirakula, the Alchon Hun king (disputed Iranian identity), is the defeated opponent in the Mandasor pillar inscription of Yashodharman.
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Mandasor (Sondani) pillar inscriptions of Yashodharman and Vishnuvardhana; Xuanzang, Records of the Western Regions (Baladitya); Bakker, H., The Alkhan (2020); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sondani
note: No battle narrative: the 'battle' is inferred from a victory pillar that says Mihirakula submitted. The alliance with the Guptas and Mihirakula's capture are later tradition.

name: Thannuris
place: Thannuris (Tell Tuneinir), on the Khabur, south of Dara, Syria
how the result was decided: A feigned retreat drew the Roman cavalry into hidden ditches; the Roman army was routed, the unfinished fort destroyed and Belisarius fled to Dara.
commanders B: Belisarius, Bouzes, Coutzes (captured or killed), Proclianus (killed), Sebastian, Basil; Jabala (Ghassanid, killed)
Iranian force: A Persian army of about 30,000 (Zacharias), its cavalry decisive, under Xerxes and Peroz of the house of Mihran.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: presumably larger (Syvanne: about 30,000 cavalry and 10,000 infantry)
losses B: heavy: most of the infantry killed or captured
sources: Zacharias of Mytilene book 9; Procopius, Wars 1.13.1-8; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Thannuris
note: Wikipedia and Battles of the Romans treat Thannuris and Mindouos as separate battles; Hughes argues Procopius compressed them into one.

date: c. 530 CE (undated; Xuanzang's story written c. 645)
name: Baladitya's capture of Mihirakula (Xuanzang's tradition, c. 530)
war: Gupta-Huna wars (Second Hunnic War, traditional account)
place: Magadha (a narrow pass or island refuge, site not named), Bihar, India
how the result was decided: Xuanzang says Baladitya captured Mihirakula and spared his life at his mother's request.
why it counts: Mihirakula, Alchon Hun king (disputed Iranian identity), is the defeated enemy in Xuanzang's story.
doubts and flags: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition. Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Xuanzang, Datang Xiyu ji; Upinder Singh, Political Violence in Ancient India (2017); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihirakula
note: Known only from a Buddhist pilgrim's report a century later; modern writers call it fanciful and may be a doublet of the Sondani victory. Included as a traditional entry.

name: Dara (530)
place: before the walls of Dara (Anastasiopolis; Oguz), Turkey
how the result was decided: The Persian army broke and fled on the third day with about 8,000 dead, leaving the field to the Romans.
commanders A: Belisarius, Hermogenes; Bouzes, Pharas, John son of Nicetas, Sunicas and Aigan
Iranian force: Perozes' 40,000 cavalry and infantry, reinforced by 10,000 from the Nisibis garrison: asawaran cavalry on the wings, the 'Immortals' in reserve and poorly armed levy infantry in the centre (Procopius 1.13-14).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: about 8,000 (3,000 cavalry, then 5,000 in the rout)
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.13-14; Zacharias of Mytilene book 9; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Dara
note: The Roman army included Hunnic and Herul units (listed as allies in Battles of the Romans); they were in Roman service and are not given as allies here.

name: Satala (530)
how the result was decided: Sittas' flank attack broke the Persian army, which retreated to Persarmenia.
Iranian force: About 30,000: Persarmenian levies, Sunitae from the Caucasus and 3,000 Sabir Huns, under Mihr-Mihroe (Procopius 1.15.1-2).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.15; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Satala (530)

name: Martyropolis (siege, 531)
how the result was decided: The Persians abandoned the siege after Kavad's death and agreed an armistice; the town held.
Iranian force: A large Persian army under three generals; no composition recorded. Sabir Huns hired by Persia raided Roman territory at the same time (Procopius 1.21).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.21; Malalas; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Martyropolis (531)

name: Callinicum (531)
place: on the Euphrates opposite Callinicum (Raqqa), Syria
how the result was decided: The Persians broke the Roman right and held the field; the Roman infantry escaped across the Euphrates at nightfall.
commanders B: Belisarius, Hermogenes, Sunicas, Simmas; al-Harith ibn Jabalah (Ghassanid)
Iranian force: Azarethes' 15,000 asawaran cavalry with about 5,000 Lakhmid Arab horse under al-Mundhir III (Procopius 1.17-18).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: heavy; Ascan, Longinus and Stephanacius killed
sources: Procopius, Wars 1.17-18; Malalas; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Callinicum
note: A costly victory: Azarethes was disgraced by Kavad for his losses.

name: Beroea (siege, 540)
how the result was decided: The Persians took and burned the town, and the garrison of the acropolis, out of water, went over to Khosrow (Procopius 2.7).
commanders B: the garrison of the acropolis; Bishop Megas negotiated
Iranian force: Khosrow I's royal invasion army; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: town burned; garrison went over to the Persians
borderline: a ransom dispute with brief fighting at the acropolis; not a named battle in Wikipedia
doubts and flags: Borderline: a ransom dispute with brief fighting at the acropolis; not a named battle in Wikipedia.
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.7; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II
note: Hierapolis, Chalcis, Apamea and Edessa bought Khosrow off without fighting in 540 and are not listed.

name: Dara (siege, 540)
how the result was decided: Dara was still invested and untaken when Khosrow, his mine countermined, took 1,000 lb of silver from the city and withdrew (Procopius 2.13.28): a siege ended by payment is a draw.
Iranian force: Khosrow I's royal army returning from Syria; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.13.16-29; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II
note: Battles of the Romans scores it a Roman defensive success; here a siege bought off while the place was still invested counts as a draw.

name: Sura (siege, 540)
place: Sura, on the Euphrates west of Callinicum, Syria
how the result was decided: After the garrison commander was killed in the first assault the Persians broke into Sura during a parley and took it.
Iranian force: Khosrow I's royal invasion army; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.5; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II

name: Antioch (540)
how the result was decided: The Persians stormed the walls when the Roman soldiers fled, beat the armed young men of the city in the streets and sacked Antioch.
Iranian force: Khosrow I's royal invasion army; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: city sacked; many inhabitants deported to Weh Antiok Khosrow
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.8-9; Malalas; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II
note: Battles of the Romans types it as a land battle; it was an assault on the city, so siege is set true here.

name: Nisibis (541)
how the result was decided: Nabedes' midday sally routed Peter's division, but Belisarius' main body drove the Persians back inside the walls with the loss of 150 men and held the field.
Iranian force: The Nisibis garrison under Nabedes, a strong force of Persian cavalry and infantry (Procopius 2.18).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: unknown (the Army of the East with Gothic and Ghassanid troops)
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.18; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Nisibis (541)
note: Outcome disputed: Battles of the Romans scores it a draw (Nisibis was not taken) and Wikipedia a Persian victory (for the rout of Peter); under this set's field test the Romans won, since the Persians were driven back into the city. Belisarius was not besieging the city, and soon judged it too strong and moved on.

name: Petra (siege, 541)
place: Petra (Tsikhisdziri), on the Black Sea coast, Georgia
how the result was decided: Persian miners brought down a tower and the garrison surrendered.
commanders A: Khosrow I, Aniabedes; Gubazes II of Lazica
Iranian force: Khosrow I's invasion army, guided by the Lazi of Gubazes II, who had invited him in; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses A: many lost to terrain, sickness and hunger
losses B: garrison surrendered and joined the Persians
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.17; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Petra (541)
note: Wikipedia gives February-June 541.

name: Sisauranon (siege, 541)
how the result was decided: After a failed assault the blockaded garrison, out of food, surrendered.
Iranian force: A garrison of 800 elite Persian horsemen under Bleschames (Procopius 2.19).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: garrison surrendered; the horsemen were sent to Italy
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.19; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Sisauranon (541)

name: Sergiopolis (siege)
how the result was decided: The Persian assault failed and the besiegers, short of water and food, withdrew.
commanders A: the garrison of about 200 (commander unknown); Bishop Candidus
Iranian force: A detachment of 6,000 (Procopius) from Khosrow's army; Ambros, a Christian Arab in al-Mundhir's service, warned the defenders.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: 6,000 (Procopius; Wikipedia gives a range up to 60,000)
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.20; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Sergiopolis

name: Anglon
place: Anglon, about 21 km from Dvin, Armenia
how the result was decided: Nabedes' men held the fortified village and routed the Roman army, which fled leaving its baggage.
commanders B: Martinus, Peter, Valerian, Isaac, Philemuth; Narses and Adolius (killed)
Iranian force: Nabedes' 4,000 men from the forces in Persarmenia, holding the village houses, the fort and a trench (Procopius 2.25).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.25; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Anglon
note: The Roman army included Herul troops (listed as allies in Battles of the Romans).

name: Edessa (siege, 544)
how the result was decided: After the siege mound was burnt and the assaults were beaten off, the siege ended in an armistice for which the still-invested city paid 500 lb of gold (Procopius 2.27.45-46): a siege ended by payment is a draw.
Iranian force: Khosrow I's royal army with siege engines and a great earth-and-timber mound; only Azarethes' division is named, and Huns appear in some modern accounts (uncertain).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.26-27; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Edessa (544)
note: Battles of the Romans scores it a Roman defensive success; here a siege bought off while the place was still invested counts as a draw. Khosrow's last assault had failed before the payment, so a Roman win is also arguable. A five-year truce followed in 545.

name: Petra (siege, 549)
place: Petra (Tsikhisdziri) and the passes into Lazica, Georgia
how the result was decided: Dagisthaeus raised the siege when Mihr-Mihroe's relief army broke through the passes; the Persian garrison held Petra.
commanders B: Dagisthaeus, John Guzes (wounded); Gubazes II of Lazica
Iranian force: A garrison of 1,500 under Mihran, relieved by Mihr-Mihroe's army of cavalry and infantry from Iberia, about 40,000 strong according to Wikipedia (Procopius 2.29-30).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses A: garrison 1,000 killed and 350 wounded; over 1,000 of the relief army killed in the passes
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.29-30; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Petra (549)
note: The Romans had breached part of the wall before the relief arrived. Mihr-Mihroe left 3,000 men in Petra.

name: Hippis
how the result was decided: The Romans and Lazi routed the Persian army on the Hippis and Chorianes was killed.
Iranian force: Chorianes' army of Persians with Alan allies (Procopius 8.1).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Procopius, Wars 8.1; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Lazic War

name: Phasis River
how the result was decided: The Romans and Lazi surprised the Persian supply corps left to provision Petra and destroyed it.
Iranian force: The 5,000 men left by Mihr-Mihroe under Fariburz to keep Petra supplied (Procopius 2.30).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: most of the 5,000; their supplies captured
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.30; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Lazic War

name: Petra (siege, 550)
how the result was decided: Bessas stormed Petra; the last defenders died when the citadel was set on fire.
Iranian force: A Persian garrison of 2,300 (Procopius); Mihr-Mihroe's relief army (mostly cavalry, with eight elephants) came too late.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: 1,570 killed and 730 captured (712 of them wounded); 500 died in the burning citadel
sources: Procopius, Wars 8.11-12; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Petra (550-551)
note: Sabir Huns allied to Rome built light rams for the assault.

name: Archaeopolis
how the result was decided: A sortie of the garrison routed the Persians assaulting the walls and Mihr-Mihroe withdrew with heavy losses.
Iranian force: Mihr-Mihroe's army of Persian cavalry and infantry, with Daylamite foot (Procopius' 'Dolomites') and elephants (Procopius 8.13-14).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Procopius, Wars 8.13-14; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Lazic War
note: An assault on a fortified town ended by a sortie; typed as a battle as in Battles of the Romans.

name: Telephis-Ollaria
place: Telephis and Ollaria, on the Phasis, Lazica, Georgia
how the result was decided: A Persian stratagem drew the Romans out of Telephis and routed them; they abandoned both strongholds and fell back to Nesos.
Iranian force: Mihr-Mihroe's army, smaller than the Roman one (Agathias 2.19-22); no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Agathias 2.19-22; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Mihr-Mihroe's campaign of 554
note: Wikipedia's campaign article dates it 553 in the infobox and the Lazic War article to summer 555.

name: Onoguris (siege)
how the result was decided: A Persian relief force of 3,000 horse routed the besieging Roman army, which fled.
commanders B: Martin, Bouzes, Wilgang the Herul, Usigardus, Dabragezas
Iranian force: The garrison of Onoguris and a relief force of 3,000 cavalry (Agathias 3.6-8).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Agathias 3.5-8; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Onoguris

name: Phasis (siege)
place: Phasis (Poti), at the mouth of the Rioni, Georgia
how the result was decided: A Roman sortie routed the besiegers and Nachoragan raised the siege.
commanders A: Martin, Justin son of Germanus, Angilas, Theodore, Valerian
Iranian force: Nachoragan's army of 60,000 (Agathias): asawaran cavalry, levy infantry (paygan), Daylamite auxiliaries fighting on foot with sword, shield and javelins, and war elephants.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: at least 10,000 soldiers (mostly levies) and about 2,000 servants (Agathias)
sources: Agathias 3.19-28; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Phasis
note: Wikipedia gives spring/July 555 to 556 for the operations around Phasis.

name: Gol-Zarriun
how the result was decided: The Hephthalites were routed near Bukhara and Ghadfar fled south into Persian territory.
Iranian force: Unknown: Khosrow I attacked the Hephthalites from the south in concert with the Turks; whether Persian troops fought at Gol-Zarriun itself is not recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the Persian presence at the battle itself is uncertain; the Turks fought it and Khosrow may have campaigned separately
doubts and flags: Borderline: the Persian presence at the battle itself is uncertain; the Turks fought it and Khosrow may have campaigned separately.
sources: Tabari; Firdawsi, Shahnameh; Bivar, 'Hephthalites', Encyclopaedia Iranica; Rezakhani, ReOrienting the Sasanians (2017); en.wikipedia Battle of Gol-Zarriun
note: The Turks took the lands north of the Oxus and the Sasanians those to the south.

name: Hadhramaut
place: Hadhramaut (near the Persian landing place; site unknown), Yemen
how the result was decided: Wahrez killed Masruq with an arrow and the Aksumite army broke and fled.
Iranian force: Wahrez's expedition: 800 men taken from the prisons, said to be Daylamites (Tabari; Ibn Qutayba gives 3,600 or 7,500), sailing in eight ships of which two were lost, joined by Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan's Yemeni followers.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: unknown (6,000-10,000 in Wikipedia's infobox, attribution unclear)
sources: Tabari (tr. Bosworth, vol. 5); Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham; Bosworth, 'Abna', Encyclopaedia Iranica; Potts, 'Arabia ii', Encyclopaedia Iranica; en.wikipedia Battle of Hadhramaut; en.wikipedia Aksumite-Persian wars
note: Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan was a Himyarite prince; 'Himyar' stands for his Yemeni followers. The details (the convicts, Wahrez's arrow) come from the Arab tradition, but the Persian conquest of Yemen is historical.

name: Sanaa (siege, 570)
how the result was decided: Sanaa fell to Wahrez, who installed Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan as a Persian vassal king.
Iranian force: Wahrez's expeditionary force (about 700 by Wikipedia's infobox), mostly Daylamite and Persian, with Sayf's Yemenis.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the tradition has Wahrez enter Sanaa soon after the field victory; the scale of the fighting at the city is unclear
doubts and flags: Borderline: the tradition has Wahrez enter Sanaa soon after the field victory; the scale of the fighting at the city is unclear.
sources: Tabari (tr. Bosworth, vol. 5); Ibn Hisham; Zakeri, Sasanid Soldiers in Early Muslim Society (1995); en.wikipedia Siege of Sanaa (570)

name: Dvin
how the result was decided: The Armenian rebels, with Roman help, took Dvin from its Persian garrison; it had changed hands once before during 572.
commanders A: Vardan Mamikonian (Red Vardan) with a Roman force
commanders B: the Persian garrison (the marzban Suren had been killed)
Iranian force: The Persian garrison of Dvin and the marzban's troops; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: John of Ephesus, Church History book 2; Sebeos; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Roman-Sasanian War of 572-591
note: Vardan's rising killed the marzban Suren and took Dvin in early 572; the Persians retook it and an Armenian-Roman force recaptured it.

name: Dara (siege, 573)
how the result was decided: Dara fell to Khosrow's assault after a four-month siege.
commanders A: Khosrow I; Izadgushnasp, Fariburz, Bahram Chobin (cavalry)
Iranian force: Khosrow I's royal army of 23,000 cavalry and 40,000 infantry (John of Ephesus), using the siege engines the Romans had left at Nisibis.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Evagrius book 5; John of Ephesus, Church History book 6; Theophylact book 3; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Dara (573)
note: The loss of Dara is said to have driven Justin II mad.

name: Nisibis (siege, 573)
how the result was decided: The Romans abandoned the siege in disorder on the approach of Khosrow's army, after Marcian's dismissal; Nisibis held.
commanders A: the garrison (Bahram Gushnasp in Wikipedia); Khosrow I (relief army)
Iranian force: The Nisibis garrison and Khosrow I's relief army coming up the Khabur; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Evagrius book 5; John of Ephesus, Church History book 6; Theophylact book 3; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Siege of Nisibis (573)

name: Sargathon
how the result was decided: Marcian defeated a Persian force near Nisibis and went on to besiege the city.
Iranian force: A Persian frontier force; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: John of Biclaro, Chronicle a. 573; Theophanes; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Roman-Sasanian War of 572-591

name: Melitene (576)
how the result was decided: Kours' division plundered the Persian camp and Khosrow withdrew across the Euphrates by night, losing many men in the crossing.
Iranian force: Khosrow I's royal army with 24 elephants; cavalry in two lines with the infantry and camp behind (Syvanne's estimate: up to 40,000 cavalry and about 50,000 infantry).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: heavy, many drowned in the Euphrates (Syvanne estimates 35,000-45,000)
sources: Evagrius book 5; Theophylact book 3; John of Ephesus, Church History book 6; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Melitene (576)
note: Before the battle Khosrow had burned Sebasteia and failed before Theodosiopolis and Caesarea without real fighting.

name: Bagrevand
how the result was decided: Tamkhusrau's army surprised and routed Justinian's army in its camp in Bagrevand.
Iranian force: Tamkhusrau's 30,000, including elite cavalry, joined by 20,000 Persarmenians (Wikipedia, after Syvanne).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: named and detailed mainly in Syvanne's reconstruction; the older literature records only a Persian victory over Justinian in Armenia in 577
doubts and flags: Borderline: named and detailed mainly in Syvanne's reconstruction; the older literature records only a Persian victory over Justinian in Armenia in 577.
sources: John of Ephesus, Church History book 6; Sebeos; Syvanne, Military History of Late Rome 565-602 (2022); Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Tamkhusrau's Armenian Campaign (577)

name: Bolorophak
how the result was decided: Tamkhusrau defeated the Roman force Justinian had left behind in Armenia.
commanders B: the Roman force left in Armenia by Justinian
Iranian force: Tamkhusrau's army of Persians and Persarmenians (as at Bagrevand).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: known as a named battle only from Syvanne's reconstruction; the site is unidentified
doubts and flags: Borderline: known as a named battle only from Syvanne's reconstruction; the site is unidentified.
sources: Syvanne, Military History of Late Rome 565-602 (2022); en.wikipedia Tamkhusrau's Armenian Campaign (577)

name: Constantina (siege, 577)
how the result was decided: Adarmahan raised the siege when Justinian's relief army approached.
Iranian force: Adarmahan's raiding army in Osrhoene; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: known as a siege only from Syvanne's reconstruction
doubts and flags: Borderline: known as a siege only from Syvanne's reconstruction.
sources: Syvanne, Military History of Late Rome 565-602 (2022); en.wikipedia Tamkhusrau's Armenian Campaign (577); en.wikipedia Maurice's Sasanian Campaigns (578-581)

name: Amida (siege, 578)
how the result was decided: Three days of Persian assaults failed and Tamkhusrau withdrew with his plunder to Arzanene.
Iranian force: Tamkhusrau's raiding army; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a short siege known in detail mainly from Syvanne's reconstruction
doubts and flags: Borderline: a short siege known in detail mainly from Syvanne's reconstruction.
sources: Menander Protector; Syvanne (2022); en.wikipedia Maurice's Sasanian Campaigns (578-581)

name: Aphumon (siege, 578)
place: Aphumon, a fortress in Arzanene, Turkey
how the result was decided: The fortress fell to Maurice's siege engines.
Iranian force: The Persian garrison of Aphumon; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: garrison captured; some 10,000 captives from Arzanene deported to Cyprus (Evagrius)
sources: Theophylact book 3; Evagrius book 5; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Maurice's Sasanian Campaigns (578-581)

name: Arzun (siege, 578)
how the result was decided: After several failed assaults Maurice accepted a large ransom from the townspeople to spare Arzun and raise the siege, so the siege ended by payment with the town untaken: a draw.
Iranian force: The Persian garrison and townspeople; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a short siege known in detail mainly from Syvanne's reconstruction
doubts and flags: Borderline: a short siege known in detail mainly from Syvanne's reconstruction.
sources: John of Ephesus, Church History book 6; Syvanne (2022); en.wikipedia Maurice's Sasanian Campaigns (578-581)
note: Wikipedia scores it a Roman success because of the ransom; under the siege test the defenders won, as for Dara 540 and Edessa 544.

name: Singara (siege, 578)
how the result was decided: Maurice took Singara by siege and destroyed it.
Iranian force: The garrison left by Mahbod, whose field army of 12,000 Persians and 8,000 Sabir Huns had withdrawn.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Menander Protector; Theophylact book 3; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Sack of Singara (578)
note: Wikipedia's title is 'Sack of Singara (578)'; Menander describes circumvallation, mining and artillery.

name: Vanand
how the result was decided: A Roman night attack destroyed most of the Persian army and captured its commander and his son.
Iranian force: The Persian army in Armenia, 'supposedly' about 50,000 (John of Ephesus); no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: most of the army; commander captured
borderline: known as a named battle mainly from Syvanne's reconstruction
doubts and flags: Borderline: known as a named battle mainly from Syvanne's reconstruction.
sources: John of Ephesus, Church History book 6; Syvanne (2022); en.wikipedia Maurice's Sasanian Campaigns (578-581)

name: Anatha (siege, 580)
how the result was decided: The besiegers lifted the siege on news of Adarmahan's invasion of Osrhoene; the fortress held.
Iranian force: The Persian garrison of Anatha, using artillery; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: known mainly from Syvanne's reconstruction; Wikipedia calls it inconclusive
doubts and flags: Borderline: known mainly from Syvanne's reconstruction; Wikipedia calls it inconclusive.
sources: John of Ephesus, Church History book 6; Syvanne (2022); en.wikipedia Maurice's Sasanian Campaigns (578-581)
note: Part of Maurice and al-Mundhir's Euphrates campaign of 580; whether Roman regulars were at Anatha is unclear.

name: Callinicum (580)
how the result was decided: Adarmahan's army was driven back into its camp and slipped away by night, leaving the field to al-Mundhir.
Iranian force: Adarmahan's raiding army in Osrhoene; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: John of Ephesus, Church History book 6; Shahid, Constantinople and the Arabs in the Sixth Century (1995); Syvanne (2022); en.wikipedia Maurice's Sasanian Campaigns (578-581)
note: A Sunday truce followed the Saturday battle; Battles of the Romans does not list it.

name: Nymphius
place: on the river Nymphius (Batman Su), near Martyropolis, Turkey
how the result was decided: Kardarigan defeated John Mystacon's army when Kours' wing failed to engage, and the Romans fled.
Iranian force: Kardarigan's army; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Theophylact book 1; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Roman-Sasanian War of 572-591

name: Constantina (582)
how the result was decided: Maurice's army defeated the Persians, killing Tamkhusrau and three other generals; Adarmahan's men withdrew.
Iranian force: The combined armies of Tamkhusrau and Adarmahan, perhaps more than 50,000 with elite cavalry (modern estimate).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: many thousands; four generals including Tamkhusrau
sources: Evagrius book 5; John of Ephesus, Church History book 6; Menander Protector; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Constantina
note: Wikipedia gives June 581 or 582.

name: Chlomaron (siege)
place: Chlomaron, a fortress in Arzanene, Turkey
how the result was decided: Philippicus abandoned the siege in panic when Kardarigan's relief army approached and fell back to Aphumon.
Iranian force: The garrison of Chlomaron and Kardarigan's rebuilt army, reinforced with levies; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Theophylact book 2; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Solachon

name: Solachon
place: the plain of Solachon, south of Dara near the Arzamon river, Turkey
how the result was decided: The Roman centre broke the Persian line and the Persians fled; many died of thirst in the retreat.
commanders A: Philippicus; Heraclius the Elder, Vitalius, Eiliphredas
Iranian force: Kardarigan's all-cavalry army of lancers and horse archers in three divisions (Theophylact book 2).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: heavy, many died of thirst; up to 1,000 more to Roman patrols
sources: Theophylact book 2; Theophanes; Whitby, The Emperor Maurice (1988); Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Solachon
note: The Roman army included Hunnic horse archers and Arab foederati (Battles of the Romans lists Huns and Christian Arabs as allies).

name: Avaze (siege)
place: the fortress of Avaze (Awaza), site unknown (Khorasan or Transoxiana)
how the result was decided: The besieged Turks surrendered and the khagan's son was taken prisoner and sent to Ctesiphon.
commanders B: Yil-Tegin (Parmuda or Birmudha), son of the khagan (captured)
Iranian force: Bahram Chobin's picked army of the previous battle (Persian cavalry, Daylamite infantry).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
doubts and flags: Traditional: Told only in the Perso-Arabic tradition (Tabari, Dinawari, Balami, the Shahnameh), which follows a romance of Bahram Chobin; the place is unidentified and modern historians accept only the general course of the war.
sources: Tabari; Dinawari; Shahbazi, 'Bahram VI Chobin', Encyclopaedia Iranica; en.wikipedia Perso-Turkic war of 588-589
note: Bahram then retook Balkh and Herat and crossed the Oxus to Paykand in 589 (fights without names in the sources).

name: Martyropolis (588)
how the result was decided: Germanus routed the Persian army and killed Maruzas, whose head and standards were sent to Maurice.
commanders A: Germanus (leader of the mutinous eastern army)
Iranian force: Maruzas' army; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: unknown (Germanus had raised about 4,000 for a raid)
losses B: about 3,000 captured; only about 1,000 reached Nisibis (Theophylact)
sources: Theophylact book 3; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Martyropolis (588)

name: Tsalkajur
how the result was decided: The Persians defeated the Roman force in Armenia (Wikipedia lists it as a Roman defeat; no details survive).
Iranian force: Persian forces in Armenia; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Roman-Sasanian War of 572-591

name: Hyrcanian Rock
place: eastern Khorasan, near Herat (site uncertain), Afghanistan
how the result was decided: Bahram's ambush broke the Turkic and Hephthalite army and killed its khagan; his son escaped.
commanders B: Bagha Qaghan ('Shaba' in the Persian tradition; killed)
Iranian force: Bahram's 12,000 picked veterans: infantry in the centre (Daylamites), cavalry behind, war elephants on the flanks and a band of 100 champions (Tabari, Dinawari).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength B: very large (the Persian tradition gives 300,000, an epic figure)
sources: Theophylact book 3; Sebeos; Tabari; Dinawari; Shahbazi, 'Bahram VI Chobin', Encyclopaedia Iranica; Jaques, Dictionary of Battles and Sieges 463; en.wikipedia Bahram Chobin; en.wikipedia Perso-Turkic war of 588-589
note: Also called the battle of Herat (588). The details of the battle come from the Perso-Arabic tradition, which draws on a romance of Bahram Chobin; the victory itself is confirmed by Theophylact and Sebeos.

name: Araxes (589)
place: on the Araxes, in Caucasian Albania, Azerbaijan
how the result was decided: The Persian vanguard was destroyed and the army broke; the Romans pursued and stripped the dead, though Bahram escaped with much of his cavalry.
Iranian force: Bahram Chobin's army of more than 20,000 in three divisions, mostly cavalry, the veterans of his Turkic war (Theophylact book 3).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the vanguard annihilated; thousands killed in the pursuit
sources: Theophylact book 3; Whitby, The Emperor Maurice (1988); Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of the Araxes (589)
note: Hormizd IV used the defeat to disgrace Bahram, who then rebelled.

name: Martyropolis (siege, 589)
how the result was decided: The Romans failed to retake Martyropolis, betrayed to the Persians in 589, and the Persians held it until Khosrow II handed it back in 591.
commanders A: the Persian garrison; Mebodes and Aphraates (relief)
Iranian force: The Persian garrison, reinforced by Mebodes and Aphraates, who beat the besiegers in the field (Theophylact book 3).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Theophylact book 3; Evagrius book 6; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Roman-Sasanian War of 572-591
note: The town had been betrayed to the Persians by the Roman officer Sittas.

name: Sisauranon (589)
place: near Sisauranon (Sisarbanon), east of Nisibis, Turkey
how the result was decided: The Persian army was routed with heavy loss and its leadership killed; the survivors fled to Nisibis.
Iranian force: Farhad's army, combining the Nisibis garrison with units withdrawn from Armenia; no composition recorded.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: very heavy; Farhad and other commanders killed
sources: Evagrius book 6; Theophylact book 3; Greatrex and Lieu, Roman Eastern Frontier II; en.wikipedia Battle of Sisauranon (589)
note: The Roman victory let Comentiolus take Akbas.

name: Nahrawan Canal
place: the Nahrawan canal, near Ctesiphon, Iraq
how the result was decided: Khosrow's outnumbered men held out in several clashes but then broke, and Khosrow fled to Roman territory.
commanders B: Khosrow II; his uncles Vistahm and Vinduyih
Iranian force: Bahram Chobin's veteran army of the eastern and northern fronts against Khosrow II's much smaller following of court troops and nobles.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: unknown; Khosrow fled with about 30 nobles
sources: Theophylact book 4; Tabari; Dinawari; Shahbazi, 'Bahram VI Chobin', Encyclopaedia Iranica; en.wikipedia Sasanian civil war of 589-591; en.wikipedia Bahram Chobin
note: Bahram then took Ctesiphon and was crowned in summer 590. His earlier defeat of Hormizd IV's general Sarames (589/590) has no place name in the sources and is not listed.

name: Blarathon
war: Revolt of Bahram Chobin (Sasanian civil war of 589-591)
place: on the Blarathon river near Ganzak, Atropatene (near Takab), Iran
how the result was decided: Bahram Chobin's army broke and he fled the field to the Turks, leaving Khosrow II and his Roman allies in possession.
commanders A: Khosrow II, Bindoe, Vistahm; Roman generals Narses and John Mystacon; Mushegh II Mamikonian
Iranian force: Khosrow II's side: about 8,000 Persian loyalists under his uncles Bindoe and Vistahm, with about 40,000 Romans and 12,000 Armenian cavalry as allies; Bahram's side: his veteran Sasanian field army from the Turkish war and the troops who had followed him from Ctesiphon.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Theophylact Simocatta 5.9-11; Sebeos 11; en.wikipedia Battle of Blarathon
note: Also in Battles of the Romans as a Roman victory with Khosrow's loyalists as allies. Most of the winning army was Roman.

name: Constantina
how the result was decided: Khosrow II's army defeated Phocas' general Germanus, who was mortally wounded, and the Romans withdrew.
Iranian force: Khosrow II's royal army, raised in 603 to avenge Maurice and support the rebel Narses at Edessa; asawaran heavy cavalry with infantry levies (normal Sasanian field army; the sources give no breakdown).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Theophanes AM 6095; Chronicle of 1234; Greatrex and Lieu 2002, 183-184
note: Site uncertain (near Constantina, or near Dara). Also in Battles of the Romans.

name: Dara (siege)
how the result was decided: Dara fell to the Persians after a siege of about nine months.
Iranian force: Khosrow II's royal army with siege engineers and mining parties (normal Sasanian field army; no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Theophanes AM 6096; Chronicle of Khuzistan; Greatrex and Lieu 2002, 184-185
note: Also in Battles of the Romans. Some modern accounts (and en.wikipedia's war article) date the fall of Dara to 605.

name: Arxamoun
place: on the Arzamon river (Zergan Su), between Dara and Edessa, Turkey
how the result was decided: On the second day the Persian elephants and infantry broke Leontius' army, which fled and was pursued; the Persians held the field.
Iranian force: Khosrow II's royal army with war elephants, infantry between the elephants and asawaran cavalry; about 45,000 (modern estimate by Syvanne).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Theophanes AM 6096; Chronicle of Khuzistan; Syvanne 2022; en.wikipedia Battle of Arzamon (605)
note: Wikipedia: 'Battle of Arzamon (605)'. Also in Battles of the Romans as Arxamoun, 604.

name: Elevard
war: Roman-Persian War of 602-628 (Persian invasion of Armenia)
how the result was decided: The Persian army was routed and its general Dzuan Veh killed; the Romans held the field.
commanders A: the Roman army in Armenia (Germanus according to en.wikipedia)
Iranian force: Dzuan Veh's Persian army sent into Armenia, with pro-Persian Armenian nobles (Sebeos; no numbers).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Sebeos 33; Greatrex and Lieu 2002, 186; Decker 2022, 210; en.wikipedia Battle of Elevard
note: Wikipedia names the Roman commander Germanus; other accounts say only that the Roman army in Armenia won. Identification of Elevard with Yeghvard is approximate.

name: Erginay
war: Roman-Persian War of 602-628 (Persian invasion of Armenia)
place: Sirakawan and the fort of Erginay, near Getik, Shirak, Armenia
how the result was decided: Datoyean broke the Roman line, plundered the camp and stormed the fort of Erginay.
Iranian force: Datoyean's large Persian army sent to Armenia after the defeat at Elevard (Sebeos; no numbers or breakdown).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Sebeos 33; Howard-Johnston 2021; Syvanne 2022; en.wikipedia Battle of Erginay (605)
note: Site of Erginay not securely identified.

name: Dhi Qar
place: Dhu Qar, between Kufa and Wasit, Iraq
how the result was decided: The Bakr ibn Wa'il coalition routed the Persian force and its Arab auxiliaries, killing its commanders.
commanders A: Hani ibn Mas'ud, Hanzala ibn Tha'laba and other Bakr chiefs
commanders B: Hamarz al-Tustari (killed), Khunubazin (Jalabzin, killed), Iyas ibn Qabisa al-Ta'i, al-Nu'man ibn Zur'a (killed), Khalid ibn Yazid (killed)
Iranian force: Imperial Persian cavalry units (about 2,000 in the Arabic tradition) with about 3,000 Arab auxiliaries of Tayy, Taghlib and Iyad under Iyas ibn Qabisa.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari i.1015-1037; Abu Ubayda in the Kitab al-Aghani; en.wikipedia Battle of Dhu Qar
note: Persian sources do not mention it; some historians think it was little more than a skirmish. Bakr ibn Wa'il led the winners; Arab tribes fought on both sides.

name: Edessa (siege, 610)
how the result was decided: Edessa fell to the Persians.
Iranian force: The Persian army operating in Mesopotamia after the fall of Mardin and Amida (normal Sasanian field army; no details).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the course of the siege is not described; it may have ended in a surrender
doubts and flags: Borderline: the course of the siege is not described; it may have ended in a surrender.
sources: Chronicle of 1234; Theophanes AM 6101; en.wikipedia (article on the war of 602-628); Siege of Edessa (disambiguation, 610)

name: Caesarea (siege)
how the result was decided: After a year's blockade the besieged Persians broke out and abandoned Caesarea, burning it, and the Romans reoccupied the city: the place was lost by its holders, as at Sestos in 479 BC.
Iranian force: Shahin's army that had taken Caesarea in 611 (Sasanian cavalry and infantry; no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Theophanes AM 6103; Nicephorus 2; Kaegi 2003, 68-69; en.wikipedia Siege of Caesarea (611-612)
note: Here the Persians were the besieged. The result is contested: Battles of the Romans scores it a Persian success, because Shahin escaped with his army, and Wikipedia calls it indecisive. By this set's siege rule the holders gave up the city and the besiegers retook it (as at Sestos in 479 BC), so it is a Roman win.

name: Adhri'at
how the result was decided: Nicetas' Roman army was defeated by the Persians at Adhri'at.
Iranian force: Shahrbaraz's army in southern Syria (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Sebeos 34; Qur'an 30.2-3 (traditionally linked); Kaegi 2003, 78; en.wikipedia (article on the war of 602-628)
note: Also in Battles of the Romans. Often identified with the defeat 'in the nearest land' of Qur'an 30.2-3.

name: Antioch
how the result was decided: After an initial Roman success the Persians defeated Heraclius' army, which retreated, leaving Antioch to them.
Iranian force: The combined armies of Shahrbaraz and Shahin, about 40,000: asawaran heavy cavalry, archers and infantry.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Sebeos 34; Theophanes AM 6104; Kaegi 2003, 75-77; en.wikipedia Battle of Antioch (613)
note: Also in Battles of the Romans.

name: Cilician Gates (613)
place: the Cilician Gates (Gulek pass) in the Taurus, Turkey
how the result was decided: After early success the Roman force was defeated at the pass and the Persians went on to take Tarsus and Cilicia.
Iranian force: The Persian army pursuing Heraclius after Antioch (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Sebeos 34; Kaegi 2003, 77-78; en.wikipedia (article on the war of 602-628)
note: Also in Battles of the Romans.

name: Damascus (siege, 613)
how the result was decided: Damascus fell to Shahrbaraz, who took many prisoners.
Iranian force: Shahrbaraz's army after its victory at Antioch (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a capture; the fighting is not described and the city may have fallen quickly
doubts and flags: Borderline: a capture; the fighting is not described and the city may have fallen quickly.
sources: Sebeos 34; Chronicle of 1234; en.wikipedia Shahrbaraz

name: Emesa (613)
how the result was decided: Nicetas won a small victory near Emesa; both sides lost heavily (about 20,000 dead in all).
Iranian force: Shahrbaraz's army in Syria (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Sebeos 34; en.wikipedia (article on the war of 602-628)
note: Also in Battles of the Romans.

name: Caesarea Maritima (siege)
how the result was decided: Caesarea, the capital of Palaestina Prima, fell to Shahrbaraz.
Iranian force: Shahrbaraz's army, joined in Galilee by Jewish rebels (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: fighting not described; the city may have capitulated (destruction was slight)
doubts and flags: Borderline: fighting not described; the city may have capitulated (destruction was slight).
sources: Antiochus Strategos; en.wikipedia Siege of Caesarea Maritima (614)

name: Tus (614)
place: near the fort of Tus (near Mashhad), Iran
how the result was decided: The Hephthalite raiders were defeated near Tus and called on the Gokturk khagan for help.
commanders A: Smbat Bagratuni (marzban of Hyrcania and Khorasan)
Iranian force: The Sasanian forces of the eastern frontier under the Armenian marzban Smbat Bagratuni, including his Armenian retainers (Sebeos).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no conventional name; known from Sebeos only
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name; known from Sebeos only.
sources: Sebeos 28; Pourshariati 2008, 139; en.wikipedia Hephthalite-Gokturk raids of 614-616

name: Jerusalem (siege)
how the result was decided: The walls were breached after a siege of about three weeks and the city fell.
commanders A: Shahrbaraz; Jewish leaders Nehemiah ben Hushiel and Benjamin of Tiberias
Iranian force: Shahrbaraz's Sasanian army with siege engines, joined by Jewish rebels from Galilee (20,000-26,000 according to later chroniclers).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Antiochus Strategos; Sebeos 34; Chronicon Paschale; en.wikipedia Sasanian conquest of Jerusalem
note: The True Cross was carried off to Ctesiphon. Also in Battles of the Romans.

name: Tus (siege, 615)
place: the fort of Tus (near Mashhad), Iran
how the result was decided: The Gokturks overran Khorasan but could not breach the fort of Tus, held by 300 men.
Iranian force: A garrison of 300 men in the fort of Tus (Sebeos).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no conventional name; known from Sebeos only
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name; known from Sebeos only.
sources: Sebeos 28; en.wikipedia Hephthalite-Gokturk raids of 614-616
note: In the same campaign a Sasanian army under Datoyean was defeated in the field by the Gokturks, and Smbat Bagratuni later crushed the Hephthalites, killing their leader in single combat (616); these engagements have no place name and are not entered.

name: Chalcedon (siege, 617)
place: Chalcedon (Kadikoy), across the Bosporus from Constantinople, Turkey
how the result was decided: Shahin took Chalcedon after investing it.
Iranian force: Shahin's army in Anatolia (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: fighting not described; the date (615 or 617) and the capture itself are disputed
doubts and flags: Borderline: fighting not described; the date (615 or 617) and the capture itself are disputed.
sources: Theophanes AM 6107; Chronicon Paschale; en.wikipedia (article on the war of 602-628)
note: In 615 Shahin reached Chalcedon and withdrew after negotiations (en.wikipedia Shahin's invasion of Asia Minor); the capture is placed in 617.

name: Alexandria (siege)
war: Roman-Persian War of 602-628 (Persian conquest of Egypt)
how the result was decided: Alexandria fell after about a year when a traitor showed the Persians an unused canal; Nicetas fled to Cyprus.
Iranian force: Shahrbaraz's army of the Egyptian expedition (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Chronicle of Khuzistan; History of the Patriarchs; en.wikipedia Sasanian conquest of Egypt
note: Also in Battles of the Romans.

date: June 619 (the rising; Li Gui executed about July 619)
name: Liangzhou (An Xinggui's rising against Li Gui, 619)
how the result was decided: An Xinggui's rising drove Li Gui into Guzang, besieged him and captured him when the people came over; Li Gui was sent to Chang'an and executed.
why it counts: Leader by descent: the brothers An Xinggui and An Xiuren, Liangzhou chiefs with the surname An, are taken by modern scholars as Sogdian (An = Bukhara; Rong Xinjiang), though the Tang histories derive the family from 'Anxi' (Parthia), which is also Iranian; their following is called Hu (and Xiongnu in the English Wikipedia's reading).
sources: Old Book of Tang, juan 55 (Li Gui); Zizhi Tongjian, juan 187; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Gui_(Liang_dynasty); Rong Xinjiang, Eighteen Lectures on Dunhuang (2013), chapters on the Sogdians
note: A coup by local Hu chiefs on Tang instructions rather than a pitched battle; the An family became Tang magnates in Liangzhou. Limited fighting, thin sources; the Turkic or Xiongnu side of the 'Hu' following is not resolved.

name: Cappadocia
place: somewhere in Cappadocia or Pontus (Mount Ophlimus, near Euchaita, in en.wikipedia), Turkey
how the result was decided: Heraclius' feigned retreat drew the Persians out of cover and his Optimatoi routed them; the Persians withdrew.
Iranian force: Shahrbaraz's field army returned from Egypt and Syria (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: George of Pisidia, Expeditio Persica; Theophanes AM 6113; Kaegi 2003, 114-116; en.wikipedia Battle of Ophlimus
note: en.wikipedia calls it the Battle of Ophlimus; Battles of the Romans calls it Cappadocia. Heraclius' route is debated.

name: Dvin (siege, 624)
how the result was decided: Dvin, the capital of Persian Armenia, was taken and sacked.
Iranian force: The garrison of the Persian provincial capital of Armenia (no details in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Sebeos 38; Howard-Johnston 2021; en.wikipedia Sack of Dvin (624)

name: Ganzak
how the result was decided: Heraclius' Arab vanguard cut down Khosrow's guard, Khosrow fled south and his army dispersed.
Iranian force: Khosrow II's own army, about 40,000, with the royal guard (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Sebeos 38; Theophanes AM 6114; Kaegi 2003, 122-126; en.wikipedia Battle of Ganzak
note: Heraclius then destroyed the fire temple of Adur Gushnasp. Also in Battles of the Romans.

name: Tigranakert
place: near Tigranakert of Artsakh (near Aghdam), Azerbaijan
how the result was decided: Heraclius routed first Shahraplakan's and then Shahin's army, taking Shahin's baggage train.
Iranian force: Two of the three Persian armies sent against Heraclius, those of Shahraplakan and Shahin, 20,000-30,000 together (modern estimate).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Movses Dasxuranci 2.10; Theophanes AM 6115; Kaegi 2003, 128-129; en.wikipedia Battle of Aghdam (625)
note: en.wikipedia's 'Battle of Aghdam (625)' is this battle (against Shahin). Battles of the Romans has it as Tigranakert; one en.wikipedia article wrongly puts it at Tigranakert (Silvan).

name: Aliovit (Archesh)
place: Archesh (Ercis), in the district of Aliovit, north of Lake Van, Turkey
how the result was decided: Heraclius' night attack destroyed Shahrbaraz's camp and Shahrbaraz barely escaped.
Iranian force: Shahrbaraz's army, part of it quartered in Archesh (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Theophanes AM 6115; Sebeos 38; Greatrex 1991, 206-208; en.wikipedia Battle of Archesh
note: Also in Battles of the Romans.

name: Sarus
place: the bridge over the Sarus (Seyhan), near Adana, Turkey
how the result was decided: After the Persians ambushed the Roman vanguard, Heraclius led the rearguard across the bridge and turned the battle; the Romans held the field and Shahrbaraz withdrew in good order.
Iranian force: Shahrbaraz's army pursuing Heraclius (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Theophanes AM 6115; Kaegi 2003, 130-131; en.wikipedia Battle of Sarus
note: A nominal Roman victory: Shahrbaraz continued his advance. Also in Battles of the Romans.

name: Constantinople (siege)
place: Constantinople, the Golden Horn and the Bosporus, with the Persian army at Chalcedon, Turkey
how the result was decided: The siege was abandoned after the Roman fleet destroyed the Slav boats, including those sent to ferry Persian troops across the Bosporus, on 7 August.
commanders B: the Avar khagan; Shahrbaraz and Kardarigan (Persian army at Chalcedon)
Iranian force: Shahrbaraz's army encamped at Chalcedon, a whole corps acting as a unit; it could not cross the Bosporus (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: about 12,000 cavalry and the city militia
strength B: about 80,000 Avars and Slavs, plus the Persian army
sources: Chronicon Paschale; Theodore Syncellus; George of Pisidia, Bellum Avaricum; en.wikipedia Siege of Constantinople (626)
note: The Persians fought chiefly as besiegers across the strait; the assault on the walls was by Avars and Slavs. Also in Battles of the Romans.

name: Lycus
how the result was decided: Theodore heavily defeated Shahin's army, which lost very heavily.
Iranian force: Shahin's new army, raised by Khosrow in 625 from 'all the able men, including foreigners' (up to 50,000 according to Theophanes).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Theophanes AM 6117; Kaegi 2003, 140-141; en.wikipedia Battle of the Lycus (626)
note: Shahin reportedly died soon after. Also in Battles of the Romans.

name: Derbent (627)
place: Derbent (Chor, the Caspian Gates), Dagestan, Russia
how the result was decided: The Turks stormed the Sasanian fortifications at Derbent and went on to plunder Albania.
Iranian force: The defenders of the Sasanian wall at Derbent, described as a lightly armed Albanian militia (Movses Dasxuranci).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a Persian force is not attested; the defenders were the militia of Sasanian Albania
doubts and flags: Borderline: a Persian force is not attested; the defenders were the militia of Sasanian Albania.
sources: Movses Dasxuranci 2.11; en.wikipedia Perso-Turkic war of 627-629

name: Tiflis (siege)
war: Roman-Persian War of 602-628; Perso-Turkic war of 627-629
how the result was decided: After a first siege by the Romans and Turks failed in 627, the Turks returned and stormed the city in the winter of 627/628.
commanders A: Heraclius, Tong Yabghu Qaghan, Bori Shad
commanders B: Stephen I of Iberia (killed); a Persian governor; Shahraplakan sent 1,000 horse
Iranian force: A Persian garrison with Iberian troops of Stephen I, reinforced by 1,000 cavalry sent by Shahraplakan.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
strength A: about 40,000 Turks left under Bori Shad, plus Heraclius' army
losses B: the garrison killed; the Persian governor and the Iberian prince tortured to death
sources: Movses Dasxuranci 2.11-14; Theophanes AM 6117; en.wikipedia Siege of Tbilisi (627-628)
note: The Turks are called Khazars in several sources; Battles of the Romans lists Khazars. The first siege was abandoned; the place fell to the second.

name: Nineveh
