place: near the ruins of Nineveh, by the Tigris (Mosul), Iraq
how the result was decided: Rhahzadh was killed and his army lost about 6,000 men but stood near the field; it withdrew afterwards, and the Romans held the battlefield.
Iranian force: Rhahzadh's army of about 12,000, with archers, in three divisions; 3,000 reinforcements arrived too late.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Theophanes AM 6118; Nicephorus 14; Sebeos 38; en.wikipedia Battle of Nineveh (627)
note: The overthrow of Khosrow II (February 628) and the peace that followed are strategic consequences. Also in Battles of the Romans.

name: Edessa (siege, 630)
war: Roman-Persian War of 602-628 (evacuation after the peace)
how the result was decided: The Persian garrison, bombarded by Theodore's siege engines, agreed to leave and the city was handed over.
Iranian force: The Persian garrison of Edessa, which refused to evacuate after the peace of 628, reportedly encouraged by the city's Jews.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Chronicle of 1234; Agapius; en.wikipedia Theodore (brother of Heraclius); Siege of Edessa (disambiguation, 630)
note: Theodore's troops then attacked the Jews of the city until Heraclius stopped them.

date: spring 630, the city taken 27 April 630 (629 in en.wikipedia's article title)
name: Ctesiphon (siege, 630)
how the result was decided: Ctesiphon fell to Shahrbaraz, who killed Ardashir III and took the throne.
factions A: Shahrbaraz (with the Parsig and Nimruzi factions)
Iranian force: Shahrbaraz's 6,000 veterans of the western army, joined by the forces of the Parsig faction (Piruz Khosrow) and of the spahbed of Nimruz, against the troops of Ardashir III's regency in the capital.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: Ardashir III and many nobles executed
sources: al-Tabari i.1061-1062; Chronicle of Seert; Pourshariati 2008, 180-183; en.wikipedia Siege of Ctesiphon (629)
note: Shahrbaraz failed at first and took the city with his allies' help. en.wikipedia's article is titled 'Siege of Ctesiphon (629)'; Pourshariati and the Shahrbaraz article give 27 April 630.

name: Ctesiphon (631)
how the result was decided: Rostam defeated Siyavakhsh's forces at Ctesiphon and took the city, deposing Azarmidokht.
Iranian force: Rostam's army of the Pahlav (Parthian) nobility from Khorasan against the forces of Azarmidokht's regime under the Mihranid Siyavakhsh.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no conventional battle name; the sources say only that Rostam defeated Azarmidokht's armies and took the capital
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional battle name; the sources say only that Rostam defeated Azarmidokht's armies and took the capital.
sources: al-Tabari i.1064-1065; Pourshariati 2008, 204-209; en.wikipedia Sasanian civil war of 628-632
note: Rostam then blinded and killed Azarmidokht and restored Boran.

name: Chains
war: Arab conquest of Persia (Khalid ibn al-Walid in Iraq)
how the result was decided: The Persian wings broke and fled; the chained infantry could not escape and was cut down, leaving the field to Khalid.
Iranian force: Hormozd's Sasanian frontier army of heavy troops, part of the infantry chained together, with many Christian Arab auxiliaries.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 12 (Sayf ibn Umar); Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; en.wikipedia Battle of Chains
note: Khalid's battles of 633 are known mostly from Sayf ibn Umar, whose details (and some of the battles) are doubted by Donner and others.

date: April 633 (12 Safar AH 12 according to Morony)
name: River
war: Arab conquest of Persia (Khalid ibn al-Walid in Iraq)
how the result was decided: With its three commanders killed in single combat, the Persian army broke and fled to its boats on the river.
Iranian force: Qarin's army sent from Ctesiphon, Persian regulars and new levies, joined by the survivors of the Chains.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 12 (Sayf ibn Umar); Morony 1984; en.wikipedia Battle of the River
note: Called the battle of al-Madhar or al-Thani in the Arabic sources.

name: Hira
war: Arab conquest of Persia (Khalid ibn al-Walid in Iraq)
how the result was decided: After a short siege of its castles al-Hira surrendered and paid tribute.
commanders B: Iyas ibn Qabisa al-Ta'i, Abd al-Masih ibn Amr ibn Buqayla
Iranian force: The Christian Arab townsmen of al-Hira (the Ibad) in the castles of the city, under its Sasanian-appointed governor; the Persian marzban Azadbeh had withdrawn.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 12; Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; en.wikipedia Battle of Hira
note: The castles named are al-Qasr al-Abyad, Qasr ibn Buqayla and Qasr al-Adasiyyin.

name: Ullais
war: Arab conquest of Persia (Khalid ibn al-Walid in Iraq)
place: Ullais, between the Euphrates and the Khaseef, Iraq
how the result was decided: After a long fight the Persian and Arab line broke and the fugitives were slaughtered (the 'River of Blood').
commanders A: Khalid ibn al-Walid, al-Muthanna ibn Haritha
commanders B: Jaban; Abd al-Aswad al-Ijli (killed) and Abjar (Christian Arab wings)
Iranian force: Imperial troops under Jaban in the centre, with Christian Arab contingents of Bakr ibn Wa'il and neighbouring tribes on both wings.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 12 (Sayf ibn Umar); Crawford 2013; en.wikipedia Battle of Ullais
note: Bahman Jadhuyih, appointed to command, had returned to Ctesiphon.

name: Walaja
war: Arab conquest of Persia (Khalid ibn al-Walid in Iraq)
place: al-Walaja, west of the Euphrates south of al-Hira, Iraq
how the result was decided: Khalid's hidden cavalry struck the Persian rear and Andarzaghar's army was destroyed.
commanders A: Khalid ibn al-Walid, al-Muthanna ibn Haritha
commanders B: Andarzaghar (died in the flight), Bahman Jadhuyih (did not arrive in time)
Iranian force: Andarzaghar's army of garrison troops drawn from across the empire, with heavy cavalry on the wings and thousands of Christian Arabs of Bakr ibn Wa'il.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 12 (Sayf ibn Umar); en.wikipedia Battle of Walaja

name: al-Anbar
war: Arab conquest of Persia (Khalid ibn al-Walid in Iraq)
how the result was decided: After archery duels, an assault on the moat and a repulsed sortie, Shirzad surrendered al-Anbar and withdrew to Ctesiphon.
Iranian force: Shirzad's Persian garrison in the fortress of al-Anbar.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 12; en.wikipedia Battle of al-Anbar
note: Called the 'Battle of the Eyes' for the Persians blinded by the Muslim archers.

name: Ayn al-Tamr
war: Arab conquest of Persia (Khalid ibn al-Walid in Iraq)
place: Ayn al-Tamr (Shithatha), west of Karbala, Iraq
how the result was decided: Khalid captured Aqqa in the field battle, the Christian Arab army surrendered, and the fortress was then stormed and its Persian garrison killed.
commanders B: Mihran son of Bahram Chobin; Aqqa ibn Qays al-Namari (captured, executed)
Iranian force: A field army of Christian Arabs (Namir, Taghlib, Iyad) under Aqqa, with Mihran's Persian regulars in the fortress.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the field army executed; the garrison killed
sources: al-Tabari, AH 12; Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; en.wikipedia Battle of Ayn al-Tamr
note: A field battle followed by the storming of the fort; entered once.

name: Husayd
war: Arab conquest of Persia (Khalid ibn al-Walid in Iraq)
place: Husayd, south-east of Ayn al-Tamr, Iraq
how the result was decided: Al-Qa'qa' attacked before the two Persian forces could unite; both commanders were killed and the survivors fled to Khanafis.
commanders A: al-Qa'qa' ibn Amr al-Tamimi, Abu Layla
Iranian force: One of two Persian field forces sent from Ctesiphon by Bahman Jadhuyih, joined by local Christian Arabs seeking revenge for Aqqa.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 12 (Sayf ibn Umar); en.wikipedia Battle of Husayd
note: The sources disagree on which commander was at Husayd and which at Khanafis.

name: Muzayyah
war: Arab conquest of Persia (Khalid ibn al-Walid in Iraq)
place: al-Muzayyah (Mudayyah), north of Ayn al-Tamr, Iraq
how the result was decided: Khalid's three-pronged night attack broke up the camp and thousands were killed; the rest fled in the dark.
commanders B: Mahbudhan (Persian commander from Khanafis), Hudhayl ibn Imran (Christian Arabs)
Iranian force: The Persian force withdrawn from Khanafis under Mahbudhan, with the Christian Arabs (Taghlib) of Hudhayl ibn Imran.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 12 (Sayf ibn Umar); en.wikipedia Battle of Muzayyah

name: Saniyy
war: Arab conquest of Persia (Khalid ibn al-Walid in Iraq)
place: al-Saniyy, on the edge of the Jazira, Iraq
how the result was decided: Khalid's night attack destroyed the Christian Arab camp and killed its leader.
Iranian force: No Persian troops are attested; the camp was of Christian Arabs (Taghlib) raised for Bahman Jadhuyih's counter-offensive.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no Persian troops attested; the Christian Arabs were Sasanian allies (en.wikipedia lists the Sasanian Empire as a belligerent)
doubts and flags: Borderline: no Persian troops attested; the Christian Arabs were Sasanian allies (en.wikipedia lists the Sasanian Empire as a belligerent).
sources: al-Tabari, AH 12 (Sayf ibn Umar); en.wikipedia Battle of Saniyy

name: Zumail
war: Arab conquest of Persia (Khalid ibn al-Walid in Iraq)
how the result was decided: The Christian Arab army scattered under a three-sided night attack and was mostly destroyed in flight.
commanders A: Khalid ibn al-Walid, Iyad ibn Ghanm, al-Qa'qa' ibn Amr
Iranian force: No Persian troops are attested; an army of Christian Arabs (Taghlib) loyal to the Sasanians.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no Persian troops attested; the Christian Arabs were Sasanian allies
doubts and flags: Borderline: no Persian troops attested; the Christian Arabs were Sasanian allies.
sources: al-Tabari, AH 12 (Sayf ibn Umar); en.wikipedia Battle of Zumail
note: Rabi'a ibn Bujayr appears as commander in some accounts, though he is said to have fallen at Saniyy.

name: Baqusiatha
how the result was decided: Jalinus' relief army, arriving too late for Kaskar, was defeated and withdrew.
Iranian force: The army of Jalinus sent by Rostam to support Narsi.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 13; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Persia; Battle of Kaskar

name: Firaz
war: Arab conquest of Persia (Khalid ibn al-Walid in Iraq)
place: Firaz, on the Euphrates between al-Qa'im and Abu Kamal, Syria
how the result was decided: In the Arabic accounts Khalid routed the coalition after it crossed the Euphrates and held the field.
commanders B: not named (Hormozd Jadhuyih on the Persian side according to some accounts)
Iranian force: At most a small body of Persian frontier troops, probably survivors of the earlier defeats, beside the Roman garrison and Christian Arabs (Taghlib, Iyad, Namir).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: Persian participation disputed
doubts and flags: Borderline: Persian participation disputed.
sources: al-Tabari, AH 12 (Sayf ibn Umar); Morony 1984; Crawford 2013; en.wikipedia Battle of Firaz
note: Also in Battles of the Romans as an Arab victory over Rome and the Sasanians. en.wikipedia calls the result disputed; Takirtakoglou suspects the tradition hides a check to Khalid.

name: Kaskar
how the result was decided: Narsi's army was defeated before Jalinus could join it; Narsi escaped and his estate was plundered.
commanders A: Abu Ubayd al-Thaqafi, Arfaja ibn Harthama
Iranian force: Narsi's own forces defending his estates, with Bindoe's sons Vinduyih and Tiruyih commanding the wings.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 13; en.wikipedia Battle of Kaskar
note: Called al-Saqatiyya in the Arabic sources; en.wikipedia's list has 'Battle of Kaskar' and 'Battle of Saqatia' as two items, but they are one battle.

date: 634 (summer or early autumn, before the Bridge)
name: Namaraq
place: the plain of al-Namariq, near Kufa, Iraq
how the result was decided: Jaban was captured and his army retreated, leaving the field to Abu Ubayd.
commanders A: Abu Ubayd al-Thaqafi, al-Muthanna ibn Haritha
Iranian force: Jaban's army sent by Rostam Farrokhzad to retake al-Hira: heavy cavalry and infantry with experienced Persian officers.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 13; en.wikipedia Battle of Namaraq

date: June - July 634 (Tabari dates it to the reign of Shahrbaraz)
name: Babylon (634)
how the result was decided: Al-Muthanna defeated Hormozd Jadhuyih's army near Babylon and pursued it towards Ctesiphon.
Iranian force: Hormozd Jadhuyih's army of about 10,000 with a war elephant (al-Tabari).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari i.2116-2117; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Rashidun Caliphate ('1st Battle of Babylon')
note: The chronology is confused: Tabari places it under Shahrbaraz (630).

name: Bridge
place: Quss al-Natif on the Euphrates, near Kufa, Iraq
how the result was decided: The Persian elephants and line broke the Arabs who had crossed the bridge; Abu Ubayd was killed and his army fled back over the river with heavy losses.
commanders B: Abu Ubayd al-Thaqafi (killed), al-Muthanna ibn Haritha (wounded)
Iranian force: Bahman Jadhuyih's army with about 20 war elephants, heavy cavalry and a deep infantry line.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 13; Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; en.wikipedia Battle of the Bridge
note: The only major Sasanian victory over the Arab invaders.

date: 635 (April or November 635 in en.wikipedia; Ramadan AH 13 or 14)
name: Buwaib
place: al-Buwayb, on the Euphrates north of al-Hira (near Kufa), Iraq
how the result was decided: Al-Muthanna let the Persians cross the river, encircled them and killed Mihran; the Persian army was routed.
Iranian force: Mihran's large Persian army sent after the victory at the Bridge (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 13 (Sayf ibn Umar); Donner 1981; en.wikipedia Battle of Buwaib
note: Local Christian Arabs (Namir, Taghlib) fought for the Muslims. Donner regards the account as unreliable. Dated 634 in many older works.

name: Qadisiyyah
how the result was decided: On the fourth day Rostam was killed and the Persian army broke and fled, leaving the field to the Arabs.
commanders A: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Khalid ibn Urfuta, al-Qa'qa' ibn Amr, Zuhra ibn al-Hawiyya, Jarir ibn Abd Allah, Tulayha, Amr ibn Ma'dikarib
commanders B: Rostam Farrokhzad (killed), Bahman Jadhuyih (killed), Jalinus, Hormuzan, Mihran Razi, Piruz Khosrow, Shahriyar ibn Kanara (killed); Armenian princes Mushegh III Mamikonian and Grigor Novirak (killed); Juansher of Albania (wounded)
Iranian force: Rostam's imperial army, about 60,000 (modern estimate about 30,000): heavy cavalry (asawaran), infantry including the Daylamite guard (later the Hamra'), Armenian and Albanian princely contingents, and about 30 elephants.
languages: Persian; Parthian; Daylami and Caspian; Armenian; other Caucasian; Indian
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 14 (Sayf ibn Umar); Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; Sebeos 42; Kennedy 2007; en.wikipedia Battle of al-Qadisiyyah
note: The date is disputed (Donner and others prefer 636 or 637; some 638).

name: Babylon (636)
how the result was decided: The Persian commanders gave way before Sa'd's army and withdrew, and Babylon submitted.
commanders B: Piruz Khosrow (Firuzan), Hormuzan, Mihran Razi, Nakhiragan
Iranian force: The Persian survivors of Qadisiyyah regrouped under Firuzan, Hormuzan, Mihran and Nakhiragan.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: some accounts describe a Persian withdrawal without a real battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: some accounts describe a Persian withdrawal without a real battle.
sources: al-Tabari, AH 16 (Sayf ibn Umar); en.wikipedia Siege of Ctesiphon (637); List of battles involving the Rashidun Caliphate ('2nd Battle of Babylon')

name: Burs
how the result was decided: Zuhra killed the garrison commander Busbuhra in single combat and the garrison gave way.
Iranian force: The Persian garrison of Burs.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 16 (Sayf ibn Umar); en.wikipedia Battle of Burs

name: Sura
place: Sura, on the Euphrates near Hillah, Iraq
how the result was decided: Zuhra's vanguard drove off the Persian rearguard at Sura.
Iranian force: A rearguard of the retreating Persian army.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a pursuit skirmish known only from Sayf ibn Umar
doubts and flags: Borderline: a pursuit skirmish known only from Sayf ibn Umar.
sources: al-Tabari, AH 16 (Sayf ibn Umar); en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Rashidun Caliphate

name: Hormizd-Ardashir (637)
place: west of Hormizd-Ardashir (Suq al-Ahwaz, Ahvaz), Iran
how the result was decided: Hormuzan was easily defeated and retreated into the city, then sued for peace.
commanders A: Sulma ibn al-Qayn, Harmala ibn Muraytah (sent by Utba ibn Ghazwan)
Iranian force: Hormuzan's Khuzestan forces, which had been raiding Maysan.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 17; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Khuzestan; List of battles involving the Rashidun Caliphate

name: Khanaqin
how the result was decided: Al-Qa'qa' overtook and defeated the remnant of Mihran's army at Khanaqin and took the town.
Iranian force: The survivors of Jalula under Mihran.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 16; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Persia

name: Tikrit (637)
how the result was decided: After a siege of about forty days the Christian Arabs inside went over and the town was stormed.
Iranian force: Al-Antaq's force from Mosul: troops called 'Rum', Persian nobles (the Shaharija) and Christian Arabs of Iyad, Taghlib and Namir (al-Tabari).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the defenders included 'Rum' and Christian Arabs; the Sasanian command is not certain
doubts and flags: Borderline: the defenders included 'Rum' and Christian Arabs; the Sasanian command is not certain.
sources: al-Tabari, AH 16; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Persia

name: Ctesiphon (siege, 637)
place: Veh-Ardashir (Bahurasir) and Ctesiphon (near Salman Pak), Iraq
how the result was decided: After a two-month siege of Veh-Ardashir the Persians withdrew across the Tigris; the Arabs forced the crossing and took Ctesiphon, and Yazdegerd fled to Hulwan.
commanders A: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Hashim ibn Utba, Zuhra ibn al-Hawiyya, Asim ibn Amr, al-Qa'qa' ibn Amr
Iranian force: The garrison of the capital with ballistae and catapults, a cavalry force at the Tigris crossing, and Yazdegerd's guard.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 16; Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; en.wikipedia Siege of Ctesiphon (637)
note: Persian engineers who had gone over helped the Arabs build siege engines.

name: Deir Kab
place: Dayr Ka'b, between Sura and Kutha, Iraq
how the result was decided: Zuhra's vanguard defeated the Persian rearguard at Dayr Ka'b.
Iranian force: A rearguard of the retreating Persian army.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a pursuit skirmish known only from Sayf ibn Umar
doubts and flags: Borderline: a pursuit skirmish known only from Sayf ibn Umar.
sources: al-Tabari, AH 16 (Sayf ibn Umar); en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Rashidun Caliphate

name: Kutha
place: Kutha (Tell Ibrahim), about 17 km from Ctesiphon's outer districts, Iraq
how the result was decided: Shahriyar was killed in a duel and his detachment's last stand collapsed.
Iranian force: A Persian detachment under the dehqan Shahriyar.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a small action known only from Sayf ibn Umar
doubts and flags: Borderline: a small action known only from Sayf ibn Umar.
sources: al-Tabari, AH 16 (Sayf ibn Umar); en.wikipedia Siege of Ctesiphon (637); List of battles involving the Rashidun Caliphate ('Battle of Kusa')

name: Jalula
how the result was decided: Drawn out of their entrenchments by a feigned retreat and cut off from the bridge over their trench, the Persians were routed and fled.
commanders A: Hashim ibn Utba, al-Qa'qa' ibn Amr, Tulayha, Amr ibn Ma'dikarib
commanders B: Mihran Razi, Farrukhzad (Khurrazad, Rostam's brother), Piruz; the Armenian Varaztirots
Iranian force: The army that withdrew from Ctesiphon, about 20,000, behind a trench with caltrops, archers and engines.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 16; Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; en.wikipedia Battle of Jalula
note: A siege of the town followed, ending in surrender on terms.

name: Hormizd-Ardashir (638)
how the result was decided: Hurqus defeated Hormuzan, who fled to Ram-Hormizd; the city submitted and paid jizya.
Iranian force: Hormuzan's Khuzestan forces.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 17; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Khuzestan

name: Tawus
war: Arab conquest of Persia (al-Ala ibn al-Hadrami's expedition to Fars)
place: Tawus, in Fars, on the way from the coast to Istakhr, Iran
how the result was decided: Two of the three Arab columns were destroyed with their commanders, the ships were burned and the survivors had to be rescued by a relief army from Basra.
commanders B: al-Jarud ibn al-Mu'alla (killed), al-Sawwar ibn Hammam (killed), Khulayd ibn al-Mundhir; al-Ala ibn al-Hadrami (organiser)
Iranian force: The Persian forces of Fars gathered against the seaborne invasion from Bahrain.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 17; Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; en.wikipedia Arab conquest of Fars
note: In al-Tabari (Sayf) Khulayd's column wins the battle at Tawus but is cut off from the sea; modern accounts treat the expedition as a defeat.

name: Hulwan
how the result was decided: The defenders were beaten at Qasr Shirin and Hulwan was taken.
Iranian force: The troops left by Yazdegerd's general Khosrowshunum to hold the pass of Hulwan.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 16; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Persia

name: Ram-Hormizd
how the result was decided: Hormuzan was defeated and fled to Shushtar.
Iranian force: Hormuzan's renewed army of Khuzestan, encouraged by Yazdegerd III.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 17; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Khuzestan; Siege of Shushtar

name: Shushtar (siege)
how the result was decided: After a defeat outside the walls and a long siege, an Iranian informer showed the Arabs a water channel into the city; Hormuzan held the citadel for a time, then surrendered.
commanders A: Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, al-Nu'man ibn Muqarrin, al-Bara' ibn Malik (wounded), Majza'a ibn Thawr (killed)
Iranian force: Hormuzan's remaining army of Khuzestan; the Asawira under Siyah al-Uswari went over to the Arabs (al-Baladhuri).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
losses B: heavy; 900 killed and 600 captured in the battle outside the city
sources: al-Tabari, AH 17; Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; Chronicle of Khuzistan; en.wikipedia Siege of Shushtar
note: Hormuzan was sent to Medina.

name: Susa (siege, 641)
how the result was decided: Susa was taken after a siege of about two months.
Iranian force: The Persian garrison of Susa.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 17; Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Persia
note: Some accounts put it before Shushtar.

name: Gundishapur (siege)
how the result was decided: Gundishapur surrendered on terms within a few days.
Iranian force: The defenders of Gundishapur (not described).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a short siege ending in surrender; fighting not described
doubts and flags: Borderline: a short siege ending in surrender; fighting not described.
sources: al-Tabari; Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Khuzestan
note: Abu Musa then took Kalbaniyya, where some inhabitants had fled.

name: Nahavand
how the result was decided: Drawn out of their fortified lines by a feigned retreat, the Persians were routed and pursued; their commander was killed.
commanders A: al-Nu'man ibn Muqarrin (killed), Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, al-Qa'qa' ibn Amr
commanders B: Piruz Khosrow (Firuzan, killed); Mardanshah (Dhu'l-Hajib) in some accounts
Iranian force: The last imperial army, levied by Yazdegerd III from Rayy, Hamadan, Isfahan, Qumis, Tabaristan, Gurgan, Azerbaijan and the two Mahs, largely of peasant levies under feudal nobles.
languages: Persian; Parthian; Daylami and Caspian; Kurdish
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 21; Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; Crawford 2013; en.wikipedia Battle of Nahavand
note: Called the 'victory of victories' by the Arab historians; the end of organised imperial resistance.

name: Spahan
place: Spahan (Isfahan, the district of Jayy), Iran
how the result was decided: The Persian army was defeated and its commander killed; the governor then came to terms.
commanders A: Abd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Itban
commanders B: Shahrvaraz Jadhuyih (killed), Padhuspan (Fadhusfan, governor of Isfahan)
Iranian force: The forces of Isfahan under a Mihranid commander (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 21; Abu Nu'aym; en.wikipedia Battle of Spahan
note: Isfahan capitulated by 644 after a siege and failed revolts.

name: Bishapur
how the result was decided: Bishapur surrendered after a siege of several weeks.
commanders B: the defenders under the marzban of Fars, Shahrag
Iranian force: The garrison and people of Bishapur in the marzbanate of Fars.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Battle of Bishapur (643-644)
note: A revolt of Bishapur under Shahrag's brother was crushed after November 644 (646 according to al-Baladhuri); not entered separately.

name: Jurmizan
how the result was decided: Isfandiyar's army was defeated and he was taken alive.
Iranian force: The forces of Azerbaijan under the Ispahbudhan lord Isfandiyar.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 22; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Azerbaijan; Muslim conquest of Northern Persia
note: His brother Bahram was then defeated by Utba ibn Farqad and fled (no place named; not entered).

name: Waj Rudh
place: Waj Rudh, between Hamadan and Qazvin, Iran
how the result was decided: The combined Persian army was routed with heavy losses and Muta was killed.
commanders B: Muta the Daylamite (killed), Isfandiyar (Isfandyadh), Farrukhzad, Abu'l-Farrukhan al-Zinabi; an Armenian contingent (Varaztirots named)
Iranian force: A coalition of the Daylamites under Muta, the forces of Rayy and of Azerbaijan under the Ispahbudhan brothers, and an Armenian contingent.
languages: Daylami and Caspian; Parthian; Persian; Armenian
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 22; Pourshariati 2008; en.wikipedia Battle of Waj Rudh
note: Al-Tabari compares it in scale to Nahavand. The death of Varaztirots there (en.wikipedia) is doubtful: he appears later in Armenia.

name: Zanjan (643)
how the result was decided: The garrison was overpowered and the city fell.
Iranian force: The Persian garrison of Zanjan.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 22; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Azerbaijan
note: en.wikipedia's Muslim conquest of Persia dates a 'Battle of Zanjan' to 651.

name: Bayrudh
place: Bayrudh, between Dawraq and Ahvaz, Iran
how the result was decided: Piruz's rising was defeated at Bayrudh the same year.
Iranian force: Persians of Khuzestan and Kurds gathered by Piruz (al-Tabari).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 23; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Khuzestan
note: A rising in a province already conquered.

name: Kerman (644)
place: in the province of Kerman, Iran
how the result was decided: The Persians of Kerman were defeated in a pitched battle and their marzban killed.
commanders A: Suhayl ibn Adi, Abd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Itban
Iranian force: The local garrisons of Kerman with the mountain people of the Qufs (Kufichis), according to al-Tabari.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 23; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Persia; List of battles involving the Rashidun Caliphate

name: Rishahr (644)
how the result was decided: Shahrag's army was defeated and he was killed.
commanders A: Uthman ibn Abi al-As (or his brother al-Hakam)
Iranian force: The army of Fars under its marzban Shahrag.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Arab conquest of Fars
note: The sources disagree whether Shahrag or his brother was killed, and on the date. Year added to the name because of the British landing at Rishahr (Reshire) in 1856.

name: Zaranj (644)
how the result was decided: Besieged in Zarang, the Sistanis capitulated and agreed to pay kharaj.
commanders A: Asim ibn Amr al-Tamimi, Abd Allah ibn Umayr
Iranian force: The people and garrison of Sistan (Sakastan) in their capital.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 23; Tarikh-i Sistan; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Sistan
note: Sistan soon revolted again.

name: Istakhr (siege, 648)
how the result was decided: Mahak was forced to surrender Istakhr.
Iranian force: The garrison of Istakhr, the Sasanian dynasty's ancestral city, under Mahak.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: fighting not described; may have been a capitulation without assault
doubts and flags: Borderline: fighting not described; may have been a capitulation without assault.
sources: Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; en.wikipedia Arab conquest of Fars; Istakhr Revolts (648-651)

name: Istakhr (649)
war: Arab conquest of Persia (Fars; revolt of Istakhr)
how the result was decided: The rebels defeated the Arab garrison and killed its commander Ubayd Allah ibn Ma'mar.
commanders A: the rebel leaders of Istakhr (supporters of Yazdegerd III)
Iranian force: The people of Istakhr in revolt, with Yazdegerd III's partisans (no details).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Arab conquest of Fars
note: A revolt of a city that had capitulated; it could also be classed as Iranian resistance. Some accounts (e.g. en.wikipedia Persian revolts against the Rashidun Caliphate) place Ubayd Allah's death later.

name: Gor (siege)
how the result was decided: Gor was taken after Istakhr fell, following an earlier interrupted siege.
Iranian force: The defenders of Ardashir I's round city of Gor (not described).
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: fighting not described in detail
doubts and flags: Borderline: fighting not described in detail.
sources: Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; en.wikipedia Arab conquest of Fars
note: Kazerun and Siraf were taken in the same campaign.

name: Istakhr (siege, 650)
how the result was decided: Istakhr was taken by storm after a siege with catapult bombardment and sacked.
Iranian force: The people and nobles of Istakhr rallied by Yazdegerd III, who had come to organise resistance and left for Gor and Kerman.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; al-Tabari, AH 29-30; en.wikipedia Istakhr Revolts (648-651); Arab conquest of Fars
note: Yazdegerd III fled to Kerman and then Sistan and Merv.

name: Tamisha
war: Arab conquest of Persia (Gurgan and Tabaristan)
how the result was decided: The fort was besieged and its defenders surrendered on terms (and, in al-Tabari, were then killed).
Iranian force: The garrison of Tamisha on the border of Gurgan and Tabaristan.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a minor siege known mainly from al-Tabari
doubts and flags: Borderline: a minor siege known mainly from al-Tabari.
sources: al-Tabari, AH 30; en.wikipedia Persian revolts against the Rashidun Caliphate
note: Sa'id's campaign forced Gurgan to pay tribute but failed in Tabaristan.

date: 651 CE (late in the year; exact date unknown)
name: Merv (651, Nezak and Mahoe Suri v Yazdegerd III)
war: Arab conquest of Iran (flight and death of Yazdegerd III)
side B: Marzban of Merv; Hephthalite principality of Badghis
how the result was decided: Yazdegerd's force was beaten and scattered and he was killed by a miller soon after.
Iranian side: Yazdegerd III's Sasanian following v Marzban of Merv
factions B: Marzban of Merv, Hephthalite principality of Badghis
why it counts: Both sides were led by Persians (Yazdegerd III; Mahoe Suri) and Nezak Tarkhan's Hephthalite horse took part (Ibn A'tham, Dinawari; Morony in Encyclopaedia Iranica).
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Ibn A'tham al-Kufi, Kitab al-Futuh; al-Dinawari, al-Akhbar al-Tiwal; al-Tabari; Morony, M., Encyclopaedia Iranica (Yazdegerd III); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yazdegerd_III
note: The fight is mentioned in a sentence by modern summaries and its place, size and course are not recorded; 'Nezak Tarkhan' may be a title.

name: Oxus River
place: Deir al-Ahnaf near Marw al-Rudh, on the Murghab, Afghanistan (en.wikipedia: on the Amu Darya, Turkmenistan)
how the result was decided: In the tradition al-Ahnaf held his ground, the Turks withdrew across the Oxus and Yazdegerd fled; his officials handed over the treasury.
Iranian force: Yazdegerd III's following with a large army supplied by the ruler of Sogdia and men of Balkh and Tokharistan, with Turkish allies; about 50,000 cavalry in the tradition.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
doubts and flags: Traditional: Known essentially from Sayf ibn Umar's account in al-Tabari, which places it in AH 22 (643) and is regarded by modern historians (e.
sources: al-Tabari, AH 22 (Sayf ibn Umar); en.wikipedia Battle of Oxus River; Muslim conquests in Afghanistan
note: Yazdegerd III was killed near Merv later in 651 by a miller after the marzban Mahuy Suri turned against him (a murder, not a battle).

date: 651 (al-Tabari places the conquest of Ray in AH 22, 642/643)
name: Ray (651)
how the result was decided: Attacked at night at the foot of the mountain and from behind by cavalry led through a hidden route, Siyavakhsh's army was routed and Ray taken.
Iranian force: The forces of Ray under the Mihranid Siyavakhsh, with help reportedly sent from Damavand, Tabaristan, Qumis and Gurgan.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: al-Tabari, AH 22; Pourshariati 2008; en.wikipedia Battle of Ray (651)
note: Farrukhzad of the House of Ispahbudhan (al-Zinabi in al-Tabari), a Persian noble, fought on the Arab side against Siyavakhsh. The date is disputed (642/643 or 651).

name: Zaranj (651)
how the result was decided: The Sistanis were defeated with heavy losses outside the walls and withdrew into Zarang; Aparviz then capitulated on terms.
Iranian force: The forces of Sakastan under its marzban Aparviz.
why it counts: Sasanian Empire: an Iranian-led state
sources: Tarikh-i Sistan; Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Sistan
note: Tribute of 1 million dirhams a year, 1,000 slave boys and 1,000 gold vessels.

date: 652 or 653 (al-Tabari's year 32); other accounts c. 654 or c. 656-657
name: Badghis
war: Arab conquest of Iran (Iranian revolts after 651: Qarin's revolt)
how the result was decided: Ibn Khazim's night attack routed the rebel army and killed Qarin; the Arabs held the field.
commanders A: Abd Allah ibn Khazim al-Sulami (for Abd Allah ibn Amir)
commanders B: Qarin (of the House of Karen; killed)
Iranian force: Qarin's levy of about 40,000 men raised in Quhistan, Tabasayn, Herat and Badghis (al-Tabari), with Hephthalite support according to modern accounts.
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
losses B: Qarin and many of his men killed
sources: al-Tabari 15, pp. 107-110; en.wikipedia Battle of Badghis (redirects to Persian revolts against the Rashidun Caliphate); Muslim conquest of Khorasan; Daryaee, Oxford Handbook of Iranian History, p. 216
note: Rashidun Caliphate. The date varies between Wikipedia articles (652, 654, c. 656-657); al-Tabari tells it after Ibn Amir's Khorasan campaign (year 32 = 652-653). The revolt briefly drove the Arabs from Nishapur and Zaranj, and the Arab garrison of Merv was besieged. Whether Hephthalite troops fought in the battle itself is not documented.

name: Herat (siege, 652)
war: Arab conquest of Iran (Iranian revolts after 651)
how the result was decided: Herat, which had revolted after first accepting terms, was attacked again, its ruler was defeated and the city was forced back to a treaty, so the place fell to the besiegers.
commanders A: al-Ahnaf ibn Qays (for Abd Allah ibn Amir)
Iranian force: The garrison and townsmen of Herat under its ruler, backed (according to the Wikipedia article) by the House of Karen and Hephthalite allies; no numbers are given.
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
borderline: thinly sourced Wikipedia article; whether the defenders were Persian or Hephthalite is not clear
doubts and flags: Borderline: thinly sourced Wikipedia article; whether the defenders were Persian or Hephthalite is not clear.
sources: al-Tabari; al-Baladhuri; en.wikipedia Siege of Herat (652); Muslim conquest of Persia
note: Rashidun Caliphate. The Muslim conquest of Persia article dates Ahnaf's siege of Herat to 651; the Siege of Herat (652) article dates it 652 and says Herat later rebelled again with the Karenids (see Badghis).

date: c. 653-654 (about two years after Rabi ibn Ziyad's conquest)
name: Zaranj (siege, 653)
war: Arab conquest of Sistan (revolt of Zaranj)
how the result was decided: The rebel city was retaken and its marzban surrendered, so the place fell to the besiegers.
commanders A: Abd al-Rahman ibn Samura (for Abd Allah ibn Amir)
Iranian force: The townsmen of Zaranj and the Sistani followers of their marzban, who had thrown out Rabi ibn Ziyad's garrison; no numbers are given.
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the fighting is not described; the city may have been retaken mainly by blockade and surrender
doubts and flags: Borderline: the fighting is not described; the city may have been retaken mainly by blockade and surrender.
sources: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; Tarikh-i Sistan; en.wikipedia Muslim conquest of Sistan; Persian revolts against the Rashidun Caliphate
note: Rashidun Caliphate. The tribute was doubled to 2,000,000 dirhams and 2,000 slaves, and Ibn Samura went on to take Bust and Zabul. Rabi ibn Ziyad's first conquest of Zaranj (651/652) (a separate entry).

name: Nishapur (siege, 657)
war: Iranian revolts during the First Fitna
how the result was decided: Khulayd besieged Nishapur until the rebels agreed to terms and their leader was taken prisoner, so the place fell to the besiegers.
commanders B: the rebel leaders of Nishapur (not named), who rallied to a daughter of Khosrow
Iranian force: The rebels of Nishapur and Khorasan, who had thrown off Arab rule during the First Fitna; no numbers are given.
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the fighting is not described; the siege ended in terms
doubts and flags: Borderline: the fighting is not described; the siege ended in terms.
sources: al-Tabari; al-Baladhuri; en.wikipedia Persian revolts against the Rashidun Caliphate
note: Rashidun Caliphate (Ali). The Wikipedia article says Khulayd besieged both Nishapur and Merv until the rebels made peace.

date: during the reign of Mu'awiya I (661-680); year uncertain, placed here at c. 670
name: Defeat of Masqala ibn Hubayra
place: the passes of Ruyan, Tabaristan (Mazandaran), Iran
how the result was decided: The Tabaristanis held the mountain passes and destroyed Masqala's army, which never returned.
commanders A: the lords of Tabaristan (commander not named in the sources used)
Iranian force: Mountain levies of Tabaristan and Ruyan under their native lords; the sources give no numbers.
why it counts: Tabaristan: an Iranian-led state
losses B: Masqala and nearly all his army
borderline: no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander); not verified online
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander); not verified online.
sources: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan (Tabaristan); Ibn Isfandiyar, History of Tabaristan
note: Umayyad Caliphate. The disaster gave rise to the Arabic proverb 'until Masqala returns from Tabaristan'. Date and numbers differ between the sources.

name: Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad's raid on Bukhara (Baykand and Ramitan)
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Umayyad raids of 673-676)
place: Baykand and Bukhara region, Zarafshan oasis (modern Bukhara Region)
allies B: Turkic horse of Transoxiana called in by Khatun
how the result was decided: Ubayd Allah beat the Bukharan and Turkic army, took Baykand and Ramitan and forced Khatun to pay tribute (about a million dirhams in the Wikipedia summary of Tabari).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Narshakhi, History of Bukhara (trans. R. N. Frye, 1954); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana
note: First Arab crossing of the Oxus to reach Bukhara. Bukhara's ruler was a Sogdian queen-regent, so the Iranian side was both led and manned by Sogdians, with Turkic allies. Details of the actual fighting are thin and partly from Narshakhi's later retelling.

name: Bukhara (Sa'id ibn Uthman, 676)
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Umayyad raids of 673-676)
allies B: Turkic allies of Bukhara; Kish and Nasaf
how the result was decided: Sa'id invested Bukhara, fought off its Bukharan and Turkic relief and Khatun bought peace and gave tribute (Tabari; Gibb).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana
note: Same expedition as the Samarkand entry that follows. Tabari's account of the first stage is brief; some retellings make Bukhara a negotiated submission rather than a siege with fighting.

date: 676 (56 AH); the city fell in three days
name: Samarkand (Sa'id ibn Uthman, 676)
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Umayyad raids of 673-676)
how the result was decided: After a hard fight against the Sogdians and Turks the Arabs took Samarkand in three days and took Sogdian hostages (Tabari; Wikipedia summary).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana
note: The fate of the Sogdian hostages and slaves at Medina is told differently in the sources. The Arabs did not hold Samarkand, so the conquest did not last.

name: Umayya ibn Abdallah's defeat at Bukhara (c. 696)
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Umayyad raids; second Fitna aftermath)
place: Beyond the Oxus, at or near Bukhara (modern Bukhara Region)
how the result was decided: Abandoned by his lieutenant Bukayr, Umayya's army was encircled and made a humiliating peace with the Bukharans (Tabari; Wikipedia).
commanders A: Umayya ibn Abdallah ibn Khalid; Bukayr ibn Wishah (second in command, who quit)
commanders B: Bukharan nobles (names not given in the summaries)
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana
note: A minor episode known only from one or two lines of Tabari. Included because Bukharans, not Turks alone, are named as the enemy; the Sogdian share of the force is not stated.

name: Zunbil's destruction of Ubayd Allah's army (698)
war: Arab conquest of Zabulistan (Umayyad wars with the Zunbils)
how the result was decided: Rutbil trapped the Arab army in the mountains, forced Ubayd Allah to pay a large tribute and give hostages, and he promised not to invade again.
why it counts: The Zunbils are said to be of Hephthalite origin (Wink); the Hephthalite identification is uncertain.
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; al-Tabari; Bosworth, C. E., Sistan under the Arabs (1968); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zunbils
note: The Arab army was called the 'army of destruction'; the better-known 'Army of Peacocks' of Ibn al-Ash'ath (c. 699-700) reached a settlement with the Zunbils and then rebelled. The Zunbils' ethnic origin (Hephthalite, Turk Shahi kin or local) is debated.

date: c. 703 (Wikipedia, 'Nezak Tarkhan'); not found in the Transoxiana summary
name: Badghis (Yazid ibn al-Muhallab against Nezak, c. 703)
side B: Nezak Tarkhan of Badghis and his allies
how the result was decided: Wikipedia states that Yazid ibn al-Muhallab defeated Nezak at Badghis in 703; I did not see this in Tabari's text.
Iranian side: Nezak Tarkhan of Badghis and his allies
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nezak_Tarkhan; al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.)
note: Nezak is called a Hephthalite ruler of Badghis (sometimes the last one); the Hephthalites' Iranian identity is debated and 'Nezak' may be a title. Weakest entry: the battle may be conflated with Nezak's alliance of 701-704.

date: 704 (Wikipedia); Musa's rebel rule at Tirmidh c. 689-704
name: Tirmidh (Musa ibn Abd Allah ibn Khazim, 704)
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Arab rebel Musa ibn Khazim and the Tokharian princes)
side B: Musa ibn Abd Allah ibn Khazim
allies B: Native princes of Tokharistan and Hephthalite lords; Turks
how the result was decided: Musa was killed and Tirmidh taken by Uthman ibn Mas'ud (Wikipedia summary of Tabari).
Iranian side: Musa ibn Abd Allah ibn Khazim
commanders B: Musa ibn Abd Allah ibn Khazim
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nezak_Tarkhan
note: The leader on the Tirmidh side was an Arab rebel; the Tokharian and Hephthalite princes were his allies (the 701-704 alliance with Nezak and Thabit and Hurayth ibn Qutba), and the share cannot be measured. Included as uncertain.

date: spring 705 (Wikipedia); sources disagree whether it surrendered or was stormed
name: Balkh (Qutayba's recovery, 705)
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba ibn Muslim)
side B: Balkh and the lords of Tokharistan
how the result was decided: Qutayba retook Balkh in spring 705 and then took the submission of Tish of Chaghaniyan and of Nezak (Wikipedia, 'Qutayba ibn Muslim').
Iranian side: Balkh and the lords of Tokharistan
commanders B: Nezak Tarkhan (Hephthalite) and local lords of Balkh
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim; al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923)
note: Little real fighting is certain; Nezak and Tish submitted. Kept because Wikipedia calls it a battle.

name: Baykand (Paykand), siege of 706
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba ibn Muslim)
place: Baykand (Paykand), the 'city of merchants', south-west of Bukhara, Uzbekistan
how the result was decided: Qutayba took Baykand after a siege of about two months; it rose again and was sacked, its men killed and others enslaved (Narshakhi; Tabari).
sources: Narshakhi, History of Bukhara (trans. R. N. Frye, 1954); al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim
note: Narshakhi and Tabari say the Baykandis fought and called in help, which is the evidence that townsmen counted. The booty (arms, merchants' goods) financed the later campaigns.

name: Tumushkath and Ramitan (Qutayba, 707)
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba ibn Muslim)
place: Tumushkath and Ramitan (Ramithana), north of Bukhara, Uzbekistan
side B: Sogdian princes of Bukhara, Kish and Nasaf
how the result was decided: Qutayba took the two towns and scattered the coalition, but then withdrew behind the Oxus to avoid a united Sogdian army (Tabari; Wikipedia).
Iranian side: Sogdian princes of Bukhara, Kish and Nasaf
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim
note: The Sogdian princes were principals; the Turkic prince Kur Maghayun commanded the allied cavalry. The next year's (708) campaign failed against the united Sogdians but no named engagement is recorded.

name: Bukhara (Qutayba's capture, 709)
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba ibn Muslim)
how the result was decided: Qutayba defeated the relief army, stormed Bukhara, imposed a 200,000-dirham tribute and a garrison, and Tarkhun of Samarkand became his vassal (Tabari; Narshakhi; Wikipedia).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Narshakhi, History of Bukhara (trans. R. N. Frye, 1954); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim
note: The conquest of Bukhara after three years of campaigning. Narshakhi adds that the Arabs settled in Bukharan houses and built the first mosque.

date: autumn 709 to spring 710 (91 AH); Nezak's capture and execution in 710 (one source says 709)
name: Nezak's revolt in Tokharistan (709-710)
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (revolt of Nezak Tarkhan)
place: Lower Tokharistan: Talaqan, Faryab, Balkh and Baghlan area, Afghanistan (Nezak's last stronghold not securely located)
side B: Nezak Tarkhan and the princes of Tokharistan
allies B: The Yabghu of Tokharistan; Princes of Talaqan and Faryab
how the result was decided: Abd al-Rahman and Qutayba crushed the revolt; Nezak was captured and executed on al-Hajjaj's orders despite a promise of pardon, and the Yabghu was sent to Damascus (Tabari; Wikipedia).
Iranian side: Nezak Tarkhan and the princes of Tokharistan
commanders A: Qutayba ibn Muslim; Abd al-Rahman ibn Muslim
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nezak_Tarkhan; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim
note: Nezak is a Hephthalite ruler of Badghis; the princes of Tokharistan were Bactrian-speaking local lords, so the Iranian side is well attested though the Hephthalite identity is debated. The sources do not give one named battle.

name: Shuman and Akharun (Qutayba, c. 710)
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba ibn Muslim)
place: Shuman and Akharun, upper Oxus valley, Tokharistan (modern Surkhandarya / southern Tajikistan)
how the result was decided: Qutayba stormed the king's citadel and the king was killed (Wikipedia, 'Qutayba ibn Muslim'; Tabari).
commanders B: The king of Shuman and Akharun (name not recorded)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim; al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.)
note: A minor Tokharian principality; location approximate.

date: 711-712 (92-93 AH); the sources are unclear on the order of events
name: Khwarazm (Qutayba's intervention, 711-712)
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba ibn Muslim)
place: Khwarazm (Kath and Hazarasp area), Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan
side A (victor if decisive): Umayyad Caliphate; Khwarazmshah Jigan as Arab client
side B: Khurrazadh and the king of Khamjird
allies B: Khwarazmian rebels who later killed the Khwarazmshah
how the result was decided: Abd al-Rahman defeated the king of Khamjird's troops and Khurrazadh and his followers were executed; a later Khwarazmian rising was put down by al-Mughira ibn Abdallah (Tabari; Wikipedia, 'Qutayba ibn Muslim').
Iranian side: Umayyad Caliphate v Khurrazadh and the king of Khamjird
factions A: Umayyad Caliphate, Khwarazmshah Jigan as Arab client
factions B: Khurrazadh and the king of Khamjird
commanders A: Qutayba ibn Muslim; Abd al-Rahman ibn Muslim; Khwarazmshah Jigan
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim; al-Biruni, Chronology of Ancient Nations (on the killing of the Khwarazmian scholars)
note: Khwarazmian princes fought on both sides: the Afrighid shah as Arab ally against his own brother. Al-Biruni's story that Qutayba killed Khwarazm's scholars and burned their books is tradition. Place is the region only.

name: Samarkand (Qutayba's siege, 712)
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba ibn Muslim)
allies A: Native levies of Bukhara, Kish, Nasaf and Khwarazm
allies B: Relief force of the princes of Shash and Ferghana
how the result was decided: Qutayba ambushed the Shash relief force, breached the walls with siege engines and Ghurak made terms; 30,000 slaves and 2,200,000 dirhams were taken (Tabari; Wikipedia).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana
note: Ghurak had overthrown Tarkhun and took the throne. He was left on it under Arab terms and later founded Farankath. Native Sogdian, Bukharan and Khwarazmian levies served in Qutayba's army (Tabari), so Iranians stood on both sides.

date: 713 (94 AH); the order and detail of the actions are uncertain
name: Khujand and Minak (Qutayba, 713)
war: Muslim conquest of Transoxiana (Qutayba's Jaxartes campaign)
place: Khujand on the Jaxartes (Tajikistan) and Minak in Ushrusana
side B: Princes of Shash, Ferghana and Ushrusana with their levies
how the result was decided: Qutayba's army fought before Khujand and at Minak and advanced to Shash; the Arabs held the field (Wikipedia, 'Qutayba ibn Muslim'; Tabari).
Iranian side: Princes of Shash, Ferghana and Ushrusana with their levies
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qutayba_ibn_Muslim; al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923)
note: Merged because the sources give only the places. The Ushrusanans were Iranian; Ferghana and Shash only partly so.

name: Namangan (Chinese restoration of the Ikhshid of Ferghana, 715)
side A (victor if decisive): Tang China; the deposed Ikhshid of Ferghana
how the result was decided: The Chinese force defeated Alutar's Arab-backed army and put the Ikhshid back on the throne (Wikipedia; Chinese annals, Cefu Yuangui).
Iranian side: Tang China v Arab occupation force
factions A: Tang China, the deposed Ikhshid of Ferghana
commanders A: Zhang Xiaosong; the Ikhshid of Ferghana (name not given)
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana; Cefu Yuangui and Xin Tangshu (Tang annals), as summarised in Gibb 1923 and Beckwith 1987
note: The Ikhshid bore an Iranian title; Ferghana's ruling house and speech were probably partly Iranian but the sources do not settle it, so qualifies is uncertain.

name: Defeat of Yazid ibn al-Muhallab in Tabaristan
place: the mountain passes of Tabaristan (Mazandaran), Iran
how the result was decided: After losing on the plain, the Tabaristanis ambushed the Arab army in the mountain passes and drove it back in a chaotic retreat; Yazid then made a tributary peace and withdrew.
Iranian force: Farrukhan's Tabaristani forces with allies he recruited from Daylam and Gilan.
why it counts: Tabaristan: an Iranian-led state
strength B: part of an army given as about 100,000 for the whole campaign
losses B: not heavy in the fighting, but many killed in the ravines during the retreat
borderline: no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander)
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander).
sources: al-Tabari (year 98); Ibn Isfandiyar; en.wikipedia Yazid ibn al-Muhallab; Farrukhan the Great; Dabuyid dynasty
note: Umayyad Caliphate. Yazid had first beaten the Tabaristanis on the plain; the Wikipedia articles describe the result as Farrukhan's successful containment of the invasion. Tabaristan stayed independent until 760.

name: Jurjan (siege, 717)
war: Yazid ibn al-Muhallab's Caspian campaign (revolt of Jurjan)
how the result was decided: Al-Tabari says Yazid besieged the rebels in their stronghold for months and took it by a mountain path, so the place fell to the besiegers.
commanders B: the rebel leaders of Jurjan (not named)
Iranian force: The Iranian townsmen and lords of Jurjan who had risen, encouraged by Farrukhan, and massacred the Arab garrison; no numbers are given.
why it counts: Iranian resistance: an Iranian-led state
losses B: many killed and executed after the fall (al-Tabari)
borderline: the siege is told by al-Tabari, but the Wikipedia articles (after Kennedy) mention only the revolt and Yazid's escape by diplomacy
doubts and flags: Borderline: the siege is told by al-Tabari, but the Wikipedia articles (after Kennedy) mention only the revolt and Yazid's escape by diplomacy.
sources: al-Tabari (year 98); en.wikipedia Yazid ibn al-Muhallab; Farrukhan the Great
note: Umayyad Caliphate. The revolt nearly trapped Yazid's army in the Caspian lands.

date: 721 (the rising began in 720-721; Kang Daibin captured by Wang Jun and sent to Xuanzong)
name: Revolt of the Six Hu Prefectures (Kang Daibin, 721)
war: Rising of the Six Hu Prefectures (Tang)
place: Six Hu Prefectures, the Ordos (Lanchi and Yanchi region), Ningxia-Inner Mongolia
side B: Hu rebels of the Six Hu Prefectures
how the result was decided: Wang Jun captured Kang Daibin soon after the Tang commanders took the field and delivered him to the emperor.
Iranian side: Hu rebels of the Six Hu Prefectures
commanders A: Zhang Yue; Wang Jun; Wang Maozhong
why it counts: Leader by descent: Kang Daibin, who led the Hu of the Six Hu Prefectures, bears the Sogdian surname Kang (Samarkand) and the prefectures were settled with Sogdians and Turks (Rong Xinjiang, de la Vaissière), so his people were Sogdian-Turkic mixed; the Turkic side of the community is large.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian, juan 212; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhang_Yue_(Tang_dynasty); Rong Xinjiang, Zhonggu Hu zu shi yanjiu (2001), on the Six Hu Prefectures; de la Vaissiere, Sogdian Traders (2005)
note: A major rising of a Sogdian-Turkic settler community in the Tang Ordos; the Tang forces were under Zhang Yue, Wang Jun and Wang Maozhong. A second Hu rising under Kang Yuanzi in 722 was separate. Individual battles and places are not itemised in the sources used, so this is a campaign-level entry.

name: Khujand (Sa'id al-Harashi against the Sogdian rebels, 721-722)
how the result was decided: At-Tar of Ferghana betrayed the Sogdians' camp; al-Harashi defeated them and massacred more than 3,000 Sogdians (Tabari; Wikipedia, 'Divashtich').
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divashtich; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim conquest of Transoxiana
note: The Sogdian nobles had fled to Khujand from Samarkand and Panjikent. Some retellings put the massacre at the end of the fight, some after surrender.

date: 722 (autumn, Wikipedia); the defeat of Divashtich near the Zarafshan and his flight to Mount Mugh
name: Mount Mugh and Panjikent (Divashtich, 722)
place: Panjikent and the fortress of Kal'ai Mug on Mount Mugh, Tajikistan
side B: Divashtich, ruler of Panjikent, and the Sogdian rebels
allies B: Ferghanan and Turkic hopes of help that did not arrive
how the result was decided: Al-Harashi won the battle by the Zarafshan, Divashtich fled to Mug, surrendered and was crucified on a Zoroastrian dakhma (Tabari; Wikipedia, 'Divashtich').
Iranian side: Divashtich, ruler of Panjikent, and the Sogdian rebels
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divashtich; Mugh Documents (Livshits, Smirnova, Bogolyubov)
note: The Mugh archive of Sogdian documents, found at the fortress in 1933, comes from Divashtich's court. The Wikipedia article does not describe a long siege, only the flight and surrender.

date: 724 (106 AH); season uncertain (Tabari has it in the summer)
name: Day of Thirst (724)
place: On the Jaxartes near Khujand, after the retreat from Ferghana (Tajikistan)
allies B: Princes of Shash and Ferghana; Remnants of the Sogdian rebellion
how the result was decided: The Arabs were trapped between the Turgesh and the Transoxianian forces, burned their baggage, broke through to Khujand with heavy losses (Wikipedia; Tabari).
commanders A: Muslim ibn Sa'id al-Kilabi; Abd al-Rahman ibn Na'im al-Ghamidi
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); H. A. R. Gibb, The Arab Conquests in Central Asia (1923); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_Thirst
note: Turgesh-led, with Sogdian, Shashi and Ferghanan allies; the Wikipedia article does not mention Alutar, so his presence is from the Divashtich and Namangan material. Muslim ibn Sa'id's expedition was against Ferghana.

name: Baykand (729)
place: Baykand, about 30 km south of Bukhara, Uzbekistan
how the result was decided: The Arabs broke through the Turgesh encirclement with a narrow victory and reached Bukhara (Wikipedia).
commanders A: Ashras ibn Abdallah al-Sulami; Qatan ibn Qutayba; Thabit Qutnah
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Baykand
note: Turgesh-led with Sogdian allies, among them the rulers of Bukhara, who had risen against Ashras's tax policy. Ghurak is listed in the infobox as a commander, but the text says only that he went over to the rebels.

name: Kamarja (siege, 729)
place: Kamarja, a fortress about 42 km west of Samarkand, Uzbekistan
allies B: Contingents of Ferghana, al-Taraband, Afshinah, Nasaf and Bukhara; Soghdian prince of al-Taraband; Khosrau, grandson of Yazdegerd III
how the result was decided: The Arab garrison held out 58 days and was allowed to leave for Dabusiyya under a negotiated agreement (Wikipedia).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Kamarja
note: Turgesh-led siege with Sogdian contingents named in the sources. The Sasanian prince Khosrau, a grandson of the last king, accompanied the Turgesh. Arab rule in Sogdia collapsed afterwards.

name: Defile (731)
place: Takhtakaracha Pass between Samarkand and Kish, Uzbekistan
allies B: Troops of the rulers of Sogdia, Shash and Ferghana
how the result was decided: The Turgesh destroyed Sawra's 12,000 and cut up Junayd's army, which escaped to Samarkand with very heavy losses (Wikipedia; Tabari; Blankinship).
commanders A: Junayd ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Murri; Sawra ibn al-Hurr al-Abani (killed)
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Defile
note: Turgesh-led with Sogdian, Shashi and Ferghanan allies; Ghurak advised the Turgesh to set the grass on fire. Tokharistan was also in revolt, which drew off about 28,000 of Junayd's men.

name: Baggage (Battle of the Baggage, 737)
place: Upper Oxus, in or near Khuttal, Tajikistan or northern Afghanistan
allies A: Contingent of al-Saghaniyan in the baggage escort
how the result was decided: The Turgesh captured most of Asad's baggage train and the Khuttal campaign failed (Wikipedia; Tabari).
commanders A: Asad ibn Abdallah al-Qasri; Ibrahim ibn Asim al-Uqayli
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Baggage
note: Turgesh-led, with Sogdians and Khuttal. The Saghan Khudah, a Tokharian prince, was killed with his contingent fighting for the Arabs, so Iranians stood on both sides. Khuttal's ruling house was Hephthalite or Turkic, which Wikipedia does not settle.

name: Kharistan (737)
place: Kharistan in Juzjan, near Maymana, Afghanistan
allies A: The Juzjan prince and his retinue
allies B: Contingents of the princes of Sughd, Shash, Usrushana and Khuttal and of the Yabghu of Tokharistan
how the result was decided: Asad surprised the scattered Turgesh, took their camp and spoils, and Suluk and Ibn Surayj fled (Wikipedia; Tabari).
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kharistan
note: Turgesh-led, with Sogdian, Ushrusanan, Shashi, Khuttali and Tokharian contingents named, and the Juzjan prince on the Arab side. About 4,000 Turgesh against 7,000 Arabs; the allied total of about 30,000 had dispersed to raid.

date: c. 739-741 (the sources do not date it exactly)
name: Jaxartes (Nasr ibn Sayyar against Shash and the Turgesh, c. 740)
war: Nasr ibn Sayyar's reconquest of Transoxiana
place: On the Jaxartes, in Shash territory (modern Uzbekistan or Kazakhstan)
how the result was decided: Nasr drove off the Turgesh and killed the chief of one of their detachments, and the ruler of Shash then came to terms (Wikipedia, 'Nasr ibn Sayyar'; Tabari).
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); Kh. Y. Blankinship, The End of the Jihad State (1994); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasr_ibn_Sayyar
note: About 15,000 Shashi troops are reported. Shash's population was partly Sogdian-speaking but its rulers had Turkic titles, so the Iranian share is unproven.

date: spring 748, after the occupation of Merv
name: Tus (748)
how the result was decided: Nasr's son Tamim was defeated at Tus and Nasr then gave up Nishapur to Qahtaba.
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasr_ibn_Sayyar
note: Qahtaba was an Arab (Tayyi'); Iranian mawali in the Khurasani army cannot be quantified, and Wikipedia stresses a heavily Arab core. This entry also stands for the fall of Nishapur, which followed without a separate battle that I could confirm.

name: Merv (748)
side B: Umayyad governor Nasr ibn Sayyar; Kharijites of Shayban
how the result was decided: The Hashimiyya army occupied Merv on 14 February 748 and Nasr fled to Nishapur.
principal opponents: Umayyad governor Nasr ibn Sayyar; Kharijites of Shayban
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Muslim; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasr_ibn_Sayyar
note: Abu Muslim's origin is debated: Wikipedia says 'most likely Persian' (born at Merv or near Isfahan) but calls the accounts doubtful. His forces were Khurasani Arab settlers plus native (Iranian) converts and officers of mixed origin; this was more a seizure of Merv after months of skirmishing than a pitched battle.

name: Jurjan
how the result was decided: The Abbasid army defeated an Umayyad force of about 10,000.
commanders B: Nubata ibn Hanzala (killed, per Tabari; unnamed in the Wikipedia article)
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution
note: Arab leader; Iranian share of the Khurasani army unquantified (see Tus). Included because the Khurasani army is a named body with a documented Iranian element.

name: Nahavand (siege, 749)
how the result was decided: Nahavand fell after Qahtaba beat the Syrian relief army; the Syrians were spared and the Khurasani units of the garrison executed.
commanders A: Qahtaba ibn Shabib al-Ta'i; Al-Hasan ibn Qahtaba
commanders B: Umayyad commanders (Syrian relief force defeated first)
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution
note: Arab leaders; Iranian share of the besiegers unquantified. The Umayyad garrison also had Khurasani units.

name: Isfahan (749)
how the result was decided: The Abbasid army defeated an Umayyad force put at 50,000, opening the way to Nahavand.
commanders B: Amir ibn Dubara (per Tabari; unnamed in the Wikipedia article)
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution
note: Arab leader; Iranian contingent unquantified. The site (Jabalaq near Isfahan) and the Umayyad commander's name are from memory of Tabari.

name: Euphrates crossing (749)
place: Euphrates near Karbala and Kufa, Iraq
how the result was decided: The Abbasids surprised Ibn Hubayra's forces at night; Qahtaba died but Ibn Hubayra fled to Wasit and Al-Hasan entered Kufa on 2 September 749.
commanders A: Qahtaba ibn Shabib al-Ta'i (killed); Al-Hasan ibn Qahtaba
commanders B: Yazid ibn Umar ibn Hubayra al-Fazari
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution
note: Arab leaders; the Kufa entry was without a major battle. Iranian share unquantified.

name: Wasit (siege, 749-750)
how the result was decided: Ibn Hubayra surrendered on promise of amnesty after the fall of the Umayyad dynasty and was then executed.
commanders B: Yazid ibn Umar ibn Hubayra al-Fazari
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution
note: Arab leaders; the Iranian element of the Khurasani army is again unquantified.

name: Chach (Tashkent), Tang capture by Gao Xianzhi (750)
war: Tang-Arab conflict in Central Asia (preceding Talas)
how the result was decided: Gao Xianzhi took the city after agreeing terms and then plundered it and sent the king to Chang'an (Tang annals).
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gao_Xianzhi; Jiu Tangshu and Xin Tangshu (biography of Gao Xianzhi)
note: Almost no real fighting: Gao is said to have taken Chach by a breach of the truce. Chach had a large Sogdian population but its king's title was Turkic. Qualifies is doubtful. The Chach prince's flight to the Arabs led to Talas (751).

date: 25 January 750 (the Abbasid Revolution article gives 16 January)
name: Zab
place: Greater Zab (left bank, near its mouth), northern Iraq
how the result was decided: Marwan II's army was completely destroyed and he fled to Egypt.
commanders A: Abdallah ibn Ali; Abu Awn Abd al-Malik ibn Yazid
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution
note: Abdallah ibn Ali was an Abbasid prince (Arab) and Abu Awn a Khurasani commander of unclear descent. The Iranian share of the Khurasani army is not given in the sources I read.

name: Damascus (siege, 750)
how the result was decided: Abdallah took the city by storm after a brief siege and killed the governor.
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 27 (The Abbasid Revolution, Williams); Daniel, The Political and Social History of Khurasan under Abbasid Rule 747-820 (1979); Shaban, The Abbasid Revolution (1970); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Revolution; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_Allah_ibn_Ali
note: Arab leader; Iranian share of the army unquantified.

name: Bukhara (revolt of Sharik ibn Shaykh al-Mahri, 751)
war: Abbasid consolidation in Transoxiana (revolt against Abu Muslim)
how the result was decided: Ziyad ibn Salih defeated and killed Sharik at Bukhara (Narshakhi; Tabari).
Iranian side: Abbasid army of Abu Muslim v Sharik ibn Shaykh al-Mahri's rebels
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Narshakhi, History of Bukhara (trans. R. N. Frye, 1954); al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.)
note: An Arab-led rising, not a native one. I could not confirm that Bukharan citizens fought for Sharik, nor give the share of Khurasani Persians in Ziyad's army. Weak entry.

date: late summer 751 (8th lunar month in ZZTJ, about Aug-Sept, Julian)
name: Tuhe (An Lushan v the Khitan, 751)
place: Tuhuzhen River, probably the Xar Moron (Xilamulun) basin, Inner Mongolia
how the result was decided: An Lushan's army, worn down by a long march in rain and heat, was destroyed by the Khitan and he escaped with a handful of riders.
commanders B: Khitan chief (name not given in the sources used)
why it counts: Leader by descent: An Lushan, ruler of Yan, was Sogdian on his father's side (New Book of Tang: 'a mixed Hu of Yingzhou, originally surnamed Kang'; his name is the Sogdian Roxshan; Pulleyblank 1955, Rong Xinjiang), but his mother was a Turk of the Ashide (Ashina) clan, his stepfather the Turk An Yanyan, and he grew up among the Turks, so the Turkic side of his family is at least as strong; here he commanded a Tang frontier army.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian, juan 216; Old Book of Tang, juan 200A (An Lushan); Pulleyblank 1955; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan
note: Before the rebellion; An Lushan, military governor of Pinglu and Fanyang, marched with about 60,000 men and Xi horse and was routed; the defeat and his later restoration to favour are part of the background of 755. Place and some details (the Xi desertion) are from ZZTJ memory and not rechecked.

name: Talas
how the result was decided: The Karluks went over to the Abbasids and the Tang army was routed.
commanders A: Ziyad ibn Salih; Abu Muslim (governor of Khurasan, directed from Samarkand)
sources: Bai Shouyi / Gibb on Talas (from memory); Beckwith, The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia (from memory)
note: Weak candidate: the field commander Ziyad ibn Salih was an Arab and I found no source stating the Iranian share of the Abbasid army; Abu Muslim (most likely Persian, origin disputed) governed the province that raised it.

name: Nisibis (754)
war: Revolt of Abdallah ibn Ali against al-Mansur
how the result was decided: Abdallah suspected treachery on all sides and fled before the battle developed, to Basra.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_Allah_ibn_Ali; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Muslim; al-Tabari, History vol. 28 (Abbasid Authority Affirmed, Kennedy); Daniel, Khurasan under Abbasid Rule
note: Abu Muslim's origin is debated (probably Persian). Abdallah's army also had Khurasanis, many reluctant to fight Abu Muslim (one account says he had 17,000 of them killed).

date: 755 (the revolt lasted about 70 days after Abu Muslim's murder)
name: Defeat of Sunpadh
how the result was decided: Sunpadh's army was routed and he fled to Tabaristan, where he was killed.
Iranian force: Sunpadh's followers, mostly from Jibal and Tabaristan: former partisans of Abu Muslim, Zoroastrians and others; no reliable numbers.
why it counts: Iranian risings: an Iranian-led state
losses B: very heavy (Ibn Isfandiyar says the bones were still visible in 912)
borderline: a rising, not a state; no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated leader)
doubts and flags: Borderline: a rising, not a state; no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated leader).
sources: al-Tabari (year 137); Nizam al-Mulk; Ibn Isfandiyar; en.wikipedia Sunpadh
note: Abbasid Caliphate. Sunpadh had taken Nishapur, Qumis and Rayy (with Abu Muslim's treasury) before the battle.

date: early 756 (about the 1st lunar month; Julian January-February); the town fell about a week after Yan Gaoqing's defection
name: Changshan (Yan Gaoqing's defence, 756)
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
