how the result was decided: Shi Siming and Cai Xide took Changshan and captured Yan Gaoqing, who was sent to Luoyang and executed.
commanders B: Yan Gaoqing (prefect of Changshan); Yuan Lüqian
why it counts: Leader by descent: Shi Siming has the surname Shi, that of the Sogdian city of Kesh, and modern scholars take his family as Turkicised Sogdian, but the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu' of Ningyi (Old Book of Tang 200), so his Sogdian descent is probable rather than certain and the Turkic side of his family is strong; An Lushan, ruler of Yan, was likewise Sogdian on his father's side but half Turkic (Turkic mother and stepfather).
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Siming; Old Book of Tang, juan 187B (Yan Gaoqing)
note: Yan Gaoqing and his cousin Yan Zhenqing (at Pingyuan) turned much of Hebei against the rebels in the winter of 755-756; Changshan, cut off and short of arms, fell after a siege of days. Li Guangbi later recaptured the town (spring 756), so Changshan changed hands twice. Dating is approximate.

date: 21st day of the 10th lunar month 756 (about Oct-Nov 756, Julian); the Qingqu fight two days later
name: Chentao Xie (Fang Guan's defeat, 756)
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
how the result was decided: Fang Guan's centre column, moving ox-carts into the Yan cavalry, was burned and routed with very heavy losses, and his other columns failed at Qingqu two days later.
commanders A: An Shouzhong; Li Guiren (Yan generals before Chang'an)
why it counts: Leader by descent: An Lushan, ruler of Yan, was Sogdian on his father's side (New Book of Tang: 'a mixed Hu of Yingzhou, originally surnamed Kang'; his name is the Sogdian Roxshan; Pulleyblank 1955, Rong Xinjiang), but his mother was a Turk of the Ashide (Ashina) clan, his stepfather the Turk An Yanyan, and he grew up among the Turks, so the Turkic side of his family is at least as strong; the Chang'an front was held by his generals under his authority.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; Old Book of Tang, juan 111 (Fang Guan)
note: A famous Tang disaster in which the chancellor Fang Guan, trying an antique ox-cart formation, lost 40,000 to 50,000 men; the Yan commanders are named An Shouzhong and Li Guiren (the An surname may point to Sogdian origin, unverified). An Lushan himself was at Luoyang, so this counts only through his role as ruler of the army. Date given loosely because the 10th lunar month of 756 straddles two Julian months.

date: about May-June 756 (4th-5th lunar month; ZZTJ), exact day not fixed here
name: Jiashan (756)
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
how the result was decided: Guo Ziyi and Li Guangbi routed Shi Siming's army, which lost (by ZZTJ) about 40,000 dead, and Shi fled.
why it counts: Leader by descent: Shi Siming has the surname Shi, that of the Sogdian city of Kesh, and modern scholars take his family as Turkicised Sogdian, but the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu' of Ningyi (Old Book of Tang 200), so his Sogdian descent is probable rather than certain and the Turkic side of his family is strong; An Lushan was ruler of Yan and the Yan army was his.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; Old Book of Tang, juan 120 (Guo Ziyi) and 110 (Li Guangbi)
note: The best Tang victory of the first campaign: Shi Siming, who had besieged Li Guangbi in Changshan, was caught in the open as Guo Ziyi's army joined Li Guangbi, and escaped on foot. The victory was thrown away when Xuanzong forced Geshu Han out of Tong Pass and the two armies had to fall back. Date and numbers are from ZZTJ and approximate.

date: Feb 756 (Linghu Chao's siege) to Jan 757 (Yin Ziqi's siege, over 60 days; Zhang Xun then withdrew to Ningling and Suiyang)
name: Yongqiu (siege, 756-757)
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
how the result was decided: Zhang Xun, with about 2,000 to 3,000 men, repulsed Linghu Chao's 40,000 and held out against repeated assaults through 756, leaving only in January 757 to move his survivors to Suiyang.
why it counts: Leader by descent: An Lushan, ruler of Yan, was Sogdian on his father's side (New Book of Tang: 'a mixed Hu of Yingzhou, originally surnamed Kang'; his name is the Sogdian Roxshan; Pulleyblank 1955, Rong Xinjiang), but his mother was a Turk of the Ashide (Ashina) clan, his stepfather the Turk An Yanyan, and he grew up among the Turks, so the Turkic side of his family is at least as strong (and after January 757 his son An Qingxu, Sogdian through his father).
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; Old Book of Tang, juan 187B (Zhang Xun)
note: Yongqiu stood across the rebels' road to the Huai and the Yangzi. The 'borrowing arrows with straw men' story is told of this siege. Linghu Chao was a defecting Tang prefect, not a Hu; Yin Ziqi's origin is not recorded in the sources used. The result is for the whole 756 siege and is the least certain part: whether the town was lost or simply abandoned in early 757 is told differently.

date: 16 Dec 755 (rising at Fanyang) to 18 Jan 756 (fall of Luoyang), Julian dates; An Lushan took the imperial title there on 5 Feb 756
name: Luoyang (An Lushan's march and capture, 755-756)
place: Luoyang (the Eastern Capital), Henan, reached by the Yellow River crossing at Lingchang and by Chenliu, Xingyang and Wuniu
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
how the result was decided: Feng Changqing's newly raised levies were beaten in a running fight from Wuniu to the city gates and Luoyang fell, whereupon An Lushan proclaimed the Great Yan there.
commanders B: Feng Changqing; Li Cheng (killed); Lu Yi (killed)
why it counts: Leader by descent: An Lushan, ruler of Yan, was Sogdian on his father's side (New Book of Tang: 'a mixed Hu of Yingzhou, originally surnamed Kang'; his name is the Sogdian Roxshan; Pulleyblank 1955, Rong Xinjiang), but his mother was a Turk of the Ashide (Ashina) clan, his stepfather the Turk An Yanyan, and he grew up among the Turks, so the Turkic side of his family is at least as strong.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; Old Book of Tang, juan 104 (Feng Changqing)
note: The rebel army was about 150,000 (claimed 200,000) from the Fanyang, Pinglu and Hedong garrisons, many of them Khitan, Xi, Tongra and Shiwei horse; Feng Changqing, with about 60,000 untrained recruits, withdrew to Shan and joined Gao Xianzhi at Tong Pass. The Chinese Wikipedia's date of 12 Dec 755 falls before the rising and is a calendar-conversion error; 18 Jan 756 follows the English Wikipedia. The 'march' stands for the Fanyang rising itself, which saw no fighting.

date: 7 Jul 756 (Julian; Lingbao fighting on the 4th day of the 6th lunar month, the pass lost within days)
name: Tong Pass (Lingbao, 756)
place: Lingbao West Plain, east of Tong Pass (Tongguan), Henan-Shaanxi border
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
allies B: Tibetan, Tuyuhun and other frontier troops
how the result was decided: Cui Qianyou's feigned weakness drew Geshu Han's army out of the pass into an ambush at Lingbao and it was destroyed; Tong Pass and then Chang'an fell.
commanders A: Cui Qianyou (in the field); An Lushan (ruler, at Luoyang)
why it counts: Leader by descent: An Lushan, ruler of Yan, was Sogdian on his father's side (New Book of Tang: 'a mixed Hu of Yingzhou, originally surnamed Kang'; his name is the Sogdian Roxshan; Pulleyblank 1955, Rong Xinjiang), but his mother was a Turk of the Ashide (Ashina) clan, his stepfather the Turk An Yanyan, and he grew up among the Turks, so the Turkic side of his family is at least as strong.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; Old Book of Tang, juan 104 (Geshu Han)
note: Geshu Han had been forced out of a strong position by Xuanzong and Yang Guozhong against his own judgement; Tang numbers are given as 80,000 to 200,000. Side note on the Tang commander: the Old Book of Tang makes Geshu Han a Turk of the Tuqishi (Turgesh) Geshu clan on his father's side with a mother who was a daughter of the king of Khotan; the Khotanese were Saka (Eastern Iranian), so on a strict descent reading the Tang commander was half Iranian too and iranian_sides could be 'both'. Not used here to qualify the battle.

date: late Jan-Feb 757 (first assaults) to 24 Nov 757 (fall, 9th day of the 10th lunar month; Julian); the last siege began in the 7th month
name: Suiyang (siege, 757)
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
how the result was decided: After about ten months the starving garrison could hold no longer; Suiyang fell and Zhang Xun, Xu Yuan and Nan Jiyun were executed.
commanders A: Yin Ziqi; Yang Chaozong; An Qingxu (ruler)
commanders B: Zhang Xun; Xu Yuan; Nan Jiyun
why it counts: Leader by descent: An Qingxu, ruler of Yan from January 757 to April 759, was An Lushan's son and so Sogdian by descent through his father (An Lushan's own family was half Turkic: Turkic mother and stepfather).
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Suiyang
note: Zhang Xun and Xu Yuan, with about 6,800 men, kept Yin Ziqi's army (put at 130,000) from the Huai and Yangzi valleys; the defenders ate horses, then people, and relief commanders such as Helan Jinming stood aside. The Yan army is said to have lost about 120,000 men in over 400 fights. An Lushan had been killed by his own son on 29 Jan 757, so An Qingxu was Yan ruler for most of the siege.

date: winter 756-57 (Dec 756 to Feb 757 or later; over a month under Shi Siming, the siege then lingered under Cai Xide)
name: Taiyuan (siege, 756-757)
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
how the result was decided: Li Guangbi, with under 10,000 soldiers, held the city by countermining and sorties against Shi Siming's 100,000 (Wikipedia, Shi Siming), and the besiegers withdrew.
why it counts: Leader by descent: Shi Siming has the surname Shi, that of the Sogdian city of Kesh, and modern scholars take his family as Turkicised Sogdian, but the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu' of Ningyi (Old Book of Tang 200), so his Sogdian descent is probable rather than certain and the Turkic side of his family is strong; the army was that of Yan, ruled by An Lushan and then An Qingxu.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Siming; Old Book of Tang, juan 110 (Li Guangbi)
note: Shi Siming left for Fanyang when An Lushan's death became known (late Jan 757); Cai Xide stayed and the siege was finally broken by Li Guangbi's sorties. The siege marks the decisive refusal of Tang Hedong to collapse. Dates are approximate.

date: late Nov to early Dec 757 (10th lunar month, Julian; Luoyang entered about 18th day, c. 3 Dec)
name: Xindian and the recapture of Luoyang (757)
place: Xindian near Shan (Sanmenxia), and Luoyang, Henan
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
allies B: Uyghur horse; Arab and other auxiliaries
how the result was decided: The Yan army broke at Xindian on sight of the Uyghur cavalry on the Tang flank, and An Qingxu abandoned Luoyang and fled to Ye.
commanders A: Yan Zhuang; Zhang Tongru; An Qingxu (ruler)
commanders B: Guo Ziyi; Li Chu; Pugu Huaien
why it counts: Leader by descent: An Qingxu, ruler of Yan from January 757 to April 759, was An Lushan's son and so Sogdian by descent through his father (An Lushan's own family was half Turkic: Turkic mother and stepfather).
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion
note: Xindian (west of Shan) was the last pitched battle for the Eastern Capital in 757; Luoyang was handed over to the Uyghurs for plunder as agreed with their prince. An Qingxu executed about 30 captive Tang officers before leaving. Whether the fight at Xindian was one day or several is not clear in the sources used; dates approximate.

date: 13 Nov 757 (Julian, 9th lunar month, renyin day, computed from the sexagenary date in ZZTJ); Chang'an recovered the next day
name: Xiangji Temple (757)
place: Plain by Xiangji Temple, south of Chang'an (Xi'an), Shaanxi
allies B: Uyghur horse; Arab contingent; Khotanese auxiliaries
how the result was decided: The Tang army, with a Uyghur cavalry ambush, destroyed the Yan army (about 60,000 beheaded) and Chang'an was retaken the next day.
commanders A: An Shouzhong; Li Guiren; Zhang Tongru (Chang'an)
commanders B: Li Chu; Guo Ziyi; Li Siye; Wang Siyi; Pugu Huaien
why it counts: Leader by descent: An Qingxu, ruler of Yan from January 757 to April 759, was An Lushan's son and so Sogdian by descent through his father (An Lushan's own family was half Turkic: Turkic mother and stepfather); the Yan army before Chang'an acted for him.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/香积寺之战
note: About 150,000 Tang against about 100,000 Yan; the Anxi and Beiting troops under Li Siye were nearly wiped out in the centre before the Uyghurs and Pugu Huaien struck the Yan rear. Chinese Wikipedia lists Khotanese troops among the Tang auxiliaries; Khotanese were Saka (Eastern Iranian), so a second Iranian contingent may sit on the Tang side, size unknown and probably under a fifth. The Gregorian date is computed (renyin = 13 Nov 757); some books give October.

date: winter 758 (Oct-Nov 758) to 7 Apr 759 (Shi Siming's relief battle, ended by a storm)
name: Ye (siege of Xiangzhou, 758-759)
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
how the result was decided: A sudden storm panicked both armies on 7 Apr 759; the Tang forces fled south and lifted the siege, and Shi Siming then took Ye and killed An Qingxu (10 Apr).
commanders A: An Qingxu; Shi Siming (relief army); Cai Xide; Tian Chengsi; Ashina Chengqing; Wu Lingxun
commanders B: Guo Ziyi; Li Guangbi; Li Siye (died in the siege); Lu Jiong; Xu Shuji
why it counts: Leader by descent: An Qingxu, ruler of Yan from January 757 to April 759, was An Lushan's son and so Sogdian by descent through his father (An Lushan's own family was half Turkic: Turkic mother and stepfather); the relief army was led by Shi Siming, probably Sogdian by descent (surname Shi; the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu', so the Turkic side is strong).
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Siming; https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/安史之乱
note: The Tang gathered nine jiedushi (200,000 or more; later sources say 600,000) with no supreme commander, only the eunuch Yu Chao'en as overseer; An Qingxu reached Ye with only about 1,300 men (Wikipedia) before reinforcements, including Shi Siming's, raised the garrison above 60,000. Ashina Chengqing was a Turk. The Yan victory left Shi Siming master of the rebellion and he murdered An Qingxu three days later.

date: autumn 759 to spring 760 (several actions around the Heyang bridgehead)
name: Heyang (759-760)
place: Heyang (Mengzhou), on the Yellow River north of Luoyang, Henan
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
how the result was decided: Li Guangbi held the Heyang bridgehead and rebuffed Shi Siming's attacks, leaving a stalemate (Wikipedia, Shi Siming).
why it counts: Leader by descent: Shi Siming has the surname Shi, that of the Sogdian city of Kesh, and modern scholars take his family as Turkicised Sogdian, but the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu' of Ningyi (Old Book of Tang 200), so his Sogdian descent is probable rather than certain and the Turkic side of his family is strong.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Siming; Old Book of Tang, juan 110 (Li Guangbi)
note: After losing Luoyang Li Guangbi kept Shi Siming from the Guanzhong by holding Heyang, an obstacle on the Yellow River crossing, for about a year; the individual engagements are not itemised here. Treated as a single entry because the sources used do not separate the actions.

date: autumn 759 (about the 9th-10th lunar month, Oct-Nov; English Wikipedia's summary puts it in April)
name: Luoyang (Shi Siming's capture, 759)
place: Luoyang (the Eastern Capital), Henan, after Bianzhou (Kaifeng)
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
how the result was decided: Li Guangbi judged the Yan army stronger, evacuated Luoyang and fell back on Heyang, and Shi Siming entered the city.
commanders B: Li Guangbi; Xu Shuji (changed sides at Bianzhou)
why it counts: Leader by descent: Shi Siming has the surname Shi, that of the Sogdian city of Kesh, and modern scholars take his family as Turkicised Sogdian, but the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu' of Ningyi (Old Book of Tang 200), so his Sogdian descent is probable rather than certain and the Turkic side of his family is strong.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Siming
note: Shi Siming declared himself emperor of Yan at Fanyang in spring 759 and marched south in autumn, taking Bianzhou when Xu Shuji went over to him. This is mostly manoeuvre with a rearguard fight rather than a set battle, hence the low confidence. The English Wikipedia (An Lushan Rebellion) lumps Bian and Luoyang under April 759; the ZZTJ narrative has the march after the Ye affair in the autumn, which is followed here.

name: al-Taq (siege)
place: the fortress of al-Taq, Tabaristan (Mazandaran), Iran
how the result was decided: After a long siege the gate was opened by Abu al-Khasib's ruse, the fortress fell and Khurshid's family was captured.
commanders A: Abu al-Khasib Marzuq, Khazim ibn Khuzayma, Rawh ibn Hatim (and Umar ibn al-Ala)
commanders B: the garrison of Khurshid (Khurshid himself had withdrawn to Daylam)
Iranian force: Khurshid's garrison and household troops in his treasure fortress; no numbers are given.
why it counts: Tabaristan: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the defenders were killed and the children taken captive
sources: al-Tabari; Ibn Isfandiyar; en.wikipedia Abbasid conquest of Tabaristan; Khurshid of Tabaristan; Khazim ibn Khuzayma al-Tamimi
note: Abbasid Caliphate. The Abbasid conquest article describes Umar ibn al-Ala taking al-Taq after prolonged fighting and, separately, Abu al-Khasib's ruse at Khurshid's fortress; they may be one siege or two.

name: Defeat of Khurshid
how the result was decided: Khurshid's counter-invasion from Daylam was repulsed and he withdrew to Daylam, where he took poison the next year.
Iranian force: An army of mountain levies that Khurshid raised in Daylam and Gilan, given as 50,000 men.
why it counts: Tabaristan: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no conventional battle name; whether a pitched battle was fought is not clear (the Abbasid conquest article says cholera was decisive)
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional battle name; whether a pitched battle was fought is not clear (the Abbasid conquest article says cholera was decisive).
sources: al-Tabari; Ibn Isfandiyar; en.wikipedia Khurshid of Tabaristan; Abbasid conquest of Tabaristan; Tabaristan
note: Abbasid Caliphate. The end of the Dabuyid dynasty; Tabaristan became an Abbasid province.

date: after April 761 (spring-summer 761; month not given in the sources used)
name: Fanyang (Gao Juren's rising and the massacre of the Hu, 761)
allies A: Turkic and Sogdian 'Hu' of the garrison
how the result was decided: Gao Juren's party defeated the Turkic and Hu forces under Ashina Chengqing and held Fanyang until Li Huaixian killed Gao and took over.
why it counts: Shi Chaoyi's order to kill Shi Siming's favoured son Shi Chaoqing in Fanyang set the garrisons against each other, and Gao Juren defeated the Yan force under the Turk Ashina Chengqing and killed the Sogdians of the city (Wikipedia, An Lushan Rebellion), but no source seen says the Sogdians were organised as a fighting unit or names a Sogdian commander (the Shi family, if Sogdian by descent, is the link; Turkic side strong).
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; Zizhi Tongjian, juan 222-223
note: A garrison fight inside Yan after Shi Siming's murder, in which the Hu (Sogdians and Turks) of Fanyang were the victims; it is the clearest attested slaughter of a Sogdian community in the rebellion. Very thinly sourced here: the date, the numbers and who commanded the Hu side are all unclear, and Gao Juren acted against, not for, Shi Chaoyi's order.

date: Feb-Mar 761 (2nd lunar month, Julian), exact day not fixed here
name: Mangshan (761)
place: Mount Mang (Beimang), north of Luoyang, Henan
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
how the result was decided: The Tang army, sent against Luoyang over Li Guangbi's objection, was beaten below Mount Mang and withdrew.
why it counts: Leader by descent: Shi Siming has the surname Shi, that of the Sogdian city of Kesh, and modern scholars take his family as Turkicised Sogdian, but the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu' of Ningyi (Old Book of Tang 200), so his Sogdian descent is probable rather than certain and the Turkic side of his family is strong.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; Old Book of Tang, juan 110 (Li Guangbi)
note: The court, under pressure from the eunuch Yu Chao'en, forced Li Guangbi to attack Luoyang though he wanted to wait; Pugu Huaien's wing, badly placed, gave way. It was Shi Siming's last victory: he was strangled by his son within weeks. Details of the battle are from memory of the ZZTJ narrative and were not rechecked.

date: spring 761 (about Mar-Apr), ended by Shi Siming's death on 18 Apr 761
name: Shan Prefecture (Shi Chaoyi's attacks, 761)
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
how the result was decided: Wei Boyu repeatedly threw back Shi Chaoyi's assaults on Shan, and the failure led Shi Siming to quarrel with his son and be killed.
why it counts: Leader by descent: Shi Siming has the surname Shi, that of the Sogdian city of Kesh, and modern scholars take his family as Turkicised Sogdian, but the Tang histories call him a 'mixed Turkic Hu' of Ningyi (Old Book of Tang 200), so his Sogdian descent is probable rather than certain and the Turkic side of his family is strong; Shi Chaoyi led the attack as his son.
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Chaoyi; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Siming
note: Shi Siming ordered his son to take a fort at Shan; after repeated failures he threatened to execute him, and the generals Luo Yue and Cai Wenjing seized and strangled the father (18 Apr 761 per Wikipedia). Included because it is a named siege that decided the dynasty's fate.

date: late autumn 762 (10th lunar month of Baoying 1; about Nov 762)
name: Luoyang (Tang-Uyghur recapture, 762)
place: Luoyang (the Eastern Capital) and the plain before it, Henan
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
how the result was decided: The Tang-Uyghur army defeated Shi Chaoyi's army in front of the city and took Luoyang, which the Uyghurs plundered.
commanders B: Li Kuo (Prince of Yong, later Emperor Dezong; nominal commander); Pugu Huaien; Dengli Khan
why it counts: Leader by descent: Shi Chaoyi, ruler of Yan from April 761 to 763, was Shi Siming's son, so Sogdian by descent through his father if Shi Siming's family was Sogdian (disputed; the Tang histories call the Shis 'mixed Turkic Hu').
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Chaoyi; https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/安史之乱
note: The second Tang-Uyghur recapture of the Eastern Capital (the first was in 757); Dengli Khan came in person and Pugu Huaien (a Turk of the Pugu tribe) commanded the Tang side. Shi Chaoyi fled north with his generals already wavering. Details of the battle (numbers, sub-fights) are not given in the sources used here.

date: Nov 762 to Feb 763 (Shi Chaoyi's flight from Luoyang to Mozhou and Fanyang; he died before 17 Feb 763)
name: Shi Chaoyi's last campaign (Weizhou-Mozhou-Fanyang, 762-763)
place: Mozhou (Renqiu), Hebei, and the road to Fanyang
allies A: Khitan, Xi, Tongra and other tribal horse and Turkic troops
how the result was decided: Pursued by Pugu Huaien and abandoned by his generals (Tian Chengsi, Li Huaixian and others went over), Shi Chaoyi was cut off and hanged himself.
why it counts: Leader by descent: Shi Chaoyi, ruler of Yan from April 761 to 763, was Shi Siming's son, so Sogdian by descent through his father if Shi Siming's family was Sogdian (disputed; the Tang histories call the Shis 'mixed Turkic Hu').
sources: Zizhi Tongjian (Sima Guang), juan 217-223; Old Book of Tang, juan 200 (An Lushan, Shi Siming) and New Book of Tang, juan 225 (traitors); Pulleyblank, The Background of the Rebellion of An Lu-shan (1955); Twitchett (ed.), Cambridge History of China 3 (1979), ch. 5; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Lushan_Rebellion; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shi_Chaoyi
note: A chain of defeats and defections, not one battle: after Luoyang the Yan generals Zhang Xiancheng, Xue Song, Zhang Zhongzhi, Tian Chengsi, Li Huaixian and Li Baozhong each went over to the Tang; Li Huaixian's men intercepted Shi Chaoyi when he tried to reach the Xi or Khitan. The dates and the sequence of the fights could not be pinned down with the sources used, so place and day are only indicative.

name: Defeat of al-Ajtham
how the result was decided: Ustadh Sis's followers defeated the Abbasid army of Marw al-Rudh and killed its commander.
Iranian force: Ustadh Sis's peasant followers from Badghis, Herat and Sistan, many of them former followers of Bihafarid; he claimed 300,000 fighting men.
why it counts: Iranian risings: an Iranian-led state
losses B: al-Ajtham and many of his men killed
borderline: a rising, not a state; no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander)
doubts and flags: Borderline: a rising, not a state; no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander).
sources: al-Tabari (year 150); Gardizi; en.wikipedia Ustadh Sis
note: Abbasid Caliphate.

name: Defeat of Ustadh Sis
how the result was decided: Ustadh Sis lost a bloody battle and fled to the mountains, where Khazim besieged and captured him.
Iranian force: The peasant army of Ustadh Sis from eastern Khorasan (Badghis, Herat, Sistan).
why it counts: Iranian risings: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a rising, not a state; no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated leader)
doubts and flags: Borderline: a rising, not a state; no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated leader).
sources: al-Tabari (years 150-151); en.wikipedia Ustadh Sis; Khazim ibn Khuzayma al-Tamimi
note: Abbasid Caliphate. Al-Mahdi is said to have pardoned 30,000 captives, a figure that does not match the 14,000.

name: Narshakh (battle)
how the result was decided: The Bukharan force killed about 700 of the White-clothed and the survivors asked for amnesty.
commanders A: Husayn ibn Mu'adh (amir of Bukhara), with the qadi Amir ibn Imran
commanders B: the White-clothed of Bukhara (leaders not named for this fight)
Iranian force: Al-Muqanna's 'White-clothed' followers from the villages of the Bukhara oasis.
why it counts: Iranian risings: an Iranian-led state
losses A: unknown (the Arab Na'im ibn Sahl killed)
borderline: a rising, not a state
doubts and flags: Borderline: a rising, not a state.
sources: Narshakhi, History of Bukhara (tr. Frye); al-Tabari
note: Abbasid Caliphate. The survivors signed a treaty, then broke it and fortified Narshakh (see Narshakh (siege)).

name: Narshakh (siege)
how the result was decided: After four months a mine brought down part of the wall, the defenders came out to treat and were killed or defeated, and Narshakh fell.
commanders A: Jibra'il ibn Yahya, Husayn ibn Mu'adh
commanders B: Hakim ibn Ahmad (killed), Khishwi (killed), Baghi (killed), Kirdik
Iranian force: The White-clothed of the Bukhara oasis under Hakim ibn Ahmad and the village chiefs Khishwi, Baghi and Kirdik.
why it counts: Iranian risings: an Iranian-led state
losses A: heavy losses in a night sortie
borderline: a rising, not a state
doubts and flags: Borderline: a rising, not a state.
sources: Narshakhi, History of Bukhara (tr. Frye); al-Tabari
note: Abbasid Caliphate. The headwoman of Narshakh was executed; Kirdik fled to al-Muqanna.

date: 779 or 780 (AH 163, al-Tabari); Narshakhi and others give 783 (AH 167)
name: Sanam (siege)
place: al-Muqanna's fortress of Sanam near Kesh (Shahrisabz), Uzbekistan
how the result was decided: The fortress fell to the besiegers; al-Muqanna poisoned himself rather than surrender.
commanders A: Sa'id al-Harashi (for the governor Mu'adh ibn Muslim and the caliph al-Mahdi)
Iranian force: Al-Muqanna's last followers from Kesh and Sughd, who earlier had Turkic allies from beyond the Jaxartes.
why it counts: Iranian risings: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a rising, not a state; no Wikipedia article; the fortress name (Sanam, Narshakhi's 'Mount Sam') varies
doubts and flags: Borderline: a rising, not a state; no Wikipedia article; the fortress name (Sanam, Narshakhi's 'Mount Sam') varies.
sources: al-Tabari (year 163); Narshakhi, History of Bukhara; en.wikipedia Al-Muqanna
note: Abbasid Caliphate. The date of the fall is disputed (779/780 or 783).

date: 782 or 783 (AH 166), after the defeat of Salm al-Farghani
name: Defeat of Farasha
how the result was decided: The rebels defeated the relief army and captured and executed its commander.
commanders B: Farasha, mawla of al-Mahdi (captured and executed)
Iranian force: The forces of the Qarinvandid and Bavandid princes of Tabaristan.
why it counts: Tabaristan: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander); place not recorded
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander); place not recorded.
sources: Ibn Isfandiyar; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Tabaristan uprising; Vandad Hormozd
note: Abbasid Caliphate (al-Mahdi).

name: Defeat of Salm al-Farghani
how the result was decided: The rebels defeated the caliphal army and Salm was killed on the battlefield.
commanders A: Vandad Hormozd and his brother Vinda-Umid (Qarinvandids), with Sharwin I (Bavandid)
Iranian force: The forces of the mountain princes of Tabaristan: the Qarinvandids under Vandad Hormozd, the Bavandids under Sharwin I and the Zarmihrids.
why it counts: Tabaristan: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander); place not recorded
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander); place not recorded.
sources: Ibn Isfandiyar; al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Tabaristan uprising; Vandad Hormozd
note: Abbasid Caliphate (al-Mahdi).

name: Defeat of Vandad Hormozd
how the result was decided: Yazid ibn Mazyad defeated Vandad Hormozd, who was wounded and then surrendered to Musa al-Hadi at Gurgan.
commanders A: Yazid ibn Mazyad al-Shaybani and Sa'id al-Harashi (under the heir Musa al-Hadi)
Iranian force: The forces of the Tabaristan princes under Vandad Hormozd (Qarinvandid) and Sharwin I (Bavandid).
why it counts: Tabaristan: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated leader); place not recorded
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated leader); place not recorded.
sources: al-Tabari; Ibn Isfandiyar; en.wikipedia Tabaristan uprising; Tabaristan
note: Abbasid Caliphate (al-Mahdi). Wikipedia's Tabaristan article credits Sa'id al-Harashi's 40,000 with the victory and dates it 784; the uprising article names Yazid ibn Mazyad and dates it 784-785. Vandad Hormozd was pardoned and kept his lands.

name: Samarkand (siege, Rafi ibn al-Layth's revolt, 809-810)
side B: Rafi ibn al-Layth and his supporters
allies B: Turks; Persian and Sogdian supporters of Rafi
how the result was decided: Rafi surrendered to al-Ma'mun and was pardoned (Tabari; Wikipedia).
Iranian side: Rafi ibn al-Layth and his supporters
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); C. E. Bosworth, The Cambridge History of Iran, vol. 4, pp. 259-261; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafi_ibn_al-Layth
note: Rafi was an Arab by descent (a grandson of Nasr ibn Sayyar) and the Iranian share of his following is only said to exist. There is no clear account of an assault on Samarkand. Included as uncertain.

date: late 811 or early 812 (not precisely dated in the secondary sources I read)
name: Asadabad Pass (811-812)
place: Asadabad pass, between Hamadan and Hulwan, Hamadan Province, Iran
how the result was decided: Abd al-Rahman ambushed Tahir's army; Tahir's cavalry counterattacked and Abd al-Rahman was killed and his army defeated.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad_(812%E2%80%93813); al-Tabari, History vol. 31
note: Named in the Wikipedia article on the siege of Baghdad but not in the Tahir biography; dating and sequence relative to Hamadan are uncertain.

name: Hamadan (811)
how the result was decided: After hard-fought engagements Abd al-Rahman's 20,000 abna were pushed back into Hamadan and blockaded, and he left seeking terms.
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 31; Bosworth, 'Tahirids', Enc. Iranica; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad_(812%E2%80%93813); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Fitna
note: Several actions around Hamadan rather than one pitched battle; precise dating is loose. Tahir's Persian descent as at Rayy.

name: Rayy (811)
place: Rayy (Shahr-e Rey, south of Tehran), Iran
how the result was decided: Tahir's 4,000-5,000 men routed Ali's army of about 40,000 abna; Ali was killed.
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 31 (Fishbein, The War between Brothers); Bosworth, 'Tahirids', Encyclopaedia Iranica / Cambridge History of Iran 4; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Fitna; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tahir_ibn_al-Husayn
note: Tahir, a Persian dehqan of Pushang near Herat (great-grandson of a mawla of the Khuza'a), commanded for al-Ma'mun. The battle opened the Khurasani advance on Baghdad.

name: Ahwaz (812)
how the result was decided: Tahir defeated and killed the Muhallabid governor and the Muhallabids of Basra then submitted.
commanders A: Tahir ibn Husayn; Harthama ibn A'yan (reinforcements)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad_(812%E2%80%93813); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tahir_ibn_al-Husayn; al-Tabari, History vol. 31
note: The Tahir article says 'Khuzistan' and the siege article 'al-Ahwaz'; the exact site is uncertain.

name: Baghdad (siege, 812-813)
how the result was decided: Tahir's men entered the city in September 813, captured al-Amin and executed him.
commanders A: Tahir ibn Husayn; Harthama ibn A'yan; Zuhayr ibn al-Musayyab al-Dabbi
sources: al-Tabari, History vol. 31 (Fishbein); Kennedy, The Early Abbasid Caliphate (1981); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad_(812%E2%80%93813); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tahir_ibn_al-Husayn
note: Tahir (Persian dehqan family) was the field commander, with Harthama ibn A'yan; Harthama was a mawla of the Banu Dabba born in Balkh, and Wikipedia does not say whether he was Arab or Persian, so he is not counted. Al-Ma'mun was in Merv.

name: Defeat of Isa ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Khalid
how the result was decided: Babak defeated the caliphal army sent against him (al-Tabari, Wikipedia).
commanders B: Isa ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Khalid
Iranian force: Babak's Khurramite highlanders of Azerbaijan.
why it counts: Iranian risings: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a rising, not a state; no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander); place not recorded
doubts and flags: Borderline: a rising, not a state; no conventional battle name (named here by the defeated commander); place not recorded.
sources: al-Tabari; en.wikipedia Babak Khorramdin; Khurramites
note: Abbasid Caliphate (al-Ma'mun).

name: Ushrusana (al-Ma'mun's expedition, 822)
side A (victor if decisive): Abbasid Caliphate; Khaydar, son of Kavus, who guided the Muslims
side B: Kavus ibn Kharakhuruh, Afshin of Ushrusana
how the result was decided: Kavus abdicated and was replaced by Haydar, who became the caliph's vassal (Wikipedia, 'Ushrusana'; Tabari).
Iranian side: Abbasid Caliphate v Kavus ibn Kharakhuruh, Afshin of Ushrusana
factions A: Abbasid Caliphate, Khaydar, son of Kavus, who guided the Muslims
factions B: Kavus ibn Kharakhuruh, Afshin of Ushrusana
commanders A: Commander of the Abbasid expedition (Ahmad ibn Abi Khalid in some accounts; not named in Wikipedia); Haydar ibn Kavus
doubts and flags: Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: al-Tabari, Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk (trans. Hawting, Blankinship, Bosworth et al.); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ushrusana; V. V. Barthold, Turkestan down to the Mongol Invasion
note: The Afshins were Iranian princes of an Iranian people. The expedition seems to have ended in a settlement after a dynastic quarrel (Kavus against his son Haydar), not a pitched battle, so the 'real fighting' is itself doubtful.

Whether Theophobos had an independent command at the sack is not stated, and a second Khurramite group (about 16,000) arrived only in September 837.

name: Anzen
place: Anzen, near Dazimon (modern Turhal), Tokat Province, Turkey

name: Amorium (siege, 838)
place: Amorium, near Emirdag (Hisarkoy), Afyonkarahisar Province, Turkey

note: Afshin (Sogdian prince of Ushrusana) was one of three major divisional commanders under the caliph, not the overall commander, so the leader link is secondary. Persian Khurramites were not among the defenders.

Iranian force: Afshin's Sajid army of Azerbaijan: the family's ghulams with Azerbaijani, Kurdish and Arab levies; composition not recorded.

how the result was decided: Rafi's forces were defeated near Bayhaq and Tus and he fled to Khwarazm, where he was killed.
commanders B: Rafi ibn Harthama; al-Mu'addal and al-Layth, sons of Ali ibn al-Layth
Iranian force: Saffarid side: Amr's Sistani, Khurasani and ghulam army. Rafi's side: his Khurasani followers, expecting Zaydid help that never came.

name: Balkh (900)
how the result was decided: Amr's army was defeated, some of his troops went over to Isma'il, and Amr was captured on the field.
Iranian force: Samanid side: about 20,000 lightly equipped horsemen of Transoxiana (dihqans, volunteers and ghulams). Saffarid side: Amr's 70,000 well-armed cavalry of Sistan and Khorasan with Turkish ghulams.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Balkh; en.wikipedia Isma'il ibn Ahmad; Narshakhi; Gardizi; Barthold, Turkestan
note: Amr was sent to Baghdad and executed in 902; the Saffarids lost Khorasan.

name: Gorgan (900)
place: Gorgan (medieval Jurjan, near Gonbad-e Kavus), Iran
how the result was decided: The Samanid army won; Muhammad ibn Zayd was mortally wounded and captured and his son Zayd was taken.
commanders B: Muhammad ibn Zayd (mortally wounded, captured); Zayd ibn Muhammad (captured); al-Hasan al-Utrush
Iranian force: Samanid side: the Khurasan army under Muhammad ibn Harun. Alavid side: Daylamite, Gilite and Tabaristani troops of Muhammad ibn Zayd.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: unknown; Muhammad ibn Zayd died of his wounds
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Gorgan (900); en.wikipedia Hasan al-Utrush; al-Tabari (year 287); al-Mas'udi

why it counts: Sajids: an Iranian-led state

how the result was decided: Yusuf routed the Armenian royal army after the Sevordi troops on Ashot's wing went over; Mushegh was captured.

commanders B: Ashot and Mushegh, sons of Smbat I (Mushegh captured)

name: Kapuyt (siege)
place: Kapuyt fortress (Kapuyt Berd), Armenia (site not securely identified)

Iranian force: Yusuf's Sajid army of Azerbaijan; composition not recorded.
why it counts: Sajids: an Iranian-led state

name: Burdidu
place: Burdidu (Burdidah) on the Burrud river, west of Chalus, Mazandaran, Iran
how the result was decided: Al-Utrush crushed the larger and better-equipped Samanid army; its survivors surrendered at Chalus and Amul opened its gates to him.
Iranian force: Alavid side: the Daylamite and Gilite converts of al-Utrush. Samanid side: the army of the governor of Tabaristan, Khurasani troops and ghulams.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: heavy; the survivors who surrendered at Chalus were massacred
sources: en.wikipedia Hasan al-Utrush; Ibn Isfandiyar; Madelung, CHI 4
note: Restored Zaydid rule in Tabaristan.

war: Samanid civil wars (revolt of Ishaq ibn Ahmad)

factions B: Ishaq ibn Ahmad (Samanid claimant in Samarkand)

Iranian force: Both sides: Samanid forces of Bukhara and Samarkand, ghulams and dihqan cavalry.

name: Queli (siege)

Iranian force: Yusuf's Sajid army, said to number about 20,000, with siege engines; composition not recorded.
why it counts: Sajids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the garrison taken; Gobron and 133 others held, Gobron executed

note: The Wikipedia infobox calls it the 'Siege of Tbilisi'. The fortress belonged to Gurgen II of Tao. The Sajids soon had to leave Tao-Klarjeti.

date: 918 (the Wikipedia article gives a first victory in 917 and this one in 918)
name: Ardabil (918)
how the result was decided: Yusuf defeated the caliphal army sent against him near Ardabil.

why it counts: Sajids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: dates (917-918) and commanders differ between accounts

name: Ardabil (919)
how the result was decided: Yusuf was defeated and captured and taken to Baghdad, where he was held for about three years.
Iranian force: Yusuf's Sajid army of Azerbaijan; composition not recorded.
why it counts: Sajids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj; Ibn Miskawayh; Madelung, CHI 4
note: Abbasid Caliphate (al-Muqtadir). The Wikipedia article does not name the victor; Mu'nis commanded the campaign (Ibn Miskawayh).

name: Marw al-Rudh (920)
war: Samanid civil wars (revolt of Ahmad ibn Sahl)
how the result was decided: Hamuya defeated and captured the rebel Ahmad ibn Sahl, who died in prison at Bukhara in 920.
factions A: Nasr II (Samanids; general Hamuya ibn Ali)
Iranian force: Both sides: Samanid forces of Khorasan, ghulams and Khurasani troops; Ahmad ibn Sahl was of an old Iranian dihqan family of Merv.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: site given only as Marw al-Rudh

how the result was decided: The Zaydid invasion of Khorasan was beaten and Lili ibn al-Nu'man was killed.
Iranian force: Samanid side: Khurasan army with Turkish ghulam officers (the Simjurids). Alavid side: Lili's Daylamite and Gilite army.

how the result was decided: Ashot's archers attacking from boats routed Beshir's army on the shore, and it fled.

Iranian force: A Sajid army under the commander Beshir, called 'Arab' by the Armenian historian; 1,000 of its men attacked Sevan island.

name: Dvin (siege, 922)
how the result was decided: Dvin withstood the joint Roman-Armenian attack.
Iranian force: The Sajid garrison of Dvin, of Muslim ('Arab') and Armenian troops.
why it counts: Sajids: an Iranian-led state

how the result was decided: The garrison, joined by the townspeople, drove off the besiegers with heavy losses.
Iranian force: The Sajid garrison of Dvin under Nasr al-Subuki, with the townspeople.
why it counts: Sajids: an Iranian-led state
strength B: unknown (well supplied, with towers, ballistae and Greek fire)
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Dvin (927); Ibn al-Athir; Runciman, The Emperor Romanus Lecapenus

name: Kufa (927)
how the result was decided: Yusuf's much larger army was routed and he was captured.
Iranian force: Yusuf's own Sajid army, mostly highland troops from Azerbaijan unused to desert war, paid from the revenues of the Jibal and north-western Iran (Kennedy).
languages: other Iranian; Turkic; Kurdish; Daylami and Caspian
why it counts: Sajids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Qarmatian invasion of Iraq; en.wikipedia Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj; Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates

name: Hamadan (931)
war: Ziyarid conquest of the Jibal (Mardavij against the Abbasids)
how the result was decided: Mardavij stormed Hamadan, where his nephew had been killed, and drove off the caliphal army sent to the Jibal.

name: Defeat of Yaqut (934)
place: on the road east from Shiraz towards Kerman, Fars, Iran (site not named)
how the result was decided: Yaqut's men fled in disorder and the road to Shiraz lay open (Kennedy).
Iranian force: About 900 Daylamite infantry under Ali ibn Buya, probably with some local volunteers.

borderline: no conventional name; the battlefield is not named in the sources checked
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name; the battlefield is not named in the sources checked.

note: Abbasid Caliphate (al-Qahir/al-Radi); Yaqut's army included the troops of Basra. Ali entered Shiraz soon after.

name: Gorgan (siege, 939)
place: Gorgan (medieval Jurjan, near Gonbad-e Kavus), Iran
how the result was decided: After a seven-month siege Makan abandoned Gorgan and fled to Rayy, and the city passed to the Samanids.
Iranian force: Samanid side: the Khurasan army of Abu Ali Chaghani (Turkish ghulams and Iranian levies). Makan's side: his Daylamite troops, with aid sent by Vushmgir.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Makan ibn Kaki; en.wikipedia Vushmgir; Ibn Miskawayh
note: Makan, a Daylamite warlord, had broken with the Samanids and allied himself with the Ziyarid Vushmgir.

name: Iskhabad
how the result was decided: Vushmgir fled early, Makan's elite units were destroyed and Makan was shot and beheaded; the Samanids held the field.
Iranian force: Samanid side: Abu Ali Chaghani's Khurasan army of Turkish ghulams and Iranian levies. Ziyarid side: Daylamite and Gilite infantry, Makan's elite Daylamite units.
languages: Persian; Daylami and Caspian; Turkic; East Iranian
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: more than half killed, the rest captured or wounded (Wikipedia)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Iskhabad; en.wikipedia Vushmgir; Ibn Miskawayh
note: The Wikipedia infobox says 'Samanid-Buyid victory', but the Buyids are not described as taking part.

name: Tabriz (siege, 942)

how the result was decided: Marzuban's Daylamites beat Daysam's Kurds and besieged Tabriz, which fell after Daysam slipped away to Ardabil.
factions B: Daysam ibn Ibrahim (ruler of Azerbaijan) and his Kurdish allies
Iranian force: Sallarid side: Marzuban's Daylamites, joined by Daysam's Daylamites who had deserted. Daysam's side: Kurdish tribesmen.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: Daysam's Azerbaijan-seated principality is treated as an Iranian state; he was a Kurdish former Sajid officer
doubts and flags: Borderline: Daysam's Azerbaijan-seated principality is treated as an Iranian state; he was a Kurdish former Sajid officer.
sources: en.wikipedia Marzuban ibn Muhammad; en.wikipedia Sallarid dynasty; Ibn Miskawayh; Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History
note: Ardabil then surrendered after Daysam's vizier was bribed.

name: Barda'a (943)
how the result was decided: The Rus routed the governor's Daylamites and volunteers within a short fight and took Barda'a.
Iranian force: The Sallarid garrison of Daylamites with local volunteers (ghazis) and Kurds.
why it counts: Sallarids: an Iranian-led state
strength B: unknown (a few hundred Daylamites and some thousands of volunteers)
sources: Ibn Miskawayh, Tajarib al-umam; en.wikipedia Sallarid dynasty; en.wikipedia Marzuban ibn Muhammad; Kennedy (2004)
note: The Rus came up the Kura. Marzuban's army then lost several engagements before the ambush (next entry).

name: Rayy (943)
how the result was decided: Vushmgir was defeated when his officers Shir Mardi and Gurigir went over to Rukn al-Dawla, and the Buyids occupied Rayy.
Iranian force: Both sides: Daylamite infantry with Turkish cavalry.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Rukn al-Dawla; en.wikipedia Vushmgir; Ibn Miskawayh
note: Rayy had been held for the Samanids; Vushmgir lost it for good.

date: 944 (AH 332); Mu'izz retreated to Ahvaz on 28 July
name: Baghdad (944)
place: the approaches of Baghdad (near al-Mada'in), Iraq
how the result was decided: Tuzun repelled Ahmad ibn Buya's attack on the approaches of Baghdad and Ahmad fell back to Ahvaz; the modern accounts (Kennedy; en.wikipedia Tuzun) have Tuzun beat him off, against the Mu'izz al-Dawla article's claim that Ahmad won the fight.
Iranian force: Ahmad ibn Buya's Daylamite infantry with some Turkish cavalry.
why it counts: Buyids: an Iranian-led state

note: Abbasid Caliphate under the Turkish amir al-umara Tuzun. The Wikipedia article on Mu'izz al-Dawla instead says Ahmad won the battle near al-Mada'in but retreated after Tuzun cut the bridge; Kennedy's verdict is followed.

name: Barda'a (siege, 944)
how the result was decided: After Marzuban's ambush killed about 700 Rus and the survivors were hemmed in and wasted by dysentery, they evacuated Barda'a, which returned to Sallarid control.
Iranian force: Marzuban's Daylamite infantry, Kurdish horse and many volunteers (Ibn Miskawayh gives his army as about 30,000).
why it counts: Sallarids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: about 700 killed in the ambush; many dead of disease
borderline: the Rus left with their loot and prisoners; the siege had been thinned when Marzuban marched against the Hamdanids
doubts and flags: Borderline: the Rus left with their loot and prisoners; the siege had been thinned when Marzuban marched against the Hamdanids.
sources: Ibn Miskawayh, Tajarib al-umam; en.wikipedia Marzuban ibn Muhammad; en.wikipedia Sallarid dynasty
note: Dated 943-944 by most; one Wikipedia article dates the raid to 945.

date: 944 (during the siege of Barda'a; one account gives winter 945-946)
name: Salmas (944)
how the result was decided: Marzuban defeated al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, who was soon recalled by Nasir al-Dawla.
Iranian force: Marzuban's Daylamite army (the rest having been left before Barda'a).
why it counts: Sallarids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: site and date uncertain; the fighting is told briefly
doubts and flags: Borderline: site and date uncertain; the fighting is told briefly.
sources: en.wikipedia Marzuban ibn Muhammad; Ibn Miskawayh
note: Hamdanids of Mosul (Nasir al-Dawla).

date: April to August 946; decisive crossing on the night of 1 August 946

note: Hamdanids of Mosul with Turkish mercenaries; allied Arab tribes blockaded western Baghdad. Peace followed at Ukbara.

name: Qazvin (948)
how the result was decided: Marzuban's army, marching on Rayy, was defeated and he was taken prisoner.
Iranian force: Both sides: Daylamite infantry with Turkish cavalry (Buyids) and Kurds (Sallarids).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Rukn al-Dawla; en.wikipedia Marzuban ibn Muhammad; en.wikipedia Sallarid dynasty; Ibn Miskawayh
note: The Sallarid dynasty article places Marzuban's defeat at Samiran castle; the other accounts place it near Qazvin. Marzuban escaped from prison in 952-953.

name: Batiha (950)
place: the Batiha marshes between Wasit and Basra, Iraq
how the result was decided: Ruzbahan held back and fled, and Imran's ambushes in the marshes destroyed much of al-Muhallabi's army; al-Muhallabi escaped by swimming.
Iranian force: A Buyid army of Daylamite infantry under the vizier al-Muhallabi and the Daylamite officer Ruzbahan.
why it counts: Buyids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Mu'izz al-Dawla; Ibn Miskawayh

name: Isfahan (955)
how the result was decided: Adud al-Dawla defeated Muhammad ibn Makan and recovered Isfahan.
factions B: Muhammad ibn Makan (Daylamite commander in Samanid service)

war: Revolt of Ruzbahan (Daylamite mutiny in Buyid Iraq)

how the result was decided: Alp-Tegin took Ghazni from Abu Bakr Lawik and settled there as its ruler.
Iranian force: Alp-Tegin's Turkish ghulams with Iranian ghazi volunteers.

factions A: Alp-Tegin (rebel Samanid commander, founder of the Ghaznavid line)

how the result was decided: The Qarakhanid army panicked and fled before Mahmud's elephants, many drowning in the Oxus.
commanders A: Mahmud of Ghazni; Altuntash (right), Arslan Jadhib (left), Nasr, Abu Nasr Farighuni of Guzgan and Abu Abdallah Muhammad al-Ta'i (centre)
commanders B: Ilig Nasr Khan, Yusuf Qadir Khan of Khotan, Chaghartigin
Iranian force: Mahmud's whole army with a front line of 500 elephants: Turkic ghulams, the Farighunid prince of Guzgan with his levies, Arab horse under al-Ta'i, Khurasani and Indian troops.
why it counts: The Farighunid ruler of Guzgan (an Iranian local dynasty) and Khurasani levies fought beside the Turkic ghulams and al-Ta'i's Arabs.
sources: Utbi; Gardizi; Barthold, Turkestan; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Kara-Khanid invasion of Khorasan
note: Also called the battle of Katar (or Sharkhiyan in some modern accounts).

name: Chach
place: plain of Chach near Hazro, between Waihind and the Indus, Pakistan
how the result was decided: After a Khokhar/Gakhar onslaught on his camp, Mahmud's guards counter-attacked and the Shahi army fled in rout, leaving 30 elephants.
commanders A: Mahmud of Ghazni; Arslan Jadhib and Abdallah al-Ta'i in the pursuit
commanders B: Anandapala and his son Trilochanapala (Hindu Shahi), with allied rajas
Iranian force: 6,000 archers, 6,000 cavalry and 10,000 infantry with the sultan's elite guard (Firishta via Wikipedia).
why it counts: The sources give arms, not peoples; inferred from the Ghaznavid recruitment of Turkic ghulams, Khurasanis and Afghans (Bosworth).
sources: Utbi; Firishta; en.wikipedia Battle of Chach; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni
note: Often called the battle of Waihind. Firishta's figures are late.

name: Nagarkot (siege, 1009)
how the result was decided: The fort capitulated after three days and its temple treasure was taken.
commanders B: Hindu Shahi refugees and the temple garrison (not named)
Iranian force: The army of Chach in pursuit: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Khurasani and Afghan troops.
why it counts: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
borderline: short siege; how much fighting is unclear
doubts and flags: Borderline: short siege; how much fighting is unclear.
sources: Utbi; en.wikipedia Battle of Chach; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni

name: Multan (1010)
how the result was decided: Mahmud defeated Dawud, took Multan and carried him off a prisoner.
commanders B: Abu'l-Fath Dawud, Ismaili amir of Multan (captured)
Iranian force: Mahmud's standing army (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
borderline: details of the fighting are thin
doubts and flags: Borderline: details of the fighting are thin.
sources: Gardizi; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni (campaign table: Battle of Multan, 1010)
note: 'Indian kingdoms' here is the Ismaili emirate of Multan.

name: Ahangaran
place: Ahangaran, the Ghurid seat on the upper Hari Rud, Ghor, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: After the advance guard was checked, Mahmud feigned a retreat, drew the Ghurids onto open ground and routed them, capturing Ibn Suri.
commanders A: Mahmud of Ghazni; Altuntash and Arslan Jadhib (advance guard)
commanders B: Muhammad ibn Suri (captured), his son Shith (captured)
Iranian force: Ghaznavid side: Mahmud's army with an advance guard of Turkic ghulam cavalry under Altuntash and Arslan Jadhib; Ghurid side: about 10,000 Ghuri highlanders.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: unknown; Ibn Suri and his son captured
borderline: the Ghurid chiefs of Mandesh long before the Ghurid state of Firuzkuh; counted civil only because the Ghurids are on the list of Persian states
doubts and flags: Borderline: the Ghurid chiefs of Mandesh long before the Ghurid state of Firuzkuh; counted civil only because the Ghurids are on the list of Persian states.
sources: Utbi; Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid campaign of Ghur; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni
note: If the early Ghurid chiefdom is not treated as a listed state, this is a Ghaznavid victory over the Ghuris (not civil).

date: 1012 (Georgian chronicle date as given by Rayfield; exact month unknown)
name: Shamkir (siege, 1012)
how the result was decided: Bagrat besieged the town and the Shaddadids bought him off with tribute, which they paid until his death in 1014.
commanders B: the Shaddadid emir (Fadl I ibn Muhammad, a Kurd)
sources: Rayfield, Edge of Empires: A History of Georgia (2012) p. 74; Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953) and 'Shaddadids', Encyclopaedia of Islam 2nd ed.; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian%E2%80%93Shaddadid_wars
note: A minor siege known from one line in a modern history; the Shaddadid emir is not named in the Wikipedia summary and Fadl I is the likely ruler. Kurdish by descent as the sources describe the dynasty.

name: Sutlej (1012)
place: on a river crossing on the road to Thanesar (the Sutlej in the campaign table), India
how the result was decided: Rama's army, posted behind the river, was driven off and Mahmud went on to sack Thanesar.
Iranian force: Mahmud's standing army (no breakdown in the sources): Turkic ghulam cavalry with Khurasani, Afghan and Indian troops and ghazi volunteers.
why it counts: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
borderline: date and site uncertain; the sack of Thanesar itself was not a battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: date and site uncertain; the sack of Thanesar itself was not a battle.
sources: Utbi; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni (campaign table: Battle of the Sutlej, 1012)

name: Tausi
place: River Tausi (Poonch or Tohi river), India
how the result was decided: Mahmud's main army routed Tunga's Kashmiris the day after their skirmish success and Trilochanapala failed to rally his men.
commanders B: Trilochanapala (Hindu Shahi); Tunga, Jayasimha, Srivardhana and Vibhramarka of Kashmir
Iranian force: The army of Nandana: Turkic ghulam cavalry, Daylamite and Afghan foot, archers.
languages: Turkic; Persian; Pashto; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Same army that fought at Nandana, where Daylamites and Afghans are named.
sources: Kalhana, Rajatarangini; Utbi; en.wikipedia Battle of the River Tausi
note: 'Indian kingdoms': the Hindu Shahis with the Lohara kingdom of Kashmir.

name: Nandana
how the result was decided: Bhimapala's force was lured into the open and routed, his elephant charge broke under archery, and Mahmud then took the fort.
commanders A: Mahmud of Ghazni, Altuntash (centre), Amir Nasr (right), Arslan Jadhib (left), Abu Abdallah Muhammad al-Ta'i (advance guard, wounded)
commanders B: Bhimapala (Hindu Shahi), Kashmiri contingent under Tunga
Iranian force: Cavalry in three divisions with Daylamite warriors and Afghan spearmen deployed to encircle the enemy, and archers against the elephants (Utbi via Wikipedia).
languages: Turkic; Persian; Pashto; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: The sources name Daylamite and Afghan foot beside the Turkic ghulam cavalry and al-Ta'i's Arabs.
sources: Utbi; Gardizi; en.wikipedia Battle of Nandana; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid-Hindu Shahi Wars
note: Also called the battle of Nardin or Nazin. One entry for the battle and the capture of the fort.

date: c. 1014-1016 (the Annazid article dates the whole sequence from 1014; Avicenna entered Shams al-Dawla's service about 1015)
name: Kermanshah (Shams al-Dawla against the Annazids, c. 1014-1016)
how the result was decided: The Annazid article says Shams al-Dawla marched on the Annazids and was defeated near Kermanshah; Avicenna, in his service, reportedly saw the battle.
commanders A: Abu'l-Shawk Faris ibn Muhammad (Annazid, a Kurd)
commanders B: Shams al-Dawla (Buyid emir of Hamadan, of Daylamite origin)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annazids ; Ibn al-Athir; Minorsky, 'Annazids', EI2; Gohlman, The Life of Ibn Sina (1974)
note: The sequence in the sources is confused (Hilal ibn Badr was killed in 1014, Tahir ibn Hilal killed by Abu'l-Shawk, then Shams al-Dawla's campaign), and I have no second source for the date of the battle. Both sides are Iranian: Kurds against a Daylamite Buyid army.

name: Khwabin (siege)
place: fortress of Khwabin, western Ghur, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: The defenders' chief was killed by an arrow shot by Mas'ud and the garrison surrendered.
Iranian force: Ghaznavid side: a detachment of Mahmud's army under the prince Mas'ud; Ghurid side: the Ghuri garrison.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a small siege; the Ghuri chiefs counted as Ghurids (see Ahangaran)
doubts and flags: Borderline: a small siege; the Ghuri chiefs counted as Ghurids (see Ahangaran).
sources: Bayhaqi; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid campaign of Ghur
note: Mas'ud's further sieges in Ghur in 1020 (Bartar, Shan, Tur) are not entered separately.

name: Lohkot (siege, 1015)
place: Lohkot (Loharkot, near Loran, Tosa Maidan route), India
how the result was decided: Mahmud abandoned the siege at the onset of winter and retreated with heavy losses.
Iranian force: Mahmud's field army (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
losses B: heavy, mostly in the winter retreat
sources: Kalhana, Rajatarangini; Gardizi; en.wikipedia Siege of Lohkot (1015)
note: Wikipedia calls the result inconclusive; under the test a raised siege is a win for the defender.

name: Hazarasp
place: near Hazarasp, on the road to Gurganj, Uzbekistan
how the result was decided: The Khwarazmian army was decisively beaten and scattered and Mahmud marched on to Gurganj.
factions B: Khwarazm (the Ma'munid regime of the army that killed Ma'mun II)
commanders A: Mahmud of Ghazni, Abu Abdallah Muhammad al-Ta'i, Altuntash, Arslan Jadhib
Iranian force: Ghaznavid side: Mahmud's main army, claimed at 100,000 horse with elephants; Khwarazmian side: about 50,000, the Turkic ghulam army of the Khwarazmshahs (with a Bukharan garrison under Alptegin) and Khwarazmian levies.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
strength A: 100,000 cavalry and 500 elephants (Wikipedia infobox; certainly exaggerated)
borderline: counted civil because the Ma'munid Khwarazmshahs were a local Iranian dynasty seated in Khwarazm
doubts and flags: Borderline: counted civil because the Ma'munid Khwarazmshahs were a local Iranian dynasty seated in Khwarazm.
sources: Bayhaqi (after al-Biruni); Gardizi; Bosworth, CHI 4; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid conquest of Khwarazm
note: Wikipedia's battle article names no site and its Mahmud article calls it the battle of Gurganj; Bosworth places the decisive battle near Hazarasp. Earlier Khumartash had routed al-Ta'i's vanguard before being beaten and captured by the sultan's guard.

date: 20 December 1018 (the body of the Wikipedia article says January 1019)
name: Kannauj (1018)
how the result was decided: Rajyapala fled without battle and Mahmud took the seven forts of Kannauj in a single day.
Iranian force: Mahmud's regulars and some 20,000 volunteers from Transoxiana (Utbi); Firishta's 100,000 horse and 20,000 foot is a late exaggeration.
why it counts: Utbi names some 20,000 Transoxianan ghazi volunteers beside the Turkic ghulam regulars.
strength A: 11,000 regulars (Sibt ibn al-Jawzi); 20,000 volunteers (Utbi); 100,000 horse and 20,000 foot (Firishta)
borderline: the Pratihara king fled; how much fighting there was at the forts is unclear
doubts and flags: Borderline: the Pratihara king fled; how much fighting there was at the forts is unclear.
sources: Utbi; Sibt ibn al-Jawzi; Firishta; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid invasions of Kannauj
note: The minor actions of the same march (Baran/Bulandshahr surrendered, Mathura plundered, Asi abandoned) are not entered.

name: Mahaban
place: Mahaban, on the Yamuna near Mathura, India
how the result was decided: Kulchand's army was routed and driven into the Yamuna, and Kulchand killed himself.
Iranian force: The Kannauj expedition: Mahmud's regulars (11,000 per Sibt ibn al-Jawzi) with about 20,000 volunteers from Transoxiana (Utbi).
why it counts: Utbi names some 20,000 ghazi volunteers from Transoxiana, mostly Persian-speaking, beside the Turkic ghulam regulars.
sources: Utbi; Nazim, The Life and Times of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazna (1931); en.wikipedia Ghaznavid invasions of Kannauj; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni
note: Utbi's casualty figure is typical of the panegyric sources.

name: Munj (siege)
how the result was decided: The fort was stormed and taken.
Iranian force: The Kannauj expedition: Turkic ghulam regulars and Transoxianan volunteers.
why it counts: Same army as at Kannauj, with many Persian-speaking volunteers (Utbi).
borderline: obscure fort; site not identified
doubts and flags: Borderline: obscure fort; site not identified.
sources: Utbi; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid invasions of Kannauj; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni

name: Sharwa
place: near Sharwa (perhaps near Meerut or Sirsawa), India
how the result was decided: Mahmud overtook Chand Rai's retreating army and defeated it, taking his elephants and baggage.
Iranian force: The Kannauj expedition: Turkic ghulam regulars and Transoxianan volunteers.
why it counts: Same army as at Kannauj, with many Persian-speaking volunteers (Utbi).
borderline: site uncertain
doubts and flags: Borderline: site uncertain.
sources: Utbi; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni (campaign table: Battle of Sharwa)

date: late 1019 (410 AH); Wikipedia's articles give October 1019, October or 15 December 1020
name: Ramganga
place: Ramganga river (the Rahib of the sources) near Afzalgarh, India
how the result was decided: Eight of Mahmud's guards swam the river, the army crossed on horses and skins, and Trilochanapala's entrenched army fled with heavy loss.
Iranian force: Mahmud's mounted army, crossing on horseback and on inflated skins (no breakdown by people in the sources).
why it counts: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
sources: Utbi; Gardizi; en.wikipedia Battle of the Ramganga; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid-Hindu Shahi Wars
note: Also called the battle of the Rahib. Mahmud then faced the Chandela Vidyadhara, whose army withdrew in the night without battle (not entered).

name: Lohkot (siege, 1021)
how the result was decided: Mahmud again gave up the siege before winter and withdrew.
Iranian force: Mahmud's field army (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
sources: Gardizi; en.wikipedia Siege of Lohkot (1015); en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni

name: Gwalior (siege, 1022)
how the result was decided: The ruler submitted after four days and gave 35 elephants, and Mahmud moved on without taking the fort; a siege ended by treaty is a draw under the test.
commanders B: the Kachchhapaghata ruler of Gwalior, vassal of the Chandelas
Iranian force: Mahmud's field army (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
borderline: short siege ended by submission; fighting not described
doubts and flags: Borderline: short siege ended by submission; fighting not described.
sources: Utbi; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni (campaign table)
note: Wikipedia lists the 1022 sieges as Ghaznavid victories.

name: Kalinjar (siege, 1022)
how the result was decided: Vidyadhara bought peace with tribute and elephants while the fort was invested and kept Kalinjar; a siege ended by treaty is a draw under the test.
Iranian force: Mahmud's field army (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
borderline: siege ended by submission; fighting not described
doubts and flags: Borderline: siege ended by submission; fighting not described.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Utbi; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni (campaign table)
note: Mahmud returned fifteen forts to Vidyadhara in exchange for his submission (as usually told).

name: Modhera
place: Mundher of the sources (probably Modhera), Gujarat, India
how the result was decided: About 20,000 Hindu fighters who barred the road were defeated and dispersed.
Iranian force: The Somnath expedition: about 30,000 cavalry with volunteers (see Somnath).
why it counts: Inferred from the usual recruitment of Mahmud's army (Bosworth).
borderline: identification of the site uncertain; known only from the Muslim chroniclers
doubts and flags: Borderline: identification of the site uncertain; known only from the Muslim chroniclers.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Sack of Somnath; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni ('Battle of Kathiawar')

name: Shamkir (siege, 1026)
how the result was decided: Frye (and the Wikipedia summary of the Georgian-Shaddadid wars) says George I launched the siege and was defeated.
commanders B: Fadl I ibn Muhammad (a Kurd), emir of Ganja
sources: Frye ed., Cambridge History of Iran vol. 4 (1975) p. 241; Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953) and 'Shaddadids', Encyclopaedia of Islam 2nd ed.; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian%E2%80%93Shaddadid_wars
note: Known from a single sentence; details of the fighting are not given. The Shaddadid ruler is inferred (Fadl I).

date: 6-8 January 1026 (the town seized 6 January, assault 7 January, the temple taken 8 January)
name: Somnath
how the result was decided: After three days of assaults and counter-attacks the Ghaznavids stormed the walls and the shrine, and the temple was sacked.
commanders B: Mandalika (Abhira overseer of the fort); Bhima I (Chaulukya) had fled to Kanthkot
Iranian force: About 30,000 cavalry and an unknown number of volunteers, each man with two camels (Ibn al-Athir via Wikipedia); the usual Ghaznavid mixture of Turkic ghulams, Khurasanis, Afghans and Indians.
why it counts: The sources give totals only; inferred from the Ghaznavid recruitment of ghulams and Persian-speaking volunteers (Bosworth).
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Gardizi; al-Biruni; Thapar, Somanatha (2004); en.wikipedia Sack of Somnath
note: The account rests on Muslim sources; Thapar and others doubt its scale. 'Indian kingdoms': the Chaulukyas and the Abhira lord of the fort.

name: Nahavand (1028)
war: Wars of Ala al-Dawla Muhammad (Kakuyid expansion in Jibal)
side B: Bavandids of Tabaristan and allied rivals
how the result was decided: Ala al-Dawla won a great victory and captured the Bavandid ruler and his sons on the field.
factions B: Bavandids of Tabaristan and allied rivals
commanders B: Abu Ja'far Muhammad, Bavandid ispahbad (captured with his two sons)
Iranian force: Kakuyid side: Ala al-Dawla's Daylamite and Turkish troops; opposing side: Tabaristani (Mazandarani) levies of the Bavandid ispahbad and Kurdish allies.
languages: Daylami and Caspian; Turkic; Kurdish; Persian
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: unknown; the Bavandid ruler and his sons captured
borderline: named only by place; details thin
doubts and flags: Borderline: named only by place; details thin.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Bosworth, 'Kakuyids', Encyclopaedia Iranica; en.wikipedia Muhammad ibn Rustam Dushmanziyar
note: The Bavandids, an Iran-seated dynasty of Tabaristan, are treated as a Persian state.

name: Ribat-i Farawa
war: Ghaznavid-Seljuk wars (the Turkmen of Arslan Isra'il in Khorasan)
place: Ribat-i Farawa (near Serdar, formerly Gyzylarbat), Turkmenistan
how the result was decided: Mahmud defeated the Turkmen bands that had beaten his governor of Tus, and drove them out towards the Balkhan mountains.
commanders B: Turkmen chiefs of the Seljuk clan of Arslan Isra'il
Iranian force: Mahmud's army in Khorasan (no breakdown in the sources): Turkic ghulam cavalry and Khurasani troops.
why it counts: Inferred from the usual recruitment of the Ghaznavid army in Khorasan (Bosworth).
borderline: details thin
doubts and flags: Borderline: details thin.
sources: Bayhaqi; Gardizi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Mahmud of Ghazni (campaign table)
note: 'Oghuz': the Turkmen followers of Arslan Isra'il, kinsmen of Tughril and Chaghri, whom Mahmud had let into Khorasan in 1025.

date: 1029 (as given in the Rawwadid article; month unknown)
name: Maragha (Wahsudan against the Oghuz, 1029)
how the result was decided: The Rawwadid article says Wahsudan, with the Hadhbani Kurds, defeated the Oghuz invaders at Maragha.
commanders A: Wahsudan ibn Muhammad (Rawwadid, of Arab descent but Kurdicised and reckoned a Kurdish dynasty)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rawadid_dynasty ; Minorsky, 'Rawwadids', EI2 and Studies in Caucasian History (1953); Ibn al-Athir
note: The Rawwadids were of Arab (Azd) origin but Kurdicised; the Hadhbani Kurds are the named unit that qualifies the battle regardless of how the dynasty is classed.

name: Sarjahan (siege)
place: Sarjahan castle, near Soltaniyeh, Zanjan, Iran
how the result was decided: Mas'ud besieged the fort, Ibrahim came out to fight and was defeated and captured, and his son submitted.
commanders A: Mas'ud, with the Daylamite Marzuban ibn Hasan
Iranian force: Ghaznavid side: Mas'ud's army with Daylamite chiefs who had come over to him; Sallarid side: Daylamite and Gilaki troops of the Musafirid ruler of Tarom.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Bayhaqi; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid campaigns in Persia
note: Mahmud had entered Rayy without resistance on 26 May 1029 (not entered: a capture without fighting).

name: Defeat of Fadl I in Georgia (1030)
place: a place on the Georgian-Armenian route home to Ganja (site not given); Georgia or northern Armenia
how the result was decided: Fadl I, returning from a successful raid into Georgia, was ambushed and his army reportedly lost about 10,000 men.
sources: Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953) p. 43; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian%E2%80%93Shaddadid_wars ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaddadids
note: Not a named battle in the sources; entered under a descriptive name because it is a real engagement with a specific loss. Location unknown.

name: Isfahan (1030)
how the result was decided: Mas'ud defeated Ala al-Dawla, who fled to the Buyids at Ahvaz, and occupied Isfahan.
Iranian force: Ghaznavid side: Mas'ud's western army of Turkic ghulams and Khurasani troops; Kakuyid side: Ala al-Dawla's Daylamite and Turkish soldiers with Kurdish allies.
languages: Turkic; Daylami and Caspian; Persian; Kurdish
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: the fighting is thinly reported; may have been more submission than battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: the fighting is thinly reported; may have been more submission than battle.
