sources: Bayhaqi; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid campaigns in Persia; en.wikipedia Muhammad ibn Rustam Dushmanziyar
note: Ala al-Dawla was then left as a tributary; Mas'ud left for Ghazni on Mahmud's death (April 1030).

name: Makran
how the result was decided: Isa's much larger army was beaten and Isa killed, and Abu'l-Askar was installed as ruler.
commanders A: Yariq-Toghmish (Ghaznavid commander), with the claimant Abu'l-Askar
commanders B: Isa ibn Ma'dan, ruler of Makran (killed)
Iranian force: Selected officers (muqaddams) and 2,000 branded (ghulam) cavalry sent by Mas'ud, with Abu'l-Askar's local followers.
why it counts: The Ghaznavid detachment was ghulam cavalry; the claimant's men were local Makranis, who spoke Iranian languages.
strength A: 2,000 branded cavalry and officers, plus the claimant's men
sources: Bayhaqi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid campaigns in Persia; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire
note: 'Makran' (new entity name): the Ma'danid amirate of Makran, seated at Kiz in present-day Pakistan.

name: Edessa (Bal's expedition, 1032)
side B: Arab tribes backed by the Roman Empire
how the result was decided: Bal took the city and killed the Arab chief, then asked Nasr al-Dawla for reinforcements; the Romans recovered Edessa in 1033.
principal opponents: Arab tribes backed by the Roman Empire
commanders A: Nasr al-Dawla Ahmad ibn Marwan (a Kurd), directing; his general Bal with 5,000 horse
commanders B: an Arab tribal chief (killed; name not given in the source consulted)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marwanids_(Diyar_Bakr) ; Ibn al-Azraq al-Fariqi; Canard, 'Marwanids', EI2
note: The page gives few details and the Roman and Arab sides (Maniakes, Banu Numayr) are not named in it. The Marwanid army is said to rely on Kurdish tribesmen, but Bal's ethnicity is not stated.

name: Dabusiyya
place: near Dabusiyya, between Bukhara and Samarkand, Uzbekistan
how the result was decided: The bloody battle had no clear victor: Ali Tegin's army fell back, Altuntash was mortally wounded, and his vizier hid his death and led the army home under a truce.
commanders A: Altuntash, Khwarazmshah (mortally wounded); his vizier Ahmad ibn Abd al-Samad
commanders B: Ali Tegin Bughra Khan, with Seljuk Turkmen allies
Iranian force: Altuntash's army of Khwarazm (Turkic ghulams and Khwarazmian troops) reinforced by Ghaznavid regulars sent by Mas'ud.
why it counts: The Khwarazm army combined Turkic ghulams with Khwarazmian levies, who spoke an East Iranian language.
sources: Bayhaqi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Battle of Dabusiyya; en.wikipedia Altuntash (khwarazmshah)
note: Wikipedia calls it a stalemate/indecisive.

name: Sarsuti (siege)
place: fortress of Sarsuti (identified either with Sarsawa near Saharanpur or a fort on the road to Kashmir), India
how the result was decided: Mas'ud took the fortress.
Iranian force: Mas'ud's army (no breakdown in the sources): Turkic ghulams, Indian troops and Khurasani soldiers.
why it counts: Mas'ud's army had a Turkic core with large Indian contingents and Iranian units (Bosworth).
borderline: site and details uncertain
doubts and flags: Borderline: site and details uncertain.
sources: Gardizi; Bayhaqi; en.wikipedia Mas'ud I of Ghazni; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire ('Siege of Sarsawa')

name: Kerman (1034)
how the result was decided: The Buyid army defeated the Ghaznavid garrison force, which retreated to Nishapur.
commanders A: Bahram ibn Mafinna, vizier of Abu Kalijar
commanders B: the Ghaznavid governor of Kerman (not named)
Iranian force: Buyid side: about 10,000 Daylamite and Turkish troops of Fars; Ghaznavid side: 4,000 cavalry, 2,500 infantry and 5 elephants.
languages: Daylami and Caspian; Turkic; Persian; Indian
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: named only by province
doubts and flags: Borderline: named only by province.
sources: Bayhaqi; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid campaigns in Persia; en.wikipedia Mas'ud I of Ghazni (dates it c. 1037)
note: An earlier Ghaznavid invasion of Kerman (1031) also failed; it is not entered for lack of detail.

date: June or July 1035 (the army left for Nasa on 19 June 1035)
name: Nasa
place: near Nasa (Nisa, by Bagir near Ashgabat), Turkmenistan
how the result was decided: The Seljuks drew Begtoghdi's army on with a feigned retreat, then fell on it and routed it.
Iranian force: About 15,000 regulars under the chamberlain Begtoghdi: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Indian, Kurdish, Arab and Khurasani units in the usual Ghaznavid mixture (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Inferred from the Ghaznavid recruitment under Mas'ud: a Turkic ghulam core with Indian, Daylamite, Kurdish, Arab and Khurasani units (Bosworth).
sources: Bayhaqi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Battle of Nasa (1035)
note: 'Oghuz': the Seljuk Turkmen under Tughril and Chaghri, not yet a state seated in Iran. Mas'ud then ceded Nasa, Farawa and Dihistan to them. The List of battles places Nasa in Tabaristan, which is wrong.

name: Hansi (siege)
how the result was decided: Mas'ud stormed Hansi after a short siege.
commanders B: the Tomara garrison of Hansi (commander not named)
Iranian force: Mas'ud's army (no breakdown in the sources): Turkic ghulams, Indian troops and Khurasani soldiers.
why it counts: Mas'ud's army had a Turkic core with large Indian contingents and Iranian units (Bosworth).
sources: Bayhaqi; Gardizi; en.wikipedia Mas'ud I of Ghazni; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire
note: Mas'ud then took Sonipat (not entered).

name: Rayy (1038)
how the result was decided: The Kakuyids defeated the Ghaznavid garrison, whose commander was killed, and the Ghaznavids abandoned Rayy.
Iranian force: Kakuyid side: Ala al-Dawla's Daylamite and Turkish troops; Ghaznavid side: the garrison of Rayy (1,500 in one infobox figure).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: thinly reported; Wikipedia's Kakuyid article speaks only of an occupation of Rayy
doubts and flags: Borderline: thinly reported; Wikipedia's Kakuyid article speaks only of an occupation of Rayy.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ghaznavid campaigns in Persia; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire

name: Sarakhs (1038)
how the result was decided: Subashi's army was routed and many were taken prisoner; Nishapur opened its gates to the Seljuks soon after.
commanders B: Subashi (commander in Khorasan), with Begtoghdi and the civil governor Abu'l-Fadl Suri
Iranian force: The Ghaznavid army of Khorasan (15,000-25,000 in an unsourced estimate): Turkic ghulam cavalry, Indian, Kurdish and Arab units and Khurasani foot.
why it counts: Inferred from the Ghaznavid recruitment under Mas'ud (Bosworth).
sources: Bayhaqi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Battle of Sarakhs (1038)
note: 'Oghuz': the Seljuk Turkmen, not yet a state seated in Iran. The 'Battle of Nishapur (1038)' article describes what was in fact the surrender of Nishapur after this battle (excluded).

name: Battle of Tashir (1040)
side A (victor if decisive): Armenian kingdom of Tashir-Dzoraget; Kingdom of Georgia
how the result was decided: The Wikipedia article on the Georgian-Shaddadid wars says the allied Armenian and Georgian force defeated Abu'l-Aswar.
principal opponents: Armenian kingdom of Tashir-Dzoraget; Kingdom of Georgia
commanders A: the Kiurikid Armenian king of Tashir-Dzoraget (David Anhoghin); Georgian auxiliary commander sent by Bagrat IV
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian%E2%80%93Shaddadid_wars (no source cited there); Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953) and 'Shaddadids', Encyclopaedia of Islam 2nd ed.
note: Weakly sourced: one line in Wikipedia without a citation. Included as a named battle with a Shaddadid commander.

name: Dandanaqan
place: Dandanaqan, between Sarakhs and Merv, Turkmenistan
how the result was decided: Mas'ud's army, worn down by thirst and harassment, broke when part of the ghulam cavalry deserted, and the sultan fled the field.
commanders A: Tughril, Chaghri Beg, Ibrahim Inal, Musa Yabghu
Iranian force: Mas'ud's main army, reportedly about 50,000 with 100-300 elephants: the Turkic palace ghulams, Indian (Hindu) cavalry and infantry, Daylamite, Kurdish, Arab and Khurasani units (Bayhaqi); part of the ghulams went over to the Seljuks.
languages: Turkic; Indian; Persian; Kurdish; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Bayhaqi's narrative names Turkic ghulams, Indians, Kurds, Arabs and Daylamite and Khurasani foot; Bosworth treats the army as a Turkic-led multi-ethnic force.
sources: Bayhaqi, Ta'rikh-i Mas'udi; Gardizi; Bosworth, The Ghaznavids and CHI 4; en.wikipedia Battle of Dandanaqan
note: 'Oghuz': the Seljuk Turkmen, who became a Persian state only by this victory (not civil). Khorasan passed to the Seljuks; Mas'ud was deposed and killed in 1041.

name: Zaranj (siege, 1040)
how the result was decided: Abu'l-Fadl went over to the Seljuks and Zaranj was occupied.
commanders B: Abu'l-Fadl Nasr, Nasrid amir of Sistan under Ghaznavid rule
Iranian force: Seljuk side: Turkmen cavalry under Ertash; defenders: the Sistani forces of the Nasrid amir.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: ended by the defender's change of side; fighting not described
doubts and flags: Borderline: ended by the defender's change of side; fighting not described.
sources: Ta'rikh-i Sistan; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Seljuk Empire
note: Civil because after Dandanaqan the Seljuks held a seat in Khorasan.

date: 1041-1042 (the Rawwadid article gives the desert of Sarab, 1041-42)
name: Sarab (Rawwadids against the Ghuzz, 1041-1042)
place: the desert of Sarab, East Azerbaijan, Iran
how the result was decided: The Rawwadid article calls it a Rawwadid defeat by a Ghuzz band that had reached Azerbaijan.
commanders B: Wahsudan ibn Muhammad (Rawwadid, reckoned a Kurdish dynasty)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rawadid_dynasty ; Minorsky, 'Rawwadids', EI2; Ibn al-Athir
note: Known from one line in the Rawwadid article; the Oghuz had already been killed or driven off in 1037-1041, so this is a second wave. The Iranian criterion rests on Wahsudan's leadership of a dynasty reckoned Kurdish.

name: Nangrahar
place: Dinur in Nangrahar, near Jalalabad, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: Mawdud defeated his uncle's army, captured Muhammad and his sons and put them to death in revenge for Mas'ud.
factions B: Muhammad (brother of Mas'ud) and his sons
commanders B: Muhammad ibn Mahmud, his sons Ahmad and others
Iranian force: Both sides were parts of the Ghaznavid army: Mawdud's Ghazni troops against the mutinous army that had deposed Mas'ud, Turkic ghulams and Indian units on both sides.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Gardizi; Ibn al-Athir; Bosworth, The Later Ghaznavids (1977); en.wikipedia Mawdud of Ghazni; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire
note: Also called the battle of Dinur.

name: Dvin
how the result was decided: As in Battles of the Romans: The Shaddadids were a Kurdish dynasty, counted here with the Muslim emirates under 'Arabs'.
commanders A: Abu'l-Aswar Shavur, Shaddadid emir of Dvin
commanders B: Michael Iasites, the magistros Constantine the Alan
why it counts: Abu'l-Aswar Shavur, Shaddadid (Kurdish) emir of Dvin, against an imperial army in which Constantine the Alan was one of the commanders (Skylitzes)
sources: Skylitzes, Constantine IX 15; Aristakes 12; en.wikipedia Abu'l-Aswar Shavur ibn Fadl
note: Abu'l-Aswar Shavur, Shaddadid (Kurdish) emir of Dvin, against an imperial army in which Constantine the Alan was one of the commanders (Skylitzes)

date: 1045-1047 (Abu'l-Shawk held out and died in April 1046; the castle fell in or about 1047)
name: Sirwan (siege, 1045-1047)
war: Seljuk conquest of the Annazid lands
place: Sirwan castle, in the Zagros between Hulwan and Shahrizur (Iran-Iraq borderland, site uncertain)
how the result was decided: The Annazid article says Abu'l-Shawk held the castle until his death in 1046 and Sirwan, the last Annazid stronghold, fell soon after.
commanders A: Ibrahim Yinal (Tughril Beg's half-brother, a Turk)
commanders B: Abu'l-Shawk Faris ibn Muhammad (Annazid, a Kurd), who died in April 1046; then his son Sa'adi
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annazids ; Minorsky, 'Annazids', EI2; Ibn al-Athir
note: The Annazids are Kurdish by descent; the defence of a hill fortress by Kurdish clans against the Seljuk Turkmen. Dates are given only by year in the source.

name: Isfahan (siege, 1047)
how the result was decided: Tughril could not enter the city and lifted the siege for tribute and the khutba; a siege ended by treaty is a draw under the test.
Iranian force: Seljuk side: Turkmen cavalry and the sultan's ghulams; Kakuyid side: Daylamite and Turkish garrison troops and the townsmen behind Ala al-Dawla's walls.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: how much fighting there was is not reported
doubts and flags: Borderline: how much fighting there was is not reported.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Tughril

date: 18 September 1048 (perhaps beginning on the evening of 17 September)
name: Kapetron
war: Seljuk-Roman wars (Ibrahim Inal's invasion of Armenia)
how the result was decided: The Roman wings drove the Turks opposite them from the field and pursued them till morning, while the Seljuk centre captured Liparit and Ibrahim withdrew with his captives; the sources disagree on who held the field and modern scholarship gives no verdict.
commanders A: Ibrahim Inal; Aspan Salarios (centre); Chorosantes (left, killed); Qutalmish
commanders B: Aaron and Katakalon Kekaumenos (Roman wings); Liparit IV of Kldekari (centre, captured)
Iranian force: Seljuk Turkmen and newly arrived Oghuz tribes, with Daylamites and 'Kabeiroi' (probably Khurasani Iranians); the left wing was led by 'Chorosantes', perhaps the Khurasani commander, and the centre by an ispahsalar (Skylitzes).
why it counts: Skylitzes names Daylamite and Khurasani ('Kabeiroi') contingents, the Khurasanis apparently forming a whole wing beside the Turkmen.
sources: Skylitzes; Aristakes Lastivertsi; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Kapetron
note: Ibn al-Athir and Aristakes treat it as a Seljuk victory; Skylitzes stresses the Roman pursuit. 'Georgia': Liparit's duchy of Kldekari.

date: 1050 to May 1051 (about a year; Tughril entered in Muharram 443; Wikipedia's Tughril article gives 1051-52)
name: Isfahan (siege, 1050)
how the result was decided: After a siege of about a year the city surrendered and Tughril made it his capital.
Iranian force: Seljuk side: Turkmen cavalry and the sultan's ghulams with siege engines; Kakuyid side: Daylamite and Turkish garrison troops and the citizens.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Nasir-i Khusraw; Bosworth, CHI 5; en.wikipedia Tughril
note: Faramurz was compensated with Yazd and Abarquh.

name: Sarmaj (siege)
place: fortress of Sarmaj, near Bisotun, Kermanshah, Iran
how the result was decided: Tughril beat Ibrahim in the field and after a four-day siege of Sarmaj Ibrahim surrendered.
Iranian force: Both sides were Seljuk Turkmen cavalry with ghulams; Ibrahim's force was his own Turkmen following in Jibal.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: one entry for a field action and a short siege
doubts and flags: Borderline: one entry for a field action and a short siege.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Tughril
note: Ibrahim was pardoned and returned to service.

name: Hupyan
how the result was decided: Toghrul defeated Alp Arslan's invading army in the Hindu Kush.
Iranian force: Ghaznavid side: Turkic ghulam cavalry under Toghrul with Indian and Afghan troops; Seljuk side: Alp Arslan's Turkmen horse from Tokharistan.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Gardizi; Bosworth, The Later Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Toghrul of Ghazna; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire
note: Civil: both the Ghaznavids and the Great Seljuks were seated in the eastern Iranian world by then.

name: Taq (siege, 1051)
place: fortress of Taq, Sistan (site not securely identified), Afghanistan
side A (victor if decisive): Sistan with a Seljuk relief army
how the result was decided: Toghrul beat the Seljuk relief army but could not take Taq and gave up the siege.
factions A: Sistan (Nasrid-Saffarid amirs, Seljuk vassals) with a Seljuk relief army
commanders A: Hilal Daraqi, commandant of Taq; Payghu (Musa Yabghu) with the relief army
Iranian force: Defenders: the Sistani garrison of the Nasrid amirs and a Seljuk Turkmen relief force; besiegers: Toghrul's Ghaznavid ghulam army.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ta'rikh-i Sistan; Bosworth, The Later Ghaznavids; en.wikipedia Toghrul of Ghazna; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire
note: Toghrul's victory over Payghu's relief army during the siege is not separately named. Toghrul then usurped the throne at Ghazni (1052) and was murdered after some weeks (not a battle).

name: Anbar (1055)
war: Buyid-Uqaylid wars (last campaigns of the Buyids in Iraq)
how the result was decided: Al-Basasiri retook Anbar and captured its commander with about 100 Khafaja soldiers.
commanders A: Arslan al-Basasiri, Turkish commander-in-chief of the Buyid al-Malik al-Rahim; Dubays I of the Mazyadids
commanders B: Abu'l-Ghana'im ibn al-Muhallaban, client of Quraysh the Uqaylid (captured)
Iranian force: Al-Basasiri's Turkish mamluks of the Buyid army of Iraq with the Mazyadid Arabs of Dubays.
why it counts: Buyids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a minor action; the Buyid regime was weeks from its end
doubts and flags: Borderline: a minor action; the Buyid regime was weeks from its end.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Al-Basasiri
note: 'Arab tribes': the Uqaylids and Khafaja (opponents) and the Mazyadids (allies). Quraysh had taken Anbar in November 1054.

date: summer 1059 (Jumada II 451; Wikipedia's Alp Arslan article gives 3 August 1059, its Tughril article 1060)
name: Rayy (1059)
side A (victor if decisive): Tughril, with his nephews Alp Arslan, Yaquti and Qavurt
side B: Ibrahim Inal and his nephews Muhammad and Ahmad
how the result was decided: Ibrahim's army was defeated and he was captured by Alp Arslan and executed with his nephews.
factions A: Tughril, with his nephews Alp Arslan, Yaquti and Qavurt
factions B: Ibrahim Inal and his nephews Muhammad and Ahmad
Iranian force: Both sides were Seljuk Turkmen armies; Ibrahim's was swollen by Turkmen discontented with Tughril's turn to settled rule, Tughril's reinforced by Chaghri's sons from Khorasan.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Bosworth, CHI 5; en.wikipedia Tughril; en.wikipedia Alp Arslan
note: Earlier in the revolt Tughril was hemmed in at Hamadan but avoided battle.

date: late November or early December 1063 (Qutalmish died on 7 December 1063)
name: Damghan (1063)
war: Seljuk succession war (Alp Arslan against Qutalmish)
place: Dihinemek, near Damghan (in the flooded Milh valley), Iran
side B: Qutalmish, with his brother Resul and his son Suleiman
how the result was decided: After a vanguard success Qutalmish's army fled when the main armies met, and Qutalmish died after falling from his horse in the flight.
factions B: Qutalmish, with his brother Resul and his son Suleiman
commanders B: Qutalmish (died in the flight), Resul and Suleiman (captured)
Iranian force: Alp Arslan's army of Khorasan (Turkmen, ghulams and Khurasani troops) against Qutalmish's Turkmen following.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Bundari; en.wikipedia Battle of Damghan (1063); en.wikipedia Alp Arslan
note: Some accounts place the battle nearer Rayy, which Qutalmish had been besieging since 15 November 1063.

name: Herat (siege, 1064)
war: Seljuk succession war (Alp Arslan against Musa Yabghu)
how the result was decided: Alp Arslan defeated Musa Yabghu and took him prisoner at Herat.
Iranian force: Seljuk Turkmen armies on both sides; Musa held Herat with its garrison and townsmen.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: whether there was a battle or only a siege and surrender is unclear
doubts and flags: Borderline: whether there was a battle or only a siege and surrender is unclear.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Alp Arslan

name: Ani (siege, 1064)
war: Alp Arslan's Georgian and Armenian campaign
how the result was decided: Ani fell to assault after a 25-day siege and was sacked.
commanders A: Alp Arslan, with Nizam al-Mulk and the young Malik-Shah
commanders B: Bagrat and Gregory, Roman commanders of the city (captured)
Iranian force: Alp Arslan's army in two columns (one under Malik-Shah and Nizam al-Mulk), with siege engines built by Arab and Persian technicians.
why it counts: Wikipedia's Siege of Ani (1064) lists Nizam al-Mulk, a Persian from Tus, as commander of one of the two divisions (with Malik-Shah) and says Alp Arslan equipped his army with Arab and Persian technicians; the troops themselves were Turkic.
losses B: heavy, with many civilians; 50,000 prisoners (Sibt ibn al-Jawzi)
sources: Aristakes Lastivertsi; Matthew of Edessa; Sibt ibn al-Jawzi; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Ani (1064)
note: Kars then submitted without a fight (not entered).

name: Kerman (1067)
how the result was decided: Alp Arslan beat the rebel's forces, Qavurt fled to Jiroft and then submitted, giving up territory after the siege of Bardasir.
commanders A: Alp Arslan; Malik-Shah (at the siege of Bardasir)
Iranian force: Alp Arslan's Turkmen and ghulam army against Qavurt's Turkmen and local Kermani and Kufichi levies.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: details thin; one entry for the 1067 battle and the 1068 siege of Bardasir
doubts and flags: Borderline: details thin; one entry for the 1067 battle and the 1068 siege of Bardasir.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Muhammad ibn Ibrahim, Ta'rikh-i Saljuqiyan-i Kirman; en.wikipedia Alp Arslan
note: Wikipedia's Alp Arslan article lists the battle (1067) and the siege of Bardasir (1068) separately.

name: Invasion of Georgia by Fadl II and his defeat (1068)
war: Georgian-Shaddadid wars (in the year of Alp Arslan's invasion of Georgia)
place: Kakheti-Kartli, along the Iori River, Georgia (site not given)
how the result was decided: The Georgians defeated the invasion and Aghsartan captured Fadl II, who was ransomed for several fortresses on the Iori and accepted a Georgian vassal emir in Tbilisi.
commanders A: Fadl II ibn Shavur (a Kurd), with about 33,000 men (as given)
commanders B: Aghsartan I of Kakheti; Bagrat IV of Georgia
sources: Minorsky, 'Shaddadids', EI2 and Studies in Caucasian History (1953); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian%E2%80%93Shaddadid_wars ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaddadids
note: The sources do not give a battle name; the Wikipedia articles on the Shaddadids and on the Georgian-Shaddadid wars differ on whether Bagrat IV or Aghsartan I won. Force size is a medieval figure.

name: Manzikert
how the result was decided: The Roman army broke during its evening withdrawal, Andronikos Doukas led the rearguard off the field and Romanos IV was captured; the Seljuks held the field.
commanders B: Romanos IV Diogenes (captured), Nikephoros Bryennios, Theodore Alyates, Andronikos Doukas
Iranian force: Alp Arslan's mounted army: his Turkic ghulams and Turkmen horse archers, with troops from Aleppo and Mosul and a Kurdish contingent (estimated at 10,000) sent by the Marwanid emir; the Romans' Pecheneg and Oghuz mercenaries went over to him.
why it counts: The core was Turkic, but the Marwanid Kurdish contingent of about 10,000 reported in the sources would be a fifth to a quarter of a 35,000-50,000 army; both figures are uncertain.
strength A: 35,000-50,000 (modern estimates; Muslim and Armenian sources give far more)
strength B: about 40,000 (close to half had deserted or been detached before the battle)
sources: Michael Attaleiates; Michael Psellos; Matthew of Edessa; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Manzikert
note: Romanos IV was released on terms; the Turkmen occupation of Anatolia that followed was largely the work of independent Turkmen bands and of the later Sultanate of Rum, not of the sultan's army.

name: Kerj Abu Dulaf (1073)
place: Kerj Abu Dulaf (between Hamadan and Arak), Iran
how the result was decided: After three days Qavurt's army broke and he was captured; Malik-Shah held the field.
Iranian force: A: Malik-Shah's ghulams with Kurdish and Arab contingents (some of his Turks mutinied in favour of Qavurt); B: Qavurt's Turkmen army with his seven sons.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Kerj Abu Dulaf; en.wikipedia Malik-Shah I
note: Qavurt, Alp Arslan's brother and ruler of Kerman, claimed the sultanate on Alp Arslan's death; two of his sons were blinded.

name: Sakalkand
how the result was decided: The Ghaznavid army overran Sakalkand and captured Uthman; the Seljuk counter-attack under Gumushtegin Bilge Beg and Anushtegin Gharchai that later drove it out is a separate action.
Iranian force: A: a Ghaznavid army (no details; Ibrahim's army was a core of Turkic ghulams with Indian, Afghan and Khalaj troops); B: Uthman's Seljuk forces in Tukharistan (Turkic).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: unknown (Uthman captured and sent to Ghazni)
borderline: obscure border fight of the Ghaznavid-Seljuk war of 1073
doubts and flags: Borderline: obscure border fight of the Ghaznavid-Seljuk war of 1073.
sources: en.wikipedia Ibrahim of Ghazna; en.wikipedia Malik-Shah I
note: Sakalkand lay in Tukharistan (northern Afghanistan); its exact site is not known. Peace followed with a marriage alliance (Gawhar Khatun and Mas'ud III).

date: c. 1074 (dated 1072-1077; recent research August or September 1075)
name: Partskhisi
how the result was decided: After a day-long battle the Georgians routed Savtegin's army.
commanders A: George II of Georgia, with Aghsartan I of Kakheti
commanders B: Savtegin (Sarang), Malik-Shah's governor of Ganja and Arran
Iranian force: The army Malik-Shah left with Savtegin in Arran, given as 48,000 horsemen (Georgian chronicle), probably with troops of the Muslim lords of Ganja, Dvin and Dmanisi.
why it counts: the Kurdish Shaddadids are listed as belligerents
sources: Georgian Chronicles (Life of George II); en.wikipedia Battle of Partskhisi; en.wikipedia Malik-Shah I
note: Wikipedia's Malik-Shah I article says Savtegin was defeated twice near Partskhisi during a campaign of 1078-1079; the date of the battle is disputed. Kakheti-Hereti fought on the Georgian side.

name: Pakpattan (siege, 1079)
how the result was decided: The fortress fell to Ibrahim.
Iranian force: Ibrahim's army; the sources give no details (the Ghaznavid army was then a core of Turkic ghulams with Indian, Afghan and Khalaj troops).
why it counts: Inferred from the usual Ghaznavid recruitment (Turkic ghulams, Indians, Afghans, Tajik and Daylamite foot); no source for this siege.
sources: en.wikipedia Ibrahim of Ghazna
note: The fortress is described as 120 parasangs from Lahore, which fits Pakpattan poorly; the identification follows Wikipedia. The Hindu opponents are not named.

date: 1085 (the Marwanid article gives 1079-1085; the end of the dynasty is dated 1085)
name: Mayyafariqin (siege, 1085)
war: Seljuk conquest of the Marwanid emirate of Diyar Bakr
how the result was decided: The Seljuk assault took Mayyafariqin and Ibn Jahir seized the Marwanid treasures; Mansur kept only Jazirat Ibn Umar (Cizre) and the dynasty ended in 1085.
commanders A: Fakhr al-Dawla ibn Jahir (former Marwanid vizier, an Arab), leading the Seljuk assault, for Sultan Malik-Shah I (a Turk) and his vizier Nizam al-Mulk
commanders B: Nasir al-Dawla Mansur ibn Nizam al-Din (Marwanid, a Kurd)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marwanids_(Diyar_Bakr) ; Ibn al-Athir; Ibn al-Azraq al-Fariqi, Ta'rikh Mayyafariqin; Canard, 'Marwanids', EI2
note: The Seljuk army was mainly Turkish (Nizam al-Mulk, a Persian, authorised the campaign as vizier but was not the ruler or field commander, so he is not counted). The Kurdish Marwanid leadership and tribal army of the defence is what qualifies the siege.

name: Darah (siege)
how the result was decided: Qizil-Sarigh abandoned the siege when Malik-Shah died; the fortress held.
Iranian force: A: the Nizari garrison of Darah (Quhistani Persians); B: Qizil-Sarigh's Seljuk army from Khorasan.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: obscure
doubts and flags: Borderline: obscure.
sources: en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts; en.wikipedia Malik-Shah I (Daru fortress)
note: The site of Darah, a dependency of Mu'minabad, is not precisely known.

name: Alamut (siege, 1092)
how the result was decided: A relief party of 300 under Dihdar Abu Ali broke through the siege lines and, with the garrison, routed the besiegers.
commanders A: Hasan-i Sabbah; Dihdar Abu Ali Ardestani (relief)
Iranian force: A: the small garrison of Alamut and about 300 Nizari volunteers from Qazvin; B: the Seljuk emir Arslan-Tash's troops (Turkic) with local levies.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
strength A: a small garrison and a relief party of 300
sources: Juvayni; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts; en.wikipedia Malik-Shah I
note: An earlier siege by the emir Yurun-Tash (undated) also failed.

name: Isfahan (siege, 1093)
how the result was decided: Berk-Yaruq lifted the siege on receiving 500,000 dinars, leaving Terken Khatun and Mahmud in Isfahan and Fars: a siege ended by treaty.
Iranian force: A: Berk-Yaruq's Turkic emirs and the Nizamiyya; B: Terken Khatun's garrison and the Isfahan troops.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: little is recorded of the fighting
doubts and flags: Borderline: little is recorded of the fighting.
sources: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Berkyaruk'

date: 1093 (486 AH; Wikipedia places it after Terken Khatun's death in 1094)
name: Kerj Abu Dulaf (1093)
place: Kerj Abu Dulaf (between Hamadan and Isfahan), Iran
how the result was decided: Isma'il's army was defeated and he was later put to death.
Iranian force: A: Berk-Yaruq's Turkic emirs and ghulams; B: Isma'il's Turkmen army from Azerbaijan and Arran.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Berkyaruk' (Kerec); en.wikipedia Berkyaruq
note: Isma'il, Berk-Yaruq's maternal uncle, had agreed to Terken Khatun's call to remove Berk-Yaruq.

name: Taliqan (1093)
how the result was decided: The Nizaris defeated and dispersed the 10,000-strong force.
commanders B: unknown (Wikipedia names al-Za'farani in connection with the fight)
Iranian force: A: Nizari fighters of Rudbar and Taliqan (Daylamite highlanders and Persian converts); B: a force of 10,000 raised mostly from the Sunnis of Rayy.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: obscure; the opponents were a Sunni militia rather than a state army
doubts and flags: Borderline: obscure; the opponents were a Sunni militia rather than a state army.
sources: en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts

name: Borujerd
how the result was decided: Terken Khatun's army was heavily defeated and withdrew to Isfahan.
commanders B: Terken Khatun's commanders; Taj al-Mulk (captured, executed 12 February 1093)
Iranian force: A: Nizam al-Mulk's former ghulams (the Nizamiyya) and the emirs who raised Berk-Yaruq; B: the army of Terken Khatun and the vizier Taj al-Mulk (Turkic emirs and ghulams).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Berkyaruk'; en.wikipedia Berkyaruq

name: Tell al-Sultan
how the result was decided: The army of Aqsunqur and Buzan broke; both were killed and Tutush held the field.
Iranian force: A: Tutush's Syrian Turkmen and the troops of Antioch; B: the armies of Aleppo and Edessa-Harran, with Kerbogha's troops sent by Berk-Yaruq.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Ibn al-Adim; en.wikipedia Tutush I
note: Aqsunqur (Malik-Shah's governor of Aleppo) and Buzan had deserted Tutush for Berk-Yaruq in 1093.

date: 25 February 1095 (17 Safar 488, about 26 February, in other reckonings)
name: Rayy (1095)
how the result was decided: Tutush's army was defeated and Tutush was killed on the field.
Iranian force: A: Berk-Yaruq's Turkic emirs and ghulams; B: Tutush's Syrian and Jaziran Turkmen with Iranian adherents such as the Kakuyid Ali ibn Faramurz.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Tutush I; en.wikipedia Berkyaruq; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Seljuk Empire (Battle of Ray)
note: The site is sometimes given as Dashlu near Rayy. Tutush's head was displayed in Baghdad. TDV records an earlier defeat of Berk-Yaruq by Tutush in Shawwal 487 (October-November 1094), which Wikipedia does not mention.

name: Lamasar (1096)
how the result was decided: The Nizaris attacked and took the castle.
commanders A: Kiya Buzurg-Ummid, Kiya Abu Ja'far, Kiya Abu Ali, Kiya Garshasb
Iranian force: A: Nizari fighters of Rudbar (Daylamites and Persians); B: the garrison of a local Daylamite lord.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a castle capture with uncertain date; Rasamuj was a local lord, not a Seljuk army
doubts and flags: Borderline: a castle capture with uncertain date; Rasamuj was a local lord, not a Seljuk army.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts
note: Lamasar became the second Nizari stronghold of Rudbar under Buzurg-Ummid.

name: Antioch (1098)
how the result was decided: The crusaders sallied from Antioch and routed Kerbogha's army after Duqaq, Soqman and the emir of Homs deserted it; the crusaders held the field.
commanders A: Bohemond of Taranto, Godfrey of Bouillon, Robert of Normandy, Robert of Flanders, Hugh of Vermandois, Adhemar of Le Puy
commanders B: Kerbogha, atabeg of Mosul; Duqaq of Damascus, Janah ad-Dawla of Homs, Soqman the Artuqid
Iranian force: Kerbogha's relief army: the troops of Mosul and the Jazira with troops from Persia, joined by Duqaq of Damascus, Janah ad-Dawla of Homs and the Artuqid Soqman.
why it counts: Latin sources such as the Gesta Francorum list Kurds and Persians among Kerbogha's relief army, and Mosul and Jazira forces regularly had Kurdish auxiliaries; Turks and Arabs were the bulk, so the Iranian part was a named component rather than a majority.
borderline: Kerbogha was Berk-Yaruq's governor of Mosul and raised a coalition; the sultan did not lead it
doubts and flags: Borderline: Kerbogha was Berk-Yaruq's governor of Mosul and raised a coalition; the sultan did not lead it.
sources: Gesta Francorum; Raymond of Aguilers; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Antioch
note: This entry is the relief battle only: the defenders of Antioch in the siege of 1097-1098 (Yaghi-Siyan) held the city under the Syrian Seljuks and are not counted as Persian.

name: Nushajan
side B: Berk-Yaruq and Amir-i Dad Habashi, with Nizari troops
how the result was decided: Sanjar's army defeated the larger army of Habashi and Berk-Yaruq, and Habashi was captured.
factions B: Berk-Yaruq and Amir-i Dad Habashi, with Nizari troops
commanders B: Amir-i Dad Habashi ibn Altuntaq (captured and killed), Berk-Yaruq
Iranian force: A: Sanjar's Khorasan army of 20,000 (Turkic ghulams and Turkmen); B: Habashi's army, larger than Sanjar's, including 5,000 Nizari Ismailis, with Berk-Yaruq's followers.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts
note: The site is uncertain: Wikipedia's Sanjar article gives 'Nushecan', its Nizari article places the fighting near Girdkuh. The Nizari commander Muzaffar took Girdkuh the same year.

name: Safidrud
how the result was decided: Berk-Yaruq's forces broke and he left the field with 50 men.
commanders A: Muhammad Tapar, the vizier Mu'ayyid al-Mulk, the mirakhur Inanch Yabgu
Iranian force: A: Muhammad Tapar's army from Ganja and Arran, with the Nizamiyya and emirs who had deserted Berk-Yaruq; B: Berk-Yaruq's Turkic emirs and ghulams.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar' and 'Berkyaruk'
note: Also written Isfidhrud; the first of the five battles between the brothers.

name: Hamadan (1101)
how the result was decided: Muhammad Tapar's army was defeated and his vizier Mu'ayyid al-Mulk captured.
commanders B: Muhammad Tapar, the vizier Mu'ayyid al-Mulk (captured)
Iranian force: A: Berk-Yaruq's Turkic emirs and ghulams; B: Muhammad Tapar's army (Turkic).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar' and 'Berkyaruk'
note: Mu'ayyid al-Mulk was executed by Berk-Yaruq.

name: Isfahan (siege, 1102)
how the result was decided: Berk-Yaruq failed to take Isfahan; Muhammad slipped out with 1,050 horsemen when supplies ran short and the siege ended without the city's capture.
Iranian force: A: Muhammad Tapar's remaining troops with the Isfahan garrison and townsmen; B: Berk-Yaruq's Turkic army.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar' and 'Berkyaruk'
note: The outcome is classed for the defender because the city did not fall, although Muhammad himself fled.

name: Ruzrawar
how the result was decided: After skirmishes the armies came to terms without a decision: Berk-Yaruq kept the title of sultan and Muhammad became malik.
Iranian force: A and B: the Turkic armies of the two brothers.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: skirmishes ended by a settlement rather than a pitched battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: skirmishes ended by a settlement rather than a pitched battle.
sources: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Berkyaruk' (Ruzraver)

name: Rayy (1102)
how the result was decided: Muhammad Tapar, who had again declared himself sultan, was defeated and fled to Isfahan with a small force.
Iranian force: A and B: the Turkic armies of the two brothers.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Berkyaruk' and 'Muhammed Tapar'

name: Khoy (1103)
place: at the gate of Khoy, Iran
how the result was decided: A charge by Ayaz's 500 horsemen routed Muhammad Tapar's army.
Iranian force: A: Berk-Yaruq's army, the decisive charge made by Ayaz's 500 cavalry; B: Muhammad Tapar's army of Azerbaijan and Arran.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar' and 'Berkyaruk'
note: The brothers divided the realm by treaty in January 1104.

name: Mosul (siege, 1104)
how the result was decided: When news of Berk-Yaruq's death arrived Jikirmish submitted and Mosul acknowledged Muhammad Tapar, who confirmed him and withdrew.
commanders A: Muhammad Tapar, the vizier Sa'd al-Mulk
Iranian force: A: Muhammad Tapar's army with sappers and siege engines; B: Jikirmish's garrison and the townsmen of Mosul, with raiders from Tell Ya'far.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Mosul (1104); TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar'
note: Wikipedia dates the end to 9 February 1104, but Berk-Yaruq died in December 1104 (Rabi II 498) and TDV places the siege when his death became known, so the siege belongs to late 1104 and early 1105. A breach was made and repaired overnight.

name: Tabas (siege, 1104)
how the result was decided: Bazghash's army took and destroyed Tabas and massacred its Nizari defenders.
Iranian force: A: Sanjar's Khorasan army under the emir Bazghash (Turkic); B: the Nizari townsmen and garrison of Tabas.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: obscure; the Nizaris lost no main stronghold
doubts and flags: Borderline: obscure; the Nizaris lost no main stronghold.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts

date: 1107 (fell Dhu'l-Qa'da 500, about July 1107; Wikipedia's Muhammad I Tapar gives 1106)
name: Shahdiz (siege)
how the result was decided: The fortress was taken tower by tower; Ibn Attash was captured and executed and the castle demolished.
factions B: Nizari Ismailis (Ahmad ibn Abd al-Malik ibn Attash)
commanders B: Ahmad ibn Abd al-Malik ibn Attash (captured, executed)
Iranian force: A: the sultan's army (Turkic ghulams and the emirs' troops); B: the Nizari garrison, about 80 men in the final fight.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Ibn al-Qalanisi; en.wikipedia Shahdiz; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar'
note: The siege was prolonged by about a year of religious debate and negotiation; the nearby Nizari fort of Khanlanjan was apparently destroyed in the same campaign.

name: Mosul (siege, 1108)
how the result was decided: Mawdud's troops entered through a breach opened by the plasterers' guild and took the city; the citadel surrendered eight days later.
commanders A: Mawdud, Sokmen al-Qutbi, Aqsunqur al-Bursuqi, Nasr ibn Muhalhal, Abu'l-Hayja
commanders B: Jawali's wife, daughter of Bursuq (Jawali himself had left)
Iranian force: A: the sultan's emirs, including the Banu Bursuq, the Shah-Armens of Akhlat and the Kurdish Annazids and Hadhabanis; B: Jawali's garrison.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Mosul (1108); en.wikipedia Mawdud
note: Counted as civil because Jawali was a Seljuk governor in revolt against the sultan.

date: from August 1109 (Muharram 503) until winter; the climax of raids from 1106
name: Alamut (siege, 1109)
how the result was decided: Neither Alamut nor Ostavand fell and the Seljuk army withdrew with the onset of winter.
commanders B: Ahmad ibn Nizam al-Mulk, Chavli Saqavu
Iranian force: A: the Nizari garrisons of Rudbar (Daylamites and Persians); B: the sultan's expeditionary army (Turkic).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts; en.wikipedia Muhammad I Tapar; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar'
note: The expedition of 1106-1109 devastated Rudbar; an eight-year war of attrition followed.

name: al-Sannabra
place: al-Sannabra (south end of the Sea of Galilee), Israel & Palestine
how the result was decided: Baldwin I's army was drawn into an ambush and routed with about 2,000 killed; the survivors took refuge on a hill and Mawdud held the field.
commanders A: Mawdud, Toghtekin of Damascus, Tamirek of Sinjar, Ayaz son of Ilghazi
Iranian force: Mawdud's army of Turks and Kurds from Mosul and Sinjar, with Toghtekin's Damascenes and Ayaz's Artuqid troops.
why it counts: Wikipedia describes Mawdud's forces as 'composed of Turks and Kurds'; the proportions are not known.
strength A: a big and strong army (no figure)
borderline: the 1113 campaign was Mawdud's, made at Toghtekin's request; it is not certain that the sultan ordered it
doubts and flags: Borderline: the 1113 campaign was Mawdud's, made at Toghtekin's request; it is not certain that the sultan ordered it.
sources: Ibn al-Qalanisi; Fulcher of Chartres; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of al-Sannabra; en.wikipedia Mawdud
note: Baldwin I escaped (Wikipedia's infobox wrongly lists him as captured). Mawdud was assassinated in Damascus later in 1113.

name: Tiginabad (1116)
how the result was decided: Bahram was defeated and fled to the Seljuk court in Khorasan.
Iranian force: A and B: Ghaznavid forces (no details; the army of the later Ghaznavids was Turkic ghulams with Indian troops and Afghans).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire; en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna
note: Tiginabad is usually placed near Kandahar; the site is approximate.

name: Ghazni (1117)
how the result was decided: Arslan Shah's army was crushed on the plain of Shahrabad and he fled to India.
Iranian force: A: Sanjar's Khorasan army (Turkic ghulams and Turkmen) with Bahram's followers; B: Arslan Shah's Ghaznavid army with war elephants.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Ghazni (1117); en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar
note: Wikipedia's lists call it the 2nd Battle of Ghazni. Sanjar's army then occupied and plundered Ghazni for 40 days; Arslan Shah was later caught in the Ughnan mountains and strangled on Bahram's orders.

name: Alamut (siege, 1117)
how the result was decided: Shirgir abandoned the sieges of Alamut and Lamasar in April 1118 on news of Muhammad Tapar's death, leaving supplies and weapons to the Nizaris.
Iranian force: A: the Nizari garrisons of Rudbar (Daylamites and Persians); B: Anushtegin Shirgir's Seljuk army (Turkic).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed Tapar'
note: One entry for the joint siege of Alamut and Lamasar; Wikipedia's dating of the start is inconsistent (1117 or 1118).

name: Multan (1119)
how the result was decided: The rebel Muhammad was defeated and killed with most of his sons.
Iranian force: A: Bahram Shah's Ghaznavid army; B: the rebel governor's Indian garrison troops.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: Wikipedia gives a battle near Multan in 1119 against Muhammad b. Ali and an undated defeat of Muhammad Bahlim near Multan; probably the same event
doubts and flags: Borderline: Wikipedia gives a battle near Multan in 1119 against Muhammad b. Ali and an undated defeat of Muhammad Bahlim near Multan; probably the same event.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna

name: Saveh
how the result was decided: Mahmud's cavalry gave way before Sanjar's elephants and Mahmud fled the field.
commanders B: Mahmud II, Ali Bar, the atabeg Ghuzoghlu, Qaraja al-Saqi
Iranian force: A: Sanjar's army of 20,000 with 18 elephants, with Nizari troops; B: Mahmud's 30,000, the Turkic emirs of western Iran and Iraq.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Bundari; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Seljuk Empire
note: Mahmud kept the western sultanate as Sanjar's subordinate.

name: Asadabad
how the result was decided: Mas'ud's army was defeated; Mahmud forgave Mas'ud and put the vizier al-Tughra'i to death.
commanders B: Mas'ud, Juyush Beg, the vizier al-Tughra'i
Iranian force: A and B: the Turkic emirs and ghulams of western Iran; Mas'ud's side was led by his atabeg Juyush Beg of Mosul.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: known from Ibn al-Athir (514 AH); the site and date were not verified online
doubts and flags: Borderline: known from Ibn al-Athir (514 AH); the site and date were not verified online.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ghiyath ad-Din Mas'ud (rebellion of c. 1120-1121)

name: Didgori
how the result was decided: The coalition army was routed and the Georgians held the field.
commanders B: Ilghazi (wounded), Tughril (Seljuk malik of Arran), Dubays ibn Sadaqa, Toghan Arslan of Bitlis
Iranian force: An expedition authorized by Sultan Mahmud II and led by the Artuqid Ilghazi: his Turkmen, the Seljuk malik Tughril of Arran and Nakhchivan (whose part is disputed), the Mazyadid Arabs of Dubays and the emir of Bitlis.
why it counts: The coalition was overwhelmingly Turkmen with Arab tribesmen; Kurdish troops of Bitlis and Dvin may have been present.
strength A: about 56,000 (Georgian sources), incl. 15,000 Kipchaks, 500 Alans and 100-500 Franks
strength B: 30,000 (Arab sources); 100,000-250,000 (modern Georgian historians); Christian sources up to 800,000
losses B: tens of thousands dead and 4,000 captured (Turkish estimate); Matthew of Edessa 400,000 killed
borderline: the Persian share is uncertain: the army was Ilghazi's, sent with the sultan's approval, and Tughril's presence is disputed
doubts and flags: Borderline: the Persian share is uncertain: the army was Ilghazi's, sent with the sultan's approval, and Tughril's presence is disputed.
sources: Georgian Chronicles; Matthew of Edessa; Walter the Chancellor; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Didgori
note: Georgia took Tbilisi in 1122.

date: 1124 (David IV took Ani in the summer of 1124; exact days unknown)
name: Ani (siege, 1124)
war: Georgian-Shaddadid wars (David IV's conquests in Armenia)
how the result was decided: David IV took the city and captured the emir; Wikipedia's Shaddadid article says without a fight, the Georgian-Shaddadid wars article says after a siege.
commanders A: David IV the Builder of Georgia
commanders B: Abu'l-Aswar Shavur II (a Kurd), emir of Ani, who was captured (Fadl IV retook Ani in 1125)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaddadids ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian%E2%80%93Shaddadid_wars ; Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953) and 'Shaddadids', Encyclopaedia of Islam 2nd ed.; Rayfield, Edge of Empires (2012)
note: Doubtful on 'real fighting': the Armenian townspeople are said to have helped the Georgians and the sources describe a quick surrender. Kept because the sources call it a siege.

name: Rudbar (1126)
how the result was decided: The Seljuk invasions of Rudbar were repelled and the commander Tamurtughan was captured.
Iranian force: A: the Nizaris of Rudbar (Daylamites and Persians); B: Seljuk troops with local support.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: recorded as campaigns without a single named battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: recorded as campaigns without a single named battle.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts
note: Part of the offensive organised by Sanjar's vizier Mu'in al-Din al-Kashi, which in Quhistan took Tarz and Turaythith with limited success; Tamurtughan was released at Sanjar's request.

name: Alamut (1129)
how the result was decided: Mahmud's attack on Alamut failed, and an Iraqi army also failed before Lamasar.
Iranian force: A: the Nizari garrisons of Rudbar; B: Mahmud II's Turkic army.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a failed attack recorded without details
doubts and flags: Borderline: a failed attack recorded without details.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts
note: It followed the lynching of a Nizari envoy in Isfahan and a Nizari raid on Qazvin.

name: Dinavar
how the result was decided: Sanjar defeated Mas'ud and Seljuk-Shah and installed Tughril II as sultan in the west.
Iranian force: A: Sanjar's Khorasan army (Turkic ghulams and Turkmen); B: the Turkic emirs of Mas'ud and Seljuk-Shah.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar
note: The caliph al-Mustarshid backed Mas'ud but did not fight at Dinavar. Mas'ud later defeated Tughril II (May 1133; site not recorded in the sources checked).

name: Hazarasp (1138)
how the result was decided: Atsiz was defeated at Hazarasp and fled.
Iranian force: A: Sanjar's army (Turkic ghulams and Turkmen); B: Atsiz's Khwarazmian army (Turkic ghulams and steppe auxiliaries with Khwarazmian levies).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Atsiz; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar
note: Sanjar gave Khwarazm to his nephew Suleiman-Shah, but Atsiz soon returned.

name: Kabud-Jama
how the result was decided: Atsiz defeated and captured the Bavandid ispahbadh Ali and occupied Gurgan.
factions B: Ala al-Dawla Ali I (Bavandids of Tabaristan)
commanders B: the ispahbadh Ala al-Dawla Ali ibn Shahriyar (captured)
Iranian force: A: Atsiz's Khwarazmian army (Turkic soldiers with Khwarazmian levies); B: the Bavandid ispahbadh's Tabaristani troops.
languages: Turkic; East Iranian; Daylami and Caspian
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: obscure
doubts and flags: Borderline: obscure.
sources: en.wikipedia Atsiz
note: Ali was released when his son pleaded for him, and Gurgan became a Khwarazmian vassal.

name: Qatwan
how the result was decided: Sanjar's army was routed with enormous losses and Sanjar fled with a handful of horsemen.
commanders B: Sanjar, Garshasp II of Yazd (Kakuyid, killed), Mahmud Khan (Qarakhanid)
Iranian force: Sanjar's great army, given as 100,000: his Turkic ghulams and Turkmen, the troops of vassals such as the Kakuyid Garshasp of Yazd and the amir of Sistan, and the Qarakhanid Mahmud Khan.
why it counts: Sanjar's army included the Kakuyid Garshasp II of Yazd (Daylamite-descended Iranian dynasty), killed in the battle, and the troops of the Banu Khalaf amir of Sistan (Persian), both named in Ibn al-Athir and Juzjani.
strength A: 20,000 to 300,000 (estimates vary; the Qarluks gave 30,000-50,000 horse)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Juvayni; en.wikipedia Battle of Qatwan
note: The Qarluks, whose appeal brought the Kara-Khitai west, fought on their side; Atsiz of Khwarazm had invited the Kara-Khitai. The amir of Sistan and Sanjar's wife were captured.

name: Gurganj (siege, 1143)
how the result was decided: Atsiz submitted and returned the plunder and captured scholars, and Sanjar withdrew without taking Gurganj: a siege ended by treaty.
Iranian force: A: Sanjar's army (Turkic); B: Atsiz's troops with the townsmen of Gurganj (Khwarazmians).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: Wikipedia's Atsiz article records the 1143 invasion of Khwarazm without describing a siege
doubts and flags: Borderline: Wikipedia's Atsiz article records the 1143 invasion of Khwarazm without describing a siege.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar; en.wikipedia Atsiz
note: Punishment for Atsiz's seizure of Merv, Nishapur and Sarakhs after Qatwan (1141), from which Sanjar expelled him in 1142.

name: Lamasar (1143)
how the result was decided: Mas'ud's attack on Lamasar and Rudbar was repelled.
Iranian force: A: the Nizari garrisons of Rudbar; B: Mas'ud's Turkic army.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a failed attack recorded without details
doubts and flags: Borderline: a failed attack recorded without details.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Nizari-Seljuk conflicts

name: Hazarasp (siege, 1147)
how the result was decided: Sanjar took the castle of Hazarasp; Atsiz fled to Gurganj, submitted and was kept as governor.
Iranian force: A: Sanjar's army (Turkic); B: the Khwarazmian garrison of Hazarasp.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar; en.wikipedia Atsiz

name: Marj Qaratakin
war: Seljuk civil war (revolt of the emirs, 1146-1147)
place: Marj Qaratakin (Qaratakin meadow, near Hamadan), Iran
how the result was decided: Boz-Aba and his allied emirs were defeated by Mas'ud; Boz-Aba lost his life.
factions B: Boz-Aba (atabeg of Fars) and allied emirs
Iranian force: A: Mas'ud's Turkic army; B: Boz-Aba's army of Fars and Khuzistan led by Turkish emirs.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed b. Mahmud' (Karategin meadow, 542/1147); en.wikipedia Ghiyath ad-Din Mas'ud
note: Boz-Aba's death is usually given as an execution after capture; the Salghurids took Fars after him (1148).

name: Ghazni (1148)
how the result was decided: Sayf al-Din defeated Bahram Shah and took Ghazni; Bahram fled to Kurram.
Iranian force: A: Sayf al-Din's Ghurid army of Ghuri highlanders; B: Bahram Shah's Ghaznavid army (Turkic ghulams, Indian troops and Afghans).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Battle of Ghazni (1148); en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna
note: Wikipedia's Ghaznavid list calls it the 3rd Battle of Ghazni, its Ghurid list the 1st.

name: Sang-i Surakh
how the result was decided: Bahram defeated Sayf al-Din and captured him with his vizier; Bahram retook Ghazni.
commanders B: Sayf al-Din Suri (captured, later crucified), the vizier Majd al-Din Musawi (captured)
Iranian force: A: Bahram Shah's Ghaznavid army, with the townsmen and troops of Ghazni who turned against the Ghurids; B: Sayf al-Din's Ghurid army.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghaznavid Empire; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty; en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna
note: The execution of Sayf al-Din provoked Ala al-Din Husayn's revenge of 1150-1151.

name: Battle of Inab
war: Wars of Nur al-Din against the Principality of Antioch
place: Inab (Tell Inab), near Apamea, Syria (exact site uncertain)
how the result was decided: Raymond's small army was encircled and destroyed, with Raymond and Ali ibn Wafa killed.
commanders A: Nur al-Din Zengi; Mu'in al-Din Unur of Damascus (contingent); the Kurdish emirs Shirkuh and Ayyub are said to have served in Nur al-Din's and Unur's armies
commanders B: Raymond of Poitiers, Prince of Antioch (killed); Ali ibn Wafa (killed)
sources: Mallett, 'The Battle of Inab', Journal of Medieval History 39 (2013); Gibb in Setton, History of the Crusades vol. 1; Ibn al-Qalanisi; Ibn al-Athir; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Inab
note: Doubtful on the Iranian criterion: the Wikipedia infobox names Ayyub, but the article text does not mention Kurds or Shirkuh, and Nur al-Din's army is described as mostly Turkish cavalry and Turkmen.

name: Jush-i Ab-i Garm
place: Jush-i Ab-i Garm (hot springs, between Tiginabad and Ghazni), Afghanistan
how the result was decided: Bahram's rallied army was routed again and he fled to Ghazni.
Iranian force: A: the Ghurid army; B: the remains of Bahram Shah's Ghaznavid army.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: obscure; the site is unknown
doubts and flags: Borderline: obscure; the site is unknown.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Ala al-Din Husayn; en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna

name: Tiginabad (1150)
how the result was decided: The Ghaznavid army was routed.
commanders A: Ala al-Din Husayn; Kharmil Sam-i Husain, Kharmil Sam-i Banji
Iranian force: A: Ala al-Din's Ghurid army of Ghuri foot and horse; B: Bahram Shah's Ghaznavid army.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Ala al-Din Husayn; en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna
note: The first of three battles of Ala al-Din's campaign of revenge.

name: Ghazni (1151)
how the result was decided: Bahram's army, reinforced by the city garrison, was routed; the Ghurids took Ghazni and burned it for seven days.
Iranian force: A: the Ghurid army of Ghuri foot and horse; B: Bahram Shah's army with the Ghazni garrison.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: army routed; the sack is said to have killed 60,000
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Battle of Ghazni (1151); en.wikipedia Bahram-Shah of Ghazna
note: The burning earned Ala al-Din the name Jahan-suz (world-burner); Bahram fled to his Indian lands.

name: Nab
how the result was decided: Ala al-Din's army was routed, after his Turkish horsemen went over to Sanjar (Juzjani), and he was captured.
Iranian force: A: Sanjar's army (Turkic ghulams and Turkmen); B: the Ghurid army of Ghuri foot and horse with Turkish (Ghuzz) mercenary cavalry.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Ahmad Sanjar; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Seljuk Empire
note: Ala al-Din had stopped paying tribute and taken Balkh; he was held two years and released for a ransom.

name: Ani (battle of Saltuk II, 1153-1154)
war: Georgian wars with the Saltukids of Erzurum
side A (victor if decisive): Kingdom of Georgia; Shaddadids of Ani
how the result was decided: Demetrius I defeated and captured Saltuk II, who was released for a ransom of 100,000 dinars.
Iranian side: Kingdom of Georgia & Shaddadids of Ani
commanders A: Demetrius I of Georgia; Fakhr al-Din Shaddad (a Kurd), emir of Ani
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaddadids ; Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953) ch. on the Shaddadids of Ani
note: Doubtful on the Iranian criterion: the Shaddadid emir is said to have warned the Georgian king of Saltuk's march, and I have no source that his troops fought in the battle. Entered as uncertain.

date: about 18-25 April 1154 (Nur al-Din's siege; the city fell on 25 April 1154)
name: Damascus (siege, 1154)
how the result was decided: After a short siege the East Gate was opened and the city passed to Nur al-Din through the mediation of Ayyub and Shirkuh; Mujir al-Din was bought out with the grant of Homs.
commanders A: Nur al-Din Zengi; Shirkuh (a Kurd), his chief emir
commanders B: Mujir al-Din Abaq, Burid ruler (a Turk); Najm al-Din Ayyub (a Kurd), senior emir in the city
sources: Ibn al-Qalanisi, Dhayl ta'rikh Dimashq; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil; Gibb in Setton, History of the Crusades vol. 1; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirkuh
note: Kurdish brothers on both sides of the walls: Shirkuh with the besiegers and Ayyub inside. The fighting was brief and the end came by surrender; counted as a siege because Nur al-Din's army invested the city for about a week.

name: Aras
place: on the Aras (Araxes) river (site unknown), Iran
how the result was decided: Sulayman-Shah was defeated; in flight he was captured by Zayn al-Din Ali Kuchuk of Mosul.
factions B: Sulayman-Shah (with Eldiguz, Malik-Shah III and Arslan-Shah)
Iranian force: A: Muhammad II's army, with the promised support of the Zengids of Mosul; B: Sulayman-Shah's coalition of Eldiguz's troops, Malik-Shah's Khuzistan forces and 3,000 men sent by the caliph.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: known from TDV; not in Wikipedia; the site 'on the bank of the Aras' as given
doubts and flags: Borderline: known from TDV; not in Wikipedia; the site 'on the bank of the Aras' as given.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi 'Muhammed b. Mahmud'
note: Eldiguz's seat was then in Arran and Nakhchivan, outside present-day Iran.

name: Ragh-i Zar
place: Ragh-i Zar, between Firuzkuh and Herat, Afghanistan
side B: Fakhr al-Din Masud of Bamiyan, with the Seljuk governors Taj al-Din Yildiz and Ala al-Din Qumach
how the result was decided: The Ghurids of Firuzkuh routed the coalition; Yildiz was killed and Fakhr al-Din taken, later restored to Bamiyan.
factions B: Fakhr al-Din Masud of Bamiyan, with the Seljuk governors Taj al-Din Yildiz (Herat) and Ala al-Din Qumach (Balkh)
commanders A: Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad (Muhammad of Ghor)
commanders B: Fakhr al-Din Masud (captured), Taj al-Din Yildiz (killed), Ala al-Din Qumach
Iranian force: The army of Ghur under the two brothers: Ghuri (Tajik) mountain infantry and cavalry with Turkic ghulams; the other side had the Bamiyan Ghurids and the Turkic troops of the Seljuk governors of Herat and Balkh.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty, Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad
note: Dated 1163 in Wikipedia's list of Ghurid battles; the Ghiyath al-Din article places it early in his reign (from 1163). Civil: a fight between Ghurid branches, joined by the governors left over from the Great Seljuk state.

date: April-October 1164 (Shirkuh entered Egypt in the spring; Amalric and Shawar besieged him in Bilbeis from about August to late October)
name: Bilbeis (siege, 1164)
war: Nur al-Din's Egyptian expeditions (Shirkuh's first Egyptian campaign)
side A (victor if decisive): Kingdom of Jerusalem; Fatimid vizier Shawar
how the result was decided: The siege ended in a negotiated mutual withdrawal in October 1164, after Nur al-Din's attack on Crusader northern Syria (Harim) forced Amalric to make terms; Shirkuh left Egypt with his army.
commanders A: Amalric I of Jerusalem; Shawar ibn Mujir, Fatimid vizier
commanders B: Shirkuh (Asad al-Din Shirkuh ibn Shadhi, a Kurd of Dvin); Saladin, his nephew
sources: Gibb, 'The Career of Nur-ad-Din' in Setton ed., A History of the Crusades vol. 1 (1969); Lev, Saladin in Egypt (1999); William of Tyre; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirkuh ; https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/wars_nur_ad_din_egypt.html
note: Shirkuh's army is described as Syrian Turks, Turkmen auxiliaries and Kurds (the Wikipedia article on Shirkuh gives 500 mamluks and Kurds out of 8,000 horse from Homs), and both Shirkuh and Saladin were Kurds, so the leader rule is what qualifies the battle; the Kurdish share of the troops is small or unknown (500 mamluks and Kurds out of about 8,000 horse in the force from Homs, plus hired Turkmen).

name: Harim (1164)
war: Wars of Nur al-Din against the Principality of Antioch and the Romans
side B: Principality of Antioch, County of Tripoli, Roman Cilicia, Armenian Cilicia
how the result was decided: Nur al-Din won a crushing victory and captured Bohemond, Raymond, Joscelin, Kalamanos and Hugh (Wikipedia 'Battle of Harim'; Ibn al-Athir).
principal opponents: Principality of Antioch, County of Tripoli, Roman Cilicia, Armenian Cilicia
commanders A: Nur al-Din Zangi, Shirkuh and Qutb al-Din Mawdud of Mosul
commanders B: Bohemond III, Raymond III, Joscelin III, Thoros II, Hugh VIII of Lusignan and Konstantinos Kalamanos
sources: Wikipedia 'Battle of Harim' (fetched 1 Nov 2026); Ibn al-Athir; William of Tyre 19.9-10
note: The Zengids were Turks; Shirkuh, Nur al-Din's emir (lord of Homs) and later conqueror of Egypt, was a Kurd of the Rawwadid family of Dvin, and Wikipedia lists him among the commanders. The page does not give his ethnicity or say what part he led, so the Iranian side is a named Kurdish commander, not a counted contingent.

date: April-August 1167 (Shirkuh moved to Alexandria after al-Babein; the Crusader and Egyptian siege ran from about July to a treaty on about 4 August)
name: Alexandria (siege, 1167)
war: Nur al-Din's Egyptian expeditions (Shirkuh's second Egyptian campaign)
side A (victor if decisive): Kingdom of Jerusalem; Fatimid vizier Shawar
how the result was decided: The siege ended by treaty: both Shirkuh's army and Amalric's left Egypt, with the Zengids evacuating Alexandria and the Franks keeping a garrison and tribute at Cairo.
commanders B: Saladin (a Kurd), left in the city by Shirkuh (a Kurd), who raised troops in Upper Egypt
sources: William of Tyre; Ibn al-Athir; Ibn Abi Tayyi; Lev, Saladin in Egypt (1999); Gibb in Setton, History of the Crusades vol. 1; https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/siege_alexandria_1167.html ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirkuh
note: Saladin, aged about 29, held the city with Syrian troops and townsmen while Shirkuh went south to draw off the besiegers. Townsmen are not counted here.

name: Battle of al-Babein
war: Nur al-Din's Egyptian expeditions (Shirkuh's second Egyptian campaign)
place: al-Babein (Babayn), near Giza and the Nile, Egypt (exact site uncertain)
side A (victor if decisive): Kingdom of Jerusalem; Fatimid vizier Shawar
how the result was decided: Amalric's knights broke up in the soft sand and slopes and Saladin's feigned retreat drew part of them off, but neither army destroyed the other; Shirkuh then withdrew upriver and Amalric returned to Cairo.
commanders B: Shirkuh (a Kurd); Saladin commanded the centre
sources: William of Tyre; Ibn al-Athir; Smail, Crusading Warfare (1956); Lev, Saladin in Egypt (1999); Baldwin in Setton, History of the Crusades vol. 1; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_al-Babein ; https://www.historyofwar.org/articles/wars_nur_ad_din_egypt.html
note: Wikipedia's infobox gives a Zengid victory but its text describes a tactical draw. Shirkuh's army of about 2,000 is described as Kurds, Turks and Bedouin (historyofwar.org); the Zengid leaders were Kurds.

name: Battle of the Blacks (Cairo, 1169)
war: Saladin's rise in Egypt (Fatimid Egypt under Saladin as vizier)
place: Cairo (the streets between the Fatimid palaces and Bab Zuwayla), Egypt
side B: Black African regiments of the Fatimid army
how the result was decided: After two days of street fighting Saladin's troops burned the Black regiments' quarter (al-Mansuriyya) and the survivors fled across the Nile to Giza, where they were granted safe-conduct and then dispersed.
principal opponents: Black African regiments of the Fatimid army
commanders A: Saladin (a Kurd), vizier, with his Syrian emirs
commanders B: the emirs of the Black regiments (not named); the revolt was set off by Saladin's execution of the palace eunuch Mu'tamin al-Khilafa
sources: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil; Ibn Abi Tayyi; Lev, Saladin in Egypt (1999); Ehrenkreutz, Saladin (1972); Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols (1977)
note: Qualifies only through Saladin's leadership; the Zengid troops with him were mainly Turks and Kurds but no figure for the Kurdish part is given. Saladin was vizier from March 1169 but did not rule Egypt in his own name until 1171.

name: Damietta (siege, 1169)
side B: Fatimid Egypt; Zengid reinforcements from Nur al-Din
how the result was decided: After about fifty days the Franks and Romans, short of food and with the Nile floods and Saladin's reinforcements against them, made a truce and withdrew.
Iranian side: Fatimid Egypt & Zengid reinforcements from Nur al-Din
commanders A: Amalric I of Jerusalem; Andronikos Kontostephanos (Roman fleet)
commanders B: Saladin (a Kurd), vizier; the Fatimid garrison commanders; Nur al-Din's Syrian relief troops
sources: William of Tyre; Ibn al-Athir; Lev, Saladin in Egypt (1999); Kinnamos; Runciman, A History of the Crusades vol. 2 (1952)
note: Qualifies through Saladin's command. The composition of his army is not recorded in the sources I used, so the Kurdish share is unknown.

date: late 1170 (December 1170 or the first weeks of 1171; sources differ)
name: Ayla (Eilat, 1170)
war: Saladin's wars against the Kingdom of Jerusalem
place: Ile de Graye (Coral or Pharaoh's Island) off Ayla (Aqaba/Eilat), Gulf of Aqaba, Egypt
how the result was decided: Saladin took the island fortress after an assault in which ships carried in sections from Cairo were used, and the Crusader garrison was captured.
sources: William of Tyre; Ibn al-Athir; Lev, Saladin in Egypt (1999)
note: The date and the exact sequence relative to Darum are uncertain (William of Tyre and Muslim sources differ). Included because it is a real assault led by Saladin before 1171.

name: Darum and Gaza (1170)
war: Saladin's wars against the Kingdom of Jerusalem
place: Darum (Deir al-Balah) and Gaza, Gaza Strip, Palestine
how the result was decided: Saladin sacked the lower town of Gaza but failed to take the Templar citadel there or the fort of Darum, and withdrew when Amalric came up.
commanders B: the Templar garrison of Gaza; Amalric I of Jerusalem (relieving)
sources: William of Tyre; Ibn al-Athir; Lev, Saladin in Egypt (1999); Ehrenkreutz, Saladin (1972)
note: Saladin's first campaign against the Franks as head of the Egyptian army. A raid with real assaults on Darum and Gaza; combined into one entry.

name: Qasr Ibrim (1172)
place: Qasr Ibrim (Ibrim, Lower Nubia), now under Lake Nasser
how the result was decided: Turan-Shah, sent by Saladin with Kurdish troops, took Ibrim, raided Nubia and returned with slaves and plunder.
sources: Wikipedia, Turan-Shah (fetched: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turan-Shah); Wikipedia, Qasr Ibrim; Vantini, Oriental Sources concerning Nubia; Ibn al-Athir (year 568 AH)
note: Saladin sent his brother Turan-Shah after Nubian raids on Aswan (late 1172-early 1173); the source says he took Kurdish troops. The year of the capture is not given precisely.

name: Ghazni (1173)
how the result was decided: The Ghurids defeated the Oghuz and took Ghazni, where Mu'izz al-Din was installed as ruler.
commanders A: Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad
Iranian force: The Ghurid army of Ghur: Ghuri (Tajik) troops with Turkic ghulams and Khalaj and Afghan tribesmen (inferred from recruitment; the sources give no detail).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Juzjani; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (3rd Battle of Ghazni), Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Muhammad of Ghor
note: The Oghuz had held Ghazni since about 1162/63, when they drove out the Ghaznavid Khusrau Shah; they are treated as invaders, not an Iranian dynasty. The Muhammad of Ghor article also gives 1169 in one passage.

name: Kerak (siege, 1173)
how the result was decided: Saladin broke off the siege on hearing that Nur al-Din was approaching and did not wish to meet him.
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982), ch. on 1173; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh
note: A joint operation of Saladin (from Egypt) and Nur al-Din that Saladin abandoned from political caution; real fighting was small.

name: Ani (siege, 1174)
how the result was decided: George III besieged and captured the city and took the emir prisoner; Ivane Orbeli was left as governor.
commanders A: George III of Georgia; Ivane Orbeli
commanders B: Shahanshah ibn Mahmud (a Kurd), emir of Ani, who was taken prisoner
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaddadids ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian%E2%80%93Shaddadid_wars ; Minorsky, Studies in Caucasian History (1953) and 'Shaddadids', Encyclopaedia of Islam 2nd ed.
note: Only a line or two in the sources I used; Ani changed hands several times between 1161 and 1199. A Muslim coalition retook it in 1175.

name: Zabid (1174)
how the result was decided: Turan-Shah took Zabid and captured Abd al-Nabi, ending the Mahdid dynasty.
sources: Wikipedia, Turan-Shah (fetched: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turan-Shah); Wikipedia, Mahdids; Ibn al-Athir; Umara al-Yamani
note: Turan-Shah captured Zabid in May 1174 and Aden later that year. Battle detail is thin; Ayyubid command is clear.

name: Suburni
war: Khwarazmian succession war (Tekish against Sultan Shah)
place: Suburni, on the approaches to Khwarazm (site unidentified), Uzbekistan
side B: Sultan Shah and Terken Khatun, with Mu'ayyid Ay-Aba of Nishapur
how the result was decided: Tekish routed the allied army and captured Ay-Aba, who was executed.
factions B: Sultan Shah and Terken Khatun, with Mu'ayyid Ay-Aba of Nishapur (Mu'ayyids of Nishapur)
commanders B: Mu'ayyid al-Din Ay-Aba (captured and executed), Sultan Shah, Terken Khatun
Iranian force: Tekish's army of Khwarazm, won with Qara Khitai help: Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic cavalry with Khwarazmian troops; the other side had Ay-Aba's Nishapur army of Turkic ghulams and Khorasani levies.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ala al-Din Tekish
note: Mu'ayyid Ay-Aba, a former mamluk of Sanjar, ruled Nishapur on his own after 1157; his line is treated as an Iran-seated local dynasty, which makes the battle civil. Tekish then took Dihistan and had Terken Khatun killed.

name: Herat (1175)
side B: Baha al-Din Toghril, former Seljuk governor ruling Herat
how the result was decided: The Ghurids defeated Toghril and took Herat and Pushang.
factions B: Baha al-Din Toghril, former Seljuk governor ruling Herat
commanders A: Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad
Iranian force: The Ghurid army of Ghur and Ghazni: Ghuri (Tajik) troops, Turkic ghulams and Khalaj and Afghan tribesmen (recruitment).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juzjani; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (Battle of Herat), Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Muhammad of Ghor
note: Civil because Toghril, a Seljuk governor left over from Sanjar's state, ruled Herat on his own (an Iran-seated ruler); if he is counted as an outsider the battle is an ordinary Ghurid victory.

name: Multan (1175)
how the result was decided: Mu'izz al-Din defeated the Qarmatian ruler and annexed Multan.
Iranian force: Mu'izz al-Din's army from Ghazni: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri (Tajik), Khalaj and Afghan contingents (inferred from recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Juzjani; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty, Muhammad of Ghor
note: The 'Qarmatians' of Multan were its local Ismaili rulers.

name: Horns of Hama
place: Qurun Hama (Horns of Hama), near Hama, Syria
how the result was decided: Saladin's smaller army routed the Zengid forces sent against him and he took the title of Sultan soon after.
commanders B: Izz al-Din Mas'ud of Mosul; Gumushtekin (regent of Aleppo)
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Wikipedia, Battle of the Horns of Hama
note: Saladin's first field victory in Syria; Kurdish emirs of his family held the principal commands. The Zengid side was Turkic.

name: Masyaf (siege, 1176)
how the result was decided: The siege ended after a short time in a truce between Saladin and Sinan, sought through Saladin's uncle Shihab al-Din of Hama, while Masyaf was still invested and untaken.
Iranian force: Sinan's garrison of Syrian Nizaris from the castles of the Jabal Bahra, with his fida'is.
why it counts: Nizari Ismailis: an Iranian-led state
borderline: The Syrian Nizaris under Sinan acted largely independently of Alamut, though under its ultimate authority.
doubts and flags: Borderline: The Syrian Nizaris under Sinan acted largely independently of Alamut, though under its ultimate authority.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Kamal al-Din; en.wikipedia Rashid ad-Din Sinan, Masyaf Castle
note: The story of Sinan's warning left in Saladin's tent is legend; the raising of the siege and the truce that followed are not doubted.

name: Uch (siege, 1176)
how the result was decided: Uch fell to Mu'izz al-Din, by tradition when the raja's wife opened the gates, and was given to Nasir al-Din Aitam.
Iranian force: Mu'izz al-Din's army from Ghazni: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri, Khalaj and Afghan contingents (recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: The town fell by betrayal; how much fighting there was is unclear.
doubts and flags: Borderline: The town fell by betrayal; how much fighting there was is unclear.
