sources: Juzjani; Firishta; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (Siege of Uch), Muhammad of Ghor
note: Wikipedia's Ghurid list names the defenders as 'Bhatis or Qarmatians'.

name: Tell al-Sultan
place: Tell al-Sultan, south-east of Aleppo, Syria
how the result was decided: Saladin defeated Sayf al-Din Ghazi's army and took its camp and baggage.
commanders B: Sayf al-Din Ghazi II of Mosul
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Wikipedia, Battle of Tell al-Sultan
note: Followed by the siege of Azaz and a truce with Aleppo.

name: Azaz (siege, 1176)
how the result was decided: Azaz surrendered to Saladin on 21 June 1176 after a siege in which a Nizari assassin wounded him.
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh
note: The Nizari attempt on Saladin during the siege was followed by his campaign against Masyaf (already in the dataset, 1176).

name: Montgisard
place: Montgisard (probably Tel Gezer), near Ramla, Israel
how the result was decided: Baldwin IV's small army caught Saladin's strung-out force at the Wadi Hasi and routed it; Saladin fled to Egypt.
commanders B: Baldwin IV; Raynald of Chatillon; Odo de Saint-Amand
sources: William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, al-Fath al-Qussi; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Saladin's nephew Taqi al-Din's son was among the dead. Qualifies by Saladin's command; the first big Ayyubid defeat.

name: Kasahrada (1178)
place: Kasahrada (Kayadara), at the foot of Mount Abu, Rajasthan, India
how the result was decided: The Ghurid army was trapped in a pass below Mount Abu and routed; Mu'izz al-Din fled back to Ghazni.
commanders A: Mularaja II (Chaulukya), Kelhanadeva of Nadol, Kirtipala, Dharavarsha of Chandravati
Iranian force: Mu'izz al-Din's army, called 'Turushka' (Turks) in Indian sources and armoured head to foot, exhausted by the march across the Thar: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri, Khalaj and Afghan contingents (recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Juzjani; Merutunga; Udayaprabha Suri; Prabandha Kosha; en.wikipedia Battle of Kasahrada
note: The Chaulukyas of Gujarat with Paramara (Chandravati) and Chahamana (Nadol, Jalor) feudatories. Merutunga's later story crediting the queen Naikidevi is thought unreliable.

name: Marj Ayyun
how the result was decided: Saladin's army routed Baldwin IV's host, captured the Master of the Temple and nearly took the king.
commanders B: Baldwin IV; Humphrey II of Toron; Odo de Saint-Amand (captured); Raymond III of Tripoli
sources: William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982)
note: Followed two months later by the fall of Jacob's Ford.

name: Jacob's Ford (Chastellet)
place: Jacob's Ford (Vadum Iacob, Chastellet), Upper Jordan, Israel
how the result was decided: Saladin undermined the new Templar fortress, stormed it on 29 August and razed it.
commanders B: Templar garrison (Odo de Saint-Amand was held prisoner); Baldwin IV (relief too late)
sources: William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, al-Fath al-Qussi; Wikipedia, Battle of Chastellet
note: The castle had been begun in 1178; about 700 defenders were killed or captured.

name: Lahore (siege, 1181)
how the result was decided: The siege ended when Khusrau Malik made peace and gave his son as a hostage; Lahore did not fall.
Iranian force: Mu'izz al-Din's army from Ghazni: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri, Khalaj and Afghan contingents (recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: How much fighting there was is unclear.
doubts and flags: Borderline: How much fighting there was is unclear.
sources: Juzjani; en.wikipedia Muhammad of Ghor, Siege of Lahore (1186)
note: The Muhammad of Ghor article calls it a failed siege; the terms (a hostage, by some accounts an elephant) make it a negotiated end. The Ghaznavids at Lahore after 1163 are not counted as Persian.

name: Belvoir (Forbelet)
place: Forbelet, near Belvoir (Kaukab al-Hawa), Jordan valley, Israel
how the result was decided: Both sides held their ground after heavy fighting; Saladin withdrew across the Jordan and the Franks kept the field only in name.
commanders B: Baldwin IV; Guy of Lusignan; Raymond III of Tripoli
sources: William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Indecisive; Saladin then raided Galilee and moved on Beirut.

name: Beirut (siege, 1182)
how the result was decided: Saladin's land and naval attack failed and he withdrew when the king's army approached.
sources: William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982)
note: A combined attack with the Egyptian fleet; broken off to turn to Syria and the Jazira.

name: Mosul (siege, 1182)
how the result was decided: Saladin broke off the siege after the Caliph's mediators intervened and moved to Sinjar and the Jazira.
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin)
note: Saladin's first attempt on Mosul; he held the lesser Jazira towns thereafter.

name: Red Sea raid of Reynald (1182-83)
place: Gulf of Aqaba and the Hijaz coast, Red Sea (al-Hawra / Rabigh)
how the result was decided: Lu'lu's Egyptian squadron destroyed Reynald's ships and killed or captured his men.
commanders A: al-Adil (ruler in Egypt); Husam al-Din Lu'lu (admiral)
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Wikipedia, Raynald of Chatillon
note: Qualifies by the Ayyubid ruler of Egypt (al-Adil, Saladin's brother) directing the response; field commander Lu'lu was not a Kurd. Details of place are approximate.

name: Amid (siege, 1183)
how the result was decided: Amid fell to Saladin and was given to his vassal Nur al-Din Muhammad of Hisn Kayfa.
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh
note: Nur al-Din Muhammad was an Artuqid, the later Hisn Kayfa line is Ayyubid; this is the point of contact between Saladin's and the Hisn Kayfa story.

name: Al-Fule (1183)
place: Jezreel valley near Merhavia, about 8 km south-east of Afula (Al-Fule), Israel
how the result was decided: The Franks held their camp and Saladin was forced to withdraw after days of skirmishing without a decisive battle.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of al-Fule (fetched); William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: The 1183 raid; the Franks avoided a full battle with their large army, which was later criticised. Saladin's field commanders named here were Turkish mamluks; Saladin himself is the basis.

name: Kerak (siege, 1183)
how the result was decided: Saladin raised the siege when Baldwin IV's relief army approached; the wedding of Humphrey IV and Isabella was in progress inside.
sources: William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Famous for the wedding of Humphrey IV and Isabella inside the castle: the lady of Kerak sent food from the feast to Saladin, who ordered the bridal tower spared. The siege was lifted on 4 December.

name: Kerak (siege, 1184)
how the result was decided: Saladin withdrew when the king's army marched to Kerak's relief.
sources: William of Tyre, Historia; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Second siege of Kerak under Saladin; the castle held and the relief army forced him to withdraw.

name: Sialkot (siege, 1185)
how the result was decided: Khusrau Malik and the Khokhars failed to take the new Ghurid fort and withdrew.
Iranian force: The Ghurid garrison of Sialkot under Husain ibn Kharmil, an Iranian lord of Guzgan; its make-up is not recorded (Turkic ghulams and Ghuri troops, by recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Juzjani; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty, Siege of Lahore (1186), Muhammad of Ghor
note: The Muhammad of Ghor article calls Sialkot an unsuccessful Ghurid siege; the Ghurid battle list and the Siege of Lahore (1186) article make it a failed Ghaznavid-Khokhar siege of the Ghurid garrison, followed here.

name: Mosul (siege, 1185-86)
how the result was decided: Saladin fell ill, left the siege and accepted terms (Mosul became his vassal in March 1186).
sources: Lyons & Jackson, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (1982); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin)
note: The second siege; the end result was a treaty of vassalage with Mosul without capture of the city.

name: Lahore (siege, 1186)
how the result was decided: Khusrau Malik surrendered Lahore after a short siege.
commanders A: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad, Husain ibn Kharmil
Iranian force: About 20,000 men under Mu'izz al-Din: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri, Khalaj and Afghan contingents (recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Juzjani; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Lahore (1186)
note: End of the Ghaznavid line: Khusrau Malik and his son were imprisoned in Gharjistan and later executed.

name: Nishapur (siege, 1187)
side B: Mengli Tegin, atabeg of Sanjar Shah
how the result was decided: Nishapur fell to Tekish after a siege of about two months.
factions B: Mengli Tegin, atabeg of Sanjar Shah (Mu'ayyids of Nishapur)
Iranian force: Tekish's army of Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic cavalry with Khwarazmian troops; the defenders were Mengli Tegin's Turkic soldiers and the townsmen of Nishapur.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ala al-Din Tekish
note: Nishapur had been ruled since 1157 by Mu'ayyid Ay-Aba and his heirs (Toghan Shah, Sanjar Shah); Tekish annexed it and sent Sanjar Shah to Gurganj.

name: Cresson
place: Springs of Cresson, near Nazareth, Israel
how the result was decided: A force of about 7,000 Muslim horse destroyed some 140 knights and their infantry, killing the Hospitaller Master; the Templar Master escaped with a handful of men.
commanders A: Muzaffar al-Din Gokboru (field commander); al-Afdal Ali (Saladin's son, nominal)
commanders B: Roger des Moulins (killed); Gerard de Ridefort
sources: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ernoul; Wikipedia, Battle of Cresson
note: Qualifies as a raid led nominally by Saladin's son al-Afdal and ordered by Saladin; the field commander Gokboru was a Turk, so the leader basis is weaker than at Hattin.

name: Hattin
place: Horns of Hattin, near Tiberias, Israel
how the result was decided: Saladin's army surrounded and destroyed the Frankish field army, capturing the king and the True Cross.
commanders A: Saladin; Taqi al-Din Umar; al-Afdal Ali; Muzaffar al-Din Gokboru
commanders B: Guy of Lusignan; Raymond III of Tripoli; Raynald of Chatillon (executed); Gerard de Ridefort
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, al-Fath al-Qussi; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Wikipedia, Battle of Hattin
note: Saladin's decisive victory; the siege of Tiberias (2-4 July) belongs with it and is not counted separately.

name: Tiberias (siege, 1187)
war: Saladin's wars (Ayyubid-Crusader wars; the Hattin campaign)
how the result was decided: Saladin's troops broke into the town on 2 July; the citadel held on briefly, which drew the Frankish army out to Hattin (Ibn al-Athir; Eracles).
commanders B: Eschiva of Bures, countess of Tripoli (citadel)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Imad al-Din al-Isfahani; Eracles; Wikipedia 'Battle of Hattin'
note: Saladin was a Kurd of the Rawwadid family of Dvin, ruling Arabs, Turks and Kurds. The Tiberias episode is the opening move of the Hattin campaign; Hattin itself is already listed.

name: Ascalon (siege, 1187)
how the result was decided: Ascalon surrendered after a hard siege when the captured King Guy ordered its handing over.
commanders B: Garrison of Ascalon (ordered to surrender by King Guy)
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: The surrender was ordered by the captive King Guy in return for promises of freedom.

name: Jerusalem (siege, 1187)
how the result was decided: After a breach in the north wall Balian negotiated a surrender and Saladin entered on 2 October.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, al-Fath al-Qussi; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Defended chiefly by townsmen and refugees under Balian; the surrender was a ransom treaty.

name: Kerak (siege, 1187-88)
how the result was decided: The castle held out for about a year and surrendered through famine.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Date of capitulation (c. November 1188) is approximate in the sources.

name: Tyre (siege, 1187-88)
how the result was decided: Saladin lifted the siege on 1 January 1188 after Conrad's sorties and the loss of his fleet in a naval action on 30 December.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Saladin's chief failure of 1187; Tyre became the base of the Third Crusade.

date: late 1188 to May 1189 (a siege of about a year)
name: Montreal (Shawbak, siege, 1188-1189)
war: Saladin's wars (Ayyubid-Crusader wars; reduction of the Transjordan castles)
how the result was decided: The starving garrison surrendered in 1189 (Ibn Shaddad; Wikipedia 'Montreal (Shobak)').
sources: Ibn Shaddad, Nawadir; Ibn al-Athir; Wikipedia 'Montreal (castle)'
note: Saladin and his brother al-Adil were Kurds ruling Egypt and Syria. Kerak and Montreal were the Frankish castles that cut the road from Egypt to Damascus; Kerak's sieges are already listed.

name: Saone (siege, 1188)
how the result was decided: Saladin's mangonels took the lower castle and the garrison surrendered on 29 July.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh
note: One of the castles taken in Saladin's 1188 northern campaign (Latakia, Saone, Bourzey).

name: Belvoir (siege, 1188-89)
how the result was decided: The garrison, after a long siege with mining, surrendered on terms in early January 1189.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: The last major fortress of Galilee to fall to Saladin.

name: Safed (siege, 1188)
how the result was decided: After a month's bombardment the Templars surrendered on terms.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh
note: Part of Saladin's reduction of the remaining Galilean castles.

name: Acre (siege, 1189-91)
how the result was decided: Acre capitulated to the Crusaders on 12 July 1191 after a two-year siege.
commanders A: Saladin; al-Adil; Taqi al-Din; Baha' al-Din Qaraqush (garrison)
commanders B: Guy of Lusignan; Philip II of France; Richard I of England; Conrad of Montferrat
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, al-Fath al-Qussi; Itinerarium Peregrinorum; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: The Ayyubid relief army under Saladin besieged the besiegers for two years; Qualifies by Saladin's command and Ayyubid princes (al-Adil, Taqi al-Din) in the field.

name: Acre (battle, 4 October 1189)
how the result was decided: The Frankish attack on Saladin's camp was repulsed after initial success and the Templar Master was killed, but the siege lines remained.
commanders B: Guy of Lusignan; Gerard de Ridefort (killed)
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Itinerarium Peregrinorum; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: The first big battle of the Acre siege; the field was held by Saladin but the Crusaders kept their siege lines.

name: Beaufort (siege, 1189-90)
how the result was decided: Reynald of Sidon's stalling failed and the castle fell to Saladin's forces in April 1190.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Ta'rikh; Wikipedia, Beaufort Castle
note: Dates are approximate; Reynald was arrested for his ruse.

name: Marw al-Rudh (1190)
place: on the Murghab near Marw al-Rudh (Bala Murghab), Afghanistan
side A (victor if decisive): Ghiyath al-Din and Mu'izz al-Din, with the rulers of Bamiyan and Sistan
side B: Sultan Shah, Khwarazmian ruler of Merv
how the result was decided: Sultan Shah was defeated on the Murghab and fled to Merv; the Ghurids annexed most of his Khorasan lands.
factions A: Ghiyath al-Din and Mu'izz al-Din (Ghurids), with the rulers of Bamiyan and Sistan
factions B: Sultan Shah, Khwarazmian ruler of Merv
commanders A: Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad
Iranian force: The combined Ghurid armies of Firuzkuh and Ghazni with the Bamiyan Ghurids and the Nasrid malik of Sistan: Turkic ghulams, Ghuri troops and Sistani contingents; Sultan Shah had Turkic troops of Merv.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juzjani; Juvayni; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (Battle of Merv), Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Muhammad of Ghor, Ala al-Din Tekish
note: Listed as 'Battle of Merv' (1190) in Wikipedia's list of Ghurid battles; the Muhammad of Ghor article puts it on the Murghab and also gives 1192. Sultan Shah, Tekish's brother, ruled Merv, Sarakhs and Tus as a rival Khwarazmshah.

date: 1191-1192 (thirteen months, after the first battle of Tarain)
name: Tabarhindah (siege, 1191)
how the result was decided: The Ghurid garrison surrendered the fort after holding out for thirteen months.
Iranian force: A Ghurid garrison of about 2,000 under Qazi Zia al-Din Tulaki; its make-up is not recorded (Turkic and Tajik soldiers, by recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: No separate article; described in the Tarain and Muhammad of Ghor articles.
doubts and flags: Borderline: No separate article; described in the Tarain and Muhammad of Ghor articles.
sources: Juzjani; en.wikipedia First Battle of Tarain, Muhammad of Ghor
note: Tabarhindah is usually identified with Bathinda (some prefer Sirhind). Mu'izz al-Din had taken it shortly before the first battle of Tarain.

name: Tarain (1191)
how the result was decided: The Chahamana counter-attack drove the Ghurids off after Mu'izz al-Din was wounded and carried away; the Rajputs held the field.
commanders B: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad (wounded), Qutb al-Din Aibak, Bahauddin Tughril
Iranian force: Mu'izz al-Din's cavalry army: mounted Turkic ghulam archers with Ghuri, Khalji and Afghan emirs and their men (Juzjani names the Ghurid, Khalji and Afghan emirs who fled); a Khalji horseman carried the wounded sultan away.
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
strength A: unknown (100,000 cavalry per Roy, an unreliable figure)
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; Hasan Nizami; Firishta; en.wikipedia First Battle of Tarain
note: Wikipedia title: 'First Battle of Tarain'. The Chahamanas of Shakambhari (Prithviraj III) with allied Rajput chiefs.

name: Arsuf
how the result was decided: Richard's counter-charge routed the Muslim army, which withdrew with the road to Jaffa open.
commanders B: Richard I; Robert of Leicester; James of Avesnes (killed)
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, al-Fath al-Qussi; Itinerarium Peregrinorum; Ambroise; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Saladin tried to break up the crusader column on its march to Jaffa and lost the field.

name: Tarain (1192)
how the result was decided: Ghurid dawn attacks and feigned retreats broke the Rajput army, which fled; Prithviraj was captured near Sursuti.
commanders A: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad, Qutb al-Din Aibak, Taj al-Din Yildiz, Nasir al-Din Qubacha, Husain ibn Kharmil, Kharbak, Mukalba, Ilah
Iranian force: Mu'izz al-Din's army of 120,000 armoured men (Minhaj): 40,000 elite horse under the sultan, 10,000 mounted archers in four divisions and a reserve of 12,000, with the commands of the Turkic slave generals Aibak, Yildiz and Qubacha and of the Ghazni lords Kharbak, Kharmil, Ilah and Mukalba, and Khalji and Afghan troops.
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; Hasan Nizami, Taj al-Ma'athir; Firishta; en.wikipedia Second Battle of Tarain
note: Wikipedia title: 'Second Battle of Tarain'. It opened northern India to the Ghurids; Prithviraj was later executed.

name: Jaffa (1192)
how the result was decided: Saladin stormed Jaffa on 28 July but Richard's relief force retook it and repulsed a Muslim surprise attack on 5 August.
sources: Baha' al-Din Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (Life of Saladin); Itinerarium Peregrinorum; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: The final battle of the Third Crusade, fought shortly before the Treaty of Ramla; Richard's small force repulsed Saladin's army.

name: Bagar
war: Ghurid campaigns in India (rebellion of Jatwan)
how the result was decided: Jatwan raised his siege of Hansi, was beaten near Bagar and was killed.
Iranian force: Aibak's Ghurid army in India: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri and Khalji contingents (recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Hasan Nizami; en.wikipedia Rebellion of Jatwan, List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (Battle of Bagar)
note: Includes the relief of Hansi, where Jatwan, a former Chahamana subordinate, had besieged the Ghurid commander Nasrat al-Din.

name: Ajmer (1194)
how the result was decided: Aibak defeated Hariraja, who burned himself, and the Ghurids reoccupied Ajmer.
Iranian force: Aibak's Ghurid army in India: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri and Khalji contingents (recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: No separate article; listed in Wikipedia's list of Ghurid battles.
doubts and flags: Borderline: No separate article; listed in Wikipedia's list of Ghurid battles.
sources: Hasan Nizami; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (Battle of Ajmer), Muhammad of Ghor, Battle of Kasahrada (1197)
note: Hariraja, Prithviraj's brother, had driven out the Ghurid vassal Govindaraja IV.

name: Chandawar
place: Chandawar (Chandwar), near Firozabad, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: The battle was hotly contested until Jayachandra was killed and his army routed.
commanders A: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad, Qutb al-Din Aibak
Iranian force: Mu'izz al-Din's army of 50,000 horsemen with Aibak's vanguard: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri, Khalji and Afghan contingents (recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Hasan Nizami; Juzjani; en.wikipedia Battle of Chandawar, Muhammad of Ghor
note: The Gahadavalas of Kannauj and Varanasi. Some date it to winter 1193-94.

date: March 1194 (19 March in the Toghrul III article; 4 March in the Tekish article)
name: Rayy (1194)
side A (victor if decisive): Tekish, with the Eldiguzid Qutlugh Inanch
how the result was decided: Toghrul III charged with about 60 guards while his amirs held back and was killed; the Khwarazmians held the field.
factions A: Tekish (Khwarazmshah), with the Eldiguzid Qutlugh Inanch
Iranian force: Tekish's Khwarazmian army of Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic cavalry, with the troops of the Eldiguzid claimant Qutlugh Inanch; Toghrul's side was his mamluks and Turkmen-backed amirs, most of whom did not fight.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Juvayni; Rawandi; en.wikipedia Toghrul III, Ala al-Din Tekish, List of battles involving the Seljuk Empire, Al-Nasir
note: End of the Seljuk sultanate of Iraq; Toghrul's head was sent to the caliph al-Nasir, who had encouraged Tekish.

name: Shamkor
war: Georgian-Seljuk wars (Georgian intervention in the Eldiguzid succession)
how the result was decided: Soslan's flank march broke Abu Bakr's army, which fled to Ganja; the Georgians took Shamkor and then Ganja.
Iranian force: Abu Bakr's Eldiguzid army of Azerbaijan and Arran, reinforced by his client Muslim emirs: Turkic mamluks and Turkmen cavalry with Kurdish and local troops (recruitment).
why it counts: The Georgian army was commanded by Queen Tamar's consort David Soslan, an Ossetian (Alan) prince of the Bagatar royal family (Georgian Chronicle of Queen Tamar; Wikipedia, Battle of Shamkor, for his command).
sources: Georgian Chronicles (Histories and Eulogies of the Sovereigns); en.wikipedia Battle of Shamkor, Georgian-Seljuk wars
note: Abu Bakr's brother Amir Amiran (Mihran) sided with Georgia and the Shirvanshah; the Georgians took the caliph's standard. Some accounts date the battle to the early 1190s.

name: Ajmer (siege, 1196)
how the result was decided: A relief army from Ghazni reached Ajmer and the besiegers withdrew.
commanders B: the Mer chiefs, with Bhima II's Chaulukyas
Iranian force: Aibak's Ghurid troops in Ajmer, relieved by an army sent by Mu'izz al-Din: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri and Khalji contingents (recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: No separate article; described in the Battle of Kasahrada (1197) article.
doubts and flags: Borderline: No separate article; described in the Battle of Kasahrada (1197) article.
sources: Hasan Nizami; Firishta; en.wikipedia Battle of Kasahrada (1197)
note: The Mers had driven the Ghurid garrison out of the Ajmer country while Aibak was in Delhi.

name: Bayana (siege)
how the result was decided: Kumarapala surrendered the fort and Bayana was put under Bahauddin Tughril.
commanders A: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad, Qutb al-Din Aibak, Bahauddin Tughril
Iranian force: Mu'izz al-Din's army with Aibak's: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri, Khalji and Afghan contingents (recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: No separate article; listed in Wikipedia's list of Ghurid battles.
doubts and flags: Borderline: No separate article; listed in Wikipedia's list of Ghurid battles.
sources: Hasan Nizami; Juzjani; en.wikipedia List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (Siege of Bayana), Muhammad of Ghor

name: Damascus (siege, 1196)
war: Ayyubid succession war (sons of Saladin v. al-Adil)
how the result was decided: Al-Adil allied with al-Aziz, took Damascus and let al-Afdal retire to Salkhad.
Iranian side: Ayyubids of Egypt v Ayyubids of Damascus
sources: Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayyubid_dynasty (fetched); Wikipedia, Al-Afdal ibn Salah ad-Din (fetched)
note: A war inside the Ayyubid family, with Ayyubid princes leading both sides; sources differ on how much fighting there was before the settlement. Exact dates are uncertain.

name: Gwalior (siege, 1196)
how the result was decided: After a long siege Sulakshanapala surrendered and accepted Ghurid rule (Wikipedia: Gwalior annexed).
commanders A: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad, Qutb al-Din Aibak, Bahauddin Tughril
Iranian force: Aibak's and Tughril's Ghurid forces: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri and Khalji troops (recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Juzjani; Firishta; en.wikipedia Siege of Gwalior (1196), Muhammad of Ghor
note: Kachchhapaghata (Parihar) ruler. Some accounts have the raja only pay tribute in 1196 and hand over the fort in 1200 after Tughril's blockade; if so the 1196 siege was a draw.

name: Kasahrada (1197)
place: Kasahrada (Kayadara), at the foot of Mount Abu, Rajasthan, India
how the result was decided: The Rajputs came down into the plain and the Ghurid cavalry routed them; Aibak then sacked Anhilwara.
commanders A: Qutb al-Din Aibak, Asad al-Din Arslan Qulij, Jahan Pahlavan, Nasir al-Din Husain
commanders B: Bhima II's commanders: Jayatasimha (killed), Dharavarsha, Prahladana
Iranian force: Aibak's Indian army reinforced from Ghazna: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Khalji and Ghuri contingents (recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Hasan Nizami, Taj al-Ma'athir; Firishta; en.wikipedia Battle of Kasahrada (1197)
note: Chaulukyas with Paramara and Naddula Chahamana allies. Wikipedia title: 'Battle of Kasahrada (1197)'.

name: Jaffa (1197)
how the result was decided: Al-Adil took Jaffa by storm before the German crusaders arrived.
commanders B: Henry of Champagne (died during the siege); garrison of Jaffa
sources: Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977); Wikipedia, Al-Adil I (fetched)
note: Henry of Champagne fell from a window to his death in the same days. The date within September 1197 is approximate.

name: Toron (siege, 1197-98)
side B: German Crusaders and Kingdom of Jerusalem
how the result was decided: The Crusaders raised the siege when al-Adil's relief army approached and news came of the death of Henry VI.
principal opponents: German Crusaders and Kingdom of Jerusalem
commanders B: Henry of Brabant; Conrad of Querfurt
sources: Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977); Wikipedia, Al-Adil I (fetched); Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Date-range as given in standard accounts of the German Crusade.

name: Guzgan (1198)
how the result was decided: The Ghurids routed a large Qara Khitai army that had invaded Guzgan.
commanders A: the Ghurid amirs of Guzgan and Balkh, for Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad
Iranian force: The Ghurid forces of Guzgan and Balkh (Husain ibn Kharmil's lordship): Turkic ghulams with Ghuri and local Tajik troops (recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: No conventional name; a pitched battle in Juzjani and Juvayni.
doubts and flags: Borderline: No conventional name; a pitched battle in Juzjani and Juvayni.
sources: Juzjani; Juvayni; en.wikipedia Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Ala al-Din Tekish
note: The Qara Khitai invaded at Tekish's request; the Ghurids took Balkh the same year.

name: Arslan-Gusha (siege)
how the result was decided: The fortress fell to Tekish after a four-month siege.
Iranian force: Tekish's Khwarazmian army (Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic troops); the defenders were Nizari garrison troops of the Alamut state.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ala al-Din Tekish
note: Wikipedia's Tekish article also says he attacked Alamut the same year without success (not listed here).

name: Damascus (siege, 1199)
war: Ayyubid succession war (sons of Saladin v. al-Adil)
how the result was decided: Al-Adil split the brothers' vassals and the siege ended when al-Kamil's reinforcements arrived in December 1199.
Iranian side: Ayyubids of Damascus v Ayyubids of Egypt and Aleppo
sources: Wikipedia, Al-Adil I (fetched); Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: Ayyubid princes led both sides; al-Adil prevailed.

name: Sack of Magadha
war: Ghurid campaigns in India (Bakhtiyar Khalji in Bihar)
how the result was decided: Bakhtiyar took the fortified monastery of Odantapuri and defeated and killed its ruler in the field outside.
Iranian force: Bakhtiyar Khalji's band of Khalaj and other Muslim horsemen from Awadh, about 200 at the start.
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: Bakhtiyar acted largely on his own as a Ghurid officer under Aibak; a raid on a fortified monastery.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Bakhtiyar acted largely on his own as a Ghurid officer under Aibak; a raid on a fortified monastery.
sources: Juzjani; Taranatha; en.wikipedia Sack of Magadha
note: The destruction of Nalanda and Vikramashila attributed to Bakhtiyar is disputed.

name: Turshiz (siege)
how the result was decided: The siege ended in a truce, the Nizaris paying 100,000 dinars, with the fort still untaken.
factions A: Qutb al-Din Muhammad (later Muhammad II), for Tekish
Iranian force: Qutb al-Din Muhammad's Khwarazmian army (Turkic cavalry and Khorasani troops); the defenders were the Nizari garrison of Quhistan.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Ala al-Din Tekish, Muhammad II of Khwarazm
note: Muhammad broke off the siege on hearing of Tekish's death (July 1200); the Tekish article dates it 1199.

name: Bilbeis (1200)
war: Ayyubid succession war (sons of Saladin v. al-Adil)
how the result was decided: Al-Adil pursued al-Afdal into Egypt and defeated him at Bilbeis; al-Afdal fled to Cairo and gave up Egypt.
Iranian side: Ayyubids of Damascus v Ayyubids of Egypt
sources: Wikipedia, Al-Adil I (fetched); Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: Ayyubid princes on both sides; al-Adil proclaimed himself Sultan on 17 February 1200.

name: Damascus (siege, 1201)
war: Ayyubid succession war (sons of Saladin v. al-Adil)
how the result was decided: Quarrels between al-Afdal and al-Zahir broke up the siege and al-Adil retained Damascus.
sources: Wikipedia, Al-Adil I (fetched); Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: The last attempt by Saladin's sons to retake Damascus; exact dates uncertain.

date: April 1201 (fell about 7 April after a few days; Ghurid list: 1200/1)
name: Nishapur (Ghurid siege, 1201)
how the result was decided: The Khwarazmian garrison surrendered Nishapur after a few days' siege.
factions B: Muhammad II of Khwarazm (garrison under Taj al-Din Ali Shah)
commanders A: Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad, Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad
Iranian force: The combined Ghurid armies of Ghiyath al-Din and Mu'izz al-Din, with war elephants brought from India: Turkic ghulams, Ghuri and Afghan contingents (recruitment).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juzjani; Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Muhammad II of Khwarazm, Ghurid conquest of Khorasan, List of battles involving the Ghurid dynasty (Battle of Nishapur)
note: Part of the Ghurid conquest of Khorasan (1200-1201), in which Merv, Sarakhs and Tus also fell.

name: Nishapur (Khwarazmian siege, 1201)
side B: Ghurid garrison under Diya al-Din Muhammad al-Ghuri
how the result was decided: The Ghurid garrison surrendered after a two-month siege and the walls were razed.
factions B: Ghurid garrison under Diya al-Din Muhammad al-Ghuri
Iranian force: Muhammad II's Khwarazmian army of Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic cavalry with Khorasani troops; the defenders were the Ghurid garrison of Ghuri and Turkic soldiers.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Muhammad II of Khwarazm
note: Muhammad retook Merv the same month.

name: Herat (siege, 1202)
side A (victor if decisive): Ghurid garrison of Herat, relieved by Husain ibn Kharmil
how the result was decided: Muhammad lifted the siege of Herat, and Ibn Kharmil destroyed a Khwarazmian detachment.
factions A: Ghurid garrison of Herat, relieved by Husain ibn Kharmil
commanders A: Umar al-Marghani, Alp Ghazi, Husain ibn Kharmil
Iranian force: The Ghurid garrison of Herat under Umar al-Marghani and Alp Ghazi, with Husain ibn Kharmil's field force from Guzgan (Turkic ghulams and Ghuri and Tajik troops, by recruitment).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Muhammad II of Khwarazm
note: In the spring of 1202 Mu'izz al-Din fought Muhammad near Merv with heavy losses on both sides (not listed separately).

date: 1202 to 12 April 1203 (some scholars date the fall to 1202)
name: Kalinjar (siege, 1203)
place: Kalinjar fort, Banda, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: With its reservoirs dry, the garrison surrendered the fort on terms and withdrew to Ajaigarh.
Iranian force: Aibak's 'huge army' with Iltutmish: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri and Khalji troops (recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Hasan Nizami, Taj al-Ma'athir; Firishta; en.wikipedia Siege of Kalinjar (1203)
note: The Chandelas of Jejakabhukti. The Taj al-Ma'athir claims 50,000 people were enslaved; Kalpi and Mahoba also fell.

date: About 1203 (scholars range 1202-1204; Ibn Bibi gives 598 AH, 1201-02)
name: Basiani
place: Basiani valley, near modern Pasinler, east of Erzurum (Turkey)
how the result was decided: Georgian Chronicle: the Georgians routed the sultan, who fell back on Erzurum, and took the Emir of Erzincan prisoner.
commanders A: David Soslan (commander of the army); Zakaria II Mkhargrdzeli (vanguard); Ivane Mkhargrdzeli
sources: Georgian Chronicle of Queen Tamar; Ibn Bibi; Rayfield (2012); Mikaberidze; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Basian; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Soslan
note: As at Shamkor, the Iranian element is the commander David Soslan, an Alan (Ossetian) prince; no Alan unit is named.

name: Gurganj (siege, 1204)
war: Ghurid-Khwarazmian wars (Mu'izz al-Din's invasion of Khwarazm)
side A (victor if decisive): Muhammad II of Khwarazm and Terken Khatun
how the result was decided: Mu'izz al-Din abandoned the siege when the Qara Khitai relief army approached.
factions A: Muhammad II of Khwarazm and Terken Khatun
commanders A: Muhammad II, Terken Khatun, Shihab al-Din al-Khivaqi; relief under Tayangu, Uthman ibn Ibrahim and Taj al-Din Bilge Khan
commanders B: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad, Husain ibn Kharmil
Iranian force: Gurganj's defenders: the citizen militia raised by Terken Khatun and the Shafi'i leader Shihab al-Din al-Khivaqi (70,000 claimed) and the Khwarazmshah's Turkic troops; the relief army was Qara Khitai and Qarakhanid.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
strength A: about 40,000 with a militia of 70,000 (claimed); Qara Khitai relief 10,000-40,000
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Gurganj (1204)
note: Civil because the Khwarazmshah's own forces held Gurganj; the Qara Khitai and Uthman of Samarkand came as allies.

name: Kakadadaha
how the result was decided: A Chandela inscription records Trailokyavarman's victory over the 'Turushkas' at Kakadadaha.
Iranian force: The Ghurid forces of the Kalinjar region; nothing is recorded (Turkic ghulams and their Ghuri and Khalji followers, by recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: Known only from a Chandela copper-plate inscription; no Persian-language source mentions it.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Known only from a Chandela copper-plate inscription; no Persian-language source mentions it.
sources: Garra copper-plate inscription; Ajaygarh inscription of Viravarman; en.wikipedia Trailokyavarman, List of wars involving Iran (before 1979)
note: Wikipedia's list of Iranian wars dates it 1205. Trailokyavarman's recovery of Kalinjar rests on the same inscriptions.

name: Nadia
how the result was decided: Bakhtiyar's raiders seized the palace, Lakshmana Sena fled east, and the Ghurid army held Nadia.
Iranian force: Bakhtiyar Khalji's Khalaj and Turkic horsemen; he rode in with 18 men disguised as horse dealers while the main body waited in a nearby forest.
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
strength A: 18 horsemen in the raid, the main army nearby
borderline: Bakhtiyar acted largely on his own as a Ghurid officer; a raid on a capital rather than a pitched battle.
doubts and flags: Borderline: Bakhtiyar acted largely on his own as a Ghurid officer; a raid on a capital rather than a pitched battle.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Ghurid conquest of Bengal
note: Sena kingdom. Wikipedia title: 'Ghurid conquest of Bengal'; a footnote there identifies Nadiya with Naoda in Rajshahi District, Bangladesh. Bakhtiyar then made Lakhnauti his capital.

name: Qarasu
war: Ghurid-Khwarazmian wars (Mu'izz al-Din's invasion of Khwarazm)
place: the Qarasu canal, east of Gurganj, Turkmenistan
side B: Muhammad II of Khwarazm, with Uthman of Samarkand
how the result was decided: The Ghurids won a costly fight at the canal and the Khwarazmshah fell back on Gurganj.
factions B: Muhammad II of Khwarazm, with Uthman of Samarkand
Iranian force: Mu'izz al-Din's invasion army with war elephants: Turkic ghulam cavalry, Ghuri, Khalji and Afghan contingents and Indian troops (recruitment); the Khwarazmians had Qipchaq and Qangli Turks.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Qarasu, Muhammad II of Khwarazm
note: Called a Pyrrhic Ghurid victory; the Ghurids killed their Khwarazmian prisoners. The Khwarazmshah had flooded the approaches by breaching dikes, holding the Ghurids for about 40 days.

name: Herat (siege, 1204)
side B: Alp Ghazi, Ghurid governor of Herat
how the result was decided: The siege ended in an agreement by which Alp Ghazi paid an indemnity, and the Khwarazmshah turned back when Mu'izz al-Din invaded Khwarazm.
factions B: Alp Ghazi, Ghurid governor of Herat
Iranian force: Muhammad II's Khwarazmian army of Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic cavalry; the defenders were the Ghurid garrison of Herat.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Muhammad II of Khwarazm, Siege of Gurganj (1204)
note: Wikipedia's wording ('Alp Ghazi surrendered for an indemnity') is ambiguous; if Herat was handed over, the besieger won. This siege provoked Mu'izz al-Din's invasion of Khwarazm.

date: 28-29 September 1204 (date per the Muhammad II article)
name: Andkhud
war: Ghurid-Qara Khitai conflicts (Mu'izz al-Din's retreat from Khwarazm)
how the result was decided: The Qara Khitai and Qarakhanids routed the Ghurids and besieged Mu'izz al-Din in Andkhud fort until he paid a ransom.
commanders A: Tayangu, Uthman ibn Ibrahim of Samarkand, Taj al-Din Bilge Khan
commanders B: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad (wounded), Husain ibn Kharmil, Nasir al-Din Aitam (killed), Aibak Yogi, Aibak Beg
Iranian force: Mu'izz al-Din's army, about 20,000 horse worn out by the retreat from Gurganj: his Turkic slave commanders (Aibak Yogi, Aibak Beg), provincial governors such as Nasir al-Din Aitam, and Ghuri and Afghan troops.
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Juzjani; Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Battle of Andkhud, Muhammad II of Khwarazm
note: Wikipedia also lists the Khwarazmians as belligerents (they had harried the Ghurid retreat at Hazar Saf); the battle itself was fought by the Qara Khitai and Uthman of Samarkand, so it is not counted as civil. The Ghurids lost Khorasan except Herat and Balkh.

name: Tirmidh (siege, 1205)
how the result was decided: The Ghurids took Tirmidh and destroyed its Qara Khitai garrison.
Iranian force: The Ghurid forces of Balkh (the Bamiyan Ghurid sphere): Turkic ghulams with Ghuri and local Tajik troops (recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Juzjani; en.wikipedia Muhammad of Ghor

name: Jhelum (1206)
place: between the Chenab and the Jhelum, Punjab, Pakistan
how the result was decided: After a fight from morning to sunset, the arrival of Aibak and Iltutmish broke the Khokhars, who were routed and massacred.
commanders A: Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad, Qutb al-Din Aibak, Iltutmish
Iranian force: Mu'izz al-Din's main army from Ghazna with Aibak's contingent from Delhi and Iltutmish's from Badaun: Turkic ghulam cavalry with Ghuri, Khalji and Afghan troops (recruitment).
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Juzjani; Hasan Nizami; Firishta; en.wikipedia Battle of Jhelum (1206)
note: Wikipedia's list of Ghurid battles has the same campaign as 'Revolt of Khokars', February-March 1205. Mu'izz al-Din was assassinated at Dhamiak on 15 March 1206 on his way back.

name: Bakhtiyar Khalji's Tibet campaign
war: Ghurid campaigns in India (Bakhtiyar Khalji's Tibet expedition)
place: Chumbi Valley, Tibet, and the Teesta crossing on the retreat, China
how the result was decided: The Tibetans trapped and drove back the army, and at the broken bridge on the retreat it was destroyed; only about 100 horsemen returned.
commanders A: Tibetan tribal leaders; the raja of Kamrup
Iranian force: Bakhtiyar's Bengal army of about 10,000 cavalry, mostly Khalaj and other Turks, with local (Deshi) Muslims, guided by Ali Mech.
why it counts: Ghurids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: A campaign rather than a single battle; Bakhtiyar ruled Lakhnauti as an autonomous Ghurid officer, and Mu'izz al-Din was killed (15 March 1206) as it began.
doubts and flags: Borderline: A campaign rather than a single battle; Bakhtiyar ruled Lakhnauti as an autonomous Ghurid officer, and Mu'izz al-Din was killed (15 March 1206) as it began.
sources: Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; en.wikipedia Bakhtiyar Khalji's Tibet campaign, Muslim invasions of Assam
note: The forces of Kamarupa (Kamrup) destroyed the bridge on the retreat. Accounts of Bakhtiyar's death (illness, or murder by Ali Mardan Khalji) differ.

name: Herat (siege, 1207-1208)
war: Khwarazmian conquest of the Ghurid lands (revolt of Husain ibn Kharmil)
side B: Herat rebels under Khwaja al-Sahib, pledged to the Ghurid Ghiyath al-Din Mahmud
how the result was decided: The Khwarazmians breached the walls and took Herat in July 1208 (or 1209).
factions B: Herat rebels under Khwaja al-Sahib (after Husain ibn Kharmil's capture), pledged to the Ghurid Ghiyath al-Din Mahmud
commanders A: Emir Jaldik, Taj al-Din Abu Bakr, Kuzlik Khan, Muhammad II
commanders B: Husain ibn Kharmil (captured, executed), Khwaja al-Sahib (executed)
Iranian force: Khwarazmian cavalry: Jaldik's 2,000 and then about 10,000 under Kuzlik Khan and Taj al-Din Abu Bakr (Turkic troops, by recruitment); the defenders were Herat's garrison and townsmen.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Revolt of Husain ibn Kharmil, Muhammad II of Khwarazm
note: Wikipedia title: 'Revolt of Husain ibn Kharmil'. The Khwarazmians also tried to flood the city by damming its water.

date: 1208 (Georgian sources put the capture of Ivane Mkhargrdzeli in 1210)
name: Khilat (siege, 1208)
how the result was decided: The Georgian siege failed and their general Ivane was taken prisoner, released under the truce of 1210.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayyubid_dynasty (fetched); Georgian Chronicles; Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: Dates differ between the Arabic and Georgian sources; the Ayyubid ruler of Khilat was al-Awhad, al-Adil's son.

name: Ganja (siege, 1213)
how the result was decided: The garrison's sortie was beaten but Ganja did not fall; the siege ended in a treaty by which Uzbek resumed tribute to Georgia.
Iranian force: Uzbek's Eldiguzid garrison of Ganja, which sortied 10,000 strong: Turkic mamluks and Turkmen troops with the townsmen (recruitment).
why it counts: Ganja's townsmen joined the sortie
sources: Georgian Chronicles; en.wikipedia Siege of Ganja (1213)
note: Wikipedia calls it a Georgian victory; under the siege test a treaty with the place still invested is a draw.

name: Karaj (1215)
war: Revolt of Mengli in Persian Iraq
place: near Karaj (Karaj of Abu Dulaf), Markazi, Iran
side A (victor if decisive): Uzbek with Hasan III's Nizaris and the caliph's army
side B: Mengli, ruler of Hamadan, Isfahan and Rayy
how the result was decided: Mengli's army was beaten on a mountain slope near Karaj and he fled to Saveh, where he was killed.
factions A: Uzbek (Eldiguzids) with Hasan III's Nizaris and the caliph's army
factions B: Mengli, ruler of Hamadan, Isfahan and Rayy
commanders A: Muzaffar al-Din Uzbek; Muzaffar al-Din Sunqur (Wajh al-Sab', for the caliph); the troops of Jalal al-Din Hasan III of Alamut
Iranian force: Uzbek's Eldiguzid army of Azerbaijan (Turkic mamluks and Turkmens) with Nizari troops sent by Hasan III; the caliph's army from Baghdad fought beside them; Mengli had his own mamluks and the troops of Persian Iraq.
languages: Turkic; Persian; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: No conventional name; a pitched battle in Ibn al-Athir.
doubts and flags: Borderline: No conventional name; a pitched battle in Ibn al-Athir.
sources: Ibn al-Athir (year 612); Juvayni; en.wikipedia Muzaffar al-Din Uzbek, Al-Nasir
note: Mengli, a mamluk of the Eldiguzids, had seized Persian Iraq; his lands were divided between Hasan III and Aghlamish. Karaj is taken to be Karaj of Abu Dulaf, not modern Karaj near Tehran.

name: Miyaneh (1217)
war: Muhammad II's campaign in western Iran
side B: Nusrat al-Din Pish-Tegin, for the Eldiguzid Uzbek
how the result was decided: The Eldiguzid force was beaten and Pish-Tegin and Uzbek's vizier were captured.
factions B: Nusrat al-Din Pish-Tegin, for the Eldiguzid Uzbek
Iranian force: A Khwarazmian army of Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic cavalry; the Eldiguzid force was Turkic mamluks and Turkmens of Azerbaijan.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: No conventional name; a minor engagement known from the narrative of Muhammad's 1217 campaign.
doubts and flags: Borderline: No conventional name; a minor engagement known from the narrative of Muhammad's 1217 campaign.
sources: Nasawi; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Muhammad II of Khwarazm, Muzaffar al-Din Uzbek
note: Uzbek then accepted Muhammad as overlord. Muhammad's march on Baghdad was stopped by snow at the Asadabad pass (not a battle).

name: Rayy (1217)
war: Muhammad II's campaign in western Iran
how the result was decided: Sa'd nearly routed the Khwarazmian vanguard but was beaten and captured.
factions B: Sa'd I ibn Zangi (Salghurids of Fars)
commanders A: Muhammad II, Taj al-Din Abu Bakr of Zuzan
Iranian force: Muhammad II's army, put at 100,000: Qipchaq and Qangli Turkic cavalry with Khorasani troops; Sa'd's Fars army was Salghurid Turkmens with Persian and Shabankara Kurdish troops.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: No conventional name.
doubts and flags: Borderline: No conventional name.
sources: Nasawi; Ibn al-Athir; Juvayni; en.wikipedia Muhammad II of Khwarazm, Muzaffar al-Din Uzbek
note: Sa'd had seized much of Persian Iraq after the murder of Aghlamish (1217); he was released as a Khwarazmian vassal.

name: Mount Tabor (siege, 1217)
how the result was decided: A Hungarian-led attack on 3 December was abandoned and a renewed attack by the Templars and Hospitallers met Greek fire and was given up on 7 December.
commanders B: Andrew II of Hungary; Templars and Hospitallers (second attack)
sources: Wikipedia, Fifth Crusade (fetched); Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Oliver of Paderborn; Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: Al-Mu'azzam's fortress; the attack ended the Syrian campaign of the first Fifth Crusade army.

name: Aleppo (1218)
how the result was decided: Al-Ashraf routed a Seljuk army at Aleppo in 1218.
commanders B: Seljuk army of Kaykaus I (commander not named)
sources: Wikipedia, Fifth Crusade (fetched; one-line mention); Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols (1977)
note: I could find only the one-line statement in the fetched page; place within the Aleppo region, month and Seljuk commander not confirmed.

name: Damietta (siege, 1218-19)
how the result was decided: Damietta fell to the Crusaders on 5 November 1219 after famine and disease had reduced the defenders.
commanders B: John of Brienne; Cardinal Pelagius; Leopold VI of Austria; William I of Holland
sources: Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Oliver of Paderborn; James of Vitry; Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub; al-Maqrizi, Suluk (Kitab al-Suluk li-Ma'rifat Duwal al-Muluk)
note: The Chain Tower fell on 25 August 1218 and al-Adil died on 31 August; al-Kamil led the defence and his brother al-Mu'azzam brought the Syrian army.

name: Fariskur (1219)
place: Ayyubid camp at Fariskur, south of Damietta, Egypt
how the result was decided: The Crusader attack on the sultan's camp was a disaster: the Hospitaller Marshal Aymar de Lairon and many Templars were killed.
commanders B: Cardinal Pelagius (his faction); John of Brienne and Ranulf of Chester (covered the retreat)
sources: Wikipedia, Fifth Crusade (fetched); Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Oliver of Paderborn; James of Vitry; Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub
note: Pelagius's faction forced the attack against the advice of John of Brienne; al-Kamil moved to Mansurah before the Crusaders took Damietta in November.

name: Khujand (siege, 1220)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
how the result was decided: The town and finally the island fortress were given up; Timur Malik broke out down the Syr Darya by boat and the Mongols held the place.
Iranian force: Timur Malik's garrison, at the end about 1,000 picked men in the island fortress, with the townsmen of Khujand.
why it counts: Khujand was a Persian-speaking (Tajik) town; Timur Malik and his professional troops were probably Turks.
sources: Juvayni; Barthold, Turkestan; en.wikipedia Siege of Khujand (1220)

name: Qazvin (1220)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire (raid of Jebe and Subutai)
how the result was decided: The Mongols stormed Qazvin, whose people fought on in the streets with knives until they were killed.
Iranian force: The townsmen of Qazvin; the Khwarazmian field forces of Iraq-e Ajam had scattered.
why it counts: Ibn al-Athir describes the defence as the townsmen's, in a Persian-speaking city.
borderline: defenders were townsmen, not the Shah's army; no Wikipedia article
doubts and flags: Borderline: defenders were townsmen, not the Shah's army; no Wikipedia article.
sources: Ibn al-Athir, year 617; Juvayni

name: Termez (siege)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
how the result was decided: Termez was stormed on the eleventh day of the siege and its people massacred.
Iranian force: The garrison and townsmen of Termez; the sources give no units or numbers.
why it counts: The defence was carried by the Persian-speaking townsmen with a small Turkic garrison, as in the other Oxus towns.
borderline: a town siege known from Juvayni, with no Wikipedia article
doubts and flags: Borderline: a town siege known from Juvayni, with no Wikipedia article.
sources: Juvayni; Rashid al-Din; Barthold, Turkestan

date: March 1220 (town surrendered 16-17 March; citadel about a month later)
name: Samarkand (siege, 1220)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
how the result was decided: A sortie with war elephants was destroyed, the town surrendered and the citadel fell about a month later.
commanders A: Genghis Khan, Chagatai, Ogedei, Jebe, Subutai
Iranian force: Qangli Turkish troops (30,000-60,000 in the medieval figures) and about 50,000 local Tajik troops with 20 war elephants; modern estimates put the garrison near 10,000.
why it counts: The medieval figures set the Turks at 30,000-60,000 against 50,000 local Tajik troops, so Iranian speakers were roughly 45-60%.
losses B: about 1,000 in the sortie; about 3,000 surrendered troops executed
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Siege of Samarkand (1220)

name: Gurganj (siege)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
how the result was decided: Gurganj fell to the besiegers after months of street fighting, and the dams were broken to flood the city.
commanders B: Khumar Tegin (proclaimed sultan; went over to the Mongols)
Iranian force: Khumar Tegin's Turkic troops and the citizens of the Khwarazmian capital, who fought quarter by quarter after the commanders gave up (Ibn al-Athir, Juvayni).
why it counts: The long street fighting was done by the citizens, who still spoke Khwarazmian (East Iranian); the Turkic commanders deserted early.
losses A: higher than usual for the Mongols
losses B: heavy; Juvayni's 1.2 million dead is a gross exaggeration
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Siege of Gurganj

name: Bamyan (siege)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
how the result was decided: Bamyan was stormed and razed after Genghis Khan's grandson Mutukan was killed by an arrow before its walls.
Iranian force: The inhabitants and garrison of Bamyan, fighting with archers and catapults.
why it counts: Bamyan, a former Ghurid capital, was defended by its Persian-speaking people.
sources: Juvayni; Juzjani; en.wikipedia Siege of Bamyan

name: Hamadan (1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire (raid of Jebe and Subutai)
how the result was decided: After the townsmen rose and killed the Mongol governor, the Mongols returned, beat their sorties and stormed the city.
commanders B: the notables of Hamadan (the ra'is and a jurist, per Ibn al-Athir)
Iranian force: The townsmen of Hamadan under their notables, with remnants of the Khwarazmian troops of Iraq-e Ajam.
why it counts: Ibn al-Athir describes the defence as the townspeople's, in a Persian-speaking city.
borderline: defenders were townsmen; no Wikipedia article
doubts and flags: Borderline: defenders were townsmen; no Wikipedia article.
sources: Ibn al-Athir, year 618; Juvayni

name: Kandahar (1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
how the result was decided: Jalal al-Din drove off the Mongol force besieging the town after two or three days of fighting.
Iranian force: Jalal al-Din's following on the march from Bust to Ghazni, Khwarazmian Turks with local troops.
why it counts: Before Parwan his following was a mix of Khwarazmian Turks and local Iranian and Afghan troops; no figures survive.
borderline: a minor action named only in the background of the Parwan article; the site may not be modern Kandahar
doubts and flags: Borderline: a minor action named only in the background of the Parwan article; the site may not be modern Kandahar.
sources: al-Nasawi; Juvayni; en.wikipedia Battle of Parwan; en.wikipedia Jalal al-Din Mangburni

name: Nasa (siege, 1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
how the result was decided: Nasa was taken after a siege of about fifteen days with mangonels and its people were massacred.
Iranian force: The townsmen and local garrison of Nasa (al-Nasawi's home town).
why it counts: The defence was by the Persian-speaking townsmen of a Khorasan town.
borderline: a town siege known from al-Nasawi, with no Wikipedia article
doubts and flags: Borderline: a town siege known from al-Nasawi, with no Wikipedia article.
sources: al-Nasawi; Juvayni; Barthold, Turkestan; en.wikipedia Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire

name: Taliqan (siege, 1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
how the result was decided: The fortress of Nusrat-Kuh was stormed after Tolui's army arrived, following a siege of some six months.
Iranian force: The garrison of the Nusrat-Kuh fortress; the sources give no units.
why it counts: A local Tajik garrison with Khwarazmian officers is assumed; the sources say nothing.
sources: Juvayni; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
note: Talaqan is identified by some with the Talaqan of Guzganan (near Maymana) rather than Taloqan in Tokharistan.

name: Merv (siege, 1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
how the result was decided: After a seven-day assault and two failed sorties the town surrendered on terms, which Tolui broke.
commanders B: Mujir al-Mulk (Wikipedia names the governor Dawud)
Iranian force: About 12,000 garrison troops and the townsmen of Merv, crowded with refugees.
why it counts: The defenders were mainly the Persian-speaking townsmen and local militia with a Khwarazmian garrison.
losses B: the population massacred (700,000 in Ibn al-Athir, 1,300,000 in Juvayni, both exaggerated)
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; en.wikipedia Siege of Merv (1221)
note: A second massacre followed a revolt in November 1221 (Shigi Qutuqu).

name: Maragha (1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire (raid of Jebe and Subutai)
how the result was decided: The Mongols stormed Maragha, driving Muslim prisoners ahead of them against the walls, and massacred its people.
commanders B: unknown (the town was ruled by a woman, per Ibn al-Athir)
Iranian force: The townsmen of Maragha; no field army defended it.
why it counts: The defenders were the townsmen of an Iranian-speaking city of Azerbaijan (Persian and Old Azari).
borderline: defenders were townsmen; the ruler is identified as the last of the Ahmadili house of Maragha only by inference
doubts and flags: Borderline: defenders were townsmen; the ruler is identified as the last of the Ahmadili house of Maragha only by inference.
sources: Ibn al-Athir, year 618; Juvayni

name: Nishapur (siege, 1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
how the result was decided: The walls were breached on 9 April and the city fell on 10 April 1221.
Iranian force: The townsmen and militia of Nishapur under the governor, with archers, crossbows and mangonels on the walls (12,000 archers at each of four gates, by one account).
why it counts: The sources describe a defence by the people of Nishapur, a Persian-speaking city.
losses B: heavy; Juvayni's 1,747,000 dead is a gross exaggeration (modern estimates 100,000-200,000)
sources: Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir; Juzjani; en.wikipedia Siege of Nishapur (1221)
note: Genghis Khan's son-in-law Toghachar had been killed in an earlier attack on the city (November 1220).

name: Herat (siege, 1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
how the result was decided: Herat surrendered after an eight-day assault; the garrison was killed and the townsmen spared.
Iranian force: The governor's Khwarazmian garrison (12,000 in later accounts) and the townsmen.
why it counts: The garrison was the Shah's (partly Turkic, partly Ghurid-Tajik) and the townsmen Persian-speaking; the proportions are not known.
sources: Juzjani; Juvayni; Sayfi Haravi; en.wikipedia Siege of Herat (1221)

name: Mansurah (1221)
place: Barmun, near Mansurah, Nile Delta, Egypt
how the result was decided: On 26 August the Egyptians attacked the Crusaders' night march, al-Kamil opened the sluices and Pelagius sued for peace on 28 August, yielding Damietta.
sources: Wikipedia, Fifth Crusade (fetched); Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Oliver of Paderborn; Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub; al-Maqrizi, Suluk (Kitab al-Suluk li-Ma'rifat Duwal al-Muluk)
note: The end of the Fifth Crusade. Al-Mu'azzam and al-Ashraf had sent troops to Egypt (their presence in the final action is not confirmed in the summary seen); al-Kamil is the Ayyubid basis.

name: Parwan
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
place: Parwan (near Jabal Saraj, north of Kabul), Afghanistan
how the result was decided: On the second day Shigi Qutuqu's army broke and fled, leaving the field to Jalal al-Din.
commanders A: Jalal al-Din, Amin Malik, Saif al-Din Ighraq, Timur Malik
Iranian force: About 10,000 Turks (Qangli) under Amin Malik on the right, Khalaj and Afghan contingents under Saif al-Din Ighraq on the left, Khwarazmian and Ghurid loyalists; many archers fought dismounted.
why it counts: Juvayni and al-Nasawi name the Turks of Amin Malik and the Khalaj, Afghan and Ghurid contingents; the Khalaj were Turkic, the Afghans Pashto-speaking and the Ghurids Persian-speaking.
sources: Juvayni; al-Nasawi; Juzjani; en.wikipedia Battle of Parwan
note: The first defeat of a Mongol army in a pitched battle by a Muslim ruler; the Khalaj and Afghans deserted over the spoils soon after.

date: autumn 1221, about a week before Parwan
name: Valiyan (1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
how the result was decided: Jalal al-Din attacked the Mongols besieging Valiyan, killed about 1,000 and drove the rest back across the river.
Iranian force: Jalal al-Din's army newly gathered at Ghazni: Khwarazmian Turks, Qangli, Khalaj, Afghan and Ghurid contingents.
why it counts: The same army as at Parwan, with Afghan (Pashto) and Ghurid (Persian) contingents beside the Turks.
borderline: a preliminary action named in the Parwan article
doubts and flags: Borderline: a preliminary action named in the Parwan article.
sources: Juvayni; al-Nasawi; en.wikipedia Battle of Parwan

name: Beylagan (1221)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire (raid of Jebe and Subutai)
how the result was decided: After the townsmen killed the Mongol envoy, Beylagan was stormed and its people massacred.
Iranian force: The townsmen of Beylagan, in the realm of the Eldiguzid atabeg Ozbeg.
why it counts: An urban defence in an Iranian-speaking town of Arran; no troops of the atabeg are mentioned.
borderline: defenders were townsmen; no Wikipedia article
doubts and flags: Borderline: defenders were townsmen; no Wikipedia article.
sources: Ibn al-Athir, year 618

name: Indus
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire
place: west bank of the Indus (near Kalabagh or Nilab), Pakistan
how the result was decided: Genghis Khan's army destroyed Jalal al-Din's army against the river; the Sultan escaped by riding into the Indus and swimming across.
commanders B: Jalal al-Din, Amin Malik (killed), Timur Malik
Iranian force: Jalal al-Din's 700 guards in the centre, Turkish troops under Amin Malik on the right and Afghan troops on the left: about 30,000 after the desertions following Parwan.
why it counts: The sources name a Turkish right wing and an Afghan left wing; the Khalaj under Ighraq had already left.
sources: Juvayni; al-Nasawi; Juzjani; en.wikipedia Battle of the Indus
note: Wikipedia lists Timur Malik as killed; other accounts have him survive. The date is also given as autumn (August-September) 1221.

name: Herat (siege, 1221-1222)
war: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire (risings after Parwan)
how the result was decided: Herat fell to the besiegers on 14 June 1222 after a siege of six to eight months.
commanders B: Malik Mubariz al-Din (of the Firuzkuh fort), Khwaja Fakhr al-Din Abd al-Rahman
Iranian force: The townsmen of Herat, who had risen for Jalal al-Din after Parwan and killed the Mongol governors, with Ghurid hillmen from Firuzkuh.
why it counts: Juzjani and Sayfi describe a defence by the people of Herat and the Ghurid hill forts, all Persian-speaking.
losses B: a seven-day massacre (1.6-2.4 million in the chronicles, impossibly high)
borderline: a rising in Jalal al-Din's name rather than his army
doubts and flags: Borderline: a rising in Jalal al-Din's name rather than his army.
sources: Juzjani; Sayfi Haravi; en.wikipedia Siege of Herat (1221)
note: Wikipedia treats both Herat sieges in one article.

date: Winter 1221-22 or early 1222 (Ibn al-Athir under 617 AH; the year is uncertain by about one)
name: Mongol defeat of the Alans and Cumans (North Caucasus)
place: Foothills of the North Caucasus, Terek-Kuban steppe (Russia); exact field unknown
allies B: Cuman khans, who withdrew after Mongol bribes
how the result was decided: Ibn al-Athir: after one indecisive fight the Mongols detached the Cumans with gifts and then crushed the isolated Alans, then turned on the Cumans.
sources: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil (year 617 AH); Kouznetsov and Lebedynsky, Les Alains (2005); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_invasion_of_Alania; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alania
note: First Mongol-Alan clash. The Alans led the coalition and bore the final defeat; the Cuman part of the coalition left the field beforehand.

name: Tabriz (siege, 1225)
how the result was decided: Tabriz surrendered to Jalal al-Din after a short siege.
factions B: Eldiguzids (Atabeg Ozbeg's capital, held by his wife)
commanders B: Malika Khatun (Ozbeg's wife); Ozbeg had fled to Ganja
Iranian force: Jalal al-Din's Khwarazmian army (Turkic cavalry with Iranian levies) against the townsmen and garrison of the Eldiguzid capital.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a short siege ending in surrender; Wikipedia treats it as a seizure
doubts and flags: Borderline: a short siege ending in surrender; Wikipedia treats it as a seizure.
sources: Ibn al-Athir; al-Nasawi; Juvayni; en.wikipedia Jalal al-Din Mangburni

name: Bolnisi
how the result was decided: The Kipchaks of the Georgian coalition went over or withdrew at Jalal al-Din's appeal, and the Georgian army was beaten from the field.
Iranian force: Jalal al-Din's Khwarazmian army of Qipchaq and Turkmen cavalry.
why it counts: No units are named for his side; his army was built on Turkic horsemen.
sources: al-Nasawi; Georgian Chronicles; en.wikipedia Battle of Bolnisi
note: The Georgian coalition included Kipchaks, Alans, Lezgins, Svans and Vainakhs.

name: Damascus (siege, 1229)
war: Ayyubid succession war (al-Kamil v. an-Nasir Dawud)
how the result was decided: After nearly two months of fighting Damascus surrendered to al-Ashraf and an-Nasir Dawud was compensated with Transjordan.
sources: Wikipedia, Al-Kamil (fetched); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayyubid_dynasty (fetched); Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: A war inside the Ayyubid family; al-Ashraf took Damascus for himself.

name: Yassıçemen
place: Yassicemen, between Sivas and Erzincan, Turkey
how the result was decided: After the allies seized part of their position the Khwarazmians abandoned the field by night and Jalal al-Din fled.
commanders B: Jalal al-Din, Jahan Shah ibn Tughril (Seljuk ruler of Erzurum)
Iranian force: Jalal al-Din's Khwarazmian army (10,000-40,000), Turkic cavalry with the troops of his ally Jahan Shah of Erzurum.
why it counts: The Ayyubid ruler al-Ashraf Musa, of the Kurdish Rawadi dynasty (Arabic-speaking by this date), personally led the Ayyubid army with Kayqubad I of Rum against Jalal al-Din (Nasawi; Humphreys).
sources: Ibn al-Athir; Ibn Bibi; al-Nasawi; en.wikipedia Battle of Yassicemen
note: On 10 August a Khwarazmian detachment of 700 beat an allied detachment of 3,000. Wikipedia also lists the Empire of Trebizond on Jalal al-Din's side.

name: Gaza (1239)
how the result was decided: The Egyptian force destroyed the Crusader raiding party near Gaza; the Count of Bar was killed and Amaury of Montfort and several hundred others captured.
commanders A: Rukn al-Din al-Hijawi (field commander; nisba of the Hakkari Kurdish emirs, not verified)
commanders B: Henry II of Bar (killed); Amaury VI of Montfort (captured); Hugh of Burgundy; Walter of Brienne
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Gaza (1239) (fetched); Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Matthew Paris, Chronica Majora; Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: Qualifies only by the Ayyubid ruler of Egypt (al-Adil II, as-Salih Ayyub being then Dawud's prisoner) directing the army; the Wikipedia article does not name the sender or any Kurdish troops. The field commander's nisba al-Hijawi may be Kurdish (Hakkari), which I could not confirm.

date: Nov/Dec 1239 to Feb 1240 (Yuanshi: 11th lunar month 1239 to 2nd lunar month 1240); older works give 1238-39
name: Siege of Maghas
war: Mongol invasion of Alania (Batu's western campaign)
place: Maghas, capital of Alania; site disputed (Ingushetia, North Ossetia, Arkhyz or the Kuban; modern Magas, Ingushetia, is named after it) (Russia)
allies A: Cuman troops; a group of Alans allied to the Mongols
how the result was decided: Juvaini and the Yuanshi: the Mongols took the walled capital after about three months and massacred its people.
commanders A: Batu (overall); Mongke and Buri (Rashid al-Din; the Alania article names Mongke and Guyuk); Shiri-gambu (Yuanshi)
commanders B: Ajis (Alan leader, captured, per the Alania article)
sources: Juvaini, Tarikh-i Jahangushay; Rashid al-Din, Jami al-tawarikh; Yuanshi (Song Zi, Shiri-gambu); Latham-Sprinkle, 'The Alan capital Magas: a preliminary identification of its location', BSOAS (2015); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maghas; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_invasion_of_Alania
note: The fall of the Alan capital ended the Alan kingdom. Alans stood on both sides (defenders, and a small allied group in the final assault); the main Iranian side is the defenders. The location is unsettled, so the coordinates give only the Ingush candidate.

date: autumn 1239; the Tower of David fell about 7 December 1239
name: Jerusalem (siege, 1239)
how the result was decided: An-Nasir Dawud's troops took the Tower of David after a siege of about three weeks and destroyed it.
commanders B: Garrison of the Tower of David
sources: Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Matthew Paris; Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: Ended the Frederick II truce for Jerusalem; the garrison surrendered the citadel.

name: La Forbie (Hirbiya)
war: Ayyubid civil war; Crusader alliance of 1244
place: Hirbiya (La Forbie), north-east of Gaza, Palestine (Gaza Strip)
side B: Ayyubids of Damascus, Homs and Kerak; Kingdom of Jerusalem and the military orders
how the result was decided: The Egyptians and Khwarazmians destroyed the allied army; over 5,000 Crusaders were killed and Walter of Brienne captured.
Iranian side: Ayyubids of Egypt v Ayyubids of Damascus, Homs and Kerak
factions B: Ayyubids of Damascus, Homs and Kerak, Kingdom of Jerusalem and the military orders
commanders A: Rukn al-Din Baybars al-Salihi; as-Salih Ayyub (ruler directing from Cairo)
commanders B: al-Mansur Ibrahim of Homs; an-Nasir Dawud of Kerak (allied); Walter IV of Brienne
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of La Forbie (fetched); Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3; Matthew Paris; Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub
note: Ayyubid princes led both sides: al-Mansur Ibrahim of Homs in person on the Syrian side, as-Salih Ayyub directing the Egyptian side.

name: Damascus (siege, 1245)
war: Ayyubid civil war (as-Salih Ayyub v. as-Salih Ismail)
how the result was decided: Damascus fell to as-Salih Ayyub's forces in 1245, ending Ismail's rule there.
Iranian side: Ayyubids of Egypt v Ayyubids of Damascus
commanders A: as-Salih Ayyub's army (Mu'in al-Din ibn al-Shaykh); Khwarazmians
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayyubid_dynasty (fetched); Wikipedia, Al-Salih Ayyub (fetched); Humphreys, From Saladin to the Mongols: The Ayyubids of Damascus 1193-1260 (1977)
note: Ayyubid princes on both sides; starting date of the siege uncertain.

name: Lake Homs (1246)
how the result was decided: Al-Mansur Ibrahim's army scattered the Khwarazmians and killed their leader.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayyubid_dynasty (fetched); Wikipedia, Al-Salih Ayyub (fetched); Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub
note: Which army carried the day (Homs and Aleppo or Egypt) is differently told; Ayyubid command is not in doubt.

name: Ascalon (siege, 1247)
how the result was decided: Fakhr al-Din stormed Ascalon on 24 October 1247 and razed it.
commanders A: Fakhr al-Din ibn al-Shaykh; as-Salih Ayyub (ruler directing)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayyubid_dynasty (fetched); Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Qualifies by the Ayyubid ruler directing the army; Fakhr al-Din was of a Khurasani shaykh family.

name: Damietta (1249)
how the result was decided: Louis IX landed on 5 June; the garrison and Fakhr al-Din's force withdrew and Damietta was occupied intact.
commanders A: Fakhr al-Din ibn al-Shaykh; as-Salih Ayyub (ill, directing from Mansurah)
commanders B: Louis IX; Charles of Anjou; Robert of Artois
sources: Wikipedia, Seventh Crusade (fetched); Joinville; Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub; al-Maqrizi, Suluk (Kitab al-Suluk li-Ma'rifat Duwal al-Muluk)
note: Qualifies by the Ayyubid Sultan as-Salih Ayyub directing; the Kinana Bedouin garrison was not Kurdish. Fakhr al-Din's family (Banu Hamawayh) is of Khurasani origin.

name: Mansurah (1250)
how the result was decided: The Egyptians killed Fakhr al-Din in the first surprise but Baybars and Qutuz rallied them and destroyed the vanguard, killing Robert of Artois.
commanders A: Fakhr al-Din ibn al-Shaykh (killed); Baybars al-Bunduqdari; Qutuz; Aybak
commanders B: Louis IX; Robert of Artois (killed); William Longespee (killed)
sources: Wikipedia, Seventh Crusade (fetched); Joinville; Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub; al-Maqrizi, Suluk (Kitab al-Suluk li-Ma'rifat Duwal al-Muluk)
note: As-Salih Ayyub had died on 22 November 1249 and his death was concealed; Turan-Shah arrived only on 28 February. The Ayyubid basis is thus indirect, via the dynasty's rule, and the leaders in the field were mamluks and Fakhr al-Din.

name: Fariskur (1250)
how the result was decided: The Egyptians surrounded the retreating Crusader army, killed or captured it and took King Louis.
commanders B: Louis IX (captured); Hugh XI of Lusignan (killed)
sources: Wikipedia, Seventh Crusade (fetched); Joinville; Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub; al-Maqrizi, Suluk (Kitab al-Suluk li-Ma'rifat Duwal al-Muluk)
note: Turan-Shah, Saladin's great-nephew and the reigning Ayyubid sultan, commanded in person; he was murdered on 2 May 1250 by the Bahri mamluks.

name: Al-Abbasa (1251)
war: Ayyubid war with the Mamluks of Egypt
how the result was decided: Yusuf's larger Syrian army was first successful but a Mamluk regiment deserted mid-battle and Yusuf fled to Damascus.
commanders A: an-Nasir Yusuf of Aleppo and Damascus
sources: Wikipedia, Seventh Crusade (fetched); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayyubid_dynasty (fetched); Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub; al-Maqrizi, Suluk (Kitab al-Suluk li-Ma'rifat Duwal al-Muluk)
note: The Ayyubid prince invaded Egypt to restore Ayyubid rule; peace in April 1253 recognised Aybak. Whether Shahrazuriyya Kurds fought in Yusuf's army is not confirmed in the sources seen.

name: Girdkuh (siege)
how the result was decided: Girdkuh surrendered to the besiegers on 15 December 1270, short of clothing, after a siege of seventeen years.
commanders A: Kitbuqa, Buri (killed December 1253); later the Ilkhans' commanders
Iranian force: The Nizari garrison of Girdkuh, reinforced from Alamut in 1254; its night sortie of December 1253 killed about 100 Mongols and their commander.
why it counts: Nizari Ismailis: an Iranian-led state
strength A: part of Kitbuqa's 5,000 horse and 5,000 foot
sources: Juvayni; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Mongol campaign against the Nizaris
note: Begun by Mongke's commanders (so the besiegers are the Mongol Empire, as for all of Hulagu's Nizari campaign) and completed under the Ilkhan Abaqa.

name: Tun (siege, 1256)
how the result was decided: Tun was taken after a week-long siege and sacked, and nearly all its people killed.
Iranian force: The Nizari townsmen and garrison of Tun in Quhistan.
why it counts: Nizari Ismailis: an Iranian-led state
sources: Juvayni; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Mongol campaign against the Nizaris
