note: Kitbuqa had already pillaged Tun in July 1253. Hulagu's army is treated as the Mongol Empire's (the invader).

name: Mount Siyalan
how the result was decided: The Nizaris of Rudbar beat back Yasur's force on the mountain, though it stayed in the district to raid.
Iranian force: Nizari fighters of the Rudbar of Alamut, Daylamite highlanders.
why it counts: Nizari Ismailis: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a small action
doubts and flags: Borderline: a small action.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Mongol campaign against the Nizaris

name: Alamut (siege, 1256)
how the result was decided: The commander of Alamut capitulated in December 1256 after a short investment, and the castle was dismantled.
Iranian force: The garrison of Alamut under its sipahsalar, who at first refused the Imam's order to surrender.
why it counts: Nizari Ismailis: an Iranian-led state
borderline: surrendered after a brief investment, with little recorded fighting
doubts and flags: Borderline: surrendered after a brief investment, with little recorded fighting.
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Mongol campaign against the Nizaris; en.wikipedia Timeline of the Ilkhanate
note: Georgian-Armenian units under David VII Ulu took part (en.wikipedia David Ulu). The Timeline of the Ilkhanate dates the capture to 20 November.

name: Maymun-Diz (siege)
how the result was decided: After three days of bombardment and a repulsed assault Khurshah surrendered on 19 November; the last defenders in the qubba were killed.
commanders A: Hulagu, Kitbuqa, Guo Kan, Balaghai and others
Iranian force: The Imam's garrison of Maymun-Diz, with its own mangonels; heavily outnumbered.
why it counts: Nizari Ismailis: an Iranian-led state
strength A: about 80,000 and 1,000 squads of siege engineers (Chinese, Khitan and Muslim)
sources: Juvayni; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Siege of Maymun-Diz
note: Hulagu's army is treated as the Mongol Empire's (the invader); if counted as the Ilkhanate (from 1256), the Nizari battles of 1256 would be civil.

name: Lambsar (siege)
how the result was decided: Lambsar fell in January 1257 after cholera broke out in the garrison.
Iranian force: The Nizari garrison of Lambsar, which refused Khurshah's order to surrender.
why it counts: Nizari Ismailis: an Iranian-led state
sources: Juvayni; en.wikipedia Mongol campaign against the Nizaris

name: Mayyafariqin (siege)
war: Mongol invasion of Syria and the Jazira
how the result was decided: Mayyafariqin fell to the besiegers on 7 April 1260 after a siege of about ten months.
commanders A: Yoshmut, Prosh Khaghbakian, Shahnshah Zakarian, al-Salih Isma'il ibn Lu'lu'
Iranian force: A small Mongol detachment under Yoshmut and a much larger Georgian-Armenian force under Prosh and Shahnshah, with Cilician Armenian units and Mosul siege engineers.
why it counts: The city was defended by its Ayyubid ruler al-Kamil Muhammad, of the Kurdish-descended Ayyubid line, against Yoshmut's Mongols and a Georgian-Armenian force (Wikipedia, Siege of Mayyafariqin; Humphreys).
losses A: unknown (the Armenian prince Sevata of Kachen killed)
sources: Kirakos; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Siege of Mayyafariqin
note: Persian role kept as principal: the Georgians and Armenians fought as vassals under Mongol command.

date: 18-24 January 1260 (citadel surrendered about a month later)
name: Aleppo (siege, 1260)
how the result was decided: Aleppo fell after six days of bombardment and the citadel surrendered about a month later.
commanders A: Hulagu, Kitbuqa, Hethum I, Bohemond VI
Iranian force: Hulagu's Mongol army with Kitbuqa's vanguard, and the troops of Hethum I of Cilician Armenia and Bohemond VI of Antioch.
why it counts: an Ayyubid (Kurdish by descent) held the city
losses B: heavy; the Muslim and Jewish inhabitants massacred
sources: Rashid al-Din; Ibn Shaddad; en.wikipedia Siege of Aleppo (1260)
note: Bohemond VI's Antioch is 'Crusaders' (Principality of Antioch).

name: Ain Jalut
place: Ain Jalut (Ma'ayan Harod), Jezreel Valley, Israel & Palestine
how the result was decided: The Mamluks held the field; Kitbuqa was killed and his army fled towards Baysan, where its rally was broken.
Iranian force: One Mongol tumen (10,000-12,000 men in all), Georgian and Cilician Armenian battalions (about 500 Armenians), the troops of the Ayyubid princes al-Ashraf Musa and al-Sa'id Hasan, and Syrian levies.
why it counts: The Mongol side included contingents of the Ayyubid princes al-Ashraf Musa and al-Sa'id Hasan (Kurdish-descended dynasty) and Qutuz's army included the Shahrazuriyya, usually described as Kurdish (Wikipedia, Battle of Ain Jalut; Amitai-Preiss).
sources: al-Maqrizi; Rashid al-Din; Abu'l-Fida; en.wikipedia Battle of Ain Jalut

name: Homs (1260)
place: near the tomb of Khalid ibn al-Walid, Homs, Syria
how the result was decided: The Muslim princes' small army routed the Mongol force, which fled the field.
commanders A: al-Ashraf Musa of Homs, al-Mansur of Hama
Iranian force: About 6,000 Mongol horsemen sent by Hulagu after Ain Jalut, in eight formations.
why it counts: The army that met Baydara's Mongols was led by the Ayyubid princes al-Ashraf Musa of Homs and al-Mansur II of Hama, of the Kurdish-descended Ayyubid dynasty, with Mamluk emirs (Maqrizi; Amitai-Preiss).
sources: Abu'l-Fida; al-Maqrizi; en.wikipedia First Battle of Homs
note: Wikipedia title: 'First Battle of Homs'.

name: Kazerun (1264)
how the result was decided: The Ilkhanid army defeated Seljuk-Shah, who had killed the Mongol governors, and took him at Kazerun.
commanders A: Ilkhanid commanders (unnamed here), with the troops of the atabegs of Yazd and Luristan
Iranian force: Ilkhanid Mongol troops with levies of the subject atabegs of Yazd and Luristan, against the Salghurid atabeg's Turkmen and Persian troops of Fars.
languages: Mongolic; Persian; Lur and Bakhtiari; Turkic
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: known from Vassaf and Rashid al-Din; commanders and site not verified on the web
doubts and flags: Borderline: known from Vassaf and Rashid al-Din; commanders and site not verified on the web.
sources: Vassaf; Rashid al-Din
note: Civil: the Salghurids of Fars and the Ilkhanate are both Persian states in this set.

name: Herat (1270)
place: Qara Su plain near Ghurian, west of Herat, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: Baraq's army broke and fled towards the Oxus, leaving the field to Abaqa.
commanders A: Abaqa, Yoshmut, Tubshin, Arghun Aqa, Samaghar, Abatai
Iranian force: Abaqa's Mongol tumens, with contingents from Kerman and Yazd on the left wing and a Georgian contingent under King David in the vanguard.
why it counts: Rashid al-Din names Kirman and Yazd contingents on Yoshmut's left wing in Abaqa's army, and the Atabegs of Yazd were ethnically Persian (Wikipedia, Battle of Herat (1270) and Atabegs of Yazd).
sources: Rashid al-Din; Vassaf; en.wikipedia Battle of Herat (1270); en.wikipedia Timeline of the Ilkhanate ('Battle of Qara-Su')
note: Also called the battle of Qara Su. The Kartid ruler of Herat, Shams al-Din, had submitted to Baraq earlier that year.

name: Alamut (1275-1276)
how the result was decided: The Ilkhanid army retook Alamut in 1276, about a year after the Nizari restoration force had seized it.
factions B: Nizari rebels (a son of Khurshah and a Khwarazmshah descendant)
commanders B: Naw Dawlat (or Abu Dawlat), son of Khurshah
Iranian force: An Ilkhanid force against Nizari partisans of Rudbar and Daylam.
languages: Daylami and Caspian; Persian; Mongolic; Turkic
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a rising, not a state
doubts and flags: Borderline: a rising, not a state.
sources: Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Mongol campaign against the Nizaris
note: One entry for the Nizari seizure (1275) and the Ilkhanid siege that ended it (1276).

date: Autumn-winter 1275 (the city, which had rebelled after submitting, resisted for five months before Bayan stormed it)
name: Siege of Changzhou (1275)
war: Yuan conquest of the Southern Song
how the result was decided: Bayan stormed Changzhou and massacred its people (Song shi, Yuan shi; Yule on Polo).
sources: Yuanshi; Songshi; Marco Polo (Yule, Book of Ser Marco Polo, notes on Alans and Chang-chou); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayan_of_the_Baarin
note: The Alan link is the weak point. Polo (and Pauthier) tie a massacre of Alans to Changzhou, but Yule argues the Alan episode belongs to Zhenzhou (see next entry). Asud troops did serve in Bayan's army, so a contingent is likely but not shown for this siege.

date: 4th lunar month 1275 (about May 1275); Polo says 1274, Tu Chi 1276
name: Zhenzhou (Yizheng), Asud garrison massacre
war: Yuan conquest of the Southern Song
how the result was decided: Songshi: Hong Fu retook the city in April-May 1275; Polo's tale is that the Alan troops billeted there were killed in the night.
doubts and flags: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
sources: Marco Polo (the Alans of 'Chang-chou'); Yule, Book of Ser Marco Polo, vol. 1 notes (dsr.nii.ac.jp/toyobunko/III-2-F-c-104/V-1/page/0037.html.en); Songshi
note: Known mainly from Polo's story of Alans killed after a feast, which Yule places at Chen-chou rather than Changzhou. Polo's '30,000 Alans' is not credible as a number.

date: Winter 1277-78; Russian chronicles give February 1278 (some works say 1277)
name: Siege of Dedyakov
war: Golden Horde suppression of the Alan revolt (Dedyakov uprising)
place: Dedyakov, an Alan town, usually placed near Vladikavkaz, North Ossetia (Russia)
how the result was decided: Russian chronicles (Nikon and related) say the Tatars with the Rus' princes took Dedyakov and burned it in February 1278.
sources: Nikon Chronicle and related Russian chronicles (s.a. 6786); Klaproth; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_invasion_of_Alania; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alans
note: The last big Alan revolt against the Horde. The Wikipedia text on the Dedyakov events is partly tagged 'citation needed'.

name: Aq Khwaja
war: Ilkhanid succession war (Arghun against Ahmad Tekuder)
place: Aq Khwaja, south of Qazvin, Iran
how the result was decided: Arghun's army defeated Alinaq's 15,000, though Arghun then fell back to Khorasan before Tekuder's main army.
Iranian force: Arghun's Khorasan army of Mongol and Turkic cavalry against Alinaq's 15,000 Ilkhanid troops; the Sufi Ala al-Dawla Simnani rode with Arghun.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Rashid al-Din; Iranica 'Argun Khan'; en.wikipedia Arghun
note: Some accounts make Alinaq the victor; Rashid al-Din and Iranica give the battle to Arghun. Arghun was captured at Kalat in July and freed by Buqa, who killed Alinaq; Tekuder was executed on 10 August 1284.

name: Marqab (siege, 1285)
how the result was decided: The Mamluks took Marqab by mining and the Hospitallers surrendered on terms on 25 May 1285.
commanders A: Qalawun; al-Muzaffar II Mahmud of Hama (Hama contingent)
sources: Wikipedia, Abu al-Fida (fetched): he was present at the attack on a Hospitaller stronghold; Abu'l-Fida, al-Mukhtasar
note: Qualifies only by the Hama contingent under the Ayyubid prince; the Hama Ayyubids were allies not leaders of the Mamluk army.

name: Tripoli (siege, 1289)
how the result was decided: Qalawun's army stormed the city, killed the garrison and razed Tripoli.
commanders A: Qalawun; al-Muzaffar II Mahmud of Hama (Hama contingent)
sources: Wikipedia, Abu al-Fida (fetched): he took part in the sieges of Tripoli and Acre; Abu'l-Fida, al-Mukhtasar
note: Qualifies only by the Hama contingent under the Ayyubid prince.

name: Acre (siege, 1291)
how the result was decided: The Mamluks stormed Acre on 18 May 1291, the last Crusader stronghold on the mainland.
commanders A: al-Ashraf Khalil; al-Muzaffar II Mahmud of Hama (Hama contingent); Abu al-Fida
commanders B: Jean de Grailly; Guillaume de Beaujeu (killed); Peter of Sevrey
sources: Wikipedia, Abu al-Fida (fetched); Abu'l-Fida, al-Mukhtasar; Runciman, A History of the Crusades, vols. 2-3
note: Abu al-Fida records his own presence and the Hama catapult force. Qualifies only by the Ayyubid prince's contingent; likely to be judged marginal.

name: Qazvin (1295)
how the result was decided: Ghazan's commanders beat Baydu's advance guard, though Ghazan then withdrew on finding Baydu's main army ahead.
Iranian force: Ghazan's Khorasan army (Nawruz's Oirat and Mongol horse) against Baydu's advance guard.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: an advance-guard action with no standard name
doubts and flags: Borderline: an advance-guard action with no standard name.
sources: Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Ghazan
note: Baydu was deposed after mass defections and executed on 4 October 1295.

name: Nishapur (1297)
how the result was decided: Ghazan's army defeated Nawruz near Nishapur; he fled to Herat, where the Kartid Fakhr al-Din handed him over.
Iranian force: Ghazan's army under Qutlugh-Shah against Nawruz's Oirat and Mongol followers in Khorasan.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: named only by place in Ghazan's biography
doubts and flags: Borderline: named only by place in Ghazan's biography.
sources: Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Ghazan; en.wikipedia Kart dynasty
note: No siege of Herat followed: Fakhr al-Din Kart surrendered Nawruz when the Ilkhanid army approached.

name: Erzincan (1299)
how the result was decided: Qutlugh-Shah defeated Sulamish's army and Sulamish fled to Mamluk Syria.
Iranian force: Qutlugh-Shah's Ilkhanid army against Sulamish's 20,000 Oirat, Mongol and Turkmen troops of Anatolia.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Rashid al-Din; Aqsara'i; en.wikipedia Ghazan; en.wikipedia Chupan
note: Civil: a revolt of the Ilkhanate's own army in Anatolia (not of the Anatolians). Sulamish returned with Mamluk help, was beaten again and burnt in Tabriz on 27 September 1299.

name: Bapheus
place: Plain of Bapheus (Koyunhisar), near Nicomedia (Izmit), Turkey; exact field unknown
how the result was decided: Ottoman cavalry broke the Roman line and Mouzalon withdrew into Nicomedia (Pachymeres).
sources: Pachymeres, Historia, book 4; Bartusis, The Late Roman Army (1997); Inalcik, 'Osman Ghazi's Siege of Nicaea and the Battle of Bapheus' (1994); Treiyer (2017); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bapheus
note: About half of Mouzalon's roughly 2,000 men were newly hired Alans, who are said to have covered the retreat rather than fought hard. Alans crossed into Roman service in 1301-02, which supports the 1302 date over 1299.

name: Apros
place: Apros, near modern Kermeyan, eastern Thrace (Turkey); exact field unknown
how the result was decided: The Catalans broke the Roman line, Michael IX was unhorsed and carried off, and the camp was looted.
commanders B: Michael IX Palaiologos; Girgon (Alan chief, in Roman service in 1305; his part at Apros is not attested here)
sources: Pachymeres, Historia; Muntaner, Chronicle; Bartusis, The Late Roman Army (1997); Jessee and Isaenko, 'The military effectiveness of Alan mercenaries in Constantinople, 1301-1306', J. Medieval Military History 12 (2014); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Apros
note: Alan cavalry held the Roman left and withdrew almost at once, which disrupted the line (Wikipedia, from Pachymeres). Whether Alans were a fifth of the army is not given.

date: Spring 1306 (Muntaner; the Wikipedia summary of Apros places an annihilation of the Alans after Apros)
name: Catalans v Alans and Turcopoles at the Balkan foothills
place: Foot of the Balkan mountains near the Bulgarian frontier, Thrace (Bulgaria/Turkey); site unknown
how the result was decided: Muntaner (via Jessee and Isaenko): a hard fight on the Bulgarian frontier went to the Catalan almogavars, who destroyed the Alan contingent.
sources: Muntaner, Chronicle; Pachymeres; Jessee and Isaenko (2014); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Apros
note: Muntaner puts Girgon's and Melik's horse at about 8,000 together. Place, date and exact order of events are poorly fixed, so this is an uncertain entry.

date: 1306 (Danishmend killed) - June 1307 (citadel taken; Wikipedia gives 5 February - 24 June 1306)
name: Herat (siege, 1306-1307)
how the result was decided: After the Kartids destroyed Danishmend's force inside Herat, Bujai's army besieged and took the citadel.
commanders B: Fakhr al-Din Kart and his garrison commanders
Iranian force: Danishmend's 10,000 Ilkhanid troops, then Bujai's besieging army with a Frankish mangonel corps, against the Kartid garrison of Herat (Tajik and Ghurid troops).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Sayfi Haravi; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Oljaitu; en.wikipedia Kart dynasty
note: Civil: the Kartids and the Ilkhanate are both Persian states in this set.

name: Gilan (1307)
how the result was decided: The Gilaks defeated Qutlugh-Shah's column and killed him, though the other Ilkhanid columns forced Gilan's submission.
Iranian force: Qutlugh-Shah's Ilkhanid column (one of four armies, others under Chupan, Sutai, Esen Qutluq, Irinjin) against the Gilaki highland and forest levies.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: Qutlugh-Shah and much of his column
borderline: civil only if the Gilaki lords count as an Iran-seated local power; otherwise an Ilkhanid defeat by local rebels
doubts and flags: Borderline: civil only if the Gilaki lords count as an Iran-seated local power; otherwise an Ilkhanid defeat by local rebels.
sources: Kashani; Rashid al-Din; en.wikipedia Oljaitu; en.wikipedia Chupan
note: The campaign as a whole ended with Gilan's submission (tributized June 1307).

name: Erbil (siege, 1310)
how the result was decided: Ilkhanid troops and Kurdish tribesmen took the citadel on 1 July 1310 and massacred its defenders.
Iranian force: Ilkhanid troops with Kurdish tribesmen (and Arabs, per the Timeline of the Ilkhanate).
why it counts: The sources name Kurdish tribesmen beside the Ilkhan's troops; their share is not known.
borderline: the defenders were Christian (Assyrian) townsmen and militia, part rebellion, part refuge from persecution
doubts and flags: Borderline: the defenders were Christian (Assyrian) townsmen and militia, part rebellion, part refuge from persecution.
sources: Bar Hebraeus (continuation); History of Mar Yahballaha; en.wikipedia Oljaitu; en.wikipedia Citadel of Erbil
note: New opponent name 'Christian rebels (Erbil)'.

name: Herat (siege, 1319)
how the result was decided: Herat held and Yasa'ur raised the siege as Ilkhanid armies approached.
factions B: Yasa'ur (rebel Chagatayid prince holding an Ilkhanid appanage)
Iranian force: The Kartid garrison and people of Herat against Yasa'ur's Chagatayid Mongol followers.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: civil only if Yasa'ur counts as a rebel Ilkhanid vassal (he held Khorasan lands from Oljaitu); otherwise a Kartid defence against a Chagatai prince
doubts and flags: Borderline: civil only if Yasa'ur counts as a rebel Ilkhanid vassal (he held Khorasan lands from Oljaitu); otherwise a Kartid defence against a Chagatai prince.
sources: Sayfi Haravi; Hafiz-i Abru; en.wikipedia Kart dynasty; en.wikipedia Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan
note: Yasa'ur was killed by Kebek's men in 1320.

date: 20 June 1319 (13 July in the Timeline of the Ilkhanate)
name: Zanjan-Rud
how the result was decided: The Ilkhan's army decisively defeated the rebel emirs, and thirty-six of them were executed.
Iranian force: The young Ilkhan's army with Chupan's following against the rebels' 40,000 (Keraite and other Mongol troops under Irinjin and the governor of Georgia, Qurumishi).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Hafiz-i Abru; en.wikipedia Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan; en.wikipedia Chupan; en.wikipedia Timeline of the Ilkhanate
note: Also called the battle near Mianeh.

date: c. 1320 (first battle; the campaign lasted 13-14 years)
name: Mubariz al-Din's campaign against the Nikudaris
how the result was decided: Mubariz al-Din's horsemen, once reinforced from Yazd, broke Nawruz's Negudaris and pursued them to Bafq.
Iranian force: Mubariz al-Din's 60 horsemen of Yazd, then reinforcements from the town; he was the Ilkhan's governor of Yazd.
why it counts: Muzaffarids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a campaign of some twenty small fights; only the first battle is described, and its date is not given
doubts and flags: Borderline: a campaign of some twenty small fights; only the first battle is described, and its date is not given.
sources: Mahmud Kutubi, Tarikh-i Al-i Muzaffar; en.wikipedia Mubariz al-Din's campaign against the Nikudaris; en.wikipedia Muzaffarids (Iran)
note: New opponent name 'Negudaris' (Nikudari, Qara'unas Mongol tribes of Sistan and Afghanistan).

name: Philippopolis (siege)
war: War with Bulgaria (George Terter II and Michael Shishman), 1322-1324
how the result was decided: As in Battles of the Romans: The defenders had about 1,000 Alan horse and 2,000 foot, with Bulgarian (perhaps also Hungarian) troops. The siege failed, but the city was taken soon afterwards when pro-imperial citizens opened the
commanders A: Ivan the Russian, his deputy Inas; the Alan chiefs Itil and Temir
commanders B: Andronikos III; the Bulgarian despot Voysil of Kopsis (ally)
why it counts: The Alan chiefs Itil and Temir with their men in the Bulgarian garrison (Kantakouzenos 1.37)
sources: Kantakouzenos book 1; Gregoras book 8; en.wikipedia Ivan the Russian
note: The Alan chiefs Itil and Temir with their men in the Bulgarian garrison (Kantakouzenos 1.37)

name: Hisn Kayfa (1334)
how the result was decided: An Artuqid force attacked Hisn Kayfa and was decisively defeated; the Ayyubids gained land on the left bank of the Tigris.
commanders A: Ayyubid emir of Hisn Kayfa (name not given in the source seen)
sources: Wikipedia, Hasankeyf (fetched): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasankeyf
note: Known only from a summary; the commanders and the exact place are not named in the source seen.

name: Jaghatu (1336)
war: Disintegration of the Ilkhanate (succession war after Abu Sa'id)
side B: Arpa Ke'un and the vizier Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad
how the result was decided: Arpa's army fell into disarray when the Uyghur contingent of Akrunj changed sides, and Ali Padshah held the field; Arpa was captured in flight and executed.
factions B: Arpa Ke'un and the vizier Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad
Iranian force: Ali Padshah's Oirat tribesmen and their allies against Arpa's larger army of Mongol and Persian regiments, including Akrunj's mostly Uyghur contingent, which defected before the fighting.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Hafiz-i Abru; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Chobanids; en.wikipedia Battle of Jaghatu
note: Iranica's Chobanids article prints the date as 18 Ramadan 735 / 10 April 1336; the Hijri year must be 736, which gives about 29-30 April 1336, the date in Wikipedia's Qara Darra article.

name: Qara Darra
war: Disintegration of the Ilkhanate (succession war after Abu Sa'id)
place: Qara Darra (Zilan valley) near Erciş, Turkey
how the result was decided: Hasan Buzurg's charge broke Musa's centre and Ali Padshah was captured; Musa fled and Hasan held the field.
commanders A: Hasan Buzurg, Hajji Taghay, Surghan, Botso Tsmedisdze (Georgian vanguard, died of wounds)
Iranian force: Hasan Buzurg's Jalayirs with the Sutayids of Diyarbakir, Chobanid troops under Surghan and a Georgian vanguard under Botso Tsmedisdze; against them the Oirats of Ali Padshah and the Uyghur emir Ogrunch.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: unknown; Ali Padshah killed or executed
sources: Hafiz-i Abru; Sharaf Khan Bidlisi; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Chobanids; en.wikipedia Battle of Qara Darra
note: Muhammad Khan was proclaimed Ilkhan on 20 July and installed at Tabriz on 25 July 1336, with Hasan Buzurg holding real power.

name: Soltaniyeh (1337)
war: Disintegration of the Ilkhanate (succession war after Abu Sa'id)
side B: Togha Temur with Musa Khan and the Oirats
how the result was decided: Togha Temur and Musa were defeated and driven from the region, Togha Temur back to Khorasan.
factions B: Togha Temur (Khorasan) with Musa Khan and the Oirats
commanders B: Togha Temur, Shaykh Ali Ke'un, Musa Khan

note: Izz al-Din Shir was spared and restored under Timurid suzerainty. Some accounts treat the garrison as Qara Qoyunlu partisans.

name: Isfahan (siege, 1387)
war: Timur's Three Years' Campaign (conquest of the Muzaffarid lands)
how the result was decided: After the townsmen rose and killed Timur's tax collectors and soldiers, the city was retaken by storm and massacred.
factions B: Townsmen of Isfahan (Muzaffarid city) in revolt
commanders B: unnamed Muzaffarid governor; the townsmen's leaders
Iranian force: Timur's army against the Persian townsmen of Isfahan.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses A: unknown; about 3,000 soldiers killed in the rising (Yazdi)
losses B: 70,000 or more killed in the massacre
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Mozaffarids; en.wikipedia Siege of Isfahan (1387)
note: Isfahan had first surrendered without a fight; the massacre followed the rising.

name: Alinja (siege)
how the result was decided: The fortress surrendered in 1401, starved out after a long blockade.
commanders A: Timur, Muhammad Miraka, Muhammad Darvish, Miran Shah, Seif ad-Din, Abu Bakr
commanders B: Tahir (son of Ahmad Jalayir), later Sidi Ahmad Ogulsai and three Georgian nobles; George VII (relief)
Iranian force: Timurid troops of Azerbaijan under Miran Shah and his commanders.
why it counts: Inferred: Miran Shah's army combined Chagatai cavalry with levies from Azerbaijan and western Iran.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Alinja, Battle of Alinja
note: The Jalayirid seat was then Baghdad, so the Jalayirids count as opponents under the seat rule. Assaults in 1388, renewed blockade in 1394 and 1396-98; the Georgian relief of 1399 is a separate entry.

name: Kondurcha River
how the result was decided: Timur's line held against the Horde's flank attacks and his counter-attack routed Tokhtamysh's army, many of whose men were trapped against the Volga.
Iranian force: Timur's army that marched across the steppe from Tashkent: Chagatai tribal cavalry in seven divisions, with Tajik foot and levies from Transoxiana and Khorasan.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); no proportions are given.
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; Nizam al-Din Shami; en.wikipedia Battle of the Kondurcha River

name: Mahanasar (siege)
how the result was decided: The Mar'ashi stronghold was taken after a siege and the sayyids were deported.
factions B: Mar'ashi sayyids of Mazandaran (Sayyid Kamal al-Din)
Iranian force: Timur's army against the Mazandarani followers of the Mar'ashi sayyids.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: known from the Persian chronicles; no Wikipedia article, and the course of the siege was not verified
doubts and flags: Borderline: known from the Persian chronicles; no Wikipedia article, and the course of the siege was not verified.
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; Zahir al-Din Mar'ashi, Tarikh-i Tabaristan
note: The Mar'ashis were an Iran-seated local dynasty, so the fight counts as civil.

name: Qal'a-i Safid (siege)
war: Timur's Five Years' Campaign (end of the Muzaffarids)
how the result was decided: Timur's troops stormed the fortress and freed the blinded Muzaffarid prince Zayn al-Abidin.
Iranian force: Timur's army against Shah Mansur's garrison of Fars.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no separate article; the storming is told in Yazdi, and Wikipedia mentions only the freeing of Zayn al-Abidin
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article; the storming is told in Yazdi, and Wikipedia mentions only the freeing of Zayn al-Abidin.
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Mozaffarids; en.wikipedia Battle of Shiraz (1393)

name: Shiraz (1393)
war: Timur's Five Years' Campaign (end of the Muzaffarids)
how the result was decided: Shah Mansur's charge reached Timur but his army was routed and he was killed in the pursuit by Shah Rukh's men; Timur held the field.
Iranian force: Timur's army with Shah Rukh's division, against Shah Mansur's 3,000-4,000 armoured horsemen of Fars.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Mozaffarids; historyofwar.org Battle of Shiraz 1393; en.wikipedia Battle of Shiraz (1393)
note: Iranica dates the execution of the remaining Muzaffarid princes to 23 May 1393; some accounts put the battle in April or May.

name: Baghdad (siege, 1393)
war: Timur's Five Years' Campaign (war with the Jalayirids)
how the result was decided: Baghdad fell to Timur at the end of August 1393 after Sultan Ahmad fled.
Iranian force: Timur's army of the Five Years' Campaign: Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik foot and Iranian levies.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); no proportions are given.
borderline: little fighting is recorded at Baghdad itself; Ahmad fled as Timur approached
doubts and flags: Borderline: little fighting is recorded at Baghdad itself; Ahmad fled as Timur approached.
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; en.wikipedia Siege of Baghdad (1393), Capture of Baghdad (1394)
note: The Jalayirid seat was Baghdad, so the Jalayirids count as opponents under the seat rule. Ahmad retook the city with Mamluk help in 1394 without a fight.

name: Tikrit (siege, 1393)
how the result was decided: The walls were undermined and brought down and the fortress was stormed on 11 December; Hasan was captured.
commanders B: Amir Hasan (chief of the band holding the fortress)
Iranian force: Timur's army, each tuman digging its own mine under the walls (72,000 diggers in Yazdi).
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); no proportions are given.
losses B: the defenders executed; towers of skulls built
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; historyofwar.org Siege of Takrit 1393
note: The fortress was held by a band that preyed on caravans; Yazdi names no overlord.

name: Astrakhan (siege, 1395)
how the result was decided: Timur's forces took and sacked Hajji Tarkhan.
Iranian force: Timur's army of the Five Years' Campaign: Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik foot and levies.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); no proportions are given.
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; en.wikipedia Siege of Astrakhan (1395)

name: Khankala (1395)
place: Khankala gorge, south-east of Grozny, Russia
how the result was decided: The main army of Simsim was almost destroyed in the Khankala gorge.
commanders B: Khour II and other Chechen nobles of Simsim
Iranian force: Timur's army after the Terek: Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik foot and Iranian levies, much larger than its opponent.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); no proportions are given.
borderline: rests on recent Chechen historical writing as presented in Wikipedia; not named in the classic Timurid histories consulted
doubts and flags: Borderline: rests on recent Chechen historical writing as presented in Wikipedia; not named in the classic Timurid histories consulted.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Khankala (1395), Timurid invasion of Simsim
note: Simsim was a Vainakh (Chechen-Ingush) principality allied to the Golden Horde.

name: Sarai (siege, 1395)
how the result was decided: Sarai was taken and burned and its craftsmen deported to Central Asia.
Iranian force: Timur's army of the Five Years' Campaign: Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik foot and levies.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); no proportions are given.
borderline: little fighting is described; it may have been a capture and sack
doubts and flags: Borderline: little fighting is described; it may have been a capture and sack.
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; en.wikipedia Siege of Sarai (1395)
note: Which Sarai (Old Sarai at Selitrennoye or New Sarai near Tsarev) is meant is not certain; New Sarai is given.

name: Terek River
how the result was decided: After some of Tokhtamysh's emirs went over, Timur routed the Horde's left wing and Tokhtamysh fled north, leaving Timur the field.
Iranian force: Timur's army of the Five Years' Campaign: Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik foot and levies from Iran and Transoxiana; Golden Horde emirs such as Aktau defected to it during the battle.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); no proportions are given.
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; en.wikipedia Battle of the Terek River, Tokhtamysh
note: Wikipedia's coordinates (43.58, 47.45) lie near the Caspian; most accounts put the battle on the middle Terek, so only the region is given. Timur was nearly killed in the battle.

name: Krishna River and the Raichur Doab (1398)
place: Krishna-Tungabhadra Doab (Raichur Doab), Karnataka, India; exact site unknown
how the result was decided: After Qazi Sirajuddin killed Prince Bukka in the Vijayanagara camp, a Bahmani force of about 4,000 scattered the disordered army and Harihara II paid a ransom and tribute (Wikipedia).
commanders A: Firuz Shah, Qazi Sirajuddin, Ahmad Shah I and Malik Na'ib
doubts and flags: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition. Whether this people was Iranian, or the leader of Iranian descent, is uncertain.
sources: Wikipedia 'Bahmani-Vijayanagar War (1398)' (fetched 1 Nov 2026); Ferishta
note: Descent of the dynasty is disputed: Wikipedia ('Bahmani Sultanate') cites Esami and Andre Wink for an Afghan origin of Hasan Gangu and Encyclopaedia Iranica for a 'Khorasani adventurer who claimed descent from Bahram Gur' (Ferishta calls the Persian pedigree flattery). Either way Iranian, so both peoples are marked uncertain. The assassination story is Ferishta's and may be embroidered; no formal battle is named.

name: Multan (siege, 1398)
how the result was decided: Multan fell to Pir Muhammad after a siege of about six months.
Iranian force: Pir Muhammad's army from his appanage of Kabul, Ghazni and Kandahar: Chagatai cavalry with levies from eastern Afghanistan.
why it counts: Inferred: Pir Muhammad's levies came from Persian- and Pashto-speaking eastern Afghanistan.
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; en.wikipedia Siege of Multan (1398)
note: The siege may have begun late in 1397.

name: Bhatner (siege)
how the result was decided: The fort was stormed, its chief surrendered, and the fort and town were destroyed.
Iranian force: Timur's Indian army (about 90,000): Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik foot and Afghan and Iranian levies.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); no proportions are given.
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; en.wikipedia Timur, Timurid conquests and invasions
note: Rai Dul Chand was the Bhati chief of Bhatner.

name: Delhi (1398)
how the result was decided: The Delhi army and its war elephants were routed before the city and the sultan fled; Delhi was sacked in the following days.
commanders B: Nasir-ud-Din Mahmud Shah Tughluq, Mallu Iqbal
Iranian force: Timur's Indian army of about 90,000: Chagatai tribal cavalry behind a ditch and caltrops, with Tajik foot, archers and Afghan and Iranian levies.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies, including Pir Muhammad's men from Afghanistan (Manz); no proportions are given.
losses B: heavy; about 100,000 civilians killed in and around the city
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; Nizam al-Din Shami; en.wikipedia Sack of Delhi (1398)
note: Before the battle Timur had some 100,000 Indian prisoners killed. Some popular accounts place the battle at Panipat; the sources put it before Delhi.

name: Alinja
war: Timurid invasions of Georgia (relief of Alinja)
how the result was decided: The Georgians broke the blockade and then defeated Abu Bakr's relief army, which fell back to Tabriz.
commanders B: Abu Bakr (son of Miran Shah), Seif ad-Din
Iranian force: Miran Shah's Timurid army of Azerbaijan under his son Abu Bakr, with the besieging force of Seif ad-Din.
why it counts: Inferred: Miran Shah's army combined Chagatai cavalry with levies from Azerbaijan and western Iran.
sources: Georgian Chronicles; en.wikipedia Battle of Alinja, Siege of Alinja
note: The Georgians freed Prince Tahir; Timur's reprisal campaign of 1399-1400 followed.

name: Meerut (siege)
how the result was decided: The fort was undermined and stormed and its defenders killed.
commanders B: the commanders of the fort (Ilyas Afghan and his son in Yazdi)
Iranian force: Timur's Indian army on its return march: Chagatai cavalry with sappers and Tajik foot.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); no proportions are given.
borderline: known from Yazdi; no Wikipedia article, and the defenders' names were not verified
doubts and flags: Borderline: known from Yazdi; no Wikipedia article, and the defenders' names were not verified.
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; en.wikipedia Timurid conquests and invasions
note: Wikipedia mentions resistance by local (Jat and khap) militias near Meerut.

name: Sagim River
how the result was decided: George VII's army was defeated and scattered.
Iranian force: Timur's army of the Seven Years' Campaign: Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik foot and Iranian levies.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); no proportions are given.
borderline: no separate article; named in Wikipedia's Timurid invasions of Georgia
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article; named in Wikipedia's Timurid invasions of Georgia.
sources: Georgian Chronicles; en.wikipedia Timurid invasions of Georgia

name: Sebaste (siege, 1400)
how the result was decided: Sivas surrendered after a short, hard siege; the Armenian soldiers of the garrison were then buried alive.
commanders B: the Ottoman garrison (Suleyman Celebi commanded in the region)
Iranian force: Timur's army of the Seven Years' Campaign: Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik foot, miners and Iranian levies.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); no proportions are given.
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; en.wikipedia Sack of Sebaste (1400)

date: 30 October 1400; the citadel surrendered by 2 November
name: Aleppo (1400)
how the result was decided: The Mamluk governors' army broke under Timur's flank attacks and fled into the city, which was then taken.
commanders B: Tamardash (Aleppo), Sudun (Damascus), Shaykh al-Mahmudi (Tripoli), Azdemir (killed) and the other Syrian governors
Iranian force: Timur's army of the Seven Years' Campaign: Chagatai cavalry wings, a centre with Indian war elephants, Tajik foot and Iranian levies.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); the Indian language entry is for the elephant crews.
sources: Ibn Taghribirdi; Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; en.wikipedia Sack of Aleppo (1400)
note: The Mamluk sultan Faraj was not present.

name: Damascus (siege, 1400)
how the result was decided: Faraj's relief army was beaten outside Damascus and withdrew to Egypt, and the city and then its citadel were surrendered to Timur.
Iranian force: Timur's army of the Seven Years' Campaign: Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik foot, siege engineers and Iranian levies.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); no proportions are given.
losses B: about 50,000 dead in the infobox, many burned in the mosques
sources: Ibn Khaldun; Ibn Taghribirdi; en.wikipedia Siege of Damascus (1400)
note: Ibn Khaldun negotiated with Timur during the siege; the city was sacked and the Umayyad Mosque burned in March 1401.

name: Baghdad (siege, 1401)
how the result was decided: Baghdad was stormed after a siege of about 40 days and sacked.
commanders B: Faraj (commander for Sultan Ahmad, who had left)
Iranian force: Timur's army of the Seven Years' Campaign, described as a Turco-Mongol army: Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik foot and Iranian levies.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); no proportions are given.
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; Ibn Taghribirdi; en.wikipedia Siege of Baghdad (1401)
note: The Jalayirid seat was Baghdad, so the Jalayirids count as opponents under the seat rule.

name: Algami Canal
place: Algami Canal between Hillah and Baghdad, Iraq
how the result was decided: Qara Yusuf's army was routed and Baghdad was recovered for the Timurids.
Iranian force: Abu Bakr's Timurid army of Azerbaijan and Iraq.
why it counts: Inferred: Chagatai cavalry with levies from Azerbaijan and western Iran.
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Algami Canal, Qara Yusuf
note: Qara Yusuf had taken Baghdad after Timur's departure for Anatolia; he fled to the Mamluks after this defeat.

name: Tortum (siege, 1402)
how the result was decided: After five days of fighting the fortress was taken and destroyed.
Iranian force: Timur's army on its way to the Ottoman war: Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik foot and Iranian levies.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); no proportions are given.
borderline: no separate article; a small fortress action named in Wikipedia's Timurid invasions of Georgia
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article; a small fortress action named in Wikipedia's Timurid invasions of Georgia.
sources: en.wikipedia Timurid invasions of Georgia

name: Ankara
how the result was decided: The Ottoman army broke after the Tatars and beylik troops went over to Timur, and Bayezid was captured in flight; Timur held the field.
commanders A: Timur, Miran Shah, Shah Rukh, Muhammad Sultan, Khalil Sultan
commanders B: Bayezid I (captured), Suleyman Celebi, Mehmed Celebi, Stefan Lazarevic
Iranian force: Timur's whole army: Chagatai cavalry wings under Miran Shah and Shah Rukh, a vanguard under his grandsons, Timur's centre with Indian war elephants, and contingents from Transoxiana, Khorasan and western Iran; the Black Tatars and Anatolian beylik troops changed sides to join it.
why it counts: Besides the Turkic-speaking Chagatai cavalry, Timur's army drew Tajik foot and contingents from Khorasan and western Iran (Manz); no proportions are given, and the deserters who joined him were Turkic.
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; Ibn Arabshah; en.wikipedia Battle of Ankara
note: Wikipedia's Timur article gives 20 July 1402; 28 July is the usual date. Timur's elephants (about 32) came from India.

name: Smyrna (siege)
how the result was decided: Mines breached the walls and the city was stormed; the Knights escaped by sea.
Iranian force: Timur's army in three divisions with miners, stone-throwers and wheeled siege towers, and a mole built to close the harbour.
why it counts: Timur's army was a core of Turkic-speaking Chagatai tribal cavalry with Tajik infantry and provincial levies (Manz); no proportions are given.
sources: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; en.wikipedia Siege of Smyrna
note: The defenders were the Knights Hospitaller of Rhodes.

date: 1403; the gates were stormed on 12 August 1403
name: Birtvisi (siege, 1403)
how the result was decided: After eight attempts, Merkit climbers stormed the gates and the fortress fell.
commanders A: Timur (ordered the siege), Shah Ibrahim of Shirvan (led the attack)
Iranian force: Timurid troops including 52 Merkit volunteer climbers, with the army of Timur's vassal Shah Ibrahim of Shirvan.
why it counts: Inferred: Chagatai troops with Shirvani forces, who spoke Persian (Tat) and Turkic.
sources: Georgian Chronicles; en.wikipedia Siege of Birtvisi (1403)

name: Nakhchivan (1406)
place: on the Aras near Nakhchivan, Azerbaijan
how the result was decided: Qara Yusuf held the field and Abu Bakr's demoralized army retreated.
commanders B: Abu Bakr Mirza (son of Miran Shah), Malik Izz al-Din of Kurdistan
Iranian force: Abu Bakr's Timurid army of Azerbaijan (Chagatai cavalry and local troops), joined by the Kurdish contingent of Malik Izz al-Din of Kurdistan; no numbers.
why it counts: The Kurdish contingent is named; the rest is inferred from Timurid recruitment (a Chagatai Turkic tribal core with native Iranian levies).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Nakhchivan (1406); en.wikipedia Qara Yusuf; en.wikipedia Qara Qoyunlu
note: Qara Yusuf took Tabriz after this battle (late 1406), so from then on the Qara Qoyunlu count as seated in Iran; here they are still the invader. The Qara Qoyunlu as a non-Persian opponent are named 'Qara Qoyunlu' (new name).

name: Gandoman
place: meadow of Gandoman, between Isfahan and Shiraz, Iran
side B: Rustam and Iskandar Sultan, his brothers
how the result was decided: Pir Muhammad won and both brothers fled the field.
factions A: Pir Muhammad (son of Umar Shaikh), ruler of Fars
factions B: Rustam and Iskandar Sultan, his brothers (Isfahan)
Iranian force: The Timurid armies of Fars and of Isfahan: Chagatai amirs with their followers and local troops; after the battle Pir Muhammad won over much of Rustam's army with an amnesty.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Pir Muhammad (son of Umar Shaikh); en.wikipedia Iskandar Sultan
note: Wikipedia says 'near Shiraz'; the village of Gandoman lies near Borujen, so the site is approximate.

name: Sardrud
how the result was decided: Qara Yusuf forestalled Abu Bakr's attack and decisively defeated the Timurid army; Miran Shah was killed.
Iranian force: Qara Yusuf's Turkmen tribal cavalry against the Timurid army of Azerbaijan and Iraq under Miran Shah and Abu Bakr (Chagatai cavalry and local troops); no numbers.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Nakhchivan (1406) (aftermath); en.wikipedia Qara Yusuf; en.wikipedia Qara Qoyunlu
note: Civil because the Qara Qoyunlu had held Tabriz since late 1406; Qara Yusuf was still nominally a Jalayirid vassal until 1410.

date: July 1414 (Iskandar defeated and captured on 21 July)
name: Isfahan (siege, 1414)
war: First Timurid war of succession (Shah Rukh against Iskandar Sultan)
side A (victor if decisive): Shah Rukh, with the princes Rustam and Bayqara
how the result was decided: Iskandar was defeated and captured and Isfahan submitted to Shah Rukh after a short siege.
factions A: Shah Rukh, with the princes Rustam and Bayqara
Iranian force: Shah Rukh's army of Khorasan with the troops of Rustam and Bayqara, against Iskandar's forces and the city of Isfahan.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Iskandar Sultan; en.wikipedia Shah Rukh; Kure Ansiklopedi, Sahruh
note: Shah Rukh's article dates Iskandar's revolt to 1413; Iskandar was executed after a further revolt in 1415.

name: Eleşkirt
war: Timurid-Qara Qoyunlu wars (Shah Rukh's Azerbaijan campaign of 1420-21)
how the result was decided: After three days of fighting the Qara Qoyunlu gave way and retreated toward Kirkuk, leaving the field to Shah Rukh.
factions B: Qara Qoyunlu (Iskandar and Ispend, sons of Qara Yusuf)
Iranian force: Shah Rukh's imperial army (Chagatai cavalry with levies from Khorasan and western Iran; about 200,000 claimed for the campaign) against the Qara Qoyunlu Turkmen cavalry and Kurdish allies.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Qara Iskander; Kure Ansiklopedi, Sahruh; en.wikipedia Shah Rukh
note: Wikipedia's Qara Iskander article places the battle at 'Yakhsi' and says the Timurids nearly lost before a ruse by Amir Shah Malik; Turkish works call it the battle of Eleşkirt (spring/summer 824). Shah Rukh then briefly occupied Tabriz.

name: Salmas
war: Timurid-Qara Qoyunlu wars (Shah Rukh's second campaign)
how the result was decided: Abu Said withdrew in the middle of the battle and submitted, and the Qara Qoyunlu retreated to Diyar Bakr, leaving the field to Shah Rukh.
commanders B: Qara Iskandar; Abu Said (deserted to Shah Rukh during the battle)
Iranian force: Shah Rukh's army of about 100,000 (Chagatai cavalry and provincial levies) against Iskandar's Turkmen cavalry.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Qara Iskander; en.wikipedia Abu Said (Qara Qoyunlu); en.wikipedia Shah Rukh
note: Shah Rukh installed Abu Said as Qara Qoyunlu ruler; Iskandar killed him after the Timurid withdrawal (1430/31).

name: Sufiyan (1436)
war: Qara Qoyunlu civil war (Jahan Shah against Iskandar)
how the result was decided: Iskandar was defeated after his emirs, including his nephew Shah Ali, betrayed him, and he fled to Alinja.
Iranian force: Qara Qoyunlu Turkmen on both sides; Jahan Shah had Timurid backing.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Qara Iskander; en.wikipedia Jahan Shah

name: Alinja (siege, 1438)
war: Qara Qoyunlu civil war (Jahan Shah against Iskandar)
place: Alinja fortress, near Julfa, Nakhchivan, Azerbaijan
side B: Qara Iskandar, then his son Shah Qubad
how the result was decided: Iskandar was murdered by his son inside the besieged fortress, which passed to Jahan Shah; he executed Shah Qubad on 23 April 1438.
factions B: Qara Iskandar, then his son Shah Qubad
Iranian force: Jahan Shah's Qara Qoyunlu Turkmen against Iskandar's remaining followers in the fortress.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: the fortress passed to the besieger after the defender's murder; the fighting is not described
doubts and flags: Borderline: the fortress passed to the besieger after the defender's murder; the fighting is not described.
sources: en.wikipedia Qara Iskander; en.wikipedia Jahan Shah
note: Iskandar sought a Mamluk alliance during the siege.

name: Baghdad (siege, 1445-46)
how the result was decided: Baghdad was captured on 9 June 1446 after a seven-month siege.
factions B: Ispend's heirs at Baghdad (Alvand Mirza, with emirs favouring Fulad Mirza)
Iranian force: Jahan Shah's Qara Qoyunlu army against the Baghdad branch of the Qara Qoyunlu with the city's garrison.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Jahan Shah
note: Civil: the Baghdad line was a branch of the Qara Qoyunlu state ruled from Tabriz.

name: Balkh (siege, 1447)
side A (victor if decisive): Abdal-Latif Mirza, governor of Balkh for Ulugh Beg
how the result was decided: Ala al-Dawla raised the siege and withdrew to Herat after Ulugh Beg's envoy intervened; Balkh did not fall.
factions A: Abdal-Latif Mirza, governor of Balkh for Ulugh Beg
Iranian force: Ala al-Dawla's Khorasan army against the garrison of Balkh.

name: Nishapur (1447)
how the result was decided: Ala al-Dawla's surprise attack defeated the encircled Abd al-Latif, who was captured.
Iranian force: Ala al-Dawla's army of Herat and Khorasan against Abd al-Latif's army; Chagatai cavalry with Khorasan levies on both sides.

sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Nishapur (1447); en.wikipedia Battle of Damghan (1447)

name: Herat (siege, 1448)
how the result was decided: The city fell at once and the citadel's resistance collapsed soon after Ulugh Beg arrived on the seventeenth day.
factions B: Ala al-Dawla Mirza's garrison (citadel of Ikhtiyar al-Din and Fort Neretu)
Iranian force: Ulugh Beg's Transoxianan army against Herat's citadel garrison, in which Tajik archers from Bakharz repelled many assaults.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Herat (1448)
note: Abd al-Latif seized 4,000 tomans from the citadel; Ulugh Beg went on to take Mashhad.

name: Tarnab
how the result was decided: After a brief engagement Ulugh Beg decisively defeated Ala al-Dawla, who fled to Mashhad.
factions A: Timurids of Samarkand (Ulugh Beg, Abdal-Latif Mirza)
Iranian force: Ulugh Beg's army of Transoxiana (reportedly 90,000) against Ala al-Dawla's army of Herat.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Tarnab (1448); en.wikipedia Abul-Qasim Babur Mirza
note: Wikipedia's Ulugh Beg article has Ulugh Beg defeat Ala al-Dawla 'at Murghab' in 1447, probably the same battle.

Iranian force: Abu Sa'id's followers against the garrison of Samarkand.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

name: Farhadgerd

factions A: Sultan Muhammad (Timurid ruler of Iraq-i Ajam and Fars)
Iranian force: Sultan Muhammad's army of western Iran against Babur Mirza's army of Khorasan; Chagatai amirs with Iranian provincial troops.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: the identification of the campaign box's 'Farhadgerd' with Babur Mirza's defeat near Mashhad in March 1450 is an inference

sources: en.wikipedia Abul-Qasim Babur Mirza; Campaignbox Second Timurid Succession Crisis ('Farhadgerd')

name: Samarkand (1451)
side A (victor if decisive): Abu Sa'id Mirza, with Abu'l-Khayr Khan's Uzbeks
how the result was decided: Abdallah was defeated and killed and Samarkand opened its gates to Abu Sa'id.
factions A: Abu Sa'id Mirza, with Abu'l-Khayr Khan's Uzbeks
Iranian force: Abu Sa'id's Timurid followers with Abu'l-Khayr's Uzbek horse as allies, against Abdallah's army of Samarkand.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

sources: en.wikipedia Abu Sa'id Mirza; en.wikipedia Abdallah Mirza; en.wikipedia Abu'l-Khayr Khan

name: Narela
war: Bahlul Lodi's wars against the Sharqis of Jaunpur
allies B: Afghan contingent of Darya Khan Lodi
how the result was decided: Darya Khan Lodi's Afghans left the Sharqi army after a tribal appeal, the army broke, Fath Khan Harawi was captured and executed, and Mahmud Shah raised the siege of Delhi.
Iranian side: Bahlul Khan Lodi v Sharqi Sultanate of Jaunpur
commanders A: Bahlul Khan Lodi; Qutb Khan Lodi; Rai Karan
commanders B: Fath Khan Harawi; Darya Khan Lodi; Mahmud Shah Sharqi (at the siege of Delhi)
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Narela (1452): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Narela_(1452); Nizamuddin Ahmad, Tabaqat-i Akbari; Ferishta, Tarikh-i Firishta
note: Bahlul, a Lodi Afghan, was fighting for the throne of Delhi against the Sharqi army; the Sharqi field commander Darya Khan Lodi was also an Afghan. Fath Khan Harawi's origin (Herat) is not treated as qualifying.

name: Samarkand (siege, 1454)
how the result was decided: The siege ended in an agreement while the city was still invested, making the Oxus the border.
Iranian force: Babur Mirza's army of Khorasan against Abu Sa'id's garrison of Samarkand.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Abul-Qasim Babur Mirza; en.wikipedia Abu Sa'id Mirza
note: The Oxus border held until Babur Mirza's death in 1457.

name: Sarakhs (1459)
how the result was decided: Reinforcements reached Abu Sa'id in time and the confederates were defeated; Sanjar was captured and the others fled.
factions B: Timurids of Khurasan and Merv (Ala al-Dawla Mirza, Ibrahim Mirza, Sultan Sanjar Mirza)
commanders A: Abu Sa'id Mirza, Amir Ali Farsi, Amir Sayyid Asil
commanders B: Ala al-Dawla Mirza, Ibrahim Mirza, Sultan Sanjar Mirza (captured, executed)
Iranian force: Abu Sa'id's outnumbered army with reinforcements under Amir Ali Farsi and Amir Sayyid Asil, against the confederate princes' armies of Khorasan and Merv.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Sarakhs (1459); en.wikipedia Abu Sa'id Mirza
note: Wikipedia gives the place as 'Khurasan, Iran'; the battle was fought between Merv and Sarakhs, on the present Turkmen side (approximate).

name: Ghwarah Marghah
how the result was decided: The Yusufzai broke the Timurid and Gigyani line and routed them.
Iranian force: The Timurid army of Kabul with its Gigyani Afghan allies; no numbers.
why it counts: A Chagatai-led army of Kabul (Tajik subjects) with Pashto-speaking Gigyani allies; proportions are not recorded.
borderline: Kabul lies at the edge of the seat rule's Greater Khorasan; the Wikipedia article is thinly sourced and its year (1460) precedes Ulugh Beg II's rule at Kabul (from 1461)
doubts and flags: Borderline: Kabul lies at the edge of the seat rule's Greater Khorasan; the Wikipedia article is thinly sourced and its year (1460) precedes Ulugh Beg II's rule at Kabul (from 1461).
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Ghwarah Marghah
note: Afghans = the Yusufzai confederacy (victors) and the Gigyani (allies of the Timurids).

name: Tabasaran (1460)
how the result was decided: Junayd was killed and his followers defeated.
commanders A: the army of Shirvanshah Khalilullah I
Iranian force: Junayd's Sufi ghazis, mostly Turkmen tribesmen from Anatolia and northern Syria (the future Qizilbash), with disciples from Ardabil.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the Safavid order before the Safavid state (1501), counted because its force fought as a principal
doubts and flags: Borderline: the Safavid order before the Safavid state (1501), counted because its force fought as a principal.
sources: en.wikipedia Shaykh Haydar
note: Wikipedia's Shaykh Haydar article places Junayd's death in battle at Tabasaran without naming the opponent; other accounts put it on the Kura against the Shirvanshah's troops.

name: Hasankeyf (siege, 1461-62)
war: Aq Qoyunlu conquest of Hisn Kayfa
how the result was decided: Uzun Hasan captured Hisn Kayfa in 1462 after a six-month siege and made his son Zeynel its governor.
commanders A: Ayyubid emir of Hisn Kayfa (name not given)
sources: Wikipedia, Hasankeyf (fetched): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasankeyf
note: The Ayyubid emir had rebelled in 1460 and tried to take Siirt; the dynasty lingered as vassals until the Ottoman conquest.

name: Jauzi Wali
side B: Sultan Mahmud Mirza, son of Abu Sa'id
how the result was decided: Husayn defeated Sultan Mahmud and took Jurjan.
factions B: Sultan Mahmud Mirza, son of Abu Sa'id
Iranian force: Husayn Bayqara's followers against Sultan Mahmud's army of Jurjan; Timurid cavalry forces.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Husayn Bayqara; Campaignbox Second Timurid Succession Crisis
note: Husayn appointed Abd al-Rahman Arghun governor of Jurjan.

name: Herat (siege, 1461)
side A (victor if decisive): Abu Sa'id Mirza's garrison of Herat
how the result was decided: Husayn raised the siege and fled to Khwarazm before Abu Sa'id returned.
factions A: Abu Sa'id Mirza's garrison of Herat
Iranian force: Husayn Bayqara's army against the garrison and people of Herat.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Husayn Bayqara; en.wikipedia Siege of Shahrukhiya

date: 1462 (a 17-day siege of the Bahmani capital; exact month not fixed in the sources used)
name: Bidar (siege, 1462)
war: Bahmani-Malwa war of 1461-1463 (Mahmud Khalji's invasion of the Bahmani Sultanate)
how the result was decided: Khalji reached the citadel but lifted the siege and withdrew when the joint army of Mahmud Gawan and Mahmud Begada of Gujarat advanced (Wikipedia, Mahmud Gawan; Ferishta).
commanders B: Mahmud Gawan (Persian-speaking Afaqi from Gawan in Gilan; regent and minister); Makhduma-i Jahan (queen mother, regent); Nizam Shah (child sultan); Mahmud Begada of Gujarat (relief army)
sources: Muhammad Qasim Ferishta, Tarikh-i Firishta (trans. J. Briggs, History of the Rise of the Mahomedan Power in India, vol. 2); H. K. Sherwani, Mahmud Gawan, the Great Bahmani Wazir (1942); R. M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 1300-1761 (2005); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmud_Gawan
note: Gawan, born in Gilan to a family of ministers of the Gilani kingdom and Persian-speaking, was one of the regents directing the Bahmani defence; the child sultan and the queen mother were nominally in charge. His personal command in the field is stated by Ferishta and the modern summaries but the details are thin.

date: November 1462-September 1463 (an earlier siege in 1461 ended in a truce)
name: Shahrukhiya (siege)
place: Shahrukhiya, on the Syr Darya, Tashkent region, Uzbekistan
side B: Muhammad Juki Mirza, with Uzbek confederates
how the result was decided: After about a year's siege Shahrukhiya surrendered on terms negotiated by Khwaja Ubaydullah Ahrar.
factions B: Muhammad Juki Mirza (Shahrukhiya), with Uzbek confederates
Iranian force: Abu Sa'id's Transoxianan army against Juki Mirza's garrison, supported by Uzbek raiding bands.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Shahrukhiya; en.wikipedia Abu Sa'id Mirza
note: Juki Mirza died in the citadel of Herat in 1464.

name: Baghdad (siege, 1464-66)
war: Qara Qoyunlu civil wars (revolt of Pir Budaq)
side B: Pir Budaq, rebel governor of Baghdad
how the result was decided: After an eighteen-month siege the city surrendered and Pir Budaq was killed.
factions A: Jahan Shah (the final assault led by his son Muhammadi)
factions B: Pir Budaq, rebel governor of Baghdad
Iranian force: Jahan Shah's Qara Qoyunlu army against Pir Budaq's followers and the Baghdad garrison.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Pir Budaq; en.wikipedia Jahan Shah; en.wikipedia Qara Qoyunlu
note: The Jahan Shah and Qara Qoyunlu articles date Pir Budaq's defeat to 1464; the Pir Budaq article has an eighteen-month siege ending in 1466.

date: 1469-1470 (monsoon-season siege during the Konkan campaign; exact months not known)
name: Khelna (siege, 1469-1470)
war: Bahmani conquest of the Konkan (Mahmud Gawan's campaign of 1469-1472)
side B: Konkan chiefs of Khelna and Sangameshwar
how the result was decided: The Bahmani army took the hill-fortress of Khelna and then the Konkan coast, ending with Dabhol and Goa (Ferishta; Wikipedia, Mahmud Gawan, dates the Konkan conquest to 1469-1472).
principal opponents: Konkan chiefs of Khelna and Sangameshwar
commanders A: Mahmud Gawan (Persian-speaking Afaqi from Gilan); Muhammad Shah III Lashkari (sultan)
commanders B: Local Hindu chief of Khelna (name not recorded in the sources used)
sources: Muhammad Qasim Ferishta, Tarikh-i Firishta (trans. J. Briggs, History of the Rise of the Mahomedan Power in India, vol. 2); H. K. Sherwani, Mahmud Gawan, the Great Bahmani Wazir (1942); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmud_Gawan
note: Ferishta names Khelna as the great hill-fort reduced after a long siege in the rains at the start of Gawan's Konkan campaign. The siege dating and the defender's name are weakly documented in the secondary sources I could check.

name: Herat (siege, 1469)
side B: the officers of the late Abu Sa'id in Herat
how the result was decided: Herat fell to Husayn on 24 March 1469 and Abu Sa'id's beaten army joined him.
factions B: the officers of the late Abu Sa'id in Herat
Iranian force: Husayn Bayqara's followers against the Herat garrison.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a short siege with little recorded fighting
doubts and flags: Borderline: a short siege with little recorded fighting.
sources: en.wikipedia Husayn Bayqara

name: Chenaran
war: Third Timurid war of succession (Yadgar Muhammad's bid for Khorasan)
side B: Yadgar Muhammad Mirza, backed by Uzun Hasan's Aq Qoyunlu
how the result was decided: Husayn defeated Yadgar Muhammad.
factions B: Yadgar Muhammad Mirza, backed by Uzun Hasan's Aq Qoyunlu
Iranian force: Husayn's Khorasan army against Yadgar Muhammad's followers with Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen troops lent by Uzun Hasan.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Husayn Bayqara; Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu
note: Yadgar was then reinforced by the Aq Qoyunlu and took Herat in July 1470.

date: August 1470 (about six weeks after Yadgar entered Herat on 7 July)
name: Herat (1470)
war: Third Timurid war of succession (Yadgar Muhammad's bid for Khorasan)
side B: Yadgar Muhammad Mirza and his Aq Qoyunlu troops
how the result was decided: Husayn retook Herat by surprise and captured Yadgar Muhammad, who was executed.
factions B: Yadgar Muhammad Mirza and his Aq Qoyunlu troops
Iranian force: A small band of Husayn's followers (850 men are mentioned) against Yadgar's followers and Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen troops.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Husayn Bayqara; Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu
note: Husayn had abandoned Herat without a battle on 7 July 1470; Wikipedia's account (garbled) also mentions his defeat of Aq Qoyunlu troops on the Murghab with 850 men.

date: Late 1472 into 1473 (Wikipedia gives 1472; Ferishta's 877 AH spans June 1472-May 1473; some modern works say 1473)
name: Belgaum (siege, 1472-1473)
war: Bahmani-Vijayanagara war (after the capture of Goa)
how the result was decided: After the failed Vijayanagara counter-attack at Goa, Gawan and the sultan besieged Belgaum and the raja surrendered, keeping his post as keeper of the fort (Wikipedia, Mahmud Gawan).
commanders A: Mahmud Gawan (Persian-speaking Afaqi from Gilan); Muhammad Shah III Lashkari (sultan)
commanders B: Raja of Belgaum (Vijayanagara feudatory; name not recorded in the sources used)
sources: Muhammad Qasim Ferishta, Tarikh-i Firishta (trans. J. Briggs, History of the Rise of the Mahomedan Power in India, vol. 2); H. K. Sherwani, Mahmud Gawan, the Great Bahmani Wazir (1942); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmud_Gawan
note: Wikipedia calls this reportedly the first known use of gunpowder in the Deccan. Belgaum later became the estate of the Bijapur noble Asad Khan Lari.

date: 1470-1472 (the Mahmud Gawan article gives February 1472, with Goa; other accounts put Dabhol earlier)
name: Dabhol (1472)
war: Bahmani conquest of the Konkan (Mahmud Gawan's campaign of 1469-1472)
how the result was decided: Dabhol was captured with Goa during Gawan's Konkan campaign (Wikipedia 'Mahmud Gawan').
commanders A: Mahmud Gawan (Afaqi minister of Gilani origin)
sources: Wikipedia 'Mahmud Gawan' and 'Bahmani Sultanate' (fetched 1 Nov 2026); Ferishta
note: Mahmud Gawan, born in Gawan in Gilan (northern Persia), was a Persian Afaqi noble who directed the Bahmani army in the Konkan; the dynasty's own descent is disputed (see Daulatabad 1347). Weak: the sources give the capture without detail, and the date varies.

date: February 1472 (Wikipedia, Mahmud Gawan); Ferishta's year 877 AH runs from June 1472
name: Goa (Bahmani capture, 1472)
place: Goa (Old Goa and the Mandovi estuary), Goa
how the result was decided: Gawan captured Goa and Dabhol in 1472, and Virupaksha's attempted counter-attack on Goa failed (Wikipedia, Mahmud Gawan; Ferishta).
commanders A: Mahmud Gawan (Persian-speaking Afaqi from Gilan); Muhammad Shah III Lashkari (sultan)
commanders B: Vijayanagara governor of Goa (name not recorded in the sources used); Virupaksha Raya II (whose counter-attack failed)
sources: Muhammad Qasim Ferishta, Tarikh-i Firishta (trans. J. Briggs, History of the Rise of the Mahomedan Power in India, vol. 2); H. K. Sherwani, Mahmud Gawan, the Great Bahmani Wazir (1942); R. M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 1300-1761 (2005); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmud_Gawan
note: Goa was a major horse-importing port of Vijayanagara; its loss was a lasting blow to that empire. Gawan commanded the expedition himself according to Ferishta.

date: 15 July 1478 (14 Rabi II 883); other dates given are 15 June and 14 August 1478
name: Khoy (1478)
place: on the Khoy river, near Khoy, Iran
side A (victor if decisive): Ya'qub, with the Anatolian Turkmen emirs
how the result was decided: Khalil broke Ya'qub's right wing but was surrounded and killed, and his army fled.
factions A: Ya'qub, with the Anatolian Turkmen emirs
commanders A: Ya'qub, Omar Bey Chagirlu, Bayandur Bey, Suleyman Bey, Mansur Bey
commanders B: Sultan Khalil (killed), Osman Bey Miranshahi, Shahali Bey Purnak, Sufi Khalil
Iranian force: Turkmen tribal cavalry on both sides: Khalil's army against Ya'qub's coalition of aggrieved Anatolian Turkmen tribesmen gathered at Diyarbakır.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Khoy (1478); en.wikipedia Yaqub (Aq Qoyunlu); Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu
note: Ya'qub entered Tabriz in September 1478 and was proclaimed sultan.

date: 1479 (one of a series of engagements of 1478-1479; exact date uncertain)
name: Rapri
war: Bahlul Lodi's wars against the Sharqis of Jaunpur
place: Rapri, Doab, near Firozabad (Uttar Pradesh, India)
how the result was decided: Husain Shah was beaten at Rapri, as in the other engagements of the war, and lost Kampil, Patiali, Shamsabad, Suket, Koil, Marhara and Jalesar.
sources: Wikipedia, Husain Shah of Jaunpur: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Husain_Shah_of_Jaunpur; Nizamuddin Ahmad, Tabaqat-i Akbari; Ferishta
note: The war of 1478-1479 is a chain of defeats at Senha, Rapri, Raigaon Khaga and the Yamuna; the chronology of the individual fights is not secure, so Rapri stands for the series.

date: c. 1480-early 1481 (Ferishta's 885-886 AH; sources disagree on the year and on Kondapalli versus Kondavidu)
name: Kondapalli (Bahmani siege, c. 1480-1481)
war: Bahmani-Gajapati wars (Bahmani invasion of Orissa's Andhra possessions)
place: Kondapalli fort near Vijayawada, Andhra Pradesh
how the result was decided: Ferishta has the Bahmani army take Kondapalli after a siege and then send Gawan on the expedition to Kanchi, but the Wikipedia articles on Kondapalli and the Bahmani invasion of Orissa put the fall of Kondavidu or Kondapalli differently (one has Purushottama retaking Kondapalli in 1481).
commanders A: Muhammad Shah III Lashkari (sultan); Mahmud Gawan (Persian-speaking Afaqi from Gilan; minister, with the army)
commanders B: Hamvira Deva (Gajapati governor; brother of Purushottama)
sources: Muhammad Qasim Ferishta, Tarikh-i Firishta (trans. J. Briggs, History of the Rise of the Mahomedan Power in India, vol. 2); H. K. Sherwani, Mahmud Gawan, the Great Bahmani Wazir (1942); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahmani_invasion_of_Orissa; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kondapalli_Fort
note: Gawan was executed in April 1481 at the end of this campaign, on the sultan's return. the chronology (Kondapalli versus Kondavidu, 1478/1480/1481) is conflicting and the sultan, not Gawan, directed the army.

name: Chirciq River
place: Chirchiq river, southeast of Tashkent, Uzbekistan
how the result was decided: Shaybani's Uzbeks turned and fled at the critical moment, the Timurid army broke, and many drowned in the river.
commanders A: Sultan Mahmud Khan of Moghulistan; Muhammad Shaybani (defected from the Timurid side)
commanders B: Sultan Ahmad Mirza, Mir Abdul Ali Tarkhan, Muhammad Majid Tarkhan
Iranian force: Sultan Ahmad Mirza's army of Samarkand and Bukhara (reportedly 150,000), with infantry, Mir Abdul Ali's contingent and Shaybani's 3,000 Uzbeks, who defected.
why it counts: The army included infantry, in Transoxiana normally Tajik levies, beside Chagatai cavalry and 3,000 Uzbeks; proportions are not recorded.
losses B: heavy; many drowned in the river
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of the Chirciq River
note: Moghulistan = the eastern Chagatai Khanate. Peace followed; Mahmud Khan gave Turkistan to Shaybani.

name: Tabasaran (1488)
place: outside Bayqird castle, Tabasaran, Dagestan, Russia
side A (victor if decisive): Aq Qoyunlu with Shirvanshah Farrukh Yasar; Shirvan
how the result was decided: Haydar and his men were cornered in a pitched battle, defeated and killed.
factions A: Aq Qoyunlu (Sultan Ya'qub) with Shirvanshah Farrukh Yasar
commanders A: Shirvanshah Farrukh Yasar; Aq Qoyunlu troops sent by Ya'qub
Iranian force: An Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen force sent by Ya'qub with Farrukh Yasar's Shirvan army, against Haydar's Qizilbash Sufi followers (Turkmen tribesmen).

name: Banaras (1494)
war: Sikandar Lodi's conquest of the remaining Sharqi lands
how the result was decided: Sikandar defeated Husain Shah, who fled to Bihar and then Bengal, ending Sharqi resistance.
sources: Nizamuddin Ahmad, Tabaqat-i Akbari; Ferishta, Tarikh-i Firishta; Cambridge History of India, vol. 3 (Lodis)

name: Shamasbi
war: Aq Qoyunlu succession wars; Safavid order's wars

Iranian force: Rustam's pursuing Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen force against Ali Mirza's small retinue of Sufis.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

doubts and flags: Borderline: described as a pursuit and killing rather than a battle; the Safavid order before the state.
sources: en.wikipedia Ali Mirza Safavi; Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu
note: Ali Mirza had helped Rustam defeat Baysunghur in 1493 (an unnamed battle); his brother Ismail escaped to Lahijan.

name: Samarkand (siege, 1496)
side B: Babur, Sultan Ali Mirza, Sultan Masud Mirza
how the result was decided: The three uncoordinated besieging armies withdrew as winter came, and the city did not fall.
factions B: Babur (Fergana), Sultan Ali Mirza (Bukhara), Sultan Masud Mirza (Hissar)

doubts and flags: Borderline: no fighting is recorded.

name: Aras (1497)
place: on the Aras (Araxes) river; exact site unknown
how the result was decided: Ahmad defeated Rustam and took the throne.
factions A: Ahmad Beg (Gövde Ahmad), with Ottoman troops
Iranian force: Ahmad's Aq Qoyunlu partisans with Ottoman troops, against Rustam's Turkmen tribal army.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Aq Qoyunlu; Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu
note: Rustam was put to death after his defeat. The country is uncertain: the Aras forms the Iran-Azerbaijan-Armenia border.

name: Samarkand (siege, 1497)
how the result was decided: After seven months Baysonqor abandoned the city and Babur entered Samarkand at the end of November 1497.
commanders B: Baysonqor Mirza; Muhammad Shaybani (Uzbek relief force, withdrew without fighting)
Iranian force: Babur's Fergana army (Chagatai begs and Moghul horse) and Ali Mirza's Bukharan troops, against Baysonqor's garrison and the citizens of Samarkand, who made sorties.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses A: considerable (Babur's best men killed or captured in an ambush at the Lovers' Cave)
losses B: considerable (many citizens killed or captured in a sortie)
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Samarkand (1497); en.wikipedia Babur
note: Wikipedia's lead says the city fell in May; its body and the seven-month length give late November. Babur held Samarkand for about 100 days.

name: Isfahan (1497)
side A (victor if decisive): Aq Qoyunlu emirs led by Ayba Sultan
how the result was decided: Ahmad was defeated and killed by the revolting emirs.
factions A: Aq Qoyunlu emirs led by Ayba Sultan
Iranian force: Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen tribal factions (the Purnak and Qajar under Ayba Sultan) against Ahmad's followers.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: Iranica, Aq Qoyunlu

name: Herat (siege, 1499)
war: Revolts of Badi' al-Zaman against Husayn Bayqara
how the result was decided: Badi' al-Zaman did not take Herat, which Husayn held until his death in 1506.
Iranian force: Badi' al-Zaman's army of Balkh against Husayn's garrison and army of Herat.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: the course of the siege is not described
