sources: en.wikipedia Badi' al-Zaman Mirza; en.wikipedia Husayn Bayqara
note: Wikipedia gives no outcome; failure is inferred from Husayn's unbroken rule at Herat.

name: Samarkand (1500)
how the result was decided: Babur's night escalade took the city and the townspeople rose and killed the Uzbek garrison.
Iranian force: Babur's band of about 240 Chagatai and Moghul followers, joined by the Persian-speaking townspeople of Samarkand.
why it counts: the Persian-speaking townsmen of Samarkand rose and fought
losses B: many of the garrison killed in the streets
borderline: a surprise capture with fighting in the streets rather than a battle or siege
doubts and flags: Borderline: a surprise capture with fighting in the streets rather than a battle or siege.
sources: Babur, Baburnama; en.wikipedia Babur; en.wikipedia Siege of Samarkand (1497)
note: Shaybani had taken Samarkand from Sultan Ali Mirza without a battle earlier in 1500; he beat Babur at Sar-i Pul and besieged him in Samarkand in 1501.

name: Jabani
how the result was decided: The Qizilbash routed Farrukh Yasar's army and the Shirvanshah was killed.
Iranian force: About 7,000 Qizilbash of the Ustajlu, Rumlu, Takkalu, Dhu'l-Qadar, Afshar, Qajar and Varsaq tribes, gathered at Erzincan in summer 1500.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: fought before Ismail's coronation at Tabriz (1501)
doubts and flags: Borderline: fought before Ismail's coronation at Tabriz (1501).
sources: en.wikipedia Ismail I
note: Ismail then took Baku; the Shirvanshahs ruled on as Safavid vassals until 1538.

name: Baku (siege, 1501)
how the result was decided: Baku fell to Ismail's besiegers in 1501.
commanders A: Ismail I (his emirs conducted the siege)
commanders B: the Shirvanshah's garrison (commander not named in the sources used)
Iranian force: Ismail's Qizilbash, about 7,000 Turkmen tribal warriors (Ustajlu, Rumlu, Shamlu, Takkalu, Dhu'l-Qadar, Afshar, Qajar) who had joined him at Erzincan in 1500.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no separate article; known from the Safavid chronicles as summarised in the Ismail I articles
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article; known from the Safavid chronicles as summarised in the Ismail I articles.
sources: en.wikipedia Ismail I and Campaigns of Ismail I (Siege of Baku in the infobox); Savory, Iran under the Safavids
note: Fought after Ismail's victory over Shirvanshah Farrukh Yassar at Jabani or Gulistan (December 1500) and before Sharur.

date: summer 1501 (July or August per Farrokh; day unknown)
name: Sharur
war: Safavid-Aq Qoyunlu war (rise of Ismail I)
how the result was decided: Alvand fled the field, which Ismail's army held; he was driven out of Azerbaijan.
Iranian force: Ismail's 7,000 Qizilbash from the Ustajlu, Rumlu, Takkalu, Dhu'l-Qadar, Afshar, Qajar and Varsaq tribes, against Alvand's Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen army of Azerbaijan and Armenia.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
strength B: more than four times Ismail's army (Savory)
losses B: up to 18,000 killed (Alam-ara-ye Safavi, a late and inflated figure)
sources: Hasan Beg Rumlu, Ahsan al-tawarikh; Savory, Iran under the Safavids; Farrokh, Iran at War; en.wikipedia Battle of Sharur
note: Some accounts place the battle late in 1501; Ismail entered Tabriz and was proclaimed shah after it.

name: Tabriz (siege, 1501)
war: Safavid-Aq Qoyunlu war (rise of Ismail I)
how the result was decided: Ismail kept Tabriz: in the Alam-ara account the palace garrison held out and Alvand's force was then defeated and dispersed.
commanders B: Alvand Beg, Osman Sultan Torkaman; Dulkadirid troops sent by Ala al-Dawla Bozkurt
Iranian force: Ismail's qurchis and Qizilbash; about 500 men under Khalvachi-oghlu defended the palace with bows and muskets (Alam-ara-ye Safavi).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
strength B: 10,000-40,000 Aq Qoyunlu and about 20,000 Dulkadirids (infobox, after the Alam-ara)
borderline: a capture whose fighting rests on one doubtful source
doubts and flags: Traditional: The fighting is known only from the anonymous popular romance Alam-ara-ye Safavi; Hasan Beg Rumlu says the notables of Tabriz received Ismail without resistance, and Ibn Kemal's violent account is hostile to the Safavids. Borderline: a capture whose fighting rests on one doubtful source.
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Tabriz (1501); Alam-ara-ye Safavi; Hasan Beg Rumlu
note: The article places Alvand's counter-attack in the context of his moves of 1502-1503; date and scale are uncertain.

name: Hamadan (1503)
war: Safavid-Aq Qoyunlu war (rise of Ismail I)
how the result was decided: Sultan Murad's army broke and he fled; the Safavids held the field.
commanders A: Ismail I; Khulafa Beg, Qipchaq Mansur Beg, Qarapiri Beg Qajar, Yegan Beg Tekelu, Bayram Beg Qaramanlu
commanders B: Sultan Murad; Ali Beg Turkman, Islamish Beg
Iranian force: About 12,000 Qizilbash horse, with Qarapiri Beg Qajar's 1,500 cavalry in reserve and Tekelu and Qaramanlu emirs on the wings, against Sultan Murad's Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen cavalry.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Hamadan (1503); Savory, Iran under the Safavids
note: Opened Iraq-i Ajam and Fars to Ismail.

name: Usta (siege)
war: Ismail I's conquest of Iran (Mazandaran campaign)
how the result was decided: The fortress fell after its water supply was cut, and Husayn Kiya was taken prisoner.
Iranian force: Ismail's Qizilbash army; no unit details are given, so this is the normal Turkmen tribal army of the first Safavid campaigns.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: garrison taken; Husayn Kiya died in captivity
borderline: no Wikipedia battle article; a siege known from the Safavid chronicles
doubts and flags: Borderline: no Wikipedia battle article; a siege known from the Safavid chronicles.
sources: Savory, Iran under the Safavids; Cambridge History of Iran vol. 6 (Savory); en.wikipedia Campaigns of Ismail I (conquest of Mazandaran, 1504)
note: In the same campaign Ismail took the fortresses of Gulkhandan and Firuzkuh. The exact site of Usta is not securely located; coordinates are for the Firuzkuh district.

name: Yazd (siege, 1504)
how the result was decided: Yazd fell to Ismail after a siege and Muhammad Karra was captured.
Iranian force: Ismail's Qizilbash army (no unit details in the sources used).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no Wikipedia battle article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no Wikipedia battle article.
sources: Savory, Iran under the Safavids; en.wikipedia Campaigns of Ismail I (conquest of Yazd, 1504)
note: Muhammad Karra, a former Aq Qoyunlu officer and lord of Abarquh, had seized Yazd; Wikipedia's campaign list counts the conquest against the Aq Qoyunlu. Ismail then sacked Tabas.

name: Trabzon (1505)
place: Trabzon province, with the pursuit to Erzincan, Turkey
how the result was decided: Selim drove off the raiders and pursued them to Erzincan, taking their arms and supplies.
Iranian force: A Qizilbash raiding force of about 3,000 horsemen.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a frontier raid known from Ottoman chronicles
doubts and flags: Borderline: a frontier raid known from Ottoman chronicles.
sources: en.wikipedia Trabzon Expedition (1505); Ottoman-Persian War (1505-1517)
note: Bayezid II kept the captured arms but answered Ismail's complaint with gifts.

name: Gwalior (siege, 1505-1506)
how the result was decided: Hit-and-run attacks and crop destruction forced Sikandar to lift the siege; the fort was not taken.
sources: Wikipedia, Sikandar Lodi: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikandar_Lodi; Ferishta; K. S. Lal on the Tomars
note: The Lodi army was largely Afghan; Sikandar was a Lodi Afghan by descent. Sikandar was ambushed at Jatwar on the retreat in 1506.

name: Erzincan (1507)
how the result was decided: Selim defeated the Safavid force and it withdrew.
Iranian force: About 10,000 Qizilbash, partly Turkmen recruited among Ottoman subjects.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Erzincan (1507); Ottoman-Persian War (1505-1517)
note: Fought while Ismail's army of about 20,000 crossed Ottoman land to attack the Dulkadirids; Selim acted without his father's approval.

name: Hormuz (1507)
war: Portuguese campaigns in the Persian Gulf (Albuquerque's first expedition)
how the result was decided: Portuguese gunfire sank or disabled much of the Hormuzi fleet and the vizier raised a white flag and accepted tribute.
commanders B: Khwaja Ata (Cogeatar), vizier of the young King Sayf al-Din; Rais Nur al-Din Fali
Iranian force: The Hormuzi fleet: 50-60 large armed merchantmen and 120-200 light oared craft carrying hired Persian bowmen.
why it counts: Kingdom of Hormuz: an Iranian-led state
losses B: 2 large ships and about a dozen light craft sunk, most of the fleet captured or burnt
borderline: the Kingdom of Hormuz was an Iran-seated island kingdom independent of the Safavids and not one of this set's Persian states
doubts and flags: Borderline: the Kingdom of Hormuz was an Iran-seated island kingdom independent of the Safavids and not one of this set's Persian states.
sources: en.wikipedia Capture of Ormuz (1507); Portuguese-Safavid wars
note: Albuquerque could not hold Hormuz in 1507-08; the Portuguese took it in 1515 (by a palace coup, no battle).

name: Narwar (siege, 1507-1508)
war: Sikandar Lodi's campaigns in Malwa and Gwalior
how the result was decided: The fort fell after a year-long siege.
commanders B: Tomara ruler of Narwar (name not secure)
sources: Wikipedia, Sikandar Lodi: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikandar_Lodi; Ferishta
note: Minor siege; included for the Lodi sultan as Pashtun leader.

name: Diyarbakır (siege, 1509)
how the result was decided: The Safavids retook Diyarbakir from its Dulkadirid defenders and executed the two princes.
commanders B: Saru Kaplan and Erdivane, sons of Ala al-Dawla Bozkurt
Iranian force: About 800 Safavid troops, the Ustajlu Qizilbash of the governor of Diyarbakir.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a recapture described in one article; the scale of the fighting is unclear
doubts and flags: Borderline: a recapture described in one article; the scale of the fighting is unclear.
sources: en.wikipedia Ala al-Dawla Bozkurt (after Yinanc, Dulkadir Beyligi)
note: The Dulkadirids had taken Diyarbakir, Mardin and Urfa in support of the Aq Qoyunlu prince Zaynal; the same article lists the death of one prince, Ahmed, under both 1509 and 1510.

name: Diyarbakır (1510)
how the result was decided: The Safavid attack routed the Dulkadirid army, whose leaders were captured and beheaded.
commanders B: Shahruh and Ahmed, sons of Ala al-Dawla Bozkurt
Iranian force: The Ustajlu Qizilbash of the Safavid governor of Diyarbakir (size not given).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: Shahruh, Ahmed and about forty others beheaded
sources: en.wikipedia Ala al-Dawla Bozkurt (after Yinanc); en.wikipedia Ismail I (Battle of Diyarbakir in the infobox)
note: Shahruh's sons Mehmed and Ali were spared and given posts by Ismail. Ismail's infobox lists a Battle of Diyarbakir dated 1511, probably this one.

name: Trabzon (1510)
how the result was decided: Selim defeated the Safavid army sent against Trabzon.
Iranian force: A Qizilbash army sent by Ismail in answer to Selim's raid into Georgia (size not given).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: known from Ottoman chronicles; few details
doubts and flags: Borderline: known from Ottoman chronicles; few details.
sources: en.wikipedia Trabzon Expedition (1510); Ottoman-Persian War (1505-1517)

name: Merv
how the result was decided: Ismail's feigned retreat drew the Uzbeks into an ambush; they were routed and Shaybani was killed in the flight.
Iranian force: About 17,000 Qizilbash cavalry under the shah.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Merv (1510); Savory, Iran under the Safavids; Iranica, Esmail I
note: Ismail had Shaybani's skull made into a drinking cup. Uzbeks here are the Shaybanids (Khanate of Bukhara).

name: Qarshi (siege)
how the result was decided: Qarshi was taken by storm and its inhabitants were massacred.
commanders A: Najm-e Sani (Yar Ahmad Khuzani), with Babur
commanders B: the Uzbek garrison of Ubaydullah Sultan's appanage
Iranian force: Najm-e Sani's army (said to be 60,000): the Qizilbash emirs of Khorasan, the governor of Herat, Biram Khan Qaramanlu from Balkh and Abdal Beg Talish, with Babur's Chagatai Turks.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: garrison and population massacred, including the poet Binai
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Ghazdewan (background); Babur, Baburnama; Savory
note: Babur, an ally (Timurids of Kabul, listed as Mughals), opposed the massacre.

name: Ghazdewan
how the result was decided: The Safavid army broke within about an hour after Biram Khan fell, and fled across the Amu Darya.
commanders A: Ubaydullah Sultan, Timur Sultan, Jani Beg Sultan, Kuchum Khan, Suyunjuk Sultan
commanders B: Najm-e Sani (captured and executed), Babur, Husayn Beg Shamlu, Abdal Beg Talish, Biram Khan Qaramanlu (killed)
Iranian force: Najm-e Sani's army: the Qizilbash emirs of Khorasan, the governor of Herat, Biram Khan Qaramanlu's Balkh contingent and Abdal Beg Talish, with Babur's Chagatai Turks.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Ghazdewan; Baburnama; Savory; Iranica, Ghojdovan
note: The Uzbeks fought from the suburbs with archers in houses and gardens. The defeat ended Babur's hopes in Transoxiana.

name: Chaldiran
place: Chaldiran plain, near Siah Cheshmeh, West Azerbaijan, Iran
how the result was decided: The Safavid cavalry broke against the Ottoman guns and Janissaries and Ismail fled the field.
commanders A: Selim I, Hadim Sinan Pasha, Hasan Pasha (killed), Biyikli Mehmed Pasha, Dukaginzade Ahmed Pasha
commanders B: Ismail I (wounded), Mohammad Khan Ustajlu (killed), Durmish Khan Shamlu, Abd al-Baqi Yazdi (killed), Sayyid Sharif al-Din Shirazi (killed), Nur-Ali Khalifa
Iranian force: Ismail's Qizilbash cavalry (Ustajlu, Shamlu, Rumlu, Takkalu, Dhu'l-Qadar and others), without artillery or infantry; Persian (Tajik) grandees such as the vakil Abd al-Baqi Yazdi and the sadr Sharif al-Din Shirazi fought and fell.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Hasan Beg Rumlu; Idris Bitlisi; Savory, Iran under the Safavids; en.wikipedia Battle of Chaldiran
note: Selim occupied Tabriz on 6 September 1514 without fighting and withdrew a week later (Capture of Tabriz (1514) and Battle of Tabriz (1514) are not separate battles).

name: Bayburt (siege)
how the result was decided: Bayburt was taken after several assaults when its commander refused to surrender.
Iranian force: A Safavid fortress garrison (size and make-up not given; frontier garrisons were Qizilbash).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no separate article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article.
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman-Persian War (1505-1517); Ismail I (infobox: Capture of Bayburt)

name: Kemah (siege)
how the result was decided: The fortress of Kemah fell to Selim's army.
commanders B: the Safavid garrison commander (not named in the sources used)
Iranian force: A Safavid fortress garrison (no details).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: listed only in the Ismail I infobox; details not checked against a detailed online source for this file

sources: en.wikipedia Ismail I (infobox: Siege of Kemah); Ottoman chronicles as summarised in Savory and Iranica
note: The last Safavid stronghold in Erzincan province; its fall preceded Selim's march on the Dulkadirids (Turnadag, 13 June 1515).

name: Ovacık
how the result was decided: Nur-Ali Khalifa was killed and his force scattered after his head was displayed.
commanders A: Biyikli Mehmed Pasha, Pir Huseyin Bey
Iranian force: About 800 Qizilbash under the Safavid khalifa Nur-Ali, partly local Anatolian adherents.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Ovacik (1515); Ottoman-Persian War (1505-1517)
note: Nur-Ali Khalifa Rumlu had been sent by Ismail into Anatolia in 1512 and fought at Chaldiran.

name: Diyarbakır (siege, 1515)
how the result was decided: The Ottoman relief force defeated the Safavid besiegers and the siege of the pro-Ottoman city was raised.
commanders A: Cemsid Bey, Yigit Ahmet, Sadi Pasha, Idris Bitlisi
Iranian force: About 10,000 Qizilbash under Qara Khan Ustajlu, brother of the fallen Mohammad Khan.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman-Persian War (1505-1517); Idris Bitlisi; Iranica, Diyarbakr
note: The townsmen had expelled the Safavid governor and declared for Selim; Kurdish chiefs organised by Idris Bitlisi joined the Ottomans (listed as Kurdish rebels against the Safavids).

date: 23 March, probably 1516 (year not stated in the source)
name: Harput (siege)
how the result was decided: Harput fell after a three-day siege.
commanders A: Cerkes Huseyin Bey, Karacinoglu Ahmet Bey
Iranian force: A Safavid fortress garrison (no details).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no separate article; minor siege
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article; minor siege.
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman-Persian War (1505-1517)
note: Placed between the relief of Diyarbakir (September 1515) and Kochisar (May 1516) in the war article.

name: Koçhisar
place: Dede Kargin, near Kiziltepe (Kochisar), Mardin, Turkey
how the result was decided: Qara Khan was killed and the Safavid army fled; the Ottomans held the field.
commanders A: Biyikli Mehmed Pasha, Deli Husrev Pasha, Idris Bitlisi, Pir Huseyin Beg
commanders B: Qara Khan Ustajlu (killed), Kangiril Sultan (governor of Baghdad), Chuka Sultan (killed), Durmus Beg
Iranian force: Qara Khan Ustajlu's Qizilbash cavalry in two wings, he on the left and the governor of Baghdad on the right.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kochisar; Ottoman-Persian War (1505-1517)
note: Opened the way for the Ottoman conquest of Mardin and Urfa.

name: Mardin (siege, 1516-1517)
how the result was decided: Mardin citadel fell in March 1517 and its Safavid garrison was killed.
commanders A: Deli Husrev Pasha, Biyikli Mehmed Pasha
Iranian force: The Ustajlu Qizilbash garrison under Suleiman Beg, brother of Qara Khan.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman-Persian War (1505-1517)
note: The Ottomans brought cannon from Diyarbakir to end the siege.

name: Khatoli
war: Rana Sanga's wars against the Lodi Sultanate
how the result was decided: Mewar sources record that Sanga routed Ibrahim's army and captured a Lodi prince, who was later released.

sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Khatoli: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Khatoli; Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan; Baburnama (Sanga's wars against Ibrahim)
note: The details come from Mewar chronicles; Babur confirms Sanga's victories over Ibrahim without naming Khatoli. The Wikipedia article on Ibrahim Lodi does not mention it.

name: Mosul (1517)
how the result was decided: The Ottomans defeated Ahmed Bey Afshar and took Mosul.
Iranian force: The Afshar Qizilbash of the Safavid governor of Mosul (no numbers).

war: Ibrahim Lodi's wars against the Tomars of Gwalior
how the result was decided: Gwalior fell and Vikramaditya surrendered.
commanders A: Azam Humayun Sarwani (c. 30,000 horse and 300 elephants)
sources: Wikipedia, Ibrahim Lodi: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibrahim_Lodi; Ferishta
note: Azam Humayun Sarwani was an Afghan noble commanding for Ibrahim Lodi.

name: Dholpur (1519)
war: Rana Sanga's wars against the Lodi Sultanate
how the result was decided: Sanga defeated the Lodi army and took the Lodi territory up to the neighbourhood of Dholpur and Bayana; Babur mentions the victory.
commanders A: Miyan Makhan; Miyan Husain Khan (for Ibrahim Lodi)
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Dholpur: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dholpur; Baburnama; Tod, Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan
note: Ibrahim Lodi, the Afghan sultan, directed the campaign through his commanders; the Lodi commanders' names are taken from memory and should be checked.

name: Teleti
how the result was decided: The outnumbered Georgians were defeated and the Safavids went on to take Tbilisi.
commanders A: Ismail I (led the invasion in person per Wikipedia)
commanders B: David X of Kartli, Prince Luarsab
Iranian force: A large Qizilbash invasion army (no numbers or units given).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia David X of Kartli; Luarsab I of Kartli; Campaigns of Ismail I
note: Kingdom of Kartli. Tbilisi was then taken by treachery and garrisoned; David X recovered it in 1524. Some accounts name Div Sultan Rumlu rather than Ismail as commander.

name: Delhi (Alam Khan Lodi's attack, 1524)
war: Lodi succession troubles and Babur's invasions
how the result was decided: Alam Khan's host (reported at 30,000-40,000) was routed by Ibrahim and Alam Khan fled back to Babur.
Iranian side: Ibrahim Lodi v Alam Khan Lodi
sources: Baburnama (Beveridge); Wikipedia, Ibrahim Lodi: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibrahim_Lodi
note: Afghan against Afghan: Alam Khan, uncle of Ibrahim, was given a Mughal escort by Babur but the fight was between Lodi forces. The details come from the Baburnama and are not confirmed in detail.

name: Lahore (1524)
how the result was decided: Babur routed Ibrahim's army and took Lahore.
commanders B: Bihar Khan Lodi (Bahar Khan); other Lodi amirs
sources: Wikipedia, Ibrahim Lodi: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibrahim_Lodi; Baburnama (Beveridge)
note: Ibrahim Lodi's army in the Punjab was Afghan; Daulat Khan Lodi, the governor, had invited Babur and then turned against him.

name: First Battle of Panipat
how the result was decided: Ibrahim Lodi was killed and his army broke before Babur's guns and flank attacks.
commanders A: Babur; Humayun; Ustad Ali Quli; Mustafa Rumi
commanders B: Ibrahim Lodi; Hamid Khan; Raja Vikramaditya of Gwalior (killed)
sources: Baburnama; Wikipedia, First Battle of Panipat: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Battle_of_Panipat; Wikipedia, Ibrahim Lodi: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibrahim_Lodi
note: The Lodi army was led by an Afghan sultan and filled with Afghan nobles and levies; Hindu contingents were also present.

name: Sharur (1527)
how the result was decided: The Ustajlu were defeated and their leader Kopek Sultan was killed.
factions A: Tahmasp I's regents (Div Sultan Rumlu, Chuha Sultan Takkalu)
commanders A: Div Sultan Rumlu, Chuha Sultan Takkalu
Iranian force: Qizilbash tribal cavalry on both sides: the Rumlu and Takkalu of the regency against the Ustajlu.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a civil-war battle named by place in Iranica, without its own Wikipedia article
doubts and flags: Borderline: a civil-war battle named by place in Iranica, without its own Wikipedia article.
sources: Iranica, Tahmasp I; Iranica, Ostajlu; en.wikipedia Tahmasp I
note: Wikipedia's Tahmasp I says Kopek Sultan was killed on Chuha Sultan's orders in 1526.

name: Khanwa
allies B: Mewat; Afghan horse; Medini Rai of Chanderi
how the result was decided: Babur's guns, wagons and flank charges broke the Rajput army; Sanga fled wounded.
commanders B: Rana Sanga; Hasan Khan Mewati; Mahmud Lodi (Afghan claimant to Delhi)
sources: Baburnama; Wikipedia, Battle of Khanwa: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Khanwa; Richards, The Mughal Empire
note: Mahmud Lodi, brother of Ibrahim, joined Sanga with the surviving Afghan chiefs of the east (some modern accounts give about 10,000 horse); the Afghans were a minority of the allied army.

name: Herat (siege, 1528)
how the result was decided: Ubaydullah raised the siege when Tahmasp's relief army approached, and was beaten at Jam.
Iranian force: The Shamlu Qizilbash garrison of Herat with the city's Tajik population.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no separate article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article.
sources: Iranica, Tahmasp I; Dickson, Shah Tahmasb and the Uzbeks (via Iranica); en.wikipedia Tahmasp I
note: Wikipedia's Tahmasp I says the Uzbeks took Herat in 1528; Iranica places the surrender after the second siege of 1529-1530 (next entries).

name: Jam
how the result was decided: The Uzbek army was broken and fled, leaving the field to the Safavids.
commanders A: Tahmasp I, Bahram Mirza, Alqas Mirza
Iranian force: About 40,000 Qizilbash cavalry with an Ottoman-style wagon laager of cannon and musketeers in the centre, Tahmasp leading 7,000 picked men.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Jam; Iranica, Tahmasp I; Savory
note: One of the first Safavid uses of field artillery and muskets.

name: Herat (siege, 1529-1530)
how the result was decided: Herat surrendered to the Uzbeks after a long siege and negotiations.
Iranian force: The Shamlu Qizilbash garrison of Herat with the townsmen.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no separate article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article.
sources: Iranica, Tahmasp I; en.wikipedia Tahmasp I
note: The garrison was allowed to leave; the Uzbeks evacuated Herat when Tahmasp returned in the summer of 1530.

name: Ghaghra
place: confluence of the Ghaghra and the Ganges, Bihar/Uttar Pradesh border, India
how the result was decided: Babur forced the river crossing under gun fire; the Afghan resistance collapsed and Mahmud Lodi abandoned his army.
sources: Baburnama; Wikipedia, Battle of Ghaghra: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ghaghra; Wikipedia, Mughal-Afghan Wars: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal%E2%80%93Afghan_Wars
note: Sher Khan Sur took part on the Afghan side before submitting to Babur.

name: Dadrah
war: Humayun's wars against the Afghans of the east
place: Dadrah (Daurah), between Lucknow and Jaunpur, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: Humayun decisively defeated the Afghan coalition and Mahmud Lodi fled to Orissa.
sources: Wikipedia, Sher Shah Suri: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sher_Shah_Suri; Erskine, History of India under Baber and Humayun
note: Sher Khan did not fight and kept his strength for Chunar. The place and the year (1531 or 1532) vary between sources.

name: Herat (siege, 1532-1533)
how the result was decided: Herat held out and the Uzbeks withdrew in October 1533.
commanders A: the Safavid governor of Herat (Sam Mirza's administration)
Iranian force: The Qizilbash garrison of Herat with the townsmen.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no separate article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article.
sources: Iranica, Tahmasp I

name: Chunar (siege, 1532)
how the result was decided: After four months Humayun lifted the siege when Sher Khan offered loyalty and gave his son Qutb Khan as hostage.
commanders B: Sher Khan (later Sher Shah); Qutb Khan (hostage)
sources: Wikipedia, Sher Shah Suri: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sher_Shah_Suri; Abbas Khan Sarwani, Tarikh-i Sher Shahi
note: Bought off while invested, so recorded as a draw.

name: Surajgarh
war: Rise of Sher Khan: Bihar and Bengal
how the result was decided: Sher Khan won decisively, Ibrahim Khan was killed and Jalal Khan fled to Bengal.
Iranian side: Sher Khan Sur v Sultanate of Bengal
sources: Wikipedia, Sher Shah Suri: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sher_Shah_Suri; Abbas Khan Sarwani, Tarikh-i Sher Shahi; Qanungo, Sher Shah
note: Afghan against Afghan: the Lohanis of Bihar fought on the Bengal side; the Bengal army was largely Bengali.

name: Kandahar (siege, 1535-1536)
how the result was decided: Kandahar held out and Kamran's relief forces drove off the Safavid besiegers.
Iranian force: The Shamlu Qizilbash of Herat under the shah's brother Sam Mirza.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: Iranica, Qandahar (history); Iranica, Tahmasp I
note: Kamran Mirza held Kandahar and Kabul for his brother Humayun; listed as Mughals. Sam Mirza was soon accused of rebellion and submitted to Tahmasp. Tahmasp took Kandahar in 1537 with little resistance (not counted) and Kamran retook it in 1538.

name: Chunar (siege, 1537-1538)
how the result was decided: The fort fell to the Mughals after a siege of more than six months.
sources: Wikipedia, Sher Shah Suri: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sher_Shah_Suri; Abbas Khan Sarwani
note: Humayun's delay at Chunar let Sher Shah take Gaur and Rohtas; the garrison was Sher Shah's Afghan troops.

name: Gaur (siege, 1538)
war: Rise of Sher Shah: conquest of Bengal
place: Gaur (Gauda), Malda district, West Bengal, India
how the result was decided: Gaur fell, Mahmud Shah was mortally wounded and Sher Shah was crowned there on 6 April 1538.
sources: Wikipedia, Sher Shah Suri: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sher_Shah_Suri; Abbas Khan Sarwani
note: Sher Shah and Khawas Khan Marwat were Pashtuns.

name: Reishahr (siege)
how the result was decided: Reishahr capitulated after a long land siege and a Portuguese naval blockade.
commanders A: Ghazi Khan Dhu'l-Qadar; Manuel do Carvalhal (Portuguese squadron)
Iranian force: The Dhu'l-Qadar Qizilbash and provincial levies of Fars under Ghazi Khan, with a Portuguese squadron blockading by sea.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a provincial revolt; counted as civil because the rebels were local Iranian lords
doubts and flags: Borderline: a provincial revolt; counted as civil because the rebels were local Iranian lords.
sources: en.wikipedia Reishahr rebellion (1539-40)
note: Reishahr lost its autonomy.

name: Chausa
how the result was decided: Sher Shah's surprise dawn attack routed the Mughal camp; Humayun escaped by swimming the Ganges.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Chausa: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Chausa; Abbas Khan Sarwani; Wikipedia, List of battles involving the Mughal Empire
note: Sher Shah's army was mainly Afghan.

name: Kannauj
place: Kannauj (battle by the Ganges near Bilgram), Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: The Mughal army was routed and Humayun lost Hindustan.
sources: Wikipedia, Sher Shah Suri: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sher_Shah_Suri; Abbas Khan Sarwani; Erskine
note: Also called the Battle of Bilgram.

name: Raisen (siege, 1543)
war: Sher Shah's conquest of Malwa and Rajputana
how the result was decided: The garrison surrendered on terms and was attacked and massacred as it marched out.
sources: Wikipedia, Sher Shah Suri: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sher_Shah_Suri; Abbas Khan Sarwani
note: Infamous for the breach of the safe conduct.

name: Sammel (Giri-Sumel)
place: Sammel (Giri), Jaitaran, Pali district, Rajasthan, India
how the result was decided: Jaita and Kumpa fought with 12,000 men and were destroyed; Sher Shah took Marwar.
sources: Wikipedia, Sher Shah Suri: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sher_Shah_Suri; Abbas Khan Sarwani; Qanungo, Sher Shah
note: Sher Shah is said to have remarked that for a handful of millet he nearly lost the empire of Hindustan.

name: Kandahar (siege, 1545)
how the result was decided: Askari surrendered the fort on 3 September 1545.
commanders A: Humayun; Bidagh Khan Qajar and the infant prince Murad Mirza (Safavid contingent)
Iranian force: About 14,000 Safavid troops lent by Tahmasp, Qizilbash cavalry under Bidagh Khan Qajar, the bulk of Humayun's army.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Humayun; Iranica, Qandahar; Iranica, Tahmasp I
note: Humayun against his brothers Askari and Kamran (both sides listed as Mughals); the Persian force made up most of the besieging army. Kandahar was handed to the Persians as agreed.

name: Kalinjar (siege, 1544-1545)
war: Sher Shah's wars against the Rajputs
place: Kalinjar, Banda district, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: The fort fell on the day Sher Shah died of wounds from a bursting shell.
sources: Wikipedia, Sher Shah Suri: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sher_Shah_Suri; Abbas Khan Sarwani
note: Sher Shah died on 22 May 1545.

name: Kandahar (surprise attack, 1545)
how the result was decided: Humayun's men surprised the Persian garrison and drove it out of the city.
Iranian force: The Qizilbash garrison left in Kandahar after the siege (no numbers).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a coup de main with little recorded fighting
doubts and flags: Borderline: a coup de main with little recorded fighting.
sources: en.wikipedia Humayun; Iranica, Qandahar
note: Humayun broke his promise to cede Kandahar to Tahmasp and made Bairam Khan governor.

name: Derbent (1547)
how the result was decided: Bahram Mirza retook Derbent from the rebels and Alqas fled to the Crimea.
commanders A: Tahmasp I, Bahram Mirza, Shahqoli Khalifa
Iranian force: Tahmasp's Qizilbash army against Alqas Mirza's Shirvan troops.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a capture in a rebellion; the scale of fighting is not described
doubts and flags: Borderline: a capture in a rebellion; the scale of fighting is not described.
sources: Iranica, Tahmasp I; Iranica, Alqas Mirza; en.wikipedia Tahmasp I
note: In the same month Alqas's field force under Mohammad Beg Afshar was routed by Shahqoli Khalifa. Alqas then went over to the Ottomans.

name: Van (siege, 1548)
how the result was decided: Van fell to the Ottoman bombardment on 25 August 1548.
commanders A: Suleiman I, Rustem Pasha (advised by the French ambassador Gabriel de Luetz d'Aramon)
commanders B: the Safavid garrison (Tahmasp I as sovereign)
Iranian force: A Safavid garrison of Qizilbash (numbers not given).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
strength A: unknown (the campaign box gives 40,000 for the campaign)
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Van (1548); Safavid campaign (1548-1549)
note: One linked title dates the siege to 1547; the narrative gives 1548.

date: Late November to December 1548 (after he took Hamadan on 5 November)
name: Isfahan (Alqas Mirza's attack, 1548)
war: Ottoman-Safavid War of 1532-1555 (Suleiman's second Persian campaign; Alqas Mirza's invasion of Persian Iraq)
how the result was decided: Alqas's attack on Isfahan, where Tahmasp had lodged his household, failed and he moved on to Shushtar, Fars and Khuzestan before retreating into Ottoman territory in January 1549 (Iranica, Alqas Mirza; Wikipedia, Alqas Mirza).
Iranian side: Alqas Mirza's force v Safavid Persia
commanders A: Alqas Mirza (Safavid prince, brother of Tahmasp); Ulama Khan Takkalu (Safavid defector, Ottoman beylerbey)
commanders B: Bahram Mirza (sent in pursuit); Shah Tahmasp I (camped at Uch Kilisa)
sources: https://iranicaonline.org/articles/alqas-alqasb-alqas-mirza-safawi; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alqas_Mirza; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman%E2%80%93Safavid_War_(1532%E2%80%931555)
note: Alqas fought for the Ottoman sultan, with Ottoman money, 600 Baghdad troops and about 8,000 tribal levies, so he counts as a Safavid prince leading Ottoman-backed troops. The Safavid dynasty is counted Iranian by descent (Kurdish or Persian origin of the sheikhs of Ardabil, Turkic-speaking by Alqas's time). Iranica names no pitched battle in this campaign, only the failed attack.

date: c. 1549-1550 (the place is given as Ambala in some accounts and as Sambla near Dinkot in others)
name: Ambala (Niazi revolt, c. 1549)
war: Niazi revolt against Islam Shah Suri
how the result was decided: Islam Shah defeated the Niazi rebels, who fled to the hills and then to Kashmir.
Iranian side: Sur Empire v Niazi Afghan rebels
commanders B: Haibat Khan Niazi (Azam Humayun); Said Khan; Shahbaz Khan
sources: Wikipedia, Haibat Khan Niazi: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haibat_Khan_Niazi; Abbas Khan Sarwani; Qanungo, Sher Shah
note: Afghan against Afghan. The Wikipedia article calls the place Sambla near Dinkot; older histories say Ambala, so the location is not secure.

name: Banihal Pass (1552)
war: Niazi revolt against Islam Shah Suri: flight to Kashmir
place: Banihal Pass, Jammu and Kashmir, India
how the result was decided: The Kashmiris blocked the pass, captured the Niazi chiefs and killed Haibat Khan, Shahbaz Khan and Said Khan.
commanders A: Haibat Khan Niazi; Said Khan; Shahbaz Khan
sources: Wikipedia, Haibat Khan Niazi: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haibat_Khan_Niazi; Abbas Khan Sarwani
note: More an ambush of fugitives than a pitched battle; included because the Niazi Afghans had fought their way to the pass.

name: Erzurum (1552)
how the result was decided: Iskender Pasha's army was routed outside Erzurum, many dying in the fortress ditch.
commanders A: Ismail Mirza (later Ismail II), Shahverdi Sultan Ziyad-oghlu, Badr Khan Ustajlu, Muhammad Khan Turkman
Iranian force: Qizilbash contingents (Ziyad-oghlu Qajar, Ustajlu, Turkman) with 1,000 Tehran and 600 Nakhchivan guards.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
strength B: unknown (Turks and Kurds of eastern Anatolia)
losses B: 2,576 killed besides those drowned, several begs captured
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Erzurum (1552); Iranica, Tahmasp I
note: Wikipedia's Tahmasp I dates Ismail Mirza's victory to May 1554.

name: Farah
place: Farah, between Mathura and Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: Sikandar defeated Ibrahim near Agra and took Delhi and Agra; Ibrahim fled east.
Iranian side: Sikandar Shah Suri v Ibrahim Shah Suri
sources: Wikipedia, Muhammad Adil Shah (died 1557): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Adil_Shah_(died_1557); Nizamuddin Ahmad, Tabaqat-i Akbari
note: Sur against Sur. The name Farah and the date come from the later chronicles and the Wikipedia article only says 'near Agra'.

name: Machhiwara
how the result was decided: The Sur army was defeated and the Mughals gained the Sutlej line and the Punjab.
sources: Wikipedia, List of battles involving the Mughal Empire: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_battles_involving_the_Mughal_Empire; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama; Wikipedia, Mughal-Afghan Wars
note: Sikandar Shah Suri was a Sur Afghan by descent; the commanders for the Sur army are from memory.

name: Sirhind
how the result was decided: The Sur army was routed, and Humayun re-entered Delhi in July 1555.
sources: Wikipedia, List of battles involving the Mughal Empire: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_battles_involving_the_Mughal_Empire; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama
note: The decisive battle of Humayun's restoration.

name: Garisi
how the result was decided: In a pitched battle the Georgians beat off the Qizilbash, whose commander Shahverdi Sultan fell, though Luarsab I was killed.
commanders A: Shahverdi Sultan Ziyad-oghlu Qajar, beglarbeg of Karabakh (killed)
commanders B: Luarsab I of Kartli (mortally wounded), Simon
Iranian force: About 25,000 Qizilbash placed under Shahverdi Sultan by Tahmasp.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses A: more than 10,000 killed or wounded (Georgian figure)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Garisi; Luarsab I of Kartli; Tahmasp I
note: Kingdom of Kartli.

name: Tughlaqabad
how the result was decided: After a day's fighting Hemu defeated Tardi Beg Khan and took Delhi.
sources: Wikipedia, Second Battle of Panipat: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Battle_of_Panipat; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama; Badauni
note: Hemu was a Hindu general, but the army he led for the Sur sultan was mainly Afghan horse; no Afghan leader is named for this battle.

name: Second Battle of Panipat
how the result was decided: Hemu was struck in the eye by an arrow, his army broke and fled, and he was captured and killed.
commanders A: Ali Quli Khan Shaibani; Bairam Khan (behind the line)
sources: Wikipedia, Second Battle of Panipat: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Battle_of_Panipat; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama
note: Hemu's army is described as mostly Afghan horse (about 30,000) with Shadi Khan Kakar, a Pashtun, commanding one wing.

name: Chhapparghatta
how the result was decided: Adil Shah was defeated and killed by Khizr Khan of Bengal.
Iranian side: Muhammad Shah Sur's Bengal v Adil Shah Suri
commanders A: Khizr Khan Sur (Bahadur Shah of Bengal)
sources: Wikipedia, Muhammad Adil Shah (died 1557): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Adil_Shah_(died_1557); Nizamuddin Ahmad, Tabaqat-i Akbari
note: Sur against Sur. The name and exact place are not given in the Wikipedia article and are taken from the later chronicles.

name: Kandahar (siege, 1557-1558)
how the result was decided: After six months of fighting Shah Muhammad surrendered the fort on terms and left for India.
commanders A: Ali Sultan Tati-oghlu Dhu'l-Qadar; Soltan Hosayn Mirza
Iranian force: A Qizilbash army under Ali Sultan Dhu'l-Qadar, fighting with bows and muskets (no numbers).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kandahar (1557-1558); Mughal-Persian wars; Soltan Hosayn Mirza Safavi
note: Akbar, under the regent Bairam Khan, could send no relief. The Safavids held Kandahar until 1595.

date: January to 25 July 1557 (the siege began in late 1556 in some accounts)
name: Mankot (siege, 1556-1557)
how the result was decided: Sikandar surrendered after about six months, on terms, once Adil Shah was dead.
sources: Wikipedia, List of battles involving the Mughal Empire: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_battles_involving_the_Mughal_Empire; Wikipedia, Muhammad Adil Shah (died 1557); Abul Fazl, Akbarnama
note: The last stand of the Sur dynasty in the north.

name: Sarangpur (1561)
how the result was decided: Baz Bahadur was defeated and fled, and the Mughals took Malwa.
sources: Abul Fazl, Akbarnama; Wikipedia, Baz Bahadur: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baz_Bahadur
note: Baz Bahadur was the son of Shuja'at Khan Sur, Sher Shah's governor of Malwa, so a Sur Afghan by descent.

name: Tsikhedidi
how the result was decided: Simon was defeated and his ally George of Kakheti was killed.
commanders A: the Persian garrison commanders of Tbilisi (not named)
commanders B: Simon I of Kartli, Prince George of Kakheti (killed)
Iranian force: The Qizilbash garrison and field troops holding Tbilisi (no details).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the opponent is not named in the Wikipedia article; Simon was campaigning to retake Persian-held Tbilisi
doubts and flags: Borderline: the opponent is not named in the Wikipedia article; Simon was campaigning to retake Persian-held Tbilisi.
sources: en.wikipedia Simon I of Kartli
note: Kingdoms of Kartli and Kakheti.

date: 1564, soon after Narrai (exact dates not fixed)
name: Chauragarh (siege, 1564)
place: Chauragarh fort, Narsinghpur district, Madhya Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: Vir Narayan was killed, the women committed jauhar and Asaf Khan took the fort and its treasure.
commanders A: Asaf Khan I (Abdul Majid Asaf Khan)
commanders B: Vir Narayan (killed); the garrison and the Rani's household
sources: Wikipedia, Mughal conquest of Garha (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_conquest_of_Garha); Wikipedia, Asaf Khan I; Akbarnama
note: Same weak origin evidence as Narrai (the nisba Harawi). Asaf Khan kept most of the loot, including 800 elephants, and rebelled in 1565.

name: Narrai
place: Narrai, between the Gaur and Narmada rivers, near Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: The Rani's army was broken and she killed herself; Asaf Khan went on to Chauragarh.
commanders A: Asaf Khan I (Abdul Majid Asaf Khan, governor of Kara)
commanders B: Rani Durgavati (died by suicide in the battle); Vir Narayan (pushed the Mughals back three times and was wounded)
sources: Wikipedia, Mughal conquest of Garha (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_conquest_of_Garha); Wikipedia, Asaf Khan I (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asaf_Khan_I); Abu'l-Fazl, Akbarnama (Beveridge trans.)
note: The origin of Asaf Khan I is thin: the Wikipedia articles do not state it; he is called Harawi (of Herat) in the Akbarnama, which makes him Persian-speaking Khurasani by origin, but this rests on the nisba. Also called the Battle of Damoh in Wikipedia's infobox.

name: Digomi
how the result was decided: Daud Khan's sortie was routed on the Digomi plain, though the Georgians could not take the Tbilisi fortress.
commanders B: Daud Khan (David XI), Tahmasp's appointee in Tbilisi
Iranian force: The Persian garrison of Tbilisi under the converted Georgian prince Daud Khan: Qizilbash troops with his Georgian followers.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Digomi; Simon I of Kartli
note: The campaign failed and the fortress stayed in Persian hands; the field fight is scored.

name: Partskhisi (1569)
place: near Partskhisi castle, Kvemo Kartli, Georgia
how the result was decided: Simon was defeated and taken prisoner.
commanders A: Persian commanders supporting Daud Khan (not named)
Iranian force: Persian (Qizilbash) troops backing Daud Khan's rule in Kartli (no details).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the opponent is implied in the source (Simon was captured by Persian forces)
doubts and flags: Borderline: the opponent is implied in the source (Simon was captured by Persian forces).
sources: en.wikipedia Simon I of Kartli
note: Earlier in 1569 Simon won at Samadlo against an opponent the source does not name (not listed). Simon was held in Alamut until 1578.

name: Hajipur and Patna (siege, 1574)
war: Mughal conquest of Bengal and Bihar
how the result was decided: The Afghan garrison nearly won at Hajipur but Akbar took the supply fort, and Daud fled from Patna into Bengal.
commanders A: Akbar; Munim Khan; Todar Mal; Man Singh
commanders B: Daud Khan Karrani; Katlu Lohani; Gujar Khan Karrani
sources: Wikipedia, Daud Khan Karrani: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daud_Khan_Karrani; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama; Banglapedia, Karrani Rule

name: Tukaroi
war: Mughal conquest of Bengal and Bihar
place: Tukaroi (Mughalmari), Balasore/Midnapore border, Odisha/West Bengal, India

commanders B: Daud Khan Karrani; Gujar Khan Karrani
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Tukaroi: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tukaroi; Wikipedia, Daud Khan Karrani: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daud_Khan_Karrani; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama
note: Daud withdrew to Cuttack and made peace, ceding Bengal and Bihar to the Mughals; the Mughal commanders are not named in the Wikipedia article and are given from memory.

name: Rajmahal
war: Mughal conquest of Bengal and Bihar
how the result was decided: After a long battle Daud was defeated, captured and executed.
commanders A: Khan Jahan Quli; Muzaffar Khan Turbati
commanders B: Daud Khan Karrani; Junaid; Qutlu Khan; Ismail Khan Lodi
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Rajmahal: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Rajmahal; Wikipedia, Daud Khan Karrani: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daud_Khan_Karrani; Banglapedia, Rajmahal, The battle of
note: The end of the Karrani Sultanate of Bengal.

name: Uzbek invasion of Khorasan (1578)

commanders B: Jalal Khan Uzbek, governor of Merv (killed)

borderline: the article names the fight inconsistently (it mentions Ashgabat and Jam); listed under the article's title
doubts and flags: Borderline: the article names the fight inconsistently (it mentions Ashgabat and Jam); listed under the article's title.
sources: en.wikipedia Uzbek invasion of Khorasan (1578)

name: Çıldır
how the result was decided: The Safavid-Georgian army was routed and thousands of prisoners were executed on the field the next day.
commanders A: Lala Mustafa Pasha (main army), Ozdemiroglu Osman Pasha, Dervis Pasha
commanders B: Mohammad Khan Tokhmaq Ustajlu (Erivan), Imam Quli Khan Qajar (Ganja), Qara Khan (wounded)

why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
strength A: unknown (Iskandar Beg Munshi claimed 100,000 for the Ottoman army)
losses B: 5,000-7,000 killed and about 3,000 captured and beheaded
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Çıldır; Lala Mustafa Pasha's Caucasian campaign; Mohammad Khan Tokhmaq Ustajlu
note: Opened Tbilisi to the Ottomans (taken by 24 August 1578).

name: Koyun Geçidi
place: Koyun Geçidi ford on the Kanik (Alazani) river, Azerbaijan
how the result was decided: The Ottomans crossed the Alazani (Qanikh) in force and drove the Safavid army into the river with heavy loss, holding the field (9 September 1578).

commanders B: Amir Khan Turkman, Murad Khan (killed), Sharaf Khan Bitlisi
Iranian force: Qizilbash cavalry of Karabakh and Shirvan (no details in the sources used).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

date: 28 November 1578 (24 or 30 November in some accounts)
name: Mollahasanli
place: Mollahasanli on the Agsu river, near Pirgasanli, Azerbaijan
how the result was decided: The surprise attack routed the Tatars, who had scattered to guard their booty, and Adil Giray was captured.

why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: about 2,000 captured, including some 30 nobles and the Ottoman sanjak-bey Piyale Beg
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Mollahasanli; Gazi II Giray; Ottoman-Safavid War (1578-1590)

name: Shamakhi (siege, 1578)
how the result was decided: The Crimean relief army caught the Safavid besiegers between two forces and routed them; the siege failed.

commanders B: Aras Khan, beglarbeg of Shirvan (killed after the defeat)
Iranian force: About 20,000 Qizilbash of Shirvan and Karabakh under Aras Khan.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Shamakhi (1578); Ottoman-Safavid War (1578-1590)
note: The Safavids besieged the Ottoman-held city; the defender won.

name: Shamakhi (1581)
how the result was decided: The Ottoman-Crimean force was decisively defeated and Gazi Giray was taken prisoner.
commanders A: Piri Muhammad Beg, Imam Quli Khan Qajar
Iranian force: Qizilbash of Karabakh and Shirvan under Imam Quli Khan Qajar and Piri Muhammad Beg (no numbers).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: described in two articles but not given a battle name
doubts and flags: Borderline: described in two articles but not given a battle name.
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman-Safavid War (1578-1590); Gazi II Giray
note: Osman Pasha then withdrew to Derbent, leaving a garrison in Baku.

name: Herat (siege, 1582-1583)
how the result was decided: After about a year of skirmishing and talks the siege ended in a truce that left Herat in Ali-Qoli Khan's hands.
commanders B: Ali-Qoli Khan Shamlu, with the boy Abbas Mirza
Iranian force: Khodabanda's army of about 80,000, Turkman, Takkalu and other Qizilbash of the west, against the Shamlu and Ustajlu of Khorasan.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: mostly minor skirmishing; Wikipedia's Abbas article also mentions a failed siege of Torbat-e Heydarieh held by Morshed-Qoli Khan in the same campaign (not listed separately)

sources: en.wikipedia Ali-Qoli Khan Shamlu; Abbas the Great; Savory
note: Wikipedia's Abbas article dates the siege to 1582, other accounts to 1583.

name: Torches
how the result was decided: After an indecisive first day the Ottoman general attack on the third day broke the Safavid army, which left the field.
commanders A: Ozdemiroglu Osman Pasha, Cafer Pasha, Haydar Pasha
commanders B: Imam Quli Khan Qajar (centre), Rostam Khan, Borhan al-Din
Iranian force: Imam Quli Khan Qajar's army of 50,000 or more, the Qizilbash of Karabakh, Shirvan and Azerbaijan, with Georgian irregulars.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Torches; Ottoman-Safavid War (1578-1590)
note: Meşaleler Savaşı, so called because fighting went on by torchlight. Ottoman allies: the Crimean Khanate, the Shamkhalate of Tarki and the Nogais. Some accounts place the battle near the Samur river.

name: Tabriz (siege, 1585-1586)
how the result was decided: The Ottoman fortress at Tabriz held and the Safavid siege was given up; the city stayed Ottoman until 1603.
commanders A: Cafer Pasha (governor of the new Ottoman fortress)
Iranian force: Hamza Mirza's Qizilbash army (no details).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

note: Hamza Mirza was murdered in his camp in Karabakh on 6 December 1586, after which the Safavid effort collapsed.

name: Alvar
place: Alvar (Elver), about 18 km north-west of Tabriz, Iran
how the result was decided: Hamza Mirza's ambush was beaten off and he fell back to the main army; the Ottomans went on to Tabriz, which surrendered on 25 September.
commanders A: Ozdemiroglu Osman Pasha, Cigalazade Yusuf Sinan Pasha, Mehmed Pasha
commanders B: Hamza Mirza; Qilinj Beg of the Pazuki (killed)
Iranian force: About 5,000 foot and 5,000 horse under Hamza Mirza hidden in the gardens: Qizilbash cavalry, musketeers and the Kurdish Pazuki tribe.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses A: 500-1,000 casualties on one side (unassigned in the source)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Alvar; Capture of Tabriz (1585)
note: Capture of Tabriz (1585), 23-25 September, followed without a separate battle and is not listed.

name: Malandari Pass (Karakar Pass)
place: between the Karakar and Malandari passes, Buner/Swat, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
how the result was decided: The Mughal column was ambushed in the defile, Birbal and about 8,000 men were killed and the army was routed.
commanders A: Raja Birbal (killed); Zain Khan Koka; Hakim Abul Fath
commanders B: Kalu Khan Yusufzai; Mirwais (son of Mullah Meru)
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Malandari Pass: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Malandari_Pass; Badauni, Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama; Wikipedia, Pir Roshan
note: Akbar's worst defeat; Todar Mal's punitive expedition followed on 19 February. Khafi Khan's figure of 40,000 dead is much higher than Badauni's 8,000.

name: Herat (siege, 1587-1589)
how the result was decided: Herat surrendered to the Uzbeks in February 1589 after more than a year's siege.
commanders B: Ali-Qoli Khan Shamlu (executed after the surrender)
Iranian force: Ali-Qoli Khan's Shamlu Qizilbash with the townsmen of Herat; no relief came because Morshed-Qoli Khan delayed it.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: the city was sacked and many inhabitants killed
sources: en.wikipedia Ali-Qoli Khan Shamlu; Abbas the Great; Savory

name: Mashhad (siege, 1589)
how the result was decided: Mashhad fell to the Uzbeks, who sacked the city and the shrine of Imam Reza.
commanders A: Abd al-Mumin, son of Abdullah Khan II
commanders B: the Safavid governor of Mashhad (not named in the sources used)
Iranian force: The Qizilbash garrison and townsmen of Mashhad (no details).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no Wikipedia article; Wikipedia's Persian-Uzbek wars and Abdullah Khan II date Abd al-Mumin's sack of Mashhad to 1583

sources: Savory, Iran under the Safavids; Iskandar Beg Munshi; en.wikipedia Persian-Uzbek wars
note: Abbas recovered Mashhad easily in April 1598.

name: Raipur (Jagat Singh's defeat, 1590)
place: Raipur, near Bishnupur, West Bengal, India
how the result was decided: The Mughal division was routed, three officers killed and Jagat Singh escaped wounded to Bishnupur.
sources: Wikipedia, Mughal conquest of Odisha: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_conquest_of_Odisha; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama
note: The place and the usual name (some histories call it Jahanabad) are not secure.

name: Subarnarekha (1592)
place: bank of the Subarnarekha river, near Jaleswar, Odisha, India
how the result was decided: After early Afghan charges, Mughal reinforcements, artillery and archery won the day; about 300 Afghans fell.
commanders A: Man Singh; Jagat Singh; Durjan Singh
sources: Wikipedia, Mughal conquest of Odisha: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_conquest_of_Odisha; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama
note: The overall Afghan commander is not named in the source; the Afghan chiefs of Orissa were the Lohani and Karrani followers of Nasir Khan.

name: Herat (1598)
how the result was decided: After Abbas's feigned retreat the Uzbeks were routed and their khan fled wounded.
commanders A: Abbas I, Allahverdi Khan, Farhad Khan Qaramanlu
commanders B: Din Mohammad Khan (wounded, killed in the flight)
Iranian force: Abbas's field force of 10,000-15,000: qurchis and Qizilbash cavalry with the new ghulam cavalry under Allahverdi Khan.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Herat (1598); Abbas the Great; Savory
note: Also called the battle of Rabat-i Pariyan; it recovered Khorasan.

name: Bahrain (1602)
how the result was decided: Persian musketeers drove the Portuguese from their fort and held the island against the Portuguese-Hormuzi counter-attack.
commanders A: Allahverdi Khan (governor of Fars); Mu'in al-Din Fali
commanders B: the Portuguese and Hormuzi garrison; Francisco de Sotomayor (counter-attack)
Iranian force: A detachment of musketeers sent by Allahverdi Khan from Fars, with the Bahraini partisans of the rebel governor.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Safavid conquest of Bahrain; Portuguese-Safavid wars
note: The governor Rukn al-Din Mas'ud had rebelled against Hormuz; Wikipedia's Abbas the Great credits Imam Quli Khan.

name: Balkh (1602)
how the result was decided: Outmanoeuvred and short of water and food, Abbas withdrew from Balkh, losing most of his cannon.
Iranian force: 40,000 troops including 10,000 musketeers and about 300 cannon.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a failed campaign and retreat rather than a set battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: a failed campaign and retreat rather than a set battle.
sources: en.wikipedia Persian-Uzbek wars; Abbas the Great

name: Tabriz (siege, 1603)
how the result was decided: The Ottoman garrison of Tabriz surrendered on 21 October 1603.
commanders A: Abbas I, Allahverdi Khan, Amir-Guna Khan Qajar
Iranian force: Abbas's reformed army: qurchis and Qizilbash, ghulam cavalry, tufangchi musketeers and the new artillery, used for the first time.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Safavid capture of Tabriz (1603); Amir-Guna Khan Qajar; Ottoman-Safavid war (1603-1612)
note: Abbas first retook and razed the Ottoman base at Nahavand.

name: Erivan (siege, 1603-1604)
how the result was decided: The fortress fell on 8 June 1604, Amir-Guna Khan's Qajars entering by the White Tower.
Iranian force: Abbas's royal army with artillery; Amir-Guna Khan's Qajar contingent led the final assault.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Amir-Guna Khan Qajar; Ottoman-Safavid war (1603-1612); Abbas the Great; Siege of Erivan (disambiguation: Siege of Erivan (1604), a red link)
note: Abbas then withdrew before the Ottoman counter-offensive with scorched-earth tactics, deporting the Armenians of the region.

name: Kandahar (siege, 1605-1606)
how the result was decided: After two months of assaults a Mughal relief army forced the besiegers to withdraw; Kandahar did not fall.
commanders A: Shah Beg Khan (governor); relief army sent by Jahangir
Iranian force: The provincial army of Khorasan under the Shamlu governor of Herat (no details).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kandahar (1605-1606); Mughal-Persian wars; Iranica, Qandahar
note: Abbas disowned the attack, made by the Khorasan governors without royal orders. Iranica dates it to 1606.

name: Sufiyan (1605)
how the result was decided: Abbas's flank feint and the Qizilbash charge routed the Ottoman army, which fled leaving the field and many commanders.
commanders A: Abbas I, Allahverdi Khan, Qarachaqay Beg, Amir-Guna Khan Qajar
commanders B: Cigalazade Yusuf Sinan Pasha, Kose Sefer Pasha (captured), Tekkeli Mehmed Pasha, Karakas Pasha, Kacar Mehmed Pasha
Iranian force: About 60,000: Qizilbash cavalry, Allahverdi Khan's ghulams, a musketeer regiment under Qarachaqay Beg, and Amir-Guna Khan's Qajars on the right wing.
languages: Turkic; Persian; Georgian; Armenian; other Caucasian
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Sufiyan; Qarachaqay Khan; Amir-Guna Khan Qajar; Iskandar Beg Munshi
note: Wikipedia's Battle of Urmia (1604) and the war article's 'Battle of Lake Urmia, 9 September 1605' describe the same defeat of Cigalazade and Kose Sefer Pasha (same commanders, about 100,000 Ottomans, about 20,000 killed) and are not listed separately.

date: 1606 (about six months, beginning three months after Sufiyan)
name: Ganja (siege, 1606)
how the result was decided: Ganja fell to the Safavids after a siege of about six months.
Iranian force: Abbas's royal army with siege artillery (no details).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: up to 2,500 killed (given as civilians in one article, as Ottoman dead in another)
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Ganja (1606); Abbas I's Shirvan campaign
note: Abbas then retook Tiflis the same year.

date: 24 July 1606 (as given on Wikipedia; year inferred from its chronology)
name: Hama (Janbulad v Yusuf Sayfa, 1606)
side B: Ottoman governors of Tripoli, Damascus and Hama

principal opponents: Ottoman governors of Tripoli, Damascus and Hama
commanders B: Yusuf Sayfa Pasha, governor of Tripoli
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Janbulad; Griswold, The Great Anatolian Rebellion (1983)
note: Ali Janbulad belonged to a Kurdish chieftain family of Kilis (the Kurd Dagh); his army was mostly sekban and local levies, so the leader rule is what qualifies it.

name: Shamakhi (siege, 1607)
how the result was decided: The Safavid assault of late June took the towers and a gate and the garrison was overrun.
commanders A: Abbas I, Allahverdi Khan, Pir Budaq Khan, Qarachaqay Beg, Zulfiqar Khan
commanders B: Ahmed Pasha, beylerbey of Shirvan (captured), Shamseddin Pasha (executed)

why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses A: many killed when a bridge over the moat collapsed
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Shamakhi; Abbas I's Shirvan campaign
note: Baku and Derbent went over to the Safavids after local risings. The Safavids took about 150 large and 500 small guns.

name: Oruc Plain (Amik Valley, 1607)
place: Oruc Plain, Amik Valley near the Afrin river, Hatay, Turkey
how the result was decided: Kuyucu Murad's army broke the rebel host, killing the lieutenant Jin Ali and capturing thousands; Ali fled.
commanders A: Grand Vizier Kuyucu Murad Pasha; Zulfikar Pasha; Tiryaki Hasan Pasha
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Janbulad; Griswold, The Great Anatolian Rebellion (1983); Kuyucu Murad Pasha (Wikipedia)
note: Ali Janbulad is described as a Kurdish tribal chief from Kilis; he led about 25,000 sekban and cavalry. The 'pyramid of 20,000 skulls' is a report, not a count.

name: Dimdim (siege)
war: Safavid campaign against the Bradost Kurds
place: Dimdim castle, west of Lake Urmia, Iran
how the result was decided: Dimdim fell after nearly a year's siege and its defenders were killed.
commanders A: Hatem Beg Ordubadi (grand vizier), Abbas I
commanders B: Amir Khan Lepzerin (Emir Khan Brada), ruler of Bradost (killed)
Iranian force: The army of Azerbaijan under the vizier Hatem Beg (no breakdown in the sources).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Dimdim; Iskandar Beg Munshi, Tarikh-e Alam-ara-ye Abbasi
note: Emirate of Bradost. A massacre in Bradost and Mukriyan followed. The siege is the subject of the Kurdish epic Kela Dimdim.

name: Bokainagar (siege, 1611)
war: Mughal conquest of Bengal: Afghan insurrection of Khwaja Usman
how the result was decided: After a failed assault in the floods and the defection of Nasir Khan and Dariya Khan, Usman abandoned the fort and it was taken by the end of November.
commanders A: Islam Khan I; Shaikh Kamal; Shuja'at Khan
sources: Wikipedia, Mughal conquest of Sylhet: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_conquest_of_Sylhet; Mirza Nathan, Baharistan-i Ghaybi

commanders B: Khwaja Usman; Khwaja Wali; Shir-i-Maydan; Khwaja Mahli; Khwaja Ibrahim; Khwaja Daud
sources: Wikipedia, Mughal conquest of Sylhet: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_conquest_of_Sylhet; Mirza Nathan, Baharistan-i Ghaybi
note: Mirza Nathan gives the Afghans about 5,000 horse, 10,000 foot and 150 elephants; the Afghans had the upper hand until a false alarm disrupted the Mughal vanguard.

name: Cambarão (siege)
how the result was decided: The Portuguese fort surrendered before a relief fleet of nine ships arrived.
Iranian force: 14,000 men of the Fars army under Imam Quli Khan (no breakdown).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Capture of Cambarão; Portuguese-Safavid wars
note: Wikipedia's Portuguese-Safavid wars dates the capture to 1615. The town was renamed Bandar Abbas.

name: Tsitsamuri
war: Abbas I's Kakhetian and Kartlian campaigns
how the result was decided: The Persian centre broke and its flanks collapsed; the Georgians held the field.
commanders A: Teimuraz I of Kakheti, David Jandieri, Nodar Jorjadze
Iranian force: About 15,000 Qizilbash sent by Abbas to put down the rising.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Tsitsamuri; Abbas I's Kakhetian and Kartlian campaigns
note: Kingdom of Kakheti. Abbas answered with the devastation and deportations of 1616-1617.

name: Erivan (siege, 1616)
how the result was decided: The Ottomans lifted the siege on 5 November and were ambushed on the retreat.
commanders A: Amir-Guna Khan Qajar (garrison), Abbas I (field army)

name: Sampagha Pass (Tirah, 1619)
war: Mughal wars against the Roshani movement
place: Sampagha Pass, Tirah, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan

date: June 1621 to February 1622 (English ships joined in January 1622)
name: Qeshm (siege, 1621-1622)
place: Portuguese fort on Qeshm Island, Iran
