name: Muscat (1622-1623)
how the result was decided: The Persian attack on Muscat was quickly repelled.
Iranian force: Fars troops with Arab allies, without English naval support (no numbers).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
strength A: about 1,000 Portuguese, 20 galliots, and about 15,000 Omanis of the Imam of Nizwa
borderline: a brief attack described in one article
doubts and flags: Borderline: a brief attack described in one article.
sources: en.wikipedia Portuguese-Safavid War (1621-1630)
note: Oman here is the Imam of Nizwa's men allied to the Portuguese.

date: 9 February to 23 April 1622 (English Old Style; 3-4 May in the Gregorian calendar)
name: Hormuz (siege, 1622)
how the result was decided: The Portuguese garrison mutinied and surrendered the fortress; the English destroyed every Portuguese ship at Hormuz.
commanders A: Imam Quli Khan; Captain Blythe (English East India Company)
Iranian force: About 3,000 Safavid troops of the Fars army landed from 200 boats, with five English warships and four pinnaces.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
strength A: about 3,000 Persians, 200 boats; 5 English warships and 4 pinnaces
losses B: the Portuguese ships at Hormuz destroyed; garrison captured
sources: en.wikipedia Anglo-Persian capture of Hormuz; Portuguese-Safavid War (1621-1630)
note: England here is the English East India Company. The last king of Hormuz, Muhammad Shah IV, was sent to Isfahan; Bandar Abbas replaced Hormuz as the port.

name: Kandahar (siege, 1622)
how the result was decided: Kandahar surrendered on 22 June 1622 after the Persians mined the walls.
commanders A: Abbas I, Ganj Ali Khan, Khosrow Sultan
Iranian force: Abbas's royal army assembled at Nishapur, without heavy cannon, relying on mining: Qizilbash, ghulams and musketeers.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Mughal-Safavid war (1622-1623); Mughal-Persian wars; Iranica, Qandahar
note: The siege is said to have lasted 45 days, which does not fit the dates given; Mughal-Persian wars wrongly gives 1621. Ganj Ali Khan became governor.

date: late 1623 to 14 January 1624 (the Safavids broke in on the evening of 12 January)
name: Baghdad (siege, 1623-1624)
how the result was decided: Baghdad fell to the Safavids on 12-14 January 1624.
commanders A: Abbas I, Qarachaqay Khan, Giorgi Saakadze
Iranian force: Abbas's royal army: Qarachaqay Khan's ghulams and musketeers, Qizilbash, and Giorgi Saakadze's Georgians.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: unknown; a large part of the Sunni population was massacred
sources: en.wikipedia Capture of Baghdad (1624); Ottoman-Safavid War (1623-1639); Blow, Shah Abbas
note: Bakr Subashi had rebelled against the Ottomans and then returned to their allegiance; his son Muhammad let the Persians in. Kirkuk and Mosul were taken in the same campaign.

name: Sohar (siege, 1623)
how the result was decided: Sohar surrendered after the Portuguese stormed a wall and fought into the streets.
commanders A: Rui Freire de Andrade, Goncalo da Silveira (wounded)
commanders B: the Persian captain of Sohar (not named)
Iranian force: A garrison of 2,000 left after the Safavid occupation of Sohar in 1622.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
strength A: about 1,000 Portuguese and about 15,000 Omani allies
sources: en.wikipedia Portuguese-Safavid War (1621-1630)
note: A garrison of 100 Portuguese and 200 Lascarins was left.

name: Khor Fakkan (1623)
place: off Khor Fakkan, United Arab Emirates
how the result was decided: The Safavid fleet withdrew after the fight and the Safavids were driven from the coast, where a Portuguese garrison was left.
Iranian force: A Safavid squadron of local vessels (no numbers).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Portuguese-Safavid War (1621-1630)
note: An accident on the Portuguese flagship let the Safavid ships escape.

name: Basra (1624)
place: Qubban and the Shatt al-Arab, near Basra, Iraq
how the result was decided: Portuguese galleys bombarded the Safavid camp from the river, the attack on Qubban failed and the Safavid army withdrew.
commanders A: Afrasiyab Pasha of Basra; the Portuguese galley squadron of Silveira (Rui Freire de Andrade's command)
Iranian force: Imam Quli Khan's Fars army, 'thousands of men' (no breakdown).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
strength A: five Portuguese galliots with Basran troops
sources: en.wikipedia Safavid invasions of Basra; Portuguese-Safavid wars; Ottoman-Safavid War (1623-1639)
note: Basra was ruled by the autonomous Afrasiyab pashas, nominally Ottoman. A second Safavid advance of about 30,000 in spring 1625 withdrew without a battle (not listed).

name: Rajmahal (1624)
place: Rajmahal on the Ganges, Jharkhand, India
how the result was decided: Ibrahim Khan Fath Jang was defeated and killed and Shah Jahan took Bengal.
commanders B: Ibrahim Khan Fath Jang, governor of Bengal (killed)
sources: Beni Prasad, History of Jahangir; Wikipedia, Shah Jahan; Ibrahim Khan Fath Jang (not fetched)
note: Ibrahim Khan Fath Jang was the brother of Nur Jahan and a son of Mirza Ghiyas Beg (Itimad-ud-Daula), the Persian from Tehran: Persian by birth. Date recalled from the standard accounts and not re-checked.

date: September 1624 (Wikipedia and Tamaskar); the Jedhe Shakavali and Basatin-us-Salatin point to October 1624
name: Bhatvadi
war: Mughal-Ahmadnagar war (Malik Ambar against the Mughals and the Bijapuri army)
how the result was decided: Malik Ambar flooded the allied route by breaching the Keli dam and routed the allied army, killing Mulla Muhammad Lari and capturing Ikhlas Khan and some 240 Bijapuri commanders and three Mughal generals (Wikipedia, Battle of Bhatvadi, after Sohoni 2016).
commanders A: Mulla Muhammad Lari (Persian from Lar; Bijapuri general, killed); Ikhlas Khan (captured); Sijahdar Khan (Mughal)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bhatvadi; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulla_Muhammad_Lari; P. Sohoni, Flushing out the Enemy: Revisiting the battle of Bhatavadi, Bulletin of the Deccan College (2016); Futuhat-i Adilshahi; Basatin-us-Salatin
note: Wikipedia (Mulla Muhammad Lari) calls him a Persian from Lar, and he was painted by Hashim as a Persian noble of the Deccan. The Iranian leadership here is of the Bijapuri contingent only;

date: autumn 1624 (October is the usual date; not re-checked)
name: Tons (1624)
place: the River Tons, near Allahabad-Benares, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: The imperial army under Parviz and Mahabat Khan defeated Shah Jahan, who fled south to the Deccan.
sources: Beni Prasad, History of Jahangir; Wikipedia, Shah Jahan; Mahabat Khan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabat_Khan)
note: Mahabat Khan (born Zamana Beg, Kabul) is 'of Persian origin' in Wikipedia; his father was Ghayur Beg Kabuli. The date and the site (the Tons near Benares) are given from memory.

name: Aghaiani
war: Abbas I's Kakhetian and Kartlian campaigns (Saakadze's revolt)
how the result was decided: The small Kakhetian force of nobles and retainers was destroyed.
Iranian force: Qarachaqay Khan's large expeditionary army: Qizilbash, ghulams and musketeers.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Aghaiani
note: Kingdom of Kakheti. The date is approximate; it preceded Martkopi.

name: Martkopi
war: Abbas I's Kakhetian and Kartlian campaigns (Saakadze's revolt)
how the result was decided: The Georgians' dawn attack destroyed the Persian camp and killed its commanders.
commanders A: Giorgi Saakadze, Zurab, Duke of Aragvi
commanders B: Qarachaqay Khan (killed), Imam Verdi Beg (killed), Yusuf Khan (killed)
Iranian force: Qarachaqay Khan's army of about 30,000, roughly half of it dispersed in Javakheti on Saakadze's advice: Qizilbash, ghulams and musketeers.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Martkopi; Qarachaqay Khan
note: Kingdoms of Kartli and Kakheti. Saakadze had served in the Persian army and turned on it. The Georgians then took Tbilisi.

name: Marabda
war: Abbas I's Kakhetian and Kartlian campaigns (Saakadze's revolt)
how the result was decided: The Georgian charge was halted by musketry and artillery, the Qizilbash counter-attacked and the Georgians were routed.
commanders A: Isa Khan Safavi, Amir-Guna Khan Qajar (mortally wounded), Rustam Khan, Shahbandeh Khan
Iranian force: About 60,000: the beglarbegs of Shirvan and Erivan with troops of northern and central Iran, musketeers in four ranks behind breastworks, artillery, and Qizilbash cavalry, reinforced from Azerbaijan.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Marabda; Amir-Guna Khan Qajar; Abbas the Great
note: Kingdoms of Kartli and Kakheti. Despite the victory Abbas accepted Kartli and Kakheti as vassal states.

name: Baghdad (siege, 1625-1626)
how the result was decided: Baghdad held; the Ottomans, their convoys cut and their attack on the relief army repulsed, lifted the siege on 4 July 1626.
commanders A: Abbas I (relief army); the Safavid garrison
Iranian force: The Safavid garrison and Abbas's relief army of Qizilbash, ghulams and musketeers (no numbers).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Baghdad (1625-1626); Ottoman-Safavid War (1623-1639)
note: The Ottomans breached the outer walls before the relief army arrived; they withdrew to Mosul.

name: Jhelum (1626)
place: the Jhelum river crossing, Punjab, Pakistan
how the result was decided: Mahabat Khan kept Jahangir in his hands after Nur Jahan's counter-attack at the crossing failed.
Iranian side: Mahabat Khan v Imperial court army
commanders B: Asaf Khan (fled); Nur Jahan (led the counter-charge on her elephant)
sources: Wikipedia, Mahabat Khan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabat_Khan); Beni Prasad, History of Jahangir; Findly, Nur Jahan
note: A Persian-against-Persian clash: Mahabat Khan (Wikipedia: 'of Persian origin', born Kabul), against Asaf Khan and Nur Jahan (Persian children of Mirza Ghiyas Beg). Mahabat's strength was Rajput troops, so the Iranian element is the leadership.

date: late 1627 (November-December, soon after Jahangir's death on 28 October; exact day not fixed)
name: Lahore (1627)
how the result was decided: Shahriyar was defeated and captured and later blinded; this secured the throne for Shah Jahan.
commanders A: Asaf Khan (Abu'l-Hasan), directing for Prince Dawar Bakhsh
commanders B: Shahriyar Mirza (Nur Jahan, his mother-in-law, backed him from Lahore)
sources: Beni Prasad, History of Jahangir; Wikipedia, Asaf Khan IV and Shahryar Mirza; Lahori, Padshahnama
note: Asaf Khan was the son of Mirza Ghiyas Beg, a Persian from Tehran, and Nur Jahan's brother. The fight itself was small and the date is recalled from memory, not fetched; Nur Jahan, also Persian, stood behind the other side.

name: Basra (siege, 1628-1629)
how the result was decided: The Safavids took outlying forts but not the city and abandoned the siege after Abbas's death in January 1629.
Iranian force: Imam Quli Khan's Fars army (no details).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Safavid invasions of Basra
note: Basra was ruled by the autonomous Afrasiyab pashas, nominally Ottoman; the campaign followed a rising against Ali Pasha led by Ibn Ilayan.

name: Mahidasht
how the result was decided: Husrev Pasha's army routed the Persians and held the field, then marched on and sacked Hamadan.
Iranian force: Zainal Khan's field army of the western frontier: Qizilbash tribal cavalry with ghulams and tufangchi musketeers (no breakdown in the sources used).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no separate Wikipedia article; named in the war article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate Wikipedia article; named in the war article.
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman-Safavid War (1623-1639); Encyclopaedia Iranica (Safi I)
note: Zainal Khan was executed by Shah Safi soon afterwards. Hamadan was sacked by the Ottomans in June 1630 without a recorded battle (excluded).

name: Baghdad (siege, 1630)
how the result was decided: The general assault of 10 October failed and Husrev Pasha raised the siege on 14 November.
commanders A: Safi Khan (commander of the citadel); Shah Safi (relief army)
Iranian force: The Safavid garrison of Baghdad (no breakdown), with a relief army forming under Shah Safi; a Safavid detachment under Khan Ahmed (probably the Ardalan Kurdish wali) took Mihriban and Pelengan in the Ottoman rear.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: heavy; 400-500 men killed inside the Narinkale, eight boats lost
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Baghdad (1630); Ottoman-Safavid War (1623-1639)
note: Some accounts give the start as 5 October. Husrev Pasha cited the failed assault, shortages and the threat to Shahrizor.

name: Sihonda
how the result was decided: Khan Jahan Lodi was cornered and killed and his head sent to Shah Jahan at Burhanpur.
sources: Wikipedia, Khan Jahan Lodi: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khan_Jahan_Lodi; Britannica, battle of Shihonda
note: Khan Jahan Lodi (Pir Khan) was an Afghan Lodi who had risen under Jahangir. The source gives the date as 1 February in the text and 3 February in the infobox.

name: Hooghly (siege, 1632)
how the result was decided: The Mughals mined and breached the wall and took the fort on 24 September, expelling the Portuguese.
commanders A: Qasim Khan Juvayni, governor of Bengal
sources: Wikipedia, Siege of Hooghly (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hooghly); Abdul Hamid Lahori, Padshahnama
note: Qasim Khan's nisba Juvayni points to Juvayn in Khurasan; the siege article does not state his origin and I did not fetch his own page, so his Persian descent is inferred from the nisba and from his place among the Irani nobles.

name: Julfar (1633)
war: Omani wars against the Portuguese and Persians (Imam Nasir bin Murshid)
place: Julfar (near Ras al-Khaimah), United Arab Emirates
how the result was decided: The Persian fort fell to the second Omani assault after two days' fighting, and the Portuguese fort was then taken.
commanders A: Imam Nasir bin Murshid, Ali bin Ahmad al-Nizawi, Khamis bin Makhzum
commanders B: Nasir al-Din al-Ajami (commander of the Persian fort)
Iranian force: The small Safavid garrison of the fort of Julfar (no details).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Capture of Julfar
note: Ya'rubid Oman. Persians and Portuguese each held a fort at Julfar and are listed together as defenders, though they were not allies.

name: Daulatabad (siege, 1633)
war: Mughal conquest of the Ahmadnagar Sultanate
how the result was decided: The fort fell in June 1633, Fath Khan was arrested and the Nizam Shahi king Husain Shah was sent to Gwalior.
commanders A: Mahabat Khan (governor of the Deccan, directed the siege); Khan Zaman (his son, led the siege works); Nasiri Khan (Khan Dauran)
commanders B: Fath Khan (minister, defended the fort); Randaula Khan; Murari Pandit; Shahaji Bhonsle (relief attempts)
sources: Wikipedia, Siege of Daulatabad (1633) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Daulatabad_(1633)); Mahabat Khan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabat_Khan)
note: Mahabat Khan was born at Kabul and Wikipedia calls him 'of Persian origin' (father Ghayur Beg Kabuli); the origin is stated but thin. This ended the Nizam Shahi dynasty.

name: Erivan (siege, 1635)
how the result was decided: After ten days of bombardment the garrison surrendered the fortress on 8 August.
commanders A: Sultan Murad IV, Tabaniyassi Mehmed Pasha
commanders B: Tahmasp Quli Khan (Emirguneoglu, governor of Erivan), Murad Agha
Iranian force: The garrison of Erivan under its Qajar governor Tahmasp Quli Khan (no breakdown).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Erivan (1635); Ottoman-Safavid War (1623-1639)
note: The governor defected, became a Sunni as Yusuf Pasha and later governed Aleppo. Murad then occupied and destroyed Tabriz, which the Safavids had evacuated without a fight (excluded).

name: Erivan (siege, 1636)
how the result was decided: The Ottoman garrison capitulated and the Safavids reoccupied Erivan.
commanders B: the Ottoman garrison commander (unnamed in the sources used)
Iranian force: Shah Safi's royal army: Qizilbash cavalry, ghulam regiments and tufangchi musketeers with artillery (no breakdown in the sources used).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman-Safavid War (1623-1639); Siege of Erivan (disambiguation, 1636 entry); Matthee, Persia in Crisis
note: The Wikipedia article on this siege is a stub; the war article says Safi retook Erivan in the spring of 1636 and defeated an Ottoman army (unnamed, not listed separately). Day and month of the surrender are not given.

name: Kandahar (1638)
how the result was decided: The Mughals routed the Safavid relief force and took its camp.
commanders A: Sa'id Khan, Qulij Khan Turani, Ali Mardan Khan (the defected Safavid governor)
Iranian force: Siyavush's relief army of 5,000-6,000 cavalry; Siyavush was qullar-aqasi (commander of the ghulam corps), so ghulam horse were probably prominent.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
strength A: about 3,000 engaged, with 8,000 cavalry and 400 musketeers nearby
sources: en.wikipedia Fall of Kandahar (1638); Mughal-Safavid War (1637-1638)
note: Ali Mardan Khan had handed the fortress to the Mughals without a fight on 11 March 1638; this entry is the field battle a month later.

name: Bost (siege, 1638)
place: Bost (Qala-i Bust, near Lashkar Gah), Afghanistan
how the result was decided: The Mughals mined and stormed the walls and Mihrab Khan surrendered the citadel on 3 September.
Iranian force: The Safavid garrison of Bost under Mihrab Khan (no breakdown).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses A: about 100 killed, 300 wounded in the assault
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Bost (1638)
note: The garrison was granted amnesty and sent back to Persia.

name: Baghdad (siege, 1638)
how the result was decided: Baghdad fell to the Ottoman assault after a 39-day siege.
commanders A: Sultan Murad IV, Tayyar Mehmed Pasha (killed), Kemankes Kara Mustafa Pasha
commanders B: Bektash Khan Gorji; Khalil Khan, Naqdi Khan, Ali Yar Khan (captured), Saru Khan (killed)
Iranian force: A greatly enlarged garrison (said to be 40,000 infantry with 100 guns) under the Georgian ghulam Bektash Khan, sallying 6,000 at a time.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: more than 20,000 killed, many in the massacre after the fall
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Baghdad (1638); Ottoman-Safavid War (1623-1639)
note: The fall of Baghdad led to the Treaty of Zuhab (17 May 1639), which left Iraq to the Ottomans.

name: Magharo
war: Wars of Teimuraz I against Rostom of Kartli and the Safavids
how the result was decided: Rostom's army with its Iranian force routed Teimuraz, who fled to Imereti.
commanders A: Rostom (Rustam Khan), Safavid vassal king of Kartli
commanders B: Teimuraz I of Kakheti, Prince David (killed)
Iranian force: An Iranian (Safavid) force of unrecorded size fighting beside Rostom's Kartlian army.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the size of the Iranian force is not recorded, so 'major ally' is a judgement
doubts and flags: Borderline: the size of the Iranian force is not recorded, so 'major ally' is a judgement.
sources: en.wikipedia Teimuraz I of Kakheti
note: Rostom was a Muslim Georgian of the Safavid court installed by the shah in Kartli. Kingdoms of Kartli and Kakheti.

name: Kandahar (siege, 1648-1649)
how the result was decided: Daulat Khan surrendered the fort on 22 February 1649 after part of his garrison mutinied.
Iranian force: Abbas II's army of about 40,000 with siege artillery; the losses name 600 Qizilbash among about 2,000 dead.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kandahar (1648-1649); Mughal-Safavid war (1649-1653)
note: Bost was taken earlier, in the summer of 1648, without a recorded battle.

name: Kandahar (siege, 1649)
how the result was decided: The Mughals could not breach the walls and retreated on 5 September 1649.
commanders B: Prince Aurangzeb, Sadullah Khan, Jai Singh I
Iranian force: The Safavid garrison of Kandahar with its artillery, and Safavid forces in the field around the city (no breakdown).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: about 3,000 men and thousands of draught animals
sources: en.wikipedia Mughal sieges of Kandahar (1649-1653); Mughal-Safavid war (1649-1653)
note: The Mughals are said to have beaten Safavid forces in the open outside the city during this campaign, but no named field battle is recorded.

date: 1649-1650 (a siege of some months; the fort fell in 1650)
name: Gandikota (siege, 1650)
war: Golconda's Carnatic campaigns under Mir Jumla (1646-1656)
place: Gandikota fort, Kadapa district, Andhra Pradesh
how the result was decided: Mir Jumla captured Gandikota in 1650 with the help of European gunners (Wikipedia, Mir Jumla II).
commanders A: Mir Jumla (Mir Muhammad Sayyid Ardestani; Persian merchant-turned-general and wazir of Golconda)
commanders B: Timma Nayaka (Timma Nayudu), the commander of the fort
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir_Jumla_II; J. Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, vol. 1 (on Mir Jumla); R. M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 1300-1761 (2005)
note: Mir Jumla was born in Isfahan (Wikipedia) of an Ardestani sayyid family and came to Golconda as a diamond merchant's clerk; he commanded the Golconda army in the Carnatic until he went over to the Mughals in 1656. His Golconda army also included Afghan, Rajput and other mercenaries.

name: Sunzha (1651)
place: near the Russian fort on the Sunzha, Chechnya, Russia
how the result was decided: The Russians won the series of fights and the Dagestani levies withdrew after plundering the countryside.
commanders A: unnamed (Terek Cossacks and the fort's garrison)
Iranian force: About 12,800 men sent by decree of Abbas II: 12,000 Dagestani levies and 800 Persian regulars from Shirvan.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a series of unnamed fights grouped here as one entry
doubts and flags: Borderline: a series of unnamed fights grouped here as one entry.
sources: en.wikipedia Russo-Persian War (1651-1653)
note: Wikipedia's infobox gives the war as a Persian victory, but its text says the Russians won the battles of 1651.

name: Kandahar (siege, 1652)
how the result was decided: The Mughals failed to breach the walls and withdrew to Kabul on 9 July 1652.
commanders A: the Safavid governor of Kandahar (unnamed in the sources used)
commanders B: Prince Aurangzeb, Sadullah Khan, Jai Singh I
Iranian force: The Safavid garrison with its artillery, whose gunners outshot the Mughal batteries (no breakdown).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
strength B: unknown (a larger, better-equipped army than in 1649)
sources: en.wikipedia Mughal sieges of Kandahar (1649-1653)
note: Uzbek raids on the Mughal supply lines (10,000 men sent by Abdul Aziz of Bukhara) contributed to the failure.

name: Sunzha fort (siege, 1653)
place: Russian fort (ostrog) on the Sunzha, Chechnya, Russia
how the result was decided: The surviving garrison slipped away to Terki on 25 March and the Persians destroyed the fort.
commanders A: Khosrow Khan (governor of Shirvan), the shamkhal of Tarki, the utsmi of Kara Qaytaq
Iranian force: About 20,000 Persians, Kumyks, Nogais and Dagestani mountaineers under Khosrow Khan, with troops from the governors of Ardabil, Erivan, Qarabagh, Astara and Derbent.
languages: Turkic; other Caucasian; Persian; Daylami and Caspian
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Russo-Persian War (1651-1653)
note: The Persians withdrew to Tarki on 1 April. The war was then settled by embassies (1653-1654).

name: Kandahar (siege, 1653)
how the result was decided: After a five-month siege the Mughals could neither breach nor starve the fortress and lifted the siege on 29 September 1653.
commanders A: the Safavid governor of Kandahar (unnamed in the sources used)
commanders B: Prince Dara Shikoh, Jai Singh I
Iranian force: The Safavid garrison with its artillery (no breakdown).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
strength B: about 70,000, with two of the heaviest Mughal guns
sources: en.wikipedia Mughal sieges of Kandahar (1649-1653); Mughal-Safavid war (1649-1653)
note: The last Mughal attempt on Kandahar, which stayed Safavid until the Afghan rising of 1709.

name: Bitlis (siege, 1655)
war: Ottoman suppression of the emirate of Bitlis
how the result was decided: The emirate lost its autonomy and was folded into the Van eyalet after Abdal Khan's clash with Melek Ahmed.
commanders A: Melek Ahmed Pasha, governor of Van
sources: Dankoff, Evliya Celebi in Bitlis (1990); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Bitlis (gives only the outcome)
note: The scale and the exact course of the fighting are not clear from the sources I checked; Evliya's account is the main one.

name: Khajwa
place: Khajwa (Khajuha), Fatehpur district, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: Aurangzeb's army surrounded Shuja's, which largely surrendered; Shuja fled to Arakan.
commanders A: Aurangzeb; Mir Jumla (led the advance to the centre under Shuja's artillery fire); Shaista Khan and Kilich Khan (reserve); Islam Khan (cavalry); Asad Khan; Haji Shafi Isfahani
commanders B: Shah Shuja; his sons Buland Akhtar, Sultan Bang and Zain-ul-Abidin; Mirza Ismail Beg
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Khajwa (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Khajwa); Wikipedia, Mir Jumla II; Shaista Khan; Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, vol. 2
note: Aurangzeb was in overall command, but Mir Jumla (born Isfahan) led the decisive advance and Shaista Khan (Persian origin, grandson of Mirza Ghiyas Beg) held the reserve. Persian generals were thus among the principal commanders; the troops were mostly Hindustani and Deccani.

name: Bakhtrioni
war: Bakhtrioni uprising (Kakhetian revolt against Safavid rule)
place: Bakhtrioni fortress and Alaverdi monastery, near Akhmeta, Georgia
how the result was decided: The Georgian rebels stormed the Turkmen-held forts of Bakhtrioni and Alaverdi and drove the settlers out of Kakheti.
commanders A: Bidzina Cholokashvili, Zaal Duke of Aragvi, Shalva and Elizbar of Ksani
commanders B: the Turkmen commanders of the Kakhetian forts (unnamed)
Iranian force: The garrisons and armed settlers of the Qizilbash Turkmen tribes planted in Kakheti by Abbas II.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: up to 80,000 Turkmen killed or expelled (an inflated figure for the whole settler population)
borderline: assaults on forts within a revolt, not a field battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: assaults on forts within a revolt, not a field battle.
sources: en.wikipedia Bakhtrioni uprising
note: Rebels were Kakhetians with Tush, Pshav and Khevsur highlanders. Abbas II later crushed the revolt and had its leaders executed, but gave up the settlement policy.

name: Ulluchay (1660)
how the result was decided: The Safavid army, stronger in artillery and firearms, won and the Dagestani coalition withdrew after heavy fighting.
commanders B: Surkhay III, shamkhal of Tarki; Kazanalp of Endirey
Iranian force: The Shirvan army of Hajji Manuchehr Khan, 15,000-30,000 strong, with artillery and musketeers (no breakdown).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: known from one recent Wikipedia article; the battle is not dated more closely
doubts and flags: Borderline: known from one recent Wikipedia article; the battle is not dated more closely.
sources: en.wikipedia Persian Invasion of Dagestan (1659-1660)
note: Wikipedia calls the war as a whole a Dagestani strategic success, the Persians withdrawing under raids.

date: about two months from mid-June; the fort fell on 14 August 1660 to a mine (not re-checked)
name: Chakan (siege, 1660)
war: Shaista Khan's Deccan campaign against Shivaji
place: Chakan fort, Pune district, Maharashtra, India
how the result was decided: After the siege the Mughals mined the wall and took the fort; Shaista Khan then held Pune and north Konkan (Wikipedia, Shaista Khan).
commanders A: Shaista Khan (Mughal governor of the Deccan, directing)
sources: Wikipedia, Shaista Khan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaista_Khan); Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times; Sabhasad Bakhar
note: Shaista Khan is 'of Persian origin' (Wikipedia): son of Asaf Khan IV, grandson of Mirza Ghiyas Beg of Tehran. The precise siege dates vary between the Marathi and Persian sources.

date: siege from about 20 February; night assault on 25 February 1662
name: Simalugarh (siege)
place: Simalugarh/Samdhara twin forts, east of the Bharali, Assam, India
how the result was decided: Dilir Khan's men scaled the walls on the night of 25 February and the thinly held garrison scattered.
commanders A: Mir Jumla (expedition commander); Dilir Khan (led the escalade)
sources: Wikipedia, Mir Jumla's invasion of Assam (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir_Jumla%27s_invasion_of_Assam); S. K. Bhuyan / E. Gait, History of Assam
note: Mir Jumla (born Isfahan) commanded; Dilir Khan Daudzai (a Pashtun) led the storming party. The twin forts were the first major Ahom line after Guwahati; Samdhara was abandoned without a fight soon after.

name: Kukurakata
place: Kukurakata on the Brahmaputra, near Kaliabor, Assam, India
how the result was decided: The Mughal flotilla destroyed the Ahom fleet (Wikipedia: a major Ahom defeat).
commanders A: Mir Jumla (expedition commander; the flotilla's own admiral is not certain)
commanders B: Ahom river-fleet commanders (not named in the source consulted)
sources: Wikipedia, Mir Jumla's invasion of Assam (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir_Jumla%27s_invasion_of_Assam); Gait, History of Assam
note: A river battle (typed 'sea' for a naval action). Mir Jumla as expedition commander is the Iranian leader; the exact Mughal admiral and the place are not settled in the source.

date: night of 5 April 1663 (the night 5/6 April in some accounts)
name: Raid on Pune (1663)
war: Shaista Khan's Deccan campaign against Shivaji
how the result was decided: Shivaji's raiders broke into the Lal Mahal, wounded Shaista Khan and killed his son, and withdrew unhurt.
commanders A: Shaista Khan (wounded: he lost fingers jumping from a window; his son was killed)
sources: Wikipedia, Shaista Khan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaista_Khan); Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times; Khafi Khan, Muntakhab al-Lubab
note: A night raid, not a pitched battle, but with real fighting among the guards and household. Shaista Khan was soon transferred to Bengal.

name: Sandwip (1665)
how the result was decided: The Mughal expedition captured the island (Wikipedia, Shaista Khan).
commanders A: Ibn Husain (admiral); Shaista Khan (governor of Bengal, directing)
commanders B: Dilawar, a runaway Mughal naval captain who held the island for Arakan
sources: Wikipedia, Shaista Khan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaista_Khan); Jadunath Sarkar, History of Bengal, vol. 2
note: Only the governor, Shaista Khan, is the documented Iranian figure; the fleet commander's origin is not stated.

date: December 1665 to January 1666 (the fort was taken about 26-27 January 1666)
name: Chittagong (1666)
how the result was decided: The Mughals won a naval action, took the territory west of the Kaladan and renamed Chittagong Islamabad.
commanders A: Buzurg Ummed Khan (overall command, Shaista Khan's son); Ibn Husain (fleet); Shaista Khan (governor, directing)
commanders B: the Arakanese governor and commanders (not named in the source consulted)
sources: Wikipedia, Shaista Khan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaista_Khan); Sarkar, History of Bengal, vol. 2; Shihabuddin Talish, Fathiyya-i-Ibriyya
note: A combined naval and land action, typed land. Buzurg Ummed Khan counts as Persian by descent through his father Shaista Khan (Persian origin per Wikipedia).

name: Harun River ferry (Attock, 1667)
place: Indus crossing near Attock (Harun river ferry), Punjab, Pakistan
how the result was decided: Artillery broke the Yusufzai formation and the cavalry completed their defeat.
sources: Military Wiki, Sixth Afghan-Mughal War (1667-1678): https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Sixth_Afghan-Mughal_War_(1667%E2%80%931678); Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, vol. 3
note: The first battle of the Pashtun rising of 1667-1678.

name: Rasht (1668)
how the result was decided: A Persian surprise attack killed about 400 Cossacks and Razin's men took to their boats.
Iranian force: Local Gilani forces of the governor of Rasht (no details).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a surprise attack on raiders, briefly described
doubts and flags: Borderline: a surprise attack on raiders, briefly described.
sources: en.wikipedia Stenka Razin
note: Razin's Don Cossacks were freebooters, not a force of the Tsar. They then sacked Farahabad by ruse (a sack, excluded).

name: Pig Island
place: off Pig Island (Svinoy, Suina), Caspian Sea
how the result was decided: Razin's Cossacks destroyed the Persian flotilla sent against them; only a few vessels escaped.
commanders B: Mamed Khan (Maenad Khan in Russian accounts)
Iranian force: A Caspian flotilla raised by the provincial governors, said to be about 50 vessels with some 3,700 men (Russian accounts).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
strength A: unknown (a few thousand Cossacks in light boats)
losses B: most of the flotilla; the commander's son captured (Russian accounts)
sources: en.wikipedia Stenka Razin; Avrich, Russian Rebels
note: The figures come from Russian accounts and are not checked against Persian sources. The island is variously placed off the Kura delta or near Baku.

name: Ali Masjid (1672)
war: Pashtun revolt against Aurangzeb (1667-1678): Afridi and Mohmand rising
place: Ali Masjid, Khyber Pass, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
how the result was decided: The Mughal army was ambushed in the gorge and largely destroyed; Muhammad Amin Khan escaped with a few followers.
commanders B: Aimal Khan Mohmand; Darya Khan Afridi
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Ali Masjid (1672): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ali_Masjid_(1672); Wikipedia, Aimal Khan Mohmand: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimal_Khan_Mohmand; Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, vol. 3
note: The casualty and force figures on Wikipedia (240,000 Mughals, 40,000 killed) are inflated and are not used.

name: Kohat (1674)
how the result was decided: The Afridi assault on the fort was repulsed with the loss of over 100 men and Tatar Khan.
Iranian side: Afridi Pashtuns v Bangash garrison of Kohat
commanders A: Darya Khan Afridi; Tatar Khan Afridi (killed)
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Kohat: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kohat; Wikipedia, Darya Khan Afridi
note: Pashtun against Pashtun; Darya Khan attacked before Khushal Khan could join him.

name: Langarkot (c. 1674)
place: Langarkot fort, near Panjpir (Swabi), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
how the result was decided: Khushal Khan's men surrounded and took the fort and the garrison commander was killed.
doubts and flags: Traditional: known only from a doubtful tradition.
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Langarkot: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Langarkot
note: Known only from a thin Pashtun tradition; the Wikipedia article's casualty figures are inconsistent.

name: Nowshera (1674)
how the result was decided: The fort was plundered, the commander killed and the garrison suffered heavy losses.
commanders B: Khushal Khan Khattak; Darya Khan Afridi; Aimal Khan Mohmand
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Nowshera (1674): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Nowshera_(1674); Wikipedia, Mughal-Afghan Wars
note: Khushal Khan Khattak, long a Mughal servant, joined the revolt here. Sources are thin and the date is not secure.

name: Gandab (Karapa Pass, 1674)
place: Gandab valley and Karapa Pass, Mohmand country, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
allies A: Rathor contingent sent by Jaswant Singh
how the result was decided: Shuja'at Khan was killed and his army was cut up in the pass; the Rathors saved the remnant.
sources: Wikipedia, Aimal Khan Mohmand: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimal_Khan_Mohmand; Military Wiki, Sixth Afghan-Mughal War: https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Sixth_Afghan-Mughal_War_(1667%E2%80%931678); pashtunhistory.com, Karapa disaster
note: Shuja'at Khan was sent in November 1673 and the disaster was in February 1674, not 1673; Gandab and Karapa are two names for one campaign.

name: Jagdalak (1675)
place: Jagdalak, between Kabul and Jalalabad, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: The Afghans defeated Fidai Khan on his way to Peshawar until Aghar Khan relieved him.
commanders B: not named in the sources seen
sources: Military Wiki, Sixth Afghan-Mughal War: https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Sixth_Afghan-Mughal_War_(1667%E2%80%931678); Wikipedia, Aimal Khan Mohmand
note: The sources seen do not say which tribes fought; they are recorded only as Afghan tribal forces on the Kabul-Peshawar road.

name: Khapush (1675)
side B: Pashtun lashkar of Aimal Khan and Darya Khan
how the result was decided: The Mughal column was ambushed, Shamsher Khan was killed and Mukarram Khan retreated wounded to Bajaur.
Iranian side: Pashtun lashkar of Aimal Khan and Darya Khan
commanders B: Aimal Khan Mohmand; Darya Khan Afridi
sources: Wikipedia, Aimal Khan Mohmand: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimal_Khan_Mohmand; Khushal Khan Khattak's verse (as cited by pashtunhistory.com)
note: The date and the exact identity of the battle (Khapush or Karapa) differ between sources.

date: c. January-21/22 September 1687 (about eight months; the fort fell when Abul Hasan surrendered)
name: Golconda (siege, 1687)
war: Mughal conquest of Golconda (Aurangzeb's Deccan wars)
how the result was decided: Golconda fell to the Mughals when Abul Hasan surrendered in September 1687 after the fort's gate was opened by traitors, while Abdur Razzaq Lari fought on to the end (J. Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, vol. 5).
commanders A: Aurangzeb; Prince Muhammad Azam; Ghazi ud-Din Khan Firuz Jang
commanders B: Abdur Razzaq Lari (Persian from Lar; commander of the Golconda army and fort); Abul Hasan Qutb Shah (Tana Shah)
sources: J. Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, vol. 5; R. M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan, 1300-1761 (2005); Maasir-i Alamgiri (Saqi Mustaid Khan)
note: Abdur Razzaq Lari defended the Fateh Darwaza and was left for dead; Aurangzeb is said to have had him treated and offered him service, which he refused. His Persian origin (Lar in Fars) comes from his nisba and from Mughal accounts; I could not fetch a dedicated page. The Qutb Shahi dynasty itself was Qara Qoyunlu Turkmen (not Iranian).

date: siege from spring 1689; the fort fell about 3 November 1689 (dates not re-checked)
name: Raigarh (siege, 1689)
how the result was decided: Zulfiqar Khan captured the fort and took Sambhaji's family, including the boy Shahu (Wikipedia, Zulfiqar Khan).
commanders B: Suryaji Pisal (betrayed the fort); Yesubai (Sambhaji's widow, captured); Rajaram escaped before the end
sources: Wikipedia, Zulfiqar Khan Nusrat Jung (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zulfiqar_Khan_Nusrat_Jung); Wikipedia list of battles involving the Mughal Empire; Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, vol. 5
note: Same origin question as for Jinji: an Iranian lineage by Wikipedia, but possibly Qaramanlu Turkmen. Dates from memory.

name: Khurma (1697)
how the result was decided: Shaykh Mani defeated a large Safavid force and captured its general.
commanders A: Shaykh Mani ibn Mughamis (Muntafiq), with Musha'sha' defectors
Iranian force: A large Safavid force from Basra (no breakdown; the Basra garrison was largely Lur and Kohgiluyeh troops).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: described in one sentence; site uncertain
doubts and flags: Borderline: described in one sentence; site uncertain.
sources: en.wikipedia Safavid occupation of Basra
note: The Safavids evacuated Basra by sea on 9 March 1701 under blockade and mutiny, before an Ottoman army arrived (no battle).

date: early 1697 (Basra occupied for the Shah on 26 March 1697)
name: Basra (1697)
how the result was decided: Farajollah Khan's Musha'sha' fighters defeated Shaykh Mani and drove him out of Basra, which was then held for the Shah.
Iranian force: The Arab followers of the Musha'sha' vali of Arabestan (Khuzestan), a Safavid governor.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the victor was a Safavid vassal vali with his own Arab tribesmen; the fight is not separately named
doubts and flags: Borderline: the victor was a Safavid vassal vali with his own Arab tribesmen; the fight is not separately named.
sources: en.wikipedia Safavid occupation of Basra
note: The Muntafiq had held Basra since 1695. Ali Mardan Khan, chief of the Fayli Lurs, then came as governor with an army from Lorestan.

name: Jinji (siege, 1690-98)
how the result was decided: The fortress capitulated on 8 January 1698 (renamed Nusratgarh), though Rajaram had escaped.
commanders A: Zulfiqar Khan Nusrat Jung (main commander throughout); Kam Bakhsh; Asad Khan; Daud Khan Panni; Dalpat Rao Bundela
commanders B: Rajaram I; Dhanaji Jadhav; Santaji Ghorpade
sources: Wikipedia, Siege of Jinji (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Jinji); Zulfiqar Khan Nusrat Jung (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zulfiqar_Khan_Nusrat_Jung); Irvine, Later Mughals
note: The origin is disputed: Wikipedia calls Zulfiqar Khan's patrilineal line Iranian (great-grandfather beglar begi of Safavid Shirvan, executed c. 1600 by Shah Abbas; grandfather Khanlar moved to India), but the Safavid Zulfiqar family is usually placed in the Qaramanlu tribe, a Turkmen Qizilbash tribe, which BRIEF3 does not count as Iranian.

name: Kandahar (1709)
how the result was decided: Mirwais's Ghilzai killed Gurgin Khan in his camp outside the city and destroyed the Georgian garrison left in Kandahar.
commanders B: Gurgin Khan (Giorgi XI of Kartli, killed)
Iranian force: Gurgin Khan's escort and the Georgian garrison of Kandahar; most of the Georgian troops were away on campaign.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a surprise attack and massacre more than a battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: a surprise attack and massacre more than a battle.
sources: en.wikipedia Hotak revolt; Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Ghilzai (Hotak) Afghans of Kandahar; the start of the Hotaki state.

name: Kandahar (siege, 1711)
how the result was decided: The besiegers, harassed by the Baloch, retreated on 26 October 1711 and the Afghans destroyed the retreating army.
commanders B: Kay Khosrow (Kaikhosro of Kartli, killed), Prince Alexander of Kartli (killed)
Iranian force: About 30,000 Georgian and Persian troops with contingents from Khorasan, Herat and Kerman.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: almost the whole army; only about 700 escaped
sources: en.wikipedia Kaikhosro of Kartli; Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Kay Khosrow had campaigned against Kandahar since November 1709; his death is dated 27 September or 26 October 1711.

name: Shamakhi (siege, 1711)
how the result was decided: Haji Davud's siege of Shamakhi failed, although he had beaten Safavid garrisons in the field.
commanders B: Haji Davud, Ali Sultan of Elisu, Ahmed Khan of Kaytag, Surkhay Khan
Iranian force: The Safavid garrison of Shamakhi (no details).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no separate article; briefly described
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article; briefly described.
sources: en.wikipedia Lezgin campaign into Shirvan
note: Lezgin and other Sunni highlanders of Dagestan and northern Shirvan. A second attempt in 1712 is described contradictorily and is not listed; a first raid stormed Shamakhi in 1707.

date: 1717 (third Omani attempt; the first two had failed)
name: Bahrain (1717)
war: Omani-Safavid conflict in the Persian Gulf
how the result was decided: The Omanis blockaded the island and took the fortress by force.
Iranian force: The Safavid garrison and the islanders; a later Persian relief army with many Bedouins was destroyed.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: unknown (heavy killing and plunder, per al-Bahrani)
sources: en.wikipedia 1717 Omani invasion of Bahrain
note: Ya'rubid Oman (Sultan ibn Saif II); Wikipedia names Al Bin Ali mercenaries. Bahrain returned to Persian rule by treaty after a payment; the year is sometimes given as 1717-1718.

name: Kafir Qala (1719)
war: Afghan rebellions (1709-1726): Abdali revolt of Herat
how the result was decided: The Abdali routed the Persian army, killed its commander and took its baggage train.
commanders A: Mohammad Zaman Khan, Asadullah Khan (Abdali of Herat)
Iranian force: Safi Quli Khan's army of Khorasan, 30,000-35,000 strong, with an artillery train under European officers.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kafir Qala (1719); Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Abdali (Sadozai) Afghans of Herat. The battle secured Herat's independence from the Safavids.

name: Dilaram
how the result was decided: Asadullah Khan was shot in the back and about 3,000 of his Abdali men were killed; Mahmud Hotak's Ghilzais held the field.
Iranian side: Hotak dynasty v Abdali Afghans of Herat
why it counts: Both armies were Pashtun: Mahmud Hotak's Ghilzais of Kandahar and Asadullah's Abdalis (Wikipedia 'Battle of Dilaram').
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dilaram; Axworthy, M., Sword of Persia (2006); Lockhart, L., The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty (1958)
note: A Pashtun against Pashtun battle between the two great tribal confederations of the day, the Ghilzai Hotaks and the Abdalis (later Durranis); it left Mahmud free to invade Kerman in 1721. The Wikipedia infobox calls Asadullah's side the Sadozai Sultanate of Herat, but the article text says Abdali.

date: 1721 (town taken; citadel held out by October 1721)
name: Kerman (siege, 1721)
war: Afghan rebellions (1709-1726): Mahmud Hotak's invasion of Persia
how the result was decided: The Ghilzai took the town but failed to storm the citadel, losing about 1,500 men, and moved on.
commanders A: the Safavid commander of the citadel (unnamed in the sources used)
Iranian force: The Safavid garrison of Kerman citadel (no breakdown).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no separate article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article.
sources: en.wikipedia Mahmud Hotak; Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Ghilzai (Hotak) Afghans of Kandahar. Mahmud had occupied Kerman town before, in 1719-1720. A further attempt on the reinforced city late in 1721 or early in 1722 also failed (included here).

name: Kura River (1721)
how the result was decided: Haji Davud's night attack on the Safavid camp routed the relief army, much of which fled.
commanders B: the beglerbegis of Ganja and Erivan
Iranian force: The provincial armies of Ganja and Erivan, about 30,000 men (60,000 in the infobox).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no separate article; site not identified
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article; site not identified.
sources: en.wikipedia Lezgin campaign into Shirvan
note: Haji Davud then took Barda and besieged Ganja, withdrawing as Vakhtang VI of Kartli marched to its relief (no battle, not listed).

name: Shamakhi (siege, 1721)
how the result was decided: Shamakhi fell when its Sunni inhabitants opened a gate to the besiegers, and the city was sacked.
commanders A: Haji Davud, Surkhay Khan of Ghazikumukh
Iranian force: The governor's garrison and the Shia townsmen of Shamakhi (no breakdown).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: 4,000-5,000 Shia inhabitants killed, with the governor; also Russian merchants
sources: en.wikipedia Sack of Shamakhi; Lezgin campaign into Shirvan
note: Lezgins and other Dagestani highlanders. The killing of Russian merchants was Peter the Great's pretext for the war of 1722-1723.

date: early 1722 (between the Kerman siege and Gulnabad)
name: Yazd (1722)
war: Afghan rebellions (1709-1726): Mahmud Hotak's invasion of Persia
how the result was decided: The garrison of Yazd beat off Mahmud's attack and he marched on towards Isfahan.
Iranian force: The garrison and townsmen of Yazd (no details).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a brief repulse, no separate article
doubts and flags: Borderline: a brief repulse, no separate article.
sources: en.wikipedia Mahmud Hotak; Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Ghilzai (Hotak) Afghans. Yazd beat off a second Hotaki attempt later in the 1720s (date not given; not listed).

name: Gulnabad
war: Afghan rebellions (1709-1726): Mahmud Hotak's invasion of Persia
how the result was decided: The Afghans routed the Persian army, which fled back to Isfahan leaving its guns.
commanders A: Mahmud Hotak, Ashraf Hotak, Amanullah Khan, Nasrullah
commanders B: Mohammad Qoli Khan (grand vizier), Ali Mardan Khan (vali of Lorestan), Rustam Khan (killed), Philippe Colombe (killed), Sayyid Abdollah (vali of Arabistan)
Iranian force: 42,000-50,000 men with 24 guns: the royal guard and ghulams (Rustam Khan), Fayli Lur horse under Ali Mardan Khan, the Arab horse of the vali of Arabistan, Persian musketeers and the artillery under the French gunner Colombe.
languages: Persian; Lur and Bakhtiari; Arabic; Turkic; Georgian
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
strength A: 10,000-11,000 (up to 18,000 in some accounts), with 100 zamburaks
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Gulnabad; Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty; Axworthy, The Sword of Persia
note: Ghilzai (Hotak) Afghans of Kandahar; Mahmud was not yet ruler of Iran, so the battle is not civil.

name: Isfahan (siege, 1722)
how the result was decided: Famine forced Shah Sultan Husayn to capitulate on 23 October 1722 and Mahmud entered Isfahan.
commanders B: Shah Sultan Husayn, Ahmad Agha (commander of the defence), Tahmasp Mirza (escaped to raise relief)
Iranian force: The remnants of the Gulnabad army, the royal guard and ghulams, and the armed townsmen of Isfahan; relief attempts failed and Vakhtang VI of Kartli refused to come.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
losses B: about 80,000 or more inhabitants died, mostly of famine
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Isfahan; Mahmud Hotak; Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Ghilzai (Hotak) Afghans. The shah abdicated in Mahmud's favour; Mahmud entered the city on 25 October. Tahmasp escaped with about 600 men to Qazvin.

name: Julfa (1722)
how the result was decided: After hours of resistance the Armenian quarter fell to the Afghans and was plundered.
Iranian force: Several hundred armed Armenian townsmen of Julfa, loyal to the Shah, who had been largely disarmed by the Persian authorities.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the defenders were loyal townsmen rather than Safavid troops
doubts and flags: Borderline: the defenders were loyal townsmen rather than Safavid troops.
sources: en.wikipedia Capture of Julfa
note: Ghilzai (Hotak) Afghans. Julfa paid an indemnity of 70,000 tomans; Farahabad was then abandoned without a fight.

name: Qazvin (1723)
war: Hotaki rule in Iran: risings against the Afghans
how the result was decided: The townsmen rose, killed many of the Afghan garrison and drove the rest out of the city.
Iranian force: Side A: the armed population of Qazvin; side B: the Ghilzai garrison Mahmud had sent after Tahmasp.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: an urban rising against a garrison
doubts and flags: Borderline: an urban rising against a garrison.
sources: en.wikipedia Mahmud Hotak; Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Civil because the Hotaki were ruling Iran from Isfahan after October 1722. Tahmasp II had fled before the Afghans arrived.

name: Rasht (1723)
how the result was decided: A Russian sortie broke the Persian force besieging the Russian barracks and the Russians held Rasht.
Iranian force: About 15,000 men, mostly untrained and poorly armed peasant levies raised by the governor of Gilan.
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Peter the Great's capture of Rasht; Russo-Persian War (1722-1723)
note: The Russians had entered Rasht in late 1722 as nominal helpers; the date may be Julian (Old Style).

date: July 1723 (the city capitulated on 26 July Julian, 6 August Gregorian)
name: Baku (siege, 1723)
how the result was decided: After a naval bombardment and landing the garrison capitulated and the Russians took Baku.
Iranian force: The garrison and townsmen of Baku (no details).
why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state
borderline: no separate article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article.
sources: en.wikipedia Russo-Persian War (1722-1723); Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty
note: Wikipedia's war article dates the capture to 26 June 1723 (7 July N.S.); Russian accounts give the capitulation as 26 July 1723 (Old Style). Derbent (August 1722) surrendered without a fight and is excluded.

name: Shiraz (siege, 1723-1724)
war: Hotaki rule in Iran: conquest of Fars
how the result was decided: Shiraz was starved into surrender after a nine-month siege and sacked.
Iranian force: Side A: Ghilzai Afghans with Sunni Dargazini settlers from Isfahan; side B: the Safavid garrison and people of Shiraz.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

why it counts: Safavids: an Iranian-led state

sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kirkuk (1733); Nader Shah's Mesopotamian campaign
