sources: en.wikipedia Nader Shah's invasion of India
note: Some accounts date the fall of the citadel to 29-30 June 1738.

name: Khyber Pass (1738)
how the result was decided: Nader's flanking march surprised and routed Nasir Khan's army, which surrendered its camp.
commanders B: Nasir Khan (Mughal subahdar of Kabul and Peshawar, captured)
Iranian force: About 10,000 picked cavalry engaged under Nader, with 12,000 under Morteza Mirza not engaged and a 6,000-man camp guard.
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
losses B: heavy; the rest captured or surrendered
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Khyber Pass (1738); Nader Shah's invasion of India
note: Nasir Khan's army was largely hastily raised Afghan tribal levies of Khyber and Peshawar. The same article says Nader entered Peshawar on 18 November, which conflicts with the battle date.

name: Karnal
how the result was decided: In under three hours Nader's army destroyed the Mughal forces that attacked it, and Muhammad Shah surrendered.
commanders A: Nader Shah, Nasrollah Mirza, Tahmasp Khan Jalayer, Fath Ali Khan Afshar, Lotf Ali Khan Afshar, Haji Khan (Kurdish horse), Ahmad Khan Abdali
commanders B: Muhammad Shah, Qamar-ud-Din Khan, Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah, Saadat Khan (captured), Khan Dauran (mortally wounded)
Iranian force: About 55,000 mounted troops (in a camp of 160,000), including some 20,000 uniformed jazayerchi musketeers, camel zamburaks, elite Kurdish horse under Haji Khan, Afshar and other Qizilbash cavalry, Abdali Afghans under Ahmad Khan and a Kakhetian contingent.
languages: Turkic; Persian; Pashto; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Georgian
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
strength B: about 75,000 on the field (up to 300,000 with camp followers), 2,000 elephants
losses A: about 1,100 (400 killed, 700 wounded); up to 2,500 killed in other figures
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Karnal; Nader Shah's invasion of India; Axworthy, The Sword of Persia
note: Heraclius (Erekle) II of Kakheti served with a Georgian contingent. The massacre in Delhi on 22 March 1739 followed a riot and is excluded.

name: Bukhara (1740)
how the result was decided: Nader's guard and artillery broke Abu'l-Fayz Khan's army, which fell back on Bukhara, and the khan sued for peace.
commanders A: Nader Shah, Reza Qoli Mirza, Lotf Ali Khan
Iranian force: Nader's guard of 3,000 and the main army with artillery (no breakdown); 8,000 under Reza Qoli Mirza were sent to Charjuy.
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
borderline: a series of fights (Qatartut, near Bukhara) grouped as one entry; dates not given
doubts and flags: Borderline: a series of fights (Qatartut, near Bukhara) grouped as one entry; dates not given.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Capture of Samarkand (1740); Nader Shah's Central Asian campaign
note: Bukhara Khanate (Ashtarkhanid). Lotf Ali Khan also beat a 20,000-strong force of Samarkand, Bukhara and Kokand; Samarkand was then taken almost unopposed (not listed). About 30,000 Uzbeks were enrolled in Nader's army.

name: Khanqah (siege, 1740)
how the result was decided: Besieged in Khanqah, Ilbars Khan surrendered and was executed with more than twenty of his amirs.
Iranian force: Nader's army with mortars, howitzers and jazayerchi (no breakdown).
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Nader Shah's Central Asian campaign; Battle of Pitnak
note: Khiva itself then submitted without a fight.

date: early November 1740 (Nader reached the area in the last days of October)
name: Pitnak
how the result was decided: Nader's cavalry routed the Khivan army, killing or capturing many in the pursuit.
Iranian force: About 20,000 men: Afshar, Marv and Atak cavalry, with Nader himself fighting the Yomut.
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
strength B: about 30,000 Uzbek and Turkmen horsemen (including 6,000 Yomut)
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Pitnak; Nader Shah's Central Asian campaign
note: Khanate of Khiva with Yomut and Aral Turkmens. Hazarasp was taken afterwards.

date: late August to 28 September 1741 (Aimaki gorge ambush on 12 September)
name: Andalal
place: Andalal and the Aimaki gorge, Gunib district, Dagestan, Russia
how the result was decided: The highlanders held the gorges and Nader's army withdrew to Derbent under constant attack, two of its contingents destroyed.
commanders A: Murtazali Khan (son of Surkhay), Ahmed Khan Mekhtuly, Qadi Pir Muhammad
commanders B: Nader Shah, Lotf Ali Khan, Haydar Bek
Iranian force: Nader's army of 100,000-150,000 at its height in Dagestan: levies from all Iran, Uzbek and Tatar auxiliaries, mounted and foot tofangchi musketeers, Georgian and other vassal contingents; the units destroyed were Haydar Bek's 4,000 and Lotf Ali Khan's 6,000.
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
losses B: 30,000 men, 33,000 animals and 79 guns (infobox); about 9,000 of the two ambushed contingents
borderline: a withdrawal under harassment rather than a single battle
doubts and flags: Traditional: The great set-piece battle of Dagestani tradition is not described in contemporary sources, which show a harried withdrawal with an ambush in the Aimaki gorge; the losses (30,000 men, 79 guns) rest on weak sourcing. Borderline: a withdrawal under harassment rather than a single battle.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Withdrawal through Andalal (1741); Gazikumukh Khanate; Nader Shah's Dagestan campaign
note: Avars and Laks of Andalal and Gazi-Kumukh. Fights at Sogratl, Megeb, Chokh and Oboch are part of this entry. Surkhay Khan had surrendered to Nader in August 1741.

name: Sohar (siege, 1742-1743)
how the result was decided: After about nine months Ahmad bin Said came to terms, keeping Sohar as governor under Persian tribute without the town being taken.
commanders A: Taqi Khan, Kalb Ali Khan; Imam Saif bin Sultan II (ally)
commanders B: Ahmad bin Said al-Busaidi (governor of Sohar); Imam Sultan bin Murshid (mortally wounded under the walls)
Iranian force: The Persian expedition landed at Julfar in October 1742 (no breakdown), with Saif bin Sultan II's followers.
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Ahmad bin Said al-Busaidi; Saif bin Sultan II
note: Ya'rubid Oman. Sources differ: one says the Persians took neither Sohar nor Muscat, another that Ahmad negotiated a surrender. The Persians took the Muscat forts by a ruse in 1743 (no battle, excluded); the killing of the last Persians at Barka (1747) was a massacre at a banquet (excluded).

name: Basra (siege, 1743)
how the result was decided: The siege was still in progress after Mosul and ended with the peace negotiated with Ahmad Pasha of Baghdad, the city untaken.
Iranian force: A detached Persian force from Khuzestan and Fars (no details).
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
borderline: mentioned only in passing; extent of fighting unknown
doubts and flags: Borderline: mentioned only in passing; extent of fighting unknown.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Mosul (1743); Longrigg, Four Centuries of Modern Iraq
note: Result by this set's rule for a siege ended by agreement while the place was invested; details not verified.

name: Kirkuk (siege, 1743)
how the result was decided: Kirkuk fell to Nader after a short bombardment.
Iranian force: Nader's main army of 1743 with a large siege train (no breakdown); the war article says the army was largely raised from Central Asian tribesmen.
languages: Turkic; Persian; Pashto; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
strength A: unknown (300,000 in the war article, an inflated figure)
borderline: listed only in the war article; details of the fighting not given
doubts and flags: Borderline: listed only in the war article; details of the fighting not given.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman-Persian War (1743-1746); Axworthy, The Sword of Persia
note: Erbil was also taken (not listed).

name: Mosul (siege, 1743)
how the result was decided: A great assault with 1,700 ladders failed and Nader lifted the siege before a negotiated peace.
Iranian force: More than 40,000 men with 390 guns and 230 mortars (no breakdown of units).
languages: Turkic; Persian; Pashto; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Mosul (1743); Ottoman-Persian War (1743-1746)
note: Wikipedia's infobox calls the result inconclusive (siege suspended, negotiated withdrawal); judged here as a defender's win because the siege was raised after the failed assault.

name: Kairarau (Rohilla invasion of Kumaon)
war: Rohilla expansion under Ali Muhammad Khan
how the result was decided: The Rohilla invaders were beaten by the combined Kumaon and Garhwal armies and had to sue for peace after sacking Almora.
commanders A: Kalyan Chand (Raja of Kumaon); Pradip Shah (Raja of Garhwal)
commanders B: Ali Muhammad Khan Rohilla; Rohilla generals including Hafiz Rahmat Khan
why it counts: The Rohilla army was drawn from Pashtun (Afghan) settlers of Rohilkhand under Ali Muhammad Khan (Wikipedia 'Rohilla'; Iqbal Husain).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohilla; Husain, Iqbal, The Rise and Decline of the Ruhela Chieftaincy in 18th Century India (1994)
note: Ali Muhammad Khan was a Hindu-born adoptee of the Pashtun Daud Khan Barech and his army was mainly Pashtun (Rohilla) mercenaries; the site and exact year are weakly sourced (one Wikipedia summary).

name: Shah Bagh (1744)
war: Rebellion of Mohammad Taqi Khan Shirazi (1744)
how the result was decided: After several hours' fighting Taqi Khan's force, with heavy losses, retreated into the fortress of Shiraz.
factions B: Mohammad Taqi Khan Shirazi (rebel governor of Fars)
Iranian force: Side A: about 30,000 royal troops under Allahverdi Khan; side B: 10,000-12,000 of Taqi Khan's Fars army.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Lur and Bakhtiari; Arabic
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Afsharid conquests in the Persian Gulf and Oman; Mohammad Taqi Khan Shirazi's Rebellion
note: Before this, Taqi Khan had ambushed Muhammad Husain Khan Qirkhli's 7,000 men in the streets of Shiraz after two or three indecisive fights (not listed).

date: early 1744 to June 1744 (two to three months)
name: Shiraz (siege, 1744)
war: Rebellion of Mohammad Taqi Khan Shirazi (1744)
how the result was decided: A defending commander opened a gate, Shiraz fell and was sacked, and Taqi Khan fled.
factions B: Mohammad Taqi Khan Shirazi (rebel governor of Fars)
commanders A: Allahverdi Khan Kirkhli, with reinforcements sent by Nader
Iranian force: Side A: Allahverdi Khan's royal army with reinforcements; side B: Taqi Khan's Fars troops and the townsmen.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: unknown (20,000 casualties in the infobox, side unclear)
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Afsharid conquests in the Persian Gulf and Oman; Mohammad Taqi Khan Shirazi's Rebellion
note: Taqi Khan was later caught and mutilated. The revolt had begun at Bandar Abbas, where the fleet commander Rustam Khan was killed by his own officers late in 1743 (a mutiny, excluded).

name: Kars (siege, 1744)
how the result was decided: After 73 days and a successful Ottoman sortie on 18-19 September, Nader raised the siege on 9 October.
Iranian force: Nader's army with 16 heavy guns (no breakdown).
languages: Turkic; Persian; Pashto; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
losses B: about 1,700 killed; nine field guns abandoned
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kars (1744)
note: Nader withdrew to deal with a revolt in Dagestan.

name: Aghsu (1745)
how the result was decided: Muhammad Khan retreated to Gazi-Kumukh and the Persians recovered Derbent and the Kura country.
commanders B: Muhammad Khan of Gazi-Kumukh (son of Surkhay)
Iranian force: Nasrollah Mirza's army of Shirvan and Azerbaijan (no breakdown).
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
borderline: described in one line; the scale of fighting is unknown
doubts and flags: Borderline: described in one line; the scale of fighting is unknown.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Gazikumukh Khanate
note: Lak and Lezgin forces of Gazi-Kumukh, backing a pretender's revolt in Shirvan.

date: 1745 (about a month's siege; month not fixed)
name: Bangarh (siege, 1745)
war: Mughal expedition against Ali Muhammad Khan Rohilla (1745)
place: Bangarh fort, Rohilkhand, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: Ali Muhammad Khan, blockaded in Bangarh, surrendered, was taken to Delhi, then pardoned and made governor of Sirhind.
commanders A: Muhammad Shah; Qamar-ud-Din Khan; Safdar Jang
why it counts: Ali Muhammad Khan's Rohilla army was Pashtun (Afghan) in composition and tradition (Iqbal Husain; Wikipedia 'Rohilla').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohilla; Husain, Iqbal, The Rise and Decline of the Ruhela Chieftaincy in 18th Century India (1994)
note: The emperor took the field himself against the rising Rohilla state; the site (Bangarh) and the length of the siege are from memory and a single summary, so the entry is uncertain.

name: Kars (1745)
how the result was decided: After ten days of fighting Nader's jazayerchi and cavalry broke the Ottoman army, which disintegrated and lost its commander.
Iranian force: About 60,000, including 40,000 elite cavalry of the Khorasan army (savaran-e sepah-e Khorasan), jazayerchi musketeers, artillery and fowj infantry.
languages: Turkic; Persian; Pashto; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kars (1745); Ottoman-Persian War (1743-1746); Axworthy, The Sword of Persia
note: Named after Kars, the Ottoman base; Wikipedia's account places both camps near Yeghevard, where the battle of 1735 was also fought, so the site is uncertain. The Treaty of Kerden (4 September 1746) followed.

name: Mosul (1745)
how the result was decided: Nasrollah Mirza inflicted a crushing defeat on Abdullah Pasha's army and its Kurdish auxiliaries.
Iranian force: Nasrollah Mirza's detached army (no breakdown).
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
borderline: described in passing; site not named
doubts and flags: Borderline: described in passing; site not named.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kars (1745)
note: Abdullah Pasha had been joined by local Ottoman troops and Kurdish tribal auxiliaries. Nasrollah's letter reporting the victory reached Nader on the last day of the battle of Kars.

date: 11 January 1748 (Wikipedia, Ahmad Shah Durrani; older accounts give 12 January)
name: Lahore (Shalimar Gardens, 1748)
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's first invasion of India (1747-1748)
how the result was decided: Shah Nawaz Khan was beaten at the Shalimar Gardens; his own Afghan regiments went over to Ahmad Shah and he fled to Delhi.
commanders A: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Jahan Khan Popalzai
why it counts: Ahmad Shah Abdali, a Pashtun (Popalzai Durrani) ruler, led an army of Durrani and Ghilzai Afghans (Ganda Singh; Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959); Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Opening battle of Ahmad Shah's first invasion; the governor's Afghan regiments (a Pashtun contingent on B) defected during the fight.

date: 11 March 1748 (Wikipedia/Sarkar; some accounts place the fighting between late February and early March)
name: Manupur
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's first invasion of India (1747-1748)
how the result was decided: A powder explosion in the Afghan camp killed about 1,000 men and Ahmad Shah, outnumbered about five to one, withdrew toward the Indus while the Mughals held the field.
commanders A: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Jahan Khan Popalzai; Shah Wali Khan
commanders B: Wazir Qamar-ud-Din Khan (killed); Safdar Jang; Mu'in al-Mulk (Mir Mannu); Prince Ahmad Shah Bahadur
why it counts: Ahmad Shah Abdali (Pashtun) led an almost wholly Afghan army (Sarkar; Ganda Singh).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34); Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959)
note: Mughal wazir Qamar-ud-Din was killed by a cannonball during the battle; Mir Mannu's pursuit of the retreating Afghans won him Lahore. Ahmad Shah's army was about 12,000 against 60,000-70,000 (Wikipedia).

name: Soltaniyeh (1748)
side A (victor if decisive): Ebrahim, with Amir Aslan Khan Afshar, governor of Azerbaijan
how the result was decided: Adel Shah's army melted away by desertion and he fled the field to Tehran, where he was seized and blinded.
factions A: Ebrahim (Ibrahim Shah), with Amir Aslan Khan Afshar, governor of Azerbaijan
commanders A: Ebrahim Mirza, Amir Aslan Khan Afshar
Iranian force: Both armies were remnants of Nader Shah's host: Afshar and other Turkic Qizilbash tribesmen with Kurdish horse and Afghan and Uzbek contingents; Ebrahim drew on the Afshar troops of Azerbaijan.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no article and no conventional name; the encounter is described only as Adel Shah's defeat by Ebrahim
doubts and flags: Borderline: no article and no conventional name; the encounter is described only as Adel Shah's defeat by Ebrahim.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Adel Shah; Ebrahim Afshar; Perry in Cambridge History of Iran vol. 7
note: The site is not named in the Wikipedia articles; Zanjan-Soltaniyeh is the usual placing of Adel's defeat in the older literature and is given as approximate.

name: Herat (siege, 1749-50)
how the result was decided: Herat fell to Ahmad Shah after a long siege.
commanders B: the Afsharid governor of Herat (not named in the sources used)
Iranian force: The Persian garrison left by Nader Shah's successors in Herat; its composition is not recorded (Afsharid garrisons were Qizilbash Turkic and Kurdish troops with local levies).
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
borderline: the Persian character of the Herat garrison after Nader's death is not well documented
doubts and flags: Borderline: the Persian character of the Herat garrison after Nader's death is not well documented.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Durrani Campaign to Khorasan (1749-1751)
note: Dates vary in the article (the campaign is dated 1749-1751, 1750-1751 and 1749-1750 in different places).

name: Semnan (1749)
how the result was decided: Ebrahim withdrew from the field when his army fell into turmoil and part of it deserted to Shahrokh; he was later captured at Qal'a-ye Qalapur.
Iranian force: Shahrokh's army of Khorasan (Turkic, Kurdish and Arab tribal leaders of Mashhad) against Ebrahim's army, which included Afghan and Uzbek troops who deserted or fled.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no article; known only as the fighting near Semnan
doubts and flags: Borderline: no article; known only as the fighting near Semnan.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Ebrahim Afshar; Adel Shah
note: Ebrahim was blinded by Musa Khan and died on the way to Mashhad.

name: Daunri (Badaun, 1749)
place: Daunri (Dauri), near Badaun, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: Qaim Khan Bangash was killed in the battle and his army broke, after which Farrukhabad was annexed to Awadh and plundered.
Iranian side: Rohilla chiefs v Bangash Nawabs of Farrukhabad
commanders A: Dunde (Dundi) Khan; Hafiz Rahmat Khan; Sa'dullah Khan
why it counts: Both armies were Pashtun: Rohilla Barech and Yusufzai chiefs against Qaim Khan Bangash, a Pashtun (Iqbal Husain; Wikipedia 'Ahmad Khan Bangash').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Khan_Bangash; Husain, Iqbal, The Rise and Decline of the Ruhela Chieftaincy in 18th Century India (1994); Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: A Pashtun against Pashtun battle: the Rohillas against the Bangash Nawab of Farrukhabad, a conflict Safdar Jang of Awadh exploited to seize Farrukhabad. Wikipedia's Ahmad Khan Bangash article calls it the Battle of Badaun and does not use 'Daunri'.

name: Turbat-i-Shaikh Jam
how the result was decided: Mir Alam Khan was killed and his army collapsed, leaving the field to the Durrani vanguard.
commanders A: Ahmad Shah Durrani, Sardar Jahan Khan Popalzai, Mir Nasir Khan I of Kalat
Iranian force: The army of Mir Alam Khan, the Arab (Khozeime) chief of Qaenat who then dominated Mashhad in Shahrokh's name; its composition is not recorded (Khozeime Arabs, Khorasani Kurds and Turks).
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
strength A: about 8,000 in the vanguard (5,000 under Jahan Khan, 3,000 Baloch horse under Nasir Khan)
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Turbat-i-Shaikh Jam
note: The Khanate of Kalat (Baloch) fought as Ahmad Shah's vassal; recorded as 'Kalat' (a new short name). The fortress of Nun surrendered after Mir Alam's death.

name: Golpayegan (1750)
side A (victor if decisive): Karim Khan Zand and Zakariya Khan
how the result was decided: Karim Khan and Zakariya Khan defeated the Bakhtiaris and took the town, though Ali Mardan recovered it soon after.
factions A: Karim Khan Zand and Zakariya Khan
Iranian force: Karim Khan's Zand and Lak tribesmen and Zakariya Khan's men against Bakhtiari tribesmen.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no article; mentioned in the campaign article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no article; mentioned in the campaign article.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Zand campaigns in Western Iran
note: The crisis at Golpayegan had drawn Karim Khan back from a campaign against the vali of Ardalan; Karim and Ali Mardan then joined forces against Isfahan.

name: Murcheh Khort (1750)
place: Murcheh Khort, north of Isfahan, Iran
side A (victor if decisive): Abu'l-Fath Khan Bakhtiari, Afsharid governor of Isfahan
how the result was decided: Ali Mardan Khan was defeated and driven off in his first attempt on Isfahan.
factions A: Abu'l-Fath Khan Bakhtiari, Afsharid governor of Isfahan
Iranian force: The army of Isfahan (largely Haft Lang Bakhtiari) against Ali Mardan's Chahar Lang Bakhtiari tribesmen.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: mentioned as a battle only in the background of the Isfahan articles
doubts and flags: Borderline: mentioned as a battle only in the background of the Isfahan articles.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Fall of Isfahan (1750); Zand campaigns in Western Iran
note: Ali Mardan then allied with Karim Khan Zand and Zakariya Khan and took Isfahan in May 1750.

name: Isfahan (siege, 1750)
side A (victor if decisive): Coalition of Ali Mardan Khan Bakhtiari, Karim Khan Zand and Zakariya Khan
how the result was decided: After a defeat of the Afsharid field force at Qahriz and several days of bombardment, the coalition broke in through the main gate and the Khwaju bridge and Abu'l-Fath Khan surrendered on 31 May.
factions A: Coalition of Ali Mardan Khan Bakhtiari, Karim Khan Zand and Zakariya Khan
commanders A: Ali Mardan Khan, Karim Khan Zand, Zakariya Khan, Shahbaz (Qaraguzlu)
Iranian force: Ali Mardan's Chahar Lang Bakhtiari (about 20,000), Karim Khan's Zand and other Lak and Lur tribesmen (about 12,000) and 2,000 Qaraguzlu, against the Haft Lang Bakhtiari and Afshar troops of the Isfahan garrison.
languages: Lur and Bakhtiari; Kurdish; Turkic; Persian
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
strength B: 15,000 at Qahriz and 50,000 in Isfahan (as given)
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Fall of Isfahan (1750); Perry, Karim Khan Zand
note: The coalition set up the Safavid prince Ismail III as puppet shah; Karim Khan later ousted Ali Mardan.

name: Mashhad (siege, 1750)
how the result was decided: After the relief army was destroyed at Chaman Zaghan the city and Shahrokh surrendered and accepted Durrani suzerainty.
Iranian force: About 8,000 Afsharid troops of the 'Persian garrison' of Mashhad, with the armed townsmen.
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Mashhad (1750); Durrani Campaign to Khorasan (1749-1751)
note: Sources conflict: Noelle has Ahmad Shah lift the siege on 10 November; Lee and Gupta have Shahrokh submit to end it. Either way Shahrokh became a Durrani vassal and kept his throne.

name: Khudaganj
place: Khudaganj, near Farrukhabad, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: Ahmad Khan Bangash surprised Nawal Rai's army in a night attack and won, which led to his recapture of Farrukhabad.
why it counts: Ahmad Khan Bangash was a Pashtun (Bangash) and his army was Pashtun (Wikipedia 'Ahmad Khan Bangash').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Khan_Bangash; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: The prelude to Ram Chatauni (13 September 1750), in which Ahmad Khan defeated Safdar Jang himself; the exact place of Khudaganj is not fixed in the source I used.

name: Ram Chatauni (1750)
war: Safdar Jang's war with the Bangash Nawab of Farrukhabad (1750-51)
place: Ram Chatauni, near Farrukhabad, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: Ahmad Khan defeated Safdar Jang in a pitched battle (Wikipedia, Ahmad Khan Bangash).
commanders A: Safdar Jang, Nawab of Awadh and Mughal wazir
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Wikipedia, Ahmad Khan Bangash (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Khan_Bangash); Wikipedia, Safdar Jang; Irvine, Later Mughals

The family also claims descent from Qara Yusuf of the Qara Qoyunlu (Wikipedia, Safdar Jang), which would make it Turkmen, so the Persian label is contested. I recall an earlier Ram Chatauni fight in 1748 between the Rohillas and Qaim Khan Bangash; it is a different battle.

name: Chaman Zaghan
how the result was decided: The relief army was destroyed and its survivors fled to the mountains.
commanders B: Mohammad Hussain Khan (Kurdish chief, killed), with two nephews of Nader Shah
Iranian force: A relief army raised by Mohammad Hussain Khan from the Kurdish and Turkic tribes of Khorasan and other Khorasani elements, with two nephews of Nader Shah.
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Chaman Zaghan; Siege of Mashhad (1750)
note: The defeat led to the surrender of Mashhad.

name: Nishapur (siege, 1750-51)
how the result was decided: The garrison threw back the assault through the breaches and Ahmad Shah retreated to Herat.
commanders A: Jafar Khan Bayat (killed), then his nephew Abbas Qoli Khan
Iranian force: A garrison of 'only a few thousand men' of the Qara Bayat amirs of Nishapur with the townsmen.
why it counts: Qara Bayat (Nishapur): an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
losses B: about 12,000 dead and thousands wounded (as given)
borderline: the Qara Bayat amirdom of Nishapur was a local Iran-seated power nominally under the Afsharids
doubts and flags: Borderline: the Qara Bayat amirdom of Nishapur was a local Iran-seated power nominally under the Afsharids.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Durrani Campaign to Khorasan (1749-1751)
note: The Afghan loss figure is high and comes from a single account.

date: autumn 1750 to early 1751 (the siege was raised when Safdar Jang's allies arrived)
name: Allahabad (siege, 1750-51)
war: Safdar Jang's war with the Bangash Nawab of Farrukhabad (1750-51)
how the result was decided: Ahmad Khan was close to taking the city when Safdar Jang's Maratha, Jat and Rohilla allies came up; the Bangash were defeated and fell back.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Wikipedia, Ahmad Khan Bangash (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Khan_Bangash); Irvine, Later Mughals; Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, vol. 1
note: Dates and the exact fighting are loose in the sources I could use; counted as a siege that was raised. Same Persian/Qara Qoyunlu caveat for Safdar Jang as above.

name: Chaharmahal (1751)
how the result was decided: Karim Khan completely defeated Ali Mardan, whose captured leaders were blinded or executed and whose foot-soldiers were taken into the Zand army.
Iranian force: Karim Khan's Zand, Lak and Lur tribesmen against Ali Mardan's Bakhtiari.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no article; described as a decisive defeat in the campaign article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no article; described as a decisive defeat in the campaign article.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Zand campaigns in Western Iran; Karim Khan Zand

name: Kirkhbulakh
how the result was decided: The Georgians routed Azad Khan's army and pursued it for about 30 km, and the siege of Erivan was lifted.
Iranian force: Azad Khan's army of Azerbaijan: a core of Afghan (Ghilzai) cavalry with the Kurdish and Turkic chiefs of Azerbaijan allied to him.
why it counts: Azad Khan (Azerbaijan): an Iranian-led state
borderline: Azad Khan was an Iran-seated warlord (Azerbaijan, Urmia and Tabriz) rather than a dynasty
doubts and flags: Borderline: Azad Khan was an Iran-seated warlord (Azerbaijan, Urmia and Tabriz) rather than a dynasty.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kirkhbulakh; Azad Khan Afghan
note: Kingdoms of Kartli and Kakheti under Erekle II. The Khan of Erivan then paid tribute to the Georgian kings.

name: Kermanshah (siege, 1752-53)
side B: Garrison of Kermanshah for Ali Mardan Khan and the pretender Soltan Hoseyn II
how the result was decided: The garrison surrendered in 1753 when Ali Mardan's promised relief failed to break through.
factions B: Garrison of Kermanshah for Ali Mardan Khan and the pretender Soltan Hoseyn II

commanders B: Abd ol-Ali Khan Mishmast, Mirza Mohammad Taqi Golestaneh; relief under Ali Mardan Khan and Esma'il Khan Feyli
Iranian force: Zand regulars with mortars and Kalhor and Zangana Kurdish tribesmen under Najaf Qoli Khan, against a garrison of Afsharid-era troops supported by Haft Lang Bakhtiari and Feyli Lurs.

losses B: the whole garrison surrendered; the relief force was destroyed
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Kermanshah; Zand campaigns in Western Iran
note: A Zand attempt under Mohammad Khan to intercept Ali Mardan's relief force in spring 1752 was repelled with heavy losses.

name: Lahore (1752)
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's third invasion of India (1751-1752)
how the result was decided: Mir Mannu was defeated outside Lahore, surrendered and was kept as Ahmad Shah's governor; Lahore was plundered.
commanders A: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Jahan Khan Popalzai
why it counts: Ahmad Shah Abdali, a Pashtun, led the Durrani and Ghilzai army (Ganda Singh).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959); Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Ahmad Shah, after a siege-like blockade of Lahore from late 1751, defeated Mir Mannu's army and secured the Punjab by treaty; Kashmir was then annexed without a battle.

name: Nahavand (1752)
side B: Ali Mardan Khan Bakhtiari, with Al-Kathir Arabs and Lurs
how the result was decided: Karim Khan defeated Ali Mardan, who fled west into Ottoman territory towards Baghdad.
factions B: Ali Mardan Khan Bakhtiari, with Al-Kathir Arabs and Lurs
Iranian force: Karim Khan's Zand, Lak, Lur and Kurdish tribesmen against Ali Mardan's Bakhtiari with Khuzestani Arab (Al-Kathir) and Lur support.
languages: Lur and Bakhtiari; Kurdish; Arabic; Persian
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

doubts and flags: Borderline: no article; described as a battle in the campaign article.

sources: en.wikipedia Zand campaigns in Western Iran

name: Astarabad (siege, 1752)
side B: Karim Khan Zand, with Ismail III
how the result was decided: The Zands failed to take Astarabad and retreated with heavy losses; the puppet Ismail III fell into Qajar hands.
factions B: Karim Khan Zand, with Ismail III
commanders A: Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar, Mohammad Mirza
commanders B: Karim Khan Zand, Musa Khan Afshar, Zakariya Khan
Iranian force: Mohammad Hasan's Qajar tribesmen and Yomut Turkmen (about 35,000, 'mainly Turkmen') against Karim Khan's Zand, Lur and Kurdish army with siege artillery (about 45,000).

name: Pari (1753)
place: near the fortress of Pari, by Malayer, Iran
how the result was decided: Azad Khan turned on the pursuing Zand army, inflicted a heavy defeat and took Karim Khan's fortress of Pari.
Iranian force: Azad Khan's Afghan cavalry with Kurdish and Turkic allies of Azerbaijan, against Karim Khan's Zand and Lur tribesmen.
languages: Pashto; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no article and no conventional name; named here after the fortress taken
doubts and flags: Borderline: no article and no conventional name; named here after the fortress taken.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Azad Khan Afghan

name: Qomsheh (1753)
side A (victor if decisive): Azad Khan Afghan, with Fath-Ali Khan Afshar
how the result was decided: The Zands withdrew after Karim Khan's half-brother Eskandar Khan was killed, and Azad's forces went on to take Shiraz.
factions A: Azad Khan Afghan, with Fath-Ali Khan Afshar
commanders B: Karim Khan Zand, Eskandar Khan Zand (killed)
Iranian force: Azad Khan's Afghans and Fath-Ali Khan's Afshar Turks against the Zand tribesmen.
languages: Turkic; Pashto; Lur and Bakhtiari; Kurdish
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no article; described in the biographies
doubts and flags: Borderline: no article; described in the biographies.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Fath-Ali Khan Afshar; Azad Khan Afghan
note: The Fath-Ali Khan Afshar article dates the attack to 1753, the Azad Khan article to 1754.

date: 26 March to 7 November 1753 (major assault on the walls failed on 5 June)
name: Delhi (siege, 1753)
war: Safdar Jang's rebellion (the Plunder of Old Delhi, 1753)
how the result was decided: Safdar Jang's assault failed, his men defected, and on 7 November he was pushed back to Ballabgarh and made peace.
commanders A: Safdar Jang; Rajendra Gossain (killed); Suraj Mal
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Wikipedia, Plunder of Old Delhi (Safdarjung's rebellion) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plunder_of_Old_Delhi); Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, vol. 1; Irvine, Later Mughals
note: A months-long investment with skirmishes rather than one battle. Najib Khan is a Rohilla (Pashtun). Safdar Jang's Persian/Qara Qoyunlu question applies as above.

name: Tabas (1754)
how the result was decided: The Persian army was routed and its commander killed; Tabas and Tun were then taken.
commanders A: Sardar Jahan Khan, Nasir Khan of Kalat
commanders B: Ali Murad Khan, governor of Tabas (killed)
Iranian force: The levies of the governor of Tabas; composition not recorded.

doubts and flags: Borderline: no article; a local governor nominally under the Afsharids.

sources: en.wikipedia Durrani Campaign to Khorasan (1754-1755)
note: Kalat (Baloch) fought as Ahmad Shah's vassal, recorded as 'Kalat' (a new short name).

name: Mashhad (siege, 1754)
how the result was decided: Shahrokh surrendered the city on 1 December after a four-month siege.
Iranian force: Shahrokh's garrison and the townsmen of Mashhad; composition not recorded.
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Durrani Campaign to Khorasan (1754-1755)
note: Ahmad Shah's name was read in the Friday sermon on 4 December; Shahrokh was reinstated as a protected ruler on 9 May 1755.

name: Kamarej
how the result was decided: Fath-Ali Khan's army was ambushed in the pass, lost heavily and fled, and Azad's forces left Kazerun and then Fars.
factions B: Azad Khan Afghan (Fath-Ali Khan Afshar in the field)
commanders A: Karim Khan Zand, Mirza Ali Beg Khurmuji, Ra'is Ahmad Shah Tangestani
Iranian force: Karim Khan's Zand troops, Kazerun townsmen and Dashtestan levies, reinforced by about 4,000 Tangestani and Khesht musketeers; against Azad Khan's main army of Afghans and Afshars under Fath-Ali Khan.
languages: Persian; Lur and Bakhtiari; Kurdish; Turkic; Pashto
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kamarej; Fath-Ali Khan Afshar
note: The turning point of Karim Khan's war with Azad Khan; Karim then retook Shiraz.

name: Sabzevar (1755)
how the result was decided: Mohammad Hasan Khan is said to have defeated the Abdali regiment.
commanders B: an Abdali regiment (Shah Pasand Khan's force, as probably meant)
Iranian force: Mohammad Hasan Khan's Qajar tribesmen and Yomut Turkmen allies with Mazandarani levies.
why it counts: Qajars of Astarabad: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
borderline: poorly documented; the Durrani campaign article reports only an unconfirmed defeat of Shah Pasand Khan by the Qajars
doubts and flags: Borderline: poorly documented; the Durrani campaign article reports only an unconfirmed defeat of Shah Pasand Khan by the Qajars.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar; Durrani Campaign to Khorasan (1754-1755)
note: The Durrani article also says Ahmad Shah defeated the Qajars after Nishapur, without place or date.

name: Nishapur (siege, 1755)
how the result was decided: Bombarded with a great Armenian-cast cannon, the elders opened the gates after about a week and the city was plundered and largely razed.
commanders B: Abbas Qoli Khan Bayat and the elders of Nishapur
Iranian force: The townsmen of Nishapur under the Bayat amirs.
why it counts: Qara Bayat (Nishapur): an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Durrani Campaign to Khorasan (1754-1755)
note: The city had revolted on a rumour that Shah Pasand Khan had been beaten by the Qajars.

name: Gulnabad (1756)
how the result was decided: Mohammad Hasan defeated Karim Khan's forces and went on to occupy Isfahan.
Iranian force: Qajar and Turkmen cavalry with Mazandarani musketeers, against Zand, Lur and Kurdish tribesmen.
languages: Turkic; Lur and Bakhtiari; Kurdish; Daylami and Caspian
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no article; listed among Mohammad Hasan's battles
doubts and flags: Borderline: no article; listed among Mohammad Hasan's battles.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar

name: Kazzaz
place: Sanjan, near Kazzaz, northwest of Isfahan (near Arak), Iran
how the result was decided: The outnumbered Zand force was broken; Mohammad Khan Zand was captured and Shaykh Ali Khan escaped with fifteen men.
commanders B: Shaykh Ali Khan Zand, Mohammad Khan Zand (captured)
Iranian force: Mohammad Hasan's veteran Qajar army with musketeers levied in Astarabad, against a weakened Zand force whose Arab musketeers had mutinied.
languages: Turkic; Daylami and Caspian; Lur and Bakhtiari; Kurdish
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: unknown (Mohammad Khan Zand and four officers captured)
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kazzaz
note: Karim Khan abandoned Isfahan for Shiraz.

date: late January 1757 (Ahmad Shah entered Delhi about 28 January)
name: Delhi (occupation and sack, 1757)
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's fourth invasion of India (1756-1757)
how the result was decided: The Mughal court submitted, Delhi was occupied and sacked for weeks, and Alamgir II was left on the throne as a vassal.
commanders A: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Jahan Khan Popalzai; Najib ad-Dawla (Rohilla)
why it counts: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) led the Afghan army, with Najib ad-Dawla's Rohilla Pashtuns.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34); Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959)
note: Little organised fighting: included because the capture and sack of Delhi is a named event of the invasion. Najib ad-Dawla, a Yusufzai Rohilla, had invited Ahmad Shah and was made his agent in Delhi.

name: Narela
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's fourth invasion of India (1756-1757)
how the result was decided: The Afghan vanguard drove back about 3,400 Marathas of Antaji Mankeshwar, who withdrew and left Delhi open.
why it counts: Ahmad Shah's army was Afghan (Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: A skirmish-sized action on the road into Delhi, known mainly from Sarkar and the Maratha letters; the date and numbers rest on a single summary of Wikipedia's account.

date: about 28 February 1757 (the day before the sack of Mathura)
name: Chaumuhan
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's fourth invasion of India (1756-1757)
place: Chaumuhan (Chaumuha), near Mathura, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: The Jats resisted at Chaumuhan with heavy losses on both sides (10,000-12,000 combined), after which the Afghans went on to sack Mathura.
commanders B: Jawahar Singh; Suraj Mal (ruler of Bharatpur)
why it counts: The Afghan column was drawn from Ahmad Shah's Durrani army (Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: The outcome is not stated outright in the sources I could check; A is inferred from the Afghan advance to Mathura next day.

name: Agra (siege, 1757)
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's fourth invasion of India (1756-1757)
how the result was decided: The Afghans plundered the town but could not take Agra Fort, and cholera in their camp forced the withdrawal to Afghanistan.
why it counts: The besiegers were Ahmad Shah's Afghan army (Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Limit of the 1757 advance; over 2,000 townspeople were killed.

name: Ballabhgarh
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's fourth invasion of India (1756-1757)
how the result was decided: The Afghans seized Ballabhgarh on about 4 March and Jawahar Singh withdrew.
commanders B: Jawahar Singh; Balram Singh (Jat chief of Ballabhgarh)
why it counts: The attackers were Ahmad Shah's Durrani army (Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Ahmad Shah's Afghans cleared the Jat forts south of Delhi on the way to Mathura and Agra.

name: Gokul
war: Ahmad Shah Durrani's fourth invasion of India (1756-1757)
place: Gokul, near Mathura, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: About 2,000 died on both sides and the Afghans withdrew without sacking Gokul.
commanders B: Naga sadhu leaders (not named in the sources checked)
why it counts: The attackers were Ahmad Shah's Afghan troops (Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: A rare check to the Afghan advance, remembered chiefly in Hindu tradition; the fighting itself is also noted by Sarkar.

name: Urmia (1757)
side B: Azad Khan Afghan, with Fath-Ali Khan Afshar of Urmia
how the result was decided: Azad Khan fled to Ottoman territory and Urmia and Tabriz passed to the Qajars.
factions B: Azad Khan Afghan, with Fath-Ali Khan Afshar of Urmia
Iranian force: Mohammad Hasan's Qajar army against Azad Khan's Afghans and the Afshars of Urmia.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: the infobox of the Mohammad Hasan article lists a 'Battle of Urmiya', but its text and the Fath-Ali Khan Afshar article say Urmia surrendered without a fight
doubts and flags: Borderline: the infobox of the Mohammad Hasan article lists a 'Battle of Urmiya', but its text and the Fath-Ali Khan Afshar article say Urmia surrendered without a fight.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar; Fath-Ali Khan Afshar

date: August-September 1757 (Marathas entered about 11 August; Najib left Delhi in September)
name: Delhi (Maratha siege of Najib ad-Dawla, 1757)
side B: Najib ad-Dawla and the Rohilla garrison of Delhi
how the result was decided: The Marathas, with Imad al-Mulk, invested Najib in Delhi and forced him to give up the capital's government and retire to his jagir.
Iranian side: Najib ad-Dawla and the Rohilla garrison of Delhi
why it counts: Najib ad-Dawla, a Pashtun (Yusufzai) Rohilla chief, led the defence (Sarkar).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Najib ad-Dawla (Yusufzai Rohilla), left as Ahmad Shah's agent in Delhi, was dislodged by Raghunathrao's Marathas; the fighting was brief and the date within 1757 is not fixed.

date: 11-13 November 1757 (Diwali; Baba Deep Singh killed 13 November)
name: Amritsar (Gohalwar, 1757)
war: Afghan-Sikh Wars: Durrani occupation of the Punjab
how the result was decided: Baba Deep Singh's Sikhs were beaten near Gohalwar on the way to Amritsar and he was killed; the Afghans desecrated the Harmandir Sahib.
commanders A: Jahan Khan Popalzai; Prince Timur Shah
why it counts: Jahan Khan Popalzai and Timur Shah, Pashtun Durranis, commanded an Afghan army (Wikipedia 'Afghan-Sikh Wars').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Sikh_Wars; Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959)
note: Prince Timur Shah, Ahmad Shah's son and viceroy at Lahore, and the general Jahan Khan commanded; Sikh accounts hold that Baba Deep Singh fought on after being wounded.

name: Kalat (siege, 1758)
how the result was decided: The siege of about forty days failed and a treaty confirmed Nasir Khan as governor under Durrani suzerainty.
Iranian side: Durrani Empire v Khanate of Kalat
why it counts: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) led the besiegers while the defenders included Baloch levies (Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Axworthy / Noelle-Karimi on Kalat (not consulted in full)
note: Ended with a treaty rather than a storm, and Nasir Khan later served Ahmad Shah with a Baloch-Brahui contingent.

name: Mastung (1758)
how the result was decided: Nasir Khan's forces were defeated at Mastung, after which he withdrew to Kalat.
Iranian side: Durrani Empire v Khanate of Kalat
commanders A: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Shah Wali Khan
why it counts: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) led the Durrani army, while Kalat's army included Baloch levies (Wikipedia 'Ahmad Shah Durrani').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani; Axworthy / Noelle-Karimi on Kalat (not consulted in full)
note: Follows Shah Wali Khan's defeat at Pringuez; Nasir Khan's army was mostly Brahui with Baloch tribal levies, so the Baloch share is a guess.

name: Sirhind (siege, 1758)
allies A: Sikh Dal Khalsa; Adina Beg Khan
how the result was decided: After about two weeks the garrison of some 15,000 Afghans surrendered and the town was sacked.
why it counts: The garrison was an Afghan force of about 15,000 (Wikipedia 'Afghan-Maratha War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Maratha_War; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Dal Khalsa Sikhs under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia and Ala Singh and Adina Beg Khan fought alongside the Marathas.

name: Attock (1758)
place: Attock fort on the Indus, Punjab, Pakistan
how the result was decided: The Marathas took Attock and raised their flag over the fort, the farthest point of their advance up the Indus.
commanders A: Raghunathrao (overall); Mahadji Shinde; Tukoji (Holkar/Shinde; Wikipedia's infobox says Scindia)
commanders B: Karim Shah; Wazirullah Khan (named in Wikipedia's infobox; their roles are not explained)
why it counts: The defenders were Ahmad Shah Durrani's Afghan garrison (Wikipedia 'Afghan-Maratha War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Attock_(1758); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Maratha_War; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: The Durrani garrisons of the Punjab were pushed out in 1758 by Raghunathrao's army with Sikh help; the garrison was Afghan, but I did not find a source naming its commanders' tribes.

name: Peshawar (1758)
how the result was decided: The Marathas defeated the Durrani force and took Peshawar, the farthest Maratha conquest.
commanders B: Durrani garrison commander (not identified in the sources checked)
why it counts: The garrison was Ahmad Shah's Afghan force (Wikipedia 'Afghan-Maratha War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Attock_(1758); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Maratha_War; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Sabaji Shinde held Peshawar until Ahmad Shah's general Jahan Khan retook the fort in 1759. The Maratha commanders' names are from memory of Sarkar, not checked here.

name: Shiraz (siege, 1758)
side B: Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar, with Fath-Ali Khan Afshar and Nasir Khan Lari
how the result was decided: The Qajars failed to take Shiraz and withdrew after Uzbek and Afghan defectors raided their camp on the night of 3 July.
factions B: Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar, with Fath-Ali Khan Afshar and Nasir Khan Lari
commanders A: Karim Khan Zand, Shaykh Ali Khan Zand, Nadr Khan Zand
commanders B: Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar, Ebrahim Khan Boghayeri, Fath-Ali Khan Afshar, Abu'l-Qasem Khan (captured), Nasir Khan Lari
Iranian force: About 10,000 Zand defenders behind fortified ramparts, against at least 27,000 Qajar troops of many peoples (many of them defectors from Azad Khan's army: Afghans, Uzbeks, Azeri Turks) with the Afshar contingent of Urmia.
languages: Lur and Bakhtiari; Kurdish; Persian; Turkic; Pashto
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Shiraz (1758); Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar

name: Astarabad (1759)
how the result was decided: The Qajar army broke and Mohammad Hasan Khan was killed in flight; Astarabad passed to the Zands.
commanders A: Shaykh Ali Khan Zand, Hoseyn Khan Develu
commanders B: Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar (killed), Agha Mohammad Khan (captured)
Iranian force: A larger Zand army under Shaykh Ali Khan with Develu Qajar and Kurdish defectors, against a smaller Qajar army of 'fickle Kurdish and Turkic tribesmen'.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: unknown (Mohammad Hasan killed, Agha Mohammad captured)
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Astarabad (1759); Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar
note: Also called the battle of Ashraf. The Mohammad Hasan article dates his death to 13 February.

name: Barari Ghat
place: Barari (Burari) Ghat on the Yamuna, north of Delhi, India
how the result was decided: Dattaji Shinde was killed on the Yamuna bank and his army fell back, ending Maratha control of the Doab north of Delhi.
commanders B: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Najib ad-Dawla; Qutb Shah (Rohilla religious leader)
why it counts: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) and Najib ad-Dawla's Rohilla Pashtuns fought the Marathas (Sarkar).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Maratha_War; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Dattaji was ambushed (some accounts say struck down when he rode forward to meet Qutb Shah); Ahmad Shah's Afghans and Najib's Rohillas were present.

name: Sikandarabad (1760)
place: near Sikandarabad, Bulandshahr district, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: Ahmad Shah's vanguard caught and destroyed the Maratha advance guard and Holkar retreated toward Agra.
commanders A: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Jahan Khan Popalzai; Najib ad-Dawla
why it counts: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) and Jahan Khan led the Durrani army, with Najib's Rohillas (Wikipedia 'Battle of Sikandrabad').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sikandarabad; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Maratha_War; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Najib ad-Dawla advised the Afghans to prepare for a fresh Maratha army from the Deccan, which Holkar's defeat preceded.

name: Tabriz (siege, 1760)
how the result was decided: Karim Khan could not take Tabriz, which Fath-Ali Khan defended, and withdrew to Tehran.
Iranian force: Fath-Ali Khan's Afshar and Shahsevan Turkic tribesmen and the townsmen of Tabriz, against Karim Khan's Zand, Lur and Kurdish army.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no article; Karim Khan briefly occupied Maragheh before the failure at Tabriz
doubts and flags: Borderline: no article; Karim Khan briefly occupied Maragheh before the failure at Tabriz.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Fath-Ali Khan Afshar

date: 22-23 July 1760 (the fort besieged until a negotiated surrender in early August)
name: Delhi (Maratha capture, 1760)
place: Delhi and the Red Fort, India
side A (victor if decisive): Maratha Confederacy; Jat kingdom of Bharatpur
how the result was decided: The Marathas took the city; the Afghan garrison held the fort for a few days, then left safely with its property under a negotiated settlement and Naro Shankar became subahdar.
commanders A: Sadashivrao Bhau; Malharrao Holkar; Jankoji Shinde; Balwantrao Mehendale
why it counts: The fort was held by Yakub Ali Khan's Afghan troops of Ahmad Shah's army (Wikipedia 'Capture of Delhi (1760)').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Delhi_(1760); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Maratha_War
note: About 100 Maratha soldiers who entered the fort were killed by the Afghan guards before the siege and bombardment began.

name: Kunjpura
how the result was decided: The Marathas encircled the fort overnight, bombarded it, and stormed in when the garrison forced a gate; the Afghan commanders were killed.
commanders A: Sadashivrao Bhau; Ibrahim Khan Gardi; Mahadji Shinde; Jankoji Shinde; Malharrao Holkar
commanders B: Najabat Khan (died of wounds); Abdus Samad Khan (governor of Sirhind, killed); Mian Qutb Shah (wounded, later executed)
why it counts: The garrison is described as Afghans and Rohillas (Wikipedia 'Battle of Kunjpura').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kunjpura; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Maratha_War; Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: About 10,000 Afghans inside and 5,000 outside under Abdus Samad Khan and Qutb Shah; the Marathas took a very large booty. Ahmad Shah crossed the Yamuna in revenge, which led to Panipat.

name: Samalkha
how the result was decided: The Afghans lost about 1,000 men and the Marathas over 2,000 and retreated slowly for days.
why it counts: Ahmad Shah Durrani (Pashtun) commanded the Afghan army (Wikipedia 'Battle of Samalkha (1760)').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Samalkha_(1760); Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: A cavalry action in the manoeuvres before Panipat; Ahmad Shah took part in person.

name: Meerut (1760)
how the result was decided: Atai Khan's 14,000 Afghans destroyed Govind Pant's foragers and killed him, cutting the Maratha supplies from the Doab.
why it counts: The attackers were a 14,000-strong Afghan contingent of Ahmad Shah's army under Atai Khan (Wikipedia 'Battle of Meerut (1760)').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Meerut_(1760); Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: The destruction of Govind Pant's force (Wikipedia gives about 12,000 horse on the Maratha side) left Bhau short of supplies and led to Panipat. The summary I checked calls the attackers only 'Afghans'; Atai Khan was a nephew of the Durrani wazir Shah Wali Khan (Sarkar, from memory).

name: Shusha (siege, 1761)
how the result was decided: The siege ended by agreement while Shusha was still invested: Panah Ali Khan gave his son Ibrahim Khalil Khan as a hostage and Fath-Ali Khan withdrew.
Iranian force: Fath-Ali Khan's Afshar and allied Turkic and Kurdish tribal forces of Azerbaijan.
why it counts: Afshars of Urmia: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
borderline: no article; the Karabakh khanate was outside present-day Iran
doubts and flags: Borderline: no article; the Karabakh khanate was outside present-day Iran.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Fath-Ali Khan Afshar
note: Karabakh Khanate (Panah Ali Khan Javanshir).

name: Third Battle of Panipat
how the result was decided: The Durrani coalition destroyed the Maratha army; Vishwasrao and Bhau were killed.
commanders A: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Shuja-ud-Daula (Nawab of Awadh); Najib ad-Dawlah; Hafiz Rahmat Khan
commanders B: Sadashivrao Bhau; Vishwasrao; Ibrahim Khan Gardi; Malharrao Holkar; Jankoji Scindia
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Wikipedia, Shuja-ud-Daula (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuja-ud-Daula); Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, vol. 2; Kashi Raj Pandit, Account of the Battle of Panipat
note: Counted for the Awadh army under Shuja-ud-Daula, a Persian by descent (Nishapuri Sayyid house; also a claimed Qara Qoyunlu descent, see Ram Chatauni). the Persian share is a named allied army, not a fifth proved.

name: Gujranwala (1761)
war: Afghan-Sikh Wars: Sikh rising after Panipat
how the result was decided: The Durrani governor of Lahore was defeated by the Sikhs near Gujranwala and fell back to Lahore, which the Sikhs then held.
commanders A: Charat Singh Sukerchakia; Jassa Singh Ahluwalia (named in Sikh tradition)
commanders B: Khwaja Ubaid Khan (Afghan governor of Lahore)
why it counts: The Durrani army of the Lahore governor was Afghan (Wikipedia 'Afghan-Sikh Wars').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Sikh_Wars; Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959)
note: The first big Sikh victory after Panipat; Wikipedia's Afghan-Sikh Wars article names a Gujranwala fight in September 1761 and another in 1762 against Jahan Khan, and I have kept only the first. The commanders are from memory.

name: Kup (Vadda Ghallughara)
war: Afghan-Sikh Wars: Ahmad Shah's sixth invasion
how the result was decided: Ahmad Shah's cavalry caught the Sikh families and warriors on the march and killed between 10,000 and 30,000 of them.
commanders A: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Shah Wali Khan; Jahan Khan Popalzai
commanders B: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia; Charat Singh; Ala Singh
why it counts: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) led the Afghan army, with the Pashtun Nawab of Malerkotla (Ganda Singh).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_Shah_Durrani
note: The Great Holocaust of Sikh memory: a surprise attack, not a pitched battle; the Sikhs regrouped within months. The Pashtun nawabs of Malerkotla and the faujdar of Sirhind joined the Afghans.

name: Qara Chaman
place: Qara Chaman (Qareh Chaman), about 80 km southeast of Tabriz, Iran
side B: Fath-Ali Khan Afshar of Urmia, with Donboli Kurds and Karabakh troops
how the result was decided: Fath-Ali Khan's baggage was overrun by a final charge of Zand gholams and he fled the field to Urmia.
factions B: Fath-Ali Khan Afshar of Urmia, with Donboli Kurds and Karabakh troops
commanders A: Karim Khan Zand, Shaykh Ali Khan Zand, Lotf Ali Khan (artillery), Ebrahim Boghayeri, Rafi' Khan Qajar
commanders B: Fath-Ali Khan Afshar, Najaf Qoli Khan (captured), Amir Guna Khan Afshar, Shahbaz Khan Donboli (captured)
Iranian force: Karim Khan's army with artillery in front and musketeers on the flanks, 300 gholams, Kurdish (Amarlu) and Shamlu and Shahsevan tribesmen and Georgian gunners; against Fath-Ali Khan's 35,000 Afshars and Shahsevan with Donboli Kurds and 1,600 Karabakh troops.
languages: Lur and Bakhtiari; Kurdish; Turkic; Georgian
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: baggage train lost; many officers and men captured and executed
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Qara Chaman; Zand campaigns in Western Iran
note: Also called Siah Chaman. Karabakh Khanate troops guarded Fath-Ali's baggage.

name: Urmia (siege, 1762-63)
how the result was decided: Urmia fell to the Zands in February 1763 after a seven-month siege, and Fath-Ali Khan was captured.
Iranian force: Karim Khan's Zand, Lur and Kurdish army against the Afshar garrison of Urmia, harried by Kurdish raids during a harsh winter.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Fath-Ali Khan Afshar; Zand campaigns in Western Iran
note: Fath-Ali Khan was executed near Isfahan in July 1764.

date: 17 October 1762 (Diwali); some accounts date the attack on the Sikh gathering earlier in the autumn
name: Amritsar (Diwali, 1762)
war: Afghan-Sikh Wars: Ahmad Shah's sixth invasion
how the result was decided: Ahmad Shah's attack on the Sikh gathering at Amritsar was fought off in a night action and he left the Punjab soon after.
why it counts: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) led the Afghan army (Ganda Singh).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959); Latif, S. M., History of the Panjab (1891)
note: Follows the Harmandir Sahib's destruction in April 1762; accounts of the result differ (Sikh sources claim a victory, Afghan sources a withdrawal after a successful attack), so the result is recorded as a draw.

name: Kasur (1763)
war: Afghan-Sikh Wars: Sikh conquests in the Bari Doab
how the result was decided: The Dal Khalsa stormed and plundered Kasur and its Pashtun ruler fell.
commanders A: Dal Khalsa chiefs (Jassa Singh Ahluwalia and Hari Singh Bhangi are named in Sikh tradition)
why it counts: Kasur was ruled by the Pashtun Khweshgi family and defended by their followers (Latif; Ganda Singh).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959); Latif, S. M., History of the Panjab (1891)
note: Tradition says the raid was provoked by the Kasur Pashtuns' seizure of a Brahmin's wife; the Khweshgi Pashtuns of Kasur were Ahmad Shah's supporters in the Bari Doab. The commanders' names are from tradition, not checked.

name: Hindon (Suraj Mal's death, 1763)
place: Hindon river near Shahdara, Delhi, India
side B: Najib ad-Dawla and the Mughal imperial army
how the result was decided: Suraj Mal was ambushed and killed on the Hindon and the Jat army withdrew to Bharatpur.
Iranian side: Najib ad-Dawla and the Mughal imperial army
commanders B: Najib ad-Dawla; Musa Khan Baloch; Sayyid Muhammad Khan Baloch
why it counts: Najib ad-Dawla, a Yusufzai Pashtun Rohilla, led the imperial forces with Baloch commanders (Sarkar).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Suraj Mal rode out with a small escort to reconnoitre and ran into a Rohilla and Baloch force; it was less a battle than a skirmish with great consequences. The Baloch commanders' names are from memory of Sarkar.

name: Sirhind (1764)
war: Afghan-Sikh Wars: Sikh conquest of Sirhind
how the result was decided: Zain Khan Sirhindi was killed and his army routed, and the Sikhs sacked Sirhind.
commanders A: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia; Ala Singh; Charat Singh
why it counts: Sirhind was held for Ahmad Shah by an Afghan force under Zain Khan (Ganda Singh).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Sikh_Wars
note: The Sikhs' revenge for the Vadda Ghallughara; Sirhind was sacked and its territory divided among the Dal Khalsa chiefs. Whether Zain Khan was himself Pashtun or an Afghan appointee is not settled in the sources I used.

name: Buxar
side B: Awadh; Mughal Empire; Nawab Mir Qasim of Bengal
how the result was decided: The Company's army routed the allied army; Shuja withdrew to Awadh and Shah Alam came to terms (Treaty of Allahabad, 1765).
commanders B: Shuja-ud-Daula; Shah Alam II; Mir Qasim; Mirza Najaf Khan (in Shah Alam's service)
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Wikipedia, Shuja-ud-Daula (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuja-ud-Daula); Mir Qasim; Mirza Najaf Khan; Dalrymple, The Anarchy; Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, vol. 2
note: Iranian element: Shuja-ud-Daula (Persian by descent; Qara Qoyunlu claim noted at Ram Chatauni) and Mirza Najaf Khan (Safavid lineage, born in Iran). Mir Qasim's 'Najafi' Sayyid house is not securely Persian, so he is not counted.

name: Delhi (siege, 1764-1765)
side B: Najib ad-Dawla and the Rohilla garrison of Delhi
allies A: Maratha Holkar forces; Sikh Dal Khalsa; Naga sannyasis
how the result was decided: Jawahar Singh withdrew from Delhi on 16 February 1765 after spending about two crore rupees without taking the city.
Iranian side: Najib ad-Dawla and the Rohilla garrison of Delhi
why it counts: Najib ad-Dawla, a Yusufzai Pashtun Rohilla, led the Rohilla defence (Wikipedia 'Battle of Delhi (1764)').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Delhi_(1764); Sarkar, J., Fall of the Mughal Empire, vols. 1-2 (1932-34)
note: Jawahar Singh came to avenge his father Suraj Mal with about 65,000 Jat, Maratha and Sikh troops (Wikipedia), and Najib ad-Dawla saved Delhi by generalship, famine-bound trench defence and bribing Holkar; Najib asked Ahmad Shah for help but none came in time.

date: December 1764 (Ahmad Shah's seventh invasion; March 1765 withdrawal)
name: Amritsar (1764)
war: Afghan-Sikh Wars: Ahmad Shah's seventh invasion
how the result was decided: Ahmad Shah's Afghans and the Dal Khalsa fought around Amritsar without a decision and the Afghans left the Punjab in March 1765, partly through mutiny in their own ranks.
commanders A: Ahmad Shah Durrani; Jahan Khan Popalzai
commanders B: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia; Charat Singh; Ala Singh
why it counts: Ahmad Shah (Pashtun) led the Afghan army (Ganda Singh).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Ganda Singh, Ahmad Shah Durrani: Father of Modern Afghanistan (1959); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan%E2%80%93Sikh_Wars
note: Ahmad Shah's last invasion; the Sikhs avoided a pitched battle and harassed the Afghans. I have a thin source for the actual engagement and its date, hence the low confidence.

name: Kora
place: Kora (Jahanabad), Fatehpur district, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: Carnac defeated Shuja's and Holkar's army, after which Shuja negotiated the Treaty of Allahabad.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Wikipedia, Shuja-ud-Daula (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuja-ud-Daula); Dalrymple, The Anarchy
note: The Kora fighting is only lightly covered in what I fetched; the main weakness is the date and place, and the Persian-by-descent label on Shuja (Qara Qoyunlu claim).

name: Kharg (1765)
how the result was decided: Mir Mahna's men captured a Dutch cargo ship and both Dutch galliots sent to escort it, with their crews.
commanders A: Mir Mahna (Mir Muhanna) of Bandar Rig
commanders B: the Dutch East India Company officers at Kharg (Baron Kniphausen's successors)
Iranian force: Mir Mahna's dhows and fighters of Bandar Rig (Arab and Persian sailors of the Gulf coast).
why it counts: Bandar Rig (Mir Mahna): an Iranian-led state
strength B: 2 galliots and a cargo ship; over 40 Europeans and 18 local sailors
borderline: Mir Mahna was a local lord of Bandar Rig, often at war with Karim Khan; the article presents him as acting for the Zands
doubts and flags: Borderline: Mir Mahna was a local lord of Bandar Rig, often at war with Karim Khan; the article presents him as acting for the Zands.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Persian-Dutch War
note: Dutch East India Company (VOC); 'Netherlands' is a new opponent name. The article's dates are garbled (1 or 22 December 1765; other accounts put the fall of Kharg on 1 January 1766).

name: Kharg (siege, 1765-66)
how the result was decided: Mir Mahna's men besieged Fort Mosselstein and took it, expelling the Dutch from Kharg.
commanders B: the Dutch commander of Fort Mosselstein (not named in the source)
Iranian force: Mir Mahna's men of Bandar Rig, landed near the Armenian quarter out of range of the Dutch guns.
why it counts: Bandar Rig (Mir Mahna): an Iranian-led state
borderline: as for Kharg (1765): Mir Mahna's relation to the Zand state is disputed
doubts and flags: Borderline: as for Kharg (1765): Mir Mahna's relation to the Zand state is disputed.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Persian-Dutch War
note: Dutch East India Company (VOC). The end of the Dutch presence in the Persian Gulf.

name: Mashhad (siege, 1769-70)
how the result was decided: Ahmad Shah did not storm the city (out of respect for the shrine of Imam Reza) and the siege ended in negotiations, Shahrokh submitting again while Mashhad was still invested.
Iranian force: Shahrokh's garrison, with sorties; Nasrollah Mirza raised a relief army from the Kurds at Chenaran.
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Durrani campaign in Khorasan (1769-1770)
note: After submitting, Shahrokh furnished troops to the Afghan army.

name: Gonabad (first, 1770)
how the result was decided: The Afghan contingent was repelled.
commanders A: Nader Mirza and Ali Mardan Khan of Tabas (reinforcements)
Iranian force: Afsharid reinforcements under Nader Mirza with the troops of Ali Mardan Khan, chief of Tabas.
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
borderline: no article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no article.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Durrani campaign in Khorasan (1769-1770)

name: Gonabad (second, 1770)
place: near Gonabad, with the pursuit to Soltanabad, Iran
how the result was decided: The Persians were defeated, Ali Mardan Khan was killed and Nader Mirza was pursued as far as Soltanabad.
commanders A: Jahan Khan, Nasir Khan Ahmadzai of Kalat
commanders B: Ali Mardan Khan of Tabas (killed), Nader Mirza
Iranian force: Nader Mirza's Afsharid troops and the forces of Tabas.
why it counts: Afsharids: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
borderline: no article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no article.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Durrani campaign in Khorasan (1769-1770)
note: Khanate of Kalat (Baloch) as Ahmad Shah's vassal.

date: 1772 (the Maratha invasion began at the turn of 1771-72; the fort's fall is not dated precisely here)
name: Pathargarh (siege, 1772)
place: Pathargarh fort, Najibabad, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: The Marathas stormed Pathargarh and Najibabad, Saadat Khan was killed and Zabita Khan fled to Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh.
commanders A: Mahadji Shinde; Tukoji Holkar; Visaji Krishna Biniwale
commanders B: Zabita Khan (son of Najib ad-Dawla); Sa'adat Khan (killed); Sayyid Khan
why it counts: Najib ad-Dawla's jagir was defended by his son Zabita Khan with Pashtun Yusufzai Rohillas (Wikipedia 'Rohilla').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rohilla; Husain, Iqbal, The Rise and Decline of the Ruhela Chieftaincy in 18th Century India (1994)
note: The Marathas, after retaking Delhi in 1771, plundered Najib's old jagir in revenge for Panipat; the Rohillas withdrew to the Terai, and Hafiz Rahmat Khan's promise of money to Shuja-ud-Daula for protection (the treaty of June 1772) was the root of the Rohilla War of 1774. The date of the fort's fall is from memory and not fixed.

date: late 1773 to 18 February 1774, when Najaf Khan retook the city (start date not fixed)
name: Agra (siege, 1773-74)
war: Najaf Khan's campaign against the Jats of Bharatpur
how the result was decided: Najaf Khan retook Agra on 18 February 1774, ending thirteen years of Jat rule (Wikipedia, Capture of Agra).
commanders B: Jat garrison commanders under Nawal Singh (not named in the source consulted)
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Wikipedia, Capture of Agra (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Agra); Wikipedia, Mirza Najaf Khan (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirza_Najaf_Khan); K. R. Qanungo, History of the Jats
note: Najaf Khan is described by Wikipedia as of 'Safavid lineage', born in Iran about 1723 and arriving at Delhi about 1740. The fighting at Agra is thinly described in what I could read.

name: Miranpur Katra
place: Miranpur Katra, Shahjahanpur district, Uttar Pradesh, India
how the result was decided: Hafiz Rahmat Khan was killed and the Rohilla army broke; Awadh and the Company then overran Rohilkhand.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Wikipedia, Shuja-ud-Daula (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuja-ud-Daula); Dalrymple, The Anarchy; Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire, vol. 3
note: Both armies are partly Iranian peoples: Awadh under a Persian-descended Nawab, and the Rohillas (Pashtuns). The Company brigade did much of the fighting.

name: Chamchamal
how the result was decided: The Persian army lost cohesion when Ali-Morad Khan was unhorsed and captured, and its retreat became a rout.
commanders A: Ahmad Pasha Baban, reinforced by Omar Pasha of Baghdad
Iranian force: About 10,000 troops sent by Karim Khan with some 2,000 Kurds loyal to the fugitive Baban pasha Mehmed Pasha.
why it counts: Zands: an Iranian-led state
losses B: 4,000-5,000 dead; 10-12 officers captured besides the commander
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Chamchamal; Ottoman-Persian War (1775-1779)
note: Baban emirate forces under Ottoman suzerainty. Ali-Morad was taken to Baghdad and later released.

name: Hella
how the result was decided: The relief force sent from Baghdad towards Basra was intercepted and driven back.
commanders A: Shaykh Ahmad and Shaykh Soltan of the Khaza'il
commanders B: unknown (a Mamluk relief force from Baghdad)
Iranian force: The Khaza'il Arab tribe acting as Zand allies; no Zand unit is described.
why it counts: Zands: an Iranian-led state
borderline: the article lists 'Zand Iran' as a belligerent but describes only the Khaza'il fighting
doubts and flags: Borderline: the article lists 'Zand Iran' as a belligerent but describes only the Khaza'il fighting.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Hella; Siege of Basra (1775-1776)
note: Khaza'il tribe of the middle Euphrates.

name: Khanaqin (1775)
how the result was decided: Nazar Ali Khan defeated Abdollah Pasha's force, inflicting heavy losses and taking much livestock.
Iranian force: A Zand detachment; composition not recorded (Zand field forces were Lak, Lur and Kurdish horse).
why it counts: Zands: an Iranian-led state
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
