place: Nafusk Pass on the road to Kahan, Marri country, Balochistan, Pakistan
how the result was decided: Clibborn's supply column, bound for the beleaguered post at Kahan, was ambushed in the pass, lost its guns and baggage and fell back to Dadhar.
why it counts: The attackers were Marri Baloch tribesmen under their chief; the Baloch are Iranian-speakers (Wikipedia and Kaye on the Kahan expeditions).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); Wikipedia 'Kahan' and 'Marri (tribe)' (not fetched)
note: A minor but well-known British reverse on the Kachhi side of the war; the date and the commander's name are from memory of Kaye and need checking.

name: Dadur (Dhadar, 1840)
war: First Anglo-Afghan War (1839-1842): Brahui revolt in Kalat
place: Dhadar (Dadur), at the mouth of the Bolan Pass, Balochistan, Pakistan
how the result was decided: Boscawen defeated Nasir Khan's attempt to drive the British from the road between Shikarpur and Quetta (FIBIS 'Battle of Dadur').
commanders B: Mir Nasir Khan II of Kalat
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://wiki.fibis.org/w/Battle_of_Dadur (fetched); Kaye (1851)
note: Weak on the Baloch share: FIBIS calls the enemy 'Brahui tribesmen', and the Khan was a Brahui. British writers of the time lumped the Khan's Brahui and Baloch levies together; the Baloch contingent is inferred.

name: Parwan Darra
place: Parwan Darra, near Charikar, Parwan Province, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: The 2nd Bengal Cavalry broke and fled and two British officers were killed, so Dost Mohammad kept the field, though he surrendered at Kabul the next evening.
commanders A: Sir Robert Sale (per Kaye); Lt. Col. William Dennie (infantry)
why it counts: Dost Mohammad, the Barakzai ruler of Kabul, led a force of Afghans and Kohistanis in his last field action (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Dost Mohammad's tactical victory, followed at once by his surrender to Macnaghten at Kabul; he was exiled to India.

name: Kotra (Dhadar, 1840)
war: First Anglo-Afghan War (1839-1842): Brahui revolt in Kalat
place: Kotra, Kachhi plain near Dhadar, Balochistan, Pakistan (site approximate)
how the result was decided: Marshall and Teasdale attacked the Brahui camp from two sides and broke it; British loss 5 killed and 30 wounded, tribal loss about 500 killed (FIBIS).
commanders B: Mir Nasir Khan II of Kalat
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://wiki.fibis.org/w/Battle_of_Kotra (fetched); Kaye (1851)
note: Weak on the Baloch share, as at Dadur: FIBIS names only Brahui tribesmen. Included because the Khanate's levies were Brahui and Baloch together and the Brief counts them as Baloch when the sources do.

name: Rigan (1841)
how the result was decided: The Aga Khan suffered a decisive defeat and fled to Afghanistan.
Iranian force: A government army (24,000 had driven him out of Bam) against the Aga Khan's followers.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no article.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Aga Khan I
note: The Aga Khan went on to Kandahar and later Sind and Bombay.

name: Dashtab (1841)
how the result was decided: The Aga Khan defeated a government force of 4,000.
Iranian force: The Aga Khan's Ismaili and tribal followers against 4,000 government troops.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no article.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Aga Khan I

date: 9-12 October 1841 (Khurd Kabul, 9 Oct; Tezin and the night attacks, 10-12 Oct)
name: Khurd Kabul Pass (1841)
war: First Anglo-Afghan War (1839-1842): Ghilzai rising of October 1841
place: Khurd Kabul Pass, between Kabul and Jalalabad, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: Sale's brigade forced the pass and fought through to Gandamak, though with heavy losses.
why it counts: The Eastern Ghilzai, a Pashtun tribal confederacy, closed the passes after the cut in their subsidies (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: The Ghilzai rising that preceded the Kabul uprising by three weeks; Sale's brigade then went on to Jalalabad.

name: Behmaru Heights
place: Behmaru (Bemaru) Heights, north of the Kabul cantonment, Kabul, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: Shelton's column on the heights was driven off, losing its gun, and the British never again left the cantonment in strength.
commanders B: Mohammad Akbar Khan (arrived 22 Nov); Abdullah Khan Achakzai; Mohammad Shah Khan
why it counts: The Afghan force that took the heights was drawn from the Kabul Pashtun chiefs and their followers under Akbar Khan, a Barakzai Pashtun (Kaye; Dalrymple).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013)
note: The decisive failure of the winter; Akbar Khan, Dost Mohammad's son, had reached Kabul the day before.

name: Charikar (1841)
how the result was decided: The garrison was overwhelmed and cut to pieces as it broke out; only a handful, including Haughton and Dr Grant, reached Kabul.
why it counts: The Kohistani Tajiks rose under their chief and destroyed the Gurkha garrison (Kaye; Dalrymple).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013)
note: Kohistan (north of Kabul) was Tajik country; names of the garrison officers are from Kaye and need checking.

date: 12 November 1841 to 7 April 1842 (Sale's brigade invested from mid-November; Akbar Khan joined in January)
name: Jalalabad (siege, 1841-1842)
how the result was decided: The garrison held through the winter and earthquake (19 Feb) and was relieved by Pollock's advance after Sale's successful sortie.
commanders B: Sir Robert Sale; Capt. George Broadfoot; Maj. Henry Havelock
why it counts: The besiegers were Pashtun tribal levies under Dost Mohammad's son Akbar Khan (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Entered with its 7 April sortie as a separate battle.

date: 2 November 1841; the cantonment was invested until the capitulation of 23 December and the evacuation of 6 January 1842
name: Kabul (uprising and siege of the cantonment, 1841)
side A (victor if decisive): Afghan insurgents of Kabul and Kohistan
allies B: Shah Shuja's government and his own troops in the Bala Hissar
how the result was decided: After repeated failures to break out, the British envoy was killed and the cantonment's garrison agreed to evacuate Kabul.
Iranian side: Afghan insurgents of Kabul and Kohistan v East India Company
factions A: Afghan insurgents of Kabul and Kohistan
commanders A: Abdullah Khan Achakzai; Mohammad Zaman Khan Barakzai (figurehead); Mohammad Akbar Khan (from 22 Nov)
commanders B: Maj.-Gen. William Elphinstone; Brig. John Shelton; Sir William Macnaghten (envoy, murdered 23 Dec); Shah Shuja ul-Mulk
why it counts: The rising was led by Pashtun chiefs (Achakzai, Barakzai, Ghilzai) with the Kabul and Kohistan Tajiks, while Shah Shuja, a Sadozai Pashtun, ruled in the Bala Hissar under British protection (Kaye; Dalrymple).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Treated as one entry covering the street fighting from Burnes's murder, the loss of the commissariat fort (9 Nov) and the investment of the cantonment; Behmaru Heights is entered separately.

date: late 1841 to about 6 March 1842 (the garrison capitulated; the exact start and end dates vary between accounts)
name: Ghazni (siege, 1841-1842)
how the result was decided: The garrison surrendered the citadel on terms, which were then broken, and was destroyed or enslaved.
commanders A: Shams ud-Din Khan (Barakzai, former governor of Ghazni)
why it counts: The investing force was Pashtun tribal and Barakzai levies under Shams ud-Din Khan (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Dates approximate; Palmer's surrender is usually put in the first week of March 1842.

name: Gandamak (1842)
how the result was decided: The remaining 20 officers and 45 men of the 44th Foot were killed or captured on the hill.
commanders A: Local Ghilzai chiefs; Mohammad Akbar Khan nearby
commanders B: Brig. Thomas Anquetil; Col. Thain (44th Foot)
why it counts: The last stand was against Ghilzai Pashtun tribesmen who first parleyed, then closed in (Kaye; Dalrymple).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Dr William Brydon reached Jalalabad on 13 January as the only man to arrive on horseback.

name: Jugdulluk (retreat from Kabul, 1842)
place: Jagdalak (Jugdulluk) Pass, Surobi District, Kabul Province, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: The remnant of the column was surrounded on the hill at Jugdulluk and broken up in the night; Elphinstone and Johnson became hostages.
why it counts: Ghilzai Pashtuns blocked the pass with barricades and held the hills above it (Kaye; Dalrymple).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013)
note: Entered separately from the September 1842 fighting at the same pass.

date: January to March 1842 (blockade and sorties; Safdar Jang's attack in early March)
name: Kandahar (siege, 1842)
side A (victor if decisive): Durrani and Ghilzai insurgents of the Kandahar region
how the result was decided: Nott repulsed the Afghan assaults and the blockade was lifted; he held Kandahar until he marched to Kabul in August.
Iranian side: Durrani and Ghilzai insurgents of the Kandahar region
commanders A: Prince Safdar Jang (Sadozai); Aktar Khan (Durrani chief of Zamindawar)
why it counts: The investing forces were Pashtun Durrani and Ghilzai levies, with Shah Shuja's son Safdar Jang as figurehead (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Wikipedia treats the whole of 1841-42 as a siege; the actions were mostly sorties against loose investment, and the names of the Afghan leaders are from Kaye and need checking.

name: Khurd Kabul Pass (retreat from Kabul, 1842)
place: Khurd Kabul Pass, east of Kabul, Afghanistan
side A (victor if decisive): Ghilzai tribesmen and Akbar Khan's followers
how the result was decided: Some 3,000 of the column were killed in the pass.
Iranian side: Ghilzai tribesmen and Akbar Khan's followers
why it counts: Pashtun Ghilzai tribesmen fired down on the column in the pass under the general direction of Akbar Khan, a Barakzai (Kaye; Dalrymple).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: First and bloodiest of the ambushes on the retreat.

date: 9-10 January 1842 (the 'Tunghee Tareekee', the Dark Defile, 10 January)
name: Tezin (retreat from Kabul, 1842)
place: Tezin valley and the Tunghee Tareekee defile, Kabul-Jalalabad road, Afghanistan
side A (victor if decisive): Ghilzai tribesmen and Akbar Khan's followers
how the result was decided: The column lost most of its remaining fighting men and followers in the defile.
Iranian side: Ghilzai tribesmen and Akbar Khan's followers
why it counts: Ghilzai Pashtuns ambushed the column in the defile (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: The exact location of the Tunghee Tareekee relative to Tezin is approximate.

name: Jalalabad (7 April 1842)
how the result was decided: The garrison marched out in three columns, routed Akbar Khan's camp and captured his guns.
commanders A: Sir Robert Sale; Capt. Henry Havelock
why it counts: Akbar Khan, a Barakzai Pashtun, led the besieging Afghan army (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); W. Dalrymple, Return of a King: The Battle for Afghanistan (2013); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: The sortie that ended the siege a week before Pollock's relief force arrived.

name: Khyber Pass (Pollock, 1842)
place: Khyber Pass (Ali Masjid), Khyber District, Pakistan
how the result was decided: Pollock turned the Afridi stockades by flank marches over the hills and cleared the pass, relieving Jalalabad on 16 April.
why it counts: The defenders of the pass were Afridi Pashtuns (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Distinct from the Second War's Ali Masjid (1878) and the Afridi capture of the Khyber forts (1897).

name: Kalat-i-Ghilzai (1842)
how the result was decided: The garrison beat off the assault with heavy Afghan loss, and was withdrawn on Nott's orders a few weeks later.
why it counts: The assault was made by Ghilzai Pashtun tribesmen (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: One of the few clear British successes of the dark months of spring 1842.

name: Ghoaine (1842)
place: Ghoaine (Goaine), on the road from Kandahar to Ghazni, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: Nott's brigades stormed the Afghan position and cleared the road to Ghazni.
why it counts: Shams ud-Din Khan, a Barakzai Pashtun, led some 10,000 Afghans against Nott (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: The site is placed only to the region between Mukur and Ghazni.

name: Ghazni (Nott's recapture, 1842)
how the result was decided: The Afghans were beaten outside the walls, and the British entered the town and demolished the citadel.
why it counts: The city was held by Afghan Pashtun levies under the same Shams ud-Din Khan (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Nott's column then marched to Kabul by Maidan, fighting a further action there on 14 September.

name: Istalif (1842)
side B: Kohistani Tajiks and Pashtuns of Istalif
how the result was decided: McCaskill stormed the town and it was sacked and burnt.
Iranian side: Kohistani Tajiks and Pashtuns of Istalif
why it counts: Istalif was a Tajik town of Kohistan and its defenders were under the Kohistani leader Mir Masjidi (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War' mentions the Tajik rising at Istalif).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Part of the reprisal for the destruction of the Charikar garrison; Mir Masjidi's presence at Istalif is from Kaye.

name: Jugdulluk (Pollock, 1842)
place: Jagdalak (Jugdulluk) Pass, Surobi District, Kabul Province, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: Pollock's flanking parties took the heights and the army forced the pass where the retreating column had perished.
why it counts: The pass was held by Ghilzai Pashtun tribesmen (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Date from memory of the despatches; needs checking.

name: Tezin (Pollock, 1842)
place: Tezin, between Jagdalak and Kabul, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: Pollock's army carried the heights and Akbar Khan fled north; Kabul was reoccupied on 15 September.
why it counts: Akbar Khan, a Barakzai Pashtun, made his last stand with some 16,000 Afghans, mostly Ghilzai levies (Kaye; Wikipedia 'First Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: J. W. Kaye, History of the War in Afghanistan (1851); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Akbar Khan's force is given as 15,000-16,000 in the sources.

name: Tiyari and Tkhuma (1843)
war: Bedir Khan's campaign against the Hakkari Assyrians
place: Tiyari and Tkhuma, Hakkari highlands, Turkey
how the result was decided: Bedir Khan broke Assyrian resistance and Mar Shimun fled to Mosul.
commanders A: Bedir Khan Beg; Nurullah Bey of Hakkari
commanders B: Shimun XVII Abraham (Mar Shimun) and the maliks
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedir_Khan_Beg; Eppel, A People Without a State (2016)
note: Nurullah Bey called Bedir Khan in after failing alone. It was a campaign of several assaults and massacres rather than a single battle, so the date and the point are approximate.

name: Hyderabad Residency (Outram's defence, 1843)
how the result was decided: Outram's guard of about 100 beat off repeated assaults for some hours, then withdrew with its guns to the river steamers and the Baloch burned the Residency.
commanders A: Major James Outram; Captain Conway (steamer Planet)
commanders B: Mir Nasir Khan Talpur and Baloch tribal chiefs
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Outram, Conquest of Scinde (1846), from memory; W. Napier, History of General Sir Charles Napier's Administration of Scinde (1851), from memory; Dalrymple/Lambrick on the conquest of Sindh, from memory
note: The attack by the Mirs' Baloch followers two days before Miani opened the fighting of the 1843 war. Numbers are from British accounts (about 8,000 attackers).

name: Miani
how the result was decided: Napier's disciplined sepoys broke the Baloch lines after hours of close fighting, and Hyderabad fell to him a few days later.
commanders B: Mir Nasir Khan Talpur; Mir Muhammad Khan Talpur; Mir Shahdad Khan Talpur
why it counts: The Talpur Amirs were Baloch by descent and their army was largely Baloch tribal levies (Wikipedia 'Talpur dynasty' and 'Battle of Miani'; Napier).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: C. J. Napier, The Conquest of Scinde (1845); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Miani (not fetched); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talpur_dynasty (not fetched; from memory)
note: Amir names are from memory.

name: Hyderabad (Dubba, 1843)
how the result was decided: Napier's brigade stormed the nullah position and Sher Muhammad fled, ending organised Baloch resistance.
commanders B: Mir Sher Muhammad Talpur of Mirpur; Hosh Muhammad Sidi (Siddi Sindhi general, killed)
why it counts: Sher Muhammad Talpur, the 'Lion of Mirpur', was a Baloch Talpur chief commanding a Baloch tribal army (Wikipedia 'Conquest of Sindh'; Napier).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: C. J. Napier, The Conquest of Scinde (1845); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Hyderabad_(1843) (not fetched); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talpur_dynasty (not fetched; from memory)
note: Included for the Baloch Talpur dynasty; the Sidi general Hosh Muhammad ('Hoshu') was a Siddi, not Baloch.

name: Shahdadpur (1843)
how the result was decided: Sher Muhammad's force was routed and he fled to the desert border, which ended organised Talpur resistance.
commanders A: Captain John Jacob (Scinde Horse), under Sir Charles Napier
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: W. Napier, Administration of Scinde (1851), from memory; not confirmed in any source I fetched (Wikipedia 'British conquest of Sindh' does not mention it)
note: Weak entry: date, commander and result are from memory and I could not fetch a source for the engagement. Sher Muhammad was the Talpur Mir of Mirpur Khas, a Baloch.

name: Trukki (Truckee, 1845)
war: Napier's campaign against the hill Baloch of the Sindh border (Jakrani, Dombki and Bugti)
place: Trukki (Truckee) fortress in the hills north of Jacobabad, on the Sindh-Kachhi border, Pakistan
side B: Jakrani, Dombki and Bugti Baloch tribes
how the result was decided: The tribes submitted by 19 March 1845 after Napier's columns invested the stronghold.
Iranian side: Jakrani, Dombki and Bugti Baloch tribes
commanders A: Major-General Sir Charles Napier; Major Beatson (blockade of the north entrance)
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://wiki.fibis.org/w/Truckee_Campaign (fetched); W. Napier, Administration of Scinde (1851), from memory
note: A frontier expedition against Baloch tribal strongholds; the amount of actual fighting at Trukki is not clear from the page I reached, so keep it as a minor entry.

date: 1847, before 4 July (the source gives no day)
name: Zeitun (Cizre, 1847)
how the result was decided: The Ottoman army of about 12,000 beat Bedir Khan's Kurds in the field and he withdrew to Evreh castle.
commanders A: Omer Pasha (Latas) per Wikipedia; Osman Pasha in other accounts
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedir_Khan_Beg; Jwaideh, The Kurdish National Movement (2006)
note: Yezdanser's defection decided the war. The name of the Ottoman field commander differs between accounts.

date: ended 4 July 1847 with Bedir Khan's surrender (start uncertain; Wikipedia says months)
name: Evreh Castle (siege, 1847)
how the result was decided: Bedir Khan surrendered the castle on 4 July 1847 and was exiled.
commanders A: Omer Pasha (Latas) per Wikipedia; Osman Pasha in other accounts
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedir_Khan_Beg; Jwaideh, The Kurdish National Movement (2006)
note: The end of the emirate of Bohtan. The length of the siege is uncertain and the coordinates are for Eruh.

name: Mayamey (1847)
how the result was decided: Salar's army was routed and fled to Joveyn.
commanders A: Muhammad Qoli Khan, Muhammad Ali Khan Maku'i, Ebrahim Khalil Khan
Iranian force: Four government regiments with 10 guns and Ebrahim Khalil Khan's 6,000, against Salar's 24,000-25,000 including 12,000 Khorasani cavalry, Turkmen and Kurdish (Shadlu) allies.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
strength A: 4 regiments and 10 guns, with about 6,000 men
borderline: no separate article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Revolt of Hasan Khan Salar
note: Salar, a Develu Qajar noble, rebelled in Khorasan from 1846.

name: Kal Yaquti (1848)
place: Kal Yaquti, a suburb of Mashhad, Iran
how the result was decided: Salar's 8,000 men were routed.
Iranian force: Government regiments of the Khorasan garrison against Salar's 8,000 Khorasani, Kurdish and Turkmen followers.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no separate article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Revolt of Hasan Khan Salar

name: Qarabaqa'ah (1848)
place: Qarabaqa'ah, about 5 farsangs from Mashhad, Iran
how the result was decided: Salar was defeated again and the Sarakhs Turkmen defected.
Iranian force: Government regiments against Salar's followers and Sarakhs Turkmen.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no separate article
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Revolt of Hasan Khan Salar

name: Mashhad (1848)
side A (victor if decisive): Hasan Khan Salar and the rising of Mashhad
side B: Qajar garrison under Hamzeh Mirza, with Yar Mohammad Khan of Herat
how the result was decided: After heavy fighting in the city Hamzeh Mirza and his Herati allies withdrew to Herat and Salar held Mashhad.
factions A: Hasan Khan Salar and the rising of Mashhad
factions B: Qajar garrison under Hamzeh Mirza, with Yar Mohammad Khan of Herat
Iranian force: The townsmen and ulema of Mashhad with Salar's 2,000 Turkmen, against the government garrison (Azerbaijan and Turkic regiments) and Yar Mohammad's Herati troops (2,000 or 19,000) with 4 guns.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: about 700 officials and soldiers in the rising; about 700 killed and 300 wounded in the later fighting
borderline: no separate article; a city rising and siege of the citadel
doubts and flags: Borderline: no separate article; a city rising and siege of the citadel.
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Revolt of Hasan Khan Salar
note: Herat under Yar Mohammad Khan Alakozai fought for the Qajar governor.

name: Fort Tabarsi
place: Shrine of Shaykh Tabarsi, near Babol (Afra), Iran
how the result was decided: Starved and reduced by attrition, the Babis surrendered under a promise of safety and were massacred.
Iranian force: Local Mazandarani forces and townsfolk, then imperial regiments (about 10,000 by the Babi account), against 540-600 Babis from 33 places (Isfahan, Boshruyeh, Miyami, Bahnemir), mostly clerics, tradesmen and merchants, with over a hundred local villagers.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)

why it counts: Qajars: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
losses A: 1,500 (infobox; 50-250 in the failed assault of 28 August)
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Second Herat War

why it counts: Qajars: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian

period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Anglo-Persian War

name: Najafgarh

how the result was decided: Nicholson's column crossed the flooded canal and routed the rebels, who lost their guns.
Iranian side: Rebel Bareilly and Nimach brigades from Delhi

sources: W. Dalrymple, The Last Mughal (2006)
note: Bakht Khan's presence in the field at Najafgarh is from memory of Dalrymple and needs checking.

commanders B: Khan Bahadur Khan (Rohilla, descendant of Hafiz Rahmat Khan)

sources: C. Hibbert, The Great Mutiny (1978); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khan_Bahadur_Khan (not fetched)

commanders B: Hamzeh Mirza Heshmat od-Dowleh, Mirza Mohammad Qavam al-Dawla
Iranian force: A large Qajar army of sarbaz regiments, Khorasani and Kurdish cavalry and artillery (commonly put at about 20,000; no figure in the pages read).

date: 1862 to 27 May 1863 (the start of the investment is not verified; Dost Mohammad died on 9 June 1863)

commanders A: Dost Mohammad Khan; Sher Ali Khan (son)

sources: T. Barfield, Afghanistan: A Cultural and Political History (2010); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dost_Mohammad_Khan (not fetched); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1863-1869)
note: Dost Mohammad's last conquest; he died of illness in the camp a fortnight later, which opened the civil war between his sons.

name: Ambela Pass

commanders A: Brig.-Gen. Sir Neville Chamberlain (wounded); Brig.-Gen. Sir John Garvock

sources: H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912); A. Swinson, North-West Frontier (1967); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambela_Campaign (not fetched)

name: Bajgah (1864)

period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1863-1869)
note: Sher Ali's first decisive victory over his half-brother's northern forces.

date: 10 May 1866 (the Wikipedia article on Abdur Rahman Khan gives '10 May'; the year is implied by the capture of Kabul in spring 1866)
name: Sheikhabad

Iranian side: Mohammad Afzal Khan's army v Sher Ali Khan's army

why it counts: Barakzai Pashtun princes led Afghan armies on both sides (Wikipedia 'Abdur Rahman Khan', fetched).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars

note: Site placed only to the region between Ghazni and Kabul.

The English account fetched never calls the defenders Tajik; the Tajik identity is inferred from the city's population and from Tajik historiography (not checked).

date: 27 Sept-2 Oct 1866 O.S. (storm on 2 Oct O.S. = 14 Oct 1866 N.S.)

period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Wikipedia 'Siege of Ura-Tyube' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Ura-Tyube (fetched; gives dates, commanders, casualties but does not mention Tajiks); Terentyev (1906); Becker (1968)
note: Ura-Tyube was a historic Tajik town of the Emirate of Bukhara and the Russian conquest of it is a standard episode of Tajik history, but the account fetched describes the defenders only as 'forces of Ura-Tyube' under Rustam Bek, not as Tajik. Included under the rule that townsmen count when the sources say they fought on the strength of the town's population;

name: Samarkand (siege, 1868)

Qualifies only under the townsmen rule. Irjar (1866), Jizzakh (1866) and Zerabulak (1868) were considered and left out: the Wikipedia accounts fetched call the Bukharan army simply 'Bukharan' and never mention Tajik fighters.

name: Black Mountain (1868)
place: Black Mountain (Tor Ghar), Hazara, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan

name: Peiwar Kotal

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986); H. B. Hanna, The Second Afghan War, 3 vols. (1899-1910)

name: Kabul Residency (siege, 1879)

place: Charasiab (Char Asiab), south of Kabul, Afghanistan

why it counts: The Afghan force was the Kabul regular regiments with Wardak, Logari and Ghilzai tribesmen (Robson; Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986); H. B. Hanna, The Second Afghan War, 3 vols. (1899-1910)
note: The way into Kabul; Roberts entered the city on 12 October.

name: Asmai Heights
how the result was decided: The Afghans took the Asmai Heights and drove the British back into Sherpur, which was invested.
commanders A: Brig.-Gen. Baker; Maj.-Gen. Sir Frederick Roberts
commanders B: Mohammad Jan Khan Wardak; Mullah Din Muhammad (Mushk-i-Alam)
why it counts: The Afghan army on the heights was the tribal host under Mohammad Jan Wardak (Robson; Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986); H. B. Hanna, The Second Afghan War, 3 vols. (1899-1910)
note: The Afghans held the heights from 14 to 22 December.

name: Chardeh Valley (1879)
place: Chardeh Valley, west of Kabul, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: Massy's cavalry was routed and lost four guns, and Roberts ordered the withdrawal of all outlying forces into the Sherpur cantonment.
commanders A: Brig.-Gen. Macpherson; Brig.-Gen. Baker; Brig.-Gen. Massy (cavalry)
commanders B: Mohammad Jan Khan Wardak; Mullah Din Muhammad (Mushk-i-Alam)
why it counts: The rising was led by Mohammad Jan Wardak and the Ghazni mullah Mushk-i-Alam, with Wardak, Logari, Ghilzai and Kohistani levies (Robson; Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986); H. B. Hanna, The Second Afghan War, 3 vols. (1899-1910)
note: Wikipedia lists neighbouring actions (Karez Mir, Takht-i-Shah, Shajui) which may overlap with this entry.

date: 15-23 December 1879 (the Afghan assault failed on the morning of 23 December)
name: Sherpur (siege, 1879)
how the result was decided: The Afghan assault on the cantonment was repulsed on 23 December and the besiegers dispersed.
commanders A: Mohammad Jan Khan Wardak; Mullah Din Muhammad (Mushk-i-Alam)
why it counts: Mohammad Jan Khan Wardak, a Wardak Pashtun, commanded the besiegers, a force of about 10,000 (Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War', fetched).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986); H. B. Hanna, The Second Afghan War, 3 vols. (1899-1910)
note: Roberts's decisive defence of Kabul; the Afghan numbers vary between 10,000 and 100,000 in different accounts.

date: autumn 1880 (the rebels held the town for some days before the Qajar army came from Tabriz)
name: Mahabad (1880)
allies A: Local Kurdish tribes loyal to the shah
how the result was decided: The rebels retreated from Mahabad when the Qajar force arrived, and the whole rising collapsed after eight weeks.
Iranian side: Qajar Iran v Kurdish rebels of Sheikh Ubeydullah
commanders A: Qajar commanders from Tabriz (not named in the source consulted)
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uprising_of_Sheikh_Ubeydullah; Jwaideh, The Kurdish National Movement (2006)
note: The Urmia siege of the same rising is already in the dataset. Whether a real fight took place at Mahabad is not clear from the source; the result is the town changing hands.

name: Ahmed Khel
place: Ahmed Khel, on the road from Ghazni to Kabul, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: Stewart's division beat off the ghazi charges and held the field; the tribal host dispersed.
commanders B: Mullah Din Muhammad (Mushk-i-Alam); Ghilzai and Hazara chiefs
why it counts: The attackers were some 15,000 Ghilzai and other Pashtun tribesmen with a Hazara following of the Ghazni mullah Mushk-i-Alam (Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War'; Hanna).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; H. B. Hanna, The Second Afghan War, 3 vols. (1899-1910); B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986)
note: The 'Ghazni 1880' of the span list is most probably this battle, fought in the Ghazni country; the battlefield is placed approximately.

name: Kandahar (siege, 1880)
how the result was decided: The garrison held until Roberts's relief force arrived on 31 August, and Ayub was routed the next day.
why it counts: Ayub Khan's Pashtun army invested the city after Maiwand (Wikipedia 'Mohammad Ayub Khan'; Robson).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986)
note: The Deh Khwaja sortie and the battle of 1 September are entered separately.

name: Maiwand
allies B: Levies of the Wali of Kandahar
how the result was decided: Burrows's brigade was routed and lost about half its strength, Afghan gunners and ghazis overrunning the line.
commanders A: Mohammad Ayub Khan; Mullah Mohammad Ghazi (ghazi leader)
why it counts: Ayub Khan, a Barakzai Pashtun prince of Herat, led an army of regulars and tens of thousands of ghazi tribesmen, while the Wali of Kandahar's Afghan levies were on the British side (Wikipedia 'Mohammad Ayub Khan'; Robson).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Ayub_Khan_(Afghanistan); B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986)
note: Ayub's Afghan victory; the Wali's levies on the British side mostly deserted before or during the fight.

name: Deh Khwaja
place: Deh Khwaja (Deh Khoja), near Kandahar, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: The sortie was driven back with heavy loss and Brooke was killed.
why it counts: The village was held by Ayub Khan's besieging Pashtun army (Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War', which lists the action as an Afghan victory).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986)
note: Date and Brooke's death are from memory of the siege narratives.

name: Kandahar (1 September 1880)
place: Kandahar (Baba Wali and Pir Paimal), Kandahar Province, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: Roberts stormed Ayub's camp and drove the Afghans from the field; Ayub fled to Herat and then to Persia.
why it counts: Ayub Khan, a Barakzai Pashtun, commanded the Afghan army (Wikipedia 'Battle of Kandahar (1880)'; Wikipedia 'Second Anglo-Afghan War', fetched).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Afghan_War; B. Robson, The Road to Kabul: The Second Afghan War 1878-1881 (1986)
note: The last battle of the war.

name: Urmia (siege, 1880)
how the result was decided: The Shia townspeople and garrison refused to surrender and the Kurds could not take the city.
commanders A: the Persian governor and garrison of Urmia (not named in the source)
Iranian force: The garrison and armed townspeople of Urmia, later relieved by Qajar forces from Tabriz.
why it counts: Qajars: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
strength B: part of a rising claimed at 80,000
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: en.wikipedia Uprising of Sheikh Ubeydullah
note: Kurdish rebels of Sheikh Ubeydullah (from Ottoman Hakkari). His columns took Mahabad and Maragheh and failed before Tabriz; the rising collapsed after about eight weeks.

date: July 1881 (Wikipedia 'Mohammad Ayub Khan' dates the reign in Kandahar from 20 July; the battle is said to coincide with the anniversary of 27 July 1880)
name: Maiwand (1881)
war: Ayub Khan's bid for the throne (1881)
how the result was decided: Ayub Khan won and took Kandahar, ruling it briefly in 1881.
Iranian side: Mohammad Ayub Khan's army v Abdur Rahman's governor of Kandahar
why it counts: Both armies were Afghan under Barakzai Pashtun leaders, Ayub against Abdur Rahman's governor (Wikipedia 'Mohammad Ayub Khan', fetched).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Ayub_Khan_(Afghanistan); M. Ewans, Afghanistan: A Short History of Its People and Politics (2002)
note: Details are thin and the Wikipedia article gives no date or numbers; it may be the same action some sources place at Karez-i-Atta.

date: 22 September 1881 (the end of Ayub's reign in Kandahar, per Wikipedia 'Mohammad Ayub Khan'; the battle is usually called Gundigan after a village near Kandahar)
name: Kandahar (Ayub Khan's defeat, 1881)
war: Ayub Khan's bid for the throne (1881)
how the result was decided: Ayub Khan was defeated outside Kandahar and fled to Persia, leaving Abdur Rahman master of the country.
Iranian side: Emirate of Afghanistan v Mohammad Ayub Khan's army
commanders A: Abdur Rahman Khan (advanced from Kabul with British support); Abdul Quddus Khan (field commander, from memory)
why it counts: Afghan Pashtun armies under Abdur Rahman and Ayub Khan, both Barakzai, fought on either side (Wikipedia 'Mohammad Ayub Khan', fetched; Ewans).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Ayub_Khan_(Afghanistan); M. Ewans, Afghanistan: A Short History of Its People and Politics (2002)
note: The battle name 'Gundigan', the date and Abdul Quddus's role are from memory and need checking.

name: Panjdeh (1885)
how the result was decided: Komarov's Russians routed the Afghans, took their guns and convoy and occupied Panjdeh.
commanders B: Naib Salar Ghaus ud-Din Khan (Yate's account) / Naib Salar Teimour Shah (Wikipedia infobox)
why it counts: The Afghan force was the regular army of the Herat border command, whose officers were Afghan (Pashtun and Herati) and whose men included Sariq Turkmen irregulars (Wikipedia 'Panjdeh incident', fetched; Yate).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panjdeh_incident; C. E. Yate, Northern Afghanistan (1888); T. Barfield, Afghanistan: A Cultural and Political History (2010)
note: The sources do not give the ethnic make-up of the Afghan troops, so the Pashtun share is unknown; the Afghan force is put at 600 to 4,700 in different accounts.

name: Ghaznigak
place: Ghaznigak, near Tashkurghan (Khulm), Samangan Province, Afghanistan
how the result was decided: Ishaq's army was beaten, many of his troops deserting, and he fled across the Oxus to Russian territory.
Iranian side: Emirate of Afghanistan v Mohammad Ishaq Khan's Turkestan army
commanders A: Ghulam Haidar Khan Charkhi; Abdur Rahman Khan (directing from Kabul)
why it counts: Abdur Rahman and his cousin Ishaq Khan were both Barakzai Pashtun, and the Amir's field commander Ghulam Haidar Charkhi was a Yusufzai Pashtun (Wikipedia 'Ghulam Haidar Khan Charkhi', fetched; Britannica 'Abdur Rahman Khan').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghulam_Haidar_Khan_Charkhi; Encyclopaedia Britannica 11th ed., 'Abdur Rahman Khan'; T. Barfield, Afghanistan: A Cultural and Political History (2010)
note: Date and place from memory (the Wikipedia article on Charkhi, fetched, dates the Turkestan revolt to 1892 and does not name Ghaznigak); the Turkestan army was mixed Pashtun, Uzbek and Tajik.

date: October to November 1888 (after the murder of Major Battye and Captain Urmston in June)
name: Black Mountain (1888)
place: Black Mountain (Tor Ghar), Hazara, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
how the result was decided: The expeditionary force marched through the clans' country, burned villages and the tribes submitted.
commanders B: Hasanzai and Akazai maliks (names not verified)
why it counts: The opponents were the Yusufzai Pashtun clans of the Black Mountain (Nevill; Wikipedia 'Black Mountain Expedition').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912)
note: Details from memory of Nevill; the 1868 expedition is entered separately.

name: Uruzgan (first battle, 1892)
how the result was decided: Zabardast Khan's force was destroyed and Faiz Mohammad Khan surrendered after a month-long siege, the Hazaras then massacring the fort's garrison.
Iranian side: Emirate of Afghanistan v Hazara rebels of Uruzgan
commanders A: Brig. Zabardast Khan; Faiz Mohammad Khan (brother)
why it counts: Abdur Rahman's army was a Pashtun-led Afghan force fighting Persian-speaking Hazara rebels (Wikipedia 'First Battle of Uruzgan', fetched; both sides Iranian under the span ruling on Hazaras).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Battle_of_Uruzgan; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazara_Uprisings
note: The Hazaras are counted here as Persian-speakers; the only source consulted is Wikipedia, which is thin.

date: 1893 (later in the year; exact date not given in Wikipedia 'Battle of Uruzgan')
name: Uruzgan (1893)
place: Uruzgan (now Uruzgan and Daikundi Provinces), Afghanistan
how the result was decided: The three Hazara leaders were captured and the rising ended, followed by massacre and displacement of the Hazaras.
Iranian side: Emirate of Afghanistan v Hazara rebels
commanders A: Abdur Rahman Khan; Ghulam Haidar Khan Charkhi; Abdul Quddus Khan
commanders B: Hussain Khan Hazara; Rasul Khan; Tajei Khan
why it counts: The Emirate's army under Pashtun commanders crushed Persian-speaking Hazara rebels in the final battle of the war (Wikipedia 'Battle of Uruzgan', fetched).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Uruzgan; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazara_Uprisings
note: Wikipedia's figure of 100,000 troops for the Emirate is unsourced; the final action took place in what is now Daikundi.

date: August to September 1894 (the Ottoman assault on the Sasun mountains)
name: Sasun (1894)
how the result was decided: The Fourth Army with the Kurdish tribal horse overran the Armenian positions on Mount Andok and the villages were sacked.
commanders B: Armenian village leaders and Hunchak organisers
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: Klein, The Margins of Empire: Kurdish Militias in the Ottoman Tribal Zone (2011); Kieser; Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People from Ancient to Modern Times vol. 2 (1997)
note: The sources single out the Kurdish tribes as active partners of the army; how formally the Hamidiye regiments were involved in 1894 is debated, and the numbers on each side are not firm.

name: Wana (1894)
how the result was decided: The attack was repulsed with heavy tribal losses, though the camp suffered about 45 killed, and a punitive expedition followed.
commanders A: Escort commander of the Waziristan Delimitation Commission (name not verified)
commanders B: Mullah Powindah (from memory); Wazir and Mahsud maliks
why it counts: The night attackers were Waziri and Mahsud Pashtuns (Nevill; Wikipedia 'Waziristan campaign (1894-1895)').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912); A. Swinson, North-West Frontier (1967)
note: Casualties, the commander's name and Mullah Powindah's role are from memory.

name: Malakand Pass (1895)
place: Malakand Pass, Malakand District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
side B: Pashtun tribes of Swat, Bajaur and Jandol
how the result was decided: Low's brigades stormed the heights and forced the pass in a day, and the force went on to the Panjkora.
Iranian side: Pashtun tribes of Swat, Bajaur and Jandol
commanders B: Umra Khan of Jandol (directing the coalition; not named on the field)
why it counts: The pass was held by some 12,000 Pashtun tribesmen of the Umra Khan coalition (Robertson, Chitral: The Story of a Minor Siege; Wikipedia 'Chitral Expedition').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: G. S. Robertson, Chitral: The Story of a Minor Siege (1898); H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912)
note: Numbers and the tribal composition are from memory of Robertson and Nevill.

name: Maizar
place: Maizar, Tochi Valley, North Waziristan, Pakistan
how the result was decided: The escort was overwhelmed during a halt, losing its commander and several officers, and fell back to Datta Khel.
commanders B: Mr. Gee (political officer); Lt.-Col. Bunny (escort commander, killed)
why it counts: The attackers were Madda Khel Wazirs, a Pashtun (Darwesh Khel) clan (Nevill).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912); A. Swinson, North-West Frontier (1967)
note: The opening of the 1897 frontier rising in Waziristan; the details of the officers killed are from memory.

name: Chakdara (siege, 1897)
war: Frontier uprising of 1897 (Malakand, Mohmand and Tirah campaigns)
place: Chakdara Fort, Lower Dir District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
side A (victor if decisive): Pashtun tribes of Swat and Dir
how the result was decided: The garrison held the fort and the lashkar was cut up by the relieving cavalry on 2 August.
Iranian side: Pashtun tribes of Swat and Dir
commanders B: Chakdara garrison (45th Sikhs), relieved by Sir Bindon Blood's cavalry on 2 Aug
why it counts: Chakdara was besieged by the same Swat Pashtun lashkar (Churchill; Wikipedia 'Siege of Chakdara').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: W. S. Churchill, The Story of the Malakand Field Force (1898); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Chakdara
note: The Guides cavalry charge of 2 August broke the besiegers.

name: Malakand (siege, 1897)
war: Frontier uprising of 1897 (Malakand, Mohmand and Tirah campaigns)
place: Malakand Pass, Malakand District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
side A (victor if decisive): Pashtun tribes of Swat and Dir
how the result was decided: The garrison held the pass through six nights of attack and the lashkar withdrew when the relief columns arrived.
Iranian side: Pashtun tribes of Swat and Dir
commanders B: Brig.-Gen. William Meiklejohn; Brig.-Gen. Sir Bindon Blood (arrived 1 Aug)
why it counts: The besiegers were Pashtun Yusufzai and other Swat tribesmen led by Mullah Sadullah, a Pashtun of Swat (Churchill; Wikipedia 'Siege of Malakand').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: W. S. Churchill, The Story of the Malakand Field Force (1898); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Malakand
note: Churchill served in the relieving Malakand Field Force and wrote the standard account.

name: Khyber forts (Afridi attack, 1897)
war: Frontier uprising of 1897 (Malakand, Mohmand and Tirah campaigns)
place: Khyber Pass (Landi Kotal, Fort Maude, Ali Masjid), Khyber District, Pakistan
side B: British posts of the Khyber Rifles
how the result was decided: The Afridis occupied the Khyber forts, which were re-taken without opposition only in December.
Iranian side: Afridi lashkar v British posts of the Khyber Rifles
factions B: British posts of the Khyber Rifles
commanders A: Mullah Sayyid Akbar (Aka Khel); Afridi maliks (names not verified)
commanders B: British officers of the Khyber Rifles (names not verified)
why it counts: The lashkar was Afridi tribesmen and the Khyber Rifles garrisons, who were themselves Afridi levies, mostly gave up their posts (Nevill; Wikipedia 'Tirah campaign').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirah_campaign
note: A named Pashtun unit (the Afridi Khyber Rifles) on the British side as well as the Afridi lashkar; the day-by-day dates are from memory.

name: Shabqadar (1897)
war: Frontier uprising of 1897 (Malakand, Mohmand and Tirah campaigns)
place: Shabqadar Fort, Charsadda District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
how the result was decided: A cavalry charge and the relief column drove off the Mohmands, who lost heavily, and the fort held.
why it counts: The lashkar was Mohmand Pashtun tribesmen raised by the Hadda Mullah (Churchill; Nevill).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: W. S. Churchill, The Story of the Malakand Field Force (1898); H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912)
note: The Mohmand Field Force's later punitive operations (Landakai and others) are not entered.

date: September to October 1897 (Agrah, Shahi Tangi and Bilot, mid to late September)
name: Mamund Valley (1897)
war: Frontier uprising of 1897 (Malakand, Mohmand and Tirah campaigns)
place: Mamund Valley, Bajaur Agency, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
how the result was decided: Jeffreys's brigades burned the valley's villages against stubborn resistance and the Mamunds submitted in October.
commanders A: Brig.-Gen. Edmond Jeffreys; Maj.-Gen. Sir Bindon Blood
why it counts: The Mamunds are a Pashtun (Tarkani) tribe of Bajaur (Churchill, who served in the campaign).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: W. S. Churchill, The Story of the Malakand Field Force (1898); H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912)
note: Treated as one entry for the valley campaign; Churchill's account describes the fights at Agrah and Bilot.

name: Saragarhi
war: Frontier uprising of 1897 (Malakand, Mohmand and Tirah campaigns): Samana
place: Saragarhi, Samana Ridge, Kohat District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
how the result was decided: The tribesmen overran the post after hours of fighting and killed all 21 defenders.
why it counts: The attackers were Orakzai and Afridi Pashtun tribesmen under Gul Badshah (Wikipedia 'Tirah campaign', fetched; Wikipedia 'Battle of Saragarhi').
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirah_campaign; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Saragarhi
note: Lockhart and Gulistan forts were also attacked on the same day; Gulistan is entered separately.

date: 18 and 20 October 1897 (taken and given up on the 18th, stormed on the 20th)
name: Dargai Heights
place: Dargai Heights, near Shinawari, Kohat-Orakzai border, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
how the result was decided: The Gordon Highlanders, with the 3rd Sikhs and Derbyshires, stormed the heights on 20 October at a cost of 199 killed and wounded.
commanders A: Gen. Sir William Lockhart; Maj.-Gen. Yeatman-Biggs; Brig.-Gen. Kempster
commanders B: Mullah Sayyid Akbar (Aka Khel Afridi); Orakzai and Afridi maliks
why it counts: The Dargai Heights were held by about 12,000 Afridi and Orakzai Pashtun tribesmen (Wikipedia 'Tirah campaign', fetched; Nevill).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirah_campaign; H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912); A. Swinson, North-West Frontier (1967)
note: Piper Findlater's piping under fire made the second assault famous; the Afridi leader's name is from memory and the site is placed to the region.

date: 9 and 11 November 1897 (Westmacott's first attack, Gaselee's second)
name: Saran Sar
place: Saran Sar, Tirah, Khyber Agency, Pakistan
how the result was decided: The position was taken on both occasions, but the first retirement was hard-pressed with 64 British casualties.
commanders A: Brig.-Gen. Richard Westmacott; Brig.-Gen. Alfred Gaselee
commanders B: Afridi and Orakzai maliks (names not verified)
why it counts: The Saran Sar ridge was held by Afridi Pashtun tribesmen (Wikipedia 'Tirah campaign', fetched).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirah_campaign
note: Wikipedia's table gives the first attack as 'before 11 Nov'; 9 November is from memory.

name: Tseri Kandao
place: Tseri Kandao Pass and the Waran Valley, Tirah, Khyber Agency, Pakistan
how the result was decided: Kempster's brigade destroyed the Waran villages but the rearguard was heavily engaged on the way back, with 72 casualties.
why it counts: The opposition on the Waran expedition was Afridi Pashtun tribesmen (Wikipedia 'Tirah campaign', fetched).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirah_campaign
note: A punitive raid on the Waran valley.

name: Bara Valley (1897)
how the result was decided: The Afridis inflicted heavy casualties on the retiring columns in four days of snow and ice, but the columns reached the Peshawar column and the Khyber forts on 14 December.
commanders A: Gen. Sir William Lockhart; Maj.-Gen. Yeatman-Biggs
why it counts: The tribesmen who harassed the withdrawal through the Bara Valley were Afridi Pashtuns (Wikipedia 'Tirah campaign', fetched).
period: Nader Shah, the Durranis and the Qajars
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirah_campaign; H. D. Nevill, Campaigns on the North-West Frontier (1912)
note: Kuki Khel and other Afridi clans; the Afridis later paid fines and gave up rifles, so the campaign ended in a British victory overall.

name: Bazar Valley campaign (Zakka Khel expedition)
place: Bazar Valley, Khyber Agency (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan)
how the result was decided: Willcocks's columns swept the Bazar Valley, destroyed towers and held the valley until the Zakka Khel submitted and paid a fine.
commanders A: Zakka Khel maliks and mullahs (names not recorded here)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bazar_Valley_campaign (title seen in search; not fetched)
note: Short expedition against the Zakka Khel section of the Afridis after raids on Peshawar; the Afridi were Pashtun tribesmen and so the lashkar qualifies.

name: Mohmand expedition of 1908
place: Mohmand hills near Matta and the Karapa pass, Mohmand Agency (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan)
how the result was decided: The Mohmand Field Force pushed into the Mohmand hills, defeated the lashkar and the tribes submitted.
commanders A: Mullah Najmuddin (the Hadda Mullah); Mohmand chiefs
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohmand_Expedition_of_1908 (title seen in search; not fetched)
note: Operations against Mohmand tribesmen stirred up by the Hadda Mullah; dates and commander roles are from memory and should be checked.

name: Bombardment of the Majlis
place: Baharestan (the Majlis building and the Sepahsalar mosque), Tehran, Iran
how the result was decided: The Cossacks shelled and took the Majlis the same day; its defenders were killed, captured or dispersed.
commanders A: Colonel Vladimir Liakhov (Persian Cossack Brigade), for Mohammad Ali Shah
commanders B: volunteers of the Tehran anjomans (no overall commander named; the speaker Esmail Momtaz od-Dowleh absent)
Iranian force: Royalists: about 800 men of the Persian Cossack Brigade under Russian officers, with artillery; constitutionalists: about 100 armed volunteers of the Tehran anjomans.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses A: not given in the sources used

war: First World War: Persian campaign (Dunsterforce and the Jangalis)
