how the result was decided: Bicherakhov's Cossacks forced the Manjil bridge and the Jangalis withdrew; the column reached Bandar Anzali a few days later.
commanders A: General Lazar Bicherakhov, with Dunsterforce elements
commanders B: Mirza Kuchik Khan (Jangalis), with German and Austrian advisers
Iranian force: The Jangali fighters of Gilan (Gilaki peasants and townsmen) with a few German, Austrian and Ottoman advisers.
why it counts: Iranian risings: an Iranian-led state
strength A: about 1,200 Cossacks with British armoured cars and a squadron of the 14th Hussars (not given in the Wikipedia article)
borderline: a rising, not a state (the Jangali movement fighting foreign troops)
doubts and flags: Borderline: a rising, not a state (the Jangali movement fighting foreign troops).
sources: en.wikipedia Dunsterforce; Dunsterville, The Adventures of Dunsterforce
note: Bicherakhov's detachment was a remnant of the Russian Caucasus Army in British pay. The British strength figures are from Dunsterville's account, not the Wikipedia article.

date: 20 July 1918 (25 July in the Wikipedia Dunsterforce article)
name: Rasht (1918)
war: First World War: Persian campaign (Dunsterforce and the Jangalis)
how the result was decided: The Jangali attack on the British garrison was repulsed after street fighting and the attackers withdrew.
commanders A: the British garrison commander at Rasht (not named in the sources used)
Iranian force: About 2,500 Jangali fighters of Gilan, with German and Austrian advisers.
why it counts: Iranian risings: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a rising, not a state (the Jangali movement fighting foreign troops)
doubts and flags: Borderline: a rising, not a state (the Jangali movement fighting foreign troops).
sources: en.wikipedia Dunsterforce; Moberly, Operations in Persia
note: Kuchik Khan made an agreement with the British in August 1918.

name: Dakka (1919)
how the result was decided: The British occupied Dakka on 13 May, repulsed an Afghan assault, counterattacked and secured the area by 17 May when the Afghans withdrew (Wikipedia).
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Dakka lay just inside Afghanistan; the Afghan army and its tribal levies fought for the border village.

name: First Battle of Bagh (1919)
place: Bagh, western Khyber Pass (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan; Afghan border)
how the result was decided: Crocker split his brigade, could not concentrate it and the British attack failed (Wikipedia).
commanders A: Salih Muhammad Khan (Afghan commander on the Khyber front; medium confidence)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Afghan irregulars had seized Bagh on 3 May; the first British counterattack failed and was repeated on 11 May.

name: Second Battle of Bagh (1919)
place: Bagh and Lower Khyber (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan)
how the result was decided: Fowler's force routed the Afghans, who lost about 100 killed and 300 wounded against 8 killed and 31 wounded (Wikipedia).
commanders A: Salih Muhammad Khan (Afghan commander on the Khyber front; medium confidence)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: The British victory that opened the Khyber to Dakka.

name: Spin Boldak (1919)
how the result was decided: The British took the fortress by escalade and so seized the initiative in the south (Wikipedia).
commanders A: Afghan garrison commander not named in the source used
commanders B: Maj.-Gen. R. Wapshare (Baluchistan Force; medium confidence)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: The only southern action of the war, on the Quetta-Kandahar road.

name: Thal (siege, 1919)
how the result was decided: Afghan assaults and bombardment were repelled and Dyer's column relieved the garrison on 1 June (Wikipedia).
commanders A: Nadir Khan (Afghan commander in the south-east)
commanders B: Brig.-Gen. Alexander Eustace (garrison); Brig.-Gen. Reginald Dyer (relief)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Nadir Khan, later King, besieged the Kurram frontier post with some fourteen battalions in the area.

name: Bazyan Pass (1919)
side A (victor if decisive): Kurdish rebels of Sheikh Mahmud Barzanji
how the result was decided: The British forced the pass against about 500 Kurds; Mahmud was wounded and captured and the Kurdish state fell.
Iranian side: Kurdish rebels of Sheikh Mahmud Barzanji
commanders B: British column of two brigades (commander not confirmed in the source consulted)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmud_Barzanji_revolts; Jwaideh, The Kurdish National Movement (2006); Eppel (2016)
note: Mahmud had seized Sulaymaniyah on 20 May 1919; the British occupied Halabja on 28 June to end the revolt. Wikipedia's other named actions of the revolt (ambushes beyond Chamchamal) have no dates.

name: Yusef Khel (1919)
place: Yusef Khel, near Thal (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan)
how the result was decided: Dyer's troops seized the Afghan camp on 3 June as the armistice took effect (Wikipedia).
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Anglo-Afghan_War
note: Pursuit action after the relief of Thal; place and date approximate.

date: January 1920 (an eight-day battle per Wikipedia; some accounts start in late December 1919)
name: Ahnai Tangi (1920)
place: Ahnai Tangi defile on the Tank Zam, South Waziristan (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan)
how the result was decided: The 2nd/5th Gurkhas held their position, the 2nd/76th Punjabis fought through to them and the Mahsuds took heavy casualties (Wikipedia).
commanders A: Mahsud maliks and mullahs (leaders not verified)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waziristan_campaign_(1919–1920)
note: The hardest fight of the Waziristan campaign, fought after the Mahsuds rose in 1919; the exact start date is uncertain.

name: Shekar Yazi
place: Shekar Yazi plain, near Salmas, Iran
how the result was decided: Amar Khan's cavalry routed the government force and killed its commander Amir Arshad, and the Iranian force dispersed.
commanders A: Simko Shikak, Amar Khan Shikak, Fars Agha, Mahmud Agha
commanders B: Amir Arshad (killed), Fathollah Khan Akbar, Major Malekzadeh, Hasan Arfa, a Swedish gendarmerie officer
Iranian force: About 1,500 gendarmes and 3,000 Azerbaijani irregulars, including the Haji-Alilu tribe of Amir Arshad.
why it counts: Qajars: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
strength A: about 200 Zibari horse in the decisive charge (Simko's whole force not given)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Shekar Yazi; Simko Shikak revolt (1918-1922)
note: The opponent is Simko's Shikak Kurds (with Zibari Kurds from across the frontier).

name: Java (1920)
side A (victor if decisive): Ossetian insurgents of the Roki and Java districts; Bolshevik detachment from Vladikavkaz
how the result was decided: The source says a Bolshevik force from Vladikavkaz helped local rebels attack a Georgian force in the Java district but does not give the outcome; by 7 June the rebels held Tskhinvali.
Iranian side: Ossetian insurgents of the Roki and Java districts & Bolshevik detachment from Vladikavkaz
commanders A: Ossetian Revkom (Ruten and Georgy Gagloev, Nikolai Gadiev, Vladimir Abaev; role in this action not stated)
commanders B: Georgian commanders not named (Valiko Jugheli led the later counter-offensive)
doubts and flags: The sources consulted do not give the result, so the battle is listed but not scored.
sources: Wikipedia 'Georgian-Ossetian conflict (1918-1920)' (fetched: 8 May 1920 declaration of a Soviet republic in the Roki area and attack on a Georgian force in the Java district)
note: The Ossetian rebels were Alans (Ossetians) assisted by a Bolshevik detachment; the fighting at Java is sketched in the source without detail.

date: 7-8 June 1920 (Ossetian Revkom takes Tskhinvali); Georgian counter-offensive from 12 June, retaking the town
name: Tskhinvali (June 1920)
place: Tskhinvali and the Liakhvi valley, South Ossetia (Georgia)
side A (victor if decisive): Ossetian insurgents with Bolshevik volunteers from North Ossetia
how the result was decided: Jugheli's People's Guard won a series of hard-fought battles from 12 June and recaptured Tskhinvali; the Revkom fled to North Ossetia.
Iranian side: Ossetian insurgents with Bolshevik volunteers from North Ossetia
commanders A: Ruten Gagloev, Georgy Gagloev, Vladimir Abaev, Nikolai Gadiev (Revkom leaders)
sources: Wikipedia 'Georgian-Ossetian conflict (1918-1920)' (fetched: Ossetian sources give 4,812-5,279 Ossetian dead in the 1920 repression and flight)
note: Largest of the three risings; the Ossetian side was an all-Ossetian insurgent force. The individual battles of the Georgian counter-offensive are not itemized in the source, so they are grouped here.

name: Tabriz (1920)
how the result was decided: The Cossacks stormed the uprising's headquarters within a few hours, and Khiabani was killed the next day.
commanders A: Brigadier Hashemi (Cossack Brigade), for Mehdi Qoli Hedayat
Iranian force: The Tabriz detachment of the Persian Cossack Brigade with some gendarmes, against Khiabani's lightly armed Democrat followers.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a short assault on the uprising's headquarters
doubts and flags: Borderline: a short assault on the uprising's headquarters.
sources: en.wikipedia Mohammad Khiabani's uprising
note: Khiabani's movement was a Democrat (not separatist) uprising; treated as civil.

date: 1921 (early 1921 in the battle article; September 1921 in the revolt article)
name: Miandoab
how the result was decided: Simko's fighters repelled the attack and forced the government troops to retreat, leaving Miandoab in Kurdish hands.
commanders A: Simko Shikak, Amar Khan Shikak, Sayyid Taha
commanders B: a detachment under Hasan Arfa (the battle article also lists Fathollah Khan, Hasan Moqaddam and Habibollah Sheibani)
Iranian force: Government troops (gendarmes and Cossack detachments; units not named in the sources used).
why it counts: Qajars: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
losses B: 200+ killed and 150 captured (most executed); 'half the army' per the revolt article
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Miandoab; Simko Shikak revolt (1918-1922)
note: The two Wikipedia articles disagree on the date; Reza Khan was minister of war from April 1921, which fits the later date better.

date: 6 March to 17 June 1921 (first clash in February)
name: Koçgiri (1921)
place: Koçgiri, Zara and Imranli districts, Sivas, Turkey
how the result was decided: The Central Army crushed the revolt: about 500 rebels killed, 32 leaders captured; the Turkish 6th Cavalry Regiment lost its commander.
commanders B: Alisan Bey; Alisher Efendi; Nuri Dersimi; Paso Misto
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ko%C3%A7giri_rebellion; van Bruinessen, Agha, Shaikh and State (1992)
note: A campaign rather than a single battle (the first clash in February 1921 went to the Kurds), so the point is the district, not a field.

name: Tasuj (1921)
place: Tasuj, north of Lake Urmia, Iran
how the result was decided: Simko defeated the government army north of Lake Urmia.
Iranian force: Government troops of the Azerbaijan command (gendarmes, Cossack detachments and Azerbaijani irregulars); units not named in the source used.
why it counts: Qajars: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
borderline: known only from a line in the revolt article
doubts and flags: Borderline: known only from a line in the revolt article.
sources: en.wikipedia Simko Shikak revolt (1918-1922)

name: Jafarabad (1921)
war: Revolt of Colonel Mohammad Taqi Khan Pesyan (Khorasan, 1921)
how the result was decided: Pesyan's gendarmes were defeated and he was killed on the field; his revolt collapsed.
factions A: Government (Qavam's cabinet) with Khorasani Kurdish levies
Iranian force: Kurmanji Kurdish tribal levies of Quchan raised by the government, against a detachment of Pesyan's Khorasan gendarmerie.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a small fight, remembered for Pesyan's death
doubts and flags: Borderline: a small fight, remembered for Pesyan's death.
sources: en.wikipedia Simko Shikak revolt (1918-1922) (note on Pesyan); Persian Cossack Brigade (infobox: suppression of Pessian's revolt)
note: The Kurds fought for the government here, not as rebels, so the battle is civil (a gendarmerie revolt).

name: Sawcubilax (1921)
how the result was decided: The Kurds broke the gendarmes' line on 7 October and Malekzadeh surrendered his headquarters the next day.
commanders A: Simko Shikak, Amar Khan Shikak, Sayyid Taha, Hamza Agha (Mamash)
commanders B: Major Malekzadeh (captured), Captain Mohammad Taqi Khan Alp (captured)
Iranian force: Major Malekzadeh's detachment of about 550 gendarmes with irregulars (550-1,500 in all), with one old gun and four machine guns.
why it counts: Qajars: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
losses B: over 700 killed, most of them shot after surrendering
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Sawcubilax; Simko Shikak revolt (1918-1922)
note: Also called the battle of Mahabad. Simko had entered Urmia on 4 October.

name: Sawcubilax (1922)
how the result was decided: Simko's forces defeated the government column and killed its commander Khalo Qurban.
Iranian force: Khalo Qurban's irregulars (former Jangali Kurdish fighters taken into Reza Khan's service).
why it counts: Qajars: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
losses B: about 200 irregulars killed with Khalo Qurban
sources: en.wikipedia Simko Shikak revolt (1918-1922)
note: Sawj Bulagh changed hands several times before the government retook it in August 1922.

name: Tabriz (1922)
how the result was decided: Fresh government troops retook Tabriz and dispersed the mutinous gendarmes, and Lahuti fled to Baku.
commanders A: fresh government forces sent to Tabriz (Mahmud Khan Puladin's troops had been beaten in the first fighting)
Iranian force: Cossack and other government units against the Tabriz gendarmerie battalion that had mutinied under Lahuti.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: poorly documented in the sources used; the scale of the fighting is uncertain
doubts and flags: Borderline: poorly documented in the sources used; the scale of the fighting is uncertain.
sources: en.wikipedia Abolqasem Lahouti; Cronin, The Army and the Creation of the Pahlavi State in Iran
note: The Wikipedia biography wrongly links Lahuti's rising with Khiabani (killed 1920); it says his men first beat Mahmud Khan Puladin's troops before fresh forces disbanded them. The usual date is February 1922.

name: Bakhtiari ambush of 1922
war: Reza Khan's tribal campaigns (Sheikh Khaz'al and the Bakhtiari)
place: Bakhtiari mountains on the route from Isfahan to Khuzestan, Iran
how the result was decided: The Bakhtiari destroyed the column; only a handful of soldiers escaped.
commanders A: Bakhtiari chiefs (not named in the source used)
Iranian force: Bakhtiari tribesmen, against a government column of 274 soldiers (12 officers).
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: no conventional name in the source used (known in Persian accounts by the valley where it happened)
doubts and flags: Borderline: no conventional name in the source used (known in Persian accounts by the valley where it happened).
sources: en.wikipedia Sheikh Khazal rebellion
note: The Bakhtiari believed the column was coming to occupy their land; it was sent to pressure Sheikh Khaz'al.

name: Sari Taj
place: Salmas region, near Chehriq (Chari castle), Iran
how the result was decided: Simko's forces were defeated and the Iranian army occupied Chari castle; Simko fled to Turkey with about 1,000 horsemen.
commanders A: commanders of Reza Khan's army in Azerbaijan (not named in the source used)
Iranian force: About 10,000 soldiers of Reza Khan's new army (the merged Cossack and gendarmerie units) with tribal levies.
why it counts: Qajars: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
sources: en.wikipedia Simko Shikak revolt (1918-1922)
note: Persian accounts call the decisive battle of 1922 the battle of Shakaryazi (not the Shekar Yazi battle of January 1920, which Simko won). The site and day need checking.

name: Boroujerd (1923)
how the result was decided: The army took Boroujerd after intense fighting.
commanders B: Lur tribal chiefs (not named in the source used)
Iranian force: Amir-Ahmadi's western division of the new army against Lur tribesmen.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: a tribal revolt of Lurs (an Iranian people not counted as separatists in this set), treated as civil
doubts and flags: Borderline: a tribal revolt of Lurs (an Iranian people not counted as separatists in this set), treated as civil.
sources: en.wikipedia Luri tribal insurgency in Pahlavi Iran

name: Gardez (1924)
how the result was decided: The government force under Muhammad Wali Khan beat the rebels, who lost about 60 against 7 government killed and 27 wounded.
Iranian side: Khost rebels v Royal Afghan army
commanders A: Mullah Abd Allah (Mullah-i Lang); Abd al-Karim
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khost_rebellion_(1924–1925)
note: First open battle of the rebellion after the Altimur Pass ambush of 22 April.

name: Khorramabad (1924)
how the result was decided: After the Lurs had beaten Colonel Fuladi's force and entered the town, Amir-Ahmadi's army retook Khorramabad and the Lur coalition broke up.
factions B: Lur tribes (Romani, Chegini, Beyranvand, Baharvand, Papi, Judaki)
commanders B: Lur tribal chiefs (not named in the source used)
Iranian force: Government troops of the western division, with aircraft in the June campaign, against a coalition of Lur tribes.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: two phases (a Lur success, then the government recapture) merged into one entry; a tribal revolt of Lurs treated as civil
doubts and flags: Borderline: two phases (a Lur success, then the government recapture) merged into one entry; a tribal revolt of Lurs treated as civil.
sources: en.wikipedia Luri tribal insurgency in Pahlavi Iran
note: The first phase (the Lur defeat of Fuladi and capture of the town) was a Lur victory.

name: Matun (siege, 1924)
how the result was decided: The siege was lifted on 29 May when the rebels withdrew, which the source attributes to bribes from Kabul.
Iranian side: Khost rebels v Afghan government garrison
commanders B: Garrison commander (not named in the source used)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khost_rebellion_(1924–1925)
note: The rebels' withdrawal was bought rather than forced, so the result rests on the siege being raised.

name: Sulaymaniyah (1924)
side B: Kurdish rebels of Sheikh Mahmud Barzanji
how the result was decided: The Assyrian Levies captured Sulaymaniyah and Mahmud's Kurdistan fell.
Iranian side: Kurdish rebels of Sheikh Mahmud Barzanji
commanders A: British-officered Assyrian Levies (commander not named in the source)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmud_Barzanji_revolts; Jwaideh (2006); Eppel (2016)
note: How much fighting there was is unclear; Mahmud had already been driven from the plain by air attack. The 1922-23 phase has no named battle in the sources I checked.

name: Bedak (1924)
how the result was decided: The government force was annihilated, its commander Abdul Hamid was killed, its guns were lost and the pass fell to the rebels.
Iranian side: Khost rebels v Royal Afghan army
commanders A: Mullah Abd Allah (Mullah-i Lang); Abd al-Karim
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khost_rebellion_(1924–1925)
note: The rebels' greatest victory; it opened the road to Kabul and the Logar valley.

name: Kulangar (1924)
how the result was decided: Two government battalions were destroyed (source summary).
Iranian side: Khost rebels v Royal Afghan army
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khost_rebellion_(1924–1925)
note: Place uncertain; follows the source's name Kulangar.

name: Pathkai (1924)
how the result was decided: The Lifeguard regiment was destroyed (source summary).
Iranian side: Khost rebels v Sar Nigahban Regiment
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khost_rebellion_(1924–1925)
note: Place is uncertain (the source gives only the name Pathkai).

name: Elazig (1925)
how the result was decided: The rebels entered Elazig and held and looted it for several days.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Said_rebellion; Olson (1989)
note: How much resistance the garrison offered is not recorded in the source I used.

name: Mus (Murat Bridge, 1925)
place: Murat Bridge on the approach to Mus from Hinis, Turkey
how the result was decided: Sheikh Abdullah's column failed to take Mus and withdrew.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Said_rebellion; Olson (1989)
note: The only clear Turkish success outside Diyarbakir in the first weeks; numbers not stated.

name: Piran (1925)
how the result was decided: Sheikh Said's men prevented the arrest of the Kurdish notables.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Said_rebellion; Olson, The Emergence of Kurdish Nationalism and the Sheikh Said Rebellion (1989)
note: The incident that started the rising; Sheikh Said spoke Zaza.

name: Diyarbakir (siege, 1925)
how the result was decided: Every assault on the four gates was repelled and the siege was lifted on 11 March.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheikh_Said_rebellion; Olson (1989); van Bruinessen (1992)
note: The turning point of the rising; the rebels numbered 5,000-10,000 and the garrison used machine guns and mortars. Sheikh Said was captured on 15 April at the Carpuh bridge near Varto.

name: Mohammerah (1925)
how the result was decided: The Persian troops reoccupied Mohammerah after the Arab rising, killing about 130 of the insurgents.
commanders A: not named in the source used
commanders B: not named (an Arab rising of Khaz'al's followers)
Iranian force: Troops of Reza Khan's army in Khuzestan, with British naval and logistic support (HMS Triad, armoured vehicles).
why it counts: Qajars: an Iranian state whose armies were largely Persian
sources: en.wikipedia Sheikh Khazal rebellion
note: Sheikh Khaz'al himself had been arrested in April 1925 without fighting. The British gave support but did not fight.

name: Demirkapi (1926)
war: Ibrahim Heski's rising (precursor of the Ararat rebellion)
place: Demirkapi, near Dogubayazit and Mount Ararat, Turkey
how the result was decided: The Kurds defeated the Turkish 28th Regiment, according to the Wikipedia summary of the Ararat revolt.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ararat_rebellion
note: I could not confirm the exact place of Demirkapi; the coordinates are for the Dogubayazit district.

name: Salmas (1926)
how the result was decided: The siege of Salmas failed: relief columns arrived, half of Simko's Shikak deserted him, and he fled to Iraq.
commanders A: relief units from Urmia, Sharafkhaneh and Khoy (the infobox lists Habibollah Sheibani)
commanders B: Simko Shikak, Haji Agha, Fattah Agha, Seyde Agha
Iranian force: The Salmas garrison and relief units of the Pahlavi army from Urmia, Sharafkhaneh and Khoy.
why it counts: Pahlavi Iran: an Iranian-led state
sources: en.wikipedia Simko Shikak revolt (1926)
note: Simko was killed in an ambush at Oshnavieh on 30 June 1930 (not a battle; excluded).

name: Bampur (1928)
war: Reza Shah's pacification of Persian Baluchistan (1928-1934)
how the result was decided: Dost Mohammad's alliances dissolved, the Iranian army easily defeated him, and he surrendered (Wikipedia 'Dost Mohammad Khan Baloch').
Iranian side: Pahlavi Iran v Barakzai Baloch of Bampur
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dost_Mohammad_Khan_Baloch (fetched); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yarahmadzai_tribe (fetched: '1928, Bampur: Reza Khan's army defeated Dost Mohammad Khan')
note: Doubtful entry: my sources record a campaign and a defeat but no named engagement or date, and the fighting may have been slight. Reza Shah was Mazandarani; Jahanbani was of the Qajar family, so the Iranian-army rule rests on Reza Shah's leadership.

name: Jabal al-Siraj (siege, 1928)
how the result was decided: The garrison surrendered and handed over funds and 18 machine guns, giving Kalakani his arsenal.
Iranian side: Saqqawists v Government garrison of Amanullah
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1928–1929)
note: Kalakani, a Tajik from Kalakan, took the arsenal that armed his march on Kabul.

date: from 14 November 1928; relief column destroyed at Nimla in December
name: Jalalabad (Shinwari revolt, 1928)
how the result was decided: The relief column was destroyed at Nimla and Ali Ahmad Khan then reached a settlement with the Shinwari, ending the government's hold.
Iranian side: Shinwari tribal rebels v Government of Amanullah
commanders B: Ali Ahmad Khan (governor of the Eastern Province)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1928–1929)
note: The revolt that opened the 1928-29 collapse of Amanullah's rule; it was a siege with an open relief battle.

name: First Battle of Kabul (1928-1929)
how the result was decided: Kalakani entered the city, the army largely mutinied, and he held Murad Beg Fort until Amanullah abdicated on 14 January.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1928–1929)
note: Kalakani was wounded on 25 December; the failed shelling of Murad Beg Fort led to the abdication.

name: Fall of Kabul (January 1929)
how the result was decided: Inayatullah abdicated and left Kabul and the Saqqawists took the Arg.
Iranian side: Saqqawists v Government of Inayatullah Khan
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1928–1929)
note: Kalakani became Emir Habibullah II, the first Tajik ruler of Afghanistan.

name: Gharm (Fuzail Maksum's raid, 1929)
how the result was decided: Fuzail Maksum's force briefly captured Gharm; Soviet forces, supplied by air, then drove them out.
commanders B: Soviet Gharm detachment (commander not identified here)
sources: Wikipedia 'Faizal Maksum' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faizal_Maksum (fetched: Garm raid/occupation spring 1929, launched from Afghanistan during Kalakani's reign); Soviet and later Basmachi literature (e.g. Olcott, 'The Basmachi or Freemen's Revolt in Turkestan', Soviet Studies 1981)
note: Fuzail Maksum, a mullah of Karategin (Gharm), is described in Soviet and later literature as a Tajik leader of the Basmachi; the Wikipedia page fetched does not state his ethnicity. Famous in Soviet military history for the airlift of Red Army troops to the Gharm area. Size of his band not established here.

name: Ghazni (1929)
how the result was decided: Sources conflict: Amanullah ordered a retreat on 26 April, but anti-Saqqawist forces re-entered Ghazni on 30 April.
commanders A: Habibullah Kalakani (commanders in the field not named in the source used)
commanders B: Amanullah Khan (ordered a retreat on 26 April)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1928–1929)
note: Amanullah's last attempt to regain the throne from the south; the result is unclear in the source used.

date: 15 April 1929 (the Soviet column then pushed on toward Mazar-i Sharif)
name: Patta-Gissar (Soviet raid, 1929)
war: Soviet incursion into northern Afghanistan (Primakov's raid, 1929)
place: Patta-Gissar, on the Amu Darya opposite Termez (Afghanistan)
how the result was decided: The Red detachment crossed the Amu Darya and overran the Afghan border post, then raided on for several weeks.
commanders B: Vitaly Primakov; Ghulam Nabi Charkhi (Afghan exile leader in Soviet pay)
sources: Wikipedia, Soviet Afghan raid of 1929 (not fetched); Kakar, Afghanistan 1929 accounts
note: Details (garrison, commanders, and the Afghan exile detachment) are from memory and should be checked; the Afghan exile leader is credited to the Soviet side.

name: Shibar Pass (1929)
how the result was decided: Sayyid Husayn's army was routed, which ended his plan to take Mazar-i Sharif.
Iranian side: Hazara militias v Saqqawist army of Sayyid Husayn
commanders A: Hazara commanders (not named in the source used)
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1928–1929)

name: Saur Revolution (Kabul)

note: A tank and air assault by one part of the Afghan army on the palace guard of another; both armies were Afghan and the leaders on both sides (Daoud, Taraki, Amin, Watanjar) were Pashtuns.

name: Tehran insurrection
place: Doshan Tappeh air base and the barracks of Tehran, Iran

strength A: tens of thousands of armed civilians (no count)
strength B: Imperial Guard and Tehran garrison (no count)
losses A: unknown (hundreds were reported killed in the three days; no agreed figure)
losses B: unknown; General Badrei and other senior officers killed

period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds

note: The Islamic Republic was proclaimed after the referendum of 30-31 March 1979; the winning faction became its government.

commanders B: Turkmen People's Cultural and Political Society (Abdollah Shoureshi), with leftist (Fedai) guerrillas

A weak entry; not to be confused with the Soviet storming of the Bala Hissar on 1 January 1980.

period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds

name: Panjshir I (April 1980)
place: Panjshir Valley, Bazarak and Pasishah-Mardan (Panjshir Province, Afghanistan)

commanders A: Mostafa Chamran; Army and IRGC commanders of Abadan
Iranian force: Revolutionary Guards, Army units with Chieftain tanks, navy marines and local fighters including Khuzestani Arabs, supplied by boat and helicopter; about 15,000 men by June 1981.

why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state

period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds

name: Operation Morvarid

how the result was decided: Iranian marines wrecked both terminals and Iranian ships and aircraft sank most of the Iraqi boats that came out, for the loss of the missile boat Paykan.

strength A: 6 amphibious ships, 2 missile boats, marines and aircraft

period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Morvarid; Razoux, The Iran-Iraq War; Cooper and Bishop, Iran-Iraq War in the Air
note: Iran's navy day (7 Azar) commemorates the operation.

name: Susangerd
how the result was decided: The Army and Revolutionary Guards broke the Iraqi ring round Susangerd and drove the besiegers back from the town.
commanders A: Mostafa Chamran (Irregular Warfare Headquarters) and Army commanders; Ali Khamenei present as Khomeini's representative (Iranian accounts)

languages: Persian; Arabic; Turkic; Lur and Bakhtiari
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Liberation of Susangerd
note: Wikipedia's title is 'Liberation of Susangerd'; its infobox dates it 17 November and its text 19 November 1980.

name: Panjshir offensive (December 1980)
place: Panjshir Valley, relief and evacuation of the Rokha post (Panjshir Province, Afghanistan)
how the result was decided: The government post at Rokha was evacuated on 27 December and the operation ended two days later with the valley largely in mujahideen hands.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Panjshir offensives: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panjshir_offensives
note: Often counted as Panjshir III. Heavy airstrikes killed about 100 civilians and 15 mujahideen according to the Wikipedia article; numbering is not fixed in the sources.

date: late January - mid-February 1981 (rebels withdrew about 14-15 February)
name: Mahabad (1981)
how the result was decided: After more than two weeks of artillery bombardment the KDPI withdrew from Mahabad, its stronghold.
Iranian side: Islamic Republic of Iran v Kurdish rebels
Iranian force: Army artillery and Revolutionary Guards (no details).
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
borderline: known from a news report only; not a standard named battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: known from a news report only; not a standard named battle.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds

note: Accounts differ on when the government finally secured Mahabad; KDPI bands stayed active round the town into 1982.

name: Operation Nasr
how the result was decided: The Iranian armoured columns ran into Iraqi tanks dug in hull-down, lost most of a brigade in the mud and withdrew across the Karkheh by 8-9 January.
commanders B: Abolhassan Banisadr (president, in personal command); Col. Meguertitch Davidkhanian
Iranian force: The Army's 16th Armoured Division (Qazvin) and 92nd Armoured Division (Ahvaz) with the 55th Airborne Brigade as infantry; the Revolutionary Guards were kept out, though Hoveyzeh's student volunteers fought on the flank.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Lur and Bakhtiari; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
strength B: about 300-330 tanks; up to 100,000 men in the sector

period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Nasr; Pollack, Arabs at War; Murray and Woods, The Iran-Iraq War
note: Also called Operation Hoveyzeh or the battle of Dasht-e Azadegan; some works call it the battle of Dezful (or Susangerd). Hossein Alamolhoda and his student volunteers were killed at Hoveyzeh in it.

name: Operation Tawakkul
place: north of Abadan, near the Mahshahr road junction, Iran
how the result was decided: The Iranian attack broke into part of the Iraqi line and took prisoners but could not hold its gains, and the siege of Abadan went on.
commanders B: not named in the sources used
Iranian force: Army armoured units on two axes and infantry including Revolutionary Guards on a third.
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Tawakkul Operation; en.wikipedia List of extensive Iranian ground operations in the Iran-Iraq War
note: Also spelled Tavakkol; the Abadan breakout planned with Operation Nasr.

name: H-3 airstrike
place: H-3 (al-Walid) air base complex, Anbar, Iraq
how the result was decided: The Phantoms reached all three airfields undetected, cratered the runways and destroyed parked aircraft and hangars without loss.
commanders A: Col. Ghasem Golchin; planners Col. Javad Fakoori, Col. Bahram Hooshyar, Col. Fereidoon Izadseta
Iranian force: Eight F-4 Phantoms from Hamadan with four F-14 escorts, tankers, a 747 command post, a C-130 and three F-5Es in a diversion.
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
strength A: 8 F-4s, 4 F-14s, 3 F-5Es and support aircraft
losses B: 27-48 aircraft destroyed (Iranian claims; Iraq admitted one MiG-21 damaged)
borderline: strike operation
doubts and flags: A strike operation (air, missile or drone attacks): listed and mapped but not scored, because its result is judged by damage claims rather than by a held field. Borderline: strike operation.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia H-3 airstrike; Cooper and Bishop, Iran-Iraq War in the Air
note: Some works date it 3 April 1981.

name: Operation Commander-in-Chief
how the result was decided: The Revolutionary Guards advanced about 3 km and held the recaptured Iraqi positions east of the Karun.
Iranian force: Revolutionary Guard units of the Abadan front.
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
losses B: 1,496 killed, wounded or captured; at least 32 tanks and APCs
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Commander-in-Chief
note: Persian name Farmandeh-ye Kol-e Qova; a rehearsal for Samen-ol-A'emeh.

name: Operation Samen-ol-A'emeh
place: east bank of the Karun, north of Abadan, Iran
how the result was decided: Iraqi forces east of the Karun broke and fled across makeshift bridges, leaving the field and their heavy equipment, and the siege of Abadan was lifted.
commanders A: Valiollah Fallahi (acting chief of staff); Mohsen Rezaee (IRGC); Army and IRGC field commanders
Iranian force: The Army's 77th Infantry Division (Khorasan), 92nd Armoured Division and an armoured brigade from Shiraz, the navy's Takavar battalion, separate IRGC brigades and local volunteers.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Arabic; Lur and Bakhtiari
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
strength A: 20,000-30,000 in the main attack, 30,000-40,000 in the diversion
losses A: about 3,000 killed or wounded; about 150 tanks
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Samen-ol-A'emeh; Murray and Woods, The Iran-Iraq War
note: Wikipedia names Chamran among the commanders, but he had been killed at Dehlaviyeh in June 1981; the C-130 crash of 29 September 1981 killed Fallahi, Fakoori, Namjoo, Kolahdouz and Jahanara on their way back from this victory.

name: Dar Khuyeh ambush
how the result was decided: Iraqi tanks ambushed the Iranian supply convoy and the Iranians abandoned at least 20 Chieftains and fell back.
Iranian force: An Iranian Army armoured convoy with Chieftain tanks.
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a sub-engagement known only from Wikipedia; its date is uncertain
doubts and flags: Borderline: a sub-engagement known only from Wikipedia; its date is uncertain.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Abadan; en.wikipedia Military operations of the Iran-Iraq War
note: Wikipedia dates it to October 1981, after the siege was lifted; it may belong to the siege of 1980-81.

name: Operation Tariq al-Quds
place: Bostan and the Chazabeh pass, Iran

Iranian force: Army 16th Armoured (Qazvin), 92nd Armoured (Ahvaz) and 77th Infantry (Khorasan) Division brigades with eight artillery battalions, IRGC Ashura, Karbala, Imam Hossein, Imam Sajjad and Imam Hassan brigades and a gendarmerie battalion; about 20,000 men.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Daylami and Caspian; Lur and Bakhtiari; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Tariq al-Quds; Murray and Woods, The Iran-Iraq War
note: Also called the liberation of Bostan.

name: Operation Matla ol-Fajr
place: Bazi-Deraz heights, Tang-e Kurak and Shiakooh, between Gilan-e Gharb and Sarpol-e Zahab, Iran

commanders A: Najaf Headquarters (IRGC) and the Army's western headquarters
Iranian force: IRGC and Basij of Kermanshah province with battalions from Tehran, Rasht, Mashhad and Hamadan, and Army units.
languages: Persian; Kurdish; Daylami and Caspian; Turkic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state

how the result was decided: The Sarbedaran who entered Amol from the forest were driven out by the Revolutionary Guards and armed townsmen after a day of street fighting.

period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia 1982 Amol uprising

name: Khiabani safe house raid
place: safe house in north Tehran (Zafaraniyeh in MEK accounts), Iran
how the result was decided: After a three-hour shootout the Revolutionary Guards stormed the house and killed Khiabani and about 20 of his comrades.
Iranian force: Government: Revolutionary Guards and security forces of Tehran; MEK: Khiabani, his bodyguards and an armed squad.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
losses B: about 22 killed, including Mousa Khiabani, Ashraf Rabiei and Azar Rezaei

doubts and flags: Borderline: a raid on a guerrilla hideout rather than a battle; no standard English name.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Time, 22 February 1982; en.wikipedia Mousa Khiabani

name: Operation Fath ol-Mobin
place: west of the Karkheh between Shush and Dezful, Iran
how the result was decided: The Iraqi forces west of the Karkheh were encircled and broken and Saddam ordered a retreat on 28 March, leaving the field and 10,000-20,000 prisoners to Iran.

languages: Persian; Turkic; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds

name: Operation Beit ol-Moqaddas
place: between the Karun and the border, from Hoveyzeh to Khorramshahr, Iran
how the result was decided: Iran crossed the Karun, drove the Iraqis from Hoveyzeh and Khorramshahr back to the border and held the field.
commanders A: Mohsen Rezaee; Ali Sayad Shirazi; Gholam Ali Rashid; Hassan Baqeri; Massoud Monfared Niyaki

Iranian force: Army 92nd Armoured, 21st Hamzeh and 16th Armoured Divisions, 55th Airborne, 23rd Special Forces and 58th Zolfaqar Brigades; IRGC Fath, Nasr and Qods headquarters with brigades such as 14th Imam Hossein, 8th Najaf Ashraf, 25th Karbala, 27th Mohammad Rasulullah, 31st Ashura and 41st Tharallah; Basij volunteers; Jihad of Construction engineers.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Daylami and Caspian; Lur and Bakhtiari; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Beit ol-Moqaddas; Murray and Woods, The Iran-Iraq War; Pollack, Arabs at War

date: 22-24 May 1982 (final phase of Operation Beit ol-Moqaddas)
name: Khorramshahr (1982)
how the result was decided: The Iranians stormed and retook Khorramshahr on 24 May, capturing most of its Iraqi garrison.
commanders A: Ali Sayad Shirazi; Mohsen Rezaee; Ahmad Motevaselian; Hooshang Samadi
Iranian force: IRGC brigades (27th Mohammad Rasulullah under Motevaselian and others), Basij, the Army's 21st Hamzeh and 92nd Divisions and navy marines under Samadi.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
strength B: about 80,000 in the sector; the city garrison about 15,000-19,000
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Khorramshahr (1982); Murray and Woods, The Iran-Iraq War
note: Wikipedia's article spans the whole operation (24 April - 24 May); the assault on the city itself was 22-24 May. 24 May (3 Khordad) is kept in Iran as Liberation Day.

date: night of 16-17 May to June 1982 (end date approximate)
name: Panjshir V (May-June 1982)
place: Panjshir Valley, from Rukha to Bazarak and Anava (Panjshir Province, Afghanistan)
how the result was decided: The Soviet-Afghan force occupied most of the valley and set up garrisons at Rukha, Bazarak and Anava, although most of Massoud's fighters escaped to the side valleys.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Panjshir offensives: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panjshir_offensives
note: The largest of the early Panjshir operations. The Soviets held the valley floor but not the decisive victory they wanted; Massoud had been warned and had evacuated much of the population.

name: Operation Ramadan
place: east of Basra, from Shalamcheh and Zeid, Iraq
how the result was decided: Iraqi counterattacks threw back each Iranian thrust toward Basra and the Iranians kept only a small strip of ground.
commanders A: Saddam Hussein; Maher Abd al-Rashid (3rd Corps)
Iranian force: Revolutionary Guard and Basij human waves with the Army's 16th, 88th and 92nd Armoured and 21st, 77th and other divisions; 90,000-150,000 men.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Lur and Bakhtiari; Kurdish; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Ramadan; Murray and Woods, The Iran-Iraq War; Pollack, Arabs at War
note: Iran's first major offensive into Iraq.

name: Operation Muslim ibn Aqil
place: heights west of Sumar, overlooking Mandali, Iran-Iraq border
how the result was decided: The Iranians took and held the heights of Giskeh and Kohneh-Rig west of Sumar in the first stage, though the second stage stalled short of Mandali.
commanders A: Mohsen Rezaee; Ali Sayad Shirazi (overall commands)
Iranian force: IRGC and Army units of the central front, about 60,000 men.
languages: Persian; Kurdish; Turkic; Lur and Bakhtiari
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Muslim ibn Aqil; en.wikipedia List of extensive Iranian ground operations in the Iran-Iraq War
note: Wikipedia's infobox calls it an Iraqi victory because Mandali was not reached; its text and the operations list record the Iranian gains of about 150 km2.

name: Operation Muharram
place: Musian and the Bayat oilfield, south-east of Dehloran, Iran
how the result was decided: The Iranians took and held Musian, the Bayat oilfield and the Dehloran road, though their advance toward al-Amarah was stopped.
Iranian force: IRGC and Army units (not named in the sources used).
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
losses A: about 4,000 killed (Wikipedia, sides not clearly labelled)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Muharram; en.wikipedia List of extensive Iranian ground operations in the Iran-Iraq War
note: Wikipedia's infobox calls it an Iraqi defensive victory because Iran did not break into Iraq; under the field test the ground taken was held.

name: Operation Before the Dawn
place: Fakkeh and Chazabeh border sector, toward al-Amarah, Iraq
how the result was decided: Iraqi trenches, artillery and aircraft stopped the Iranian human-wave attacks, and Iran called off the offensive after a week with only marginal ground.
Iranian force: Revolutionary Guard and Basij infantry in human waves, supported by Army infantry, armoured and airborne divisions and artillery; about 200,000 men in the sector (Wikipedia).
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Before the Dawn; Murray and Woods, The Iran-Iraq War
note: Persian name Valfajr-e Moqaddamati; launched for the fourth anniversary of the revolution.

name: Operation Dawn 1
place: Jabal Fauqi and the Fakkeh oilfield, north of Fakkeh, Iran-Iraq border
how the result was decided: The Iranian attack was beaten off with heavy losses and the Iranians were back on their start lines within days.
Iranian force: Revolutionary Guard infantry and the Army's 92nd Armoured Division.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Dawn (1983); en.wikipedia List of extensive Iranian ground operations in the Iran-Iraq War

date: July 1983 (the Khost garrison was blockaded intermittently from 1980 to 1991)
name: Khost (siege, 1983)
how the result was decided: The Wikipedia Soviet-Afghan War article mentions the July 1983 siege without stating the outcome; the town stayed in government hands until 1991.
Iranian side: Mujahideen of Paktia and Khost v Democratic Republic of Afghanistan
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Soviet-Afghan War: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet%E2%80%93Afghan_War
note: Included from a one-line mention; a weak entry. Khost was an Afghan army garrison among Pashtun tribes (Zadran, Mangal, Jadran); the later relief operation is Magistral (1987-88).

name: Operation Dawn 2
how the result was decided: Iran took the Haj Omran heights and held them against the Iraqi counterattack, in which Iraq first used mustard gas.

commanders B: Iraqi northern front (corps not named in the sources used)

strength A: 16 IRGC and 7 Army battalions, 1,500 militiamen, 800 peshmerga

losses B: several thousand killed on both sides (no split)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds

name: Operation Dawn 3
how the result was decided: The sources conflict: Iran claimed the border heights north of Mehran, Iraq claimed to have destroyed the encircled Iranian force before pulling back, and Wikipedia calls it an Iraqi victory without independent support.
Iranian force: Army and Revolutionary Guard infantry, about 50,000 in the mountains (not named in the sources used).
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Dawn 3; Christian Science Monitor, 10 August 1983
note: Persian Valfajr-3; Iraq tried chemical rounds from helicopters here. Wikipedia's claim that Iraq 'captured Mehran' is doubtful, as Iraq had held it since 1980.

name: Operation Dawn 4
how the result was decided: Iran took the Penjwin valley and held it against Iraqi counterattacks with Republican Guards and gas, stopping about 15 km inside Iraq.
commanders A: IRGC division commanders Mehdi Bakeri (31st Ashura), Qasem Soleimani (41st Tharallah), Mehdi Zeinoddin (17th Ali ibn Abi Taleb), Morteza Ghorbani (25th Karbala), Hossein Kharrazi (14th Imam Hossein), Ahmad Kazemi (8th Najaf Ashraf)
Iranian force: IRGC divisions 31st Ashura (Azerbaijan), 41st Tharallah (Kerman), 17th Ali ibn Abi Taleb (Qom), 25th Karbala (Mazandaran), 14th Imam Hossein and 8th Najaf Ashraf (Isfahan): 47 infantry, 4 armoured, 4 mechanized and 3 artillery battalions, with 17 Army infantry and 8 artillery battalions and PUK peshmerga.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Daylami and Caspian; Kurdish
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Dawn-4; Murray and Woods, The Iran-Iraq War
note: Persian Valfajr-4; the allies were PUK peshmerga and KDP elements of Iraqi Kurdistan.

name: Operation Dawn 5
place: toward the Baghdad-Basra highway (Wikipedia places it near Basra; other accounts in the Kut - al-Amarah sector), Iraq
how the result was decided: The Revolutionary Guard and Basij waves came within a few kilometres of the highway but were thrown back, Iran keeping only minor ground.
Iranian force: Revolutionary Guard and Basij infantry, 100,000-150,000 men, with little armour or artillery.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Dawn 5; en.wikipedia Battle of the Marshes
note: Persian Valfajr-5, a preliminary to Kheibar; the site is uncertain (Wikipedia's 'Military operations' article places Dawn 5 and 6 near Kut al-Amara).

name: Operation Dawn 6
place: east of the Baghdad-Basra highway, toward Ali al-Gharbi and al-Amarah, Iraq
how the result was decided: The Iranians took a strip of Iraqi ground about 5 by 10 miles east of the Baghdad-Basra highway and still held it when the operation was called off on 24 February, though they stopped 10 miles short of the highway.
Iranian force: Army regulars, Revolutionary Guards and Basij in human-wave assaults.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Dawn 6; en.wikipedia Battle of the Marshes
note: Persian Valfajr-6, launched with Kheibar; the site is uncertain.

name: Operation Kheibar
place: Majnoon Islands and the Hawizeh Marshes toward al-Qurna, Iraq
how the result was decided: The Iranians took the Majnoon Islands and kept them, though their thrust from the marshes to the Basra-Baghdad road near al-Qurna was thrown back by armour and gas.
commanders A: Mohsen Rezaee; Hossein Kharrazi (wounded); Hamid Bakeri (killed)
Iranian force: Revolutionary Guard and Basij infantry carried by boats and helicopters, about 250,000 men, with the Army's 92nd Armoured Division and four navy commando battalions (about 2,400 men).
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Kheibar; en.wikipedia Battle of the Marshes; Murray and Woods, The Iran-Iraq War
note: Wikipedia's 'Battle of the Marshes' covers the same fighting (with Dawn 5 and 6). Start dates vary: 14, 22 or 24 February (the Persian date 3 Esfand 1362 is 22 February). Iraq used mustard and nerve gas at scale; 49 of 50 Iranian helicopters were reported lost on 27 February.

name: War of the Cities (1984)
place: Dezful and ten other Iranian cities; Basra and Iraqi border towns
how the result was decided: Iraqi aircraft and missiles struck eleven Iranian cities and killed many civilians, while Iran could answer only with artillery and a few air raids on Basra, Baghdad and border towns.
commanders A: Saddam Hussein (Iraqi Air Force and missile forces)
commanders B: Iranian Army artillery and Air Force
Iranian force: Iranian air defences, Army artillery shelling Basra and border towns, and Air Force raids.
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
losses B: about 1,200 Iranian civilians killed in February (other figures up to 4,700)
borderline: strike operation; War of the Cities phase
doubts and flags: A strike operation (air, missile or drone attacks): listed and mapped but not scored, because its result is judged by damage claims rather than by a held field. Borderline: strike operation; War of the Cities phase.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia War of the cities; en.wikipedia Military operations of the Iran-Iraq War
note: The first phase of the War of the Cities; Iraqi FROG and Scud missiles had already hit Dezful in 1982-83. A UN-brokered moratorium on attacking cities followed in June 1984.

name: Hazara Valley (1984)
place: Hazara side valley, Panjshir (Panjshir Province, Afghanistan)
how the result was decided: The Soviet battalion was ambushed and decimated, with an estimated 60 dead, according to the Wikipedia article on the Panjshir offensives.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Panjshir offensives: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panjshir_offensives
note: A single ambush-and-battle within Panjshir VII; the Soviet side was entirely Soviet army, so only side B qualifies.

name: Panjshir VII (April-September 1984)
how the result was decided: Some mujahideen infrastructure was destroyed, but most fighters escaped, and the Soviet-Afghan force left the upper valley in September, keeping only the lower Panjshir.
commanders A: Marshal Sergei Sokolov (Soviet defence minister, directing)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Panjshir offensives: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panjshir_offensives
note: The biggest Panjshir offensive, with about 2,600 Afghan army troops beside the Soviets; heavy Soviet losses to mines and ambushes (see the Hazara Valley battle of 30 April).

name: Arabi Island incident
place: over the Persian Gulf near Arabi Island, Saudi Arabia
how the result was decided: Saudi F-15s guided by a US AWACS shot down one Iranian Phantom and crippled a second, and the Iranian reinforcements turned back.
commanders B: Iranian Air Force, Bushehr base (not named)
Iranian force: Two F-4 Phantoms from Bushehr, then eleven more scrambled.
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
losses B: 2 F-4s (one shot down, one written off), 2 aircrew killed
doubts and flags: A strike operation (air, missile or drone attacks): listed and mapped but not scored, because its result is judged by damage claims rather than by a held field.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia 1984 Arabi Island incident; en.wikipedia Iran-Iraq War
note: Also called the action of 5 June 1984 or the Fahd Line incident; a US E-3 AWACS tracked the Iranian aircraft and guided the Saudi fighters but took no part in the fighting.

name: Eruh and Shemdinli raids (1984)
how the result was decided: PKK squads attacked gendarmerie posts in both towns and withdrew; the town posts were not held.
commanders A: PKK local commanders (Mahsum Korkmaz in the Eruh group)
doubts and flags: The sources consulted do not give the result, so the battle is listed but not scored.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Marcus, Blood and Belief: the PKK and the Kurdish Fight for Independence (2007); McDowall, A Modern History of the Kurds (2004)
note: The PKK's first armed action, taken as the start of its insurgency. It was a hit-and-run attack of two small groups with few dead, so it is a marginal battle; the result is left open because neither side held the field in a meaningful sense. Semdinli is at 37.30N 44.57E.

name: Operation Ashura
how the result was decided: Iran retook about 50 km2 of the Meymak heights, held since 1980, and kept them.
Iranian force: Revolutionary Guards with Army support (units not named in the sources used).
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Ashura (Iran)

name: Operation Dawn 7
place: Mehran sector, Ilam (or Chazabeh, Khuzestan: the sources disagree), Iran
how the result was decided: The sources conflict: Wikipedia's article places it at Chazabeh and calls it inconclusive, halted after a few days by Iraqi flooding, while Wikipedia's survey of operations says it retook Mehran.
Iranian force: Army and Revolutionary Guard units (not named in the sources used).
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
borderline: poorly documented operation; place and result uncertain
doubts and flags: Borderline: poorly documented operation; place and result uncertain.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Dawn 7; en.wikipedia Military operations of the Iran-Iraq War
note: Persian Valfajr-7, code 'Ya Zahra'.

name: Panjshir IX (1985)
how the result was decided: The Soviets pushed the mujahideen back and installed a garrison at Peshghur after Massoud's men had overrun the post there and taken about 500 prisoners.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Panjshir offensives: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panjshir_offensives
note: Launched to disrupt a planned exchange of the captured Afghan officers, most of whom were killed in circumstances that remain disputed. The article gives no firm dates.

name: Operation Badr
place: Hawizeh Marshes and the Baghdad-Basra highway north-east of al-Qurnah, Iraq
how the result was decided: Iraqi counterattacks with Republican Guard reserves drove the Iranians back across the Tigris and retook the highway within days; Iran kept only part of the marshes.
commanders A: Sultan Hashim Ahmad al-Tai, Jamal Zanoun, Hisham Sabah al-Fakhri
commanders B: Mohsen Rezaee, Mehdi Bakeri (killed; listed as missing)
Iranian force: About 100,000 men, mostly IRGC (Pasdaran) infantry and Basij volunteers with anti-tank weapons, crossing the marshes by boat and the Tigris on pontoon bridges; Mehdi Bakeri's 31st Ashura Division among them.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
losses A: 2,000 killed, 6,000 wounded, 3,000 captured; 100 tanks, 11 helicopters, 4 aircraft
losses B: 10,000 killed (11,000-17,000 in other estimates), 20,000 wounded, 2,000 captured
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Badr (1985); List of extensive Iranian ground operations in the Iran-Iraq War; Cordesman and Wagner, Lessons of Modern War II
note: Iraq used chemical weapons in the counteroffensive. Mehdi Bakeri, commander of the 31st Ashura Division (raised in Azerbaijan), was killed.

date: 22 March-8 April 1985 (other sources: from 4 March into June 1985)
name: War of the Cities (1985)
place: Tehran, Tabriz, Shiraz and Isfahan (Iraqi raids); Baghdad and Kirkuk (Iranian strikes)
how the result was decided: Iraqi bombers (Tu-22, Tu-16, MiG-25) reached Tehran and other cities and Iran's first Scud missiles and air raids reached Baghdad; neither side stopped the other's strikes, so the exchange has no winner by the test.
commanders A: IRIAF and IRGC missile command (commanders not named in the source used)
Iranian force: Iranian air defences (HAWK batteries, anti-aircraft guns, F-14 and F-4 interceptors of the IRIAF) against the Iraqi raids, and Iranian air raids and Scud-B missiles fired at Baghdad by the IRGC's new missile units.
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
borderline: War of the Cities phase (strike campaign against cities), not a single battle
doubts and flags: A strike operation (air, missile or drone attacks): listed and mapped but not scored, because its result is judged by damage claims rather than by a held field. Borderline: War of the Cities phase (strike campaign against cities), not a single battle.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia War of the cities (second campaign); Cordesman and Wagner, Lessons of Modern War II
note: Iraq's answer to Operation Badr. The first round (February 1984) is a separate entry.

name: Maravar (1985)
how the result was decided: The Soviet column was ambushed in the valley and lost heavily, reportedly dozens killed, before it withdrew.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Isby, War in a Distant Country (1989) (not fetched; from memory); no Wikipedia article of that title was found
note: One of the worst single Soviet reverses of the Kunar campaigns; recorded from memory, so unit names, day and casualty figures are uncertain and the entry is weak. The Kunar fighters were mostly Pashtuns, with some Nuristanis nearby.

name: Operation Quds-1
place: Hawizeh Marshes (Hur al-Hawizeh) east of the Tigris, Iraq
how the result was decided: The IRGC took the Iraqi posts of Abu Dharr and Abu Laila and held about 180 square km of the marshes.
Iranian force: IRGC marsh infantry in boats, apparently including the 25th Karbala Division of Mazandaran.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a limited operation; the English article rests on Iranian sources
doubts and flags: Borderline: a limited operation; the English article rests on Iranian sources.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Quds-1
note: Code name 'Ya Mohammad Rasoolullah'. Iraq used chemical weapons on the first day.

name: Operation Quds-2
place: Northern Hawizeh Marshes, al-Bayda and Umm al-Naaj lake, Iraq
how the result was decided: The IRGC broke up the Iraqi counterattack around al-Bayda and held about 15 square km of the northern marshes (Iranian figures).
Iranian force: IRGC amphibious marsh infantry.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
losses B: 312 killed; 30 boats and 15 water-police posts destroyed (Iranian claims)
borderline: a limited operation; the English article rests on Iranian sources
doubts and flags: Borderline: a limited operation; the English article rests on Iranian sources.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Quds-2
note: Further operations Quds-3 to Quds-5 (summer 1985) have no English articles and are not listed.

date: 15 July-9 September 1985 (stages from 24 July and 9 September)
name: Operation Ghader
place: Heights above Sidakan, Erbil Governorate, Iraq (launched from Oshnavieh)
how the result was decided: The Iranians took and held several heights overlooking Sidakan, up to 35 km inside Iraq, though Iraqi counterattacks kept them from their final objectives.
Iranian force: Iranian Army ground forces (the first large operation planned by the Artesh alone after Badr), with IRGC units and Army aviation and air force support.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
losses B: Iranian claims: about 2,000 killed and 3,000 wounded (another report: 1,020 killed and wounded)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Ghader; List of extensive Iranian ground operations in the Iran-Iraq War
note: Also spelt Qader. Iran later withdrew from some of the captured positions; the article calls the result limited. One aim was to cut the supply routes of the Iranian Kurdish opposition (KDPI) based in Iraq.

date: 9/10 February-10 March 1986 (fighting on the peninsula into April)
name: First Battle of al-Faw
how the result was decided: The Iranians took the tip of the peninsula and al-Faw town (14 February) and held them against every Iraqi counterattack to the end of the operation.
commanders A: Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, Mohsen Rezaee, Ali Sayad Shirazi, Esmaeil Sohrabi, Morteza Ghorbani, Hossein Kharrazi, Amin Shariati
commanders B: Maher Abd al-Rashid, Hisham Sabah al-Fakhri, Saadi Tuma Abbas
Iranian force: Operation Valfajr 8: about 240 Navy SEALs and frogmen leading an amphibious night crossing of the Shatt al-Arab, then IRGC divisions (25th Karbala, 27th Mohammad Rasulullah, 41st Tharallah, 31st Ashura, 14th Imam Hossein, 17th Ali ibn Abi Taleb, 8th Najaf, 5th Nasr, 19th Fajr) with Basij, Army artillery and aviation; 133,000 men at the height.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
strength A: 22,000-25,000 at the start; 133,000 at the height
strength B: 1,000-5,000 at the start; 82,000 at the height
losses A: 10,000 killed, 25,000 wounded (about 10,000 of them by chemical weapons) (estimates)
losses B: 3,000 killed, 9,000 wounded, 2,105 captured; 74 aircraft, 400 tanks (Iranian claims)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia First Battle of al-Faw; List of extensive Iranian ground operations in the Iran-Iraq War; Murray and Woods, The Iran-Iraq War
note: Iranian name Valfajr 8 (Dawn 8). A feint toward Basra near al-Qurnah opened the operation. Iraq retook the peninsula in April 1988 (Second Battle of al-Faw).

name: Operation Dawn 9
place: Border heights east of Sulaymaniyah (Chwarta sector), Iraq; later phases toward Rawanduz
how the result was decided: Iraqi counterattacks contained the Iranians short of Sulaymaniyah and Rawanduz and retook Mangesh; Iran kept only a few border heights.
commanders B: IRGC commanders (not named); Masoud Barzani (KDP peshmerga)
Iranian force: IRGC infantry with Iranian paratroopers, and Iraqi Kurdish peshmerga (about 1,000 at Mangesh) attacking the Iraqi rear.
languages: Persian; Kurdish; Turkic; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
losses B: more than 2,500 killed or wounded (Iranian claim)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Dawn 9
note: Iranian name Valfajr 9, a diversion for al-Faw. Wikipedia's result: 'Iranian strategic failure, minor gains for Iran'. The Kurdish ally was the KDP (Iraqi Kurdish rebels).

date: April 1986 (about two weeks; exact dates not verified)
name: Zhawar (1986)
place: Zhawar Kili base complex, near Khost (Khost Province, Afghanistan)
how the result was decided: The government force captured and demolished the Zhawar tunnel and supply complex, although the mujahideen reoccupied the site after it withdrew.
Iranian side: Democratic Republic of Afghanistan v Mujahideen of Jalaluddin Haqqani
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Jalali and Grau, The Other Side of the Mountain: Mujahideen Tactics in the Soviet-Afghan War (1998) (not fetched; from memory)
note: A large Afghan army operation (several thousand men) against the main mujahideen supply base on the Pakistan border; the Soviets gave advisers and air support. Dates and numbers are from memory.

name: Mehran (1986)
how the result was decided: The Iraqi II Corps took the town and the heights around it from the Iranian garrison.
Iranian force: A small Iranian garrison of Army and IRGC troops holding the town and the border heights.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Mehran (1986); Cordesman and Wagner, Lessons of Modern War II
note: Saddam's 'dynamic defence' answer to the loss of al-Faw; he offered to trade Mehran for al-Faw and Iran refused. Wikipedia's 'Battle of Mehran (1986)' covers both this capture and the Iranian recapture (Operation Karbala-1), listed separately here.

name: Operation Karbala-1
place: Mehran and the Qalavizan heights, Ilam Province, Iran
how the result was decided: The Iranians retook Mehran and the Qalavizan and Hamrin heights by 3 July and beat off the Republican Guard counterattack of 4 July.
commanders A: IRGC and Army commanders (Mohsen Rezaee, Ali Sayad Shirazi)
Iranian force: IRGC divisions with Army artillery battalions and Army aviation AH-1 Cobra helicopters with TOW missiles.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Mehran (1986); List of extensive Iranian ground operations in the Iran-Iraq War
note: Wikipedia title 'Battle of Mehran (1986)'. The casualty figures in the infobox are not assigned to sides clearly.

name: Operation Karbala-3
place: Al-Amaya (al-Umayyah) and al-Bakr oil terminals off al-Faw, Iraq
how the result was decided: The Iranians held part of the al-Amaya terminal for about 24 hours before Iraqi naval infantry, special forces and shore missiles drove them off on 2 September.
Iranian force: About 2,000 IRGC naval men in light boats armed with machine guns, rockets and mortars.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Karbala-3
note: Also called the Battle of al-Umayyah. Later Iranian attacks on the terminal (4-5 September, 21-22 November 1986) also failed.

name: Operation Karbala-2
how the result was decided: The Iranians took several heights (1600-2435) and part of the Haji Omaran road and held them.
Iranian force: 28 IRGC battalions under the Seyyed al-Shohada 4th Corps, among them the 9th Badr brigade (Iraqi Shia exiles), 12th Qaem, 21st Imam Reza, 105th Quds and 155th Shohada.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Arabic; Lur and Bakhtiari
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Karbala-2
note: The Karbala-4 article says Karbala-2 and Karbala-3 failed to move the Iraqi lines; the result is the Karbala-2 article's.

name: Operation Fath 1
place: Kirkuk oil refinery and installations, Iraq
how the result was decided: The raiders struck the refinery, power station, SAM sites and bases around Kirkuk and withdrew with all their equipment.
commanders A: Mohammad-Baqer Zolqadr (IRGC Ramazan Headquarters); PUK commanders
Iranian force: About 300-400 IRGC special forces of the Ramazan Headquarters (66th Airborne and 75th Zafar special brigades) with about 2,000 PUK peshmerga.
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
losses A: IRGC none, several wounded; PUK minimal
losses B: 600 killed and wounded, dozens captured (Iranian claim)
borderline: a raid on installations rather than a battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: a raid on installations rather than a battle.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Fath 1
note: Also called Operation Wahdat. The PUK (Patriotic Union of Kurdistan) was the Iraqi Kurdish ally; the PUK was the larger force but the operation was planned and led by the IRGC.

name: Operation Karbala-4
place: Umm al-Rasas and the Shatt al-Arab islands west of Minu, toward Abu al-Khasib, Basra Governorate, Iraq
how the result was decided: The Iraqis stopped the crossing on the road to Basra and the Iranians withdrew across the Shatt al-Arab after three days.
commanders A: Saddam Hussein, Khalil al-Dhouri, Jawad Rumi
Iranian force: About 60,000 IRGC and Basij of the Najaf, Quds, Karbala and Nouh corps, led by frogmen of the 25th, 41st, 7th and 14th divisions.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Karbala-4; List of extensive Iranian ground operations in the Iran-Iraq War
note: The 175 divers whose remains came back to Iran in 2015 were lost here.

name: Operation Karbala-5
place: Fish Lake, the Jasim river and Shalamcheh, east of Basra, Iraq
how the result was decided: The Iraqis held their last lines about 15 km from Basra and then pushed the Iranians back toward Shalamcheh; Iran kept only a strip of ground east of the city.
commanders A: Saddam Hussein, Maher Abd al-Rashid, Dhia al-Din Jamal, Khalil al-Dhouri
commanders B: Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, Mohsen Rezaee, Ali Sayad Shirazi, Hossein Kharrazi (killed), Esmail Daghayeghi (killed)
Iranian force: 150,000-200,000 men: about 70% IRGC and Basij (Najaf, Quds, Karbala and Nouh corps, the 9th Badr division of Iraqi exiles among them) and 30% Army with artillery and armour.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Basra; List of extensive Iranian ground operations in the Iran-Iraq War; Murray and Woods, The Iran-Iraq War
note: Wikipedia title 'Siege of Basra'; the city was never invested, so it is scored as a field battle. The largest battle of the war.

name: Operation Karbala-6
place: Naft Shahr and Sumar sector, south of Qasr-e Shirin, Kermanshah Province, Iran
how the result was decided: Iraqi armour counterattacked and encircled the Basij, the Iranian advance stalled and the Iraqis held their line.
Iranian force: About 10,000 Basij with the Army's 77th Mechanized Division of Khorasan (M47 and M48 tanks) and the IRGC 31st Ashura Division of Azerbaijan.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Karbala-6; List of extensive Iranian ground operations in the Iran-Iraq War
note: A diversion for Karbala-5. Iran claimed Naft Shahr and Naft Khaneh; Wikipedia's result is 'operational failure; successful Iraqi defence; limited Iranian advance'.

name: War of the Cities (1987)
place: Tehran, Isfahan and Qom (Iraqi raids); Baghdad and Basra (Iranian missiles)
how the result was decided: Iraqi raids hit Tehran, Isfahan and Qom (about 3,000 civilians killed) and eleven Iranian long-range missiles hit Iraqi cities (at least 300 killed); both sides' strikes reached their targets, so there is no winner by the test.
commanders A: IRIAF and IRGC missile command (not named)
Iranian force: Iranian air defences (HAWK batteries, anti-aircraft guns, F-14 and F-4 interceptors of the IRIAF) against the Iraqi raids, and Iranian air raids and Scud-B missiles fired at Baghdad by the IRGC's new missile units.
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
losses A: about 3,000 civilians killed in Iranian cities
losses B: at least 300 killed in Iraqi cities
borderline: War of the Cities phase (strike campaign against cities), not a single battle
doubts and flags: A strike operation (air, missile or drone attacks): listed and mapped but not scored, because its result is judged by damage claims rather than by a held field. Borderline: War of the Cities phase (strike campaign against cities), not a single battle.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia War of the cities (third and fourth campaigns); en.wikipedia Siege of Basra
note: Fought alongside Karbala-5. Wikipedia lists a third campaign (17-25 January 1987) and a fourth (February-April 1987), merged here because the fourth has no details.

name: Operation Karbala-7
place: Haj Omran highlands and Kurda Mand (Gerdmand) mountain, Erbil Governorate, Iraq
how the result was decided: The Iraqis held the summit of Kurda Mand, the Iranians' objective, and beat back the follow-up attack of 11-12 March, though Iran kept some of the Haj Omran highlands.
Iranian force: IRGC infantry; the units are not named in the source used.
languages: Persian; Turkic; Kurdish; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian; Arabic
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Karbala-7
note: Wikipedia's result: 'Iraqi defensive victory; Iranian tactical failure; Iran captures Haj Omran highlands'.

name: Operation Karbala-10
place: Mawat (Mavout) axis, Sulaymaniyah Governorate, Iraq (from Baneh and Sardasht)
how the result was decided: The Iranians and the PUK advanced about 34 km and kept the ground they took, though they were halted at Mawat and the Shakh Qoolan heights.
Iranian force: IRGC infantry with a few thousand PUK peshmerga.
languages: Persian; Kurdish; Turkic; Lur and Bakhtiari; Daylami and Caspian
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state

note: The fight is the capture of the city by the uprising, not the later Iraqi return. Dates inside March are approximate. Townsmen fought as well; the defecting jash militia is the main armed element.

period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds

name: Tamarasheni and Eredvi (May 1992)
place: Tamarasheni and Eredvi (Georgian villages north of Tskhinvali), South Ossetia (Georgia)

date: Early June 1992 (before the ceasefire of 10 June)
name: Teki (June 1992)
how the result was decided: The Georgian advance took Teki and Georgian artillery shelled Tskhinvali, until the ceasefire of 10 June.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia 'South Ossetia war (1991-1992)' (fetched: early June Georgian advance and capture of Teki)
note: Georgian push in the last phase of the siege of Tskhinvali (already in the dataset), ended by Russian pressure and the Dagomys agreement of 24 June 1992. The site of Teki is placed approximately.

date: 30 October-6 November 1992 (open fighting on the night of 30 October and about a week after)

period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
