note: The source describes no named battle, only a week of fighting in the district and on Vladikavkaz's edge; Included as a named conflict. The Ossetian forces were Alans; much of the violence was against civilians, so this is a campaign-type entry.

date: 10-12 December 1992 (the Popular Front's entry into the capital)

note: Both armies were Tajik (Kulobi/Hissari Popular Front against Garmi, Pamiri and Dushanbe-based opposition). The date 10 December is from standard histories; one source fetched dates an earlier Safarov offensive on the capital to Sept-Oct 1992.

date: 11-12 February 1993 (operation; killings of civilians continued for days)
name: Afshar (1993)

period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds

note: A military attack on Wahdat positions in a Hazara neighbourhood that turned into the Afshar massacre (Amnesty International). Borderline for a battle entry because the massacre of civilians dominates the record; kept as a named operation with real fighting.

factions A: Islamic Republic of Iran Air Force

commanders A: Not identified (one Russian account names a Tabarov among the planners)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds

date: 1 January to about June 1994 (heaviest fighting January-February)
name: Kabul (1994)

period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1992-1996): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1992%E2%80%931996)
note: The worst fighting of the 1992-96 civil war in the capital; the Afghanistan Justice Project cites about 25,000 killed between January and June 1994. The Uzbek Junbish is not counted.

name: Spin Boldak (1994)
place: Spin Boldak, on the Pakistan border (Kandahar Province, Afghanistan)
how the result was decided: The Taliban took the town and the large Hezb-i Islami arms depot after a short fight, which gave them their first stock of heavy weapons.
commanders B: Local Hezb-i Islami commander (not verified here)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1992-1996): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1992%E2%80%931996)
note: The first notable Taliban action; fighting was short and the numbers are not firmly recorded, so the entry is weak. Both sides were Pashtun.

name: Kandahar (1994)
side B: Kandahar commanders and Hezb-i Islami forces
how the result was decided: The Taliban took the city and its airport and arsenal on 5 November, and the rival commanders fled or submitted.
Iranian side: Taliban v Kandahar commanders and Hezb-i Islami forces
factions B: Kandahar commanders and Hezb-i Islami forces
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1992-1996): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1992%E2%80%931996)
note: The Taliban's take-over of their home city: some real fighting at the airport and the Kandahar garrison, but mostly negotiated surrender of the warlords.

name: Charasiab (1995)
place: Charasiab and the southern approaches of Kabul (Kabul Province, Afghanistan)
how the result was decided: Massoud's offensive retook Charasiab on 19 March and drove the Taliban back from Kabul, their first major defeat.
Iranian side: Islamic State of Afghanistan v Taliban
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1992-1996): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1992%E2%80%931996)
note: Followed the Taliban's capture of Ghazni (January) and Maidan Shahr (10 February) and the killing of Wahdat's Mazari in Taliban custody on 13 March; the Taliban went on to retreat to Maidan Shahr and Ghazni.

name: Operation Steel (1995)
place: Zap, Haftanin and Metina areas of northern Iraq (Duhok and Erbil Governorates)
how the result was decided: Turkish troops overran PKK camps in northern Iraq and then withdrew after six weeks, without breaking the PKK.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia 'Turkish military operations in Iraq' and 'Kurdish-Turkish conflict' (fetches failed; from memory); McDowall (2004); Marcus, Blood and Belief: the PKK and the Kurdish Fight for Independence (2007)
note: The largest Turkish operation of its time, with air support and the passive consent of the KDP. Both sides' casualty claims differ greatly.

date: 4 April to 11 May 1995 (Taliban attack 4 April; Ismail Khan recaptured the town 11 May)
name: Farah (1995)
how the result was decided: The Taliban took Farah after killing about 800 government soldiers, but Ismail Khan recaptured the town on 11 May and held the west until the Taliban attacked again in September.
Iranian side: Taliban v Islamic State of Afghanistan
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1992-1996): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1992%E2%80%931996)
note: The two-step fight is merged into one entry; the exact dates come from the Wikipedia summary of the civil war.

name: Herat (1995)
how the result was decided: The Taliban took Shindand air base and then entered Herat on 5 September, and Ismail Khan fled to Mashhad.
Iranian side: Taliban v Islamic State of Afghanistan
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1992-1996): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1992%E2%80%931996)
note: The Taliban's first conquest of a Persian-speaking city. Some accounts credit an informal Dostum-Taliban understanding for the collapse of Ismail Khan's front.

name: Tavildara (May 1996)

period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds

note: Both sides Tajik. Part of the opposition's spring 1996 offensive; the government later held it again until the opposition recaptured it in August 1996.

name: Koysanjaq incursion (1996)

Iranian side: Islamic Republic of Iran v Kurdish rebels

period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds

note: Iran called it self-defence against KDPI raids. On 4 August 1996 the KDPI declared a unilateral halt to cross-border attacks, ending its 1989-1996 insurgency. The incursion prompted Masoud Barzani to call in the Iraqi army against the PUK (Erbil, 31 August 1996).

name: Erbil (1996)
side B: Patriotic Union of Kurdistan; Iraqi National Congress
how the result was decided: The Iraqi Republican Guard and the KDP took Erbil in a day, and the PUK and INC fighters withdrew.
Iranian side: Iraq v Patriotic Union of Kurdistan
factions B: Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, Iraqi National Congress

commanders B: Kosrat Rasul Ali (PUK Peshmerga, about 3,000); Jalal Talabani

note: The KDP asked Baghdad for help after an Iranian incursion on the PUK side in July 1996. Both Kurdish parties fought, so Kurds are on both sides. About 700 INC and PUK prisoners were reportedly executed afterwards.

date: 16 August 1996 (confirmed by the government on 20 August)
name: Tavildara (August 1996)

note: Both sides Tajik. The government had tried to hide the defeat; Rahmonov then reshuffled his security chiefs. Commander attribution to Ziyoyev is inferred from his command of the Tavildara front.

name: Kabul (1996)
how the result was decided: After the Taliban took Sarobi on 25 September, Massoud judged his forces nearly encircled and withdrew north, and the Taliban entered Kabul and proclaimed the Islamic Emirate.
Iranian side: Taliban v Islamic State of Afghanistan

commanders B: Ahmad Shah Massoud; Burhanuddin Rabbani; Gulbuddin Hekmatyar (prime minister; withdrew)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Afghan Civil War (1992-1996): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghan_Civil_War_(1992%E2%80%931996)
note: Massoud pulled out rather than fight it to a finish, so the real combat was at Sarobi and on the eastern approaches. Najibullah was taken from the UN compound and killed.

name: Sulaymaniyah (1996)

doubts and flags: Borderline: Iranian participation is only alleged ('allegedly with support of Iranian forces'); both principals were Iraqi Kurdish parties (PUK as side_a, KDP as side_b, both under 'Kurdish rebels').

note: Dostum's Junbish (Uzbek) split when Malik turned on him; the Taliban's defeat here was one of the largest of the war. Leaders' names are from memory and uncertain.

name: Operation Hammer (1997)

period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds

note: Weakly documented: the capture followed Mazar and seems to have involved little set-piece fighting, though the Hazara retreat was contested. A weak entry; the Hazara guerrilla war that continued is not covered.

name: Shomali Plain (1999)

date: 5 September 2000 (siege and offensive from about late July 2000; start date not verified)
name: Taloqan (2000)
side B: United Front forces of Ahmad Shah Massoud
how the result was decided: The Taliban captured Taloqan, Massoud's headquarters town, on 5 September 2000 after a siege, and the United Front held the line north and east of the city.

factions B: United Front forces of Ahmad Shah Massoud

name: Scud strikes on MEK camps (2001)
place: MEK camps in Iraq (Camp Ashraf and others), Iraq
how the result was decided: Dozens of Scud-B missiles were fired at MEK bases across Iraq, but no reliable account of hits or damage is available.
Iranian force: Government side: IRGC ballistic-missile units firing Scud-B missiles from western Iran; MEK side: the NLA camps.
why it counts: Iranians on both sides (a civil war of the Iranian states)
borderline: strike operation; not verified in Wikipedia; number of missiles uncertain
doubts and flags: A strike operation (air, missile or drone attacks): listed and mapped but not scored, because its result is judged by damage claims rather than by a held field. Borderline: strike operation; not verified in Wikipedia; number of missiles uncertain.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: contemporary press reports (Reuters, BBC, April 2001); not covered by the Wikipedia articles fetched
note: Recorded from contemporary reports; the date and scale should be checked.

name: Herat (uprising, 2001)
how the result was decided: The city fell to Ismail Khan's forces on 12 November 2001 and the Taliban fled toward the mountains.
commanders A: Ismail Khan (Northern Alliance); Tommy Franks; Yahya Rahim Safavi and Qasem Soleimani (IRGC)
Iranian force: IRGC Quds Force agents in Herat, directed by Safavi and Soleimani, who were to enter the city covertly and start the uprising; the fighting force was about 5,000 Northern Alliance militiamen.
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia 2001 uprising in Herat
note: 'Afghans' here is the Northern Alliance of Ismail Khan.

date: late November to 7 December 2001 (negotiated surrender announced 6 December; city entered 7 December)
name: Kandahar (2001)
side A (victor if decisive): Pashtun forces of Hamid Karzai and Gul Agha Sherzai
how the result was decided: The Taliban agreed a surrender on 6 December, Sherzai's men took the airport and city on 7 December, and Mullah Omar left.
Iranian side: Pashtun forces of Hamid Karzai and Gul Agha Sherzai v Taliban
factions A: Pashtun forces of Hamid Karzai and Gul Agha Sherzai
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan
note: The fall of the Taliban's capital after air attacks and the fights at Shin-Narai, Sayyd Alma Kalay and Camp Rhino; the surrender rather than a final assault ended it. Pashtuns on both sides.

date: 11-26 November 2001 (siege; surrender negotiated 21-23 November; city taken 25-26 November)
name: Kunduz (siege, 2001)
how the result was decided: After about two weeks of siege and air attack, the Taliban and foreign fighters surrendered in stages on 23-26 November and the Northern Alliance took the city.
Iranian side: Northern Alliance v Taliban garrison of Kunduz
commanders A: General Mohammad Daud Daud (Tajik); Abdul Rashid Dostum (Uzbek)
commanders B: Taliban and volunteer commanders in Kunduz (not individually verified)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan (the page treats the surrender briefly)
note: The last Taliban stronghold in the north. Numbers in the garrison vary widely (perhaps 10,000) and the foreign volunteers were a large share. The captives from Kunduz were taken to Qala-i-Jangi.

date: 5-10 November 2001 (Baluch 5 November; Tangi Pass 8-9 November; city entered 10 November)
name: Mazar-i-Sharif (2001)
place: Mazar-i-Sharif and the Tangi Pass (Balkh Province, Afghanistan)
how the result was decided: The Northern Alliance forced the Tangi Pass on 9 November and entered Mazar-i-Sharif on 10 November as the Taliban retreated, the first major city to fall.
Iranian side: Northern Alliance v Taliban garrison of the north
commanders A: Atta Muhammad Nur (Tajik); Mohammad Mohaqiq (Hazara); Abdul Rashid Dostum (Uzbek)
commanders B: Taliban commanders of Balkh (Mullah Nurullah Nuri, governor)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan
note: The first great success of the US-Northern Alliance campaign, helped by American special forces (ODA 595 and 534) and B-52 strikes. Dostum's Junbish (Uzbek) is not counted as Iranian. The Taliban were mostly Pashtun.

date: 25 November to 1 December 2001 (prisoner revolt and its suppression)
name: Qala-i-Jangi (2001)
place: Qala-i-Jangi fortress, west of Mazar-i-Sharif (Balkh Province, Afghanistan)
side A (victor if decisive): Northern Alliance guards of Dostum's Junbish
how the result was decided: Dostum's forces, with AC-130 and aircraft support, crushed the revolt over six days; of the prisoners (estimates range from about 300-500 up to 1,000) only 86 survived, and about 50 Northern Alliance soldiers died (Wikipedia).
principal opponents: Northern Alliance guards of Dostum's Junbish
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan
note: Doubtful for the Iranian rule: the prisoners were mostly Pakistanis, Uzbeks, Arabs and Chechens, with an unmeasured number of Afghan Taliban (Pashtun), and the guards were mainly Dostum's Uzbeks. Kept because it is a famous battle in the assigned span; qualification uncertain.

name: Taloqan (2001)
how the result was decided: The Northern Alliance took Taloqan in a quick infantry assault on 11 November, before the first planned bomb was dropped.
commanders B: Taliban commanders of Takhar (not recorded here)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan; Wikipedia, Taloqan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taloqan
note: Retaking Massoud's old headquarters town; the Taliban garrison gave way quickly.

name: Tarin Kowt (2001)
side A (victor if decisive): Pashtun anti-Taliban militia of Hamid Karzai
how the result was decided: Karzai's force held Tarin Kowt after the town rose against the Taliban, and the Taliban counter-attack was beaten off with American close air support.
Iranian side: Pashtun anti-Taliban militia of Hamid Karzai v Taliban of Uruzgan
factions A: Pashtun anti-Taliban militia of Hamid Karzai
commanders B: Taliban commanders of Uruzgan (not recorded here)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan
note: The first Pashtun uprising in the south. Pashtuns fought on both sides; the Taliban counter-attack came from Kandahar and was destroyed by air power.

date: about 3-5 December 2001 (bridge battle; friendly-fire bombing 5 December; the Wikipedia invasion article dates it only to late November)
name: Sayyd Alma Kalay (2001)
place: Sayyd Alma Kalay bridge over the Arghandab, near Shawali Kot (Kandahar Province, Afghanistan)
side A (victor if decisive): Pashtun anti-Taliban force of Hamid Karzai
how the result was decided: Karzai's force took the bridge, opening the road to Kandahar, and the Taliban then entered the surrender talks.
Iranian side: Pashtun anti-Taliban force of Hamid Karzai v Taliban
factions A: Pashtun anti-Taliban force of Hamid Karzai
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan
note: Fought two days; the 5 December friendly-fire bombing killed American soldiers and Afghans and wounded Karzai. The exact dates are uncertain.

date: air attacks from mid-November; main ground fighting 12-17 December 2001
name: Tora Bora (2001)
place: Tora Bora cave complex, White Mountains (Nangarhar Province, Afghanistan)
how the result was decided: The Eastern Alliance and American air power took the cave complex by 17 December, but bin Laden and a number of fighters escaped into Pakistan.
Iranian side: Eastern Alliance v Al-Qaeda and Taliban remnants
commanders A: Hazrat Ali (Pashtun); Haji Zaman Ghamsharik (Pashtun); Haji Zahir (Pashtun)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, United States invasion of Afghanistan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_invasion_of_Afghanistan
note: The anti-Taliban militias were Pashtun and did most of the ground fighting; the defenders were largely Arab al-Qaeda fighters with some Afghan Taliban and local tribesmen, so the Iranian share on side B is small.

name: Operation Anaconda (Shah-i-Kot)
place: Shah-i-Kot Valley and Arma Ghar, near Gardez, Paktia (Afghanistan)
how the result was decided: After two weeks of air strikes and ground sweeps the coalition and Afghan militia held the valley and ridges while most of the enemy slipped away into Pakistan.
Iranian side: United States-led coalition v Al-Qaeda, Taliban and Haqqani-network fighters
commanders A: Maj. Gen. Franklin Hagenbeck (CJTF Mountain); Zia Lodin (Pashtun commander of the Afghan Interim Administration militia); Zakim Khan; Kamal Khan
commanders B: Saif ur-Rahman Mansur (Zadran Pashtun, Haqqani network); Tohir Yuldashev (IMU, not Iranian)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Operation Anaconda: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Anaconda; Wikipedia, List of military operations in the war in Afghanistan (2001-2021)
note: The first large set-piece battle after Tora Bora. About a thousand Afghan militiamen under Zia Lodin (Pashtun) fought on the coalition side, and the enemy included local Pashtun Taliban and Haqqani fighters alongside the foreign fighters, so both sides had an Iranian element; the enemy's share of Pashtuns is a guess.

name: Operation Viking Hammer
place: Khurmal, Sargat and the Ansar al-Islam enclave near Halabja, Sulaymaniyah Governorate, Iraqi Kurdistan
side A (victor if decisive): United States; Patriotic Union of Kurdistan
how the result was decided: US special forces and about 1,000-plus PUK Peshmerga drove Ansar al-Islam out of its mountain strongholds in three days.
factions A: United States, Patriotic Union of Kurdistan
commanders A: Col. Charles Cleveland (US 10th SFG); PUK Peshmerga commanders
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia 'Operation Viking Hammer' and 'Peshmerga'; Briscoe et al., Weapon of Choice (2003); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peshmerga
note: Ansar al-Islam was itself mostly Kurdish (with Arab volunteers), so Kurds were on both sides. The Peshmerga formed the bulk of the ground force.

name: Operation Mountain Viper
allies A: Afghan Militia Forces and early Afghan National Army
how the result was decided: The coalition forces killed over a hundred Taliban and the group dispersed from the Daychopan valleys, though they returned in 2004.
commanders A: US task force commanders (not named in the sources consulted)
commanders B: Local Taliban commanders (Mullah Dadullah's network; individuals not named in the sources consulted)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, List of military operations in the war in Afghanistan (2001-2021): Operation Mountain Viper (30 Aug-Sep 2003, Dey Chopan, Zabul)
note: One of the first big engagements with the regrouped Taliban in the south. Taliban fighters in Zabul were Pashtun (Tokhi, Hotak and Kakar tribesmen); commander names not checked, so the commander list is a placeholder.

date: 16 March to April 2004 (main fighting 16-18 March; Shakai agreement 24 April)
name: Battle of Wana (2004)
war: Insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (War in North-West Pakistan)
side B: Ahmadzai Wazir tribal militants of Nek Muhammad Wazir
how the result was decided: The army failed to capture or destroy the militants and ended the operation with the Shakai agreement (24 April 2004) with Nek Muhammad, which many Pakistani commentators called a militant success.
Iranian side: Ahmadzai Wazir tribal militants of Nek Muhammad Wazir
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Wana: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Wana; Wikipedia, War in North-West Pakistan
note: The first major Pakistani army operation in the tribal areas after 2001, against the Wazir militants sheltering Uzbek and Arab fighters. The Frontier Corps also fought on the government side (a Pashtun force), but the main Iranian side is the militants.

name: Dera Bugti (March 2005)
place: Dera Bugti and the Sui gas field, Balochistan, Pakistan
how the result was decided: Several days of shelling and gun battles ended in a ceasefire with the Frontier Corps still in the town and the Bugti militia in the hills.
commanders B: Frontier Corps Balochistan (Major-General Shujaat Zamir Dar, IG FC)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurgency_in_Balochistan (fetched: Bugti uprising 2005-06); BBC and Dawn reports, March 2005, from memory
note: The Bugti are Baloch under a hereditary Baloch chief. Casualty figures (dozens killed, including civilians) are disputed and from memory.

date: 27 June to mid-July 2005 (main battle 28 June, Abbas Ghar)
name: Operation Red Wings
place: Korengal and Pech area near Asadabad, Kunar Province (Afghanistan)
how the result was decided: A four-man SEAL team was compromised and three killed, a rescue helicopter was shot down with 16 more US dead, and only Marcus Luttrell survived, sheltered by villagers; the militia lost an estimated 30-35.
commanders A: Lt. Michael Murphy (SEAL team leader); Cdr. Erik Kristensen
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Operation Red Wings: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Red_Wings
note: Famous for the book and film Lone Survivor. The enemy were Kunar mountain fighters; Ahmad Shah's own origin (Pashtun or Nuristani/Pashai) is not firmly settled in the sources, so qualification is doubtful.

date: 3 April 2006 (PJAK attacks); Iranian shelling and incursion near Mount Qandil 21-28 April 2006
name: April 2006 Iran-Iraq cross-border raids
theatre: Iranian Kurdistan and the Qandil mountains
place: Iran-Iraq border near Mount Qandil, Iraq and north-western Iran
how the result was decided: PJAK's three raids of early April and Iran's retaliatory shelling and brief incursion near Mount Qandil each struck and withdrew, and Wikipedia records the result as indecisive.
Iranian side: Islamic Republic of Iran v Kurdish rebels
Iranian force: Iranian border garrisons and security forces, then IRGC artillery and troops in a brief cross-border incursion (units not named).
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
losses B: about 10 militants killed in the Iranian shelling (reports)
borderline: a series of raids and shelling rather than one battle
doubts and flags: Borderline: a series of raids and shelling rather than one battle.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia April 2006 Iran-Iraq cross-border raids; Iran-PJAK conflict
note: PJAK said its raids avenged the killing of 10 Kurdish demonstrators at Maku in February 2006. The Iraqi defence ministry reported nearly 100 Iranian shells on the Qandil area.

name: Operation Mountain Thrust
place: Kandahar, Helmand, Uruzgan, Zabul and Paktika provinces (Afghanistan)
how the result was decided: The coalition reported over a thousand Taliban killed and pushed them from several districts, but the Taliban regrouped in Panjwayi within weeks.
Iranian side: ISAF and Operation Enduring Freedom v Taliban
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, List of military operations in the war in Afghanistan (2001-2021); Wikipedia, Operation Mountain Thrust
note: The largest offensive since 2001 at the time; Pashtun Taliban on one side and Afghan National Army units fighting beside the coalition. Reported enemy losses are coalition claims.

name: Battle of Musa Qala (2006 siege)
side B: Taliban and local tribal fighters of Upper Helmand
how the result was decided: The British garrison in the district centre was withdrawn under the 17 October 2006 agreement with the elders, and the Taliban soon took the town (February 2007).
Iranian side: ISAF v Taliban and local tribal fighters of Upper Helmand
factions B: Taliban and local tribal fighters of Upper Helmand
commanders A: Brig. Ed Butler (UK Task Force Helmand); Lt. Col. Stuart Tootal (3 PARA)
commanders B: Local Taliban commanders (Mullah Salaam and others)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Musa Qala: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Musa_Qala
note: A long siege of the district centre including Operation Snakebite (August 2006). The Afghan police posted there fought beside the British; the Taliban side was Pashtun (Alizai and Ishaqzai).

name: Tarateni (Kohlu, death of Akbar Bugti, 2006)
place: Tarateni, mountains of Kohlu district, Balochistan, Pakistan (cave site approximate)
how the result was decided: Akbar Bugti, aged 79, was killed in the operation; the army also lost several officers and soldiers (Wikipedia gives at least 60 soldiers and 7 officers dead; official figures were lower).
commanders A: Pakistan Army field commanders (not named in my sources)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurgency_in_Balochistan (fetched); Dawn and BBC, 27 August 2006, from memory
note: An armed assault on a hideout, not a field battle, but it is the best-documented single fight of the 2005-06 war and triggered the wider insurgency.

name: Operation Medusa (Battle of Panjwaii)
place: Pashmul, Panjwayi and Zhari districts, Kandahar Province (Afghanistan)
how the result was decided: After several days of heavy fighting and air strikes ISAF cleared the Pashmul pocket and the Taliban withdrew, although they later returned to the area.
commanders A: Brig. Gen. David Fraser (Canadian, Task Force Orion)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Operation Medusa: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Medusa
note: The biggest NATO ground battle in Afghanistan up to that date. About 1,000-1,500 Taliban stood to fight; Afghan National Army units were part of the assault force.

name: September 2006 Sardasht incident
place: Iran-Iraq border near Sardasht, West Azerbaijan, Iran
how the result was decided: By the Iranian account, Iranian security forces killed over 30 PJAK fighters and wounded 40 in the clash; PJAK did not contest the field and then declared a unilateral ceasefire.
Iranian side: Islamic Republic of Iran v Kurdish rebels
Iranian force: Iranian border and security forces of the IRGC (units not named).
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
borderline: a small border clash known mainly from one side's claims
doubts and flags: Borderline: a small border clash known mainly from one side's claims.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia September 2006 Sardasht incident; Iran-PJAK conflict
note: Only the Iranian casualty claim is reported; the outcome rests on it. Iran rejected PJAK's ceasefire offer.

name: 2007 West Azerbaijan clashes
place: Khoy and the Turkish border districts of West Azerbaijan, Iran
how the result was decided: After the loss of an IRGC helicopter near Khoy, the IRGC counter-offensive killed 47 rebels for 17 soldiers by its own count, but neither side drove the other from the area and Wikipedia gives the result as indecisive.
Iranian side: Islamic Republic of Iran v Kurdish rebels
commanders A: IRGC commander Said Qahari (killed in the helicopter crash of 24 February); other commanders not named
Iranian force: IRGC ground forces and the regular army's 3rd Corps in West Azerbaijan, with IRGC helicopters.
why it counts: Islamic Republic of Iran: an Iranian-led state
losses A: 17 soldiers killed (25 February-1 March), plus 8-20 IRGC killed in the helicopter crash (Iranian and PJAK figures)
losses B: 47 killed (Iranian figure, 25 February-1 March); 17 killed 22-24 February (unsourced)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: en.wikipedia 2007 West Azerbaijan clashes; Iran-PJAK conflict
note: The Wikipedia infobox misdates the clashes to 2006; the text and the Iran-PJAK article give 2007. Iran blamed the helicopter crash on weather; PJAK claimed to have shot it down.

name: Operation Achilles
place: Sangin and Kajaki districts, Helmand Province (Afghanistan)
how the result was decided: ISAF secured the Kajaki dam area and Sangin valley and the Taliban lost ground and several commanders, though the Taliban held much of northern Helmand.
commanders A: Brig. John Lorimer (UK Task Force Helmand)
commanders B: Mullah Dadullah (southern commander, killed 12 May 2007); Mullah Mansour Dadullah
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, List of military operations in the war in Afghanistan (2001-2021): Operation Achilles
note: At the time the largest NATO operation of the war (about 4,500 troops). Real fighting around Sangin and Kajaki; outcome claimed as a success by ISAF.

name: Battle of Chora
side A (victor if decisive): Netherlands, Australia and the Afghan National Army
allies A: Afghan National Army; Afghan National Police
how the result was decided: Dutch, Australian and Afghan forces, with air support, held the Chora district centre against a Taliban assault and the attackers withdrew.
Iranian side: Netherlands, Australia and the Afghan National Army v Taliban
factions A: Netherlands, Australia and the Afghan National Army
commanders A: Dutch Task Force Uruzgan and Australian task group commanders (not named in the sources consulted)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, List of military operations in the war in Afghanistan (2001-2021): Battle of Chora (15-19 Jun 2007)
note: Taliban attempted to take the Chora district centre; the Dutch fought their first major action in Uruzgan. Commander names were not checked.

name: Daglica (2007)
how the result was decided: The PKK overran the Turkish army post, killing about 12 soldiers and taking 8 prisoners, and withdrew into Iraq.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia 'Kurdish-Turkish conflict'; press reports (BBC, Reuters, Oct 2007); from memory
note: The attack led Turkey to win parliamentary approval for the cross-border operations of December 2007 and Operation Sun in 2008. The Turkish counter-attack in the area claimed dozens of PKK dead.

date: 25 October to December 2007 (mopping up into early 2008)
name: First Battle of Swat (Operation Rah-e-Haq)
war: Insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (War in North-West Pakistan)
place: Swat Valley (Matta, Kabal, Imam Dheri, Khwazakhela), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (Pakistan)
side A (victor if decisive): Pakistan Army, Special Service Group and Frontier Corps
side B: Tehrik-e Nifaz-e Shariat-e Mohammadi and Swat Taliban of Maulana Fazlullah
how the result was decided: The army retook Matta, Khwazakhela and Fazlullah's headquarters at Imam Dheri by December, though Fazlullah escaped and the Taliban returned in force in 2008.
principal opponents: Pakistan Army, Special Service Group and Frontier Corps
Iranian side: Tehrik-e Nifaz-e Shariat-e Mohammadi and Swat Taliban of Maulana Fazlullah
commanders B: Maulana Fazlullah (Swati Yusufzai); Muslim Khan; Maulana Shah Dauran
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Swat (2007) / Operation Rah-e-Haq: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Swat_(2007)
note: The first major army operation in Swat after the 2007 uprising of Fazlullah's followers. The Pakistan Army is not counted as Iranian; the Frontier Corps also fought on the government side.

name: Second Battle of Musa Qala
how the result was decided: The coalition and Afghan army advanced into the town, the Taliban withdrew north on 10 December and Afghan troops entered the centre on 12 December.
commanders A: Brig. Andrew Mackay; General Mahayadin Ghori (Afghan National Army)
commanders B: Abdul-Mannan; Abdul-Rahim; Abdul-Matin Akhund; Abdul-Bari Akhund
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Musa Qala: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Musa_Qala
note: Operation Snakepit/Mar Lek: about 4,500 ISAF and Afghan troops against 200-2,000 Taliban (figures differ). Mullah Salaam's later defection made the town a government base.

name: Operation Zalzala (South Waziristan, 2008)
war: Insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (War in North-West Pakistan)
place: Ladha, Sararogha and Makeen, South Waziristan (Pakistan)
how the result was decided: The army relieved besieged forts and retook Ladha, but Baitullah Mehsud kept control of the Mehsud heartland and a peace agreement followed in February 2008.
commanders A: Pakistani XII Corps and 14th Division commanders (not named in the sources consulted)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Operation Zalzala (2008): recalled from memory; not fetched
note: Fighting around Fort Ladha and Sararogha in the winter of 2007-2008 after the TTP's formation. Dates and outcome come from memory and are weak.

name: Operation Sun (2008)
place: Zap, Avashin and Hakurk areas of northern Iraq
how the result was decided: Turkey withdrew after eight days, claiming hundreds of PKK dead against 27 Turkish soldiers, while the PKK kept its bases and claimed victory.
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia 'Operation Sun (2008)' (from memory); press reports (BBC, 29 Feb 2008)
note: The first Turkish ground operation in Iraq since 1997 and the only one stopped by US and Iraqi pressure and winter weather. Casualty claims on both sides conflict.

date: 29 April to 8 September 2008 (also given as April-September)
name: Battle of Garmsir (2008)
how the result was decided: The Marines pushed the Taliban out of Garmsir district and held the district centre; the offensive ended on schedule in September.
Iranian side: United States and Britain v Taliban
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, List of military operations in the war in Afghanistan (2001-2021): Battle of Garmsir (Apr-8 Sep 2008)
note: A Marine battalion landing team cleared the southern Helmand river valley. Start date given loosely.

name: Battle of Shok Valley
how the result was decided: After six hours of fighting and heavy air support the team and the Afghan commandos broke out of the valley with the wounded; the insurgent force was driven off with heavy losses.
Iranian side: United States with Afghan commandos v Hizb-i Islami fighters
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Shok Valley: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Shok_Valley
note: Qualifies only through the Afghan commando contingent (about a hundred men beside 12 Americans); the Hizb-i Islami fighters in Nuristan were largely Nuristani/Pashai, so their qualification is not claimed.

name: Battle of Wanat
side B: Taliban, Hizb-i Islami and local Waygal valley fighters
how the result was decided: The US and Afghan soldiers held the vehicle patrol base after being overrun in part, losing nine US dead, and the attackers withdrew after air strikes.
principal opponents: Taliban, Hizb-i Islami and local Waygal valley fighters
commanders A: Capt. Matthew Myer; Lt. Jonathan Brostrom
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Wanat: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Wanat
note: Qualifies only through the Afghan National Army platoon (about two dozen men beside about 48 Americans); the attackers were largely Nuristani, who are not Iranian. The Army's ethnic composition (Pashtun and Tajik) is not given in the sources.

name: Battle of Bajaur (Operation Sher Dil)
war: Insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (War in North-West Pakistan)
place: Bajaur Agency (Khar, Loi Sam, Charmang), Federally Administered Tribal Areas (Pakistan)
side A (victor if decisive): Pakistan Army and Frontier Corps with pro-government tribal lashkars
side B: Tehrik-i Taliban Pakistan and TNSM fighters of Maulana Faqir Muhammad
how the result was decided: The army and Frontier Corps cleared Loi Sam, Charmang and Khar and the militants accepted a ceasefire in February 2009, losing their stronghold in the agency.
Iranian side: Pakistan Army and Frontier Corps with pro-government tribal lashkars v Tehrik-i Taliban Pakistan and TNSM fighters of Maulana Faqir Muhammad
factions A: Pakistan Army and Frontier Corps with pro-government tribal lashkars
factions B: Tehrik-i Taliban Pakistan and TNSM fighters of Maulana Faqir Muhammad
commanders A: Maj. Gen. Tariq Khan (Inspector General, Frontier Corps)
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia, Battle of Bajaur: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bajaur
note: A six-month operation in Bajaur; the Frontier Corps and the Pashtun tribal lashkars were singled out in the fighting on the government side, the militants were Tarkani Pashtun.

date: 7-9 August 2008 (Roki Tunnel, Java and Gufta Bridge, before and into the battle of Tskhinvali)
name: Liakhvi Gorge (August 2008)
place: Liakhvi Gorge, Java and the Gufta Bridge, South Ossetia (Georgia)
side A (victor if decisive): Russia; South Ossetian militia and volunteers
how the result was decided: Georgia failed to block the Roki Tunnel and Gufta, the Russian and Ossetian column got through and the battle of Tskhinvali began.
Iranian side: Russia & South Ossetian militia and volunteers
commanders A: Col. Kazachenko (693rd regiment), Taymuraz Mamsurov (South Ossetian leader in the first convoy from Java)
commanders B: Georgian commanders not named in the source
period: The Islamic Republic, Afghanistan and the Kurds
sources: Wikipedia 'Battle in the Liakhvi Gorge' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_in_the_Liakhvi_Gorge (fetched)
note: Qualifies through the South Ossetian militia and volunteers (Alans), singled out in the source, fighting beside Russian regulars; the Battle of Tskhinvali itself is already in the dataset. Fighting for the Georgian-held villages (Kekhvi, Kurta, Achabeti, Tamarasheni) is not itemized in the source.

name: Tskhinvali (2008)
place: Tskhinvali, South Ossetia (Georgia, de facto South Ossetia)
